title: Skipped monorepo deployments no longer count against limits
description:
Deployments that Vercel automatically skips in a monorepo no longer count against your deployment rate limits. Teams with monorepos now get more deployments from the same limits.

Vercel skips a project's deployment when its source code and internal dependencies haven't changed, using Turborepo's package graph and lockfile analysis to determine which projects a commit affects.

Skipping is enabled by default for new monorepo projects. You can turn it on for existing projects under Build and Deployment in the project's settings.

Learn more about skipping unaffected projects and deployment limits.

Read more

title: Routing Middleware now supports Python
description:
You can now write routing middleware in Python for FastAPI, Flask, Django, and other Python frameworks. It runs before requests reach your app, and can rewrite, redirect, or answer them.

To set it up, point the proxy entrypoint in vercel.toml at your proxy:

Your middleware is an ASGI or WSGI app that runs separately from your main app, with only the packages in the vercel.proxy dependency group of your pyproject.toml. Add the packages your middleware imports to that group:

The vercel-proxy package provides utilities for writing routing middleware on Vercel, including a Proxy app that routes requests by path:

Requests that match no route continue to your app unchanged.

For more information, see the Routing Middleware Python reference.

Read more

description:
You can now deploy apps to Vercel without an account using Vercel CLI. Share prototypes faster with a live URL before signing in to claim your project.

From a project directory that isn't linked to Vercel, run:

title: Kimi K3.1 Pro and Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed are available now in AI Gateway
description:
Kimi K3.1 Pro from Moonshot AI is now available on AI Gateway, along with Kimi K3.1 Pro Highspeed, a faster version for interactive use.

K3.1 Pro is the first model in Moonshot's K3.1 series. It builds on Kimi K3 with improvements in coding, 3D modeling, financial analysis, and agentic tasks, and keeps the 1M-token context window and image input.

For coding, K3.1 Pro handles work ranging from small fixes in an existing codebase to building a full project, including long agent runs with many steps. It builds front-end pages and interactive scenes with stronger typography and animation than earlier Kimi models. In finance, it can carry a task from start to finish, such as building a linked financial model with adjustable assumptions and scenarios, or writing research grounded in source documents. K3.1 Pro makes fewer factual errors than earlier Kimi models on difficult prompts.

Moonshot AI plans to release the model weights by November 4: support for more providers will follow.

Call either model through the AI SDK, the Chat Completions, Responses, and Anthropic Messages APIs, or a coding agent connected to AI Gateway. For Highspeed, use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in place of the model name below.

Use moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro as the model name:

To use it in Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and more, install the latest Vercel CLI and run setup:

Then select moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro or moonshotai/kimi-k3.1-pro-highspeed in the agent. See the coding agents guide for details.

Try Kimi K3.1 Pro in the model playground.

AI Gateway provides a unified API for calling models, tracking usage and cost, and configuring retries, failover, and performance optimizations for higher-than-provider uptime. It includes built-in custom reporting, Zero Data Retention support, budgets for API keys, routing rules, and more.

AI Gateway reflects provider pricing with no markup and does not charge a platform fee on inference, including on Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) requests.

You can view all language models available on AI Gateway.

Read more

title: Vercel CLI adds Spend Management
description:
You can now view and manage your team's Spend Management budget from the Vercel CLI. Run vercel budgets and you, or the scripts and agents you run, get back your current spend and the active budget.

View, set, and remove a budget

This is the same On-Demand Budget shown in your team's billing settings. Setting a budget does not stop usage on its own. The --pause flag pauses production deployments of all projects when spend reaches 100%.

List budget alert history

You can now see your budget alert history. Run vercel budgets alerts for the full log, filtered with --since, --until, --limit, and --json. A bare vercel budgets prints the three most recent alerts.

Managing budgets requires the Owner or Billing role. Spend Management is available at no additional cost to Pro teams and to Enterprise teams on the Flexible Commitment plan.

Full reference now available in the vercel budgets CLI reference. Read more about Spend Management.

Read more

title: Customizable widgets for project cards
description:
The Overview tab in the dashboard now lets you choose which metric appears on each project card.

Project cards used to show a fixed Real Experience Score in the top right, but not everyone on your team watches the same signal. You can now swap that slot for whichever metric matters for that project. A security-sensitive project can show firewall activity, while a marketing site project shows traffic.

Available widgets

  • Firewall: allowed requests, denied requests

  • Observability: alerts, edge requests, function invocations, error rate

  • Speed Insights: Real Experience Score, LCP, CLS

  • Web Analytics: visitors online, visitors, page views

Pick per project

Open the switcher in the top right of any project card. The menu shows the current value for each available metric. When you select one, your choice is saved for that project and follows your account across refreshes and devices.

Enable features from the card

If a project does not have a feature enabled, you can start the enable flow from the widget menu without leaving the Overview tab. This is available for Speed Insights Plus, Web Analytics, and alerts.

Get started

Open your team’s Overview tab and use the switcher on any project card.

Read more

title: Create custom monitors in Vercel Observability
description:
You can now create custom monitors to get alerts based on your Vercel Observability query results.

For example, you can track signals such as AI Gateway costs, Core Web Vitals and other performance metrics, Workflow and external API failure rates, or Vercel Sandbox CPU time.

Each monitor tracks a single metric, such as response time, or a ratio of two metrics, such as errors divided by total requests. Choose statistical anomaly detection or a fixed threshold, then configure the detection window, filters, and grouping.

To create a monitor, inspect a chart’s query in Observability, start from a preset, or open Settings > Alerts for your team.

You can also define a custom monitor in a JSON file and create it with vercel monitors add in the Vercel CLI. Run vercel monitors schema --type custom for the schema and examples.

Receive alerts through email, Slack, Vercel Inbox, push notifications, or team-level webhooks. You can also add context for Vercel Agent to use when investigating an alert.

Custom monitors are available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus, at $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. Built-in alerts remain included with Observability Plus.

Create a custom monitor or learn more in the configuration documentation.

Read more

title: HarnessAgent now supports image inputs for all harness adapters
description:
The AI SDK HarnessAgent layer now accepts image inputs across every harness adapter.

Pass images alongside text in the standard AI SDK message format: a content array mixing { type: 'text' } and { type: 'file' } parts.

Image input is processed by the harnesses' underlying vision models and supported across all available adapters: Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, Deep Agents, fx, GitHub Copilot, Grok Build, OpenCode, Pi.

Read the HarnessAgent image inputs documentation to get started.

Read more

title: Vercel Agent sessions now cost 67% less
description:
Vercel Agent sessions in the dashboard and Slack now cost 67% less on average. We rebuilt how Agent manages context, reducing the tokens needed per session and improving prompt-cache reuse. These improvements are live and require no action.

What changed:

  • Workflow-based CLI skills: Updated Vercel CLI skills give agents clearer guidance for common workflows and error recovery. Other agents using these skills also benefit.

title: Vercel Agent can now validate alerts before paging
description:
Vercel Agent can now investigate alerts from Vercel monitors before they reach your paging system. With validation enabled for a webhook destination, only alerts Agent classifies as Critical are sent to it.

To enable validation:

  1. Open a monitor’s notification settings and create or link a webhook destination for your paging system, such as incident.io.

  2. Select Critical Only next to that destination.

You can also configure notification destinations with the Vercel CLI using vercel monitors notifications. Add --critical-only when linking or updating a webhook destination.

Agent checks logs and metrics to assess impact. For example, it can identify health-check errors that don’t affect customers or confirm sustained 5xx errors affecting checkout requests. You can also add context to each monitor to guide Agent’s investigation.

Alert validation is available on Pro and Enterprise plans with Observability Plus. Observability Plus includes ten Agent investigations per billing cycle, with additional investigations billed separately. Custom monitors cost $0.0035 per GB of data scanned. To get started:

  2. For Twilio, Notion, and X, use the webhook URL from Connect and follow its instructions to complete setup in the provider’s settings.

  3. Add a trigger destination to choose the project and endpoint that should receive events.

You can turn triggers on or off later in the connector’s settings.

In the connector’s Observability tab, select Live to watch incoming trigger events.

These connectors join existing trigger support for Slack, Discord, Microsoft Teams, GitHub, and Linear.

title: Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available on Vercel
description:
Node.js 26 LTS is now Generally Available for builds and Vercel Functions.

This release includes:

  • HTTP/2 by default for built-in fetch (Undici 8) lets multiple requests share a connection with servers that support it. This can reduce latency when your functions call APIs or databases over HTTP.

  • Temporal API offers an alternative to Date with immutable values and built-in time zone and calendar support.

  • V8 version 14.6, the updated JavaScript engine, adds features such as Map.prototype.getOrInsert() to retrieve an existing value or insert a default when a key is missing.

Using Node.js 26

Node.js 26 is the default for all new projects.

  • Automatic upgrades: If engines.node in your existing project’s package.json allows 26, such as >=20, your Node.js builds on Vercel will use 26 on the next deployment.

  • Manual upgrades: Set engines.node to 26.x in your project's package.json and redeploy.

  • Prebuilt deployments: Use Vercel CLI version 65.8.0 or later to deploy Node.js 26 Functions.

  • HTTP/1.1 in Functions: To keep HTTP/1.1, set the VERCEL_FETCH_DISABLE_H2 environment variable to 1 and redeploy.

Minor and patch updates to Node.js 26 roll out automatically for builds and Vercel Functions.

Read the Node.js version documentation to learn more.

title: Vercel Flags starts 7x faster and no longer extends function duration
description:
On Vercel, the Vercel Flags SDK now initializes faster on cold starts, and usage reporting no longer keeps functions running after the response.

Faster cold starts

Two changes speed up SDK initialization on cold starts:

  • The SDK loads and parses the flags datafile bundled with your deployment as soon as the client is created, so it’s ready before your code evaluates its first flag.

  • Every function invocation now includes the current datafile revision, so the SDK can check whether the bundled datafile is up to date without a network request.

In internal testing, eliminating the network wait reduced p75 cold-start SDK initialization time from over 70 ms to 10 ms, roughly 7x faster.

After initialization, flag reads are effectively instant. Across cold and warm invocations, p99 flag-read latency is under 1 ms.

Usage reporting no longer extends function duration

The SDK previously used waitUntil for usage reporting, keeping functions running after the response was sent. It now passes usage events to the Vercel runtime, so reporting no longer adds to function duration.

Update @flags-sdk/vercel to version 1.5.3 or later and redeploy your application:

Learn more in the Flags SDK documentation.

title: Simplifying runtime caching on Vercel
description:
Today, we’re bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache, giving developers one product for data caching across frameworks and APIs. If you use Next.js fetch caching or unstable_cache, you won’t need to change your code. Pro and Enterprise projects will get larger storage allocations.

Runtime Cache lets your code reuse fetched or computed data across requests without operating a separate caching service. Over the past year, we’ve improved read performance during traffic bursts, increased storage budgets, and made cache usage easier to investigate.

Why we built Runtime Cache

Data Cache was originally launched as Vercel’s data caching service for the Next.js App Router, used by fetch caching and unstable_cache. Unlike CDN caching, which stores complete HTTP responses, Data Cache stores data your application uses to generate those responses. A product page, for example, can reuse cached catalog data while rendering a personalized response for each visitor.

We wanted developers to have access to that service without depending on Next.js. Last year, we introduced Runtime Cache with a direct API: getCache from @vercel/functions. Applications can use it for feature flag lookups in Routing Middleware, caching CMS content during builds, and data caching in SvelteKit and Nuxt apps.

Frameworks can expose this service through their own APIs, too. On Vercel, Next.js itself uses the Runtime Cache API for 'use cache: remote', which caches function and component outputs.

How Runtime Cache works

The infrastructure behind Runtime Cache is a distributed caching service shared by many teams. A Go API handles requests, backed by Redis fleets in every Vercel region. Every hour, the service handles more than 440 million reads and moves more than 18 TB of data.

Each region has its own cache. A cache hit takes one round trip to the cache service in the region where your code runs. Vercel handles authentication with short-lived credentials, so you don’t need to manage API keys.

On a cache miss, your app or framework fetches or computes the value and writes it to that region’s cache. The service doesn’t check other regions for a cached copy.

Each cached entry stores its tags and write time. When the service reads an entry, it checks a separate tag store in the same region for those tags’ invalidation timestamps. If any tag was invalidated after the entry was written, the entry is stale.

For example, an application can tag all its cached product data with catalog. When the catalog changes, invalidating that tag writes a single timestamp, even if a million entries share the tag. The service doesn’t need to find and delete those entries individually.

The invalidation immediately updates the tag store in the region receiving the request. Vercel’s shared tag infrastructure, also used by the CDN, distributes the timestamp through the global push pipeline, typically reaching other regions within a few hundred milliseconds.

Your app or framework chooses what to cache and handles misses. Runtime Cache handles regional storage, authentication, and distributing tag invalidations across regions.

What we’ve shipped

Faster reads during traffic bursts

Checking whether an entry is still fresh adds a dependency to every cache hit. During traffic bursts, a slow shard in the tag store could delay reads even when the cached value was already available.

We added circuit breakers that let reads temporarily check freshness using tag timestamps cached in memory, so they can proceed without waiting for the slow shard to respond. During this fallback, a read can briefly treat recently invalidated data as fresh.

We enabled the breakers in every region in August. During the heaviest bursts in our largest region, p99 cache-service read latency fell to about one fifth of its previous level at comparable traffic. On-call alerts for this failure mode stopped.

More storage and fewer evictions

We raised Runtime Cache storage budgets for Pro projects in June and Enterprise projects in October, giving applications more room for data they reuse. This reduces the need to evict cached entries to make room for new data. Among Enterprise projects with frequent evictions, cache miss rates roughly halved within a day.

More visibility into cache behavior

We’ve added deployment markers, revalidation causes, and write utilization to the Runtime Cache view in Observability. These help you compare changes in cache behavior with releases, see why entries are refreshed, and identify data that gets written to the cache but rarely read.

Bringing Data Cache into Runtime Cache

We’re simplifying caching on Vercel by consolidating on Runtime Cache. Until now, Next.js fetch caching and unstable_cache have used Data Cache, while getCache and 'use cache: remote' have used Runtime Cache. The migration brings all four APIs under Runtime Cache, so you and coding agents have one set of storage budgets and usage tools to work with.

If you use fetch caching or unstable_cache, nothing changes in your code. On Pro, each project and environment gets its own storage allocation, with 8x the space of Data Cache’s previous team-wide pool. Enterprise projects get 10x their previous Data Cache storage.

Previously unbilled Data Cache reads and writes will follow Runtime Cache pricing. New teams use Runtime Cache automatically, and existing teams will receive their migration and billing details in advance.

See the changelog for the rollout, pricing, and early opt-in details. Before migrating, review your cache usage and follow the optimization guide to reduce unnecessary reads and writes.

title: Introducing Geist Serif
description:
Geist started as a monospace typeface for developers, built for the editors and terminals where they spend their day doing their work. From there it grew into Geist Sans for product interfaces, and then into Geist Pixel, which was inspired by the grids of early computer screens.

Today, we're adding a new member to the family: Geist Serif.

Geist Serif is a high-contrast display serif built on the same foundations as Geist Sans, Geist Mono, and Geist Pixel. It has fine, saw-toothed serifs and sharp hairlines, and it was drawn to communicate messages powerfully both in the physical world and on the high-density screens on modern devices.

Same system, new voice

At Vercel, Geist Sans runs the product. For headlines, though, we wanted a second voice, one that belongs to the same system, instead of a stranger picked from a drop-down menu.

A lot of tech brands have moved away from clean sans-serifs to get some personality back, and many of them borrow from vintage computer ads. Geist Serif takes a different path: toward fashion, editorial design, and magazine headlines. It's our homage to the artists behind Rolling Stone and Harper's Bazaar.

From the beginning, each Geist family has read from a chapter of type history: the Swiss design movement, early terminal and DOS computing, and now editorial print.

Display first

Geist Serif began as a set of sketches by Evil Rabbit, which Andrés Briganti then expanded. The first letters already showed an expressive serif, in the spirit of typefaces like Victor Serif and Stanley.

When Mark Davis took over the drawings, we made the first release a display face for headlines, posters, and other large sizes, while work on the full family continued. Print has always struggled to hold fine hairlines and sharp serifs, but today's displays can handle a high level of detail. We wanted the new face to take full advantage of modern screens, so we thinned every downstroke by 50% and tightened the sidebearings to push the contrast as far as it would go.

Each serif has a wedge on one side and a curve on the other, so the proportions are classical and look beautiful in print, but the construction is new and optimized for digital devices.

From the first prototype to today

The first prototype of Geist Serif was shared on April 1, 2026. Here's the same word, Geist, in that prototype, compared with the display drawing shipping today.

Geist grew teeth

The goal was to honor our original intent and keep the serif closely tied to the sans, even when the letters sit on top of each other. Geist Serif’s stems match Geist Sans, and the two share widths and postures.

The saw-toothed serifs and high contrast give Geist an editorial voice. One phrase kept coming up as each character was drawn: “Geist grew teeth.”

Four families, one x-height

Geist Serif uses the same cap height and x-height as Geist Sans, so you can drop it into any Geist layout without moving a line. Mix Sans, Mono, Pixel, and Serif in the same sentence and every word looks the same size.

Metric

Geist Sans

Geist Serif

Four variants, one axis

Like Geist Pixel, Geist Serif has a variable axis that swaps the shape of every dot in the font, including those on i and j and in punctuation. The axis is called Element Shape (ELSH), and it gives you four variants: Regular with round dots (the default), Square, Triangle (a nod to the Vercel logo), and Heart.

Each variant also ships as its own static file. If you use the variable font, pick a variant with font-variation-settings:

Crafted by hand

In July the font had 227 glyphs. It now has 894 and covers 352 Latin-script languages, and we worked through more than 52,000 kerning pairs to get the spacing right. Some of the details are tiny. The eye of the g, for example, is tilted exactly 7°.

Specs at a glance

Geist Serif ships with:

  • 1 weight (Regular)

  • 4 variants (Regular, Square, Triangle, Heart)

  • 894 glyphs

  • 5 stylistic sets (ss01 to ss05)

  • 352 supported languages

Getting started

Geist Serif ships in the same package as the rest of the family:

Exports and CSS variables:

  • GeistSerif (variable, all shapes): --font-geist-serif

  • GeistSerifRegular: --font-geist-serif-regular

  • GeistSerifSquare: --font-geist-serif-square

  • GeistSerifTriangle: --font-geist-serif-triangle

  • GeistSerifHeart: --font-geist-serif-heart

Each one has its own entry point, so you only ship the font file you use. For example, in layout.tsx with GeistSerifRegular:

You can also download the font files, test every stylistic set, and inspect each glyph at vercel.com/font.

What’s next

Regular is the first style we’re releasing, and the rest of the family is already in progress. We’re testing future versions while building this one, so this release is just the start.

Weights from Thin to Black

The variable font will range from Thin (100) to Black (900). In this week’s proofs, the g in Black is the letter we can’t stop looking at.

Toward a text face

To explore a text version, we built a foundry tool that measures strokes, including where they meet, and thickens the display outlines. It edits the outlines directly, so we can set real words and see which strokes need more weight.

Italics, built rule by rule

We’re also developing an italic generated entirely in Python. We slanted existing italics back upright and compared them with their romans. With the angle removed, the remaining differences show up clearly, and we turned them into rules we can test and revise. This italic won’t be the final version, but breaking glyphs in code helps us find the limits faster.

More scripts and Google Fonts

Cyrillic support is planned to match Geist Sans and Geist Mono, and Geist Serif will come to Google Fonts after launch.

One family

With Geist Sans, Geist Mono, Geist Pixel, and now Geist Serif, the family runs from UI text and code to expressive display type, and all four feel at home together.

Download Geist Serif and start building.

Thank you to everyone who made Geist Serif possible.

None of this would have been possible without an incredible group of people behind the scenes.

Huge thanks to Andrés Briganti for starting this journey with me and drawing the first version that everything else grew from, and to Mark Davis for carrying it across the finish line with obsessive craft, from the expanded glyph set and variable axis to every last kerning pair. Thanks also to Patrick McDonald and Marijana Pavlinić for the poster designs, to Luis Gutierrez Rico for the motion and incredible magic, to Christopher Kindl for shipping the package and rebuilding the landing page down to the smallest details, and to Zahra Jabini for the coordination and technical support that brought it all together. This was a true team effort, and I’m grateful to have built it with all of you.

title: Blocking malicious npm packages before and during installation
description:
Vercel now checks for blocked npm packages before and during dependency installation in builds, helping prevent malicious install scripts from running.

The checks use a blocklist of specific package versions selected for blocking because of malware or security vulnerabilities, with new rules typically reaching new builds within minutes.

  • Before installation, Vercel checks supported lockfiles, including when dependencies are restored from the build cache.

  • During installation, Vercel blocks affected public npm downloads.

Existing checks of installed dependencies and function outputs continue before deployment.

These protections apply automatically to new builds on all plans, with no configuration required.

If a blocked dependency is detected, Vercel fails the deployment, identifies the package and version in the error, and attempts to invalidate the affected build cache. Update the dependency to a safe version and update the lockfile, then redeploy.

title: Vercel MCP now supports Client ID Metadata Documents
description:
Any MCP client can now ask to connect to Vercel MCP. You still log in and approve each connection, but the client no longer has to be reviewed by Vercel first. Previously, Vercel reviewed and allowlisted each client and its redirect URIs by hand, and anything not on the list was rejected.

To connect, a client publishes a Client ID Metadata Document (CIMD), a JSON file on its own domain that describes it, and uses that file's HTTPS URL as its OAuth client_id. This follows the MCP authorization spec, which now recommends CIMD over Dynamic Client Registration.

Because Vercel hasn't reviewed these clients, the consent screen shows where each one comes from: its name, its logo, and the hostname that serves its metadata document, for example "Claude Code by claude.ai". CIMD clients don't get the Vercel verified badge, so the hostname is what you're trusting when you approve.

Apps already registered with Vercel are unchanged.

Read the Vercel MCP documentation to connect your client.

title: Introducing Vercel Schedules
description:
Cron jobs are useful for work that needs to happen regularly. You can use them to do things such as back up your database on a schedule, or keep data in sync between two systems.

You define them once in code and then can update them by editing their config and redeploying. But today, agents interact with users as work evolves, and schedules need to be updated in real time.

We built Vercel Schedules to allow agents and applications to create, change, or cancel one-time and recurring schedules through code, without redeploying.

What are Vercel Schedules?

Schedules builds on the static approach used by Vercel Cron Jobs, but are designed to let users and agents decide when work should happen while your application is still running. A schedule tells Vercel when to trigger a task and where to send it. Your application provides the code that carries out the work.

You can use schedules for both static and dynamic jobs:

  • Static schedules keep the timing in vercel.json or Build Output API configuration and sync when you deploy. You can use them to call private functions or HTTP paths, or send messages to Queue topics.

  • Dynamic schedules let your app create and manage schedules through the JS SDK, CLI, or API as it runs. They support one-time and recurring work through Queue topics.

You can also test scheduled work on Preview deployments and in custom environments before running it in Production.

How Schedules works

Take this example: A user could ask an agent with web access, “Tomorrow morning, summarize the top five stories on Hacker News.” The traditional solution would be storing the request and its schedule time in a database, then using a cron job to check for work that is due.

With Schedules, an agent can create a schedule that records the request and when to run it, without a separate database and polling job. The example below defines an AI SDK tool that gives an agent this capability.

When the task is due, Vercel uses Queues to deliver the saved request to your app. Your app provides code to read that request, check the user’s current permissions, and start the agent. The agent fetches the top five Hacker News posts with a web tool, then returns a summary for your app to save for the user.

If you already build agents with fx’s JavaScript library, libfx or Pi’s agent library, you can add a similar scheduling tool. The eve agent framework uses Vercel Schedules to provide dynamic scheduling tools for production agents hosted on Vercel.

Run recurring application jobs

You can schedule recurring work with Vercel Schedules. Schedules can be created dynamically via the JS SDK, API, and CLI, or set up in your project’s configuration.

For example, to create a job that cleans up expired records every day, you could define a schedule that invokes a private function in your chosen time zone:

Vercel calls this cleanup code directly, without exposing it at a public URL. It checks that each call comes from the scheduling service, so you don’t have to add that check yourself.

If your app already uses the Nitro 3 server framework, its experimental integration lets you run the recurring jobs in your existing scheduledTasks configuration as private functions.

You can also try the agent task and cleanup locally with vercel dev, then test them on a Preview branch or in a custom environment before production. Use Run Schedule in your project’s Schedules tab to try either task without waiting, and see when past runs happened.

Get started

Vercel Schedules is now in Public Beta, and you can use it for the recurring tasks your application already runs. When a user or agent chooses when work should happen, your code can create and manage a schedule for that task.

To get started, check out the Vercel Schedules skill and read the documentation.

title: MiniMax H3 Image and Highspeed now available on AI Gateway
description:

title: Test Reviewer Capacity Before Raising an AI Queue Limit
description:
A larger queue still needs a review reservation

An AI drafting service has two items waiting for review. One reserves two review units and the other reserves one. The current window has a declared capacity of three units. Raising the queue limit to fifty creates room for more item records, while the review budget is already fully reserved. A rule that checks only the item count will admit another draft into that window.

The Python fixture below reproduces that error. Its corrected admission function passes 21 local tests. A controlled copy with the budget check removed fails two tests. Both failures admit work that should remain held. The tests also check snapshot freshness, a changed ledger version and repeated delivery of the same work item. You can copy the complete function and test file into an empty directory and reproduce the assertions.

The example uses fictional review units and a fixed clock. An owner supplies the budget and each item's declared cost. The code makes a decision about those inputs. Estimating actual reviewer availability and evaluating the quality of reviewed work remain separate operating tasks. The tests were run locally by an AI agent in Python 3.14.7, without model calls or a production queue.

An AI agent prepared this tutorial, code and synthetic fixtures and ran the local checks. Human manuscript review has not been performed. The author affiliation is Pharos Production. The reported observations come from the included local fixture.

Decide what the review budget represents

Choose a unit that the review owner can explain. A team might start with fixed units for predefined review classes, with a difficult item reserving more than a routine one. Another team might allocate minutes after measuring its workflow. Either approach needs a documented mapping from work to the reservation it consumes. This fixture uses integers so the examples stay deterministic and easy to inspect.

In Google's SRE Workbook chapter on identifying and recovering from overload, the authors write "The team should work together to decide what measures to use." The chapter discusses team workload and overload. It gives a reason to involve the receiving reviewers when selecting an input to an admission policy. It supplies no conversion from a generated answer's length to a person's available review capacity.

For W-117, assume every reservation belongs to one review scope and one planning window. Item A reserves two units. Item B reserves one. Both remain unresolved. A proposed item C costs two. With a capacity of five, C fits exactly. With a capacity of three, C must wait. The same arithmetic applies when the item-count limit is fifty because that limit constrains a different part of the state.

Keep the total declared window capacity separate from used reservations. Recomputing used units from the current reservation ledger avoids treating a previously calculated free balance as current. The fixture sums all retained reservations. Completion, cancellation and reassignment require their own approved transitions before a reservation disappears. Treating a lost acknowledgement as completion would release capacity while the original work could still need review.

A review unit can be revised as the team learns more. Save the mapping version with the operating configuration and apply changes deliberately. An item that becomes more expensive after an artifact changes needs an explicit revision decision. The admission path should make that change visible instead of silently reducing another item's allocation.

Define the state passed to the function

The ledger contains the review scope, the planning window and a monotonically advancing version. It also carries the window's start and end and the reservations already accepted. The snapshot supplies the declared capacity for that same scope, window and ledger version. Its capture time lets the policy decide how old the observation is when new work arrives.

Input Meaning in this fixture Acceptance boundary
Ledger scope and window Identity of the budget being reserved Snapshot must address the same pair
Ledger version Revision of the reservation state A new reservation advances it
Start and end Fixed window bounds Start is inclusive, end is exclusive
Snapshot capture time When capacity was observed Within the window and at or before decision time
Maximum age Configured freshness allowance Age equal to the allowance is accepted
Work ID and revision Identity of the requested review An existing ID must retain its accepted cost and revision
Work cost Positive integer units to reserve Existing plus requested cost must fit the total budget
Queue limit Maximum retained reservation count Current count must be below the limit for new work

All times in the fixture are integer ticks in the same synthetic clock domain. W-117 starts at tick 90 and ends at tick 160. A capacity snapshot captured at tick 100 is checked at tick 110. The maximum permitted age is thirty ticks. These values are chosen inputs for the demonstration. A deployed service needs an agreed clock source and a policy for observations delayed by collection or transport.

The function expects a well-formed internal dictionary envelope with the documented keys. It validates the integer values relevant to the rule, including rejection of booleans as integers. A public-facing adapter would need its own schema, payload bounds and authorization checks before building that envelope. Keep that adapter's rejected input separate from a valid request receiving a HOLD decision.

An existing reservation is checked before the freshness requirements for new admission. A matching replay returns ALREADY_ADMITTED and the existing ledger. That path retrieves an earlier allocation. It gives no permission to reserve more work. A cost or revision change under an existing work ID raises a conflict, so the caller must resolve the identity instead of letting duplicate delivery rewrite history.

Implement the reservation decision

Save the following file as admission.py. The return value contains a decision, a reason and a copied ledger. HOLD returns the prior state. ADMITTED adds one reservation and advances the version. ALREADY_ADMITTED returns the existing allocation. All three results can be displayed to an operator without converting a held item into a failed review.

The checks run before the returned state is committed. In a real service, the caller must atomically compare the version and persist the update. This pure function gives the caller a state transition to attempt. The database section later explains the additional boundary needed when two workers compete for the same capacity.

from copy import deepcopy


def integer(value, name, minimum=0):
    if type(value) is not int or value < minimum:
        raise ValueError(f"{name} must be an integer >= {minimum}")
    return value


def admit(ledger, snapshot, work, *, now, queue_limit, max_age):
    """Plan one reservation. The caller must commit it atomically."""
    for name in ("scope", "window"):
        if not isinstance(ledger[name], str) or not ledger[name]:
            raise ValueError(f"ledger {name} is required")
    for name in ("id", "revision"):
        if not isinstance(work[name], str) or not work[name]:
            raise ValueError(f"work {name} is required")
    cost = integer(work["cost"], "cost", 1)
    integer(now, "now")
    integer(queue_limit, "queue_limit")
    integer(max_age, "max_age")
    integer(ledger["version"], "ledger version")
    integer(ledger["start"], "window start")
    integer(ledger["end"], "window end")
    if ledger["end"] <= ledger["start"]:
        raise ValueError("window end must follow start")
    for item in ledger["reservations"].values():
        integer(item["cost"], "reserved cost", 1)
        if not isinstance(item["revision"], str) or not item["revision"]:
            raise ValueError("reservation revision is required")

    def result(decision, reason, state=None):
        return {
            "decision": decision,
            "reason": reason,
            "ledger": deepcopy(ledger if state is None else state),
        }

    existing = ledger["reservations"].get(work["id"])
    reservation = {"cost": cost, "revision": work["revision"]}
    if existing is not None:
        if existing != reservation:
            raise ValueError("work identity conflicts with reservation")
        return result("ALREADY_ADMITTED", "EXISTING_RESERVATION")

    integer(snapshot["captured_at"], "snapshot time")
    integer(snapshot["version"], "snapshot version")
    capacity = integer(snapshot["capacity"], "capacity")
    if (snapshot["scope"], snapshot["window"]) != (
        ledger["scope"], ledger["window"]
    ):
        return result("HOLD", "SCOPE_MISMATCH")
    if not ledger["start"] <= now < ledger["end"]:
        return result("HOLD", "WINDOW_CLOSED")
    if not ledger["start"] <= snapshot["captured_at"] <= now:
        return result("HOLD", "INVALID_SNAPSHOT_TIME")
    if now - snapshot["captured_at"] > max_age:
        return result("HOLD", "STALE_SNAPSHOT")
    if snapshot["version"] != ledger["version"]:
        return result("HOLD", "VERSION_CONFLICT")
    if len(ledger["reservations"]) >= queue_limit:
        return result("HOLD", "QUEUE_FULL")
    used = sum(item["cost"] for item in ledger["reservations"].values())
    if used + cost > capacity:
        return result("HOLD", "REVIEW_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED")
    updated = deepcopy(ledger)
    updated["reservations"][work["id"]] = reservation
    updated["version"] += 1
    return result("ADMITTED", "RESERVED", updated)

The strict comparison in the budget check matters. Used units plus requested units equal to capacity are permitted. An item exceeding the budget by one unit is held. The queue-slot check remains independent, so a request can be held because the queue is full even when unused review units remain. The reason is selected from the first applicable new-work check in the function.

A caller should keep those reasons distinct in its records. A capacity owner can update an old snapshot, whereas a queue owner may need to resolve accepted work. Combining both into a generic busy response makes it harder to determine what action could change the result. Save the request identity and the state version beside the decision so a later reviewer can reproduce the same branch.

Run the complete test file

Save this second file as test_admission.py beside admission.py. The cases use the standard library's unittest framework. Each test starts with the same ledger and modifies only the condition it is testing. That makes the two budget regressions easy to trace back to the capacity rule.

The assert_held helper checks the returned decision and reason together. It also compares the entire returned ledger and the original input against the prior state. A function that reports HOLD while dropping item B would therefore fail the same contract. The success test inspects the actual reservation and the advanced version, then another test confirms that the caller's dictionaries were preserved.

from copy import deepcopy
import unittest

from admission import admit


class AdmissionTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.ledger = {
            "scope": "ai-draft-review", "window": "W-117", "version": 7,
            "start": 90, "end": 160,
            "reservations": {
                "A": {"cost": 2, "revision": "r1"},
                "B": {"cost": 1, "revision": "r1"},
            },
        }
        self.snapshot = {
            "scope": "ai-draft-review", "window": "W-117", "version": 7,
            "captured_at": 100, "capacity": 5,
        }
        self.work = {"id": "C", "revision": "r1", "cost": 2}
        self.options = {"now": 110, "queue_limit": 50, "max_age": 30}

    def check_admission(self):
        return admit(self.ledger, self.snapshot, self.work, **self.options)

    def assert_held(self, reason):
        before = deepcopy(self.ledger)
        result = self.check_admission()
        self.assertEqual((result["decision"], result["reason"]), ("HOLD", reason))
        self.assertEqual(result["ledger"], before)
        self.assertEqual(self.ledger, before)

    def test_exhausted_budget_despite_larger_queue(self):
        self.snapshot["capacity"] = 3
        self.assert_held("REVIEW_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED")

    def test_over_budget(self):
        self.work["cost"] = 3
        self.assert_held("REVIEW_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED")

    def test_exact_fit_reserves_and_advances_version(self):
        result = self.check_admission()
        self.assertEqual(result["decision"], "ADMITTED")
        self.assertEqual(result["ledger"]["version"], 8)
        self.assertEqual(result["ledger"]["reservations"]["C"], {"cost": 2, "revision": "r1"})

    def test_queue_slots_are_an_independent_limit(self):
        self.options["queue_limit"] = 2
        self.assert_held("QUEUE_FULL")

    def test_stale_snapshot(self):
        self.options["now"] = 131
        self.assert_held("STALE_SNAPSHOT")

    def test_snapshot_at_age_boundary(self):
        self.options["now"] = 130
        self.assertEqual(self.check_admission()["decision"], "ADMITTED")

    def test_future_snapshot(self):
        self.snapshot["captured_at"] = 111
        self.assert_held("INVALID_SNAPSHOT_TIME")

    def test_snapshot_before_window(self):
        self.snapshot["captured_at"] = 89
        self.assert_held("INVALID_SNAPSHOT_TIME")

    def test_closed_window(self):
        self.options["now"] = 160
        self.assert_held("WINDOW_CLOSED")

    def test_window_not_started(self):
        self.options["now"] = 89
        self.assert_held("WINDOW_CLOSED")

    def test_wrong_scope(self):
        self.snapshot["scope"] = "other-queue"
        self.assert_held("SCOPE_MISMATCH")

    def test_wrong_window(self):
        self.snapshot["window"] = "W-118"
        self.assert_held("SCOPE_MISMATCH")

    def test_stale_version(self):
        self.snapshot["version"] = 6
        self.assert_held("VERSION_CONFLICT")

    def test_replay_retains_existing_reservation(self):
        self.work = {"id": "A", "revision": "r1", "cost": 2}
        result = self.check_admission()
        self.assertEqual(result["decision"], "ALREADY_ADMITTED")
        self.assertEqual(result["ledger"], self.ledger)

    def test_replay_with_changed_cost_raises(self):
        self.work = {"id": "A", "revision": "r1", "cost": 1}
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.check_admission()

    def test_replay_with_changed_revision_raises(self):
        self.work = {"id": "A", "revision": "r2", "cost": 2}
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.check_admission()

    def test_old_snapshot_replay_is_a_read_of_existing_work(self):
        self.work = {"id": "A", "revision": "r1", "cost": 2}
        self.snapshot["captured_at"] = 0
        result = self.check_admission()
        self.assertEqual(result["decision"], "ALREADY_ADMITTED")
        self.assertEqual(result["ledger"], self.ledger)

    def test_success_does_not_mutate_inputs(self):
        before = deepcopy((self.ledger, self.snapshot, self.work))
        self.check_admission()
        self.assertEqual((self.ledger, self.snapshot, self.work), before)

    def test_zero_cost_raises(self):
        self.work["cost"] = 0
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.check_admission()

    def test_boolean_capacity_raises(self):
        self.snapshot["capacity"] = True
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.check_admission()

    def test_new_work_after_prior_admission_needs_new_snapshot(self):
        self.ledger = self.check_admission()["ledger"]
        self.work = {"id": "D", "revision": "r1", "cost": 1}
        self.assert_held("VERSION_CONFLICT")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    unittest.main(verbosity=2)

Run python3 -m unittest -v test_admission.py from that directory. The supplied corrected fixture ran 21 tests successfully in the local execution. The recorded elapsed duration was 0.001 seconds. That small local duration describes this test process on the machine used for the article. It carries no implication about review latency, model throughput or a deployed service's response time.

For the controlled failure, copy both files to a separate directory and change only the condition if used + cost > capacity to if False. Run the same command there. The local run kept nineteen tests passing and failed test_exhausted_budget_despite_larger_queue and test_over_budget. Both expected a held decision and received ADMITTED with reason RESERVED. Restore the original condition and rerun the corrected file before adopting any part of the example.

Read the exception tests as input-contract checks. Their expected result is ValueError, so a conflicting revision cannot become an ordinary held request that the caller retries indefinitely. The caller needs to correct the identity or invoke an authorized change process. The boolean-capacity test also matters in Python because booleans participate in integer behavior. The explicit type check keeps a supplied True from becoming a one-unit budget.

The test suite uses independent setup for every case. A prior success cannot accidentally consume capacity needed by a later assertion. The test for a stale snapshot after admission deliberately carries the returned ledger into the next call, preserving the old snapshot to expose the version conflict. That case models the change the caller must recognize after another reservation becomes authoritative.

Keep the failure output with the corrected output. A green result alone cannot show whether the tests would notice removal of the decision that protects the budget. Here the deliberate defect demonstrates sensitivity to that particular fault. Other defects require their own relevant assertions, especially once the function is attached to persistence or a queue transport.

Follow the two budget outcomes through the ledger

With the initial capacity of five, the ledger has three units reserved and C requests two. The function returns ADMITTED, adds C at revision r1 and changes the ledger version from seven to eight. The original ledger passed into the call still has only A and B. That input preservation allows a caller to retain the pre-decision state for a comparison or failed commit.

Now use capacity three with the same queue limit of fifty. The function returns HOLD with reason REVIEW_BUDGET_EXHAUSTED. The returned ledger keeps A and B unchanged at version seven. C stays outside this admission ledger. A real intake service should retain C in its own pending-request record and give it an owner or an appropriate response. This small fixture has no transport or pending-request database.

Configuration Used units Requested units Outcome Ledger version after planning
Capacity five, queue limit fifty 3 2 ADMITTED 8
Capacity three, queue limit fifty 3 2 HOLD, review budget exhausted 7
Capacity five, queue limit two 3 2 HOLD, queue full 7
Matching replay of A Existing allocation retained No new allocation ALREADY_ADMITTED 7

The snapshot-age boundary is tested separately. At tick 130, the snapshot from tick 100 is exactly thirty ticks old and new admission can proceed. At tick 131, it is stale and the function returns HOLD. The window itself closes at tick 160. An expired window blocks new admission even when a snapshot would otherwise be recent enough.

Existing A and B remain visible after every held decision. An operator can still identify the work already promised to reviewers. Raising a limit or pausing intake should preserve those commitments. A dashboard that counts only items admitted after the latest configuration change would hide the backlog that determines how much of the current budget is already occupied.

Refresh capacity with an identified owner

The reservation ledger can be current while the declared budget is wrong. A reviewer may become unavailable after the capacity owner published the snapshot. The version check detects changes to the ledger it names. It cannot discover an absence or a changed operating commitment that nobody recorded. The service needs a defined source for capacity and a way for the owner to reduce it when circumstances change.

A reduced capacity can fall below units already reserved. Leave those commitments visible and hold new admission while the owner examines them. The budget predicate naturally holds a new request in that state because existing cost plus a positive requested cost exceeds the new capacity. Resolving the overcommitment requires a recorded decision about accepted work, such as reassignment or an agreed delay. The admission function has no authority to make that choice.

Freshness should cover the source's actual update process. A polling adapter can attach the current time to a value fetched from an old cache, making the wrapper appear fresh. Keep the original capacity observation time through the adapter and distinguish it from retrieval time. The fixture's captured_at field represents the observation time. The owner needs to confirm that the supplying component preserves that meaning.

Store the capacity-policy revision alongside operating decisions. This example passes maximum age and queue limit directly to the function. A deployment might load them from configuration. When those values change, save the effective revision with the admission record so the same input can be replayed under the rule that originally evaluated it. A decision log should identify both the reservation version and the configuration used to judge it.

Treat work identity and content revision as a contract

Repeated delivery of A with cost two and revision r1 returns ALREADY_ADMITTED. The allocation survives intact and the ledger version stays seven. That result supports a caller recovering after an acknowledgement was lost. The caller can search for the original work identity and present the earlier outcome without inventing a new reservation.

A request for A at cost one raises ValueError. A request for A at revision r2 also raises ValueError. The conflict forces the integration to decide whether the caller made an error or the artifact really changed. Reviewing a new revision can create additional work even when the task keeps the same friendly title. The policy should define whether a revision replaces unfinished work or needs a separately reserved review.

The fixture allows retrieval of a matching existing reservation using an old snapshot. The result describes the recorded reservation and leaves the state unchanged. A new item with that same old snapshot still passes through the freshness checks. Keeping these paths distinct is useful during an outage when the service can read previous decisions but cannot establish a current capacity observation.

Retain an immutable content reference with each real review task. The fixture's r1 label represents a version supplied by the caller. A production implementation should be able to retrieve the exact artifact it names. If a document changes under the same label, matching the label will preserve allocation arithmetic while leaving the reviewer with the wrong material.

Put the check and reservation inside one commit boundary

Two workers can read version seven and each plan a reservation against the same remaining capacity. The pure function can return a valid update to both. Only an atomic persistence rule prevents both updates from becoming independently accepted work. Use the storage system's transaction or conditional-write mechanism to compare the expected ledger version when committing the reservation.

If one worker commits version eight, the other worker's commit against version seven must fail. The losing worker then rereads the authoritative ledger, obtains a valid capacity observation for that state and reevaluates its original work request. The next decision may be a budget hold or a successful admission. Reusing the earlier proposed result after a failed compare would discard the protection provided by the version field.

Keep the queue message aligned with the durable reservation. A transactional outbox is one way to record the accepted work and a publishable message together. The relay can deliver that message more than once, so the reviewer-facing consumer still needs stable task identity. Persisting a reservation and losing the message creates a recovery task. Sending work before the reservation commits creates a different gap because reviewers can receive work the ledger never accepted.

An unknown commit result needs investigation using the original work ID. First read the durable reservation or its decision record. A network timeout after a successful commit can leave the caller uncertain while capacity is already reserved. Creating another work ID during that uncertainty can allocate capacity twice. The replay test checks the function's behavior once the original reservation is visible. It does not execute the database failure or relay recovery.

Add integration tests at those boundaries before enabling automatic retries. Save evidence for one winning reservation under concurrent attempts, recovery after a lost commit response and duplicate message delivery. Verify the consumer's task record and the reservation ledger together. Those observations extend the local policy test into the components that actually promise work to reviewers.

Carry unresolved work into the next planning decision

A new planning window needs an explicit transition. W-117 can close while A remains unresolved. Copying a fresh capacity number into a new window without accounting for A can make previously promised work disappear from the planning view. The owner should decide how unfinished reservations affect the next window and retain the link to the original commitment.

The fixture handles one ledger and supplies no rollover function. At the closed boundary it preserves the existing reservations and holds new work. That behavior gives the operator time to reconcile what remains before publishing a successor window. The receiving owner needs the work identities, artifact revisions and remaining obligations, together with the capacity basis selected for the new period.

Completion also needs a defined evidence rule. A reviewer opening an item does not establish that its review is finished. Rework may require another allocation after findings are returned. Cancellation should name who authorized releasing the reservation and whether a queued copy can still reach a reviewer. Record those transitions separately so an admission log can explain why used capacity changed.

Priority handling is another policy decision. The example admits work in call order and retains a single queue-slot limit. A service with urgent work may reserve some capacity for that class or require a named override. Test the override's accounting and visibility before treating it as an operating path. A manually approved urgent item should remain visible in the same budget explanation.

Use the fixture as a release question

Before increasing an AI queue limit, inspect what the change permits when every declared review unit is already reserved. Run the exhausted-budget case, the freshness boundary and the repeated-work case against the candidate implementation. Inspect the retained unresolved items and the reason returned to the caller. A larger limit should lead to a comprehensible decision under each of those states.

The local result here establishes the behavior of a small function over synthetic inputs. The next engineering decision is whether the surrounding storage and message flow preserve the same reservation contract. Keep that decision attached to the tested implementation and the review owner's current capacity definition so a queue configuration change has an inspectable basis.
