  • GitHub: Loop Origin (@LoopOrigin)

title: How a Privacy-First Online Image Editor Works Without Uploading Your Photos (WebAssembly + On-Device AI)
description:
Most online image editors follow the same pattern. You pick a file, the browser uploads it, a server processes it, and a result comes back. It is simple to build, and it quietly means every photo you edit passes through someone else's infrastructure.

Browsers no longer need that arrangement. With WebAssembly, the Canvas API, and models that run on the client, the work of a photo editor, background remover, and image converter can happen on the device in front of you.

Akhouri Systems built APIC, a free browser-based editor, around that constraint. This article documents how a privacy-first online image editor is put together when nothing is uploaded, which trade-offs come with that design, and what users can reasonably expect from it.

Why "no upload" is an architecture decision, not a slogan

Privacy claims are cheap. Architecture is harder to fake.

When image processing happens on a server, privacy depends on policy: retention windows, access controls, and trust. When processing happens on the device, the image never leaves the browser tab, so there is nothing to retain and nothing to leak in transit.

That changes a few things for anyone building or choosing an online photo editor:

  • Sensitive images stay local. ID photos, product prototypes, client work, family pictures.
  • There is no upload queue. Speed depends on the user's hardware, not on server load.
  • Large files are no longer a bandwidth problem. A 40 MB photo does not need to travel anywhere.
  • Offline use becomes possible. After the first load, much of the tooling does not need a connection.

The cost is that the client has to do real work. The rest of this article is about how that work gets done.

The building blocks of a browser-based image editor

1. Canvas for live editing

Filters, brightness, contrast, saturation, blur, rotation, and flipping are all operations on pixel data, and the Canvas API handles them well. Because the work is local, sliders update the preview live with no round trip.

For more demanding color work, the same approach scales up. APIC's advanced panel includes a live histogram with shadow and highlight clipping indicators, RGB curves, an 8-band HSL mixer, three-way color grading, clarity, and grain. It can also export a 33×33×33 3D LUT as a .cube file, so a grade built in the browser can be reused in tools such as DaVinci Resolve, Premiere, or Photoshop.

One honest limitation: spatial effects like clarity, sharpening, vignette, and grain are not purely color transforms, so they cannot be baked into a LUT. The export covers the color-only parts of the grade.

2. WebAssembly for the heavy lifting

JavaScript alone is not the right tool for neural-network inference on a full-resolution photo. WebAssembly gives near-native execution inside the browser sandbox, which is what makes on-device AI practical. Every AI feature below runs this way.

3. Model caching so the cost is paid once

On-device AI has a real first-run cost: the model has to be downloaded. A well-behaved implementation downloads it once, caches it in the browser, and reuses it afterward.

For background removal, APIC offers three tiers so users can match the model to their device:

Tier First download Best for
Light about 5 MB Phones and quick cut-outs
Fast about 44 MB Everyday use
Maximum about 176 MB Highest accuracy, multi-pass, desktop-class hardware

After the first run, the model loads from cache, and nothing is sent to a server at any point. If a download fails, the app retries automatically and surfaces a retry button rather than failing silently.

On-device AI background removal

Background removal is a segmentation problem: classify every pixel as subject or not, then turn that mask into transparency. Doing this locally means the full-resolution original stays in memory on the user's device.

Two details matter for quality:

  • Edge refinement. Raw masks tend to leave hard or jagged boundaries. A refinement pass smooths them.
  • Color-fringe removal. Pixels at the edge often carry color from the old background. Removing that spill is the difference between a cut-out that looks pasted on and one that looks natural.

For output, keep transparency by exporting to PNG or WebP. JPEG has no alpha channel, so it will flatten the result.

Removing objects with on-device inpainting

Object removal is a different problem from background removal. You paint over what you want gone, such as a stray person, a sign, or a blemish, and a model fills the region so it blends with its surroundings.

APIC uses two engines, which illustrates a useful design pattern, graceful degradation:

  • MI-GAN (about 28 MB) is lightweight enough to run on phones.
  • LaMa, a large Fourier-convolution inpainting network (about 208 MB), gives the most accurate fills for big or complex areas, and is intended for desktop-class devices.

If a model cannot load, the tool steps down automatically: Ultra, then MI-GAN, then a quick patch fill. Only the area around the brush is processed, and the fill is color-matched and re-grained to match the original photo, which avoids the telltale "too clean" patch.

A practical tip that applies to any inpainting tool: paint slightly outside the object, so shadows and reflections are covered too.

Compressing an image to an exact file size

A common real-world task is hitting an upload limit: "under 200 KB" for a form, "under 1 MB" for a CMS. Guessing a quality slider is tedious.

A better approach is to search across quality levels and keep the highest one that fits the target. APIC's compress image online tool works this way. If the target is impossible at any quality, it reduces the dimensions as a fallback and reports the actual resulting size rather than pretending it hit the number.

Resizing without the muddy look

A single large downscale is a classic source of soft, blurry results. Resampling in several half-size steps preserves more detail, and every pixel is recomputed at full quality. The tool leaves the image uncropped and unstretched unless you deliberately change the aspect ratio. You can specify exact pixels or a percentage, with an aspect-ratio lock.

Converting formats: PNG, JPG, WebP, BMP, ICO, PDF

Format conversion is where most people start. The practical rules of thumb:

  • PNG: lossless, supports transparency. Best after background removal.
  • JPEG: small files, no transparency. Best for photos.
  • WebP: small files and transparency. A strong default for the web.
  • BMP: uncompressed.
  • ICO: app and favicon icons.
  • PDF: a single-page document from an image.

All six conversions run locally, so converting a private document scan does not involve a third party.

Social media sizes without the guesswork

Every platform has its own dimensions for profile pictures, banners, covers, posts, and stories, and they change. APIC's Social tab holds exact-size presets for 15 networks, including Instagram, YouTube, Facebook, X, TikTok, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Snapchat, Threads, Bluesky, Discord, Twitch, and Spotify.

Two features make this more useful than a list of numbers: safe-zone guides that show where a platform crops or covers your image, and ZIP export so you can download every size for a network at once.

Batch processing and an offline desktop version

Single-image tools only go so far. A batch studio takes many images through background removal, resizing, compression, and conversion in one pass and returns one ZIP, again processed entirely on the device.

For people who want no browser involved at all, there is also a Windows desktop build that runs fully offline with the edit, convert, and compress tools.

A note on accounts and what data is involved

Being specific here matters, because "no upload" can be misread. The editing tools work without an account. Signing in with Google is optional, and it uses your name, email, and photo for the account. The images themselves are not uploaded.
We request you to signing in APIC even when it is optional because it will help us to send you guys update emails.

Frequently asked questions

What is a privacy-first online image editor?
It is an editor that processes images on your own device instead of sending them to a server. Editing, conversion, compression, resizing, and AI features all run in the browser.

Can AI background removal run without uploading the photo?
Yes. A segmentation model can run in the browser through WebAssembly. The model downloads once, is cached, and processes the image locally.

Is there a free online photo editor that keeps images on-device?
APIC is one. It is free, has no paid tiers, and runs its tools locally.

How do I compress an image to a specific size in KB?
Use a compressor that searches for the highest quality under your target size, such as the Compress tool in APIC.

Which format keeps a transparent background?
PNG and WebP. JPEG does not support transparency.

Does it work on phones?
Yes. Lighter model tiers exist specifically for phones, with heavier ones recommended for desktop hardware.

Where to try it

If you want to see these techniques in practice, APIC is a free online photo editor, background remover, and image converter that runs in your browser, with no uploads of your images.

We are interested in how other engineers approach on-device processing. Which tasks have you moved from the server to the client, and what held you back? Share your experience in the comments.

title: A citation list is a flat file; the research is a graph
description:
I kept losing the shape of a literature review. I'd export forty references, read the abstracts in order, and end up with a folder of notes that told me what each paper said but not how the papers related. The thing I actually needed - which result depends on which earlier result, who cites whom, where a cluster stops - isn't in a flat list.

That's the problem I built LiteratureMap around. Not summarization. Structure.

A list hides the edges

A bibliography is an array. Each entry has authors, a year, a title, a venue. You can sort it, you can filter it, but nothing in that array encodes a relationship. The relationship is the interesting part: paper B extends paper A, paper C contradicts B, paper D is the survey that ties A, B, and C together.

Modeled properly, the literature is a directed graph. Nodes are papers. Edges are citations, with a direction - the citing paper points back to the cited one. Once you have that, questions that were painful become queries. Which papers are the common ancestors of a cluster? Which node has many incoming edges and few outgoing ones, meaning it's a foundation everyone builds on but nobody extends? Which pair of clusters has no connecting edge, which is a candidate gap?

The 'Citation relationship graph' feature is exactly that view. It draws what builds on what, who cites whom, and where the gaps are. I'm careful with the word 'gap' though.

'Gap finder' is a hint, not a verdict

A missing edge in a graph is not proof of an unanswered research question. It can mean the two clusters genuinely haven't been connected, or it can mean I didn't give the tool enough papers for the connection to show up, or that the connection exists in a paper outside the set. The gap finder surfaces a structural observation; it doesn't certify novelty.

That distinction matters because 'find a gap' is the kind of claim that sounds authoritative. I'd rather the tool say 'here is where the graph is sparse' and let a researcher decide whether that sparsity is meaningful. Combined with 'Theme clusters', which groups papers by shared subject, you get a readable overview of a field's shape. But it's a starting map. You still read the papers. I would not cite a gap from the map as evidence in a paper without checking the primary sources myself.

Why an exportable outline is the real output

A picture of a graph is pleasant but hard to write from. The 'Exportable outline' feature matters more than it sounds: it turns the structure back into text you can drop into a related-work section. Clusters become headings, the foundational nodes become the paragraphs you open with, and the sparse regions become the questions you pose at the end.

That round trip - papers in, graph, outline out - is the whole design. The input is a set of papers or a topic. The tool draws the relationship graph, groups themes, flags gaps, and hands back an outline. Nothing in that chain decides what's true about the field. It rearranges what you gave it so the structure is visible.

The limits I won't paper over

The map is only as complete as the set of papers you feed it. Feed it a narrow slice and the graph will look confident about a field it has barely seen. That's the failure mode I worry about most, because a clean diagram reads as thorough even when the input was thin.

It's also not a systematic review, a citation database, or a live audit of the literature. It doesn't fetch papers, verify citations, or tell you whether a result has been replicated. It's decision-support for organizing reading, closer to a whiteboard than to a reference manager. If you need completeness for a review article, this is a first pass, not the final word.

LiteratureMap is useful precisely because it makes a structure visible that a flat list hides. Just don't mistake a clean graph for a complete one.

FAQ

What do I actually put in?

A set of papers or a topic. The tool draws the relationship graph between them, groups themes, flags gaps, and returns an exportable outline.

Does the gap finder prove a research gap is real?

No. It flags where the graph is sparse. A missing edge might be a real opening or just a paper you didn't include. Check the primary sources.

Is this a citation database or a systematic review?

Neither. It's a way to see the shape of a set of papers. It doesn't fetch papers, verify citations, or claim completeness.

Can I use the output directly in a related-work section?

The exportable outline is a starting draft. I'd verify every claim against the papers before citing it.

title: • After a layoff and divorce, I built an app studio at my kitchen table
description:
I’m sharing this today not to look back at what I lost, but to celebrate what love and resilience can build when you refuse to give up.

Twelve months ago, my life was completely reset. I lost my job in a layoff, and shortly after, my marriage ended. Suddenly, I was raising my 2-year-old on my own with a tight budget. There were plenty of days when I skipped meals just to make sure my kid had everything they needed.

In those quiet moments at the kitchen table, watching my toddler smile without a care in the world, something shifted inside me. Instead of feeling defeated, I felt an overwhelming surge of purpose. That little kid gave me a superpower I didn't know I had.

Turning a Kitchen Table Into a Studio

I decided I wasn't going to wait for someone else to hand us a lifeline—I was going to build one with my own two hands.

Every night after tucking my kid in, I turned my kitchen table into a workspace. Fueled by hope, cheap coffee, and the joy of building something meaningful, I spent four hours coding. One app turned into two, and two turned into a small collection. Every bug I fixed and every feature I shipped was a small victory for our future.

Meet Shivaya

I named my solo studio Shivaya. To me, Shivaya stands for renewal, inner strength, and the beauty of starting fresh. Every single app under Shivaya was born out of late-night determination and pure love for my kid.

Today, seeing our apps live on Google Play fills me with gratitude:
👉 Check out Shivaya apps on Google Play

We don't have big investors or a fancy office, just unstoppable momentum and a bright road ahead.

If you’re starting over right now, please know this: rock bottom isn't the end of your story—it’s the solid foundation you get to rebuild on. You are stronger than you think. ✨

Fellow solo devs and builders—how do you manage your late-night coding schedule alongside family life? Would love to hear your thoughts or feedback on our apps in the comments!

title: How to Migrate From Webflow to Shopify Without Losing SEO
description:
Moving platforms changes every URL, template, and tag on your site. Here's the process I use so the rankings you've already earned come with you.

Most SEO losses after a migration aren't caused by the new platform. Shopify is perfectly capable of ranking. They're caused by three avoidable things: old URLs that lead nowhere, titles and content that quietly change in transit, and nobody checking the results after launch.

The principle behind everything below is simple. Search engines need to find every important old page, land on its closest new equivalent, and find the same content and signals when they arrive. A migration that does that keeps most of what it had. One that doesn't spends months recovering.

On a Webflow-to-Shopify migration for a motorcycle brand, I audited the Webflow storefront first and then built the product import with Matrixify. This is the process I follow, in five phases: baseline, map, build, launch, monitor.

First: Does the Whole Site Need to Move?

Before planning redirects, check whether a full migration is actually the right call. Many brands keep Webflow for the marketing site, the blog, and the landing pages, and move only the store to Shopify.

That changes the SEO plan significantly. Your blog and brand pages stay put, and the redirects only need to cover commerce URLs: products, categories, and anything tied to the cart. Less moves, so less can go wrong. If your marketing content ranks well and your problem is store functionality, this split is worth considering. It's the kind of architecture I cover under Webflow development alongside the Shopify build.

If you are moving everything, the rest of this post applies in full.

Phase 1: Baseline Everything Before You Touch Anything

You can't tell whether a migration worked without a record of what you had. Capture this before any build work begins:

A full crawl of the Webflow site. Use Screaming Frog or a similar crawler. Export every URL with its status code, title tag, meta description, H1, canonical, and indexability. This spreadsheet becomes the source of truth for everything that follows. Don't rely on the Webflow designer's page list, because it won't show you everything search engines have indexed.

Search Console data. Export top pages and top queries. Search Console only keeps around sixteen months of data, so export it now rather than after launch.

Analytics by landing page. Pull organic sessions and revenue by landing page from GA4. This tells you which pages actually earn money, which is not always the same as which pages get traffic.

Backlinks. Export the pages on your site that have external links pointing at them (Search Console's links report is free, and paid tools show more). These URLs must redirect precisely, because they carry authority from other sites.

Existing Webflow redirects. Copy out everything in Webflow's 301 redirect settings. Redirects that live in Webflow stop working the moment your domain points at Shopify, so every one has to be rebuilt.

Custom code. Note everything in Webflow's head and footer code: analytics, ad pixels, schema markup, verification tags. None of it carries over automatically.

Then rank your pages. Anything with organic traffic, revenue, or backlinks is tier one. These get hand-checked at launch. Everything else is tier two.

One more thing worth doing at this stage: audit the conversion flow of the existing store. A migration is the cheapest moment to fix leaks you'd otherwise carry across to the new platform. A CRO and website audit done before the build means the new store launches better than the old one, not merely equal to it.

Phase 2: Map the URLs

This is the phase that decides most of the outcome. Webflow and Shopify structure their URLs differently, so a large share of your pages will change address.

Typical patterns look like this, though your crawl is the source of truth because Webflow setups vary:

Page type Typical Webflow URL Shopify URL
Homepage / /
Product /product/slug /products/handle
Category /category/slug /collections/handle
Blog post /blog/slug /blogs/blog-handle/slug
Static page /about /pages/about

Shopify's prefixes (/products/, /collections/, /pages/, /blogs/) are fixed. You can't remove them, so every one of these URLs needs a redirect.

Keep slugs identical to handles wherever you can. If the Webflow product slug is carbon-slip-on-exhaust, make the Shopify handle carbon-slip-on-exhaust. The mapping becomes mechanical, and mechanical means fewer mistakes.

Build the redirect map in a spreadsheet. Columns: old URL, new URL, page type, priority tier, notes. Shopify redirects are exact-path matches and, in the built-in tool, there are no wildcards. You can't write "send everything under /product/ to /products/" as one rule. Generate the full list with a spreadsheet formula instead. If you need pattern-based rules, redirect apps support them.

Import in bulk. Shopify accepts a CSV with two columns, "Redirect from" and "Redirect to", using relative paths that start with a slash. Matrixify can also import redirects as part of the same migration job. Check the current redirect limit for your plan against the size of your list, because standard plans have a cap.

Redirect to the closest equivalent, not the homepage. When a product won't exist on the new store, send it to the most relevant collection or a similar product. Mass redirects to the homepage can be treated by Google as soft 404s, and the visitor who arrives gets nothing useful anyway.

Flatten chains. If an old Webflow redirect sends A to B, and B is now being redirected to C, update A to go straight to C. Chains slow things down and leak authority.

Remember images. Image files on Webflow's CDN can't be redirected to Shopify's CDN. If images bring you search traffic, expect some movement. Keep file names descriptive and alt text intact on the new store to give those images the best chance.

Phase 3: Build for SEO Parity

The goal on the new store is parity first, improvement second. Rebuild what's ranking before you try to make it better.

Match titles, descriptions, and H1s. Take them straight from the baseline crawl. In Shopify, each product, collection, page, and blog post has its own search engine listing fields. If you're using Matrixify for the product import, SEO title and description can be imported in the same sheet instead of being typed in by hand.

Migrate the catalogue deliberately. Webflow lets you export products as CSV from the Ecommerce panel. Map that export to Shopify's structure, with particular attention to variants and options, which Webflow and Shopify model differently. Shopify's native importer handles simple catalogues. Matrixify handles complex ones, including metafields. Check the plan limits against your catalogue size, because the free tier only covers a small number of items per file.

Move the blog and pages. Export Webflow CMS collections as CSV, then import them into Shopify blogs and pages. Preserve publish dates and slugs. Blog URLs will change shape because of the /blogs/ prefix, so they need redirects like everything else.

Rebuild structured data. Shopify themes include product schema out of the box, but Webflow custom code won't carry over. Test product pages in Google's Rich Results Test, and re-add any Article, FAQ, or Organization schema you were using.

Re-implement tracking. Recreate analytics, conversion tracking, and ad pixels deliberately, and test that they fire. Missing tracking after launch makes every later comparison unreliable.

Update internal links. Links inside your content that point to old URLs should be rewritten to the new ones. Redirects work, but internal links that rely on redirects waste crawl budget and slow pages down.

Check the theme's speed on staging. Premium themes plus a pile of apps is how many Shopify stores end up slower than the Webflow site they replaced. Test Core Web Vitals before launch, not after.

Resist changing everything at once. If rankings matter, don't rewrite all copy, restructure all URLs, and redesign every template on the same day you switch platforms. Migrate like-for-like first, then iterate. If you are redesigning, keep the content and headings of your top-ranking pages as close to the original as you can.

Phase 4: The Launch Checklist

Before the cutover:

  • Import the full redirect list before pointing the domain, so redirects are live the moment traffic arrives
  • Lower your DNS TTL a day or two ahead so the change propagates quickly
  • Pick a low-traffic window, avoid launching just before a peak sales period, and don't launch when no one can monitor it
  • Freeze content changes on the Webflow site during the migration window, so nothing new needs redirecting at the last minute

At the cutover:

  • Update DNS using the values shown in Shopify's domain settings, and confirm HTTPS works on both the root domain and www
  • Set the primary domain so one version of the URL is canonical
  • Remove the storefront password. A password-protected store can't be crawled, and leaving it on after launch is one of the most damaging mistakes on this list

Immediately after:

  • Crawl your tier-one URLs from the redirect map and confirm each returns a 301 to a page that returns a 200, with no chains
  • Submit the new sitemap (/sitemap.xml) in Search Console
  • If the domain name has stayed the same, you don't need Search Console's change-of-address tool. That's only for moving to a different domain
  • Keep the Webflow project as a backup until you're confident the redirects are working. Don't delete anything yet

Phase 5: Monitor for the First 90 Days

Launch isn't the finish line. Most recoverable problems get found in the first few weeks, and only if someone is looking.

Daily in the first week:

  • Search Console's page indexing report, for new 404s, redirect errors, and pages excluded unexpectedly
  • Crawl errors on tier-one URLs
  • GA4 organic landing pages compared against your baseline

Weekly after that:

  • Clicks and impressions for top pages and queries, compared against your pre-migration export
  • Rankings for your priority keywords
  • A fresh crawl to catch redirect chains, broken internal links, and canonical problems

When you find a 404 that had traffic or backlinks, add the redirect immediately and note it for the next review.

Some movement in rankings in the weeks after a migration is normal while search engines reprocess the site. What matters is the pattern. A sustained drop on pages you redirected correctly points to something else: changed titles, thinner content, slower pages, or weaker internal linking. Compare against the baseline and investigate those first.

The Mistakes I See Most Often

If you only take a short list from this post, take this one:

  • Redirecting everything to the homepage instead of mapping page by page
  • Leaving the storefront password on after launch
  • Forgetting the blog, or forgetting that blog URLs change
  • Ignoring old Webflow redirects, which then break or form chains
  • Rewriting titles and content during the move, so you can't tell what caused any drop
  • Losing tracking and structured data because it lived in Webflow custom code
  • Launching with no baseline to compare against
  • Deleting the old site before the redirects are verified

Every one of these is preventable with the spreadsheet from Phase 1 and the crawl from Phase 4.

The Principle Underneath

A migration is a data problem more than a design problem. Everything that earned you rankings, the URLs, the titles, the content, the links pointing in, has to arrive intact at the other end. The store you're moving to can be better than the one you're leaving. But it can only inherit the old one's search performance if you treat the move as something to be mapped, built, verified, and monitored, rather than something that happens on launch day.

If you're planning a move from Webflow and want it handled with the SEO work built in, I do Shopify development and migrations through Webko, and I offer a free three-page mockup so you can see the new design before committing to anything.

I'm a freelance web designer and developer specializing in Shopify web design and Webflow development for e-commerce brands globally. I run Webko, a web design studio focused on high-converting e-commerce storefronts.

Connect with me on LinkedIn or explore my work on GitHub.

title: The Best Next.js CRM Templates in 2026 (Compared)
description:
A CRM looks like a dashboard but behaves like an app. Beyond charts, it needs a contacts list you can search and filter, a pipeline where deals move between stages, deal records with values and close dates, tasks tied to people, and a fast way to jump between all of them. CRM templates differ mostly in two things: whether there's a real database behind the screens, and how much of that daily workflow is actually built. This is an honest comparison of four Next.js CRM templates, one of them ours, plus two open-source CRMs worth knowing about if what you really want is a CRM rather than a template.

What to check before you pick one

  • Backend or UI kit - does it save contacts and deals to a real database, or run on mock data you replace?
  • The pipeline - can you drag deals between stages, and can you also move them without dragging? WCAG 2.2 requires a non-drag alternative, like a click or a menu, and keyboard users need one too.
  • Workflow depth - contacts, deals, and tasks are the minimum; email, calendar, CSV import, and forecasting are where kits differ.
  • License for client work - if you're building a CRM for a client, check which tier allows it.
  • Version currency - Next.js 16 and Tailwind v4 are current; check package.json, not the README.

The best Next.js CRM templates in 2026

1. NextCRM - Best open-source full-stack CRM

NextCRM is an MIT-licensed, actively maintained CRM built on Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, and shadcn/ui, with PostgreSQL through Prisma 7. Unlike the UI kits below, it's a working application with a real database: modules for contacts, accounts, opportunities, invoicing, projects, and documents. If you want a free CRM you can run and extend rather than a set of screens to wire up, it's the strongest Next.js option. The tradeoff is the usual one for a full app: you inherit its data model and its opinions, and you're running a database from day one.

2. Elite CRM - Best focused, designed CRM front end

Elite CRM is ours: a dark-first CRM front end that covers the daily sales workflow tightly rather than broadly. Contacts with search, status filters, and a table/grid toggle; a five-column Kanban pipeline with per-stage totals, days-in-stage risk flags, and drag-and-drop between stages; a deals table with multi-select and bulk actions; tasks bucketed into overdue, due today, and upcoming; and analytics with a revenue chart, win/loss donut, conversion funnel, and rep leaderboard. A Cmd+K command palette searches contacts, deals, and tasks, and one global slide-over panel opens any record without leaving the page. It's built on Next.js 16, React 19, and Tailwind v4 ("Indigo Console", Geist Sans and Mono) with a light theme, and ships an automated WCAG 2.2 AA check.

The honest tradeoffs: it's front end only, with contacts, deals, and tasks in a typed mock-data layer and no database, auth, or email. Deals you drag between stages live in page state and reset on reload. And dragging is the only way to change a deal's stage - there's no keyboard or click alternative yet, which matters if your users rely on a keyboard. It's also narrower than Frontkit's kit below: no email, calendar, CSV import, or forecasting.

See Elite CRM - Elite CRM - contacts, a drag-and-drop Kanban pipeline, deals with bulk actions, tasks, and analytics, with Cmd+K search and a global detail panel. Next.js 16, dark-first with a light theme. From $79, one-time.

3. Frontkit CRM Dashboard Kit - Best for breadth

Frontkit's CRM Dashboard Kit is the broadest CRM UI kit we found: 42 screens across ten sections on Next.js 16, Tailwind v4, and shadcn/ui. Beyond contacts, deals, and a Kanban pipeline, it includes companies with a CSV import wizard, revenue forecasting, four analytics dashboards, an email inbox with compose and sequences, a calendar, and an activity log. Its pipeline drag-and-drop uses @hello-pangea/dnd, a library that supports keyboard dragging. Like Elite CRM, it's front end only on mock seed data. Pricing is per tier - Solo lists at $165 and Agency at $349, and the page showed a 40% discount when we checked - and only the Agency tier allows client delivery; Solo and Team are for internal projects.

4. shadcn-crm-dashboard - Best free starter

KaraBharat's shadcn-crm-dashboard is an MIT-licensed CRM dashboard UI on Next.js 15, React 19, Tailwind v4, and shadcn/ui, meant to be forked as a base. It's free and clean, but it's a starting point rather than a finished CRM, and it hasn't been updated since April 2025 - so plan to upgrade Next.js and build out the workflow yourself.

If you want a CRM, not a template

Two open-source CRMs are worth knowing about if what you actually need is a working CRM for your own team rather than a template to build a product on. Neither is a Next.js template, which is why they aren't ranked above.

  • Atomic CRM, from Marmelab - an MIT-licensed CRM built with React and react-admin on Supabase, with contacts, a Kanban deals board, tasks, and email capture. It's designed as a framework you extend in TypeScript, and it's actively maintained.
  • Twenty - a full open-source CRM product you can self-host, positioned as a Salesforce alternative. Its license is mostly AGPL-3.0, with some enterprise features under a commercial license, so read it carefully before building a service on top of it.

Side-by-side comparison

Template Backend Workflow Pipeline drag Price
NextCRM PostgreSQL + Prisma Contacts, accounts, opportunities, invoicing, projects Full app Free (MIT)
Elite CRM None - typed mock data Contacts, pipeline, deals, tasks, analytics, Cmd+K Mouse only, resets on reload From $79
Frontkit CRM Dashboard Kit None - mock data 42 screens incl. email, calendar, CSV import, forecasting Keyboard-capable library $165 list (Solo)
shadcn-crm-dashboard None Dashboard UI starter Not a focus Free (MIT)

How to choose

  • You want a free CRM with a real database you can run and extend - NextCRM.
  • You want a polished, focused CRM front end for your own product and will connect the backend - Elite CRM.
  • You need the widest set of CRM screens, including email and calendar, or keyboard-accessible pipeline dragging - Frontkit's CRM Dashboard Kit.
  • You want a free UI base to build on - shadcn-crm-dashboard.
  • You just need a CRM for your team - Atomic CRM or Twenty.

In a CRM, the data model is the product. Before choosing a template for its screens, sketch the records you'll actually store - contacts, companies, deals, stages, activities - and check the template's types fit them. Re-shaping a data model later touches every screen.

See dashboard templates - Browse every TheKitBase dashboard template - Elite CRM for sales pipelines, and SaaS Dashboard Pro for SaaS admin. Next.js 16, Tailwind v4, light and dark.

title: Why my inbox triage tool refuses to ask for your Gmail password
description:
The first question I get about EmailTriage is why it doesn't connect to Gmail. I could have built an OAuth flow, requested read access, and synced messages in the background. I didn't, and the reason isn't privacy theater. It's that the connection is the expensive part of the problem, and most of what people need from triage doesn't require it.

Triage is a classification task over a finite batch. You have a pile of messages, you want to know which ones need a reply today, which ones you can read later, and which ones are noise. That's a labeling problem, not a synchronization problem. Once I framed it that way, the architecture got small.

The permission I didn't want to ask for

An inbox integration means tokens, refresh logic, scopes, a consent screen, and a background job that keeps state in sync. Every one of those is a surface I'd have to maintain. It also means the tool sees your whole mailbox, including threads that have nothing to do with the batch you're trying to clear. For a founder pasting twenty messages before a flight, that's overkill.

So EmailTriage works on bulk paste. You copy a set of emails into one field and get each one labeled. That's the entire input contract. No tokens, no background sync, no stored mailbox state. The feature list calls this 'No inbox access needed', and it's the decision I'm most attached to because it removes a whole category of failure: nothing breaks at 3am because a refresh token expired, because there is no refresh token.

The trade-off is real, though. There's no incremental update. If a new reply lands in a thread, it isn't in your batch until you paste it again. There's no threading context beyond what you copy. I'd rather be honest about that than pretend a paste box is a full mail client.

Three labels, and why only three

I spent more time than I'd like on the label set. Inside the tool, the output is ACTION, READ, or LOW. ACTION means the message needs a response and gets a draft reply. READ means it's worth your attention but not a reply. LOW means it can wait or be ignored.

Fewer labels is a deliberate constraint. A taxonomy with eight categories sounds more precise, but in practice it pushes the hard judgment onto the person doing the triage: is this 'urgent' or 'important but not urgent'? Three buckets force a choice that maps to a real behavior - reply now, read later, skip. The draft replies attach only to ACTION items, which keeps the tool from generating text nobody asked for.

The 'Auto label' and 'Draft replies' features are the two halves of that. Labels sort the pile; drafts give you a starting sentence for the ones that matter. Neither is a decision. I treat the draft as a first pass you edit before sending, not as something to fire off untouched.

Where the paste approach gets awkward

The interesting failures are all about input quality. Paste a forwarded chain with five quoted replies and the boundaries between messages get fuzzy. Paste HTML-heavy marketing mail and the useful sentence is buried under markup. Paste two emails with the same subject and no separator and you get one blob.

These aren't bugs I can fully fix with a smarter model, because the ambiguity is in the input itself. What I can do is be clear that the tool works on a batch of discrete messages and that you get better labels when each message is distinguishable. That's an honest limit of the format, not a hidden one.

Long threads are the other weak spot. A single email in a long conversation often only makes sense with the history, and a paste doesn't carry that history reliably. If a message looks like it references something you can't see, the honest move is to open your mail client and read the thread. The tool is a sorting aid for a batch, not a substitute for reading your mail.

What this is and isn't

EmailTriage is decision-support for clearing a pile of messages. It labels and drafts; you decide and send. It doesn't connect to your inbox, schedule sends, or guarantee that a labeled LOW item is actually unimportant. For a busy operator who wants to turn a wall of unread mail into three buckets and a few reply starters, that's the whole job. If you need continuous sync or full-thread awareness, a paste-based tool is the wrong shape and I'd say so.

FAQ

Does it need access to my inbox?

No. You paste a batch of emails and get labels and draft replies back. There's no OAuth, no token, and no background sync.

Why only three labels?

ACTION, READ, and LOW map to three real behaviors: reply now, read later, skip. A bigger taxonomy moves the hard judgment back onto you.

Are the draft replies ready to send as-is?

Treat them as a first pass. I'd review and edit before sending; the tool drafts, you decide.

What if my emails are messy or part of a long thread?

The labels depend on the text you paste. Forwarded chains and quoted replies can blur message boundaries, so for context-heavy threads, read the original in your mail client.

title: Getting Started with Swift on Android: A Beginner's Guide to the Official SDK
description:
A beginner-friendly introduction to the official Swift SDK for Android

1. Introduction

For most of its life, Swift was known as the language for iPhone, iPad and Mac apps. That changed with Swift 6.3, which shipped the first official Swift SDK for Android. You can now compile Swift code for Android devices using official tools published on swift.org, instead of relying on unofficial community toolchains.

This tutorial walks you through the whole path from zero: what the pieces are, how to install them, how to build your first Swift program for Android, and how Swift fits into a real Android app. No previous Android experience is needed, but basic familiarity with Swift and the terminal will help.

What you will learn

  • What the Swift SDK for Android is, and what it is not
  • How to install the toolchain, the SDK and the Android NDK
  • How to cross-compile and run a "Hello, world" program on an emulator or device
  • How to share Swift code between an iOS app and an Android app

2. How it works: the three pieces

Building Swift for Android needs three components that work together:

Component What it does
Host toolchain The Swift compiler and tools running on your Mac or Linux machine.
Swift SDK for Android Libraries, headers and resources that let the compiler target Android (a cross-compilation SDK).
Android NDK Google's Native Development Kit, which provides the Android system libraries your Swift code links against.

Important: Xcode cannot build Android apps by itself. The Swift SDK for Android is used from the command line (Swift Package Manager) or from Android Studio via Gradle. SwiftUI and UIKit do not run on Android; for the user interface you typically use Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, or a third-party tool such as Skip.

3. Prerequisites

  • A Mac (macOS) or a Linux machine
  • Android Studio, with an emulator set up or a physical Android device with USB debugging enabled
  • Around 5 GB of free disk space for the toolchain, SDK and NDK
  • A terminal you are comfortable using

4. Step-by-step setup

Step 1: Install swiftly

swiftly is the official Swift toolchain manager. It lets you install and switch between Swift versions. On macOS:

curl -O https://download.swift.org/swiftly/darwin/swiftly.pkg && \
installer -pkg swiftly.pkg -target CurrentUserHomeDirectory && \
~/.swiftly/bin/swiftly init --quiet-shell-followup && \
. "${SWIFTLY_HOME_DIR:-$HOME/.swiftly}/env.sh" && \
hash -r

On Linux, follow the swiftly instructions at swift.org/install.

Step 2: Install a matching Swift toolchain

The host toolchain must be the same version as the Android SDK you install next. For example, for the latest release:

swiftly install latest
swiftly use latest
swift --version

Step 3: Install the Swift SDK for Android

Go to swift.org/install, open the Android section, and copy the install command for the SDK that matches your toolchain version. It looks like this:

swift sdk install <SDK-URL-FROM-SWIFT.ORG>.artifactbundle.tar.gz \
  --checksum <CHECKSUM-FROM-SWIFT.ORG>

Tip: Always copy the URL and checksum from swift.org rather than from a blog post. The checksum protects you from a corrupted or tampered download, and it changes with every release.

Check that it installed correctly:

swift sdk list
# Example output:
# swift-6.x-RELEASE_android

Step 4: Install the Android NDK and link it

In Android Studio, open Settings > Languages & Frameworks > Android SDK > SDK Tools, tick NDK (Side by side) and install the version recommended in the swift.org Android guide. Then point your shell at it (macOS paths shown; on Linux the SDK usually lives in ~/Android/Sdk):

export ANDROID_HOME=$HOME/Library/Android/sdk
export ANDROID_NDK_HOME=$ANDROID_HOME/ndk/<your-ndk-version>
export PATH=$PATH:$ANDROID_HOME/platform-tools

Finally, run the setup script that ships inside the SDK bundle. It links the NDK to the Swift SDK:

cd ~/Library/org.swift.swiftpm || cd ~/.swiftpm
./swift-sdks/<your-sdk-name>.artifactbundle/swift-android/scripts/setup-android-sdk.sh

You should see a success message saying the NDK sysroot was linked.

5. Your first Swift program on Android

Step 5: Create a package 

mkdir hello && cd hello
swift package init --type executable
swift build
.build/debug/hello      # prints: Hello, world!

This first build runs on your own machine. Now cross-compile the same code for Android.

Step 6: Cross-compile for Android 

# For the emulator (x86_64):
swift build --swift-sdk x86_64-unknown-linux-android28 --static-swift-stdlib

# For a real phone (arm64):
swift build --swift-sdk aarch64-unknown-linux-android28 --static-swift-stdlib

The number 28 is the minimum Android API level (Android 9). --static-swift-stdlib bundles the Swift standard library into the binary so you don't have to copy it separately.

Step 7: Run it on the emulator or device

Start your emulator (or connect your phone), then push the binary plus the C++ runtime from the NDK and run it:

adb push .build/x86_64-unknown-linux-android28/debug/hello /data/local/tmp/
adb push $ANDROID_NDK_HOME/toolchains/llvm/prebuilt/*/sysroot/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-android/libc++_shared.so /data/local/tmp/
adb shell "cd /data/local/tmp && LD_LIBRARY_PATH=. ./hello"
# Hello, world!

🎉 Congratulations! You just ran Swift code on Android. For a real phone, swap x86_64 for aarch64 in the first two paths.

6. Writing code that works on both platforms

The most practical use of Swift on Android today is sharing your app's core logic: models, validation, networking and business rules. You write it once in a Swift package and use it in both apps. When something needs to differ, use a compile-time platform check:

public struct Greeter {
    public init() {}

    public func greeting(for name: String) -> String {
        #if os(Android)
        let platform = "Android"
        #elseif os(iOS)
        let platform = "iOS"
        #else
        let platform = "another platform"
        #endif
        return "Hello, \(name)! Running Swift on \(platform)."
    }
}

Many existing packages already work: more than a quarter of the libraries on the Swift Package Index were marked as Android-compatible when the SDK launched. Check a package's page on swiftpackageindex.com before you depend on it.

7. From a program to a real Android app

Running a terminal program is the first milestone. To build an actual app with screens, you have two main options:

Option A: Kotlin UI + shared Swift logic

Build the user interface in Android Studio with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose, and call your Swift package from Kotlin using swift-java, the official Java/Kotlin interoperability project. The official swift-android-examples repository on GitHub shows complete working setups. This is the best fit for teams that already have an Android app.

Option B: SwiftUI everywhere with Skip

Skip is a third-party tool that works inside Xcode. You write a SwiftUI app and Skip produces a native Android version, running on the iOS simulator and an Android emulator side by side. It is the closest thing to "Xcode for Android". Check its website for current features and pricing.

8. Common problems and fixes

Problem Fix
swift sdk list shows nothing The SDK install failed or ran with a different toolchain. Re-run the install command with the toolchain active.
Build errors about missing headers or sysroot The NDK isn't linked. Re-run setup-android-sdk.sh after setting ANDROID_NDK_HOME.
Version mismatch error Toolchain and SDK versions must match exactly. Check with swift --version.
libc++_shared.so not found on device Push it from the NDK sysroot (Step 7) and set LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
"Exec format error" on device Wrong architecture. Use x86_64 for most emulators and aarch64 for phones.

9. Resources

  • Official getting-started guide: Swift SDK for Android – Getting Started
  • Downloads and install commands: swift.org/install
  • Java/Kotlin interop: swiftlang/swift-java
  • Example apps: swiftlang/swift-android-examples
  • Community discussion: the Android category on forums.swift.org
  • Skip: skip.dev

10. Wrapping up

Swift on Android is young but official, and it is improving with every release. Start small: get "Hello, world" running, then move one piece of shared logic, such as a model or a validation rule, into a Swift package that both your iOS and Android apps use. Feedback and questions are welcome in the comments below!

title: Unified CLI Framework Reduces Development Boilerplate and Integrates Autocomplete
description:
The Fragmentation Crisis in Modern CLI Development

Traditional command-line interface development operates as a fractured distributed system disguised as a single binary. When building a CLI using legacy toolchains, a developer is forced to maintain three distinct, decoupled artifacts for every single command, flag, and argument: the core execution logic, the static documentation (typically written in archaic roff for manpages or markdown for tldr), and the interactive shell completion scripts for bash, zsh, and fish.

This multi-file architecture imposes a heavy synchronization tax. When a flag's default value or type changes in the implementation code, that modification does not automatically propagate to the completion script or the manual page. Instead, the developer must manually update three separate code paths. This creates structural drift: the documentation tells the user one thing, the shell completion engine emits another set of tokens, and the underlying parser crashes on unhandled inputs. The internal consistency of the toolchain shatters under the weight of manual duplication.

The mechanical cost of this fragmentation manifests as severe cognitive friction and context-switching overhead. Terminal users evaluate CLI usability through instant, zero-latency feedback loops like robust tab-completion. Yet, implementing native shell completion traditionally requires writing brittle wrapper scripts that parse terminal state machines by hand. Developers waste countless hours wrestling with shell-specific completion arrays—such as compgen in Bash versus compdef in Zsh—rather than shipping business logic. The tooling fails because it treats documentation and shell integration as afterthought add-ons rather than direct compilation targets of a single source of truth.

Evaluating Approaches to CLI Construction

To resolve this crisis, engineering teams typically choose between three flawed patterns:

  • Manual Boilerplate Authoring: Writing redundant parsing logic and shell scripts by hand. This breaks down immediately at scale, leading to widespread version drift between code and documentation.
  • Custom Glue Scripts: Attempting to patch together documentation generators and parsers with custom shell scripts. This creates brittle maintenance bottlenecks where any upstream change to the language runtime breaks the build pipeline.
  • Unified Schema-Driven Toolchains: Defining flags, arguments, and metadata once in a structured format (such as the Go-based uf toolchain approach) to programmatically drive execution parsers, multi-language code generation, and shell completion scripts simultaneously.

Decision Rule: If your project requires maintaining command-line tools across multiple shell environments or expects high-frequency updates to CLI flags, never rely on manual boilerplate or disparate documentation files. You must adopt a data-driven schema propagation model where a unified definition file acts as the single source of truth, compiling directly into runtime parsers, native tab-completions, and structured manpages to eliminate synchronization drift entirely.

Enter uf: Redefining CLI Ergonomics and Documentation

Traditional command-line documentation relies on decoupled artifacts: static man pages authored in brittle roff macros and community-driven tldr snippets. This multi-artifact burden imposes a severe synchronization tax on software development workflows. When a flag default or argument type changes in the core execution logic, the manual update path to the documentation file is easily severed. The internal mechanism of failure is structural drift: parsers accept updated parameters while legacy man pages continue referencing deprecated syntax, forcing developers into an expensive debugging loop defined by false-positive error messages and high cognitive friction.

uf attacks this fragmentation by treating the command-line interface as a distributed compiler target. Instead of maintaining separate documentation files, uf utilizes a single-source-of-truth schema where flag definitions, validation rules, and descriptions are declared once. This data-driven propagation compiles runtime execution parsers, native tab-completions, and structured documentation concurrently from the exact same definition source. Consequently, documentation drift becomes mechanically impossible because any mismatch between code and help text breaks compilation before it ever reaches the terminal environment.

Comparative Evaluation of Documentation Architectures

Architecture Maintenance Mechanism Failure Mode
Manual man / roff Hand-written formatting macros decoupled from code execution. Silent desynchronization; documentation lies about flag behaviors and defaults.
Static tldr / Markdown Crowdsourced snippet files stored independently from the source repository. Incomplete coverage of edge-case flags and nested subcommands; frequent staleness.
uf Unified Schema Single definition source driving runtime code and help strings simultaneously. Fails at compile-time if documentation metadata desynchronizes from parser logic.

By shifting documentation generation downstream from the unified schema, uf ensures that inline help output is dynamically context-aware. Terminal developers no longer suffer from context-switching fatigue caused by jumping between separate manual pages and source code. However, this approach stops working effectively when a CLI relies on hyper-dynamic, runtime-evaluated command plugins whose parameters cannot be statically resolved during the initial schema compilation phase. For standard static or hierarchical CLI tooling, the operational rule is absolute: if a project requires multi-artifact synchronization, enforce a single schema definition source or accept inevitable documentation drift.

Five Scenarios in Action: Autocomplete, Polyglot Generation, and Beyond

When building production command-line tooling, architectural friction concentrates at the boundary where the developer's intent meets the shell's execution environment. To evaluate how a single-source-of-truth toolchain like uf eliminates this drag, we must examine five distinct operational scenarios. Each scenario exposes a specific failure mode of legacy multi-artifact setups and demonstrates the mechanical resilience of schema-driven compilation.

  • Scenario 1: Native Shell Completion Synthesis in fish Mechanism: Instead of hand-authoring brittle complete -c command blocks that inevitably drift when flags are renamed, uf reads the unified schema and compiles native fish completion streams directly. Observable Effect: Pressing tab triggers zero-latency state machine introspection. If a flag type changes from string to integer, the type constraint is embedded directly into the completion candidate buffer, preventing invalid parameter injection before execution ever hits the binary parser.
  • Scenario 2: POSIX-Compliant Autocomplete Propagation for zsh and bash Mechanism: Legacy workflows rely on manual compgen or compdef functions—fragile text scripts that parse terminal state machines via regex hacks. Under uf, the schema acts as a distributed compiler target, outputting exact completion word-lists and completion functions tailored to the quirks of legacy shell completion arrays (compgen -F). Failure Avoided: This completely halts structural drift where missing completions cause silent shell fallbacks to local file-path completion.
  • Scenario 3: Polyglot Code Generation and Target Mapping Mechanism: While Go serves as the primary runtime target, multi-language ecosystems require cross-compiling command structures. Template-driven code generation maps the unified schema directly into client bindings or parallel parsers in other languages. Decision Rule: If your system requires multi-language SDKs interacting with CLI subcommands, never maintain separate parser files; use a single declarative schema to emit typed bindings, eliminating the maintenance tax of manual synchronization scripts that break when upstream runtimes shift.
  • Scenario 4: Context-Aware Inline Help Generation vs. Decoupled Manuals Mechanism: Traditional man pages (written in roff macros) and crowdsourced tldr snippets live in separate files decoupled from execution code. When a developer modifies a validation rule, the manual is bypassed. uf mechanically extracts structured documentation straight from the validation attributes at compile time. Failure Mode: If documentation text desynchronizes from code logic, compilation halts entirely. Documentation drift becomes physically impossible because code and help output share a single compilation lifecycle.
  • Scenario 5: Handling Hyper-Dynamic Plugin Architectures (Boundary Conditions) Mechanism: While static schema compilation excels at predictable flag topologies, it strikes a hard architectural wall when confronted with runtime-evaluated command plugins whose parameters cannot be resolved until external services boot. Operational Boundary: Under hyper-dynamic conditions where flags are fetched from remote databases at runtime, static uf compilation fails to emit valid shell states. The solution here is to switch from static compilation to a dynamic schema-introspection hook, trading compile-time safety for runtime flexibility.

By enforcing a strict data-driven propagation model across these five scenarios, developers discard the synchronization tax of legacy toolchains. The CLI transitions from a fragmented collection of shell scripts and documentation files into a unified, mechanically verifiable compilation target.

The Broader Impact on Developer Productivity

Traditional command-line tool development is crippled by a multi-artifact maintenance burden. Engineers traditionally maintain three decoupled silos per command or flag: core execution logic, static documentation (such as roff-based man pages or markdown tldr files), and shell completion scripts (written via brittle primitives like compgen or compdef). When a flag default changes in the execution parser, that change rarely propagates automatically to the completion scripts or documentation. This decouples the code from its metadata, creating structural drift. The internal mechanism of this failure is straightforward: the shell completion state machine attempts to match input against outdated word-lists, encountering unexpected tokens that trigger silent completion failures or invalid parameter injections into the binary parser.

To evaluate construction patterns, we must contrast manual boilerplate authoring and custom glue scripts against unified schema-driven toolchains like uf. Manual boilerplate creation introduces extreme redundancy and version drift at scale, while custom glue scripts act as fragile maintenance bottlenecks where upstream language runtime changes shatter build pipelines. The optimal architectural choice is a single-source-of-truth schema that compiles directly into runtime parsers, native tab-completions, and structured documentation simultaneously. By treating the CLI as a unified compilation target rather than a collection of scattered files, documentation drift becomes mechanically impossible: any type mismatch between code and metadata halts compilation before the binary ever reaches the terminal.

In cross-language ecosystems, this architectural consolidation extends directly into polyglot code generation. Maintaining separate parser implementations across multiple languages introduces a heavy synchronization tax, where client libraries diverge in their argument-parsing behavior. Template-driven code generation solves this by mapping the unified schema into client bindings and parallel parsers for diverse languages. Decision Rule: If scaling CLI tools across multi-language environments, never maintain decoupled wrapper parsers; mandate a single declarative schema to emit typed bindings, eliminating manual synchronization overhead entirely.

However, this schema-driven model encounters hard boundary conditions when applied to hyper-dynamic plugin architectures. Static schema compilation fails entirely when command parameters are runtime-evaluated—such as resource identifiers fetched dynamically from remote databases or live APIs during execution. Under these conditions, attempting to enforce static compile-time safety causes compilation deadlocks because the parameters do not yet exist in the source tree. The operational workaround requires trading compile-time safety for runtime flexibility by substituting static compilation targets with dynamic schema-introspection hooks, proving that while unified toolchains dominate static CLI design, complex runtime environments demand graceful fallback mechanisms.

title: How Do You Make a Bama Bound AI Clip Loop Without a Visible Jump? A Tail-to-Head Crossfade in ffmpeg, With a Seam Score
description:
Checked November 11, 2026. I build bamabound.app, which turns one photo of one person into a vertical clip of them holding a red I'M BAMA BOUND banner. The test clip in this post is synthetic (a red box swaying over a green field, with beeps), not a real person.

People ask some version of this a lot: "How do I make my Bama Bound video loop smoothly on my story / on a website / on a screen at a grad party?"

Players already repeat short videos. The problem is the moment where they do. A Bama Bound clip follows the reference timing of about eight seconds in a 9:16 frame, with the original soundtrack attached (FAQ). The last frame and the first frame were never meant to meet, so every repeat has a visible jump: the banner snaps from one side to the other, and the audio clicks.

This post fixes that with one ffmpeg graph and gives you a number to check the result instead of squinting.

The idea: crossfade the tail into the head

Split the clip into three parts:

| head (0..F) |          mid (F..D-F)          | tail (D-F..D) |

Then build a new clip: mid, followed by tail with head fading in on top of it. The output ends on the head's last frame, which is exactly where mid begins. So when the player jumps back to the start, frame N flows into frame N+1 of the original motion. No snap.

The cost is length: the output is D - F seconds. With F = 0.5, an 8 s clip becomes 7.5 s.

Audio gets the same treatment with acrossfade, so the beat doesn't click at the seam.

The script

Full file: loop_clip.py (Python 3, numpy, ffmpeg/ffprobe on PATH).

def make_loop(src, dst, fade):
    w, h, fps, dur = probe(src)
    body = dur - fade
    v = (f"[0:v]split=3[a][b][c];"
         f"[a]trim=0:{fade},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[head];"
         f"[b]trim={fade}:{body},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[mid];"
         f"[c]trim={body}:{dur},setpts=PTS-STARTPTS[tail];"
         f"[head]format=yuva420p,fade=t=in:st=0:d={fade}:alpha=1[hf];"
         f"[tail][hf]overlay=shortest=1[seam];"
         f"[mid][seam]concat=n=2:v=1:a=0,format=yuv420p[v]")
    if has_audio(src):
        v += (f";[0:a]asplit=3[x][y][z];"
              f"[x]atrim=0:{fade},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[ah];"
              f"[y]atrim={fade}:{body},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[am];"
              f"[z]atrim={body}:{dur},asetpts=PTS-STARTPTS[at];"
              f"[at][ah]acrossfade=d={fade}:c1=tri:c2=tri[as];"
              f"[am][as]concat=n=2:v=0:a=1[aout]")
    # then: ffmpeg -i src -filter_complex v -map [v] -map [aout] ... dst

Why not xfade?

My first version used xfade=transition=fade. It failed with:

The inputs needs to be a constant frame rate; current rate of 1/0 is invalid

After trim + setpts, the branches lose their frame-rate metadata, and xfade refuses them. Adding fps= up front didn't fix it either. Fading the head's alpha channel in and overlaying it on the tail does the same blend and doesn't care about frame-rate metadata. If you control your input, xfade works too, but the alpha version has been less fussy for me.

Measuring the seam

"Looks smooth to me" isn't a test. The script grabs the last frame and the first frame as grayscale arrays and reports the mean absolute pixel difference (0 = identical, 255 = opposite). It also reports the difference between two neighbouring frames in the middle of the clip, because that's the honest target: a good seam should look like any other frame step, not like a freeze.

def seam(path):
    w, h, fps, dur = probe(path)
    last = frame(path, max(dur - 1.5 / fps, 0), w, h)
    first = frame(path, 0, w, h)
    return float(np.abs(last - first).mean())

Results on a test clip

I ran it on two synthetic 480x854, 30 fps, 8 s clips: one with heavy film grain on the grass, one with no grain.

Clip Seam before Seam after (F=0.5 s) Normal frame step Length
grainy field 7.5 5.2 5.1 8.00 → 7.50 s
clean field 2.0 0.9 0.7 8.00 → 7.50 s

With F = 1.0 on the grainy clip, the seam was 4.5 and the clip 7.0 s.

Two things to notice:

  • The grainy "before" seam looks small (7.5) but the jump is real. Grain makes every frame differ by about 5, so the number only means something next to the normal frame step. That's why the script prints both.
  • After the crossfade, the seam lands right at the normal frame step (5.2 vs 5.1, 0.9 vs 0.7). That's the goal: the loop point stops being special.

Picking the fade length

  • 0.3 to 0.5 s is enough when the banner moves slowly at the start and end. You lose little length.
  • 1 s helps when the start and end poses are very different, but you'll see a soft double image of the banner for that second. For text that has to stay readable, that ghosting is worse than a tiny jump.
  • Don't go past about a quarter of the clip. You'd be cutting the part people came for.

Where a loop-ready file helps

  • A TV or laptop at a grad party, where a media player repeats the clip all night.
  • A website hero or a <video loop muted playsinline> embed.
  • A story that auto-replays while people read the caption.

TikTok, Reels and Shorts loop on their own. A seamless file just stops the repeat from looking like an edit.

What this doesn't do

  • It doesn't change the soundtrack's musical phrase. If the song is mid-word at 7.5 s, the crossfade blends two words. Listen once before posting.
  • It re-encodes (libx264 -crf 18). Keep your original download too.
  • It can't fix a clip that has a frozen or black lead-in from screen recording. Trim that first, then loop.

Prices, if you're making the clip itself

On the live pricing page today, one Bama Bound generation is $7.98 at 480p, $9.98 at 720p, $16.98 at 1080p and $24.98 at 4k, with tax added at checkout (pricing). There's no free tier and no subscription. Loop-ready output isn't a product feature, which is why this script exists.

And as always with this meme: it's a joke format, not an admission letter. The real Bama Bound is the University of Alabama's orientation program, which has nothing to do with it (about the meme).

title: Японское ударение в одной цифре: генерируем рисунок тона из словарной записи
description:
Японское ударение в одной цифре: генерируем рисунок тона из словарной записи

Если вы делаете карточки для Anki, словарь или тренажёр японского, рано или поздно захочется показывать ударение. В японском оно тональное: слоги различаются не громкостью, а высотой — высоко (H) или низко (L). Хорошая новость для разработчика: хранить для каждого слова таблицу H/L не нужно. В словарях ударение записывают одним числом, а рисунок из него восстанавливается в несколько строк кода.

Что означает число

Число — это номер моры, после которой тон падает:

  • 0 — хэйбан: тон поднимается после первой моры и не падает, даже на частице после слова;
  • 1 — атамадака: высокая только первая мора;
  • от 2 до n−1 — накадака: тон падает внутри слова;
  • n — одака (n — число мор): тон высокий до конца слова и падает на частице.

Классический пример — три слова «хаси»: 箸 (палочки) — [1], 橋 (мост) — [2], 端 (край) — [0]. Внутри слова 橋 и 端 звучат одинаково, LH, а различаются только тоном частицы: はしが.

Шаг 1: делим слово на моры

Мора — единица японского ритма. Каждый знак каны — одна мора, кроме маленьких ゃ, ゅ, ょ (и катаканных ャ, ュ, ョ, ァ, ィ, ゥ, ェ, ォ): они прилипают к предыдущему знаку. При этом っ, ん и ー — полноценные отдельные моры.

const toMoras = kana => kana.match(/.[ゃゅょャュョァィゥェォ]?/g) ?? [];

toMoras('きょう');   // ['きょ', 'う'] — 2 моры
toMoras('がっこう'); // ['が', 'っ', 'こ', 'う'] — 4 моры

Шаг 2: рисунок по числу 

// accent: 0 — хэйбан, 1 — атамадака, 2…n−1 — накадака, n — одака
function pitchPattern(kana, accent) {
  const moras = toMoras(kana);
  const word = moras.map((_, i) => {
    if (accent === 1) return i === 0 ? 'H' : 'L';
    if (i === 0) return 'L';                       // первая мора низкая
    return accent === 0 || i < accent ? 'H' : 'L'; // высоко до места падения
  });
  return { moras, word: word.join(''), particle: accent === 0 ? 'H' : 'L' };
}

pitchPattern('はし', 1);   // { word: 'HL',  particle: 'L' } — 箸, палочки
pitchPattern('はし', 2);   // { word: 'LH',  particle: 'L' } — 橋, мост
pitchPattern('はし', 0);   // { word: 'LH',  particle: 'H' } — 端, край
pitchPattern('こころ', 2); // { word: 'LHL', particle: 'L' } — 心, сердце

Отсюда уже легко нарисовать линию тона над словом в интерфейсе — так, как это делают словари ударений.

Где брать числа

  • OJAD (Online Japanese Accent Dictionary) — показывает рисунок тона для слов и целых фраз.
  • Словарь ударений NHK — стандарт для токийского произношения.
  • Викисловарь — в японских статьях часто указан номер ударения.

Ограничения

  • Это токийская норма. Кансайское произношение устроено иначе.
  • При спряжении глаголов и в сложных словах ударение смещается — одного числа из словаря для каждой формы недостаточно.
  • В живой речи подъём после первой моры бывает сглажен, особенно если вторая мора — ん, ー или っ.

Для учебного приложения этого обычно хватает: показать рисунок, дать послушать и повторить. Примеры с аудио и тренажёр, где ИИ оценивает произношение, собраны в разделе японское ударение на Japanese Zen.

title: Pygame Non-Blocking World Generation: Keep Menus Responsive
description:
I've put together a small Pygame snippet to address a common issue in games with procedurally generated worlds: keeping the main menu responsive during long world generation tasks. When a game's main loop handles extensive operations like world generation directly, the UI can freeze, leading to a poor user experience.

This snippet demonstrates a method for running the world generation process in a separate thread. By offloading this work, the main game loop remains free to process user input, render the main menu, and handle other immediate tasks. This prevents the application from appearing unresponsive while the world is being built in the background.

The code provides a basic example of how to set up and manage a separate thread for a computationally intensive task within a Pygame application. It's intended for developers who are building Pygame projects that involve significant setup time before gameplay can begin and want to maintain a smooth user interface during that period.

Pygame Non-Blocking World Generation

title: How to Analyse a Legacy Codebase Before Refactoring: A Developer's Guide
description:
Refactoring an existing application can be more challenging than building a new one.

When developers work with a legacy codebase, they often encounter outdated frameworks, undocumented business logic, tightly coupled modules and dependencies that are difficult to identify.

The biggest challenge is understanding how the application works before changing it.

A small modification in one module can affect several other components, particularly in enterprise applications with complex integrations.

In this guide, we will explore a practical approach to analyzing a legacy codebase before starting a refactoring project.

1. Start by Understanding the Project Structure

Before modifying any code, understand how the application is organized.

Start by examining:

  • Source code directories.
  • Application modules.
  • Configuration files.
  • Shared libraries.
  • Database connection settings.
  • API integrations.
  • Build and deployment files.

For example, a typical enterprise application might have the following structure:

banking-application/
│
├── src/
│   ├── authentication/
│   ├── customers/
│   ├── transactions/
│   └── payments/
│
├── config/
├── database/
├── integrations/
├── tests/
└── deployment/

Understanding this structure helps developers identify the main functional areas and locate important components.

2. Identify Dependencies Between Modules

One of the most important steps in legacy application analysis is dependency mapping.

A module rarely works independently. It may depend on shared services, databases, external APIs or other application components.

Start by examining:

  • Import statements and package dependencies.
  • API calls between services.
  • Database queries and stored procedures.
  • Shared libraries.
  • External integrations.
  • Background processing jobs.

Consider this simplified transaction workflow:

Customer Request
       |
       v
Authentication Service
       |
       v
Transaction Module
       |
       v
Payment Gateway
       |
       v
Transaction Database
       |
       v
Notification Service

Before modifying the transaction module, developers should understand how these components interact.

Dependency mapping helps identify the potential impact of changes.

3. Find Undocumented Business Logic

Legacy applications often contain business rules that are not properly documented.

These rules may exist inside:

  • Conditional statements.
  • Stored procedures.
  • Database triggers.
  • Configuration files.
  • Batch processing logic.
  • Custom application functions.

For example:

def calculate_transaction_fee(amount, customer_type):

    if customer_type == "premium":
        return amount * 0.01

    elif customer_type == "standard":
        return amount * 0.02

    return amount * 0.03

This simple example contains business logic that may affect other application workflows.

In larger applications, such rules may be distributed across multiple modules.

Before refactoring, developers should identify these rules and understand their expected behavior.

4. Assess Technical Debt

Technical debt accumulates as applications evolve.

Quick fixes, duplicated functionality, outdated dependencies and tightly coupled components can make applications difficult to maintain.

Look for common indicators:

Technical issue Potential impact
Duplicate code Difficult maintenance
Outdated libraries Compatibility and security concerns
Tight coupling Changes affect multiple modules
Complex functions Difficult debugging
Missing documentation Knowledge gaps
Unsupported frameworks Modernization challenges

Not every technical issue needs immediate attention.

Priorities issues based on application criticality, maintenance effort and business impact.

5. Analyze Application Behavior Before Making Changes

Source code does not always tell the complete story.

Runtime behavior, configurations, database interactions and scheduled processes may influence how an application operates.

Use a combination of:

  • Static code analysis.
  • Application logs.
  • Unit and integration tests.
  • Runtime dependency analysis.
  • Database inspection.
  • API monitoring.

This helps developers understand how the application behaves in real environments.

6. Use AI to Support Legacy Code Analysis

AI-assisted development tools can help developers understand unfamiliar codebases.

They can assist with:

  • Explaining complex functions.
  • Summarizing code modules.
  • Identifying potential dependencies.
  • Generating initial technical documentation.
  • Finding repeated code patterns.
  • Explaining unfamiliar programming constructs.

However, AI-generated explanations are not automatically accurate.

Developers should validate suggestions against the actual implementation, configuration, tests and runtime behavior.

AI should support engineering analysis, not replace engineering judgement.

7. Create a Refactoring Plan

Once the application has been analyzed, prepare a structured refactoring plan.

A practical checklist includes:

  • Identify critical application modules.
  • Document application dependencies.
  • Identify undocumented business rules.
  • Review third-party libraries.
  • Assess technical debt.
  • Identify high-risk components.
  • Establish regression test coverage.
  • Priorities refactoring activities.

This provides a clearer path for making changes without unnecessarily disrupting existing functionality.

8. Common Mistakes to Avoid

When working with legacy applications, avoid these common mistakes:

Rewriting without understanding: Replacing code before understanding existing functionality can introduce unexpected behavior.

Ignoring dependencies: A change in one component may affect several connected systems.

Trusting outdated documentation: Always validate documentation against the actual implementation.

Skipping regression testing: Existing functionality must be tested after refactoring.

Relying entirely on AI: AI-generated insights require technical validation and human oversight.

Conclusion

Legacy application refactoring requires more than improving code quality.

Developers need to understand application architecture, dependencies, business rules and technical debt before making significant changes.

A structured analysis approach helps reduce uncertainty, identify risks and establish a stronger foundation for application modernization.

title: Trending in self-hosting and Kubernetes: week of 10 November 2026
description:
Four things that picked up attention this week, with what we think of each. The originals are linked; read them. This page only tells you why they matter for a small self-hosted setup.

1. An empty resources: {} quietly downgrades your pods on Kubernetes 1.34 to 1.36

Original: An Empty resources: {} Makes Kubernetes 1.34 to 1.36 Pods BestEffort on devops-daily.com (also on dev.to).

The claim: if a pod sets spec.resources: {} at pod level, the kubelet classifies it as BestEffort even when every container has requests and limits. The authors measured it on k3s 1.34, 1.35 and 1.36: oom_score_adj jumped to 1000, and next to a busy neighbour a pod that requested half a CPU got 0.06 to 0.08 cores instead of about 0.57. A namespace quota that blocks BestEffort pods rejected it. On 1.37.1 the classes were correct. GitLab Runner's Kubernetes executor generates that empty block from version 18.10.0 to 19.4.3.
