title: FastAPI Fundamentals & Dependency Injection: Explained from Absolute Zero ⚡
description:
⚡ FastAPI Fundamentals & Dependency Injection: Let's Learn from ZERO!

Ever wondered how FastAPI receives requests, validates data, calls your Python functions, connects to databases, handles authentication, and organizes a real-world backend? 🤔

In this post we'll learn it all from scratch, with simple examples, real-life analogies, Python code, and folder structures. No prior backend knowledge needed! 🚀

1. 🤔 What exactly is FastAPI?

Imagine you're building Instagram. Your app has:

  • ⚛️ A React frontend
  • 🐍 A Python FastAPI backend
  • 🐘 A PostgreSQL database

A user clicks the Like button. What happens?

⚛️ Frontend (React)
   User clicks Like
        │  HTTP request
        ▼
⚡ Backend (FastAPI)
   Receives request, validates data, executes logic
        │  Database query
        ▼
🐘 PostgreSQL Database
   Stores the like information
        │
        ▼
⚡ FastAPI returns a response
   200 OK → { "message": "Post liked successfully" }

📌 FastAPI is a modern Python web framework used to build APIs. An API (Application Programming Interface) lets two software applications communicate.

FastAPI helps us:

  1. 🛣️ Create API endpoints
  2. 📥 Receive data from frontend applications
  3. ✔️ Validate incoming data
  4. 🧠 Execute business logic
  5. 🗄️ Communicate with databases
  6. 📤 Return responses in JSON
  7. 📖 Automatically generate API documentation 
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/")
def home():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}
  • from fastapi import FastAPI imports the FastAPI class
  • app = FastAPI() creates our application
  • @app.get("/") creates a GET endpoint at the root URL
  • def home() is the Python function that handles the request
  • return sends the response back to the client

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/ and you get:

{
  "message": "Hello World"
}

That's your first FastAPI endpoint! 🎉

2. 📬 Understanding API Parameters

When a frontend calls a backend, it often needs to send information:

  • Which post should we retrieve?
  • Which page of posts should we show?
  • What data should we save?
  • Which user is making the request?

FastAPI has three parameter types you need to know:

  1. 🛤️ Path parameters
  2. ❓ Query parameters
  3. 📦 Body parameters

2.1 🛤️ Path parameters

Values passed directly inside the URL path. You have 100 posts and want post number 25:

GET /posts/25

Here 25 is the path parameter, because it's part of the URL path itself.

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/posts/{post_id}")
def get_post(post_id: int):
    return {
        "post_id": post_id,
        "message": "Post retrieved",
    }
  • {post_id} is a dynamic placeholder
  • The actual value comes from the URL
  • FastAPI extracts it and passes it to your function

When you request GET /posts/25, FastAPI internally calls:

get_post(post_id=25)

Response:

{
  "post_id": 25,
  "message": "Post retrieved"
}

Notice we wrote post_id: int. What if somebody sends GET /posts/hello? FastAPI automatically validates the value. Since "hello" can't become an integer, it returns a validation error (HTTP 422). You don't write that validation yourself! ✨

Real-life examples: /users/10, /posts/25, /comments/100, /products/500.

🧠 Path parameters generally identify a particular resource.

2.2 ❓ Query parameters

Extra values passed after a ? in the URL. Want only 10 of your 100 posts?

GET /posts?limit=10
GET /posts?limit=10&skip=20
  • /posts = endpoint
  • ? = start of query parameters
  • limit=10 = a query parameter
  • & separates multiple query parameters 
@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(limit: int = 10, skip: int = 0):
    return {
        "limit": limit,
        "skip": skip,
    }

limit: int = 10 means limit should be an integer, and if the user doesn't provide it, use 10. Same idea for skip, defaulting to 0.

Request Response
GET /posts {"limit": 10, "skip": 0}
GET /posts?limit=5 {"limit": 5, "skip": 0}
GET /posts?limit=20&skip=40 {"limit": 20, "skip": 40}

Real-life uses:

Query parameter Purpose
?limit=10 Get 10 records
?page=2 Get page 2
?search=deepika Search for something
?sort=latest Sort by latest
?category=technology Filter by category

In a social feed, query parameters are perfect for pagination, filtering and searching, like GET /feed?limit=10&cursor=abc123.

2.3 📦 Body parameters (request body)

A user wants to create a new post and must send a caption, image URL and location. That data usually goes in the request body:

POST /posts

{
  "caption": "Beautiful evening!",
  "image_url": "https://example.com/image.jpg",
  "location": "Bengaluru"
}

from pydantic import BaseModel


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str
    image_url: str
    location: str


@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(post: PostCreate):
    return {
        "message": "Post created",
        "caption": post.caption,
    }
  • PostCreate is a Pydantic model
  • post: PostCreate tells FastAPI to expect request-body data matching that model
  • post.caption and post.image_url access the values

2.4 ⚖️ Path vs Query vs Body

Type Role Example Question it answers
🛤️ Path Identifies which resource GET /posts/25 Which post? Post 25
❓ Query Controls how we retrieve GET /posts?limit=10 How many posts? 10
📦 Body Carries data to create/update POST /posts + {"caption": "My new post"} What do we save? The caption

🧠 Quick rule: Path = which resource? · Query = how should we retrieve it? · Body = what data are we sending?

3. ✔️ Pydantic Models: Request and Response Schemas

Imagine your frontend sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": "twenty",
  "email": "not-an-email"
}

Age is a string instead of an integer, and the email isn't valid. Should your backend blindly accept that? Obviously not! We need a way to validate incoming data. Enter Pydantic.

3.1 🛂 What is Pydantic?

📌 Pydantic is a Python library for data validation and parsing. It checks whether incoming data follows the structure and rules we've defined.

Think of it as an airport security checkpoint ✈️: before passengers enter, their details are checked. Before request data reaches your business logic, Pydantic validates it.

3.2 🏗️ Creating a Pydantic model 

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int
    email: str

BaseModel is Pydantic's base class. We inherit from it to create a model.

Field Expected type
username String
age Integer
email String

3.3 ✅ Valid data arrives 

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": 22,
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

Pydantic validates it, creates a Python model object, and you access user.username, user.age, user.email.

3.4 ❌ Invalid data arrives 

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "age": "hello",
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

"hello" can't become an integer, so FastAPI automatically returns:

{
  "detail": [
    {
      "type": "int_parsing",
      "loc": ["body", "age"],
      "msg": "Input should be a valid integer"
    }
  ]
}

💡 FastAPI handles this request-validation error automatically. You don't write manual if checks for every field.

3.5 📏 Validation rules 

from pydantic import BaseModel, EmailStr, Field


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str = Field(min_length=3, max_length=20)
    age: int = Field(ge=18, le=100)
    email: EmailStr
  • min_length=3: username needs at least 3 characters
  • max_length=20: username can't exceed 20 characters
  • ge=18: age must be greater than or equal to 18
  • le=100: age must be less than or equal to 100
  • EmailStr: validates email format

📝 EmailStr requires the optional email-validator package.

3.6 🕳️ Optional fields and defaults 

class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    age: int
    bio: str | None = None
  • str | None means the value can be a string or absent/null
  • = None provides a default value

3.7 🔄 Request schemas vs Response schemas

🎯 A VERY important distinction in real backends!

A user creates an account and sends:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@example.com",
  "password": "secret123"
}

That's a request schema. But should we return the password? Absolutely not! 🙅 We return:

{
  "id": 101,
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

That's a response schema.

from pydantic import BaseModel


# Incoming data
class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str
    password: str


# Outgoing data
class UserResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    username: str
    email: str

Connect them in FastAPI:

@app.post("/users", response_model=UserResponse)
def create_user(user: UserCreate):
    return {
        "id": 101,
        "username": user.username,
        "email": user.email,
        "password": user.password,
    }

Even though the function returns a dict containing the password, the response_model filters the output to the fields in UserResponse. The client never sees the password. 🔐

Why separate request and response schemas?

  1. ✔️ Validate incoming data
  2. 🎛️ Control outgoing data
  3. 🔒 Prevent sensitive information from being exposed
  4. 📜 Maintain a clear API contract
  5. 🧹 Make code easier to maintain

Common naming conventions:

Model Purpose
UserCreate Incoming user creation data
UserUpdate Incoming user update data
UserResponse Outgoing user data
PostCreate Incoming post creation data
PostResponse Outgoing post data
LoginRequest Login credentials

4. 💉 Dependency Injection (DI): The MOST Important Concept!

Don't worry about the big name. Let's use a simple example.

4.1 🚨 First, the problem

Whenever a user views their feed, your backend needs a database:

def get_feed():
    db = connect_to_database()
    posts = db.get_posts()
    return posts

Now imagine 20 endpoints needing database access. Would you write db = connect_to_database() inside all 20 functions? That causes:

  1. 🔁 Repeated code
  2. 😩 Hard to maintain
  3. 🧪 Hard to test
  4. 🔌 Hard to manage database connections

What if one function provided the database connection whenever another function needed it? That's the basic idea of Dependency Injection.

4.2 🧩 What is a dependency?

📌 A dependency is something a function or class needs to do its work.

def get_feed(db):
    posts = db.get_posts()
    return posts

Here db is a dependency, because get_feed() depends on it. Other examples:

  • 🗄️ Database session
  • 👤 Authenticated user
  • ⚙️ Configuration settings
  • 📝 Logger
  • 🌍 External API client
  • ⚡ Cache connection

4.3 💉 What is Dependency Injection?

📌 Dependency Injection means: instead of creating everything a function needs by itself, we provide those things from outside.

❌ Without DI:

def get_feed():
    db = connect_to_database()
    return db.get_posts()

The function creates its own dependency.

✅ With DI:

def get_feed(db):
    return db.get_posts()

The dependency is provided from outside. This is more flexible. For example, during testing you can pass in a fake database instead of the real one. 🧪

4.4 🎯 What is Depends() in FastAPI?

FastAPI has a built-in function, Depends(), to declare dependencies:

from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


def get_database():
    return "Database connection"


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(db=Depends(get_database)):
    return {
        "database": db,
        "message": "Posts retrieved",
    }

get_database() is our dependency provider. Now the interesting part:

def get_posts(db=Depends(get_database)):

Depends(get_database) tells FastAPI: "Before executing get_posts(), run get_database() and inject its result into the db parameter."

Client sends GET /posts
        ▼
FastAPI sees Depends(get_database)
        ▼
Executes get_database()
        ▼
Injects the returned value into db
        ▼
Executes get_posts(db)
        ▼
Response returned

You never manually call get_database() inside get_posts(). FastAPI resolves it for you. That's the beauty of Depends()! ✨

4.5 🗄️ A practical example: database dependency

With PostgreSQL and SQLAlchemy, we create a database session provider:

from app.database import SessionLocal


def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
    finally:
        db.close()
  • db = SessionLocal() creates a new database session (a temporary working connection to the database)
  • yield db hands the session to the function that requested it
  • finally: db.close() closes the session after the request finishes, even if an exception occurs

🤔 Why yield instead of return? A generator dependency lets FastAPI run cleanup code after the request completes.

Now use it in an endpoint:

from fastapi import Depends
from sqlalchemy.orm import Session


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts(db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    posts = db.query(Post).all()
    return posts
  • db: Session is the expected SQLAlchemy session type
  • Depends(get_db) tells FastAPI how to provide it
  • db.query(Post).all() retrieves all Post records

We never created the session manually. FastAPI manages its lifecycle through the dependency.

📝 This is a simplified synchronous SQLAlchemy example. Async SQLAlchemy uses an async session and an async dependency.

4.6 🔐 DI for authentication

A user wants to create a post. Before allowing it we check: Is the user logged in? Is their token valid? Which user is this? Create a dependency:

def get_current_user():
    # Validate access token
    # Find user in database
    # Return authenticated user
    return current_user

Then use it:

@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(current_user=Depends(get_current_user)):
    return {
        "message": "Post created",
        "user": current_user.username,
    }

What happens:

  1. The client sends a request
  2. FastAPI sees Depends(get_current_user)
  3. It runs the authentication dependency
  4. The dependency validates the user's identity
  5. It returns the authenticated user
  6. FastAPI injects that user into current_user
  7. The endpoint executes

If authentication fails, the dependency can raise an HTTP 401 or 403, and the endpoint won't run normally. With 15 endpoints needing authentication, you reuse the same dependency instead of repeating token logic 15 times. ♻️

5. 🔄 Inversion of Control (IoC)

You understand DI, so IoC is easier now.

5.1 🤔 What is IoC?

📌 Inversion of Control means transferring the responsibility of managing something from your code to an external framework or system.

❌ Without IoC, you decide when to create the session, how to pass it, and when to close it:

def get_posts():
    db = create_database_session()
    try:
        return db.get_posts()
    finally:
        db.close()

✅ With IoC using FastAPI:

def get_posts(db=Depends(get_db)):
    return db.get_posts()

FastAPI manages dependency resolution and the cleanup lifecycle for the request. You simply declare what you need. Control has shifted from your endpoint to the framework. That's Inversion of Control. 🎛️

5.2 🔗 Relationship between IoC and DI

Concept Meaning
IoC The general principle of handing over control
DI A technique used to implement IoC
Depends() FastAPI's mechanism for declaring dependencies 
Inversion of Control (IoC)   → the general design principle
        ▼
Dependency Injection (DI)    → a way to achieve IoC
        ▼
FastAPI Depends()            → a built-in dependency mechanism

🎤 Interview-ready explanation

"Inversion of Control is a design principle where the responsibility of managing dependencies is transferred from our application code to the framework. In FastAPI, we achieve this using Dependency Injection through Depends(). For example, instead of manually creating database sessions inside every route, we declare Depends(get_db), and FastAPI resolves and manages the dependency."

6. 🗂️ APIRouter: Organizing API Endpoints

As your app grows, you might write everything in one file:

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/users")
def get_users():
    pass


@app.post("/users")
def create_user():
    pass


@app.get("/posts")
def get_posts():
    pass


@app.post("/posts")
def create_post():
    pass


@app.get("/comments")
def get_comments():
    pass

Imagine 100 endpoints in one file! 😵 We need to split them by responsibility. That's APIRouter.

6.1 🤔 What is APIRouter?

📌 APIRouter is a FastAPI class that organizes related endpoints into separate modules.

Think of dividing a company into departments: the user department handles users, the post department handles posts, the comment department handles comments, the auth department handles authentication.

6.2 📁 Recommended folder structure 

backend/
└── app/
    ├── api/
    │   ├── users.py       # User endpoints
    │   ├── posts.py       # Post endpoints
    │   └── comments.py    # Comment endpoints
    └── main.py            # Main application

6.3 🛠️ Creating a router

users.py:

from fastapi import APIRouter

router = APIRouter()


@router.get("/")
def get_users():
    return {"message": "All users"}


@router.get("/{user_id}")
def get_user(user_id: int):
    return {"user_id": user_id}


@router.post("/")
def create_user():
    return {"message": "User created"}

router = APIRouter() creates a separate router. Instead of @app.get("/") we write @router.get("/"), because these endpoints belong to the router, not directly to the main app.

6.4 🔌 Connecting the router to the main app

main.py:

from fastapi import FastAPI

from app.api import users

app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(
    users.router,
    prefix="/users",
    tags=["Users"],
)
  • include_router() registers the router with the main app
  • prefix="/users" means every endpoint in that router starts with /users
  • tags=["Users"] groups these endpoints under a Users section in Swagger docs
Router endpoint Final endpoint
@router.get("/") GET /users/
@router.get("/{user_id}") GET /users/{user_id}
@router.post("/") POST /users/

6.5 ✅ Why use APIRouter?

  1. 🧩 Modularity: separate related endpoints
  2. 🛠️ Maintainability: easier to modify code
  3. ♻️ Reusability: routers can be included in different apps
  4. 📖 Readability: easier for developers to understand
  5. 📈 Scalability: suitable for large backends

⚠️ Important: APIRouter does not create a separate server or application. It organizes routes inside one FastAPI application.

7. 📖 Automatic Interactive Documentation: Swagger UI and ReDoc

One of FastAPI's coolest features! You create 50 endpoints. How will your frontend developer know which endpoints exist, which methods they support, what parameters and request body they need, and what they return? You could write docs manually, but FastAPI generates them automatically! 🪄

7.1 🧪 Swagger UI

An interactive interface to explore and test your API. After starting your app, visit:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs

You can:

  1. View all endpoints
  2. Expand an endpoint
  3. See required parameters
  4. Enter request data
  5. Click Try it out
  6. Click Execute
  7. View the response and HTTP status code

You can test your backend without writing any frontend code! 🎉

7.2 📚 ReDoc

Another automatically generated documentation interface:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/redoc

It presents your API in a more reference-oriented, organized layout.

7.3 ⚖️ Swagger UI vs ReDoc

Feature Swagger UI ReDoc
URL /docs /redoc
Interactive testing Yes Primarily documentation-focused
API exploration Yes Yes
Layout Interactive interface Reference-style documentation
Generated automatically Yes Yes

Both are generated from FastAPI's OpenAPI schema.

7.4 📜 What is OpenAPI?

📌 OpenAPI is a standard specification that describes your API: available endpoints, HTTP methods, request parameters, request body schemas, response schemas and authentication requirements.

FastAPI generates it automatically at:

http://127.0.0.1:8000/openapi.json

Swagger UI and ReDoc read this schema to display the docs.

7.5 🪄 How does FastAPI generate docs automatically? 

@app.get("/posts/{post_id}")
def get_post(post_id: int):
    return {"post_id": post_id}

FastAPI understands the HTTP method (GET), the endpoint (/posts/{post_id}), the parameter name (post_id) and its type (integer). Likewise:

class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str
    image_url: str

FastAPI understands the request-body structure, and:

@app.post("/posts", response_model=PostResponse)

tells it the expected response schema. It collects all this into OpenAPI docs. That's why type hints and Pydantic models matter so much in FastAPI. 💡

8. 🎯 Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

SRP is one of the five SOLID principles of object-oriented design. Let's focus on just this one.

8.1 🤔 What is SRP?

📌 A function, class, or module should have one clear responsibility, or one reason to change.

Think of a restaurant 🍽️: the chef prepares food, the cashier handles payments, the waiter takes orders, the manager manages operations. If one person did everything, it'd be chaos. Similarly, we shouldn't put all backend responsibilities into one function.

8.2 ❌ The problem: without SRP 

@app.post("/posts")
def create_post(post: PostCreate):
    # Validate user
    # Connect to database
    # Check image URL
    # Create post in database
    # Send notification
    # Return response
    return {"message": "Post created"}

This function handles too many responsibilities:

  1. Receiving the HTTP request
  2. Validating user permissions
  3. Handling database operations
  4. Executing post creation logic
  5. Sending notifications
  6. Returning the HTTP response

Change notification logic? Modify this function. Change database logic? Modify it again. It becomes hard to maintain. 😩

8.3 ✅ Applying SRP: separate responsibilities 

🛣️ Router Layer      posts.py             Receives HTTP requests, reads parameters, calls services, returns responses
        ▼
🧠 Service Layer      post_service.py      Contains business logic and rules
        ▼
📚 Repository Layer   post_repository.py   Handles database operations (insert, update, retrieve)
        ▼
🗄️ Database           Stores application data

A. Router layer (posts.py)

@router.post("/")
def create_post(
    post: PostCreate,
    db: Session = Depends(get_db),
):
    return post_service.create_post(db, post)

Its job: receive the request, get the request data, obtain the database dependency, call the service, return the result. It doesn't need to know the internal business rules.

B. Service layer (post_service.py)

def create_post(db, post):
    if not post.caption:
        raise ValueError("Caption is required")

    return post_repository.create(db, post)

Its job: implement business rules, decide what should happen, coordinate the required operations (like checking whether a user is allowed to create a post).

C. Repository layer (post_repository.py)

def create(db, post):
    new_post = Post(caption=post.caption)

    db.add(new_post)
    db.commit()
    db.refresh(new_post)

    return new_post

Its job: talk to the database (insert, retrieve, update, delete).

Why is this better? If your database changes, you modify the repository layer without rewriting all your HTTP endpoints. If business rules change, you update the service layer. The app becomes easier to maintain and test. 🧪

📝 These layers are an architectural choice, not a mandatory FastAPI requirement. Small apps can have fewer layers. The key is to avoid mixing unrelated responsibilities.

9. 🧵 Putting Everything Together: A Real FastAPI Example

Let's build a mini Instagram backend with an endpoint to create posts.

backend/
└── app/
    ├── api/
    │   └── posts.py              # Routes
    ├── schemas/
    │   └── post.py               # Pydantic models
    ├── services/
    │   └── post_service.py       # Business logic
    ├── repositories/
    │   └── post_repository.py    # Database operations
    └── main.py                   # Application entry point

Step 1: create Pydantic schemas (schemas/post.py)

from pydantic import BaseModel


class PostCreate(BaseModel):
    caption: str


class PostResponse(BaseModel):
    id: int
    caption: str

Step 2: create the repository (repositories/post_repository.py)

def create_post(db, caption):
    new_post = {
        "id": 1,
        "caption": caption,
    }
    return new_post

📝 A simplified repository using a dictionary instead of a real SQLAlchemy database.

Step 3: create the service (services/post_service.py)

from app.repositories import post_repository


def create_post(db, post):
    return post_repository.create_post(db, post.caption)

Step 4: create the router (api/posts.py)

from fastapi import APIRouter, Depends

from app.schemas.post import PostCreate, PostResponse
from app.services import post_service

router = APIRouter()


def get_db():
    return "Database session"


@router.post("/", response_model=PostResponse)
def create_post(
    post: PostCreate,
    db=Depends(get_db),
):
    return post_service.create_post(db, post)

Step 5: connect the router (main.py)

from fastapi import FastAPI

from app.api import posts

app = FastAPI()

app.include_router(
    posts.router,
    prefix="/posts",
    tags=["Posts"],
)

Start the server:

uvicorn app.main:app --reload

Visit http://127.0.0.1:8000/docs, find POST /posts/, and send:

{
  "caption": "My first post!"
}

Expected response:

{
  "id": 1,
  "caption": "My first post!"
}

9.1 🔍 What happened internally?

  1. 🌐 Frontend sends the request: POST /posts/ with JSON data
  2. 🛣️ FastAPI identifies the route: it finds the matching endpoint in the posts router
  3. ✔️ Pydantic validates request data: checks that the caption is a string
  4. 💉 Dependency Injection happens: FastAPI sees Depends(get_db) and resolves the database dependency
  5. 🧠 Router calls the service: post_service.create_post(db, post)
  6. 📚 Service calls the repository: the repository performs the database operation
  7. 📤 Response model validates output: FastAPI uses PostResponse to validate and serialize the response
  8. 🔙 Response goes back to the frontend as JSON

This is how everything you've learned works together in a real backend. 🎯

10. 📋 Quick Revision: Everything at a Glance

Concept What it does Example
FastAPI Python framework for APIs FastAPI()
Path parameter Identifies a resource /posts/10
Query parameter Filters or controls retrieval ?limit=10
Body parameter Sends structured data JSON request body
Pydantic Validates and parses data BaseModel
Request schema Defines incoming data PostCreate
Response schema Defines outgoing data PostResponse
Depends() Injects dependencies Depends(get_db)
IoC Transfers control to a framework FastAPI manages dependency resolution
APIRouter Organizes endpoints APIRouter()
Swagger UI Interactive API testing /docs
ReDoc API documentation /redoc
SRP One clear responsibility per component Separate router and service

11. 🎤 Interview Questions

1. What is FastAPI?
A modern Python web framework used to build APIs. It supports automatic request validation, dependency injection, asynchronous programming and automatic API documentation.

2. What's the difference between path and query parameters?
Path parameters identify a particular resource, whereas query parameters provide additional filtering, sorting or pagination information.

3. What is Pydantic?
A Python data validation library. It validates incoming data based on the types and rules defined in our models.

4. Why do we need separate request and response schemas?
Request schemas validate incoming data, while response schemas control the structure of outgoing data and prevent unwanted fields, such as passwords, from being exposed.

5. What is Dependency Injection?
A technique where required objects or services are provided to a function from outside instead of the function creating them internally.

6. What is Depends() in FastAPI?
FastAPI's built-in mechanism for declaring dependencies. FastAPI resolves them and injects their results into endpoint functions.

7. What is Inversion of Control?
A design principle where control over certain operations is transferred from application code to a framework or external component. FastAPI implements this through dependency injection.

8. What is APIRouter?
It organizes related API endpoints into separate modules, making large applications modular and maintainable.

9. What's the difference between Swagger UI and ReDoc?
Swagger UI provides an interactive interface for exploring and testing APIs. ReDoc provides a documentation-focused interface.

10. What is SRP?
The Single Responsibility Principle says a component should have one clear responsibility. In FastAPI, we apply it by separating route handling, business logic and database operations.

12. 🧪 Test Yourself!

Try these before peeking at the answers! ❤️

  1. You want to retrieve post number 50 using /posts/50. What type of parameter is 50?

    • A) Query parameter
    • B) Path parameter
    • C) Body parameter

  2. Which library validates incoming request data using BaseModel?

    • A) SQLAlchemy
    • B) Uvicorn
    • C) Pydantic

  3. What does Depends(get_db) do?

    • A) Deletes the database
    • B) Asks FastAPI to provide a database dependency
    • C) Creates a new API endpoint

  4. Which component organizes related API endpoints?

    • A) APIRouter
    • B) BaseModel
    • C) ReDoc

  5. Where can you interactively test your FastAPI endpoints by default?

    • A) /redoc
    • B) /openapi.json
    • C) /docs

  6. Which layer should contain business logic?

    • A) Router
    • B) Service
    • C) Frontend

👀 Click to reveal answers
  1. B: 50 is part of the URL path, so it's a path parameter
  2. C: Pydantic validates data using BaseModel
  3. B: It asks FastAPI to resolve and inject the get_db dependency
  4. A: APIRouter groups related endpoints
  5. C: /docs opens Swagger UI for interactive testing
  6. B: The service layer holds business logic

13. 🧭 What to Remember in Your Own Backend

When you open your own FastAPI project, try to identify:

  • 🛣️ api/: where are the routes?
  • ✔️ schemas/: what request and response structures are defined?
  • 🧠 services/: where is the business logic?
  • 📚 repositories/: where are database operations performed?
  • 💉 Depends(): how are dependencies provided?
  • 🗂️ APIRouter: how are endpoints grouped?
  • 🚪 main.py: where are routers registered and the app created?

Once you can spot these in real code, you'll understand how a professional FastAPI backend is structured instead of just memorizing definitions.

🚀 What's Next?

Pick one endpoint and trace its complete flow: frontend request → router → dependency → service → repository → database → response. That's far more valuable than memorizing 50 definitions. 💡

If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend learning FastAPI. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨

title: What Is React? Explained Simply for Beginners
description:
Originally published on CodingCush.

React is a free JavaScript library for building user interfaces, the parts of a website or app that people actually see and click. Instead of writing one giant page of code, you build small reusable pieces called components, like buttons, cards, menus and forms, and React puts them together on the screen. You describe what the screen should look like, and React updates it automatically when your data changes. That simple idea is why React powers so many modern websites, from small blogs to huge social networks.

A Short History: Where Did React Come From?

React was created by Meta, the company behind Facebook and Instagram. Engineers there were struggling to keep a fast-growing interface in sync, and updating everything by hand was slow and full of bugs. React was released in 2013, and other developers quickly adopted it.

Today React is open source, so anyone can use it for free. A huge community builds tools and tutorials around it, so when you get stuck, someone has almost certainly solved the same problem before.

The Big Idea: Components

Think of a page like Lego bricks. A header is one brick, a product card another, a footer another. In React, each brick is a component: a small JavaScript function that returns markup for that piece.

Components are reusable. Build a Button once and use it ten times with different text and colours. Build a ProductCard once and show fifty products without copying fifty blocks of HTML. Change the component in one place, and every copy updates.

If this idea is new to you, our guide to React components, props and state walks through it slowly with more examples, so keep that open in another tab while you practise.

Your First React Component

Here is a tiny but complete React component. It shows a greeting and a button that counts how many times you click it:

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

  return (
    <div>
      <h2>Hello from React!</h2>
      <p>You clicked {count} times.</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(count + 1)}>
        Click me
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}

export default Counter;

The function returns markup that looks like HTML. The {count} part inserts a JavaScript value into that markup. When you click the button, setCount changes the value, and React redraws just that piece with the new number. You never wrote code to find and rewrite the paragraph by hand.

That strange HTML-inside-JavaScript syntax has a name: JSX. JSX lets you write markup inside your JavaScript files, which feels odd for about a day and then feels completely natural. Under the hood, tools convert JSX into regular JavaScript before the browser runs it.

The official React documentation (react.dev) — the Quick Start page creates a first component in a few lines.

Props and State: Passing Data and Remembering Things

Two words you will hear every day in React are props and state. Props are inputs passed from a parent component to a child, like passing ingredients to a chef. A ProductCard might receive a name, a price and an image as props, and simply display them. Props flow one way, from parent to child, which makes data easy to follow.

State is data a component remembers and can change: whether a menu is open, what a user typed, or the click count above. When state changes, React re-renders the component. Props are given to a component; state is owned by it.

The best way to learn both is by building. The official tutorial at react.dev/learn teaches components, props and state step by step with interactive examples you can edit in the browser, so you see results instantly without installing anything.

Declarative UI: Describe the Result, Not the Steps

React uses a declarative style. Declarative means you describe what the interface should look like for a given state, instead of listing every step to change it. Compare these two approaches for a loading spinner. In plain JavaScript you might write: find the spinner element, show it, find the button, disable it, and later remember to reverse all of that. In React you write something like: if loading is true, show the spinner and disable the button.

Your code becomes a description of the screen at any moment, rather than a diary of changes. That makes interfaces easier to predict and debug: when something looks wrong, you check the state, because the screen is simply a reflection of it.

What Is the Virtual DOM?

You will often hear that React is fast because of the virtual DOM. Here is the plain version. The DOM is the browser's live model of your page. Changing it directly, again and again, can be slow. React keeps a lightweight copy of the page structure in memory, called the virtual DOM.

When state changes, React updates this copy, compares it with the previous copy, and applies only the smallest real changes to the actual page. If one price on a page of fifty products changes, React updates that one price instead of rebuilding the whole list.

React vs Plain JavaScript

React is still JavaScript, so why not skip it? For tiny pages, plain JavaScript is perfectly fine. As an app grows, though, keeping the screen and the data in sync by hand becomes painful. This table sums up the difference:

Feature Plain JavaScript React
Building the UI You create and update elements manually You build reusable components
Updating the screen You find elements and change them yourself React updates the screen when state changes
Reusing code Copy and paste, or custom functions Components are reused by design
Code organisation Can get messy in large apps Each component keeps its markup and logic together
Learning curve Nothing extra to learn Needs JSX, props, state and hooks
Best for Small pages and simple effects Interactive apps with lots of changing data

Neither side wins everywhere. React earns its place when an interface has many moving parts that depend on shared, changing data.

Where Is React Used?

React runs parts of Facebook, Instagram and countless dashboards, shops and streaming sites. Companies like it because it is fast, well supported and easy to hire for.

React also reaches beyond the browser. React Native uses the same component ideas to build real mobile apps for Android and iOS, so learning React opens a door to app development too. Frameworks such as Next.js build on top of React, adding routing, server rendering and better search engine support for public websites. You can explore what the library offers on the homepage at react.dev, which links to the docs, the blog and the community resources.

Who Should Learn React, and What Comes First?

Learn React if you want to build modern web apps, apply for front-end jobs, or create projects like dashboards and online stores. Job listings ask for React constantly.

But do not start with React on day one. First learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript, especially functions, arrays, objects and methods like map and filter. Weak JavaScript makes React feel twice as hard. Our step-by-step beginner roadmap for learning React lays out the order to follow, week by week.

A good first project is a to-do list, a weather app using a free API, or a small shop page with a working cart. Keep projects small and finish them. Finishing beats perfect, every single time.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is React a language or a framework?

React is a JavaScript library, not a language and, strictly speaking, not a full framework. It focuses on the user interface. You add other tools for routing, data fetching and styling as your app needs them, or use a framework like Next.js that bundles those choices for you.

Is React hard for beginners?

React is beginner-friendly if your JavaScript basics are ready. JSX and state take a few days to feel normal. Most confusion comes from shaky JavaScript, not from React itself, so strengthen functions, arrays and objects first and React will click much faster.

Is React free to use?

Yes. React is completely free and open source under the MIT licence. You can use it for personal projects, client work and commercial products without paying anything, and the official documentation and community resources are free as well.

Can I build mobile apps with React?

Yes, through React Native. It uses React components and JavaScript to build genuine Android and iOS apps from one codebase. The concepts you learn for the web, like components, props and state, transfer directly, which makes it a popular next step after web React.

Conclusion

React is a JavaScript library for building interfaces from small, reusable components. You describe what the screen should look like, keep changing data in state, pass data down with props, and let React update the page efficiently for you. Learn HTML, CSS and JavaScript first, then build tiny projects one at a time. Start small today, and the components will soon start making sense.

title: Python Packaging & Environment Config for Services: venv, Poetry, pip-tools, Pydantic Settings & 12-Factor Explained 🐍
description:
🐍 Python Packaging & Environment Config for Services: Let's Learn from ZERO!

When you build a backend service (for example a FastAPI social-feed app), writing Python code is only one part of the job. You also need to know:

  • 📦 How to manage packages and dependencies
  • 🏠 How to create and manage virtual environments
  • 🔐 How to configure a service without hardcoding values
  • 🗂️ How to organize a professional backend project
  • 🌍 How to manage development, testing and production environments
  • 🧭 How to follow the 12-factor app principles

I'll explain what each concept means, why we need it, how it works, and give practical examples. Let's go! 🚀

1. 🖼️ The Big Picture

Imagine you're building an Instagram-like backend with FastAPI. It needs:

  • ⚡ FastAPI to create APIs
  • 🗄️ SQLAlchemy to talk to PostgreSQL
  • ✔️ Pydantic to validate data
  • 🦄 Uvicorn to run the app
  • 🔄 Alembic for database migrations
  • 🧪 pytest to test the app

These are all external Python packages. But then:

  • ❓ How does Python know which packages your project needs?
  • ❓ How do we make sure your teammate's laptop and the production server use compatible versions?
  • ❓ How do we configure database URLs and secret keys without putting them in code?

That's exactly what Python packaging and environment configuration solve.

Your Python Service (FastAPI backend)
        │
        ├── 📦 Packaging        → Poetry / pip-tools  → Dependencies
        ├── 🔐 Configuration    → Pydantic Settings   → Environment variables
        └── 🗂️ Project Structure → app/ · tests/ · alembic/ · pyproject.toml
                  │
                  ▼
   ✅ Reliable Service: Development → Testing → Production

📦 PART 1: Python Packaging

2. 🤔 What is Python packaging?

A package is reusable code written by someone else (or by you) that you can install and use.

Package Purpose
FastAPI Build APIs
SQLAlchemy Work with databases
Pydantic Validate data
Uvicorn Run ASGI applications
pytest Test Python code
Alembic Manage database migrations
pydantic-settings Manage application configuration

Instead of writing all this yourself, you install existing packages:

pip install fastapi

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()

📌 Python packaging is the process of organizing, declaring, managing and distributing your project's dependencies and metadata. In simple words: it tells Python what your project needs and how those requirements should be installed.

3. 🔗 What are dependencies?

A dependency is something your project needs in order to work correctly.

from fastapi import FastAPI
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

This project depends on FastAPI and SQLAlchemy. Without them you'd get:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'fastapi'

🧩 Two types of dependencies

1️⃣ Direct dependencies: packages your project explicitly uses (fastapi, sqlalchemy, pydantic).

2️⃣ Transitive dependencies: packages your direct dependencies need internally.

Your application
    │
    └── FastAPI              (direct dependency)
          │
          └── Starlette      (transitive dependency)
                │
                └── other internal dependencies

You never installed Starlette directly, but it arrives because FastAPI needs it.

🚨 Why is dependency management important?

You develop with FastAPI 0.115. Your teammate installs the latest version, which changed something. Now:

  • ✅ Your code works on your laptop
  • ❌ Your teammate's code breaks
  • ❓ The production server behaves differently

That's the dependency/version consistency problem. We solve it with tools like Poetry and pip-tools.

🏠 PART 2: Virtual Environments

4. 🤔 What is a virtual environment (venv)?

Two projects, different needs:

Project FastAPI SQLAlchemy
🅰️ Project A 0.100 2.0
🅱️ Project B 0.115 2.0

If you install everything into one global Python, packages conflict. 💥

📌 A virtual environment is an isolated Python environment for one project. Think of a separate room 🚪 for each project, each with its own installed packages.

Project A → Environment A → FastAPI 0.100, SQLAlchemy 2.0
Project B → Environment B → FastAPI 0.115, SQLAlchemy 2.0

🛠️ How to create one

Open a terminal inside your project folder (social-feed/).

Step 1: create it

python -m venv .venv
Part Meaning
python Run Python
-m Run a Python module
venv Use Python's built-in virtual environment module
.venv Name of the environment folder

Step 2: activate it

Windows PowerShell:

.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1

Windows Command Prompt:

.venv\Scripts\activate.bat

macOS / Linux:

source .venv/bin/activate

You'll see (.venv) in your prompt. ✅

Step 3: install packages

pip install fastapi uvicorn sqlalchemy

Step 4: deactivate

deactivate

📥 What is pip?

pip is Python's package installer:

pip install fastapi      # install
pip uninstall fastapi    # uninstall
pip list                 # list installed packages
pip show fastapi         # details about one package

🧠 venv creates an isolated environment. pip installs packages into it. They solve two different problems.

🧰 PART 3: Dependency Management Tools

5. 🎭 What is Poetry?

📌 Poetry is a Python dependency management and packaging tool. Think of it as a project manager for your packages.

It helps you:

  1. Add and install dependencies
  2. Manage package versions
  3. Create and manage virtual environments
  4. Maintain dependency lock files
  5. Build and package Python projects

Why Poetry when pip exists? pip installs packages, but managing a whole project's dependencies and reproducible installs takes extra work. Poetry combines several tasks into one workflow.

🚀 Create a project with Poetry

Step 1: install Poetry using the official installation guide.

Step 2: create a project

poetry new social-feed

social-feed/
│
├── pyproject.toml
├── README.md
├── social_feed/
│   └── __init__.py
└── tests/
    └── __init__.py

Step 3: add dependencies

poetry add fastapi
poetry add sqlalchemy
poetry add uvicorn

Poetry automatically updates pyproject.toml and the lock file.

Step 4: add development dependencies (needed while developing/testing, not for running the app)

poetry add --group dev pytest
poetry add --group dev ruff
  • 🧪 pytest is for testing
  • 🧹 ruff is for linting and code quality

Step 5: install everything

poetry install

Step 6: run commands inside Poetry's environment

poetry run pytest

📄 What is pyproject.toml?

The standard configuration file of modern Python projects. It can contain the project name, version, Python version requirement, dependencies, dev dependencies, build system info, and tool configurations.

[tool.poetry]
name = "social-feed"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "A social media backend"
authors = ["Developer"]

[tool.poetry.dependencies]
python = "^3.12"
fastapi = "^0.115"
sqlalchemy = "^2.0"
uvicorn = "^0.30"

[tool.poetry.group.dev.dependencies]
pytest = "^8.0"
ruff = "^0.9"
Configuration Meaning
name Project name
version Project version
python Supported Python version
fastapi Application dependency
pytest Development dependency

📝 fastapi = "^0.115" allows compatible versions under Poetry's caret rules. It does not mean exactly 0.115 is always installed.

🔒 What is poetry.lock?

When Poetry resolves your dependencies, it creates poetry.lock, which records the exact resolved versions:

fastapi = 0.115.6
starlette = 0.41.3
pydantic = 2.10.4

(These versions are illustrative.)

If you and your teammate have the same lock file, you both install the same resolved versions instead of independently getting different ones. 🎯

Useful commands:

poetry install          # install from project config + lock file
poetry update           # update within allowed constraints, refresh lock file
poetry show             # display installed/resolved packages
poetry add requests     # add a dependency
poetry remove requests  # remove a dependency

🧠 pyproject.toml = the dependencies and constraints you want. poetry.lock = the exact resolution. For an application, commit both to Git.

6. 🔧 What is pip-tools?

📌 pip-tools works alongside pip. It helps you keep a clean list of direct requirements and generate a fully pinned requirements file.

It provides two commands: pip-compile and pip-sync.

🤔 Why do we need it?

Your project directly needs fastapi, sqlalchemy, uvicorn, but those have their own dependencies. You want a file with the exact versions of everything. pip-compile generates it.

🪜 Step-by-step workflow

Step 1: install

pip install pip-tools

Step 2: create requirements.in (your human-maintained list of direct dependencies)

fastapi
sqlalchemy
uvicorn

Step 3: compile

pip-compile requirements.in

This generates requirements.txt, for example (simplified):

fastapi==0.115.6
sqlalchemy==2.0.36
uvicorn==0.34.0
starlette==0.41.3

The real output also includes transitive dependencies, and can include hashes when configured.

Step 4: sync

pip-sync requirements.txt
File Purpose
requirements.in Human-maintained list of direct dependencies
requirements.txt Compiled, pinned dependency list
  • pip-compile reads your declarations, resolves compatible versions, and produces a pinned file
  • pip-sync makes the active environment match the compiled file by installing missing packages and uninstalling packages not listed

⚔️ Poetry vs pip-tools

Feature Poetry 🎭 pip-tools 🔧
Dependency management Yes Yes
Virtual environments Built-in support Uses venv or another tool
Dependency lock poetry.lock Compiled requirements.txt
Add dependencies poetry add Edit the .in file
Install poetry install pip-sync
Build/package support Yes Not its main purpose
Workflow Integrated tool pip-based workflow
  • Poetry: you want an integrated project + dependency workflow
  • pip-tools: your team prefers the traditional pip + requirements.txt ecosystem but wants reliable locking

⚠️ Choose one primary dependency workflow per project. Don't maintain conflicting lock systems.

🔐 PART 4: Configuration Management

7. 🤔 What is application configuration?

Your FastAPI backend connects to PostgreSQL:

postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/social_feed

It also needs a database URL, secret key, API port, debug mode, CORS allowed origins, and session expiry duration. These are configuration values. They tell your app how to behave in a particular environment.

🚫 Why shouldn't we hardcode configuration? 

DATABASE_URL = "postgresql://root:password123@localhost:5432/social_feed"

What's wrong?

  1. 🔓 Security: the password sits in your source code. Push it to GitHub and someone may see it.
  2. 🌍 Environment differences: development uses localhost:5432/social_feed_dev, production uses production-server:5432/social_feed. You don't want to edit source code on every deploy.
  3. 🛠️ Maintenance: if the password changes, you'd have to modify the code.

✅ The solution: environment variables

📌 An environment variable is a named value provided to a running process by its environment.

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/social_feed

import os

database_url = os.getenv("DATABASE_URL")

Same code, different configuration

Development                 Production
DATABASE_URL=localhost      DATABASE_URL=cloud-db
DEBUG=true                  DEBUG=false
        │                           │
        └──────────┬────────────────┘
                   ▼
     Same Python application, no source-code changes ✨

8. ⚡ What is Pydantic Settings?

You know Pydantic validates data:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class User(BaseModel):
    name: str
    age: int

User(name="Deepika", age="twenty") raises a validation error. But what if we want to validate our application's configuration?

  • Is DATABASE_URL provided?
  • Is DEBUG a valid boolean?
  • Is SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS a valid integer?
  • Is the secret key available?

📌 Pydantic Settings is a library built on Pydantic that loads, validates and manages application settings from environment variables and other supported sources.

Step 1: install

pip install pydantic-settings

Step 2: create settings.py

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    DATABASE_URL: str
    SECRET_KEY: str
    DEBUG: bool = False
    SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS: int = 7

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        extra="ignore",
    )

Line by line:

Line Meaning
BaseSettings Base class that lets your class load values from environment variables
DATABASE_URL: str Must be a string. No default, so it's required
SECRET_KEY: str Also required
DEBUG: bool = False Boolean, defaults to False
SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS: int = 7 Integer, defaults to 7
env_file=".env" Also load values from a .env file
extra="ignore" Ignore extra entries that aren't defined as fields

Step 3: create a .env file in your project root

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/social_feed
SECRET_KEY=my-super-secret-key
DEBUG=true
SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS=7

Step 4: create a settings object

settings = Settings()

What happens:

  1. Pydantic Settings looks for the values
  2. It reads environment variables and the configured .env file
  3. It converts values to the required types where valid
  4. It validates required fields
  5. It creates the settings object 
print(settings.DATABASE_URL)
print(settings.DEBUG)                # True  (converted from "true")
print(settings.SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS)  # 7    (converted from "7")

💥 What if a required value is missing?

Remove SECRET_KEY and run Settings(). Pydantic raises a validation error, because SECRET_KEY is required and has no default.

That's good! 🎉 Instead of starting with incomplete configuration, the app fails early and tells you what's missing. This is called fail-fast configuration validation.

Step 5: use settings across your app

app/config.py:

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    DATABASE_URL: str
    SECRET_KEY: str
    DEBUG: bool = False

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        extra="ignore",
    )


settings = Settings()

In another file:

from app.config import settings

print(settings.DATABASE_URL)

Now every part of your app reads from one centralized configuration.

🔄 The configuration flow 

.env file / environment variables
        │   DATABASE_URL, SECRET_KEY, DEBUG
        ▼
Pydantic Settings   → reads, converts and validates values
        ▼
Settings object     → settings.DATABASE_URL
        ▼
Application components → database, security, API, services

⚖️ Environment variable vs .env file

Environment variable .env file
A variable supplied to a running process A text file containing key-value pairs
Can be set by the OS, shell or hosting platform Commonly used for local development
Exists in the process environment Must be loaded by an app or library
Doesn't require a physical file Is a physical file

📝 Pydantic Settings gives environment variables higher priority than .env values. So a production environment variable can override a local file value.

🛡️ Security rule

🚨 Never commit your real .env file containing passwords and secrets to GitHub.

.gitignore:

.env
.venv/
__pycache__/
.pytest_cache/

Instead, commit a .env.example so teammates know which settings they need, without exposing secrets:

DATABASE_URL=
SECRET_KEY=
DEBUG=false
SESSION_EXPIRE_DAYS=7

For production, use your hosting provider's environment-variable or secret-management facility.

🗂️ PART 5: Standard Python Service Project Layout

9. 🤔 What is project structure?

Imagine your whole backend lives in one main.py: routes, database connections, authentication, business logic, queries, configuration, even tests. It works at first, but as the project grows the file becomes huge and unmaintainable. 😵

Professional apps separate responsibilities into folders and files. That's a project layout.

10. 🏗️ Recommended FastAPI service structure 

social-feed/
│
├── app/                    # Main application code
│   ├── api/                # API routes and endpoints
│   ├── models/             # Database models
│   ├── schemas/            # Request/response validation
│   ├── services/           # Business logic
│   ├── repositories/       # Database access logic
│   ├── common/             # Shared utilities and exceptions
│   ├── config.py           # Application configuration
│   ├── database.py         # Database connection
│   └── main.py             # FastAPI entry point
│
├── tests/                  # Automated tests
│   ├── test_auth.py
│   ├── test_feed.py
│   └── test_users.py
│
├── alembic/                # Database migrations
│   ├── versions/
│   ├── env.py
│   └── script.py.mako
│
├── pyproject.toml          # Project and tool configuration
├── poetry.lock             # Locked dependency versions
├── alembic.ini             # Alembic configuration
├── README.md               # Project documentation
├── .env                    # Local configuration (NOT committed)
└── .gitignore              # Files Git should ignore

Let's understand each part. 👇

10.1 📁 app/: the main application folder

Where your actual backend code lives (main.py, config.py, database.py, and the sub-folders).

10.2 🛣️ api/: API routes

An API route defines how your backend responds to HTTP requests:

@router.get("/users")
def get_users():
    return {"message": "All users"}
  • @router.get defines a GET endpoint
  • /users is the endpoint path
  • The function runs when a matching request arrives 
api/
    routes/
        auth.py
        users.py
        posts.py
        feed.py

Each file handles a group of endpoints.

10.3 🗄️ models/: database models

A model describes a database table using Python classes (with an ORM like SQLAlchemy):

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"

    id = Column(Integer, primary_key=True)
    username = Column(String)
    email = Column(String)

🧠 Models = how data is stored in the database.

10.4 ✔️ schemas/: data validation

Schemas define the structure of incoming and outgoing data:

from pydantic import BaseModel


class UserCreate(BaseModel):
    username: str
    email: str

A registration request might contain:

{
  "username": "deepika",
  "email": "deepika@example.com"
}

🧠 Models = database structure. Schemas = API data structure and validation. They are not the same thing!

10.5 🧠 services/: business logic

Where the application rules live. Imagine a user wants to follow another user. The service checks:

  1. Does the target user exist?
  2. Is the user trying to follow themselves?
  3. Does the follow relationship already exist?
  4. If all valid, create the follow relationship 
def follow_user(current_user, target_user):
    if current_user.id == target_user.id:
        raise ValueError("Cannot follow yourself")

    # Follow business logic goes here

🧠 Services = what the application should do.

10.6 📚 repositories/: database access

A repository is the layer that talks to the database:

def get_user_by_id(db, user_id):
    return db.query(User).filter(User.id == user_id).first()

🧠 Repository = how we retrieve or store data. Service = why and when we do it. This separation makes code easier to test and maintain.

10.7 🧰 common/: shared utilities

Reusable code used in many places:

common/
    exceptions.py
    security.py
    responses.py
    pagination.py

10.8 ⚙️ config.py: configuration

Defines and loads application settings. Other modules import the settings object instead of reading environment variables independently.

10.9 🔌 database.py: database connection

Typically contains the engine, the session factory, session management and the ORM base class:

from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker

engine = create_engine(settings.DATABASE_URL)

SessionLocal = sessionmaker(
    bind=engine,
    autoflush=False,
)

10.10 🚪 main.py: application entry point 

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/health")
def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy"}

Start it with:

uvicorn app.main:app --reload
  • uvicorn: the ASGI server
  • app.main: the main.py module inside the app package
  • app: the FastAPI application object
  • --reload: auto-reload when code changes (development)

10.11 🧪 tests/: testing 

def test_addition():
    assert 2 + 3 == 5

For a backend: test_auth.py, test_posts.py, test_feed.py, test_database.py. Run them with:

pytest

10.12 🔄 alembic/: database migrations

A database migration is a controlled change to the database schema. Say your users table has id, username, email, and later you want to add profile_picture. Instead of changing the database manually:

alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add profile picture"
alembic upgrade head

🧠 Alembic = version control for database schema changes.

11. 🔗 How all the folders work together

A user sends GET /posts/101:

1. 🌐 Client sends HTTP request       GET /posts/101
        ▼
2. 🛣️ API layer                       receives the request, identifies the endpoint
        ▼
3. 🧠 Service layer                   applies business rules
        ▼
4. 📚 Repository layer                fetches the post from the database
        ▼
5. 🗄️ Database                        returns post information
        ▼
6. ✔️ Schema / API response           formats and validates the response

{
  "id": 101,
  "caption": "Beautiful day!",
  "username": "deepika"
}

Each folder has one specific responsibility. That's why professional projects are structured this way. 🎯

📝 PART 6: Config as Code

12. 🤔 What is Config as Code?

📌 Config as Code means defining and managing application configuration through structured, version-controlled code or configuration files, rather than manually changing settings in different places.

Instead of scattering this through your code:

if environment == "production":
    database = "production_db"
else:
    database = "development_db"

centralize it:

class Settings(BaseSettings):
    DATABASE_URL: str
    DEBUG: bool = False
    SECRET_KEY: str

✅ Why is this useful?

  1. 🤝 Consistency: everyone follows the same configuration structure
  2. 🛠️ Maintainability: change configuration without editing many files
  3. 🌍 Environment separation: development, testing and production can use different settings
  4. ✔️ Validation: Pydantic checks the values
  5. 📖 Documentation: the settings class tells developers what the app expects

⚖️ Config as Code vs hardcoding

Hardcoding Config as Code
Values written directly in application logic Values are centralized
Changing values may require source changes Values can come from the environment
Secrets may accidentally enter Git Secrets can be supplied externally
Harder to manage environments Easier to manage environments

⚠️ Important: Config as Code does NOT mean putting every secret into a Python file and pushing it to GitHub. It means managing the configuration structure systematically while supplying sensitive values securely from the environment or a secret manager.

🧭 PART 7: 12-Factor App Principles

13. 🤔 What is a 12-Factor App?

📌 The 12-Factor App is a methodology for building modern, scalable, maintainable software-as-a-service applications that run reliably across different environments and deployment platforms.

You don't need to memorize all 12 immediately. This topic focuses on Codebase, Dependencies, Config, but here's the complete picture:

# Factor Principle
1 📂 Codebase One codebase tracked in version control, with multiple deployments
2 📦 Dependencies Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies
3 ⚙️ Config Store configuration in the environment
4 🔌 Backing services Treat databases, caches and other services as attached resources
5 🏗️ Build, release, run Separate building, releasing and running
6 🧍 Processes Run the app as one or more stateless processes
7 🚪 Port binding Export services through port binding
8 📈 Concurrency Scale out using processes
9 ♻️ Disposability Fast startup and graceful shutdown
10 🪞 Dev/prod parity Keep development, staging and production as similar as possible
11 📜 Logs Treat logs as event streams
12 🛠️ Admin processes Run administrative tasks as one-off processes

Let's go through them. 👇

14. 📂 Factor 1: Codebase

One codebase tracked in version control, with multiple deployments.

You have one backend project in GitHub (SocialFeed/) and deploy the same codebase to Development, Staging and Production. You don't need three separate codebases. You maintain one and configure it differently:

              GitHub Repository
                     │
          ┌──────────┼──────────┐
          ▼          ▼          ▼
     Development   Staging   Production

Development → development database
Staging     → staging database
Production  → production database

Why? Separate codebases slowly drift apart. A bug fix might reach production but get forgotten in development. One source of truth in Git makes collaboration easier.

15. 📦 Factor 2: Dependencies

Explicitly declare and isolate dependencies.

Explicitly declare: clearly specify the packages your project requires:

[project]
dependencies = [
    "fastapi",
    "sqlalchemy",
    "pydantic-settings",
]

Isolate: keep dependencies separate from other projects:

python -m venv .venv

Why? Imagine your project works only because you manually installed a package on your laptop and forgot to list it in requirements.txt or pyproject.toml. Your teammate clones the project and it crashes. That's the undeclared dependency problem. Never rely on packages being installed accidentally or globally.

16. ⚙️ Factor 3: Config

Store configuration in the environment.

Development: DATABASE_URL=localhost, DEBUG=true. Production: DATABASE_URL=production-database, DEBUG=false. The same code runs in both; only the supplied configuration differs.

What counts as configuration?

  • Database URLs
  • API keys and secret keys
  • External service URLs
  • Environment-specific feature flags
  • Credentials
  • Runtime settings

What should NOT be configuration? Application code and internal business logic. A function that calculates a user's feed ranking is business logic, not configuration.

17. 🔌 Factor 4: Backing Services

A backing service is an external service your app depends on: PostgreSQL, Redis, an email service, cloud storage, external payment APIs.

Your app shouldn't care whether PostgreSQL runs locally or on a cloud server, as long as it can connect using the configured details:

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://localhost/social_feed

Later you can switch to a hosted PostgreSQL URL without rewriting your database logic. Treat external services as attached resources that can be configured.

18. 🏗️ Factor 5: Build, Release, Run

Deployment is separated into three stages:

  1. 🔨 Build: convert source code into a deployable artifact, including dependencies
  2. 📦 Release: combine the build with the configuration for a particular deployment
  3. ▶️ Run: start the application from that release

Example: Build = install dependencies and prepare the app. Release = provide the production database URL and secrets. Run = start the FastAPI server.

Why separate them? So you can deploy the same built application with different configurations without rebuilding everything.

19. 🧍 Factor 6: Processes

Execute the app as one or more stateless processes.

A process is a running instance of a program, for example what starts when you run uvicorn app.main:app.

Stateless means the process shouldn't rely on its local memory or filesystem as the permanent storage of important user data or session state.

  • ❌ Poor: store a user's session only in one process's memory. If the process restarts, the session disappears.
  • ✅ Better: store sessions in a shared database or suitable external storage.

This matters especially when multiple app instances run. Important persistent data belongs in backing services, not just inside a process's memory.

20. 🚪 Factor 7: Port Binding

The app makes itself available through a network port:

uvicorn app.main:app --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000
  • 0.0.0.0 → listen on all available network interfaces
  • 8000 → the port

Your app is then reachable at http://localhost:8000. The service should be self-contained and expose itself through a port.

21. 📈 Factor 8: Concurrency

100 users hit your app at once. You can scale using multiple processes or instances:

            Incoming requests
                    │
          ┌─────────┼─────────┐
          ▼         ▼         ▼
        App 1     App 2     App 3
          └─────────┼─────────┘
                    ▼
               PostgreSQL

A load balancer distributes requests among instances. This is horizontal scaling: instead of making one server bigger, you add more instances. Scale by running more processes.

22. ♻️ Factor 9: Disposability

Processes should start quickly and shut down gracefully. When your platform restarts your backend, a good app should:

  • Start without unnecessary delays
  • Accept requests once ready
  • Stop accepting new requests when shutting down
  • Finish ongoing work where possible
  • Close database connections cleanly

FastAPI supports lifespan events:

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    print("Application starting")
    yield
    print("Application shutting down")


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)

Code before yield runs on startup, and code after it runs on shutdown. In a real service, you'd initialize and clean up shared resources here.

23. 🪞 Factor 10: Dev/Prod Parity

Keep development, staging and production as similar as practical. Imagine:

Development:  Python 3.12, PostgreSQL 16, FastAPI
Production:   Python 3.10, MySQL, different dependency versions

It works in development but fails in production. Why? The environments are too different. 12-factor encourages minimizing gaps in three areas:

  • ⏱️ Time: reduce the time between writing code and deploying it
  • 👥 Personnel: developers stay involved in deployment
  • 🧰 Tools: use similar technology across environments

24. 📜 Factor 11: Logs

A log is a record of something that happened inside an application:

INFO: Application started
INFO: User logged in
WARNING: Database response was slow
ERROR: Failed to create post

12-factor says: treat logs as event streams. The app writes logs to stdout (and errors to stderr) instead of depending on a particular log-file location. The hosting platform collects and stores them.

import logging

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO)
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

logger.info("Application started")
logger.error("Unable to connect to database")

Your app generates logs; the execution environment handles their collection and storage.

25. 🛠️ Factor 12: Admin Processes

Admin processes are one-time tasks that help maintain or operate an app:

  • Database migrations
  • Creating an administrator account
  • Importing initial data
  • Running maintenance scripts
  • Cleaning old records 
alembic upgrade head            # apply database migrations
python scripts/create_admin.py  # create an administrator account

These aren't normal HTTP request-handling operations. The principle: run them using the same codebase, configuration and environment as the app.

🏗️ PART 8: Putting Everything Together

26. 🧵 Setting up a clean FastAPI service

Your mentor says: "Create a clean Python service with dependency management and environment-based configuration." Here's how:

Step 1: create the project

mkdir social-feed
cd social-feed

Step 2: create and activate a virtual environment

python -m venv .venv
.venv\Scripts\Activate.ps1      # Windows PowerShell
# source .venv/bin/activate     # macOS / Linux

Step 3: install dependencies

pip install fastapi uvicorn sqlalchemy pydantic-settings
pip install pytest ruff          # development tools

Step 4: save dependencies

pip freeze > requirements.txt

This records the installed packages and versions. For a more controlled workflow, use requirements.in + pip-compile instead.

Step 5: create the project structure

social-feed/
│
├── app/
│   ├── api/
│   ├── models/
│   ├── schemas/
│   ├── services/
│   ├── repositories/
│   ├── common/
│   ├── config.py
│   ├── database.py
│   └── main.py
│
├── tests/
│   └── test_health.py
│
├── alembic/
│   └── versions/
│
├── .env
├── .env.example
├── .gitignore
├── requirements.txt
└── README.md

Step 6: add configuration (app/config.py)

from pydantic_settings import BaseSettings, SettingsConfigDict


class Settings(BaseSettings):
    DATABASE_URL: str
    SECRET_KEY: str
    DEBUG: bool = False

    model_config = SettingsConfigDict(
        env_file=".env",
        extra="ignore",
    )


settings = Settings()

Step 7: create your .env

DATABASE_URL=postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/social_feed
SECRET_KEY=local-development-secret
DEBUG=true

Step 8: create the FastAPI app (app/main.py)

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/health")
def health_check():
    return {"status": "healthy"}

Step 9: run it

uvicorn app.main:app --reload

Open http://localhost:8000/docs to see the Swagger documentation. 🎉

Step 10: test it (tests/test_health.py)

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from app.main import app

client = TestClient(app)


def test_health_check():
    response = client.get("/health")

    assert response.status_code == 200
    assert response.json() == {"status": "healthy"}

pytest

🎉 You've connected packaging, virtual environments, configuration, project structure and testing in one small service.

📝 This is a learning skeleton. A production service also needs proper database initialization, secret management, logging, migration setup and deployment configuration.

⚖️ PART 9: Differences You Must Never Confuse

Concept What it does
venv Creates an isolated Python environment
pip Installs Python packages
Poetry Manages dependencies, environments and packaging
pip-tools Compiles and synchronizes pinned dependencies
pyproject.toml Stores project metadata and tool configuration
poetry.lock Records resolved dependency versions
requirements.txt Lists pinned packages for installation
Pydantic Validates data
Pydantic Settings Loads and validates application configuration
.env Stores local environment configuration values
config.py Defines and exposes application settings
alembic/ Manages database schema migrations
tests/ Contains automated tests

⚠️ PART 10: Common Beginner Mistakes

  1. ❌ Installing packages globally. Always use the project's environment.
  2. ❌ Not maintaining dependency files. Your teammate should be able to recreate the environment.
  3. ❌ Committing .env to GitHub. Never expose real passwords or secret keys.
  4. ❌ Hardcoding database URLs. Use environment-based configuration.
  5. ❌ Putting everything in main.py. Separate routes, services, repositories and models.
  6. ❌ Confusing models and schemas. Database representation and API validation are different.
  7. ❌ Using different package versions everywhere. Maintain consistent dependency resolution.
  8. ❌ Ignoring production configuration. Production secrets should come from secure deployment configuration, not development files.

🧪 PART 11: Test Your Understanding!

Try these before peeking at the answers! ❤️

  1. Which tool creates an isolated Python environment?

    • A) pip
    • B) venv
    • C) Pydantic
    • D) Alembic

  2. What is the primary purpose of poetry.lock?

    • A) Store database passwords
    • B) Store API routes
    • C) Record resolved dependency versions
    • D) Store test cases

  3. Which library helps load and validate environment-based application settings?

    • A) pytest
    • B) SQLAlchemy
    • C) Pydantic Settings
    • D) Uvicorn

  4. Where should business logic generally live in a layered FastAPI project?

    • A) services/
    • B) tests/
    • C) alembic/
    • D) schemas/

  5. Which 12-factor principle says configuration should be stored in the environment?

    • A) Codebase
    • B) Config
    • C) Processes
    • D) Logs

  6. What should you do with a real .env file containing secrets?

    • A) Push it to GitHub
    • B) Put it in tests/
    • C) Add it to .gitignore
    • D) Rename it main.py

👀 Click to reveal answers
  1. B: venv creates isolated environments (pip just installs packages)
  2. C: poetry.lock records exact resolved dependency versions
  3. C: Pydantic Settings loads and validates configuration
  4. A: services/ holds business logic
  5. B: Factor 3, Config
  6. C: Add .env to .gitignore and commit a .env.example instead

🎤 PART 12: How to Explain This to Your Mentor

Python packaging and environment configuration help us build maintainable and reproducible backend services. We use dependency management tools like Poetry or pip-tools to declare and lock package versions, so the same dependencies can be installed across development and production. We use virtual environments to isolate project dependencies and avoid conflicts between projects. For configuration, we use Pydantic Settings to load and validate environment variables such as database URLs, secret keys and debug settings, instead of hardcoding them. We organize the service into modules such as app, tests and alembic, with clear responsibilities for API routes, business logic, database access, testing and migrations. Finally, we follow the 12-factor methodology, particularly explicitly declaring dependencies and keeping environment-specific configuration outside the codebase, which makes the service easier to deploy, maintain and scale.

🏁 Five Key Takeaways

  1. 📦 Packaging: manage the packages your project needs
  2. 🏠 Virtual environments: isolate dependencies for each project
  3. 🎭 Poetry / pip-tools: maintain consistent, reproducible dependencies
  4. ⚙️ Pydantic Settings: read and validate environment-based configuration
  5. 🧭 12-factor principles: build services that are portable, maintainable and deployment-friendly

🚀 What's Next?

Don't just memorize the terms. Build one small FastAPI service with a .venv, pyproject.toml, config.py, .env and a tests/ folder. Once you've done it yourself, these concepts become much easier to explain. 💡

If this post helped you, drop a ❤️ or 🦄 and share it with a friend learning Python backend development. Happy coding! 👩‍💻✨
