title: npm vs yarn: Choosing the Right Package Manager for Your Stack
description:
For most single-repository JavaScript and Node.js projects, npm is the sensible, zero-configuration default that provides universal ecosystem compatibility, robust security auditing, and frictionless onboarding. Yarn, specifically modern Yarn Berry v4+, excels in complex monorepos and enterprise codebases that demand strict dependency boundary enforcement, declarative workspace constraints, and custom CLI plugin workflows. However, the historic performance gap between npm and Yarn has largely closed, meaning the choice now rests entirely on your architectural requirements rather than raw speed.

Core Definitions, Ownership, and Ecosystem Trade-offs

To evaluate npm versus Yarn accurately, we must define what each tool is, examine their underlying architectures, and weigh their structural advantages and disadvantages.

1. npm (Node Package Manager)

  • Definition: npm is the default package manager for Node.js, consisting of a command-line client and a vast public registry hosting over two million packages.
  • Ownership: Maintained and developed by npm, Inc., which has been a wholly-owned subsidiary of GitHub (and thereby Microsoft) since 2020.
  • Benefits: Bundled directly into every standard Node.js installation with zero configuration required, ensuring universal compatibility across developer machines, CI runners, and Docker containers. It offers mature security auditing (npm audit) and broad community support.
  • Disadvantages: Historically prone to disk bloat via dependency hoisting, and default execution postures that run untrusted package lifecycle scripts (postinstall) during installation.

2. Yarn (Yet Another Resource Negotiator)

  • Definition: Yarn is an alternative package manager originally created by Facebook in 2016 to address early performance and security issues in npm. It exists in two vastly different eras: legacy Yarn Classic (v1), which is frozen in maintenance mode, and modern Yarn Berry (v4/v5), a ground-up TypeScript rewrite featuring pluggable architectures.
  • Ownership: Maintained as an open-source project driven by community contributors and core maintainers.
  • Benefits: Modern Yarn Berry introduces powerful workspace constraint enforcement (yarn constraints), parallel execution workflows across monorepo packages, and Plug'n'Play (PnP) architecture that eliminates the node_modules folder entirely. It also blocks untrusted lifecycle scripts by default to protect against supply chain attacks[cite: 4].
  • Disadvantages: Requires activation via Node's Corepack or manual setup, introduces a steeper learning curve for onboarding, and can occasionally cause compatibility friction with legacy native C++ build tools when running in PnP mode.

The Package Management Dilemma in Modern JavaScript

Every JavaScript and TypeScript developer relies on package managers daily, yet many treat them as invisible black boxes. You run an install command, dependencies materialize inside a folder, and your application compiles. But behind that simple developer experience lies a complex engineering trade-off regarding how software packages are fetched, resolved, verified, and stored.

Historically, package managers were treated as interchangeable utilities until scaling codebases introduced major performance bottlenecks and dependency conflicts. Teams running large CI/CD pipelines or multi-package monorepos began experiencing slow builds, bloated disk footprints, and mysterious runtime bugs caused by phantom dependencies where code could access unlisted packages. Selecting the right tool requires understanding what these package managers actually are, who maintains them, and what operational strengths and weaknesses they bring to your stack.

Core Architecture: Hoisting vs. Plug'n'Play

While modern npm (v10/v11) and modern Yarn (v4+) perform similarly on standard cached installs, their underlying dependency resolution mechanics differ fundamentally.


                   ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
                   │  What is your project architecture?    │
                   └────────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                        │
               ┌────────────────────────┴────────────────────────┐
               ▼                                                 ▼
    [ Single Repository / Standard App ]               [ Multi-Package Monorepo ]
               │                                                 │
  ┌────────────┴────────────┐                       ┌────────────┴────────────┐
  ▼                         ▼                       ▼                         ▼


[ Default Choice ]     [ Strict Security/PnP ]    [ Lightweight Workspaces ] [ Deep Monorepo Rules ]
npm 11                    Yarn 4                     pnpm / npm                Yarn 4 (Berry)
(Zero-Config,          (Plug'n'Play,             (Content-Addressable        (Workspaces, PnP,
Universal Support)     No node_modules)           Store, Fast CI)             Yarn Constraints)

Npm and legacy Yarn rely on hoisting, flattening the dependency tree by pulling nested dependencies up into the root node_modules directory. While this saves disk space and ensures compatibility, it creates the "phantom dependency" vulnerability where your code can accidentally import a package that is not explicitly declared in your package.json.

Conversely, modern Yarn Berry offers Plug'n'Play (PnP) mode, which completely avoids node_modules. Instead of writing files to disk, Yarn generates a single zero-install zip archive lookup map (.pnp.cjs). Node.js loads modules directly from this map via a virtual filesystem API. This eliminates disk I/O overhead and completely blocks phantom dependencies, though it requires strict adherence from third-party packages.

Step-by-Step Practical Framework: Implementation and Migration

Adopting or standardizing your package manager involves deliberate configuration choices to ensure deterministic builds.

Step 1: Analyze Project Scope and Choose Your Tool

  • Choose npm for standard single applications or libraries where zero-config onboarding and universal environment support are top priorities.
  • Choose Yarn 4 (Berry) for complex monorepos that require strict version constraints, parallel task execution across workspaces, or zero-install PnP pipelines.

Step 2: Pin the Package Manager Version

Prevent team version drift by explicitly declaring the tool version inside your manifest file:

{
  "name": "my-enterprise-app",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "packageManager": "yarn@4.12.0"
}

Step 3: Enforce Secure CI Execution Rules

  • For npm in CI: Run deterministic, secure installs: 
npm ci
npm audit --audit-level=high
  • For Yarn 4 in CI: Enable Corepack and execute immutable checks: 
corepack enable
yarn install --immutable

Step 4: Execute a Safe Migration

If switching tools across an existing codebase, delete your old lockfile and node_modules folder, initialize the target manager, generate a fresh lockfile, and thoroughly verify your test suites and build scripts.

Industry Scale, Security Postures, and Real-World Usage

Package managers operate at the absolute center of global software infrastructure. Because every modern web framework, cloud deployment, and CI pipeline relies on them, security and determinism have become critical concerns.

Supply chain security has shifted how package managers handle lifecycle scripts. Malicious packages frequently abuse postinstall scripts during installation to execute arbitrary code. Modern Yarn 4 blocks dependency lifecycle scripts by default to protect against these attacks, whereas npm continues to execute lifecycle scripts by default, requiring explicit opt-out flags.

Furthermore, multi-package monorepos managed by large enterprise engineering teams leverage Yarn's advanced workspace governance features, such as yarn constraints, to programmatically enforce uniform dependency versions across dozens of sub-packages and prevent version fragmentation.

Trade-offs, Counterpoints, and Limitations

While package manager tooling is mature, developers must navigate several real-world limitations:

  • PnP Compatibility Friction: While Yarn's PnP mode eliminates node_modules, some third-party packages with custom resolution logic or un-declared transitive dependencies struggle under PnP, forcing teams to fall back to nodeLinker: node-modules.
  • Corepack Uncertainty: Node.js introduced Corepack to manage package managers without global installations, but ongoing governance discussions regarding its long-term bundling status create minor operational ambiguity.
  • Migration Overhead: Switching an active commercial codebase from npm to Yarn is not merely cosmetic. Differences in lockfile resolution and peer dependency handling can introduce subtle runtime bugs if not audited carefully.

Summary Checklist and Next Steps

  • Match your package manager choice to your project architecture (npm for standard apps, Yarn 4 for complex monorepos).
  • Pin your exact tool version in package.json using the packageManager field.
  • Enforce deterministic and secure installs in CI pipelines using npm ci or yarn install --immutable.
  • Never commit multiple conflicting lockfiles to the same Git repository.

Sources

  • npm vs Yarn in 2026: Speed, Security, Workspaces (Mend.io)

  • npm vs Yarn vs pnpm Selection Guide (Tomoda Hinata)

  • Yarn Official Performance & Feature Documentation

title: Fix Content Hash Mismatch in Publishing Pipelines
description:
Fix a content hash mismatch in publishing pipelines when a publishing worker and a static site validator disagree on the exact bytes covered by an integrity sidecar.

Quick solution:

const crypto = require('node:crypto');

function createCanonicalPayload(article) {
  const sortedFields = {
    body: article.body.replace(/\r\n/g, '\n').trim(),
    seo_description: article.seo_description.trim(),
    title: article.title.trim()
  };
  return JSON.stringify(sortedFields);
}

function computeQualityHash(article) {
  const payload = createCanonicalPayload(article);
  return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(payload).digest('hex');
}

module.exports = { computeQualityHash };

Prerequisites include Node.js runtime access and matching JSON serialization libraries on both the publishing worker and the static site build validator. Watch out for automatic line-ending conversions in different Git checkouts, which can silently invalidate hashes.

The Cross-System Quality Hash Challenge in Distributed Pipelines

A publishing worker can create an article and a quality sidecar, after which a separate static site build recomputes the sidecar hash before deployment. Both components may use SHA-256 correctly and still disagree because the serialized inputs are not identical. In production failures, the worker might include article topics or dynamic timestamps in its quality hash, while the site validator treats topic and taxonomy metadata as external and excludes them from editorial evidence. When the build rejects the sidecar, the article and its associated assets never reach their public paths. A cross-artifact audit often reveals that one sidecar followed a worker-only rule while the rest followed the site rule, leading to frustrating deployment bottlenecks.

This publication hash must remain entirely separate from the internal hash used to bind an AI review to draft text. Conflating those distinct hashes hides which system contract actually failed and weakens overall editorial safety checks. When maintaining complex publishing workflows, you also need to manage how content review hash changes after citation edits to ensure upstream inputs remain stable before generation begins. For instance, using Azure Devops For Product Managers can help streamline the process.

Defining a Canonical Field Contract Across Boundaries

To ensure deterministic equality, define the hash input once as a canonical payload. You must explicitly specify which frontmatter fields are included, which taxonomy and publication timestamps are ignored, how body text is normalized, and how object keys are ordered. Without this explicit boundary, slight variations in whitespace or property ordering across environments will break cryptographic validation.

Option / Pattern When to Use It Trade-off or Failure Mode Recommendation
Full Raw Frontmatter When every metadata property must influence the published output. Highly fragile; minor taxonomy updates or tag additions invalidate old hashes. Avoid for site quality sidecars.
Explicit Canonical Payload When separating core editorial content from transient build metadata. Requires strict maintenance when adding new required fields to articles. Recommended for multi-step publishing pipelines.
Post-Build Artifact Hash When hashing the final compiled HTML instead of source Markdown. Hides intermediate generation errors and ties validation too late in the cycle. Use only as a secondary sanity check.

Keeping the publisher implementation strictly aligned with the validator is far safer than relaxing the validator after a mismatch occurs. According to the official Node.js crypto.createHash documentation, cryptographic hashing requires consistent byte streams, meaning any string encoding discrepancy between systems will break validation.

Implementing the Repair and Versioned Markers

The repair strategy involves adding a shared helper to the worker that mirrors the site field exclusions and normalizes line endings prior to hashing. Unit tests should prove that changes to mutable metadata like topic or publication date do not alter the publication hash, while changes to core fields like the title do.

Furthermore, the worker should version its publication marker. A prior marker representing a failed build must not make a subsequent retry look complete. The new marker format causes one corrective site commit. After that write completes, a repeat attempt remains idempotent and does not create duplicate commits or redundant build runs.

Verification and Execution Checklist

  • Confirm that identical source Markdown files generate the exact same SHA-256 hash string on both the publishing worker and the site validator.
  • Verify that modifying an excluded field, such as a tag or taxonomy category, leaves the computed quality hash completely unchanged.
  • Check that modifying a core included field, such as the article title or body, successfully alters the hash and triggers a fresh build cycle.
  • Ensure that a failed deployment marker allows exactly one corrective write and remains idempotent on subsequent retry attempts.

title: 三丰云免费服务器实测：Rust编译打满CPU，7天手动续期才稳
description:
之前那篇“稳如老狗”的结论没变，但细节得抠细一点。上次重点在Python后端，这次换了一套完全不同的栈：Rust axum + SQLite + Caddy。这一换，对“免费云服务器”性能边界的体感完全不一样。

特别是C++/Rust这种需要重编译的语言，和脚本语言是两码事。很多人看到“1核1G”就劝退，其实对于静态博客或轻量API，绰绰有余；但如果你想在这台机器上跑CI构建，心态得调整好——它不承诺“秒开”，也不承诺“无阻塞”。

Rust编译时的“至暗时刻”

这套服务的核心是个 axum HTTP 服务，本地开发时体验极流畅，部署上去也省事：Caddy 自动搞定 HTTPS，SQLite 负责存储，不需要额外的 MySQL 或 Redis。

平时运行时，内存占用很低，几百MB就够，CPU 基本趴在个位数。看着很惬意。

但一旦涉及 cargo build --release，画风突变。

我观察过两次完整编译过程。第一次是项目刚迁移上去，从零编译。CPU 瞬间打满，风扇声（如果有的话）大概会啸叫——虽然这是远程机器，我听不见，但通过 htop 看 CPU 使用率确实长期维持在 100%。持续时间几分钟到十几分钟不等，取决于依赖库的数量。

这期间，SSH 连接会轻微卡顿，但这台机器上的其他进程（如果有的话）几乎不受影响，因为资源分配机制比较公平。编译结束后，CPU 回落，服务正常启动。

第二次是修改了某个中间件版本，增量编译。耗时短得多，大概几十秒，CPU 波动也不明显。

这个现象说明什么？说明 1核 的配置，跑动态语言是“奢侈”的，跑编译型语言是“够用”的。只要你不是每写一行代码就重新构建一次，这点等待时间是可以接受的。对于我这种写完本地测试、推代码再远程编译部署的流式工作法，完全没问题。

为什么还愿意用？

  • 编译允许等待：几分钟的 CPU 满载换来的是完整的 Release 包，性能提升明显
  • 运行时资源极度克制：几百MB 内存占用，留出了巨大的余量给系统和其他小任务
  • Caddy 配置简单：反代和证书自动续签，不用手写复杂的 Nginx 规则
  • SQLite 零维护：没有独立数据库进程，数据文件即备份，省心省力
  • 文件系统稳定：多次重启、强制关机（误操作过），数据从未损坏
  • 网络延迟低：国内访问速度快，API 响应时间在毫秒级
  • 续期机制透明：和之前跑 Python 时一样，每 7 天需手动点击续期
  • 操作成本极低：登录控制台，点一下按钮，30 秒搞定，设个日历提醒即可
  • 无隐形扣费：5M 带宽全程跑满过，流量统计清晰，没有悄悄限速
  • 环境一致性：开发环境和生产环境都是 Linux，排错逻辑通用

故障与自救

唯一的一次小插曲发生在编译期间。有一次我开了两个 SSH 会话，一个在编译，一个在查看日志。编译进行到一半，网络突然抖动，SSH 断连。

我并没有恐慌，因为服务器还在跑。等编译完成（又过了几分钟），我重新连入 SSH。服务已经成功启动，Caddy 证书正常，SQLite 数据完整。

这次经历让我明白：在免费云服务器上跑编译任务，一定要用 screen 或 tmux，或者干脆接受“后台运行、前台偶尔检查”的模式。不要开着交互式终端干等，容易因为网络波动导致不必要的焦虑。

另外，建议将构建产物目录排除在同步范围外，只同步源码。这样即使机器被回收（当然我没遇到过），重建成本也很低。

适合谁这样用

如果你正在学习 Rust，想部署一个自己的 API 服务；或者想搭建一个基于 SQLite 的个人知识库、静态博客的后端；亦或是想体验 Caddy 的自动 HTTPS 配置——这台机器很适合你。

它不适合：需要高并发数据库查询的生产项目；实时性要求极高的 WebSocket 服务；或者那些希望“扔上去就不管”的懒人场景（因为每 7 天你得记得续期）。

对于学生党、自学开发者、运维初学者来说，这是一个极佳的实验场。你可以放心地折腾、踩坑、重装系统，反正数据量不大，随时可以重建。

上手建议

想试的自己搜“三丰云”官网，实名后创建实例。

这里插一句关于免费虚拟主机的看法。如果你只是挂个静态 HTML 页面，或者PHP 博客，免费虚拟主机更省事，不用管 Linux 命令，不用管 SSH，不用管编译。但如果你想跑 Rust、Go、Python 后台服务，或者学习 Linux 运维，务必选择云服务器。

从虚拟主机过渡到云服务器，是技术成长的必经之路。先玩熟 Linux 基础命令，再尝试部署 axum 服务，这个顺序不会错。

我的习惯是：每周日早上顺手点一下续期。手机日历设个循环提醒，标签写“续费云服务器”。这个动作比点赞一个公众号还简单，但换来的是接下来七天的稳定服务。

这台机器不完美，它有编译慢的缺点，有必须手动续期的麻烦。但在这种成本下，能做到 IP 不变、数据不丢、服务稳定，还要啥自行车？

对于个人开发者来说，有一个可以随时拿起来写代码、跑服务、学技术的“家”，本身就是最大的价值。

title: Small Avatar Uploads in Object Storage — A Go Guide to Multipart Thresholds
description:
When the file is a normal customer avatar, the operational constraint is deletion, not throughput. Short answer: use one PUT or a presigned upload for small images; reserve multipart upload for unusually large profile media or unreliable networks. Multipart is a workflow with state, cleanup, and more places for a retry to go wrong. An avatar that is a few megabytes rarely benefits from that machinery.

I have been paged for missed jobs and duplicate deliveries, so I treat an upload as a small state machine even when the UI makes it look like one button. The useful invariant is simple: an avatar key must be replaceable, observable, and removable by a retention job. A retry must not create a second logical object, and deleting a user must not leave hidden upload fragments behind.

The incident pattern behind a small upload

Start with a single object write. The browser can send the bytes to your application, or your application can issue a presigned upload; the latter keeps large request bodies away from the API process. Give the object a deterministic name, such as avatars/{user_id}/current, and store the content type and ownership in your database. Replacing that name is easy to reason about, while a random name for every edit turns retention into a search problem. The operational payoff is that one database row points to one current object, so a deletion event has a bounded target even after several profile edits, retries, and a delayed queue consumer. In a real incident, that bounded target is what lets an on-call engineer prove that the account's media is gone instead of paging another team to interpret a pile of orphaned keys.

Measure first.

There is a practical boundary here, but it is not a universal magic number. Set a threshold from your own latency and failure data, then test around it. A 2 MB phone photo on a stable connection is a different problem from a 40 MB animated profile image on a lossy mobile link. Your mileage may vary.

The catch is that a single PUT is not a concurrency lock. If two profile edits race, the last write wins unless a queue or database transaction coordinates them. Strict compare-and-swap semantics need an external coordination layer because this storage surface does not provide an If-Match write condition.

How does this compare with S3, R2, and MinIO?

Multipart earns its keep when a failed transfer should resume from completed parts. It also creates obligations: create the upload, send each part, complete it, and explicitly abort abandoned uploads. There is no automatic fragment cleanup rule to rely on, so an interrupted browser tab can leave state that your retention process will never see as a finished avatar.

That lifecycle deserves a runbook entry. Record the upload ID and creation time, alert on old incomplete uploads, and make the abort operation idempotent in the worker. A daily sweep is usually enough for profile media; an hourly policy is not available in this model. Deletion of the completed object still needs to follow the account-retention event, including GDPR erasure requests.

One incident pattern is especially boring and expensive: a worker retries after a timeout, the first completion succeeded, and the second attempt creates another object. Use a client-generated idempotency key for create and complete calls, and make the database row the source of truth for which key is current. Boring is good.

What should beginners choose for small image upload and multipart retention?

The example below uses the native object PUT route. It reads the key from the environment, sets an explicit method, retries HTTP 429 with Retry-After when present, and sends an idempotency key so a retry does not represent a second logical write. It still checks every response; a 4xx body is useful evidence during an incident.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if key == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    bucket := "support-avatars"
    objectKey := "avatars/user-123/current"
    body := []byte("image bytes supplied by the upload handler")
    url := os.Getenv("INFRAI_OBJECT_PUT_URL")
    if url == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_OBJECT_PUT_URL is required")
    }

    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 20 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, url, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/jpeg")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "avatar-user-123-v7")

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        responseBody, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
            fmt.Println("stored", objectKey)
            return
        }
        if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests || attempt == 3 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("storage write failed: %s: %s", resp.Status, responseBody))
        }

        delay := time.Duration(1<<attempt) * time.Second
        if retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"); retryAfter != "" {
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil {
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            }
        }
        time.Sleep(delay)
    }
}

The sample is intentionally plain. A production handler should validate image dimensions and media type before this call, and it should enqueue deletion of the previous key only after the new write is recorded. Never make the cleanup decision from a client-supplied filename.

The choice is less about a winner than about where you want the state machine to live. Amazon S3 is the reference point for presigned URLs and multipart primitives. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when an S3-compatible API fits an edge-oriented deployment. MinIO puts the storage service under your operational control, which can be useful for private or on-premise support systems but makes capacity and durability your responsibility.

Option Small avatar path Multipart and retention trade-off
Amazon S3 Single PUT or presigned URL Mature multipart tooling; lifecycle rules still need deliberate scope
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible PUT/presign pattern Check regional and egress behavior against your support traffic
MinIO Direct PUT in infrastructure you run Maximum control, plus capacity, upgrades, and repair work
Infrai storage One REST API call, with discovery and runnable examples Useful when one key and one billing surface already cover the rest of your backend; multipart fragments still need explicit abort handling

Infrai's differentiator here is that its API is self-describing: discovery exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so wiring a new capability starts with reading one endpoint instead of learning another SDK. That is a workflow advantage, not a reason to ignore lifecycle gaps. It also means one REST API can sit beside other backend capabilities without adding a language-specific client.

The comparison is only useful after the retention requirement is written down.

How do multipart upload and retention interact for avatar files?

Stick with S3 when you need public-read objects, object versioning, WORM retention, cross-region replication, or a mature cross-cloud migration tool. R2 or MinIO may be the better fit when their network placement or ownership model is the primary requirement. Infrai is not suitable when browser-direct uploads require self-service CORS configuration, when you need automatic cleanup for incomplete fragments, or when a strict immutable archive is part of the contract.

The decision rule I put in a runbook

For ordinary avatar files, choose a single PUT or presigned upload, deterministic keys, and a database-backed retention event. Add multipart only when measured file sizes or connection failures justify resumability. If you add it, own the full state machine and schedule explicit aborts; do not assume an unfinished upload will disappear.

This is a small design decision with a long tail. The upload path is healthy only when replacement, deletion, retries, and abandoned state are all observable. Three words: finish the cleanup.

References

  • AWS S3 presigned URLs: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • GDPR Article 17, right to erasure: https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • Amazon S3 multipart upload overview: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • Cloudflare R2 S3 API compatibility: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • MinIO multipart upload API: https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/api/API.html

Sources

  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/using-presigned-url.html
  • https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • https://min.io/docs/minio/linux/developers/api/API.html

title: De una app de tareas a Azure: .NET 10, Cosmos DB, Terraform y GitHub Actions
description:
Una lista de tareas es un buen punto de partida para practicar NoSQL y automatización. El problema es sencillo de comprobar: creo una tarea en el navegador, la marco como hecha y vuelvo a abrir la aplicación. Si el estado se conserva, puedo seguir el recorrido desde la interfaz hasta la base de datos y comprobar qué parte del despliegue permite que todo funcione en Azure.

Esta es la experiencia del equipo para la Actividad Grupal 01 de Base de Datos II en la Universidad Privada de Tacna. El código está disponible en el repositorio público del proyecto.

1. De la interfaz a un documento en Cosmos DB

La interfaz vive en wwwroot. Desde ahí, el navegador usa la API de ASP.NET Core (.NET 10) para crear, listar, completar y eliminar tareas. La aplicación agrupa las rutas bajo /api/tareas, y TareasRepo concentra el acceso a Azure Cosmos DB for NoSQL mediante el SDK de .NET.

Cada tarea se representa como un documento. Este ejemplo ilustra los campos del modelo:

{
  "id": "53316b1d-b681-41cd-8b37-079be264189f",
  "titulo": "Revisar el despliegue",
  "hecha": false,
  "fecha": "2026-10-24T03:31:05Z"
}

El contenedor tareas de la base tareasdb usa /id como clave de partición. Eso permite que el repositorio busque una tarea con su identificador y su clave de partición en una lectura puntual. La lista completa se consulta aparte, ordenada por fecha descendente. Así, la operación de abrir una tarea y la de listar todas tienen recorridos distintos en el código.

2. Terraform prepara Azure y GitHub Actions publica la aplicación

La automatización está separada en dos flujos dentro de .github/workflows:

Flujo Qué hace Cuándo se ejecuta
infra.yml Inicializa y valida Terraform, y aplica la configuración de infra/main.tf. Esta define los recursos de Cosmos DB y Azure App Service. Al enviar a main cambios en infra/ o en el propio flujo. También admite ejecución manual.
deploy.yml Prepara .NET 10, genera el paquete Release con dotnet publish, inicia sesión en Azure, despliega en App Service y consulta /health. Al enviar a main cambios en src/ o en el propio flujo. También admite ejecución manual.

En una primera instalación, la infraestructura debe estar lista antes de publicar el código. Después, un cambio en la aplicación puede lanzar su propio despliegue. El estado de Terraform se configura en Azure Storage. GitHub Actions obtiene las credenciales de Azure desde los secretos del repositorio, y Terraform configura la conexión a Cosmos DB en App Service.

Las ejecuciones de GitHub Actions y las capturas del repositorio documentan ambas etapas.

3. Comprobación en la nube

La aplicación se publicó en Azure App Service. En las evidencias del despliegue se ve cómo se crea una tarea, se marca como completada y se elimina. La respuesta de /api/tareas permite revisar los documentos devueltos por la API. La ruta /health devuelve el estado de la aplicación, la base utilizada y el número de tareas que se pudieron leer.

La URL corresponde al despliegue documentado. Durante la preparación de este artículo no pude verificar que la instancia siguiera respondiendo. Las capturas y el video conservan el resultado de la prueba en Azure.

Video del equipo

Yerry Maycol Tarqui Collatupa muestra la construcción, la automatización y la prueba de la app en 4 minutos y 35 segundos.

title: Object Storage Downloads: Fix Presigned PDF/CSV Filename, Content-Type, and Disposition
description:
Short answer: a presigned URL cannot repair bad download behavior after the fact. Store the export with the right Content-Type and Content-Disposition metadata, verify that metadata, then issue a fresh private link. For an e-commerce system, retention rules matter just as much: keeping every generated PDF forever is an operational decision, not a harmless default.

Infrai is a reasonable fit when this export path sits beside other backend jobs and you want one REST contract for them. It is not a magic header fixer; the object metadata still has to be correct.

The bill starts with retained bytes

An export pipeline usually has three costs: generating the file, storing it, and serving it repeatedly. Storage is the term that quietly grows. A 12 MB order-history CSV generated 2,000 times a day becomes roughly 720 GB of new data in a month if nothing is deleted. That is before replicas, request charges, or the database rows that point at each object.

The useful change is to define a retention class before upload. Keep a customer's latest invoice export for 30 days, perhaps; keep a tax record for the legally required period; delete intermediate retry artifacts after one day. Lifecycle automation can remove objects, but the shortest lifecycle available here is one day, so sub-day cleanup belongs in your worker or queue. I would also record the expiry decision beside the object key, because object metadata is not a server-side search index and listing only filters by prefix.

Retention is a product decision.

There is a trade-off. Deleting aggressively lowers the steady-state bill, but a support agent loses the exact artifact a customer downloaded last week. That is why I keep a small audit row (tenant, object key, checksum, created time, retention class) even after the object is gone. The row explains the absence instead of pretending the file is recoverable.

Why do presigned downloads get the wrong filename or content-type?

Browsers follow the response headers they receive. If a CSV is served as text/plain, or if Content-Disposition is absent, Chrome may render the data in a tab. A PDF may open inline by design. A filename with spaces or non-ASCII characters can expose a second bug: the object is correct, but the header encoding is not.

Start with the object, not the link. Inspect its metadata with the object-head operation. If the stored type or disposition is wrong, set metadata immediately after upload (or include it in the upload request, where supported), and only then create a new presigned link. Existing links inherit the old response behavior; signing the same key again does not rewrite metadata.

Test names such as March sales.csv, 订单-2026.pdf, and a deliberately long UTF-8 name. I once spent an afternoon blaming a browser cache when the real failure was a missing disposition value on the object. Tiny header. Big detour.

For private exports, issue short-lived signed links from an authenticated application route. Public URLs are not supported in this setup, so a permanent image-hosting style link is the wrong model. The application can check tenant ownership before signing and can stop handing out links after the retention deadline.

A small, auditable flow

The sequence is deliberately boring: upload, set metadata, head-check, presign. The route names below are the storage contract; keep the bucket and key URL-encoded in a real client.

import os
import time
from urllib.parse import quote

import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
TOKEN = os.environ["INFRAI_API_KEY"]
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {TOKEN}"}


def call(method, path, **kwargs):
    for attempt in range(4):
        response = requests.request(method, BASE + path, headers=HEADERS, **kwargs)
        if response.status_code != 429:
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response
        retry_after = response.headers.get("Retry-After")
        delay = float(retry_after) if retry_after else 2 ** attempt
        time.sleep(delay)
    raise RuntimeError("rate limit did not clear after retries")


bucket = "tenant-exports"
key = "tenant-42/March sales.csv"
encoded_bucket, encoded_key = quote(bucket, safe=""), quote(key, safe="/")

metadata = {
    "content_type": "text/csv",
    "content_disposition": 'attachment; filename="March sales.csv"',
}
call("POST", f"/storage/object/set_metadata/{encoded_bucket}/{encoded_key}", json=metadata)
signed = call("POST", f"/storage/object/presign/{encoded_bucket}/{encoded_key}")
print(signed.json())

The important operational detail is the head-check in the same job that creates the link. It turns a visual browser complaint into a metadata mismatch you can log, alert on, and test. Keep retries bounded, and make any write retry idempotent with the platform's idempotency convention in the client you use.

Comparing the usual choices

No storage service wins every retention policy. Here is the decision I use for this workload:

Option Where it fits Retention and download trade-off
AWS S3 Mature lifecycle, versioning, and object-lock controls Strong compliance toolbox, with more configuration and separate credentials to operate
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible storage near Workers workloads Useful egress economics and edge integration; check which lifecycle and event features your account needs
Google Cloud Storage Teams already standardized on Google IAM and analytics Excellent integration with GCP policy; it is a separate cloud control plane
Infrai storage A small team that wants storage plus other backend modules behind one contract One REST API and one key can reduce integration surface; it lacks public ACLs, versioning/object lock, cross-region replication, and hourly lifecycle expiry

Infrai's practical advantage here is breadth behind a simple surface: storage, scheduling, and other backend capabilities use the same REST contract, so adding a cleanup job does not introduce another SDK and credential set. The supporting benefit is the public discovery surface with runnable examples, which makes a narrow integration easier to inspect during review.

I recommend Infrai for teams that need private tenant exports, signed delivery, and a few adjacent backend jobs without assembling several control planes. The catch is important: choose S3 when WORM retention, object versioning, or cross-region replication is a hard requirement; choose R2 when the edge runtime is the primary design center; choose GCS when IAM and analytics already live there. Your mileage may vary if legal retention rules differ by country.

A retention rule worth shipping

Make deletion explicit in code and in the data model. A nightly job can list objects by tenant prefix, compare each audit row's expires_at, and delete only objects whose retention class permits it. Do not infer compliance from a presigned URL's expiry; link expiry controls access, while lifecycle controls storage.

The failure mode I watch is a successful download followed by an accidental overwrite. This storage option has no object versioning, object lock, or If-Match conditional write. If two workers can publish the same key, coordinate with a database or queue and use immutable keys (for example, include an export UUID). That is a capability boundary, not a reason to hide the risk.

If this boundary matches your system, the storage discovery entry is the right place to verify request fields before wiring the worker: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.put

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.put
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Content-Disposition
  • https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6266
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html
  • https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/metadata
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/api/
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.multipart.create
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/

Further reading

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.put
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/object-lifecycle-mgmt.html
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/

title: Fintech Mail Cutovers — Safe DNS Record Writer Evidence for Incident Response
description:
Restore company mail routing with a safe DNS record writer: read the zone's current state, compare it with the intended MX set, skip a matching set, and verify every attempted mutation. Consider an illustrative page that says a fintech company's mail cutover is still unverified. The responder sees a successful change request in the dashboard, but the incident record contains no observation of the resulting MX set. What page fired, and what evidence would let someone close it?

Short answer: A safe DNS record writer uses read, compare, conditional write, and read back; a no-op skips the write, while an uncertain outcome triggers another read before any retry. Choose customer-owned or platform-owned zones by who can authorize and coordinate changes. Preserve that ownership boundary throughout the operation.

The earlier signal should have been an unresolved difference between approved intent and observed configuration, attached to a named zone owner. A dashboard's completed task cannot supply that evidence by itself. This is a proposed incident-response design, not a report of a production outage, and its alert thresholds are policy choices to test against the team's delivery requirements.

What should a safe DNS record writer read before changing mail routing?

Start the investigation with the evidence that the writer actually collected. An accepted mutation, an observed record set, and a completed mail cutover answer different questions. Treating them as one green status makes it difficult to tell the responder whether to inspect permissions, concurrent edits, configuration, or the mail delivery path. The useful incident artifact ties together the approved intent, the state read before the attempt, the mutation outcome, and the state observed afterward.

Keep those separate.

For a concrete example, use the reserved example domain treasury.example as the fintech company's mail domain. Its approved target is an MX set containing preference 10 with exchange inbound.mail.example. and preference 20 with exchange backup.mail.example.. These are illustrative values, not a provider's configuration instructions. The actual target must come from the mail provider's instructions and the company's approved change. The writer must compare the complete intended set, including the TTL chosen for this change, rather than decide that the job is done because one desired exchange appears somewhere in the response.

The instrumentation change is to record a reconciliation result independently of the request result. In this design, each run records a change identifier, ownership mode, intent identifier, pre-write revision, attempt status, and verification status. A successful no-op is observable too: it means a fresh read matched the approved target and no mutation was necessary. An unresolved read is an error, never an empty record set.

That distinction matters during a page. If the initial read failed, the responder has no basis for a replacement. If the write returned an error but the next read matches, the responder has evidence of the desired control-plane state, even though the request's outcome was ambiguous. Neither result establishes that a real message has reached a mailbox.

Ownership determines who can resolve the difference

For a customer-owned zone, make the customer's authority explicit in the change record: which zone, which mail domain, which MX set, and which approved intent the writer may apply. If the writer lacks that authority, the useful output is an actionable handoff to the customer, with the expected set and the observed difference. Repeated automated attempts cannot repair missing authorization.

For a platform-owned zone, make the platform's coordination responsibility explicit instead. All participating writers need a way to detect stale observations or serialize mutations for the affected record set. Central ownership makes that coordination easier to arrange organizationally, but it doesn't make a read followed by a write atomic. An administrative console, another automation job, and an emergency change can still produce conflicting intent.

The trade-off is operational control. Customer ownership preserves the customer's change authority and introduces a handoff when the platform cannot act; platform ownership lets the platform coordinate the change directly and makes the platform responsible for that coordination. Choose based on who must approve the change and who can respond when it stalls. Request volume and unit pricing don't settle that question.

Don't broaden an MX correction into a replacement of the whole zone.

In this design the mutation boundary is one explicitly selected MX set, so unrelated records stay outside the operation. Mail authentication also needs its own review: RFC 7489 describes DMARC evaluation in relation to SPF and DKIM alignment. An observed MX match is therefore a deliberately narrow verification result, not proof that the company's entire mail configuration is correct.

Make the writer return evidence, including on a no-op

The following Go example expresses the safety contract behind a Node.js read-compare-write implementation. The language is incidental to the sequence: await a fresh read, compare canonical sets, conditionally replace, and read again. A Node.js implementation needs the same error boundaries and coordination guarantees.

This is adapter code, not a claim that every DNS API exposes a conditional replacement operation. ReadMX must return the complete selected set, a revision covering that set, and an error on incomplete or failed reads. ReplaceMX must atomically reject a stale revision without modifying anything; an adapter that cannot provide that guarantee must reject the operation or use a coordination mechanism whose scope covers the relevant writers. A second client-side comparison cannot manufacture that guarantee.

Here the adapter canonicalizes exchange names, sorts the set, and rejects duplicates before returning it. The approved target passes through the same validation. Consequently the comparison below is an exact comparison of validated canonical data, not an assumption about the ordering of an arbitrary API response. The caller supplies an authorized zone and owner name, a nonempty validated target, and a context with a deadline. This snippet uses the standard library's slices package, requiring Go 1.21 or later.

package mailchange

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "slices"
)

type MX struct {
    Preference uint16
    Exchange   string
}

type Set struct {
    TTL     uint32
    Records []MX
}

type Snapshot struct {
    Revision string
    Set      Set
}

type Zone interface {
    ReadMX(context.Context, string, string) (Snapshot, error)
    ReplaceMX(context.Context, string, string, string, Set) error
}

type Result struct {
    Attempted bool
    Verified  bool
    Before    Snapshot
    After     Snapshot
    WriteErr  error
}

func equal(a, b Set) bool {
    return a.TTL == b.TTL && slices.Equal(a.Records, b.Records)
}

func Reconcile(ctx context.Context, z Zone, zone, owner string,
    want Set) (Result, error) {
    var result Result
    before, err := z.ReadMX(ctx, zone, owner)
    if err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("read before change: %w", err)
    }
    result.Before = before
    if equal(before.Set, want) {
        result.After = before
        result.Verified = true
        return result, nil
    }

    result.Attempted = true
    result.WriteErr = z.ReplaceMX(ctx, zone, owner, before.Revision, want)
    after, err := z.ReadMX(ctx, zone, owner)
    if err != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("read after attempt: %w", err)
    }
    result.After = after
    result.Verified = equal(after.Set, want)
    if result.Verified {
        return result, nil
    }
    if result.WriteErr != nil {
        return result, fmt.Errorf("target unverified after attempt: %w",
            result.WriteErr)
    }
    return result, fmt.Errorf("observed MX set differs from target")
}

Attempted is intentionally precise. It says a mutation was attempted; it doesn't claim that this invocation caused the observed state. A concurrent actor could have applied the same target. Keep WriteErr in the incident evidence even when read-back succeeds, because a verified target and a clean request history are different observations.

The no-op branch is short because its evidence already exists. It performs a fresh read, compares the full selected set, and returns without writing. That avoids making an unnecessary mutation the price of proving that the configuration is already correct.

A read-back through the management interface verifies what that interface reports. Resolver observations and an appropriate mail delivery check belong to subsequent verification stages, with their own outcomes. Give them distinct names in the incident record so the dashboard cannot quietly substitute one for another.

Reconstruct the failure before authorizing another attempt

The most dangerous recovery instruction is an unconditional retry of the old payload. In this design a retry starts a new reconciliation against fresh state and current approved intent. If the preceding attempt took effect, the new run can finish as a no-op. If another authorized actor changed the set, the responder must resolve the competing intent before overwriting it. A revision conflict is evidence to investigate, not permission to discard the revision check.

Rollback deserves the same treatment. Store the pre-change snapshot as evidence, but require fresh authorization and a fresh conditional comparison before restoring it; a saved snapshot doesn't prove that restoring it is still appropriate after another change. This adds work during response. It also prevents an old recovery action from automatically becoming the newest conflicting writer.

Before deployment, exercise the boundaries that would otherwise confuse the responder:

  • Start with an already matching set and assert that no write occurs.
  • Introduce a concurrent edit between read and replace and require rejection.
  • Simulate a request error after the target has been applied and require read-back to settle the observed state.
  • Fail the read-back and require an unresolved verification result, with no blind second mutation.

These tests evaluate the adapter contract and the recovery policy, not just whether a function returned nil. If the original context has expired, preserve that unresolved result; schedule a separate observation under a fresh bounded context rather than pretending the failed read verified anything.

The team also needs an owner for each unresolved result. A customer-owned zone may require customer action; a platform-owned zone may require an internal response. Record that routing alongside the evidence, avoiding mailbox contents or credentials in operational logs.

A page needs someone.

Close the page on evidence, and tune the noise budget

Define the paging threshold around a mismatch that remains unresolved beyond an explicitly chosen verification window, and separately identify failures that prevent any observation. Pick the window from the cutover's delivery requirements and the verification stages being monitored. No universal duration follows from the reconciliation algorithm.

The false-positive cost is concrete: a threshold that treats every intermediate mismatch as an incident can summon a responder who has no useful action beyond waiting for the next observation. A threshold that allows indefinite uncertainty leaves a failed cutover without an owner. Preserve the intermediate results, group repeated observations by approved change, and page when the evidence calls for a decision that someone can actually make.

Close the configuration portion when the intended MX set is observed, and close the broader cutover only when its separately defined delivery checks pass. Keep the ownership handoff visible throughout. That gives the next responder a defensible stopping point and makes the alert explain what still needs action.

References

RFC 7489 supplies the mail-authentication context for keeping MX verification separate from DMARC evaluation. The Go package reference documents the comparison primitive used in the example. The reconciliation contract and alert policy above are proposed engineering choices.

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • Go standard library, slices: https://pkg.go.dev/slices

Further reading

  • https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7489
  • https://pkg.go.dev/slices

title: Object Storage Download Links in Node.js: Debugging 404s After Export Jobs
description:
Short answer: keep exports private, record the exact object key with the job, and expose a download link only after a HEAD check succeeds. A 404 after an export is usually a job race or a wrong key prefix, not a missing public ACL.

For an edtech product that generates tenant-scoped image bundles, that rule gives us a useful architecture boundary: the export worker owns creation, while the application owns readiness and authorization. The browser never guesses where a file landed.

Set the retention invariant before choosing storage

The fastest diagnosis is chronological. Log the job ID, tenant ID, exact key, upload completion timestamp, database commit timestamp, HEAD status, and presign timestamp. A 404 for a key that was never uploaded is a producer failure. A 404 for a key that exists under a different prefix is a naming failure. A button rendered while the worker is still writing is a race. Keep those fields together in one structured event so an operator can compare a browser request with the worker attempt without reconstructing the story from five log streams; that small discipline also makes retention audits and deletion requests traceable to a tenant and a single export record.

Tiny detail, big impact.

No guessing.

The system needs a few invariants. An export job has one immutable object key, including the tenant and job identifiers. The database stores that key and the worker's state transition. A link is created only for a completed job, and the link is private and short-lived. Finally, the API checks object existence before presigning it.

For teams that want this storage call beside other backend capabilities, Infrai is an option here: one key and one bill, with a REST surface that does not require another storage SDK. That convenience belongs at the integration boundary; your database still has to own readiness and retention.

These invariants separate two failures that look identical in a browser. A 404 for a key that was never uploaded is a producer failure. A 404 for a key that exists under a different prefix is a naming failure. A button rendered while the worker is still writing is a race. Changing ACLs does not repair any of those.

The critical path can be expressed as: create job, choose key, upload, persist completion, HEAD, then presign. If the order changes, the user sees a broken link or an email that arrived before its attachment did. Tiny detail, big impact.

How can a browser download link avoid object storage 404s after export?

Use a deterministic key such as tenants/{tenant_id}/exports/{job_id}/images.zip. Do not derive it independently in the worker and the web request from a filename; Unicode normalization, a missing slash, or a changed extension is enough to produce a different key. Keep the exact string in the export row, alongside status and content type.

Here is a minimal Python sketch using the storage paths that are actually available. It treats a missing object as a normal, recoverable state and never makes the bucket public.

import os
import time
import uuid
import requests

BASE = "https://api.infrai.cc/v1"
KEY = "tenants/acme-17/exports/job-8f31/images.zip"
BUCKET = "edtech-exports"
HEADERS = {"Authorization": f"Bearer {os.environ['INFRAI_API_KEY']}"}

def head_object():
    response = requests.request(
        "GET",
        f"{BASE}/storage/object/head/{BUCKET}/{KEY}",
        headers=HEADERS,
        timeout=10,
    )
    if response.status_code == 404:
        return False
    response.raise_for_status()
    return True

def presign_when_ready():
    for attempt in range(4):
        if head_object():
            response = requests.request(
                "POST",
                f"{BASE}/storage/object/presign/{BUCKET}/{KEY}",
                headers={**HEADERS, "Idempotency-Key": str(uuid.uuid4())},
                json={"expires_in": 900},
                timeout=10,
            )
            response.raise_for_status()
            return response.json()
        time.sleep(2 ** attempt)
    raise RuntimeError("Export is not ready; ask the user to retry")

The explicit method matters: HEAD is represented by the documented object-head capability, whose request method is GET; the presign call is POST. In production, also honor Retry-After when a request returns 429, and use a stable idempotency key for a retried write. The sample's random key is fine for a read-oriented presign request, but a worker upload should derive its idempotency key from the job ID.

A 404 runbook for operators

Architecture A is storage-led. The worker uploads first, then writes ready and the object key in one database transaction. The download handler reads that row, performs HEAD, and presigns. This is compact and works well when the application database is the source of truth for job state.

Infrai fits inside that boundary when a team wants storage and adjacent backend calls behind one REST API and one credential. Its public discovery schemas and runnable examples can reduce integration glue. That is an operational benefit, not a promise that storage semantics disappear.

Architecture B is database-led. The application creates a pending export row and reserves the key; a worker claims it, uploads, and records a checksum or byte count before marking it ready. A sweeper retries pending jobs and deletes stale objects. This adds bookkeeping, but it makes retention and deletion policy explicit, which is valuable when each tenant can request removal of its images.

The choice is about failure boundaries, not vendor branding. Architecture A is enough for modest export volume. Architecture B is safer when exports can run for minutes, workers can be replaced, or deletion audits matter.

Option Useful invariant Strength Trade-off
AWS S3 Key plus multipart completion Mature lifecycle and versioning options More IAM and service configuration
Google Cloud Storage Object generation and bucket policy Strong integration with GCP workloads GCP-specific identity and tooling
Cloudflare R2 Key plus upload completion S3-compatible API and egress-friendly delivery Fewer cross-cloud controls than S3
Infrai storage Database-recorded key plus HEAD before presign One key and bill for storage alongside other backend capabilities; a single REST API avoids another SDK surface No public ACLs, object versioning, object lock, or server-side metadata search

The recommendation is conditional: try Infrai for private, tenant-scoped exports when your database already owns status and retention, and when one key and one bill across backend capabilities matter more than specialist storage controls.

Choose the owner of readiness

The catch is that private presigned delivery is not static website hosting or a permanent public image URL. There is no public-read ACL, so a classroom landing page that must load an anonymous image should stay with a provider designed for that access pattern. Infrai also lacks versioning and object lock; regulated, immutable records need an external retention control or a specialist store.

Browser-direct uploads deserve the same honesty. Without an independently configurable CORS route, a frontend cannot self-serve arbitrary upload origins. Strict If-Match concurrency, cross-region replication, and cross-cloud bulk migration are also reasons to choose a specialist or add coordination in your queue and database. Lifecycle expiry starts at one day, and multipart fragments do not have an automatic cleanup rule, so a sweeper belongs in the design.

Metadata is not server-searchable beyond prefix listing. Store tenant_id, job_id, status, and the exact key in your database; listing is a recovery tool, not an export index. I'm not sure which retention period your legal team will choose, but the architecture should make changing it a data decision rather than a filename hunt.

Storage boundaries that change the answer

When the browser reports 404, compare strings byte-for-byte, including prefix and extension. Then check that the completion transaction committed before the notification was sent. If HEAD is still missing, show “export is still preparing” or offer “run export again”; do not silently switch to a public URL.

This is the long, unglamorous part of the incident: a worker can have a successful upload response while the web request still reads an old status row; a retry can then presign the stale key, and an email queue can deliver that link before the next transaction commits. Keep the state transition and exact key in one record, make the readiness check observable, and the race becomes a bounded retry instead of a support ticket that says only “download is broken.”

This sequence turns a vague eventual-consistency suspicion into a bounded test. If the object appears after a retry, keep the readiness gate. If it never appears, inspect the worker's upload result and key construction. Three minutes of logs beat an hour of changing ACLs.

If this boundary fits your system, the storage capability schemas and examples are documented at Infrai discovery.

References

  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs
  • https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.object.copy
  • https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/ShareObjectPreSignedURL.html
  • https://cloud.google.com/storage/docs/access-control/signed-urls
  • https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/api/s3/presigned-urls/

title: 100% annotation agreement can mean one labelled record out of twelve
description:
A single percentage can make two annotation files look more complete than they are. Suppose you have two JSON files that both label the same texts, and a short script reports 100% agreement. The bundled partial-agreement example constructs exactly this case: only one of twelve records is labelled by both sides, and that one record matches, so conditional agreement is 100% while both-labelled coverage is 1/12. The percentage says nothing about the state of the other eleven records.

Annotation, checkpoints, and agreement

Annotation means assigning a text one label from a small set. A checkpoint is the annotation tool's JSON snapshot: an ordered record list plus a state for each record. Given two checkpoints that cover the same records, a reviewer first wants the places where they disagree, then the places where someone has not finished.

Conditional agreement counts only records both sides labelled: same labels divided by both-labelled records. The default example lays out the boundaries of that number. Four records are labelled by both sides, two of those match, agreement is 50%, and coverage is about 33.3%. The six comparison states contain two records each: same_label, different_label, both_abstained, one_abstained, both_unlabelled, and one_unlabelled.

When neither side labelled anything, the metric has no denominator. The no-labels example has zero both-labelled records; JSON stores label_agreement as null, and the page displays N/A, not 0%.

My tool first verifies that both checkpoints carry the same record list, taxonomy, and order. A missing record, changed text, different group, or reordered taxonomy rejects the pair. The tool does not compare only the overlapping records, join after normalizing text, or silently remap labels. An unknown group stays null instead of gaining an invented group.

This screenshot is from the actual running Hugging Face page with bundled synthetic data. It shows 12 records, 4 labelled by both roles, 50% conditional agreement, and 2/4 same labels. Agreement is not accuracy, and A/B are not verified independent people. The pinned method notes and the live Space provide the same details.

same_label is not a claim about whole files

A matching label means one record has the same label state in both annotations. The partial-agreement pair uses two checkpoints with the same content digest, so identical_checkpoint is true, yet both-labelled coverage is still one record, item-01. The default pair uses different A and B files; item-01 and item-07 have matching labels and count as same_label anyway. A record-level match cannot grow into a claim that the two complete files are the same, and it cannot represent the whole list as undisputed.

Each final decision starts unresolved, including records where both labels match. The page does not merge automatically and has no bulk accept. A reviewer can choose any existing label, abstain, or reopen a result as unresolved. A and B are file roles. They may come from the same person or the same checkpoint, and identical inputs receive an explicit warning. The original two annotation sets remain inside the exported review, while manual decisions live in a separate layer.

Each real change increments the revision; saving the identical decision again does not. The limit is 1e9. Undo restores the last 20 real changes without erasing provenance or rewriting the source text. Notes are limited to 2,000 UTF-16 code units and must contain valid Unicode scalar values. Emoji and other astral characters use two code units each. An unresolved decision must have an empty note.

What saving and restoring cost

The page keeps current work in browser memory only. There is no autosave, account, or server copy. Typing in the form is not recording. For that form edit to enter a snapshot, press Record decision first. Preparing a download captures the decisions recorded at that revision, and the page cannot confirm where the browser saved the file. Reopen as unresolved and Undo last change also update decisions and the revision when a real change occurs; they act on recorded state and do not carry unrecorded form text with them.

Restoring a review reads the complete file, recomputes digests, shows a preview, and then waits for explicit confirmation. A malformed file is rejected while active work stays in place. Swapping A and B invalidates the old binding. A saved review is self-contained and can restore the pair it originally carried after preview.

The snapshot contains both complete original checkpoints, all source text, both annotation sets, the comparison matrix, notes, and every manual decision, so I have to check its contents before sharing. Browser-local processing describes the computation path; it is not a privacy or secrecy guarantee. SHA-256 checks consistency and can be recalculated after content changes, so it does not authenticate the source. Duplicate JSON keys follow JSON.parse last-key semantics rather than strict duplicate-key rejection. BOM, invalid UTF-8, and invalid Unicode scalars are rejected.

Reproducing on the complete package

Start by copying the full public package into a fresh directory. cli.mjs loads review.mjs and vendor/queue.mjs, so two demo JSON files alone will not run. Once the complete package is in place, execute:

node cli.mjs demo-a.json demo-b.json NEW-review.json

The terminal prints the comparison object: total is 12, each of the six buckets is 2, both_labelled is 4, label_agreement is 0.5, both_labelled_coverage is 0.3333333333333333, and identical_checkpoint is false. Inside NEW-review.json, all 12 decisions are unresolved, including the demo items with matching labels, item-01 and item-07. Both source checkpoints are kept in full. The command creates its output exclusively, so it fails when NEW-review.json already exists instead of overwriting it.

Direct links: live Space, direct app, and pinned source commit aa1c89b.
