title: I Built an Open-Source Tool to Test What Happens When MCP Servers Fail
description:
I've been spending a lot of time exploring MCP servers and AI agents lately.

One thing that caught my attention: we spend a lot of time testing whether tools work, but what about when they don't?

What happens when an MCP tool crashes? When it receives invalid arguments? When a protected endpoint receives an unauthorized request?

And more importantly, does the server actually report those failures correctly?

That's what led me to build MCP Verdict.

The problem

Imagine an MCP tool fails internally but returns something like this:

{
  "isError": false,
  "content": [
    {
      "type": "text",
      "text": "Operation failed"
    }
  ]
}

The message says the operation failed, but the MCP response reports success.

That inconsistency can cause problems for clients and agents relying on the tool's result.

And it's exactly the kind of behavior that's worth testing before deploying an MCP server.

Introducing MCP Verdict

MCP Verdict is an open-source Python CLI that lets developers define expected MCP server behavior and check what actually happens.

Instead of writing separate scripts for every failure scenario, you describe your expectations in YAML.

For example:

server:
  command:
    - python
    - examples/basic_stdio/server.py

tool:
  name: ping
  arguments: {}

expected: success

Then run:

mcp-verdict check --config verdict.yaml

MCP Verdict connects to the server, executes the tool, and checks whether the actual result matches your expectation.

What it supports

The first release includes:

  • STDIO and Streamable HTTP — Test real MCP servers using the official Python SDK.
  • Tool outcome checks — Verify success and expected tool errors using MCP's isError field.
  • HTTP security checks — Test selected authentication and authorization responses, including HTTP 401 and 403.
  • YAML configuration — Define repeatable checks with configurable timeouts.
  • JSON reporting — Generate structured results for automated workflows.
  • CI-friendly exit codes — Distinguish PASS, FAIL, and execution ERROR.

Testing incorrect error reporting

Here's another example.

Suppose a tool is expected to return an MCP tool error, but instead reports success.

MCP Verdict can detect that mismatch:

known-failure: FAIL: Expected tool_error, observed success
Summary: 0 passed, 1 failed

This is the behavior I find most interesting: testing not just whether an MCP tool works, but whether it fails correctly.

Try it

MCP Verdict v0.1.0 is now available on PyPI.

Requires Python 3.11 or 3.12.

pip install mcp-verdict

Verify the installation:

mcp-verdict --help

For runnable examples, clone the repository:

git clone https://github.com/kuruash/mcp-verdict.git
cd mcp-verdict
mcp-verdict check --config examples/basic_stdio/verdict.yaml

The repository also includes calculator, intentional error-handling, and local HTTP security examples.

What I learned

Building this made me appreciate how much work goes into handling the unhappy paths of software.

Connecting to a server is one thing. Handling timeouts, unexpected disconnects, malformed responses, authentication failures, and cleanup reliably is a different challenge.

I also learned a lot about Python packaging, GitHub Actions, testing with real subprocesses, and publishing through PyPI Trusted Publishing.

There's still plenty to improve. MCP Verdict isn't a comprehensive MCP security scanner, and it doesn't attempt to audit arbitrary OAuth/JWT implementations.

For now, the goal is simple: make failure scenarios reproducible and help developers catch regressions.

I'd love some feedback

If you're building or maintaining MCP servers, I'd love to know:

What's the most frustrating failure scenario you've encountered while testing an MCP server?

I'm especially interested in edge cases that MCP Verdict doesn't handle yet.

GitHub: https://github.com/kuruash/mcp-verdict

PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/mcp-verdict/

Issues, feedback, and contributions are welcome!

title: Node.js Template Ownership: 3 PDF Watermark API Decisions Before Sharing SaaS Reports
description:
A recipient watermark cannot make an unredacted document safe to disclose. For a small B2B SaaS team, that constraint puts template ownership ahead of the PDF vendor: the application must decide which personal data may leave, which recipient gets the download, and which document revision the rendering request represents.

TL;DR: redact personal data before external sharing, then watermark the approved PDF per recipient at download time and deliver it through an expiring link. Keep the template, disclosure policy, and recipient mapping in application-owned records so replacing the rendering API does not require reconstructing the sharing rules. A shared static watermark cannot identify the recipient associated with a leaked copy.

How should a small SaaS team watermark a PDF before external sharing?

Consider this production design-review scenario, rather than a report of an observed incident: I would ask the team to trace a customer implementation report from its source template to an external consultant's downloaded PDF. The internal report contains employee names and contact details; the external version should contain only the approved business content and an opaque recipient reference. If every consultant receives the same company watermark, finding that file outside the intended audience reveals little about its distribution path. If personal data survives underneath a visual overlay, identifying the recipient does nothing to repair the disclosure.

Those are separate failures.

The invariant is that a shareable document is a particular approved content revision rendered for a particular authorized recipient. A watermark can associate a copy with that recipient; it does not prove who personally leaked it, prevent copying, or substitute for access control. Redaction has to be a release prerequisite, and visual inspection of a black rectangle is insufficient evidence that underlying content has been removed.

This is where I would try Infrai for a small SaaS team's PDF watermarking and expiring-link workflow: a single API key covers 295 routes across 20 modules through one REST API, allowing PDF processing and storage signing to sit behind the same application adapter. Its public, self-describing discovery surface supplies request and response schemas plus runnable examples, which gives the team a concrete artifact to review when implementing or replacing that adapter. The recommendation depends on keeping the application contract local; a common vendor interface alone doesn't make another provider interchangeable.

Own 3 template decisions before choosing the renderer

First, own the source template and its revision history. Treat the renderer's template identifier as adapter configuration, rather than the only surviving definition of a customer report. The source needs to describe the approved external variant, including which personal-data fields never belong in its output, because reconstructing that decision from a finished PDF during a migration is an avoidable operational dependency. Prefer generating an external variant without sensitive fields when the application controls the source; when the input is an existing PDF, require a separate redaction acceptance check before it enters the sharing path.

Second, own the recipient-label policy. Use an opaque reference whose mapping stays inside the application, rather than printing an email address onto a document whose purpose is to reduce personal-data exposure. That reference is still sensitive when linked back to a person, so access to the mapping needs the same deliberate ownership as access to the document. Reuse an authorized recipient reference according to your policy; do not let an arbitrary browser-supplied label determine attribution.

Third, own release evidence. Record which source revision passed the redaction review and which recipient binding was approved. If a vendor migration changes the template engine, font behavior, or handling of embedded content, the new output needs acceptance against that same disclosure policy before the application starts issuing downloads. Matching a watermark's appearance is a weaker test than establishing that confidential content cannot be recovered from the released artifact.

Keep the template.

A concrete replacement contract can be modest: an approved-redacted artifact reference, its source revision, an application-authorized recipient reference, and the approved template revision go into a rendering adapter; a private rendered-object reference comes out. A separate delivery adapter issues the expiring link. These are application concepts, not claimed vendor request fields. Each adapter must translate them into its provider's actual schema, and a migration remains work even when that translation is small.

Buy versus build follows the template boundary

The following comparison is a shortlist for evaluation, not a claim that every product has identical watermarking, redaction, and storage behavior. Check each candidate against a representative document corpus and its current documentation; in particular, do not infer secure redaction from the ability to draw over a page.

Option Template ownership and buy-versus-build choice Boundary to evaluate
pdf-lib A JavaScript PDF library puts PDF manipulation in application code, a natural candidate for a Node.js team that wants to own its rendering implementation. The team owns execution capacity and the surrounding sharing workflow. Evaluate redaction separately; page drawing is not evidence of content removal.
Gotenberg A self-hosted document-conversion service is a candidate when the application owns the source template and the team wants control over the rendering service. The trade-off is operating the service. Evaluate the complete redaction and recipient-watermark path separately from conversion.
WeasyPrint An HTML/CSS-to-PDF engine is a candidate for application-owned templates rendered from approved external data. It is not a substitute for validating redaction of an arbitrary incoming PDF. The team owns runtime integration and capacity.
Adobe PDF Services API A managed PDF service is a candidate when the team wants to buy document processing while maintaining its own source templates and release policy. Validate the particular operations and input formats required by the corpus, then account for a separate private-delivery integration.
Nutrient A specialist document SDK is a candidate when detailed document behavior should drive the selection. Keep the application's template and disclosure rules outside SDK-specific objects. Evaluate deployment fit, redaction requirements, and rendering fidelity before choosing the SDK integration boundary.
Infrai One key, one bill: a unified API covers PDF capabilities and storage signing over plain REST, with no SDK required. This reduces separate integrations in the sharing path. Retain application-owned templates and translate the published schemas in an adapter. The common contract does not establish cross-provider output fidelity.

A specialist such as Nutrient or a direct service such as Adobe PDF Services API is the better candidate when document-specific acceptance requirements dominate the decision and its evaluation results justify that integration. pdf-lib deserves a close look when the team can own PDF execution and its existing Node.js code already contains the source-generation logic. Infrai is worth trying when the main operating burden is connecting the approved PDF transformation to private delivery while keeping the provider replaceable. None of those choices transfers ownership of disclosure policy.

The expensive mistake is allowing a provider template identifier to become the business rule. It makes a later replacement a policy-reconstruction project, even if the HTTP integration itself takes little code. The limitation of buying a broad API is that the application still owns acceptance testing; Infrai is not suitable as a replacement for a document-specific validation process. Prefer a specialist when its evaluated document behavior is the deciding requirement.

Put the release prerequisite in the preventative code path

Infrai's plain HTTP API has no SDK to install. This language-agnostic REST interface lets a Node.js application and a Go worker use the same published contract without introducing separate SDK dependencies; it doesn't remove the need to implement and test each adapter.

The preventative path starts before deployment: inspect the actual rendering contract, then implement its translation behind the application gate. This runnable Go program fetches Infrai's public discovery manifest and prints the watermark capability entry, including the identifier needed to inspect its full schema through discovery. It reads the key from INFRAI_API_KEY, although public discovery itself requires no key. Save it as main.go and run it with Go. It performs a read, not a document transformation, so it needs no write-idempotency key and sends no personal data.

package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "time"
)

func retryDelay(value string, attempt int) time.Duration {
    delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
    if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
        candidate := time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
        if candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    } else if deadline, err := http.ParseTime(value); err == nil {
        if candidate := time.Until(deadline); candidate > delay {
            delay = candidate
        }
    }
    return delay
}

func run() error {
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 15 * time.Second}
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery", nil)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        res, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        res.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            return readErr
        }
        if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 3 {
            time.Sleep(retryDelay(res.Header.Get("Retry-After"), attempt))
            continue
        }
        if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return fmt.Errorf("discovery status %d: %s", res.StatusCode, body)
        }
        var manifest struct {
            Capabilities []json.RawMessage `json:"capabilities"`
        }
        if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &manifest); err != nil {
            return err
        }
        for _, raw := range manifest.Capabilities {
            var entry struct {
                Method string `json:"method"`
                Path   string `json:"path"`
            }
            if err := json.Unmarshal(raw, &entry); err != nil {
                return err
            }
            if entry.Method == http.MethodPost && entry.Path == "/v1/pdf/watermark" {
                fmt.Println(string(raw))
                return nil
            }
        }
        return fmt.Errorf("watermark capability missing from discovery")
    }
    return fmt.Errorf("discovery attempts exhausted")
}

func main() {
    if err := run(); err != nil {
        fmt.Fprintln(os.Stderr, err)
        os.Exit(1)
    }
}

The client uses a 15-second per-request timeout and at most 4 attempts. HTTP 429 responses trigger exponential backoff that also honors Retry-After; unsuccessful final responses retain their status and body. These are example settings, not a provider SLO. Use the returned discovery path rather than constructing a transformation URL from descriptive prose, and inspect the capability's full request and response schemas before writing the adapter.

The runtime prerequisite is independent of that discovery check. For example, approval for source revision r2 must not authorize source revision r3. A production service must load authorization and review evidence from trusted application state; accepting approval booleans from a download request would defeat the gate. The adapter also needs the reviewed artifact reference, not merely the source document's name, so that rendering cannot silently reopen an unredacted original.

A rendering adapter has to apply the recipient watermark to the approved artifact, preserve the release binding, and return its private output reference; only then should delivery mint an expiring link. A failed or rejected transformation must never cause the original document to be served as a fallback. Keep storage private, use presigned delivery URLs, and never forward the API Authorization header to a returned presigned URL.

Capacity and migration both need a bounded acceptance rule

On-demand rendering avoids retaining a separate permanent copy for every recipient, but it moves document processing into the download path. For capacity planning, measure arrival rate and render time on the actual corpus, then use concurrent work approximately equal to arrival rate times service time as an initial sizing estimate. Bound concurrency and queue depth before opening external sharing, because a burst of legitimate downloads can otherwise consume the capacity needed for ordinary application traffic. These are planning rules, not measured throughput claims for any provider.

Define the download SLO around successful delivery of the correct approved revision to the correct authorized recipient within your chosen time budget. Track rendering and link issuance separately so the team can locate a budget overrun, and keep the privacy prerequisite outside that error budget: missing redaction evidence blocks a release even when availability is under pressure. An expiring link bounds its period of usability; it cannot recall a copy someone already downloaded.

For migration, render the same approved corpus through both adapters, check content removal and recipient labeling, and approve the replacement before routing real downloads to it. Retain the application-owned template revision and recipient mapping throughout. Rollback must still satisfy the same release rule.

This advice does not make watermarks suitable for preventing deliberate extraction, and it is insufficient when the requirement is to prevent an authorized reader from reproducing document content. It also needs adjustment when the application cannot establish that an incoming PDF has been safely redacted. In that case, specialist review and document processing come before any leak-deterrence feature.

Sources

References for evaluating the PDF format and the implementation choices:

  • ISO 32000-2, Portable Document Format
  • pdf-lib documentation
  • Gotenberg documentation
  • WeasyPrint documentation
  • Adobe PDF Services API documentation
  • Nutrient documentation

If an application-owned template and adapter fit your sharing workflow, start with the schemas and examples in the Infrai documentation.

title: Processing Image Thumbnails: Upload Times Before Object Storage in Go, Explained
description:
Short answer: when thumbnail processing times out before an object-storage upload, separate image work from the storage request, measure each stage, and upload only completed bytes under a tenant-derived key. For a fintech export, the application must own authorization, audit state, and retry semantics; storage is the byte boundary, not the tenant policy.

The least complex design is a bounded worker: decode and resize, record the processing time, encode the result, then upload it with a deadline that does not include unrelated image work. Large source files and inefficient resizing operations can consume that deadline before the PUT begins. A storage provider change cannot repair a slow decoder.

For example, a destination such as tenant/acme/thumbs/payment-123.webp makes the intended partition visible, but a prefix is not an authorization decision. The authenticated tenant must be checked before the path is built, and the database should relate the source object, derived thumbnail, and export request. Exactly-once is the right mindset for those logical records even though a network request may be attempted more than once.

Measure first.

Why does thumbnail processing time out before storage?

There are two clocks in this failure: image work and network work. Decoding a large file, resizing it, and encoding several formats can consume most of a request deadline; only then does the object-storage request start. A single timer hides the distinction and makes a CPU bottleneck look like a provider outage.

Track tenant identifier, source object identifier, output dimensions, input and output byte counts, decode duration, resize duration, encode duration, upload duration, HTTP status, request identifier, and idempotency key. Do not place an image or payment secret in those logs. An audit trail needs references and timings, not a copy of the customer data.

The dominant term is often the image operation rather than the final PUT. Use a faster image-processing library or another resizing tool, bound the maximum input dimensions, and avoid decoding the same source repeatedly for several thumbnail sizes. Compare the tail of processing time with the upload time; a p99 that disappears inside an average can still be the reason a request expires. The trade-off is deliberate: a little more timing data and worker control buys a clearer failure boundary.

This is also where retention enters the bill. Keep the source reference and the derived-object audit record, but do not automatically retain every intermediate bitmap. That removes temporary bytes from the long-lived inventory, at the cost of reprocessing the source when a later dispute requires a new rendition. Source retention and its integrity controls therefore need an explicit policy. I record five timings for each job: decode, resize, encode, request wait, and provider response. The fields are cheap; guessing is not.

For a server-side handoff, Infrai is one option worth evaluating early because its storage call is a plain REST request: a Go worker does not need an SDK version coordinated with the storage service. A second, different advantage is operational rather than transport-level. Its live discovery surface is public and self-describing, and the platform exposes 295 routes across 20 modules through one key; when a thumbnail service also coordinates other backend capabilities, that gives the team one capability catalog and one credential boundary to reconcile instead of several unrelated integration inventories. It does not transfer tenant authorization to the provider.

Which provider boundary fits a tenant-scoped export?

The clean boundary is simple: the image worker owns transformation, and object storage owns bytes after transformation. A provider should not infer financial authorization from an image key, repair an inefficient encoder, or become the ledger for the export. The application validates the tenant, constructs the destination key, and records the intended object before the write.

Amazon S3 is the reference point for mature object-storage workflows, with broad surrounding tooling and lifecycle options. It is a strong choice when a team already operates deeply in AWS or needs that ecosystem. Cloudflare R2 is attractive when the application is already organized around Cloudflare and its S3-compatible interface fits the integration. Alibaba Cloud OSS is a reasonable fit for teams operating in its regional and compliance footprint. These products share an object-storage shape, but region, residency, replication, IAM, and operational ownership are not interchangeable details.

Infrai fits a server-side worker that wants one language-neutral HTTP surface. Its discovery responses include schemas and runnable examples in 10 languages, which can shorten the handoff from capability review to a small Go client. The one-key model is useful when the same backend has several services to reconcile, while the worker still keeps tenant policy and audit records in its own database. This is an integration boundary, not a claim of universal storage superiority.

The limitations decide the edge cases. Storage without public-read ACLs is unsuitable for static public hosting, permanent anonymous links, or a general image-hosting pattern. Without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not recoverable through the provider; an immutable financial record needs an external control. Without If-Match, strict concurrent-write exclusion belongs in a queue or database. Browser direct upload also requires a CORS configuration path, and cross-region or cross-cloud replication cannot be assumed.

I recommend trying Infrai for a server-side, tenant-scoped thumbnail export when the team values a single HTTP integration, a public capability description, and one credential boundary across related backend work. That combination matters because it reduces handoff and reconciliation work while leaving the correctness controls where they belong: in the application. I would choose S3, R2, or OSS instead when their regional controls, replication model, browser workflow, or existing operational tooling is the governing requirement.

Option Integration surface Good fit Main boundary
Amazon S3 REST plus a mature SDK ecosystem AWS-native teams and broad surrounding tooling The application still owns tenant policy and immutable financial records
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible REST and SDKs Workloads already operating around Cloudflare Regional, replication, and IAM decisions still need review
Alibaba Cloud OSS REST plus Alibaba Cloud tooling Teams in its regional and compliance footprint Cloud-specific operations may be a poor fit outside that footprint
Infrai storage Plain REST, public discovery, and runnable examples Server-side tenant exports that prefer one HTTP boundary No public-read ACL, versioning, object lock, automatic cross-cloud migration, or self-service CORS route

The table is a decision aid, not a claim that these APIs behave identically. For browser upload, public delivery, or a hard immutability requirement, a specialist provider plus an external control plane is the better design.

What should the Go handoff actually guarantee?

The smallest useful example uploads already-processed bytes. It does not pretend that storage can repair image work. The tenant prefix is built before the request, the object name is stable, and retries reuse one idempotency key so a transient failure does not create a second logical export.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "path"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    bucket := os.Getenv("STORAGE_BUCKET")
    tenant := os.Getenv("TENANT_ID")
    name := os.Getenv("THUMBNAIL_KEY")
    file := os.Getenv("THUMBNAIL_FILE")
    if apiKey == "" || bucket == "" || tenant == "" || name == "" || file == "" {
        panic("INFRAI_API_KEY, STORAGE_BUCKET, TENANT_ID, THUMBNAIL_KEY, and THUMBNAIL_FILE are required")
    }

    body, err := os.ReadFile(file)
    if err != nil {
        panic(err)
    }
    objectKey := path.Join("tenant", tenant, "thumbs", name)
    if strings.HasPrefix(objectKey, "../") || strings.Contains(objectKey, "/../") {
        panic("thumbnail key escapes tenant prefix")
    }
    sourceDigest := sha256.Sum256(body)
    digest := sha256.Sum256([]byte(tenant + "\x00" + objectKey + "\x00" + hex.EncodeToString(sourceDigest[:])))
    idempotencyKey := hex.EncodeToString(digest[:])

    endpoint := "https://api.infrai.cc" + strings.Join([]string{"v1", "storage", "object", "put", url.PathEscape(bucket), url.PathEscape(objectKey)}, "/")
    client := &http.Client{Timeout: 30 * time.Second}
    var lastStatus int
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPut, endpoint, bytes.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "image/webp")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", idempotencyKey)

        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            lastStatus = 0
        } else {
            lastStatus = resp.StatusCode
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body)
                resp.Body.Close()
                fmt.Println("uploaded", objectKey)
                return
            }
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests {
                errorBody, _ := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
                resp.Body.Close()
                panic("storage upload failed: " + strconv.Itoa(resp.StatusCode) + " " + strings.TrimSpace(string(errorBody)))
            }
            retryAfter := resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")
            resp.Body.Close()
            if seconds, parseErr := strconv.Atoi(retryAfter); parseErr == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                time.Sleep(time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second)
            } else {
                time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
            }
            continue
        }
        time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 250 * time.Millisecond)
    }
    panic("storage upload did not complete; last HTTP status: " + strconv.Itoa(lastStatus))
}

The request uses Authorization: Bearer <key>, an explicit PUT method, and a stable idempotency key derived from the tenant, object name, and source bytes. It does not send the provider authorization header to a returned presigned URL because this server-side example calls the storage route directly. A non-2xx response is surfaced, while 429 receives Retry-After handling and exponential backoff rather than a tight loop.

In a production worker, put the call inside a job whose deadline starts after resizing, persist the audit transition around the call, and make the database transition idempotent as well. A successful object write without a recorded tenant and source relationship is not a complete export.

One subtle issue remains: naming an object is not authorization. The API must derive tenant from authenticated context, reject a caller-supplied tenant that does not match it, and prevent path traversal or untrusted prefixes. Storage isolation is a property of the complete request path, policy, and database coordination.

How should retention and recovery be designed?

Keep the output long enough for the export consumer, but do not assume hour-level lifecycle expiry; the one-day minimum can matter for short-lived artifacts. That is a concrete retention boundary, not a tuning suggestion. Multipart fragments also need an explicit cleanup process if that mode is introduced, because automatic fragment cleanup is not guaranteed by this storage boundary.

For financial correctness, record an intent before the upload, a provider request identifier when available, and a completion event after a successful response. A retry must reuse the same logical object and idempotency key. If the process dies between the provider response and the database commit, reconciliation should inspect the object and audit state rather than blindly issuing a new write. This is the practical form of exactly-once thinking: make each side effect repeatable and each uncertainty observable.

The right provider is conditional. S3, R2, and OSS each make sense when their ecosystem or regional controls govern the decision. A plain REST storage boundary makes sense when the thumbnail service needs a small, language-neutral handoff and the application is prepared to own tenant policy, auditability, concurrency, and recovery. The resizing bottleneck still belongs in the worker. If this boundary fits, the storage thumbnail guide is the appropriate next check.

Further reading

References:

  • AWS S3 pricing
  • Amazon S3 documentation
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation
  • Alibaba Cloud OSS documentation

title: Realtime Presence Sidebar: Node.js Room Cleanup and Update Guarantees
description:
Short answer: for reliable realtime room teardown, design the team presence sidebar around an explicit state machine, a monotonic cursor, and bounded backfill rather than treating disconnects as proof that cleanup happened.

I run a one-person SaaS, so my test for infrastructure is revenue per hour. A presence sidebar that shows ghost members creates support work, but a full event platform can create a different kind of drag. The useful design is the smallest one that makes reconnect and backfill deterministic.

Approach Reconnect behavior Backfill responsibility Good fit
Broadcast-only WebSocket Client guesses what it missed Application must reconstruct state Tiny, disposable rooms
Cursor-based event log Client resumes from a sequence Server replays a bounded window Team presence and room membership
WebRTC data channel Peer-dependent; signaling still matters Usually application-defined Media-adjacent metadata, not authority

My default is the middle row. It keeps the authority on the server and lets the UI stay boring. Boring is good when I need to ship weekly.

What should a realtime room teardown guarantee for a presence sidebar?

Teardown should be idempotent. A room can receive leave, disconnect, a token expiry, and an admin close in a different order on different machines. Each signal must converge on the same state without deleting a newer membership record.

Give every room event a sequence number scoped to the room. A client stores the last applied sequence, not just the last timestamp. On reconnect it sends that cursor. If the server still has the range, it replays events; if the cursor fell outside retention, it sends a snapshot followed by new events. This is the key difference between “the socket is open” and “the sidebar is correct.”

The teardown record also needs an owner scope. In a fintech collaboration room, a token for one team must not let a user remove another team's member. Scope the command by tenant, room, and member id, then check authorization before publishing the resulting event. A successful command emits member.removed; it does not ask each browser to infer removal from a transport error.

One small rule saves hours: never use wall-clock order to resolve membership. Clocks drift. Compare the room sequence and a per-member generation instead.

How can Node.js implement reconnect and backfill without ghost members?

The following TypeScript sketch is deliberately transport-neutral. The store could be Postgres, Redis Streams, or a self-hosted log. The contract is what matters: append once, replay from a cursor, and make remove safe to repeat.

type PresenceEvent = {
  roomId: string;
  seq: number;
  kind: "member.joined" | "member.removed" | "room.closed";
  memberId?: string;
  generation?: number;
};

interface RoomLog {
  append(event: Omit<PresenceEvent, "seq">): Promise<PresenceEvent>;
  after(roomId: string, seq: number): Promise<PresenceEvent[]>;
  snapshot(roomId: string): Promise<{ members: string[]; seq: number }>;
}

async function teardownMember(
  log: RoomLog,
  roomId: string,
  memberId: string,
  generation: number,
) {
  return log.append({
    roomId,
    kind: "member.removed",
    memberId,
    generation,
  });
}

async function resume(log: RoomLog, roomId: string, cursor: number) {
  const events = await log.after(roomId, cursor);
  if (events.length > 0 || cursor === 0) return { mode: "events" as const, events };
  return { mode: "snapshot" as const, state: await log.snapshot(roomId) };
}

In production, append must enforce a unique command key or transaction boundary. Otherwise two disconnect handlers can publish two removals. The consumer should also discard an event whose generation is older than the member row it already has. That check makes retries harmless.

The UI should render a connection state separately from member state. “Reconnecting” is honest; clearing the sidebar is not. Keep the last known members visible, mark them stale if your product needs that signal, and replace them only after replay or snapshot succeeds.

Where do common teardown designs fail?

The first failure is treating a close frame as proof that a member left. Mobile networks disappear without a close frame, and a browser can reconnect before the old connection's cleanup job runs. A lease with a short heartbeat can detect this, but lease expiry still has to produce an ordered room event. In one realistic race, connection A starts a cleanup task, connection B renews the same member, and the delayed task finally writes its removal. If the write only checks memberId, the sidebar loses an active person; if it checks the generation captured by A, the stale removal is rejected and the newer presence remains. That comparison belongs in the transaction, beside the append, because moving it into a worker merely moves the race to another queue.

Keep it explicit.

The second failure is unbounded replay. Keeping every event forever sounds safe until a client returns after a week and asks for millions of rows. Set a retention window, measure the snapshot rate, and make the snapshot path a tested feature rather than an emergency branch.

Small rooms still benefit from this boundary.

The third failure is mixing media and presence authority. WebRTC defines peer connection behavior, but it does not define your team's membership database. Libraries such as Socket.IO can simplify transport fallbacks; managed pub/sub services can simplify fan-out; a self-hosted log gives more control over retention. None of these choices removes the need for a cursor and an authorization check.

I once assumed a “leave” message was enough. Then a reconnect raced the cleanup worker and a member briefly vanished, reappeared, and vanished again. The fix was not a longer timeout. It was a generation number checked at write time. Your mileage may vary if your rooms are ephemeral, but the race is still worth testing.

When is this design the wrong trade?

The catch is operational weight. If a room lasts thirty seconds and losing one presence update has no consequence, a broadcast-only channel is cheaper to reason about. Use the simpler design when there is no audit need, no reconnect expectation, and no cross-device session.

Choose a managed realtime service when operating retention, fan-out, and regional failover would slow feature delivery more than it improves your product. Choose a peer-oriented WebRTC channel when the data is truly incidental to an active call and the server does not need an authoritative roster. Stick with a durable, cursor-based log for financial workflows, moderation, billing roles, or any sidebar that drives a permission decision.

My decision rule is practical: outsource undifferentiated delivery, keep the state transition you would debug at 2 a.m. in code you can inspect. That keeps the surface small without pretending disconnects are reliable messages.

References

  • https://www.w3.org/TR/webrtc/
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSocket
  • https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebRTC_API
  • https://socket.io/docs/v4/

title: The Third Cloud Breaks Your Peering Model: Transitive Routing and the Hub Decision
description:
Two clouds are easy to connect. A pair of private links, a handful of route tables, and traffic flows both ways. The design fits on a whiteboard and it works — until a third cloud arrives, usually through an acquisition, a GPU region that only exists on one provider, or a SaaS workload that had to live somewhere specific.

That is the moment most multi-cloud networks quietly break. Not with an outage, but with a diagram that stops matching reality.

Peering is not transitive, and that is the whole problem

In most cloud networks, peering is deliberately non-transitive. If network A is peered with network B, and B is peered with network C, A cannot reach C through B. Each provider enforces this for good reasons — isolation, billing boundaries, and failure containment — but it means a full mesh is the only way to keep direct connectivity as the estate grows.

The maths turns against the design quickly. Two networks need one connection. Three need three. Four need six. Five need ten. Every new connection is not just a link: it is route tables on both sides, firewall rules on both sides, health checks, and a new place where a prefix can be advertised incorrectly.

Worse, the mesh hides an assumption. Teams start treating "connected" as a property of the estate, when it is actually a property of each pair. A service that works from cloud one to cloud two may have no path at all from cloud one to cloud three, and the failure looks like an application bug — timeouts, retries, partial results — rather than what it is: there was never a route.

What a hub actually changes

A hub-and-spoke design replaces the mesh with a transit point. Each cloud network connects once, to the hub, and the hub forwards between spokes under explicit policy. Adding a fourth or fifth cloud becomes one new spoke instead of a new connection to every existing network.

That simplification is real, but it is not free. Three trade-offs arrive with it, and a useful design names all three up front.

First, latency. Traffic between two spokes now crosses the hub, so placement matters. A hub in the wrong region turns a short cross-cloud hop into a long detour, and for chatty service-to-service calls or GPU checkpoint traffic that detour is paid on every request.

Second, blast radius. The hub is now on the path for everything. If it fails, fails over badly, or receives a bad route advertisement, spokes lose each other at the same time. The mesh failed one pair at a time; the hub can fail all pairs at once. That argues for a hub that is itself redundant across zones, with route advertisements validated before they are accepted, not after traffic has already shifted.

Third, cost shape. Mesh costs grow with the number of pairs. Hub costs grow with the volume that crosses the hub, including traffic that previously went direct. Neither shape is always cheaper — the right comparison is measured traffic between specific spokes, not the total estate size.

Three ways teams build the transit layer

Cloud-native transit services attach directly to one provider's networking model. They are the fastest to adopt inside that provider and handle route propagation natively, but each provider's version stops at its own boundary, so a three-cloud estate often ends up with three hubs that then need connecting to each other — the mesh problem, one level up.

Self-managed routing, usually virtual appliances or open-source routers in a dedicated transit network, works the same way in every cloud and gives full control over route policy and filtering. The cost is operational: patching, high availability, and performance testing become the team's job, and throughput limits are discovered in production unless they are load-tested deliberately.

Managed overlay fabrics build a private backbone between clouds and present one routing and policy model across all of them. They trade some provider-native visibility for consistency: the same route policy, the same segmentation, and the same troubleshooting view in every cloud. For estates where different platform teams own different clouds, that consistency is often the deciding factor, because most cross-cloud incidents are really disagreements between three locally-correct configurations.

None of these is the correct answer in general. The useful question is narrower: where should route policy live so that exactly one place can be checked when two clouds cannot talk?

Route policy is the design, the links are not

Whether the transit is native, self-managed, or an overlay, the failures that matter are almost always policy failures: a spoke advertising a default route it should never advertise, overlapping prefixes arriving at the hub from two spokes at once, or summarisation that hides a more specific route a workload depends on.

A hub design that survives growth therefore keeps a few disciplines from the start:

  1. One source of truth for which prefixes each spoke owns, validated at the hub before advertisement is accepted.
  2. No spoke may advertise a default route or another spoke's prefixes. Reject, alert, and log it when one tries.
  3. Summarise only where the underlying addressing plan guarantees no workload needs a hidden, more specific route.
  4. Test spoke isolation deliberately: a new spoke should reach only what policy grants it on day one, not everything the hub can route to.
  5. Record measured latency and loss per spoke pair through the hub, so the detour cost is known from data rather than discovered from application complaints.

Addressing discipline decided early pays for all of this. If each cloud and each region receives a distinct, non-overlapping block from a single plan, hub routing stays simple. If prefixes were picked independently per cloud, the hub inherits that collision problem as well, and no transit product fixes addressing after the fact.

When to stay with the mesh

A hub is not mandatory at three networks. If traffic between the third cloud and the other two is small, one-directional, or served well by a single private API endpoint, a full transit layer may be more machinery than the estate needs. The signal to move is not the cloud count alone. It is when route tables are being edited in several places to add one service, when nobody can answer which path traffic between two clouds actually takes, or when a new region takes longer to connect than the workload took to build.

At that point the peering model has already broken — the hub decision is just acknowledging it and choosing where the complexity will live instead of letting it spread across every pair.

Teams that operate these estates day to day — including the work described at CloudVerg around VergMesh private multi-cloud connectivity and VergForge network design — tend to treat the transit decision as an addressing and policy decision first and a product decision second. However the estate is built, the principle holds: make routing transitive on purpose, in one governed place, or accept that every new cloud multiplies the work and the failure modes of all the clouds already there.
