title: 1 of 41 Cold Emails Bounced. That's 2.4% or 1.9%, Depending on What You Divide By
description:
On Nov 9 I sent 41 first emails for cold outreach for Posting Dude, a backlink service I run. A day later my sending tool said 40 were delivered and 1 bounced.

1 in 41 is 2.4%. My pause line is 2%. So I should stop, right?

Except that batch wasn't the whole stream. Counting every first email I'd sent in that sequence so far, it was 1 bounce in 53. That's 1.9%. Under the line.

Same bounce, two answers. Here is how I decided, the small script I now run before any follow-up goes out, and the two DNS cases that would have bounced if I hadn't looked.

Why bother before the follow-up

Follow-ups are where a dirty list hurts twice. A bounced address in step 1 is one bad send. Leave it in the sequence and it bounces again on day 4, and again on day 11. Google's sender guidelines literally say to "automatically unsubscribe recipients who have multiple bounced messages" (Google's email sender guidelines). Mailbox providers keep score, and repeat bounces are the cheapest way to lose it.

So the check runs the day after the first batch, before day 4.

The 5 steps

1. Send the first email to a small batch. 41 people, not the whole list. If the list is bad, you find out on 41 addresses instead of 400.

2. A day later, pull the delivery status of every message. Not "sent". Sent only means your tool accepted it. You want delivered / bounced per address, from your sending tool's API or export. Mine gave 40 delivered, 1 bounced.

3. Divide by first emails only. Follow-ups go to people who already received mail from you, so they barely bounce (mine: 0). If you put them in the denominator your rate looks better than your list really is. Batch: 1/41 = 2.4%. Stream: 1/53 = 1.9%.

4. Set the pause line before you look. Mine is 2%, decided before the first send. Under it, keep going. Over it, stop and clean the list before anything else goes out. Deciding after you see the number is how 2.4% turns into "basically 2".

5. Never follow up a bounced address. Pull it out of the sequence the same day, so day-4 only goes to inboxes that actually took mail.

So which number won?

Both, for different decisions.

  • Stream-wide (1.9%) decides whether the sequence keeps running. It was under the line, so day-4 follow-ups stay scheduled for Nov 13.
  • Batch (2.4%) decides how fast I grow. That batch was over the line, so the next batch stayed at about 40 instead of going up. I only raise it if the next batch comes back with 1 bounce or fewer.

The one bounce was a role inbox (a support@ address), and it's suppressed now. Also, to be clear about results: zero human replies so far. One auto-ticket reply, which doesn't count. A clean list doesn't make people answer; it just stops you from burning the domain while you find out.

The script

No dependencies, Node 18+. Feed it a CSV export: email,step,status,code, where step is first or followup and code is the SMTP enhanced status code if your tool gives one.

// node bounce-check.mjs sends.csv [pauseLine=0.02]
// sends.csv columns: email,step,status,code   (step = first | followup)
import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";

const [file, pauseArg = "0.02"] = process.argv.slice(2);
const pauseLine = Number(pauseArg);
const rows = readFileSync(file, "utf8").trim().split("\n").slice(1)
  .map((l) => { const [email, step, status, code = ""] = l.split(",").map((s) => s.trim());
    return { email: email.toLowerCase(), step, status: status.toLowerCase(), code }; });

const firsts = rows.filter((r) => r.step === "first");
const bounced = (r) => r.status === "bounced";
const hard = (r) => bounced(r) && !r.code.startsWith("4"); // 5.x.x or no code = treat as permanent
const firstBounces = firsts.filter(bounced);
const rate = firstBounces.length / firsts.length;

console.log(`first emails: ${firsts.length}, delivered: ${firsts.filter((r) => r.status === "delivered").length}, bounced: ${firstBounces.length}`);
console.log(`bounce rate vs first emails: ${(rate * 100).toFixed(1)}%  (pause line ${(pauseLine * 100).toFixed(1)}%)`);
console.log(rate > pauseLine ? "STOP: over the pause line. Clean the list before anything else goes out." : "OK: under the pause line.");

// never follow up an address that bounced hard, anywhere in the stream
const dead = new Set(rows.filter(hard).map((r) => r.email));
const soft = new Set(rows.filter((r) => bounced(r) && !hard(r)).map((r) => r.email));

async function mx(domain) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://dns.google/resolve?name=${domain}&type=MX`).then((r) => r.json());
  if (res.Status === 3) return "NXDOMAIN (domain doesn't exist)";
  const recs = (res.Answer || []).filter((a) => a.type === 15).map((a) => a.data);
  if (recs.length === 0) return "no MX (mail falls back to the A record, risky)";
  if (recs.length === 1 && /^0 \.$/.test(recs[0])) return "null MX (domain says it takes no mail)";
  return "ok";
}

const due = firsts.filter((r) => r.status === "delivered" && !dead.has(r.email));
const keep = [];
for (const r of due) {
  const verdict = await mx(r.email.split("@")[1]);
  if (verdict === "ok") keep.push(r.email); else console.log(`skip ${r.email}: ${verdict}`);
}
for (const e of soft) console.log(`hold ${e}: soft bounce (4.x.x), retry later, don't sequence it yet`);
for (const e of dead) console.log(`suppress ${e}: hard bounce`);
writeFileSync("followups.csv", "email\n" + keep.join("\n") + "\n");
console.log(`follow-ups due: ${keep.length} -> followups.csv`);

I used Google's DNS-over-HTTPS endpoint because the box I run this on intercepts plain DNS. If yours doesn't, dns.promises.resolveMx works too.

Run against a made-up 7-row file (fake people, real domains), today:

first emails: 7, delivered: 5, bounced: 2
bounce rate vs first emails: 28.6%  (pause line 2.0%)
STOP: over the pause line. Clean the list before anything else goes out.
skip cara@example.com: null MX (domain says it takes no mail)
skip dev@no-such-domain-2026-11-11.com: NXDOMAIN (domain doesn't exist)
hold eli@outlook.com: soft bounce (4.x.x), retry later, don't sequence it yet
suppress support@shop.example: hard bounce
follow-ups due: 3 -> followups.csv

The parts that are easy to get wrong

Hard vs soft. RFC 3463 splits delivery failures into 4.x.x ("persistent transient failure", a full mailbox, a server that's down) and 5.x.x ("permanent failure", not likely to work if you resend). Suppress 5.x.x for good. Hold 4.x.x and retry later, but don't let it ride the sequence on autopilot. If your tool gives no code, treat it as hard. Guessing soft is how dead addresses get three emails.

"Delivered" doesn't mean the domain takes mail now. Some status APIs report what happened at send time. A day later a startup can be gone. That's why the script re-checks MX right before follow-ups.

Null MX. example.com publishes an MX record of 0 . today. That's RFC 7505's "null MX": the domain is telling you it accepts no mail at all. A naive check that only asks "is there an MX record?" passes it. The script catches it.

No MX at all. Mail then falls back to the domain's A/AAAA record. Sometimes that works, often it's a web server that won't take mail. I skip these for cold follow-ups; you might not.

If you'd rather eyeball one domain than run a script, the free email DNS checker on Uno (a directory I run) shows MX, SPF and DMARC with a plain verdict, including "this domain can't receive mail". And before any of this, your own sending domain needs SPF, DKIM and DMARC set up, which I wrote up in this SPF/DKIM/DMARC check before a launch email. The longer playbook on picking who to email in the first place is in how to send cold emails to your first B2B customers.

What I'd tell myself a week ago

  • Pick the pause line before the first send, and write it down.
  • Bounce rate is per first email. Keep follow-ups out of the denominator.
  • Look at both the batch and the stream. They answer different questions.
  • One bounce in 41 isn't a crisis. One bounce you email three times is a habit.

What pause line do you use for cold email, and do you count it per batch or per sequence? I picked 2% mostly by gut and I'd like to hear where other people landed.

title: Calcutta Hacks — Where Heritage Meets Technology
description:
1. Project Overview

Calcutta <Hacks/> is the official website developed for Apex Circle's 24-hour heritage hackathon in Kolkata. The event brought together technology enthusiasts, developers, designers, and innovators to explore the intersection of technology, creativity, and cultural heritage.

The goal was to create a digital platform that communicated the event's identity, presented essential information, and provided participants with a clear and engaging experience.

Rather than building another conventional hackathon landing page, the objective was to create a website that reflected Kolkata's cultural identity while maintaining a modern technology-focused visual language.

I contributed to the Web Team, focusing on frontend development, component architecture, responsive layouts, and the overall user experience.

2. The Problem

Hackathon websites are often treated as simple promotional landing pages. However, an event website needs to do more than look attractive.

Potential participants need to understand the event, discover its purpose, explore important information, and know how to participate without navigating through confusing sections.

The key challenges were:

  • Information Architecture: Presenting event details, schedules, speakers, themes, and participation information in an organized structure.
  • Visual Identity: Representing Kolkata's heritage and cultural identity without compromising the modern technology-focused appearance.
  • User Experience: Making important information easy to discover and understand.
  • Responsive Design: Delivering a consistent experience across mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.
  • Frontend Maintainability: Structuring the codebase so components and sections could be reused and maintained efficiently.

3. The Solution

I contributed to building a responsive, component-driven React website that served as the event's primary digital information platform.

The approach focused on three major areas:

A. Heritage Meets Technology

The visual direction balanced Kolkata's cultural identity with a modern hackathon aesthetic. The intention was to make the event recognizable and visually distinct rather than relying on a generic developer-event template.

B. Structured Information Experience

Event-related information was organized into clearly defined sections, helping visitors understand the event, explore its themes, discover schedules and speakers, and find participation information.

C. Responsive Frontend Architecture

The interface was developed using reusable React components and Tailwind CSS, with attention to consistent styling, responsive behavior, and maintainable code.

4. My Responsibilities

As part of the Apex Circle Web Team, my responsibilities focused on frontend engineering.

  • Developed frontend interfaces using React.js.
  • Implemented responsive layouts using Tailwind CSS.
  • Built reusable and modular UI components.
  • Organized website sections into a structured page architecture.
  • Worked on the visual presentation of event information.
  • Improved consistency across different screen sizes.
  • Focused on maintainable component structures and clean implementation.
  • Worked on translating the event's identity into a digital experience.

5. Key Features & Website Experience

Event Information

A structured presentation of the hackathon, its purpose, and essential event details.

Event Schedule

A dedicated information experience for communicating event activities and schedules.

Speakers & Themes

Organized sections for presenting speaker information and the event's central themes.

Participation Information

Clear presentation of participation-related details to help potential attendees understand how to get involved.

Responsive Interface

Layouts designed to adapt to mobile, tablet, and desktop screen sizes.

Reusable UI Components

A component-based approach to reduce duplication and maintain consistency across the website.

6. Technical Architecture

The project followed a frontend-only architecture.

Frontend Layer

  • React.js — Component-based UI development.
  • JavaScript — Application logic and interface behavior.
  • Tailwind CSS — Styling and responsive layouts.

Architecture Approach

  • Component-based development.
  • Reusable UI elements.
  • Separation of page sections and presentation components.
  • Responsive utility-based styling.

Backend: Not implemented.

Database: Not implemented.

Authentication: Not implemented.

API Integration: No custom backend API was implemented.

The project was intentionally limited to the frontend scope required for the hackathon website.

7. Design & User Experience Decisions

The primary design challenge was balancing two different identities:

  • Kolkata's cultural and historical heritage.
  • The innovation, experimentation, and energy of a technology hackathon.

The website needed to feel modern without losing its connection to the event's identity.

My frontend implementation prioritized:

  • Clear content hierarchy.
  • Consistent spacing and typography.
  • Responsive section layouts.
  • Reusable visual patterns.
  • Easy navigation through event information.
  • Consistent presentation across devices.

8. Challenges & How I Approached Them

Challenge 1: Balancing Heritage with a Modern Technology Identity

A conventional technology-event design would not communicate the cultural theme effectively.

Approach: The visual direction was designed around the relationship between Kolkata's heritage and modern innovation.

Challenge 2: Organizing Multiple Categories of Information

Hackathon websites contain different types of information, including event details, schedules, speakers, themes, and participation instructions.

Approach: I used a structured section-based layout to make information easier to discover.

Challenge 3: Responsive Layout Development

A website that looks good on desktop may not translate well to smaller screens.

Approach: I used Tailwind CSS responsive utilities and adaptable layouts to maintain usability across different screen sizes.

Challenge 4: Maintaining Reusable Code

Building every section independently can lead to duplicated markup and inconsistent styling.

Approach: I followed a reusable React component approach to improve consistency and maintainability.

9. Project Scope & Limitations

This project was developed as a frontend-only hackathon website.

The implementation focused on the visual interface, responsive layouts, component architecture, and event information presentation.

The following functionality was outside the project's implementation scope:

  • Backend services and server-side business logic.
  • Database storage and management.
  • User authentication and authorization.
  • Custom registration APIs.
  • Admin dashboard and content management.
  • Server-side participant data processing.

This distinction is important: the project demonstrates frontend development and UI engineering, not a complete full-stack event management platform.

10. What I Learned

Working on Calcutta <Hacks/> helped me understand that building a good event website requires more than writing React components.

Key takeaways:

  • Translating an event's identity into a consistent digital experience.
  • Organizing complex information into understandable sections.
  • Building reusable React components.
  • Developing responsive interfaces with Tailwind CSS.
  • Understanding the importance of frontend architecture and maintainability.
  • Working as part of a collaborative web development team.
  • Making implementation decisions within a defined project scope.

11. Project Outcome

The project delivered a dedicated frontend website for Apex Circle's Calcutta <Hacks/> 24-hour heritage hackathon.

It brought the event's identity, information, and participation experience into one digital platform while demonstrating my contribution to frontend engineering as part of the Web Team.

The biggest takeaway: A successful event website is not simply a collection of attractive sections. It is an organized digital experience that communicates the event's identity and helps its audience find the information they need.

Project Credits

Project: Calcutta <Hacks/>

Organization: Apex Circle

Contribution: Frontend Development — Web Team

Technologies: React.js, JavaScript, Tailwind CSS

Project URL: https://cuttahacks.abhishek-nexgen.xyz/

title: Scaffold Production-Ready Express.js with a Built-in Django-Style Admin Panel
description:
Tired of setting up Express boilerplate from scratch, configuring MVC, migrations, and building admin dashboards manually?

Meet express-mod-cli 🚀 — a production-ready Express.js CLI generator with modular MVC architecture, built-in Django-style admin dashboard, Zod validation, JWT auth, SQL migrations, and multi-database support.

✨ Key Features:

  • 🎛️ Django-Style Admin Panel: Instant dashboard at /admin with Classic, Modern, and Top-Menu themes (express-mod-cli add-admin).
  • 🏗️ Modular MVC Architecture: Clean domain-driven folders.
  • 🗄️ Multi-Database Support: Connect MongoDB, PostgreSQL, and MySQL simultaneously in one app (add-db).
  • ✅ Zod Schema Validation: Automatic request sanitization and schema generation.
  • 🔐 Authentication: Complete JWT refresh token rotation, roles, and password reset (add-auth).
  • 🟦 TypeScript & JavaScript: Full first-class support.

⚡ Quick Start: 

npx express-mod-cli create my-app --db mongodb
cd my-app
npx express-mod-cli add products name:string price:number
npx express-mod-cli add-auth
npx express-mod-cli add-admin
npm run dev

Check out the documentation and npm package:

  • 📦 NPM: https://www.npmjs.com/package/express-mod-cli
  • 🐙 GitHub: https://github.com/nizamseu/express-mod-cli

title: Should you learn Node.js, Django or Laravel first in Nepal?
description:
For most beginners in Nepal, learn Node.js first. JavaScript shows up in Kathmandu job posts for all three stacks, and SQL matters more than whichever framework you pick.

That is our answer, and we should say up front that Saarathi Academy in Old Baneshwor, Kathmandu teaches Node.js in its Backend Engineering course. So check the reasons below yourself. We also say when Django or Laravel is the better first pick.

Why do Laravel jobs in Kathmandu still ask for JavaScript?

Many Kathmandu companies use PHP and Laravel. That is true, and our own course page says so. But look at what those jobs ask for.

A Tekkon Nepal post on merojob for a Full Stack Developer (PHP/Laravel) listed PHP, MySQL, Laravel, Vue.js and CSS. Its requirements also named JavaScript and jQuery. Vue.js is a JavaScript framework.

Laravel itself needs JavaScript tools. The Laravel installation guide says you should install Node and npm, or Bun, to build your app's frontend files. So a Laravel developer uses Node tools on the first day.

The reverse is not true. A Node.js developer never needs PHP. If you learn JavaScript first, it stays useful in whichever job you take. If you learn PHP first and later join a Node team, you start a new language.

What do backend job posts in Nepal ask for in every stack?

We read four Kathmandu backend posts on merojob from 2024 and 2025. Two asked for Laravel and two asked for Node.js.

Every one of them asked for SQL, through MySQL, PostgreSQL or both. A backend post from a financial institution listed Laravel next to MySQL and PostgreSQL. A NodeJS Developer post from Citizen Infotech listed JavaScript, Git, RESTful API, SQL and PostgreSQL. A Node.js and NestJS post from GCG International asked for PostgreSQL and TypeScript.

Three of the four also asked for Git or REST API design. The framework was one line in each post. The rest was the same in every stack: how a request travels, how to design tables, how to write a JOIN, how to work with Git.

The tests look the same too. Mid-sized companies are most of the market here, and they usually start with a written test at their office. The questions are string and array problems by hand, plus SQL joins and normalisation, which means organising database tables well. No framework question decides that round.

So spend more of your first months on SQL than on any framework. Many beginners do the opposite.

When is Django the better first backend?

Pick Django if you already write Python with ease. Maybe you used it in college, or you want to move toward data or AI work later.

Django gives you a lot from the start, including an admin site to add, change and delete data. But the official Django tutorial expects you to know Python already. It uses functions and imports without teaching them. If Python is new to you, you learn two hard things at once, and that is slow.

Don't pick Django because a video called it easy. Pick it because you already know Python.

When is Laravel the better first backend?

Pick Laravel if you already have a job offer, an internship or a family business that runs on PHP. Then the fastest way to useful work is the stack in front of you.

Laravel has clear rules about where each file goes, and its documentation is friendly to beginners. Those are real strengths. They do not change our pick for someone who starts from zero with no employer yet.

Why Node.js for a beginner with no stack yet?

The first reason is one language. The Node.js introduction says frontend developers can write server code "without the need to learn a completely different language". You learn JavaScript once and use it on the server, in the browser, and in the Vue.js part of a Laravel job.

The second reason is a small first step. A Node server can be one short file, built with the node:http module that comes with Node. You see the raw request and response before any framework hides them. Express, Django and Laravel all wrap that same request, so the lesson carries over.

Our course follows this order. JavaScript and TypeScript are taught from zero in Weeks 2 and 3. Your first HTTP server uses Node's built-in http module in Week 3, before any framework. Express comes in Week 4 and NestJS in Week 5. Weeks 6 and 7 are about databases: SQL, PostgreSQL, data modeling, indexes and transactions. MySQL is covered only at awareness level, but the SQL you write carries over to it.

What can you try tonight?

Install the LTS version of Node.js from nodejs.org. Copy the example server from the Node.js introduction page into a file named server.js. Run node server.js and open http://127.0.0.1:3000 in your browser.

Now change res.statusCode = 200 to 404, save, and stop the server with Ctrl+C. Start it again and open your browser's developer tools on the Network tab. Reload and find the 404 there. You will read status codes like this in Node, Django and Laravel alike.

If you want the full order of topics, the Backend Engineering syllabus is public, week by week, and the course page has the rest.

title: From Booking Requests to Confirmed Bookings: Designing Reliable Server-Side Events
description:
A form submission is easy to track. A confirmed booking is harder.

In booking-based businesses, the customer may submit a request, reserve multiple seats, change plans, or cancel before attending. If all of those actions are counted as conversions, marketing reports can look successful while overstating actual business outcomes.

I worked on this problem in a booking attribution project where the goal was to connect campaign information, booking requests, CRM status changes, and analytics events.

This article describes the event-design decisions and testing approach. The code examples are simplified illustrations, not copies of production code.

1. Define the business outcome before the event

The first challenge was semantic, not technical.

Consider these stages:

  • Request created: Someone submits a booking form.
  • Booking confirmed: The booking is accepted and recorded as confirmed.
  • Booking cancelled: A previously requested or confirmed booking is cancelled.
  • Attendance recorded: Someone actually shows up.

These stages are related, but they are not interchangeable.

A request tells us that someone expressed interest. A confirmation tells us that the business secured a booking. Attendance tells us something different again.

The tracking model must preserve those distinctions.

In our project, the primary marketing outcome was a confirmed booking, not simply a form submission.

2. Model events around state transitions

Rather than sending an indistinguishable conversion every time something changes, define separate event types.

For example:

booking_created
booking_confirmed
booking_cancelled

A useful event record might look like this:

{
  "event_type": "booking_confirmed",
  "booking_id": "example-123",
  "event_id": "example-123:confirmed:1",
  "seat_count": 3,
  "source": "facebook",
  "campaign": "example_campaign",
  "occurred_at": "2026-10-15T14:40:00Z"
}

This is an illustrative schema, not an actual customer record.

Several properties are important:

  • booking_id connects the event to a business record.
  • event_id identifies the event for duplicate protection.
  • seat_count separates reservations from reserved places.
  • source and campaign preserve available attribution context.
  • occurred_at records when the business event happened.

A confirmation should be generated from the actual booking state, not inferred from a thank-you page.

3. Connect the website, CRM, and reporting pipeline

The implementation connects several parts of an existing booking system.

The simplified data flow is:

Campaign / source information
          |
          v
     Booking form
          |
          v
     Booking record
          |
          v
   CRM status transition
          |
          v
   Server-side event queue
          |
          +----> Google Analytics 4
          |
          +----> Meta Conversions API

The website captures a request. The booking system remains responsible for booking status. The integration layer turns relevant state changes into analytics events.

This separation matters because marketing tools should not decide whether a customer has been confirmed. That decision belongs to the business system.

The server-side layer can then provide consistent delivery, validation, and retry handling.

4. Make event processing idempotent

Duplicate events are one of the easiest ways to corrupt conversion reporting.

They can occur when:

  • A webhook is delivered more than once.
  • A request times out and gets retried.
  • A scheduled job processes a previously attempted event.
  • A status update is replayed.
  • Browser and server tracking report the same action.

A useful design principle is:

Processing the same business event twice should not produce two business conversions.

For example, an idempotency key can combine the booking ID, transition type, and a transition version:

booking-123:confirmed:1

Conceptually, the server-side processing logic becomes:

Receive event
    |
Validate event and consent
    |
Check idempotency key
    |
    +-- Already processed --> Do not create another event
    |
    +-- New event --> Store event and enqueue delivery
                              |
                              v
                       Send to platforms
                              |
                              v
                       Record delivery status

The event record and its queue entry should be created reliably together. A retry should reuse the same event identity rather than create a new conversion.

It is also important to distinguish accepted by an API from visible in an analytics report. Those are separate verification steps.

5. Don't confuse bookings with seats

One booking request can cover multiple people.

Suppose a customer requests three seats and the booking is confirmed.

That can mean:

  • One booking request.
  • One confirmed booking.
  • Three confirmed seats.

If the dashboard reports three bookings instead of three seats, the result is misleading.

A correct report needs explicit metric definitions.

For example:

Metric What it counts
Requests Booking requests submitted
Confirmed bookings Booking records confirmed
Confirmed seats Places within confirmed bookings
Cancelled bookings Bookings cancelled
Attendance Actual attendance records

This is especially important for events, appointments, group activities, and other businesses where one customer action can represent several participants.

6. Respect consent and attribution limits

Campaign parameters are useful, but they should only be processed and forwarded to analytics platforms when the applicable consent requirements are satisfied.

In this implementation, consent is part of the tracking flow rather than an afterthought.

There is also a difference between knowing the campaign associated with a booking request and identifying the exact Instagram conversation that produced it.

Those are different levels of attribution.

The current system can preserve available campaign information and report booking statuses. It does not establish a verified one-to-one match between every individual Instagram Direct conversation and a specific booking.

Reporting should communicate that boundary instead of implying a level of certainty that the data cannot support.

7. Test the business workflow, not just the tag

A successful network request does not prove that the overall tracking implementation is correct.

Testing should cover the complete path from an initial booking request to the final business status.

My checklist includes:

  1. Create a test booking request.
  2. Verify that a booking record is created.
  3. Confirm that the correct source information is retained when permitted.
  4. Check that request and confirmation events are separate.
  5. Confirm a booking containing multiple seats.
  6. Replay the same event and verify duplicate protection.
  7. Test cancellation or another status change.
  8. Check the queue and destination API responses.
  9. Verify reporting independently of API acceptance.
  10. Repeat relevant tests with consent declined.

Test records must also be distinguishable from real business results.

In the real project, some screenshots and counts come from integration tests. They demonstrate configured workflows, not proven increases in customers, sales, or revenue.

8. The lesson: measure verified states

A useful conversion-tracking system is not simply one that sends more events.

It is one that answers precise questions:

  • What actually happened?
  • Which system is authoritative for that outcome?
  • How do we prevent duplicate reporting?
  • Which attribution details are known?
  • Which details are still unknown?
  • Can the reported result be traced back to a business record?

When these questions are answered, analytics becomes much more useful for operational decisions.

I documented the real project, including implementation screenshots and its current limitations, in this booking attribution case study.

The broader principle applies beyond bookings: track confirmed business outcomes as distinct states, and test the entire data path before trusting a conversion report.

AI disclosure: AI tools were used to assist with drafting and structuring this article. The content was subsequently reviewed and edited by the author based on practical project experience.

title: The draw is 24% of the outcomes and 0.8% of the labels: auditing class collapse in a three-way model
description:
A three-class classifier that reports one label per row is not a three-class classifier. It is a ranking function collapsed to a decision, and the collapse is where the information dies. On our platform, 11,177 of 46,189 settled predictions ended in a draw; the label draw was emitted 360 times.

Every number below comes from the live production table, queried today, not estimated.

Two distributions that are required to match, and don't

The base table stores one row per model per match with the realised outcome attached. Two distributions matter: what happened, and what the model said would happen. If the second is a faithful compression of the first, they should be close.

-- D0: outcome distribution vs emitted-label distribution
WITH actual AS (
  SELECT actual_result AS cls, count(*) AS n
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
  GROUP BY 1
),
emitted AS (
  SELECT prediction_direction AS cls, count(*) AS n
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled
  GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT 'actual' AS side, cls, n,
       round(100.0 * n / sum(n) OVER (), 2) AS pct
FROM actual
UNION ALL
SELECT 'emitted', cls, n,
       round(100.0 * n / sum(n) OVER (), 2)
FROM emitted
ORDER BY side, n DESC;
side class rows share
actual home 20,445 44.26%
actual away 14,238 30.83%
actual draw 11,177 24.20%
actual NULL 329 —
emitted home 18,819 40.74%
emitted away/draw 10,997 23.81%
emitted away 10,085 21.83%
emitted home/draw 5,928 12.83%
emitted draw 360 0.78%

The draw happens 24.20% of the time and is named as the sole answer 0.78% of the time — a 31× under-representation. 16,925 rows name it as one of two outcomes; 27,647 rows chose strictly between home and away and could not be correct if the match finished level.

That last set is the interesting one. Of those 27,647 binary picks, 6,269 (22.68%) finished level. The ceiling was set by the label vocabulary, not the analysis.

Why the headline accuracy hides it

Reported accuracy by output arity on rows with a settled outcome:

arity rows hit rate
single 32,223 18,857 58.52%
double 13,608 7,385 54.27%

58.52% on single-label rows looks like a margin over chance. But chance for a 44/31/24 class split under a majority-class strategy is 44.26% — and the "single" bucket is not homogeneous: 4,490 of those rows had a compound single label (home/draw, away/draw) and 27,647 were strictly two-class. Averaging them reports neither.

This is a binary classifier wearing a three-class schema: any binary classifier over football outcomes pays a fixed 22.68% tax on the subset it is applied to. A genuine three-class system moves that tax into calibrated probability on the draw.

The audit query that should be a unit test

Aggregate accuracy is what lets this bug live for 46,000 rows. Per-class precision and recall make it visible in one screen:

-- D1: per-class precision / recall on the collapsed label set
WITH base AS (
  SELECT actual_result, string_to_array(prediction_direction, '/') AS picked
  FROM ai_predictions
  WHERE settled AND actual_result IS NOT NULL
),
exploded AS (
  -- a compound label is a set; a single label is a set of one
  SELECT actual_result, unnest(picked) AS cls FROM base
),
per_class AS (
  SELECT cls,
         count(*)                                    AS emitted_n,
         count(*) FILTER (WHERE actual_result = cls) AS correct
  FROM exploded
  GROUP BY cls
),
totals AS (
  SELECT actual_result AS cls, count(*) AS actual_n FROM base GROUP BY 1
)
SELECT c.cls, c.emitted_n, c.correct,
       round(100.0 * c.correct / c.emitted_n, 2) AS precision_pct,
       round(100.0 * c.correct / t.actual_n,  2) AS recall_pct
FROM per_class c
JOIN totals t USING (cls)
ORDER BY c.emitted_n DESC;

Result on the 45,860 rows with a non-null outcome:

class times emitted correct precision recall
home 24,564 13,154 53.55% 64.34%
away 20,941 8,399 40.11% 58.99%
draw 17,159 4,601 26.81% 41.16%

Draw precision of 26.81% hides the shape of the failure: draw alone hit 78 of 360 (21.67%), while away/draw hit 5,920 of 10,997 (53.83%) and home/draw hit 3,272 of 5,928 (55.20%). The compound labels are not predicting a draw — they express uncertainty between two outcomes, and the draw is an escape hatch. Recall on the draw is 41.16%: 6,576 draws were named by no label at all.

The most damning row: 283 distinct models emitted draw at least once across 46,189 predictions, and the busiest did it 4 times. No model here has learned to identify draws. Some occasionally guess.

Scoring both systems on one yardstick

Accuracy cannot compare a one-hot label with a distribution. Log loss can. The emitted label is scored as a probability vector (1.0 on the named class, split evenly for compounds) against the market-implied probability from the quoted three-way price, normalised to sum to one. 45,110 of 46,189 rows survive the price sanity filter.

import math

def implied(prices):
    inv = [1.0 / p for p in prices]
    s = sum(inv)
    return [x / s for x in inv]

LL_MARKET = LL_MODEL = BRIER_DRAW = 0.0
n = 0
for actual, ph, pd, pa, direction, arity in rows:
    mh, md, ma = implied((ph, pd, pa))
    LL_MARKET += -math.log(max({"home": mh, "draw": md, "away": ma}[actual], 1e-12))
    BRIER_DRAW += (md - (1.0 if actual == "draw" else 0.0)) ** 2

    if arity == "single":
        q_true = 1.0 if direction == actual else 0.0
    else:
        parts = direction.split("/")
        q_true = 1.0 / len(parts) if actual in parts else 0.0
    LL_MODEL += -math.log(max(q_true, 1e-12))
    n += 1

print(n, round(LL_MARKET / n, 4), round(LL_MODEL / n, 4), round(BRIER_DRAW / n, 4))
# 45110  0.9683  13.4625  0.1812

Log loss 0.9683 for the market-implied probabilities, 13.4625 for the emitted label — a factor of 13.9. That is what a zero looks like inside a logarithm: every row where the model picked a compound and the outcome was the excluded class contributes -log(0), clamped at 1e-12, or 27.6 nats.

This is not a claim that market probabilities are a good model. It is a claim about representation: a probability vector can be scored and improved; a one-hot label can only be counted, and counting rewards the majority class. The draw Brier of 0.1812 is what a real three-class output would have to beat.

What actually carries draw information

If confidence carried draw-risk signal, high-confidence binary picks would convert to draws less often. They don't. Draw rate among single picks restricted to home or away (27,647 rows, 6,269 draws):

confidence rows ended in draw draw rate
3 5,340 1,247 23.35%
4 5,188 1,013 19.53%
5 5,870 1,343 22.88%
6 5,426 1,314 24.22%
7 2,852 667 23.39%
8 1,705 437 25.63%
9 400 86 21.50%

Flat, and mildly inverted at the top: a model that says 9 is no less likely to be level than one that says 4. That is the expected failure when confidence is attached to a binary comparison and the third class was pruned before scoring — the pruning discards the evidence.

The market-implied draw probability, on the same 45,110 rows, is calibrated in the ordinary sense:

implied draw probability rows observed draw rate
0.0 – 0.1 688 6.40%
0.1 – 0.2 6,851 16.09%
0.2 – 0.3 34,460 25.11%
0.3 – 0.4 3,111 38.89%

Mean implied 0.2423 against an observed 24.20%. The information is already in a column we store, and it is thrown away at the label step.

The imbalance is structural, not random

Draw rates are not uniform across competitions. On 78,553 finished matches the overall draw rate is 24.69% (19,392 draws), and competition buckets with at least 500 settled rows span 15.49% to 30.42%:

competition matches draw rate
Argentina reserve league 674 30.42%
Spain RFEF third tier 1,635 29.60%
Italy fourth tier 898 27.17%
German regional league 667 27.14%
Club friendlies 5,297 26.79%
Norway third tier 594 15.49%

A single global threshold for "is this a draw?" is therefore wrong by about 15 percentage points. A per-class correction must be conditioned on the competition, and that requires a calibrated probability rather than a relabelled decision — you cannot attach a competition prior to a one-hot output.

Six rules that would have prevented this

  1. Store the distribution, not the decision. A row should carry p_home, p_draw, p_away; the label is a rendering derived at read time. Ours stores prediction_direction and a 1–10 integer, so every metric above had to reconstruct intent from a string.
  2. Never score a three-class problem by accuracy. Log loss and per-class recall, in the same query as the headline number.
  3. Assert a per-class floor in CI. If the draw is emitted in under 10% of rows while the observed base rate is 24%, fail the build.
  4. Measure compound labels separately. home/draw at 55.20% precision is not three-class capability; it inflates the "single" hit rate whenever the draw lands.
  5. Condition on competition before claiming a threshold. A 15.49%–30.42% spread makes one global cut miscalibrated for every league it touches.
  6. Score against market-implied probability. It is the only genuine distribution in the schema and it is already calibrated on our own rows — without it, a 0.78% draw rate looks like a modelling choice rather than a defect.

Two integrity facts

The 46,189 settled predictions cover 16,724 distinct matches, and only 3,736 (8.09%) join to matches on id; the rest carry a match_id from an older identifier space. Every per-competition number above was computed from matches directly — joining predictions to competitions would have dropped 92% of rows and produced a confident, wrong table.

Second: 329 settled rows have actual_result IS NULL and 121 have hit IS NULL while settled is true. They are excluded explicitly with FILTER.

The point

A 24% versus 0.8% gap is not a dataset problem. Twenty-four percent is an ordinary share for the third class of a football outcome. The imbalance was manufactured by the output format: the model emitted a label, the vocabulary had three slots, and the scoring loop only rewarded the slot that appeared most. Fixing it needs no better model — three numbers instead of one string, and a refusal to ship a three-class system whose per-class recall is never measured for one of its classes.

The draw was never hard to predict. It was hard to record.

Analytics and research content. Not betting advice. 18+

title: NestJS Request Lifecycle & SOLID Design Principles
description:
1. Introduction

NestJS provides a structured request-handling mechanism that processes incoming HTTP requests through different components before returning responses to clients.

These components include Middleware, Guards, Interceptors, Pipes and Exception Filters.

Apart from request handling, NestJS applications benefit from software design principles such as the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) and Single Responsibility Principle (SRP).

These principles help developers build applications that are maintainable, reusable and loosely coupled.

In this blog, we will understand the NestJS request lifecycle and important SOLID design principles using practical backend examples.

2. NestJS Request Lifecycle

What is the Request Lifecycle?

The request lifecycle describes the sequence of operations performed when an HTTP request enters a NestJS application and a response is returned to the client.

For example, when a user requests an Instagram profile:

GET /users/101

The request passes through different stages before the application sends the response.

Request Lifecycle Flow

Client Request → Middleware → Guards → Interceptors → Pipes → Controller → Service → Response

Main stages

  1. Middleware: Executes operations before the route handler pipeline.
  2. Guards: Determines whether the request is allowed to access a route.
  3. Interceptors: Executes logic before and after the route handler.
  4. Pipes: Validates and transforms incoming arguments.
  5. Controller: Handles the HTTP request.
  6. Service: Executes business logic.
  7. Exception Filters: Handle exceptions and generate appropriate error responses.

Exception filters are not a normal step in every successful request. They handle exceptions when they occur.

3. Middleware

What is Middleware?

Middleware is a function that executes during the request-response cycle before the route handler is executed.

It has access to the request object, response object and the next middleware function.

Why do we use Middleware?

  • Logging incoming requests.
  • Tracking request information.
  • Adding request metadata.
  • Processing certain headers.
  • Implementing general request-processing operations.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  NestMiddleware
} from '@nestjs/common';

import {
  Request,
  Response,
  NextFunction
} from 'express';

@Injectable()
export class LoggerMiddleware
implements NestMiddleware {

  use(
    req: Request,
    res: Response,
    next: NextFunction
  ) {
    console.log(
      `${req.method} ${req.originalUrl}`
    );

    next();
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • NestMiddleware: Interface used to define NestJS middleware.
  • use(): Executes when a request reaches the middleware.
  • req: Contains incoming request information.
  • res: Represents the HTTP response.
  • next(): Passes control to the next middleware or request-processing stage.

For example, if a user sends:

GET /users/101

The middleware logs:

GET /users/101

4. Guards

What are Guards?

Guards are components used to determine whether a request is allowed to access a particular route.

They are commonly used for authentication and authorization.

Why do we use Guards?

Consider an Instagram application.

Suppose a user wants to access a protected profile endpoint.

GET /users/profile

Before allowing access, the application checks whether the user has an authenticated session.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  CanActivate,
  ExecutionContext
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class AuthGuard implements CanActivate {

  canActivate(context: ExecutionContext): boolean {

    const request = context
      .switchToHttp()
      .getRequest();

    return !!request.session?.userId;
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • CanActivate: Interface implemented by guards.
  • ExecutionContext: Provides information about the current request and handler.
  • switchToHttp(): Accesses the HTTP request context.
  • getRequest(): Retrieves the request object.
  • canActivate(): Returns whether access is allowed.

If the user has a valid session containing userId, access is granted.

Otherwise, access is denied.

Applying the Guard 

@UseGuards(AuthGuard)
@Get('profile')
getProfile() {
  return 'User profile';
}

The guard checks the request before the controller handler executes.

5. Interceptors

What are Interceptors?

Interceptors are components that execute logic before and after a route handler.

They can intercept the execution of a request and process its result.

Why do we use Interceptors?

  • Logging execution time.
  • Transforming response data.
  • Implementing caching.
  • Monitoring application performance.
  • Handling common response-processing logic.

Example 

import {
  Injectable,
  NestInterceptor,
  ExecutionContext,
  CallHandler
} from '@nestjs/common';

import { Observable, tap } from 'rxjs';

@Injectable()
export class LoggingInterceptor
implements NestInterceptor {

  intercept(
    context: ExecutionContext,
    next: CallHandler
  ): Observable<any> {

    console.log('Before request handler');

    const startTime = Date.now();

    return next.handle().pipe(
      tap(() => {
        console.log(
          `Execution time: ${Date.now() - startTime}ms`
        );
      })
    );
  }
}

Understanding the code

  • NestInterceptor: Interface used to create interceptors.
  • intercept(): Executes before the route handler.
  • next.handle(): Passes execution to the next stage and returns an Observable.
  • tap(): Performs a side effect when the response data is emitted.

An interceptor can perform operations before and after the controller handler.

6. Pipes

What are Pipes?

Pipes are components used to validate or transform incoming data before it reaches the controller method.

Why do we use Pipes?

  • Validating request parameters.
  • Converting data types.
  • Transforming incoming values.
  • Preventing invalid input from reaching business logic.

Example: ParseIntPipe 

import {
  Controller,
  Get,
  Param,
  ParseIntPipe
} from '@nestjs/common';

@Controller('users')
export class UsersController {

  @Get(':id')
  getUser(
    @Param('id', ParseIntPipe) id: number
  ) {
    return {
      userId: id
    };
  }
}

Understanding the code

Suppose the frontend sends:

GET /users/101

The URL parameter initially comes as a string.

ParseIntPipe converts it into a number.

If the incoming value is not a valid integer, NestJS returns a validation error.

Other Common Pipes

  • ValidationPipe
  • ParseIntPipe
  • ParseBoolPipe
  • ParseUUIDPipe
  • DefaultValuePipe

7. Exception Filters

What are Exception Filters?

Exception Filters are components used to handle exceptions and customize the error responses returned to clients.

They help manage errors in a consistent way.

Why do we use Exception Filters?

  • Handling application errors.
  • Returning appropriate HTTP status codes.
  • Customizing error messages.
  • Centralizing error-handling logic.

Example 

throw new NotFoundException('User not found');

If a requested user does not exist, NestJS can return:

{
  "statusCode": 404,
  "message": "User not found",
  "error": "Not Found"
}

Common HTTP Exceptions

Exception HTTP Status
BadRequestException 400
UnauthorizedException 401
ForbiddenException 403
NotFoundException 404
ConflictException 409
InternalServerErrorException 500

NestJS provides built-in exception handling. Custom exception filters can be implemented when specific error formatting or handling is required.

8. Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)

What is DIP?

The Dependency Inversion Principle is one of the five SOLID design principles.

It states that high-level modules should not depend directly on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

In simple terms, business logic should depend on a contract rather than a specific implementation.

Without DIP

Consider a service that directly creates a PostgreSQL database object.

class PostgreSQLDatabase {

  saveUser() {
    console.log('User saved');
  }
}

class UsersService {

  private database = new PostgreSQLDatabase();

  createUser() {
    this.database.saveUser();
  }
}

Here, UsersService is tightly coupled to PostgreSQLDatabase.

If we want to change the database implementation, the service may need modification.

Applying DIP

First, define an abstraction.

interface UserRepository {
  saveUser(): void;
}

Then create an implementation.

class PostgreSQLDatabase
implements UserRepository {

  saveUser() {
    console.log('User saved in PostgreSQL');
  }
}

Now the service depends on the abstraction.

class UsersService {

  constructor(
    private database: UserRepository
  ) {}

  createUser() {
    this.database.saveUser();
  }
}

Now UsersService does not directly depend on PostgreSQLDatabase.

Benefits of DIP

  1. Reduces tight coupling.
  2. Improves flexibility.
  3. Makes unit testing easier.
  4. Supports replacing implementations.
  5. Improves maintainability.

In NestJS, dependency injection tokens and provider configurations can be used to inject different implementations of an abstraction.

9. Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)

What is SRP?

The Single Responsibility Principle is another important SOLID design principle.

It states that a class should have one responsibility and one reason to change.

Without SRP

Consider a class that handles multiple responsibilities.

class UserManager {

  createUser() {}

  deleteUser() {}

  sendEmail() {}

  generateReport() {}

  connectDatabase() {}

}

This class manages users, sends emails, generates reports and connects to the database.

This makes the class difficult to maintain.

Applying SRP

Separate the responsibilities into different classes.

class UsersService {
  createUser() {}
  deleteUser() {}
}

class EmailService {
  sendEmail() {}
}

class ReportService {
  generateReport() {}
}

class DatabaseService {
  connectDatabase() {}
}

Now every class has a clearly defined responsibility.

SRP in a NestJS Application

Class Responsibility
UsersController Handle user HTTP requests
UsersService User business logic
PostsController Handle post HTTP requests
PostsService Post business logic
AuthService Authentication operations
PrismaService Database connectivity

Benefits of SRP

  1. Improves code readability.
  2. Makes debugging easier.
  3. Reduces complexity.
  4. Improves code reusability.
  5. Makes testing easier.

10. Practical Application in an Instagram Backend

Consider an Instagram-style backend built using NestJS, Prisma and PostgreSQL.

When a user requests their profile:

GET /users/profile

The application may perform the following operations:

  1. Middleware logs the incoming request.
  2. AuthGuard checks the authenticated session.
  3. An interceptor records request execution time.
  4. Pipes validate incoming parameters when required.
  5. UsersController receives the request.
  6. UsersService executes the business logic.
  7. PrismaService communicates with PostgreSQL.
  8. The response is returned to the frontend.

If an exception occurs, NestJS exception handling returns an appropriate error response.

DIP helps separate the business logic from specific database implementations, while SRP ensures that each class has a clear responsibility.

11. Difference Between Middleware, Guards, Interceptors, Pipes and Filters

Component Main Responsibility
Middleware Processes incoming requests
Guards Controls access to routes
Interceptors Processes execution before and after handlers
Pipes Validates and transforms input
Exception Filters Handles exceptions

These components work together to create a structured request-processing mechanism.

12. Conclusion

NestJS provides several components to manage HTTP requests and application behavior effectively.

Middleware handles incoming request processing, Guards manage route access, Interceptors process execution and responses, Pipes validate and transform input, and Exception Filters handle errors.

Along with these components, SOLID principles such as DIP and SRP help developers write loosely coupled, maintainable and reusable code.

Understanding these concepts is important for developing scalable backend applications using NestJS.

title: Auditable Human-Agent Teams for Autonomous X-ray Experimentation
description:
arXiv:2611.12933v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Closed-loop autonomous experimentation can accelerate scientific discovery, but implementation effort limits accessibility. Agentic systems may lower this barrier, although sustained operation on physical instruments remains largely unexplored. Here, using coding-agent infrastructure grounded in validated scientific methods, we demonstrate autonomous synchrotron X-ray experiments on nanoparticle superlattices under evolving, human-defined objectives. Complete human-agent and agent-agent transcripts enable an audit that reconstructs decision provenance and characterizes the division of cognitive labor. Across three experiments, 61-67% of messages involved interpretation or judgment, while the share of methodological and scientific contributions increased from 46% in the setup-focused first experiment to 56-61% in later experiments. Provenance showed that 59-68% of error corrections involved multiple participants and that about half of all decisions incorporated the input of another participant. These results may guide design principles for multi-agent scientific systems and inform future agent harnesses, model training, and accessible autonomous experimentation.

title: EarthRecord: From Pixels to Land Change with Multimodal Agents over Four Decades of Satellite Imagery
description:
arXiv:2611.12934v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: While multimodal agents now carry out complex data analysis with tools, their ability to turn decades of satellite imagery into reliable land-change analysis, crucial for Earth observation science, remains unmeasured. Existing benchmarks fall short: they pose questions on curated images or give agents preprocessed inputs, leaving out the raw multi-sensor archives where such analysis begins. We introduce EarthRecord, a benchmark built on the raw record of 56 sites: four decades of Landsat, MODIS, VIIRS, and Sentinel-2 data, with cloud masking and cross-sensor harmonization left to the agent. It poses 238 land-change questions across ten analysis tasks, scored against withheld references from global products, agreement among methods, and visual interpretation. Two controls test what answers rest on: the closed book removes the record, and instrument pairs alter one satellite's data while nothing changes on the ground. Evaluations of twelve multimodal agents reveal that leading agents complete most analyses end to end but falter when an answer requires mapping from imagery. Further analysis shows that the record moves answers from prior knowledge to the pixels but not yet to the real change on the ground: when one satellite's data are altered, half of the right answers follow the alteration. EarthRecord thus provides a principled platform for measuring and advancing agents from pixels to land change.

title: Train on prefill, monitor at decode: Using sparse autoencoders for topic monitoring
description:
arXiv:2611.12935v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Topic monitoring is the task of labelling the topic of each token in a model's response during generation. Activation-based monitors that run at generation time have so far been trained to detect harmful content and are limited to two or three classes. We introduce TopicScope, a framework for training causal topic classifiers on SAE features that assign a topic to every token, so that the label can change partway through a response. We train three detector architectures on synthetic multi-topic conversations covering seven topics. Across Gemma-3 1B and 4B, monitors trained on features extracted from prefill hidden states were able to generalise to decoding. We also found that the classifiers are robust to perturbations, losing at most 5 macro-F1 points when off-topic asides are inserted, topics are removed or sections are reordered. Ablations conducted to understand the contribution of the SAE revealed that classifiers reaching baseline performance without it were several times larger. Our findings show that compact topic monitors can be trained inexpensively in prefill and deployed during generation. More broadly, our work shows where SAEs are useful beyond safety classification. Our code, dataset and checkpoints are available at https://github.com/Mercity-AI/SAE-Guardrails and https://huggingface.co/collections/Mercity/online-guardrails-using-sparse-autoencoders-6ac602940468c62fefb2b9e8

title: LandslideFM: A Foundation Model Towards Unified Landslide Perception and Understanding
description:
arXiv:2611.12936v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Intelligent landslide detection is essential for disaster prevention. However, existing models primarily focus on isolated visual tasks, require extensive labeled data, and lack deep analytical and scene-understanding capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose LandslideFM, the first unified foundation model that connects visual perception tasks with contextual interpretation of landslides. Specifically, LandslideFM adapts to multiple visual tasks via a Source-Agreement Graduated Trust semi-supervised learning framework that leverages limited labeled data alongside abundant unlabeled data. Furthermore, predicted landslide regions provide explicit spatial guidance to a Vision-Language Model adapted through parameter-efficient fine-tuning, enabling comprehensive landslide reasoning. To support training and evaluation in this domain, we also present LandslideVL, the first benchmark for intelligent landslide analysis, combining visual imagery and newly introduced textual prompts. Comprehensive experiments across public datasets and LandslideVL demonstrate that LandslideFM achieves superior quantitative and qualitative performance. Most importantly, LandslideFM surpasses general-purpose VLMs in specialized landslide reasoning and scene analysis. Our code is released at https://github.com/wangshanwen001/LandslideFM.

title: Tracing Psychometric Inference in Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.12937v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Do large language models represent psychological constructs internally, or do they only generate outputs that resemble psychometric structure? We address this question using a cross-persona paradigm across 14 model variants from two families (Llama 3 and Qwen 2.5, 0.5B-14B, base and instruct). Given responses on one psychological scale from real individuals (N = 272 Taiwanese university students), models predict responses on six other scales. At the behavioral level, larger variants reproduce and amplify human cross-scale correlations; amplification persists after correcting the seven-scale human correlations for measurement attenuation. We then examine whether this structure is reflected internally. Contrastive direction analysis finds geometry aligned with the human matrix in larger instruct variants, but little alignment in base variants under this assay. Across models, geometry strength is associated with behavioral amplification (r = 0.68, p = 0.008; partial r = 0.69 controlling for log size). To relate internal structure to output behavior, a matched activation-probing paradigm shows that probe slopes vary less than behavioral slopes (1.38-1.77 vs 0.52-1.53). A synthetic control shows that ridge probing can inflate these slopes; after subtracting a baseline based on a reliability proxy from another analysis, adjusted slopes remain associated with behavior (r = 0.88). We term the measured probe-behavior gap readout attenuation. These results establish decodability and geometric alignment under the tested assays, without showing that the measured directions mediate the cross-persona answers.

title: Graph Visualizations in Prompts for Knowledge Graph Question Answering
description:
arXiv:2611.12938v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: We study when and how multimodal input improves knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) in large vision--language models. Using a controlled evaluation over 1,500 WebQSP and CWQ questions and six VLMs within a fixed KGQA pipeline, we compare text-only prompting against text-plus-graph visualization at the per-question level and analyze performance changes as a function of reasoning complexity, model size, and image layout. Adding a graph image yields an average gain of 1.85 F1 points, driven by strong precision improvements on low-complexity questions (+4.65 F1). Mixed-effects and regression analyses show that these multimodal gains do not depend strongly on model scale, but are highly sensitive to graph layout: image-only settings sharply degrade performance, hierarchical Graphviz layouts outperform less organized renderings, and decomposing large subgraphs into separated paths yields the largest improvements. Taken together, the results indicate that visual prompting primarily aids KGQA by enhancing prediction precision in low-complexity contexts, provided that visual design respects cognitive and perceptual constraints. To optimize both accuracy and inference efficiency, we argue for adaptive visual prompting policies that selectively append diagrams to small, visually sparse subgraphs with well-structured layouts, avoiding unnecessary visual clutter and token overhead on complex queries. We conclude by relating these findings to a visual notation design theory, outlining how principled diagram encoding can guide future multimodal VLM prompting.

title: Reinforcement Learning based control of Cancer Chemotherapy treatments
description:
arXiv:2611.12940v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Reinforcement Learning has achieved tremendous success in recent years. Extending its scope from the traditional complex games such as Atari, Go, Pokeman, and Chess, reinforcement learning has caught researchers' attention on modelling real-life scenarios. Personalized medicine and the dynamic treatment regimen are two such preliminary research fields; researchers are focusing their mindsets currently. Estimating the optimal dynamic treatment regimens from the observational real clinical data is being popularized among the researchers, widening its scope towards more advanced versions of reinforcement learning algorithms.
  This research is about a research study that focused on reinforcement learning techniques that have been approached in the context of cancer chemotherapy treatments. Primarily this thesis addresses the result of the study by means of the state-of-the-art on reinforcement learning techniques used in generating the optimal policy for sequential treatments, including the existing online reinforcement learning approaches. Thereby a simulation for cancer chemotherapy via traditional Q-learning would be presented. Secondly, the study will extend towards using offline reinforcement learning in the optimal policy generation. Thus, the proposed solution follows a data-driven approach, which works on the real human colon cancer clinical data.
  The novelty of the proposed solution resides in the implementation of an offline reinforcement learning approach by means of a model-based architecture using the conservative Q-learning and the model-based offline policy optimization algorithm. As per the experimental results and the evaluations, it was revealed that the proposed Chemo RL model caters well the problem of cancer chemotherapy treatment scheduling and serves as a supportive model for the junior oncologists in deciding their treatment decisions.

title: AI Governance Should Prioritize Control and Knowledge Boundaries Over Limiting Intelligence
description:
arXiv:2611.12941v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: The rapid proliferation of autonomously acting AI agents makes the governance of agentic systems urgent. We propose the competence circuit, summarized as IKC + KC + C, that decomposes an agent's real-world impact into three pathways: intelligence-mediated discovery, procedural know-how, and direct control. Using the canonical fast-takeoff debate as a stress test, we formalize the conditions for intelligence-mediated fast takeoff as a conjunction jointly sufficient for fast catastrophic supremacy, showing that most rely on rapid knowledge acquisition or control attainment rather than intelligence alone. We operationalize epistemic intelligence as hypothesis-selection efficiency and validate this framework via stochastic simulation on NK fitness landscapes across six scenarios spanning the conjunctive chain. An analytic bound supported by the simulations shows that intelligence-driven speedup is capped by the ratio of competing intelligence levels regardless of task difficulty. The simulations also expose a fast-takeoff dilemma: a large intelligence-driven speedup multiplier materializes only when the hypothesis space is noisy, but the absolute timescale remains constrained by the time required for capability-critical tests, so a large multiplier need not imply rapid progress. Simulations also indicate that institutional chokepoints disproportionately slow down superintelligent agents when mandatory authorization delays are large relative to the negligible time these agents spend on unproductive search. We argue that the dominant safety levers are restricting control and enforcing knowledge boundaries rather than limiting intelligence alone, and this applies to agentic systems at any capability level. Purely digital domains weaken these bottlenecks, strengthening the case for architectures that intentionally "put physics in the loop."

title: Tabular Foundation Models vs Tuned Gradient Boosting for Telecom Churn: A Profit- and Calibration-Aware Evaluation
description:
arXiv:2611.12942v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Tabular foundation models (TFMs) predict from a labelled context in a single forward pass. A recent benchmark reported that they decisively outperform tree ensembles for customer churn, but it compared them with untuned gradient-boosted trees (GBDTs) and scored only ranking metrics, while a retention campaign is judged in money. We re-evaluate TabPFN-2.5, TabPFN-3.5, TabPFN-3.5-Fast and TabICL v2 against Optuna-tuned GBDTs on five public telecom churn datasets over 10 seeded splits. We separate three questions: whether a model ranks churners well, whether that ranking earns more expected maximum profit (EMP), and whether its probabilities can drive a threshold policy. With a split-aware test and Holm correction over 20 pre-declared comparisons, TabPFN-3.5 earns significantly more EMP than the best tuned GBDT on Cell2Cell (1.9%) and Iranian (7.6%), and these two gains also hold against each of the three tuned GBDTs separately. On Orange it is ahead in all 10 splits (14.3%), but the gain is not significant after correction (Holm p = 0.155). The splits resample the same datasets, so these results do not stand for independent operators. TabICL v2, the earlier benchmark's leader, beats the best tuned GBDT only on Iranian, not all three of them, and underpredicts Orange churn by 2.1 points on a 7.3% base rate. On the datasets and splits where we tested them, a substantially larger tuning budget and a duplicate-aware split leave the main conclusions unchanged. Retuning the baseline cuts the earlier headline gap from 6.1 to 4.0 PR-AUC points without closing it. The licence of the TabPFN-3.5 weights we used (License v1.0), not scoring cost, is what stands between its gains and production use.

title: SetPrint: Black-Box LLM Fingerprinting via Setwise Correspondence of Response Changes
description:
arXiv:2611.12950v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Black-box LLM fingerprinting aims to determine whether a target model was derived from a source model when only the output responses to input queries are observable. One way to reveal this relationship is to perturb each query and observe the resulting responses of both models, yielding two corresponding sets of response variations. These sets provide two complementary sources of information: the relations among response changes within each set, and the correspondence of response changes between the two sets. Existing approaches, however, have not fully exploited both. We introduce \textbf{SetPrint}, a training-free method that jointly captures both within-set relations and between-set correspondence. SetPrint expresses each response change relative to the mean change of its own set, and then compares changes from the two models that were induced by the same perturbation. On LeaFBench, SetPrint consistently outperforms existing training-free black-box fingerprinting methods. Further analyses attribute these gains to both within-set relations and between-set correspondence.

title: Agent Architecture Cost-Success Trade-offs: A Controlled Evaluation across Enterprise-Style SOPs
description:
arXiv:2611.12953v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Enterprises increasingly use large language model agents to execute standard operating procedures (SOPs): long, branching, tool-intensive workflows. Yet there is little controlled evidence for choosing among competing agentic architectures. Holding the model, tasks, and tools fixed and varying only the architecture, we compare four designs (a function-calling single agent, a skill-augmented agent, centralized multi-agent orchestration, and a triage swarm; eight arms) across 13 enterprise SOPs, and introduce a skill-definition quality rubric to build matched high and low-quality skill corpora. Three takeaways emerge. (1)~\textbf{There is no universal best architecture; the right choice is SOP-dependent.} On a given SOP, task success ranges from under $10\%$ on the hardest to near $100\%$ on the easiest; no architecture is statistically separable in aggregate, and added structure only plausibly pays off on complex, branching SOPs (a directional, not yet significant, trend). (2)~\textbf{Added architecture cost must be justified by a task-success gain.} Every coordinated arm (multi-agent or skill-augmented) spends $1.4$--$4.7\times$ the tokens and $2.6$--$5.8\times$ the latency of the single agent for gains that are usually small and rarely significant, making the single agent the efficient default; high-quality skills do lift success (to $73.1\%$ from $67.4\%$) while degraded skills fall below it. (3)~\textbf{Implementation quality outweighs the single- versus multi-agent choice.} A plausible multi-agent implementation loses to the single agent, yet a targeted redesign of it becomes the only arm to significantly beat the baseline ($75.6\%$ vs.\ $67.4\%$).

title: Physics2Weight: Direct Neural Network Architecture and Weight Generation from Physical Laws Using Large Language Models
description:
arXiv:2611.12954v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled weight-space programming (WSP), which directly generates neural network weights without gradient-based optimization. However, extending WSP to physical problems remains challenging, particularly in achieving both solution accuracy and physical consistency. In this paper, we propose Physics2Weight (PtW), a framework that extends WSP to solving partial differential equations by directly generating neural network weights and editing architectures based on governing equations and initial and boundary conditions. PtW introduces physics-constrained prompting and physics-guided architecture editing, combined with iterative weight refinement from WSP, to improve solution accuracy and physical consistency without gradient-based optimization. Experiments on four PDEs, namely the heat, advection, Burgers', and Allen--Cahn equations, demonstrate lower solution errors than conventional physics-informed neural networks, while revealing limitations in satisfying the governing equations for nonlinear PDEs.

title: Embodied Science Agents: Making Embodied Experimental Design Learnable
description:
arXiv:2611.12958v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Recent advances in large models have accelerated AI for Science toward agentic science, where AI agents autonomously conduct scientific discovery. Realising this vision requires closing the loop between computational reasoning and physical experimentation, positioning self-driving laboratories (SDLs) as critical enablers. However, existing SDLs exhibit a fundamental paradox: foundation model integration has increased linguistic sophistication while severing physical grounding. By treating models as disembodied planners that output symbolic workflows for separate robotic systems, current architectures inherently block the development of embodied experimental intuition. We argue that overcoming this paradox requires embedding \emph{learnability} along three interdependent axes: cognitive learnability (learning what to investigate), experimental learnability (learning where to search), and embodied learnability (learning how to act). Building on this view, we introduce the Embodied Science Agent (ESA), which unifies digital intelligence with physical embodiment through three synergistic components: a Digital Agent that provides cognitive and experimental learnability via memory-based reasoning and Bayesian optimisation, an Embodied Agent that provides embodied learnability via generalisable instrument control, and an Embodied Unified Interface for seamless coordination. We validated ESA in autonomous wastewater treatment experiments, navigating over 200 million possible conditions. Through 15 continuous rounds, ESA raised the final solution transmittance from 82\% to 99.7\%, corresponding to a 98.5\% reduction in residual dye concentration and near-complete decolourisation, while its learned visuomotor policies generalised across varying instrument placements, a promising step toward next-generation SDLs for autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Monitoring One Channel Is Not Communication Control: Causal Evidence for Adaptive Reallocation of Joint Message--Route Codes
description:
arXiv:2611.12959v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Monitoring a visible channel can change how learned agents communicate without removing why communication is useful. We test this distinction in an end-to-end game where a sender and receiver learn a discrete protocol and route policy without communication supervision. In two independent 20-seed batches, 20/20 and 19/20 protocols form. Online partial coverage increases shadow-route share over no monitoring by .701 [.574,.826] and .575 [.412,.737], while task accuracy remains .905/.913 and signed frozen message contribution remains .592/.563. Complete coverage removes most selective migration without removing communication. Frozen interventions, including a fresh pre-outcome confirmation, show that route is semantic: joint message--route shuffling changes .668 of receiver predictions and route alone retains .388 accuracy versus .25 chance. A corrected explicit-silence cost makes 18/20 policies fully silent and lowers mean sending to .050, but its strict complete-suppression gate fails because two seeds retain communication. Failed semantic-evasion and operational gates further bound the result. The evidence supports adaptive reallocation of a joint message--route code under partial monitoring, not open-world route discovery, emergent encryption, or a universal defense.

title: IIT Patna at "ICPR 2026 TVRID Competition on Privacy-Preserving Person Re-Identification from Top-View RGB-Depth Camera"
description:
arXiv:2611.12960v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Privacy-aware person re-identification (Re-ID) from top-view cameras replaces frontal appearance with anthropometric shape, while depth sensing further reduces color-based identity cues. The ICPR 2026 TVRID competition evaluates this setting using 86 identities captured by four synchronized Intel RealSense D455 cameras with RGB and Depth streams across flat, ascent, descent, and oblique viewpoints. Performance is measured using mAP and CMC@1 across within-camera in/out, ascent-descent, and flat-oblique scenarios. The competition had 147 registered participants and 33 final submissions. Three teams from IIT Patna participated: 'abhinavkumar03' and 'sjkdgfhl_' ranked 5th and 7th among 31 ranked participants, and 'vivek katuri' reached 77.67% CMC@1 / 85.20% mAP on the RGB track. This paper presents the methods of the two top-10 teams. Methodology 1 (abhinavkumar03) achieves 93.51% mAP and 90.42% CMC@1 on Depth, ranking 4th of 28, while Methodology 2 (sjkdgfhl_) reaches 99.63%/99.35% on RGB and 86.26%/80.34% on Depth. Both substantially outperform the 57.19% track-average Depth mAP, with Methodology 1 yielding a 7.3-point gain over Methodology 2. These results demonstrate the importance of depth representation and supervision for privacy-preserving Re-ID.

title: RBLA+: Efficient Rank-Specific LoRA Adapter Extraction for Federated Fine-Tuning with Heterogeneous Clients
description:
arXiv:2611.12961v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Federated fine-tuning with low-rank adaptation (LoRA) reduces communication and computational overhead by training and exchanging compact trainable LoRA factors. Clients may use different LoRA ranks to meet adapter communication budgets and accommodate different local adaptation needs. The server must process these differences during aggregation and construct adapters at each client's rank for local training. We distinguish pre-aggregation alignment, which handles factor dimensions and scaling conventions before aggregation and rank-specific LoRA adapter extraction, which constructs client-sized pairs from the aggregated global model.
