A cached plan avoids repeated optimization work, but it does not allow execution to bypass the schema-lock queue. A query using OPTION (RECOMPILE) adds compilation on every execution, increasing pressure and the number of waiting requests during a convoy.

Recompilation is not inherently wrong, but it must be considered when planning maintenance against hot tables.

Why the Symptoms May Be Intermittent

Temporary relief can occur when the waiting Sch-M request is cancelled by a client timeout, a configured lock timeout, or an explicit operator action. Removing that request allows the queue to drain.

When that happens:

  1. The queued Sch-S requests can be granted.
  2. A burst of queries completes.
  3. A later compilation detects stale statistics again.
  4. Another statistics update requests Sch-M.
  5. The convoy returns.

This produces a repeating pattern:

Blocking -> temporary relief -> blocking -> temporary relief

Intermittent success does not prove that the index operation is healthy. It may indicate that the head waiter is repeatedly cancelled and requested again.

Risk Factors

The likelihood and impact of this pattern increase when several of the following are true:

Risk factor Why it matters
Very large table or index Extends the period during which schema locks and resource pressure exist
High write rate Makes statistics stale more quickly and increases index-maintenance overhead
Frequent recompilation Adds compilation work and more requests during the vulnerable window
Tight application timeouts Converts short blocking into visible request failures quickly
Limited transaction-log capacity Can slow or fail the operation
Insufficient free storage Online and resumable operations may temporarily require both old and new index structures
High CPU or I/O utilization Extends build duration and affects foreground workload
Fixed client or tool timeout May terminate the operation after hours of work
No tested abort procedure Increases recovery time when application health degrades

Plan the Change Before Running It

1. Measure the Target

Collect at least:

  • Table and index size
  • Row count
  • Current write rate
  • Peak and off-peak workload
  • Available database and temporary storage
  • Existing index definition
  • Edition and engine-version support for online and resumable operations
  • Temporary-database capacity when using options that require it
  • Planned MAXDOP and its effect on duration and resource use
  • Recovery model and transaction-log backup throughput
  • Replication, availability, or disaster-recovery constraints

Do not estimate duration solely from a development or staging database. Index build time does not scale linearly across different hardware, data distributions, workload levels, and log configurations.

2. Establish Success and Abort Thresholds

Define measurable thresholds before execution, such as:

  • Maximum acceptable blocked-query count
  • Maximum lock-wait duration
  • Maximum application error or timeout rate
  • CPU, I/O, and log-utilization limits
  • Maximum operation duration
  • Minimum free-storage reserve

3. Choose the Execution Model

Use the simplest model that provides enough safety:

Model Appropriate when
Application schema-migration step The operation is small, predictable, and the tool's command timeout exceeds the expected duration
Extended-timeout maintenance command The operation is long but can safely remain attached to its initiating tool
Separate maintenance job The operation must run independently or in a low-traffic window
Resumable index operation The work must be divided into bounded windows or survive process restarts
Scheduled maintenance framework Many databases require auditable, scheduled, retryable execution

Long-running data and index operations should generally be separated from fast schema changes. A routine application rollout should not depend on a multi-hour physical data operation finishing in the same execution window.

4. Test with Production-Like Conditions

A useful rehearsal should include:

  • Representative data volume and distribution
  • Concurrent reads and writes
  • Queries that commonly recompile
  • Monitoring of lock waits and blocking chains
  • An intentional pause or abort
  • Validation of retry or resume behavior

The goal is not only to prove that the index can be created. It is to prove that the system remains operable while it is being created.

Execution Safeguards

Run During the Lowest Practical Traffic Window

Lower traffic reduces:

  • Foreground workload contention
  • Data changes that must be reflected in the new index
  • Transaction-log generation
  • The probability of statistics becoming stale during the operation
  • The number of queries affected by an unexpected blocking chain

An online operation should still be scheduled thoughtfully. "Online" is a concurrency feature, not a maintenance-window substitute.

Use Low-Priority Lock Waiting

For supported operations, use WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY so the index operation's own lock requests do not indefinitely block normal workload. Test all syntax against the deployed engine version and edition; support differs between CREATE INDEX and ALTER INDEX ... REBUILD.

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
REBUILD
WITH
(
    ONLINE = ON
    (
        WAIT_AT_LOW_PRIORITY
        (
            MAX_DURATION = 5 MINUTES,
            ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = SELF
        )
    )
);

ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = SELF favors workload availability by cancelling the index operation if it cannot obtain the required lock within the specified period. For a non-resumable operation, cancellation discards completed build work and rollback can take time. ABORT_AFTER_WAIT = BLOCKERS can terminate user sessions and should be used only with explicit operational approval.

Choose the duration based on the workload's latency objectives. Do not copy a large value without understanding how long the operation may remain pending.

This option reduces blocking caused by the index operation's own lock requests. It does not prevent a separate statistics-update Sch-M request from queueing while the build holds Sch-S.

Consider Resumable Index Operations

Where supported, resumable operations reduce the cost of interruption:

CREATE INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable] ([KeyColumn])
WITH
(
    ONLINE = ON,
    RESUMABLE = ON,
    MAX_DURATION = 120 MINUTES
);

If the operation reaches MAX_DURATION, it pauses rather than discarding all progress. It can later be resumed:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
RESUME WITH (MAX_DURATION = 120 MINUTES);

Inspect resumable operations with:

SELECT
    object_id,
    index_id,
    name,
    state_desc,
    percent_complete,
    page_count
FROM sys.index_resumable_operations;

Resumability introduces operational responsibilities:

  • A paused operation consumes storage.
  • Writes may need to maintain both index structures.
  • Operations requiring a table-level exclusive lock, such as TRUNCATE TABLE, some ALTER TABLE statements, and offline index rebuilds, cannot proceed while the index is paused.
  • Automation must detect and resume, complete, or abort abandoned operations.

Resumability does not prevent the lock-convoy pattern while the operation is actively running. Enable it only when someone owns monitoring and cleanup for paused work.

Control Automatic Statistics Updates Deliberately

For a verified lock-convoy risk, temporarily disabling automatic statistics updates can prevent a statistics update from requesting Sch-M during the vulnerable period. Treat this as a last-resort mitigation after scheduling, low-priority waiting, resumability, and active monitoring have been considered.

Prefer the narrowest effective scope. Inspect the current table-level settings before changing them:

EXEC sys.sp_autostats N'dbo.LargeTable';

If testing confirms that table-scoped suppression addresses the risk, record the existing state, disable updates for the target table, and restore the recorded state afterward:

EXEC sys.sp_autostats N'dbo.LargeTable', N'OFF';

-- Run the controlled index operation here.

-- Restore each statistic to its previously recorded setting.

If a database-level change is required, first record is_auto_update_stats_on from sys.databases and restore that original value rather than hard-coding ON. A database-level change affects every table; stale statistics can accumulate and query quality can degrade. Switching to asynchronous automatic statistics does not eliminate this risk because the statistics update can still request the incompatible lock.

Use this mitigation only when:

  • The lock-convoy mechanism has been validated for the workload.
  • The maintenance window is bounded.
  • The setting change is monitored.
  • Re-enabling is part of the mandatory cleanup path.
  • Critical statistics are updated manually afterward when appropriate.

After the index operation has finished, update other affected statistics when appropriate. The newly created index already receives index statistics during creation.

UPDATE STATISTICS [dbo].[LargeTable];

The appropriate sampling level depends on table size, workload, and maintenance budget. A full scan can itself be expensive.

Ensure cleanup runs even after cancellation, timeout, or failure, and alert if any temporary statistics configuration remains in place.

Avoid Unnecessary Recompilation During the Window

If application behavior permits, reduce avoidable compilations during maintenance:

  • Reassess unconditional OPTION (RECOMPILE) usage.
  • Avoid unnecessary plan-cache clearing.
  • Do not combine unrelated schema changes with the index operation.

Do not remove recompilation hints blindly. They may exist to solve parameter-sensitivity or plan-quality problems. Any query change requires independent performance validation.

Monitoring During the Operation

Find Active Requests and Blockers 

SELECT
    r.session_id,
    r.status,
    r.command,
    r.wait_type,
    r.wait_time,
    r.wait_resource,
    r.blocking_session_id,
    r.percent_complete,
    r.cpu_time,
    r.total_elapsed_time
FROM sys.dm_exec_requests AS r
INNER JOIN sys.dm_exec_sessions AS s
    ON s.session_id = r.session_id
WHERE
    r.database_id = DB_ID()
    AND s.is_user_process = 1
    AND r.session_id <> @@SPID
ORDER BY r.total_elapsed_time DESC;

percent_complete is populated only for some commands and may remain zero for an index operation.

Look specifically for:

  • LCK_M_SCH_M
  • LCK_M_SCH_S
  • A growing number of blocked sessions
  • A head blocker associated with statistics or index maintenance
  • Increasing application timeout rates

Inspect Locks on the Target Object 

SELECT
    tl.request_session_id,
    tl.resource_type,
    tl.request_mode,
    tl.request_status,
    tl.resource_associated_entity_id
FROM sys.dm_tran_locks AS tl
WHERE
    tl.resource_database_id = DB_ID()
    AND tl.resource_type = N'OBJECT'
    AND tl.resource_associated_entity_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable')
ORDER BY
    tl.resource_associated_entity_id,
    tl.request_session_id;

This DMV does not expose queue order. Correlate it with sys.dm_exec_requests, sys.dm_os_waiting_tasks, and SQL text when deeper investigation is required. Capture evidence before terminating an operation, provided doing so does not delay recovery.

Monitor Resource Health

At minimum, track:

  • CPU
  • Data-file and log-file I/O latency
  • Transaction-log usage and growth
  • Database and temporary-storage free space
  • Query latency and timeout rate
  • Deadlocks
  • Blocking duration
  • Index-operation progress

Database health and application health must be observed together. A database command can be progressing normally while the application is already outside its service objectives.

Abort and Recovery

Stopping a non-resumable index operation can require a lengthy rollback. The database may remain under resource pressure while that rollback proceeds.

If a verified statistics-related LCK_M_SCH_M waiter is causing the convoy, cancelling that waiting session may drain the queue while preserving the index build. Confirm the session's identity and SQL text first; cancelling it also cancels the triggering query.

Before execution, document:

  1. How to identify the index session.
  2. The exact command used to stop or pause it.
  3. Whether progress will be preserved.
  4. How rollback progress will be monitored.
  5. Which temporary database settings must be restored.
  6. How statistics and index state will be validated afterward.
  7. When the operation may be retried.

For a resumable operation, prefer PAUSE when the goal is to preserve progress:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
PAUSE;

If the partial operation must be discarded:

ALTER INDEX [IX_Example]
ON [dbo].[LargeTable]
ABORT;

ABORT discards saved progress and may take time. Confirm the supported syntax and behavior for the deployed engine version before the maintenance window.

Post-Change Validation

Do not declare success when the DDL statement returns. Verify:

  • The intended index exists and is enabled.
  • The index definition matches the approved design.
  • No resumable operation remains paused unexpectedly.
  • Temporary database settings have been restored.
  • Statistics are sufficiently current.
  • Blocking and timeout rates have returned to baseline.
  • Query plans use the new index where expected.
  • Write latency has not regressed unexpectedly.
  • Data and log files have adequate free space.
  • The maintenance record reflects the final state.

Example checks:

SELECT
    i.name,
    i.type_desc,
    i.is_disabled,
    i.is_hypothetical,
    i.has_filter,
    i.filter_definition
FROM sys.indexes AS i
WHERE i.object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable');

SELECT
    s.name AS statistic_name,
    sp.last_updated,
    sp.rows,
    sp.modification_counter
FROM sys.stats AS s
OUTER APPLY sys.dm_db_stats_properties(s.object_id, s.stats_id) AS sp
WHERE
    s.object_id = OBJECT_ID(N'dbo.LargeTable')
ORDER BY sp.last_updated;

Recommended Operational Checklist

Before

  • [ ] Measure table, index, log, and storage requirements.
  • [ ] Estimate duration using representative data and workload.
  • [ ] Confirm online and resumable feature support.
  • [ ] Identify queries that frequently compile or recompile.
  • [ ] Select a low-traffic window.
  • [ ] Define success, pause, and abort thresholds.
  • [ ] Prepare monitoring queries and dashboards.
  • [ ] Test pause, resume, abort, and cleanup behavior.

During

  • [ ] Monitor application latency and error rate.
  • [ ] Monitor Sch-S and Sch-M waits.
  • [ ] Watch the blocking chain, not only the index session.
  • [ ] Track CPU, I/O, storage, and transaction-log health.
  • [ ] Pause or abort when a predefined threshold is crossed.

After

  • [ ] Confirm the final index definition and state.
  • [ ] Restore temporary database settings.
  • [ ] Enable statistics auto update as needed.
  • [ ] Confirm no resumable operation remains paused.
  • [ ] Validate critical query performance.
  • [ ] Record actual duration, resource usage, and lessons learned.

Final Takeaways

  1. Online does not mean lock-free. Online index operations still interact with schema locks and can affect production traffic.
  2. A waiting Sch-M request can create a lock convoy. Later Sch-S requests may queue behind it even though they are compatible with the lock currently being held.
  3. Automatic statistics can create a head waiter, and recompilation can add pressure. All new statements need schema stability; frequent recompilation adds more work and requests during the convoy.
  4. Large index changes need an operational design. Maintenance windows, monitoring, abort criteria, and cleanup are part of the implementation.
  5. Resumable operations reduce interruption cost but require lifecycle management. Paused work must be visible, owned, and completed or aborted.
  6. Temporary configuration changes must be bounded and reversible. If automatic statistics are disabled, restoring them is a mandatory recovery action.
  7. Separate slow maintenance from routine application rollout when scale demands it. Fast schema changes and multi-hour physical data operations have different operational requirements.

The safest index change is not the one with the most options in its WITH clause. It is the one whose production behavior has been estimated, rehearsed, observed, and made recoverable.

title: What type scale is a site really using? Measuring it from computed font sizes
description:
"Modular scale, ratio 1.25" is a nice thing to put in a design doc. When you inherit a site, or want to match one, you rarely get that doc. You get a page and DevTools.

Here is how I measure the scale a page actually uses, what it looked like on three demo sites I built, and where the single "ratio" number stops being useful.

Step 1: list the sizes, weighted by text

Clicking headings one by one in DevTools misses sizes and tells you nothing about which size carries the body text. Instead, walk every visible text node and add up characters per computed font size. Paste this in the console:

(() => {
  const sizes = new Map();
  const walk = document.createTreeWalker(document.body, NodeFilter.SHOW_TEXT);
  while (walk.nextNode()) {
    const text = walk.currentNode.textContent.trim();
    const el = walk.currentNode.parentElement;
    if (!text || !el.checkVisibility()) continue;
    const px = Math.round(parseFloat(getComputedStyle(el).fontSize));
    sizes.set(px, (sizes.get(px) || 0) + text.length);
  }
  return [...sizes].sort((a, b) => b[0] - a[0]);
})()

On Northwind Roasters, a fictional coffee shop I use for demos, at 1280px wide it returns [size in px, characters] pairs:

[[64, 44], [40, 30], [22, 50], [17, 486], [15, 85], [14, 145]]

Run it at the viewport you care about. If the headings use clamp() or media queries, a phone width gives different numbers.

Step 2: the base is the size with the most text

486 characters at 17px, far more than anything else, so the body size is 17px, not the 16px you might assume. That matters: if you rebuild this site with Tailwind's default text-base (16px), every paragraph comes out a pixel smaller and the line lengths change.

Step 3: a ratio from the steps above the base

Sizes above the base: 22, 40, 64. If the scale were geometric, each step would multiply by the same ratio r, so 17 × r³ = 64:

const ratio = (base, above) => (Math.max(...above) / base) ** (1 / above.length);
ratio(17, [22, 40, 64]); // 1.556

A second demo site, Ledgerline (a fictional accounting app), has a 16px base and 18, 20, 28 and 60 above it:

ratio(16, [18, 20, 28, 60]); // 1.392

That is close to the augmented fourth (1.414) from the classic named ratios. Close is all it is.

Why the ratio is only a summary

Go back to Northwind and look at the actual steps:

  • 22 / 17 = 1.29
  • 40 / 22 = 1.82
  • 64 / 40 = 1.60

No single ratio there. If you regenerate the scale from base 17 and ratio 1.556, you get 26.4, 41.1 and 64. The h1 matches, the h2 is close, and the h3 is 4.4px too big. That is a visibly different card title.

The third site shows how fragile the number is. Afterhours (a fictional dev tool) gives sizes above its 16px base of 19, 20 and 66:

ratio(16, [19, 20, 66]); // 1.604
ratio(16, [19, 66]);     // 2.031

The 20px size covers 10 characters on the whole page, probably one stray label. Drop it and the "ratio" jumps from 1.60 to 2.03. In practice this site has a huge display heading and then body-ish sizes, and no ratio describes that well.

So I use the ratio as a one-line description ("base 17, grows about 1.56 per step") and keep the measured sizes as the actual tokens:

:root {
  --text-sm: 0.875rem;    /* 14px */
  --text-base: 1.0625rem; /* 17px */
  --text-xl: 1.375rem;    /* 22px, h3 */
  --text-4xl: 2.5rem;     /* 40px, h2 */
  --text-6xl: 4rem;       /* 64px, h1 */
}

Measure line height and tracking too

Size alone does not make a heading look right. Click one heading per step in DevTools and read line-height and letter-spacing from Computed. On Northwind:

Step Size Line height Letter spacing
h1 64px 1.04 -1.28px (-0.02em)
h2 40px 1.1 -0.4px (-0.01em)
h3 22px 1.25 0
body 17px 1.6 0

The pattern is the usual one: the bigger the text, the tighter the leading and tracking. The other two sites tighten their h1 harder: Afterhours at 66px uses -2.64px (-0.04em), Ledgerline at 60px uses -2.7px (-0.045em). Convert tracking to em when you copy it, so it still fits if you change the size.

The short version

  1. List sizes weighted by characters, at the viewport you care about.
  2. The size with the most text is the base.
  3. Compute a ratio if you want a description, but copy the real sizes.
  4. Take line height and letter spacing with each step.

If you'd rather not do this by hand, I made a Chrome extension, Stylasso, that reads the type scale along with the fonts and colors and gives base, ratio and each step's line height and tracking. The numbers above match its output for these demo sites, except that it drops the stray 20px size on Afterhours (that's where its 2.031 comes from). There's a short guide here: find out what font a website is using, with its type scale. The snippet works fine without it.

Written with help from an AI assistant. The sizes come from running the snippet above on the three demo pages, and the ratios from the code in this post.

title: MySQL ENUM vs CHECK Constraint: Which Value List Changes Copy the Table
description:
Disclosure: I build Schemity, a desktop ERD tool - this post is from our blog and uses it for the examples.

TL;DR: On MySQL 8.4, appending a value to the end of an ENUM of up to 255 values is a metadata change that takes no time, while inserting one in the middle, reordering, or removing one copies the whole table and holds back writes. Removing a value that rows still hold fails with error 1265. An enforced CHECK on a VARCHAR copies the table for every change to its list, appends included, and a lookup table needs no ALTER TABLE at all.

On MySQL 8.4, an ENUM is the cheapest value list to extend and among the most expensive to edit any other way. Appending a value to the end of the list changes only the table definition and finished in 0.00 seconds on a million rows. Inserting a value in the middle, reordering the list or removing a value copies the whole table and holds back writes while it does, and removing a value that rows still hold fails outright. A CHECK (status IN (...)) on a VARCHAR copies the table for every change to its list, appends included. So whether ENUM or CHECK is the better choice depends on how the list will change, not on how it looks today.

Everything below ran on MySQL 8.4.11 in a throwaway Docker container on a laptop. The table is tasks, with 1,000,000 rows and a status ENUM('open','done','blocked') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open' column. 400,000 rows hold open, 599,964 hold done and 36 hold blocked. Each change ran on a fresh copy of the table, and the timings are there to compare kinds of change, not to predict your server.

MySQL ENUM vs CHECK constraint: which is cheaper to change?

The ENUM is cheaper only for an append within its storage width (and a change of letter case): every other ENUM edit, and every edit to an enforced CHECK list, copies the table.

MySQL stores an ENUM value as a number, the position of the value in the list, and keeps the strings in the table definition. Appending a string leaves every stored number pointing at the same value, so there is nothing to rewrite. Anything that moves a value to a different position, or takes one away, changes what the stored numbers mean, so MySQL rebuilds the table to write them again. The online DDL reference says it in one line: "Adding members in the middle of the list causes renumbering of existing members, which requires a table copy."

Change to status on 1,000,000 rows What MySQL does Time
Append 'archived' at the end INSTANT 0.00 s
Insert 'review' between 'open' and 'done' Copies the table (INSTANT and INPLACE refused, 1846) 1.58 s
Reorder to ('done','open','blocked') Copies the table 1.50 s
Remove 'archived', which no row holds Copies the table 1.53 s
Remove 'blocked', which 36 rows hold Fails, ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 2 -
Change the case of 'done' to 'Done' INSTANT, and every row now reads Done 0.00 s
Append a 256th value to a 255-value ENUM Copies the table 1.46 s
Append a 9th member to an 8-member SET Copies the table 1.39 s
Append a 10th member to a 9-member SET INSTANT 0.00 s
Add 'archived' to CHECK (status IN (...)) on a VARCHAR(20) Copies the table (INSTANT and INPLACE refused, 1845) 1.65 s

Neither MySQL nor PostgreSQL can alter a check constraint's expression, so changing the list means DROP CHECK and ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK, and adding a check makes MySQL read every row to validate it. MySQL does that by copying the table, even when the new list only adds a value and no row could fail it. The DROP CHECK alone is instant; it is the ADD that costs. PostgreSQL can split the cost with NOT VALID and a later VALIDATE CONSTRAINT; MySQL has no equivalent. Its NOT ENFORCED check is added instantly, but it enforces nothing, and switching it to ENFORCED copies the table.

A copy is not only slow, it holds back writes. On the same table grown to 3,000,000 rows, inserting 'review' in the middle of the list copied for 4.94 seconds. A single-row INSERT sent 0.7 seconds in waited 4.33 seconds, while a SELECT by primary key sent at the same moment came back at once. Appending 'archived' to the same 3,000,000 rows took 0.00 seconds.

Does adding a value to a MySQL ENUM copy the table?

Not if the value goes at the end and the list stays within the same storage width.

An ENUM takes 1 byte per row up to 255 values and 2 bytes from 256 up to its limit of 65,535; a SET takes 1, 2, 3, 4 or 8 bytes for its up to 64 members, per the storage requirements table. When an append crosses one of those widths, every row has to be rewritten at the new width, so the append copies the table like any other change. That is why the 9th SET member copied and the 10th did not, and why the 256th ENUM value copied. Few lists ever reach 255 values, but 8 SET members is an easy boundary to cross.

To make the cost visible before production, name the algorithm in the migration:

ALTER TABLE tasks
  MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'done', 'blocked', 'archived') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
-- Query OK, 0 rows affected (0.00 sec)

ALTER TABLE tasks
  MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'review', 'done', 'blocked') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open',
  ALGORITHM=INSTANT;
-- ERROR 1846 (0A000): ALGORITHM=INSTANT is not supported.
-- Reason: Need to rebuild the table to change column type. Try ALGORITHM=COPY/INPLACE.

The second statement changes nothing and says why. Without the clause it would have copied the table, because MySQL picks the cheapest algorithm it can and does not name it; the only sign is 1000000 rows affected instead of 0 rows affected, after the copy has run. The same clause catches a migration generated from a model where someone inserted 'review' where it reads well, rather than at the end.

Order matters for a second reason. MySQL sorts an ENUM by position, not alphabetically, so ORDER BY status on this table returns open, done, blocked. Appending keeps that order stable; putting a new value anywhere but last in a sort means inserting it or reordering the list, and both copy the table.

How do I remove a value from a MySQL ENUM?

Move every row off the value first, then remove it, and expect the removal to copy the table.

With strict mode on, the MySQL 8.4 default, removing a value that any row holds fails before anything changes: ERROR 1265 (01000): Data truncated for column 'status' at row 2. Without strict mode, the same statement succeeds with one warning per row, 36 here, and those rows now hold the empty string, which the ENUM documentation calls the error value, with index 0. SELECT status + 0 shows it. Nothing tells the application that 36 tasks lost their status. So before the change:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM tasks WHERE status = 'blocked';   -- 36
UPDATE tasks SET status = 'open' WHERE status = 'blocked';
ALTER TABLE tasks MODIFY status ENUM('open', 'done') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'open';

Renaming a value is the same three steps: append the new name (instant), move the rows with an UPDATE, remove the old name (a copy). On a large table the UPDATE is the expensive step, one transaction over every row that holds the value, so run it in batches and have the application accept both names while the rows move. Changing 'done' to 'completed' in place is refused INSTANT with 1846 and fails with 1265 on rows holding 'done'. There is no shorter route, with one exception: a change of letter case only. Under a case-insensitive collation such as the default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci, relabelling 'done' as 'Done' was instant and every row read back as Done. Under utf8mb4_bin or utf8mb4_0900_as_cs the same statement failed with 1265, because there 'done' and 'Done' are different values. The default follows the same rule: DEFAULT 'Open' on a list holding 'open' is accepted under _ci and stored as 'open', and refused on a status ENUM('open','done') COLLATE utf8mb4_bin column with ERROR 1067 (42000): Invalid default value for 'status'.

If the copy is too expensive, the alternative is not to remove the value at all: leave it in the list, stop the application writing it, and remove it the next time the table is rebuilt for another reason.

Which should you use: ENUM, CHECK or a lookup table?

Use an ENUM for a list that only grows at the end, a lookup table for a list that changes often or carries data of its own, and a CHECK when portability matters more than the cost of changing it.

ENUM VARCHAR + CHECK Lookup table + foreign key
Add a value Instant at the end; a copy anywhere else Copies the table An INSERT, no ALTER TABLE
Remove a value rows still hold Fails, 1265 (strict) Fails, 3819 (Check constraint 'c_status_check' is violated.) Fails, 1451 (Cannot delete or update a parent row)
Storage per row 1 byte (up to 255 values) The string itself The string or a numeric key
Sort order Position in the list Collation order By label after a join, or a sort column you add
Moves to PostgreSQL or SQL Server Needs converting As written As written

The removal row matters as much as the add row: every option refuses to orphan a row, but only the lookup table does it without an ALTER TABLE on the table that holds the rows. Its cost is a join to read the label and one more table in the diagram.

How Schemity shows what an ENUM change costs

Schemity's impact analysis reports which MySQL ENUM edits copy the table and how many rows hold a value you removed, before the migration runs.

Schemity is database design software that reads your live database, shows the impact of every schema change before it runs, and keeps the diagram as a file in Git. After you connect to MySQL, an ENUM column's values appear in the field dialog's Values box, and editing them there becomes a planned ALTER TABLE ... MODIFY statement.

Impact analysis applies the rules measured above:

  • Append a value and there is no finding, because MySQL changes only the definition. Append the 256th ENUM value or the 9th SET member and the table rewrite appears.
  • Insert, reorder or remove a value and the findings include "Rewrites tasks to change status" with the row estimate, and a note that changing the type of status holds back writes to tasks while it reads the same estimated rows.
  • Remove a value and a "Can fail on existing data" finding appears ("Loses data" on a server without strict mode), with "Count exactly" to count the rows that still hold it. The count runs only when you ask, as a read-only SELECT COUNT(*) that matches the removed values, so 36 blocked rows show up before MySQL reports them as error 1265.
  • A change of letter case is matched the way the column's collation compares: no finding under _ci, a failing removal under _bin or _cs.

Appending archived after open, done and blocked in the Values box is the first case, and the Impact drawer stays empty:

Remove blocked instead and the same drawer shows three findings: the change can fail on existing data, it rewrites tasks, and it holds back writes while it reads the estimated ~997.6K rows, 42 MB on disk.

Schema lint adds one rule for the same column type: mysql-enum-default-not-listed reports an ENUM or SET default that is not one of its values, which MySQL refuses with error 1067, compared under the column's collation. That is how the diagram lets you see the impact of every change to a value list: the append and the insert look alike in a migration file, and only one of them copies the table.

MySQL ENUM changes, in one list

Only an append within the same storage width, or a change of letter case under a _ci collation, is free; everything else rewrites the table or fails.

  • Appending to an ENUM or SET is INSTANT, unless it crosses 255 ENUM values or a SET storage width (8, 16, 24 or 32 members).
  • Inserting in the middle, reordering and removing a value copy the table and hold back writes until the copy ends.
  • Removing a value that rows hold fails with 1265 in strict mode and silently empties those rows without it; move them first.
  • Changing an enforced CHECK list copies the table every time, appends included; a lookup table changes with an INSERT.
  • Add ALGORITHM=INSTANT to an append so MySQL refuses, rather than copies, if the change is not one, and set lock_wait_timeout so even an instant change cannot queue reads behind an open transaction.

The other MySQL ALTER TABLE changes that copy, from a VARCHAR crossing 255 bytes to a foreign key added with checks on, are timed in MySQL ALTER TABLE: which changes lock the table, and what happens to the statements before a failed one is covered in which failed migrations roll back. The same choice on PostgreSQL, where enums are a type of their own, is compared in Postgres enum vs check constraint vs lookup table, and if you are converting a MySQL schema to PostgreSQL, every ENUM needs that decision anyway.

title: Introducing Go++
description:
My dear fellow developers,

I’d like to take a moment of your time to announce that I’ve been working on an experimental project called Go++, a superset of Go that compiles to plain Go; the project is still in early stages and definitely not ready for production use but I was hoping to get some early feedback from the community that could help steer it in the right direction.

I love Go and its simplicity, but many a time I’ve wished it allowed me to express my intent a little more succinctly and Go++ is an attempt towards exactly that but while remaining firmly grounded to the Go runtime and its awesome and mature standard library and the ecosystem.

In a nutshell, Go++ currently offers things like:

  • Classes and polymorphism
  • Generics
  • Multiple inheritance
  • Function and method overloading
  • Named and default arguments
  • Enums and structural records
  • Extension methods
  • String interpolation
  • Safe nil walking and fallbacks
  • Exceptions
  • Annotations and introspection
  • and more!

One important project constraint driving the compiler has been to compile a Go project without any modifications thus letting developers incrementally adopt Go++ features as they see fit for the problem at hand.

The project has grown beyond the compiler itself and now includes a CLI, formatter, language server/VS Code extension, testing, and some opinionated built-in packages for HTTP routing, serialization, ORM and more.

Go developers can quickly try it with:

go install github.com/telgatech/gpp@main
gpp init hello
cd hello
gpp run

Detailed documentation including getting started guide and sources available at:
https://gpp.telga.in/
https://gpp.telga.in/guide/getting-started
https://github.com/telgatech/gpp

I’d love feedback from Go developers who are willing to give it a spin—particularly around the language design, Go interoperability, tooling, rough edges, and anything that feels surprising or inconsistent.

If you try it, let me know what works, what breaks, and what you’d like to see next.

title: UECA-React 3.2.2: two bugs that lost state without a word
description:
Part 5. Earlier: converting a vibe-coded MVP, the origin story, an AI agent testing the framework, UECA-React 3.2.

UECA-React 3.2.2 is a patch with no new API. It fixes two bugs that lost state without a word: no error, no warning, no failing test.

A new route kept the old screen

In UECA a component's id is its identity: DOM id, bus address and cache key. So a router can give each route its own screen through the id:

"/items/:itemId": (p) => (
    <ItemScreen
        id={"itemScreen-" + p?.itemId}
        routeParams={p}
    />
),

Going from item 1 to item 2 changes only the id, so React keeps the element. UECA kept its model too and renamed it: no init, and item 2 opened with item 1's state. It turned up while checking the shipped agent skills against 3.2.1, whose scaffold router had exactly this shape.

Now the id is the element's key. A new id gets its own model, and the old one waits in the cache until its id comes back.

An edit went nowhere 

editor: useNestedEditor({
    data: UECA.bind(() => model.entity, "nested"),
}),

The owner and the child share one object, so the child's edits land in the entity. When the owner reloaded the entity and the nested object came back equal but as a new instance, UECA treated it as no change. The child kept the old instance, and its edits went into an object the entity no longer held. This one was reported from a real application.

Now the child takes the new instance, without running onChange, since the value didn't change.

Also

  • React 16.14 is the minimum. Earlier 16.x versions could never load the package; the peer range now says so.
  • The programming guide, the agent skills and the app scaffold are corrected against the code. If you scaffolded an app from 3.2.1, compare your dialogs and REST client with the new scaffold.

Upgrading 

npm install ueca-react@3.2.2

npx ueca-react-skills

The second command refreshes the agent skills in your project. Details are in the changelog.

npm · Docs and demo

title: A pre-start version guard for self-hosted services (after the LNbits 1.7.0 advisory)
description:
On 8 November the LNbits team told operators to shut their servers down after attackers created unauthorized accounts and withdrew funds. One operator reported losing 2,285,545 sats. On 10 November, version 1.7.0 shipped as an urgent security update, with a clear instruction: upgrade before you restart.

That instruction is easy to break by accident. A systemd unit restarts after a reboot, a container comes back with an old image, and the vulnerable version is serving requests again before anyone checks.

Here is a small guard you can put in front of any self-hosted service: it reads the installed version, compares it with a minimum you set, and exits non-zero if the version is too old, so the service never starts.

The script 

// version-guard.mjs
// usage: node version-guard.mjs <path-to-pyproject.toml> <min-version>
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const [file, min] = process.argv.slice(2);
if (!file || !min) {
  console.error('usage: node version-guard.mjs <pyproject.toml> <min-version>');
  process.exit(64);
}

const text = readFileSync(file, 'utf8');
const m = text.match(/^version\s*=\s*"([^"]+)"/m);
if (!m) {
  console.error(`no version line found in ${file}`);
  process.exit(65);
}

const parse = (v) => v.replace(/^v/, '').split(/[.-]/).slice(0, 3).map((n) => parseInt(n, 10) || 0);
const cmp = (a, b) => {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) if (a[i] !== b[i]) return a[i] - b[i];
  return 0;
};

const installed = m[1];
if (cmp(parse(installed), parse(min)) < 0) {
  console.error(`refusing to start: installed ${installed} < required ${min}`);
  process.exit(1);
}
console.log(`ok: installed ${installed} >= ${min}`);

Wire it into systemd 

[Service]
ExecStartPre=/usr/bin/node /opt/guards/version-guard.mjs /opt/lnbits/pyproject.toml 1.7.0
ExecStart=/opt/lnbits/start.sh

If ExecStartPre fails, systemd doesn't run ExecStart. The unit fails, and you see it in systemctl status and your alerts.

Check it against the latest upstream release

To get told when upstream moves past your pin, compare with the GitHub releases API:

// latest-release.mjs
const res = await fetch('https://api.github.com/repos/lnbits/lnbits/releases/latest', {
  headers: { 'User-Agent': 'version-guard' },
});
const { tag_name } = await res.json();
console.log(tag_name);

Run it from cron and diff the output against your pinned minimum. A change means it's time to read the release notes.

Notes

  • The version parser handles 1.7.0, v1.7.0 and 1.7.0-rc1 (pre-release tags compare equal to the release; tighten it if that matters to you).
  • Point the guard at whatever file your install uses as the source of truth for its version.
  • A guard can only stop a restart. It does nothing for a server that is already running. When a project says "shut down now", shut it down first.

Sources: Bitcoin Magazine on LNbits 1.7.0, Crypto Briefing, Bitcoin.com News.

title: Zustand: React State Without the Boilerplate
description:
Picture a small shop page with a cart icon in the corner. A visitor adds a tote bag and a mug. Three parts of the page need to know what happened: the cart icon showing the count, the cart drawer listing the items, and the checkout button showing the total. If each part keeps its own copy of the cart, the numbers drift apart. The usual fix is to lift the state up to a shared parent, but that turns every middle component into a courier for data it never uses. That is the problem Zustand sets out to solve, and the question is whether a tiny store does the job better than the tools React already ships with.

What I would check before using it

My first check is how much state needs sharing. One cart icon and one list on the same page can live in a parent component, and a library buys nothing there. Once three or more distant parts read the same state, or it must survive a route change, a shared store earns its keep. Count the readers first.

My second check is the learning curve, and Zustand is light here. A store is a function call with state fields plus the functions that change them. No provider, no reducer, no action types. Anyone who knows useState can read a Zustand store, and that matters, because the cost of a library is paid whenever someone new opens the file.

My third check is how components subscribe. With React context, every reader re-renders on any change, even parts it never touches. Zustand lets each component pick just the slice it needs, so the cart icon re-renders on a count change and ignores a price edit. On a small shop that is invisible; on a busy page it is the difference between a snappy interface and one that stutters.

My fourth check is the escape hatches. Zustand also works outside React, through its vanilla store, so the same cart logic runs in a plain script or a test. That beats context, which only exists inside a React tree.

My verdict, as judgement: use Zustand when several components share state that changes a lot and you want the simplest tool. Skip it when the state lives in one component, or when you need time travel debugging or a strict action log. The recommendation flips when the shared state shrinks to one parent and child, or the team needs a framework's guardrails rather than a plain object's freedom.

One small shop cart, run end to end

The example is a small shop cart built with the vanilla version of Zustand, so it runs in plain Node with no React at all. The store holds an array of cart items and three actions: add an item, remove one by id, and clear the cart. A total function computes the price from the items, so the total can never drift out of sync with the list. A subscriber logs the item count and total after every change, standing in for the parts of a page that would re-render in React.

Here is the store and the script that drives it. The products are a canvas tote bag at $18, a ceramic mug at $14.50, and a notebook set at $9.25:

const { createStore } = require("zustand/vanilla");

const products = [
  { id: 1, name: "Canvas tote bag", price: 18.0 },
  { id: 2, name: "Ceramic mug", price: 14.5 },
  { id: 3, name: "Notebook set", price: 9.25 },
];

const cartStore = createStore((set, get) => ({
  items: [],
  addItem: (product, qty = 1) =>
    set((state) => {
      const existing = state.items.find((i) => i.id === product.id);
      if (existing) {
        return {
          items: state.items.map((i) =>
            i.id === product.id ? { ...i, qty: i.qty + qty } : i
          ),
        };
      }
      return { items: [...state.items, { ...product, qty }] };
    }),
  removeItem: (id) =>
    set((state) => ({ items: state.items.filter((i) => i.id !== id) })),
  clearCart: () => set({ items: [] }),
  total: () =>
    get().items.reduce((sum, i) => sum + i.price * i.qty, 0),
}));

cartStore.subscribe((state) => {
  const count = state.items.reduce((n, i) => n + i.qty, 0);
  console.log(`Cart changed: ${count} item(s), total $${state.total().toFixed(2)}`);
});

console.log("Adding 2 tote bags and 1 mug...");
cartStore.getState().addItem(products[0], 2);
cartStore.getState().addItem(products[1], 1);

console.log("Adding 3 notebook sets...");
cartStore.getState().addItem(products[2], 3);

console.log("Removing the mug...");
cartStore.getState().removeItem(2);

console.log("Final cart:");
for (const item of cartStore.getState().items) {
  console.log(`- ${item.qty} x ${item.name} @ $${item.price} = $${(item.price * item.qty).toFixed(2)}`);
}
console.log("Grand total: $" + cartStore.getState().total().toFixed(2));

This is the real output from running it with Node:

Adding 2 tote bags and 1 mug...
Cart changed: 2 item(s), total $36.00
Cart changed: 3 item(s), total $50.50
Adding 3 notebook sets...
Cart changed: 6 item(s), total $78.25
Removing the mug...
Cart changed: 5 item(s), total $63.75
Final cart:
- 2 x Canvas tote bag @ $18 = $36.00
- 3 x Notebook set @ $9.25 = $27.75
Grand total: $63.75

Three things are worth noticing. First, the total is always computed from the items, never stored separately, so adding a notebook set moves the total from $50.50 to $78.25 with no extra code. Second, the subscriber fired exactly once per change, which is how a React component would know to re-render. Third, adding the same product twice creates no duplicate line: the second tote bag merged into the existing one by raising the quantity, which is the behaviour a real shop wants.

The thing that went wrong was a direct push into the state array. Instead of calling the addItem action, I reached into the store and pushed a pen set straight onto the items array:

cartStore.getState().items.push({ id: 4, name: "Pen set", price: 6.5, qty: 1 });

Reading the store afterwards showed 2 items, so the push had worked, but the subscriber never fired. Here is the real output from that run:

Items before the bad line: 1
Items after direct push: 2
Subscriber calls after direct push: 0
Adding a notebook set the proper way...
Subscriber fired, call #1
Items now: Canvas tote bag, Pen set, Notebook set
Subscriber calls total: 1

The push changed the data without telling anyone. In React the cart icon would still show the old count, because no re-render was triggered, and the pen set would only appear after the next real update forced a render. That is a silent bug: nothing throws, nothing looks broken, and the page quietly shows stale numbers. The fix is the rule Zustand is built around: never touch the state object directly, always go through set. The addItem action creates a new array with the spread operator, and that new array is what wakes the subscribers. Keep that rule and the store stays honest; break it and the store lies to the page.

Common mistakes and how to fix them

First, mutating state directly, as in the broken run above. The symptom is a store holding new data while the page shows old numbers, with no error anywhere to point at. The fix is to always change state through set with a new array or object, using the spread operator or map and filter, and never push, splice, or assign onto state from getState.

Second, subscribing to the whole store. A component that reads the entire store re-renders on every change, even one it never displays, so a price edit re-renders the cart icon. The fix is to select only the slice it needs, for example just the item count or just the total, and let the rest of the store change without disturbing it.

Third, holding a stale snapshot. Calling getState once, saving the result, and reading it later gives you the state as it was at that moment, not as it is now, so a total computed from it stays frozen while the cart keeps changing. The fix is to call getState fresh inside the action that needs it, or to subscribe, so the value you read is always current.

My call on Zustand

Zustand does one job and stays out of the way: it holds shared state in an object and tells the components that care when it changes. The cart above needed a short store, a computed total, and a subscriber, and nothing in it was new. That is the whole appeal, and also the limit: dozens of tangled stores can turn that freedom into a hunt for which action changed what. For a shop cart, a theme toggle, or a dashboard, it is the right size. Try it on one shared piece of state and see whether the code gets shorter. If it does, keep going; if the state was never shared, a store was never needed.

Further reading

  • Zustand documentation, https://zustand.docs.pmnd.rs/
  • React docs, Managing State, https://react.dev/learn/managing-state
  • React docs, Sharing State Between Components, https://react.dev/learn/sharing-state-between-components

Originally published at https://practicaldevblog.blogspot.com/2026/11/zustand-react-state-without-boilerplate.html

title: The 10-Minute Collision Window: Killing Duplicate Bank SMS Transactions
description:
When you build an automated transaction ingestion pipeline from banking SMS notifications, your biggest enemy is not malformed text.

Your biggest enemy is duplicate delivery.

Telecommunication networks and banking infrastructure duplicate messages regularly:

  1. Network Retransmission: If a phone travels through a weak cellular zone or hands off between cell towers, carrier SMS gateways frequently deliver the same message twice.
  2. Dual Bank Alerts: Many Indian banks send two distinct notifications for a single POS transaction: first an authorization alert from the card processor (e.g. Visa or Mastercard), followed minutes later by an SMS from the issuing bank confirming the debit.
  3. Inbox Re-Scanning: When a user runs a historical inbox scan, the scanner will encounter messages that were already captured in real-time by the application's background BroadcastReceiver days earlier.

If an expense tracker records both alerts, your account balance is deducted twice, ruining your ledger.

However, fixing this with naive deduplication is even more dangerous: it can cause silent data loss.

Here is how a subtle regression in FinLedger led to the discovery of the deduplication collision dilemma, and how we solved it with a calibrated four-factor matching engine.

The Flawed Query: When Deduplication Causes Silent Data Loss

In an early development sprint, FinLedger implemented a straightforward duplicate detection query in SQLite. The logic attempted to catch both identical timestamps and identical transactions:

-- The Flawed Early Query
SELECT * FROM transactions 
WHERE dateTimestamp = :timestamp 
   OR (amount = :amount AND accountId = :accountId);

Can you spot the catastrophic flaw in this logic?

Look closely at the OR condition:

flowchart TD
    subgraph SilentLoss["The Danger of Naive Deduplication"]
        MorningCoffee["9:00 AM: Buy Coffee for Rs. 150.00 at Starbucks"] --> Insert1["Inserted into Ledger:
        Amount: 150.00, Time: 9:00 AM"]

        LunchCoffee["1:30 PM: Buy Coffee for Rs. 150.00 at Starbucks"] --> Check["Deduplication Query:
        'Does a transaction exist with Amount = 150.00 on this account?'"]

        Check -->|YES: Matches Morning Coffee!| Drop["Catastrophic Bug:
        Lunch coffee dropped as 'Duplicate'!
        Rs. 150 quietly vanishes from ledger tracking."]
    end

Because the query used an over-broad OR clause:

  1. If you bought two coffees of the exact same price (Rs. 150.00) on the same day, the second coffee was rejected as a duplicate!
  2. Even worse, if you ran automated bills where two subscriptions (e.g., Spotify and iCloud) processed at the exact same second (dateTimestamp), the second subscription was discarded!

This was a severe accounting bug discovered during regression testing (documented under TASK-H4.4 in the FinLedger codebase). We were dropping genuine financial transactions to prevent duplicate SMS alerts.

The Four-Factor Matching Engine (DuplicateDetectionTest.kt)

To prevent duplicate bank alerts without dropping legitimate recurring transactions, we completely rewrote the deduplication predicate.

A candidate transaction is only classified as a duplicate if all four discriminating factors match simultaneously:

flowchart TD
    Candidate["Incoming SMS Candidate"] --> Factor1{"1. Amount Match:
    abs(a - b) < 0.005
    (Within half a paisa)"}

    Factor1 -->|No| Safe["Insert as Unique Transaction"]
    Factor1 -->|Yes| Factor2{"2. Time Window:
    abs(t1 - t2) <= 10 Minutes
    (600,000 ms)"}

    Factor2 -->|No| Safe
    Factor2 -->|Yes| Factor3{"3. Polarity Match:
    candidate.type == seen.type
    (DEBIT vs CREDIT)"}

    Factor3 -->|No| Safe
    Factor3 -->|Yes| Factor4{"4. Entity Match:
    candidate.merchant == seen.merchant"}

    Factor4 -->|No| Safe
    Factor4 -->|Yes| Duplicate["CONFIRMED DUPLICATE:
    Drop without corrupting balances"]

Let's examine why each factor is essential.

1. Amount Precision (Half a Paisa)

In financial math, floating-point numbers cannot be compared with direct equality (==). The engine verifies that:
abs(seen.amount - candidate.amount) < 0.005
This accounts for minuscule floating-point rounding quirks while strictly preserving distinct transactions.

2. The 10-Minute Collision Window (600,000 ms)

Why 10 minutes?

  • Cellular network retries and carrier message duplication almost always occur within 60 to 180 seconds.
  • Secondary bank authorization alerts for POS machines occasionally experience 5 to 7 minute delays during peak server loads.
  • However, it is virtually impossible for a human being to purchase the exact same item, for the exact same price, at the exact same merchant, within a 10-minute window without it being an accidental duplicate tap or double-charge.
  • If you buy coffee at 9:00 AM and another coffee at 1:30 PM, the delta is 270 minutes—well outside the collision window. Both are correctly preserved.

3. Transaction Polarity (Type Matching)

A debit followed immediately by a credit (such as an instant refund or reversed payment) carries the same amount, timestamp, and merchant. By verifying that candidate.type == seen.type, an incoming refund credit of Rs. 500 is never dropped because of the original Rs. 500 debit alert.

4. Counter-Party Normalization

The merchant name must match after string normalization (stripping trailing UPI reference numbers and whitespace). If you pay Rs. 500 for a taxi and Rs. 500 for groceries five minutes later, the distinct merchant identifiers ensure neither transaction is dropped.

Testing with Automated Regression Suites

To guarantee that future refactoring never reintroduces duplicate data loss, FinLedger maintains a comprehensive unit test suite in DuplicateDetectionTest.kt.

The test suite systematically asserts against real-world edge cases:

  • Two different transactions occurring at the exact same millisecond (e.g. simultaneous automated investments) are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts at different merchants are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts and merchants separated by 11 minutes (660,000 ms) are asserted as NOT duplicates.
  • Identical amounts, merchants, and accounts arriving within 3 minutes with matching transaction references are asserted as DUPLICATES and successfully consolidated.

Key Takeaway

Deduplication in financial software cannot be treated as a simple database uniqueness constraint.

Real-world banking alerts are messy, delayed, and asynchronous. By establishing a strict multi-factor collision window—spanning amount precision, time delta, transaction polarity, and merchant identity—FinLedger eliminates redundant SMS alerts without ever losing a penny of user data.

FinLedger is a privacy-first, offline-first personal finance application for Android that models bank accounts, credit cards, and cash without double-counting.

Explore FinLedger on Google Play: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.devanshufinance.app

title: How to Reduce Azure SQL Costs: A Practical Checklist (2026)
description:
Originally published at SQL & Cloud Lab.

This post was drafted with AI assistance.

Azure SQL is easy to start and easy to overspend on. Most teams size their databases once, during migration, and never look again, so they keep paying for capacity they do not use. The good news is that the biggest savings usually come from a handful of changes that take hours, not weeks.

This checklist walks through those changes in the order I would apply them: measure first, then fix licensing and commitments, then architecture, then queries.

1. Right-size from real usage, not from the old server

The most common mistake is sizing Azure to match the on-premises server's hardware. Old servers were bought for peak load plus growth, and often sat at 10 to 20 percent CPU.

  • Check at least two to four weeks of CPU, data IO, log IO and memory usage.
  • In Azure SQL Database, sys.dm_db_resource_stats shows usage for roughly the last hour at 15-second intervals, and sys.resource_stats in the master database keeps longer history.
  • If average usage stays low and peaks are short, scale down one tier and watch for a week. 
-- Average and peak usage over the last hour (Azure SQL Database)
SELECT
    AVG(avg_cpu_percent)       AS avg_cpu,
    MAX(avg_cpu_percent)       AS max_cpu,
    AVG(avg_data_io_percent)   AS avg_data_io,
    AVG(avg_log_write_percent) AS avg_log_write
FROM sys.dm_db_resource_stats;

Scaling an Azure SQL Database up or down is an online operation that usually completes in minutes, so it is low risk to try a smaller size.

2. Use Azure Hybrid Benefit

If your organisation already owns SQL Server licences with Software Assurance (or qualifying subscriptions), Azure Hybrid Benefit lets you apply them in the vCore purchasing model so you stop paying for the SQL licence again. For many workloads this is the single largest saving. It does not apply to the DTU model or to serverless compute, so check which model each database uses.

3. Buy reserved capacity for steady workloads

Production databases that run 24x7 at a predictable size are the most expensive thing to run on pay-as-you-go. Reserved capacity commits you to a vCore amount for one or three years in exchange for a lower rate, and it can be combined with Azure Hybrid Benefit. Reserve only the baseline you are confident about; burst above it on pay-as-you-go.

4. Use serverless for dev, test and intermittent workloads

The General Purpose serverless tier bills compute per second and can auto-pause when idle, leaving only storage charges. It is ideal for development and test databases and for apps used mainly in business hours.

Watch for anything that keeps the database awake: open SSMS windows, connection pools, monitoring probes and scheduled jobs. A serverless database that never pauses can cost more than a small provisioned one.

5. Put small databases in an elastic pool

If you run many small databases with uneven load, such as one per customer, an elastic pool lets them share a fixed amount of compute. Because their peaks rarely happen at the same time, the pool can be much cheaper than sizing each database for its own peak.

6. Trim backup, replica and storage costs

  • Backup retention: keep long-term retention only where policy requires it, and review whether geo-redundant backup storage is needed for non-production databases.
  • Replicas: geo-replicas and failover groups are billed as full databases. Make sure each one is still required.
  • Allocated space: after large deletes, check allocated versus used space before paying for a bigger maximum size.

7. Tune the top queries before buying a bigger tier

A missing index or one bad query can push a database two tiers higher than it needs. Before scaling up, open Query Store, sort by total CPU or duration, and fix the top five queries. That often frees enough headroom to scale down instead.

-- Top 5 queries by total CPU time (Query Store)
SELECT TOP (5)
    q.query_id,
    SUM(rs.count_executions) AS executions,
    SUM(rs.avg_cpu_time * rs.count_executions) / 1000 AS total_cpu_ms,
    MAX(qt.query_sql_text) AS query_text
FROM sys.query_store_runtime_stats rs
JOIN sys.query_store_plan p        ON rs.plan_id = p.plan_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query q       ON p.query_id = q.query_id
JOIN sys.query_store_query_text qt ON q.query_text_id = qt.query_text_id
GROUP BY q.query_id
ORDER BY total_cpu_ms DESC;

8. Set budgets, alerts and review Azure Advisor

Savings drift back without monitoring. In Cost Management, create a budget per subscription or resource group with alerts at 80 and 100 percent. Review Azure Advisor cost recommendations monthly; it flags idle and under-used databases for you.

Quick checklist

Action Effort Typical impact
Right-size from real usage Low High
Azure Hybrid Benefit Low High (if licences exist)
Reserved capacity Low High for 24x7 workloads
Serverless for dev/test Low Medium
Elastic pools Medium Medium to high
Backup and replica review Low Low to medium
Query tuning Medium Medium to high
Budgets and alerts Low Prevents drift

Final thoughts

Start with measurement, because every other decision depends on it. Then apply licensing and commitment discounts to what you truly need, and only then look at architecture and queries. Prices and offers change, so confirm the numbers for your region in the Azure Pricing Calculator before committing.

title: Figma handoff checklist: what developers need from designers
description:
Moving a design from Figma into code should feel like a smooth transition, but it often turns into a frustrating guessing game. Designers hand over a clean file, developers start building, and immediately the questions begin. What happens when this button is hovered? How does this card look on an iPad? Where are the actual image files?

When design files lack structure, projects slow down, budgets stretch, and the final product starts drifting away from the original vision. You end up wasting hours in meetings clearing up details that should have been obvious in the layout.

Whether you are working with my team on a Figma to Next.js build or partnering with any other developer, establishing a solid handoff routine saves everyone time. Here is a practical checklist of what developers actually need from designers to build pixel-perfect, responsive websites without the constant back-and-forth.

Organized components and variants

In modern web development, websites are built using reusable pieces rather than static pages. If a designer hands over a file with fifty separate button frames that all look slightly different, a developer cannot easily tell which one is the master component. It creates massive amounts of redundant code and inconsistent user interfaces.

A proper design file uses master components with clear variants for different styles and properties. If a button has primary, secondary, and ghost styles, those should live inside a single component set rather than scattered across the artboard. This mirrors how React and Next.js developers build user interfaces using props and reusable modules.

Clean component structures also make future updates much easier. When a brand color changes or a border radius gets updated, editing the master component propagates that change everywhere. Developers appreciate seeing explicit component states mapped out clearly in the design file.

  • Use master components for repeating elements like cards, buttons, form fields, and navigation bars.
  • Group variations such as hover, active, disabled, and loading states inside the component properties.
  • Avoid detached instances or unlinked copies that look like components but lack systemic rules.

Clear interactive and responsive states

Static screens only tell half the story of a modern website. Users interact with buttons, hover over cards, type into input fields, and trigger error messages. If these states are missing from the design file, developers have to invent them on the fly, which rarely matches what the designer intended.

Designers should explicitly show what happens during interaction. What does a submit button look like when clicked? How does an error message display when a form field is left blank? Providing these extra frames eliminates guesswork during coding.

Responsive behavior across screen sizes needs the same level of clarity. Instead of assuming a desktop layout simply shrinks down for mobile, designers should define how multi-column grids collapse, when text sizes scale down, and how navigation menus transform into mobile hamburger drawers.

  • Design hover, focus, and active states for all clickable elements.
  • Provide explicit error, success, and loading states for forms and interactive widgets.
  • Include distinct layout frames for mobile, tablet, and desktop viewports rather than relying on automatic scaling.

Design tokens for colors, typography, and spacing

Consistency is what separates a professional website from a messy collection of web pages. When designers use arbitrary font sizes like 15px, 17px, and 18px across different pages, or use slight variations of a brand blue hex code, it creates visual clutter and bloats the codebase.

Design tokens act as a single source of truth for design decisions. They define a strict system for colors, typography scales, border radii, shadows, and spacing increments. When these tokens are clearly documented in Figma, developers can translate them directly into configuration files like Tailwind CSS.

Using a consistent spacing scale, such as increments of four or eight pixels, ensures that margins and paddings look harmonious throughout the site. It also speeds up development because engineers do not have to inspect every single padding value manually.

  • Establish a defined color palette with descriptive names like primary, background, and muted rather than raw hex codes.
  • Use a typographic scale that limits font sizes to a deliberate set of options.
  • Stick to a consistent spacing grid for margins, padding, and layout gutters.

Proper asset preparation and export readiness

One of the most common bottlenecks in a web project is waiting for image and icon assets. If icons are embedded as flattened bitmap graphics or complex vector paths with thousands of stray points, they cannot be used effectively on the web.

Developers need vector assets exported as clean SVG files that can scale infinitely without losing quality. Raster images like photographs should be supplied in high resolutions so they can be optimized and converted into modern formats like WebP or AVIF for fast loading times.

Organizing these assets into dedicated pages or sections within Figma prevents developers from hunting through old artboards to find the right logo or illustration. Naming layers logically, such as icon-search or logo-header, makes exporting a quick, automated process.

  • Export all icons as clean, optimized SVG files.
  • Provide high-resolution source images for photography and illustration.
  • Use clear, logical naming conventions for all layers and asset frames.

Practical takeaways for your next handoff

A successful design handoff is not about delivering a massive document; it is about clear communication and structured systems. When designers and developers speak the same language around components, tokens, and responsive behavior, projects move forward without unnecessary friction.

Before sending your next design file over for development, take a quick pass to clean up unused artboards, check your component states, and verify your color and typography systems. Taking ten minutes to organize your file saves hours of clarifying questions down the road.

Want help with this? See my Figma → React / Next.js service, or send me your site for a free review.
