title: Time zones are the bug: a price feed that is wrong at midnight
description:
A fee comparison showed a price that was wrong for about six minutes every night, and only for some exchanges. Not stale, not missing — wrong. The kind of wrong that makes a user screenshot it and ask why your numbers do not match the exchange's own page.

The cause was not the price feed. It was the day boundary.

Every exchange resets on its own midnight

Trading fee tiers are usually computed per rolling period, but several exchanges reset allowances and volume counters on a calendar day in the exchange's local time. So the question "what is my fee tier right now" depends on what time it is where the exchange's accounting lives, not where the user is and not where your server is.

An aggregator that normalises everything to UTC — which is the correct instinct for storage — quietly moves that boundary. For an exchange at UTC+8, the tier resets at 16:00 UTC. If your code resets at 00:00 UTC, then between 16:00 and 24:00 UTC you are computing today's tier against yesterday's volume, and the fee you display is off by whatever the tier step is.

Six minutes was not the error window. Six minutes was how long it took someone to notice.

Three timestamp shapes, one of them a trap

The same normalisation bug shows up in three forms, and only the third is obvious:

  1. Epoch milliseconds. Unambiguous. Convert and move on.
  2. ISO 8601 with an offset (2026-11-11T09:00:00+08:00). Unambiguous if you keep the offset.
  3. ISO 8601 without an offset (2026-11-11T09:00:00). This is the trap. Every parser will assume something — server local, UTC, or browser local — and all three assumptions are wrong for at least one exchange. The string looks like a timestamp and behaves like a guess.

If you parse shape 3 with a default timezone, you get a value that is correct in one environment and wrong in another. That is the worst failure mode available: it passes local tests and fails in production, or passes in production and fails after a deploy moves the container's TZ.

Store the exchange's clock, not just the instant

The fix that held up was to stop treating time as a single instant and store two things:

  • the instant, in UTC, for ordering and display;
  • the exchange's local date, as a plain YYYY-MM-DD string, for anything that resets on a day boundary.

The second field is what makes tier logic testable. You are no longer asking "what time is it", you are asking "which of the exchange's days does this belong to", and that question has one answer regardless of where the code runs.

def exchange_day(ts_utc: datetime, tz: ZoneInfo) -> date:
    """The calendar date the exchange would print on a statement."""
    return ts_utc.astimezone(tz).date()

Two lines, and it removes an entire class of bug — the one where the same input produces different output depending on the machine.

Test the boundary, not the middle

The test that would have caught this is not "does the fee match for a sample trade". It is:

  • freeze the clock at 23:59 exchange-local and assert tier A;
  • freeze it at 00:01 exchange-local and assert tier B;
  • run both with TZ=UTC, TZ=Asia/Shanghai and TZ=America/New_York.

If the answers differ between the three runs, you have a timezone dependency in business logic, and it will surface as a support ticket at the worst possible hour. If they agree, you have actually fixed it rather than moved it.

The same discipline applies to rounding, which has the same shape of problem — the value is fine, the rule about when to apply it is what breaks. Rounding is a business rule, not a formatting detail, and it fails in the same quiet way: correct on the happy path, wrong at the edge, invisible until someone adds up a month of trades.

Cache the answer, but not the boundary

One more thing worth saying, because it is how this bug survived a deploy: the tier was cached. The cache key was the exchange and the account, with a TTL of an hour. That is a perfectly reasonable cache — and it made the bug persist for up to an hour after the real value changed.

If a value has a day-boundary dependency, the boundary belongs in the cache key, not just the TTL. Otherwise the cache outlives the fact. The general case for rarely-changing data is the same problem in slower motion: a TTL is a guess about when data changes, and a guessed boundary is a bug waiting for the one day it matters.

None of this is exotic. It is the ordinary cost of aggregating numbers that other people computed under assumptions they never wrote down. The exchanges are not wrong to reset on their own day; we were wrong to assume they reset on ours.

If you want to see what the output looks like when the boundaries are handled correctly, the comparison this work feeds is at fipst.com — the tier figures there are computed in exchange-local time, and the timestamps carry the offset they were computed with.

title: How to Route Users to the Nearest Healthy Region Automatically (and How Fast Each Method Fails Over)
description:
Route users to the nearest healthy region with latency-based or geo-based DNS routing backed by health checks, an anycast global load balancer, or a platform that combines deployment and routing behind a global endpoint. How fast traffic moves away from a failed region depends on how quickly health checks detect the failure and how long clients hold onto the old DNS answer. Failover is often slower than expected when nobody has measured the full chain from detection to the last cached client. This guide compares the three methods, works out worst-case failover times from each provider’s documented defaults, and explains how to test the result.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

Three methods route each user to the nearest healthy region automatically:

  • Platforms with a built-in global endpoint. A platform like Control Plane deploys one workload definition to multiple locations and routes each user to the nearest location where the workload is healthy, using the workload’s own readiness probes, with no per-service DNS records or external health checks to configure.
  • DNS routing with health checks. Amazon Route 53, Azure Traffic Manager, and Google Cloud DNS answer each query with the closest healthy endpoint. Failover time is health check detection plus DNS TTL plus resolver and client caching.
  • Anycast global load balancers. AWS Global Accelerator, Google Cloud’s global external Application Load Balancer, and Azure Front Door announce anycast IP addresses from edge locations and forward traffic to healthy backends. Failover avoids DNS caching; with default health checks it ranges from about 10 to 30 seconds (Google Cloud) to about 90 seconds or more (Global Accelerator, and Azure Front Door with Microsoft’s example settings), and tuning brings it lower.

Failover time is detection (health check interval × failure threshold) plus propagation (DNS TTL and caching, near zero for anycast) plus the time long-lived connections take to close. Test by failing a health check on purpose and timing the shift with synthetic probes and with real clients that cache DNS.

How do I route users to the nearest healthy region automatically?

Automatic region routing rests on two building blocks: choosing the nearest region, and removing an unhealthy region from the pool.

Choosing the nearest region can be done by latency or by geography. Latency-based routing uses the provider’s latency measurements between the user’s network (identified by the resolver’s IP, or the client subnet when the resolver sends EDNS Client Subnet) and each region, then returns the lowest-latency region. Geolocation routing maps the user’s IP to a country or subdivision and returns a pre-assigned region. VPNs and mobile carriers can make a geographically close region slower than a distant one, and both methods see the resolver’s location instead of the user’s when the resolver does not send EDNS Client Subnet.

Removing an unhealthy region requires active health checks. The routing system probes each regional endpoint on a schedule. If a probe fails a configured number of times in a row, the region is marked unhealthy and excluded from routing answers. When it passes enough consecutive checks, it is added back.

DNS routing with health checks

DNS routing services answer each query by latency or geolocation policy and stop returning an endpoint’s IP once it fails its health check. Resolvers and clients cache answers for the TTL and sometimes longer, so some clients keep reaching the failed region until their cached answer expires. Weighted, geolocation, and failover policies give fine-grained control over which users reach which region.

Anycast global load balancers

Managed anycast load balancers announce the same anycast IP addresses from many edge locations. BGP delivers each client to a nearby edge, which forwards traffic to the closest healthy backend region. When a region fails its health checks, the edge stops sending it traffic. The anycast IP and BGP announcements stay the same, so failover waits on neither DNS TTL nor BGP convergence. Plain anycast setups that you run yourself fail over by withdrawing a region’s BGP route instead.

Platforms with a built-in global endpoint

Some platforms run one workload definition in multiple regions behind a global endpoint that handles health-aware routing, which removes much of the work of configuring DNS records, health checks, and failover policies separately for each service.

How fast each routing method fails over

Values are defaults and configurable ranges documented on each provider’s own pages. Detection time is roughly the health check interval multiplied by the failure threshold (Traffic Manager marks an endpoint unhealthy only after tolerated failures plus one consecutive failure; Front Door and Cloudflare use sample- and quorum-based rules). Propagation covers DNS TTL plus resolver and client caching for DNS methods, or the time the edge takes to stop sending to a failed backend for anycast methods. Totals are estimates from documented defaults.

Method How it picks a region Health check defaults Detection time (defaults) Propagation delay Worst-case switch time (estimate) Notes
Amazon Route 53 latency or geolocation routing with health checks Latency or geolocation DNS policy 30 s interval × 3 failures (default; threshold 1 to 10); fast checks: 10 s interval ~90 s (standard); ~30 s with fast checks TTL you set (AWS recommends 60 s or less with health checks) plus resolver and client caching ~2.5 minutes to several minutes Checkers run from multiple regions; the endpoint is marked unhealthy when 18% or fewer of checkers report it healthy.
Azure Traffic Manager (performance routing) Latency-based DNS 30 s interval; tolerated failures 3 (range 0 to 9); probe timeout 10 s ~2 min (marked degraded after the fourth consecutive failure) Profile TTL (Azure CLI default 30 s; can be set as low as 0 s) plus resolver and client caching ~2.5 minutes to several minutes Supports custom headers in probes. Microsoft says failover can complete under 10 s after an endpoint goes unhealthy with 10 s probes, 0 tolerated failures, and TTL 0.
Google Cloud DNS routing policies with health checks Geolocation, weighted round robin, or failover DNS policy External endpoints: 30 to 300 s interval × unhealthy threshold (Google Cloud default 2); internal load balancers: their own health check (default 5 s × 2) ~60 s at the 30 s minimum interval for external endpoints; ~10 s for internal load balancer targets TTL you set plus resolver and client caching ~1 minute plus TTL to several minutes Public zones health-check external IPs, including a global external Application Load Balancer VIP; private zones health-check internal load balancers.
AWS Global Accelerator Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy endpoint group 30 s interval × 3 (default; interval 10 or 30 s, threshold 1 to 10) ~90 s No DNS change; the anycast IPs stay advertised and the edge sends new connections to the next healthy endpoint group ~90 to 120 s These settings apply to EC2 and Elastic IP endpoints; ALB and NLB endpoints use Elastic Load Balancing target-group health checks.
Google Cloud global external Application Load Balancer Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy backend 5 s interval × 2 failures, 5 s timeout (defaults) ~10 to 15 s No DNS change; the anycast VIP stays advertised and Google’s front ends stop sending requests to unhealthy backends ~10 to 30 s Fastest defaults in this table. Each backend service can set its own health check.
Azure Front Door Anycast; routes to the nearest healthy origin 30 s probe interval in the health-probes doc (the CLI reference says 240 s); healthy if at least x of the last n probes succeed No documented default sample counts; ~90 s with Microsoft’s example (30 s, 5 samples, 3 required) No DNS change; the edge stops routing to unhealthy origins ~90 s or more with that example Every edge location probes origins independently. Latency sensitivity picks among healthy origins; it does not decide health.
Cloudflare Load Balancing Steering policy (failover, geo, proximity, dynamic latency, and others), DNS-only or proxied (anycast) 60 s interval, 5 s timeout, 2 immediate retries (defaults in Cloudflare’s API schema); minimum interval by plan ~15 to 75 s per failed check cycle, plus 60 s for each extra consecutive failure you require Proxied: no client DNS change. DNS-only: the load balancer TTL plus resolver caching ~75 s (proxied) to several minutes (DNS-only) Minimum interval is 60 s on Pro, 15 s on Business, and 10 s on Enterprise. Health is decided by a majority of data centers per region, then a majority of regions.

Shortening the health check interval, lowering the failure threshold, and reducing the DNS TTL improve every value in the table. After tuning, measure with real clients and real traffic, since detection times on paper leave out caching.

What decides how fast traffic moves to another region?

Failover time is the sum of several independent delays, so shortening one delay cuts the total only by that amount, and the slowest delay usually dominates.

Health check interval and failure threshold. Detection time follows from the interval and the threshold. A 30-second interval with a threshold of 3 means up to 90 seconds pass before the system acts. Lower values speed detection but raise the risk of flapping if probes are flaky.

What the health check actually tests. A TCP port check confirms the process is listening but says nothing about whether it can serve requests. An HTTP check on a path that exercises the request path catches failures a port check misses. Leave out dependencies every region shares: if a shared database fails, every region fails its check at once, and Route 53 then treats all endpoints as healthy. Set probe timeouts shorter than the interval.

DNS TTL and real-world caching. The TTL tells resolvers how long to cache an answer, but some recursive resolvers and client operating systems apply a minimum floor, and browsers and connection pools reuse addresses for the life of a connection. Measure how resolvers in your client population actually honor TTLs.

Connection reuse and long-lived connections. gRPC streams, WebSocket connections, and HTTP/2 pools can stay open for minutes or hours and are unaffected by DNS changes until they close or error out. Use reasonable idle timeouts and retry logic with backoff that re-resolves DNS on reconnect.

Warm capacity in the surviving region. If the surviving region cannot absorb the redirected traffic, failover succeeds at the routing layer and fails at the application layer. Autoscaling helps, but new instances take time to become ready. Running active-active with enough headroom in each region to absorb the largest region’s share of traffic avoids this gap. The guide on how to run an app across multiple regions with routing, databases, and failover covers the full architecture.

How do I deploy one application to multiple regions with a single configuration?

Routing works only if every region runs the same application version and has enough capacity to serve traffic.

  • Infrastructure as code modules. Terraform or Pulumi can parameterize a deployment module by region and apply it to several regions in one pipeline. Adding a region means adding an entry to a list.
  • Kubernetes with GitOps tooling. Argo CD ApplicationSets, or Flux bootstrapped on each cluster against the same repository, deploy to multiple clusters from one Git repository. Federating health signals across clusters needs additional tooling.
  • A platform that deploys one definition to many locations. A workload deployed to a Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), a named set of locations across one or more clouds, runs in every location from one definition, with no per-region pipeline or cluster configuration to maintain.

Whichever method you use, the pipeline should verify that every region converges on the same version. Staged region-by-region rollouts are safe only when old and new versions are backward-compatible. The best multi-region and multi-cloud networking platforms compares platforms that handle multi-region deployment and networking.

How do I test that failover works?

Run this checklist at launch and on a regular schedule.

  • Fail a health check on purpose. Stop the application in one region or return an unhealthy response from the health check endpoint, and record when the routing system reacts.
  • Measure the shift with synthetic probes from several regions. Run HTTP probes from at least three locations, record when each starts reaching the new region, and compare it to the worst-case switch time in the table.
  • Test with real clients that cache DNS. Synthetic probes often resolve DNS fresh on every request, so use a browser, a mobile device, or a CLI with DNS caching enabled.
  • Check capacity in the surviving region. Watch CPU, memory, latency, and error rates, measure how long autoscaling takes to reach steady state, and confirm new instances pass readiness checks before they receive production traffic.
  • Test failback. Restore the failed region, confirm traffic rebalances, and watch for flapping if the healthy threshold is too low.
  • Run the test under load. A failover test on an idle system does not reveal capacity problems.
  • Document the results. Record detection time, propagation time, and total switch time, and adjust health check settings, TTLs, or capacity against your SLA targets.

Lessons from real regional outages are collected in how companies stay online during AWS us-east-1 outages.

How Control Plane routes users to the nearest healthy location

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A workload runs in every location of its GVC, so routing always has a set of identical locations to choose from. Adding a location provisions it for every workload in the GVC; removing one drains its replicas and shifts traffic to the locations that remain, without touching a workload definition.

On Control Plane, every workload gets its own global endpoint (its canonical endpoint), and each custom domain you route to it gets one too. Control Plane DNS geo-routes clients to the nearest location where the workload is healthy, using the workload’s own readiness probes, so a location drops out of DNS answers when the workload there stops reporting ready. Each GVC also has an alias endpoint; by default it is health-checked only with a basic TCP probe, so point its alias workload link at a workload to make the alias follow that workload’s health.

Control Plane’s location routing options, set per location on the GVC, reshape that default for every endpoint in the GVC:

  • A priority tier per location. Lower tiers are preferred, and within a tier the lowest-latency location wins. If every location in the preferred tier is unavailable, traffic moves to the next tier, which lets you prefer one region and keep others as backup.
  • A latency offset that nudges a location up or down in the latency ranking.
  • A latency threshold past which a location is treated as unavailable. If every location exceeds its threshold, Control Plane ignores the thresholds so traffic is not dropped.

For TCP or UDP traffic that should bypass the HTTP ingress, you can enable a direct load balancer on a workload. Control Plane then creates a load balancer in each location and registers each one as a Geo DNS target with latency-based routing.

During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had workloads active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds, with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry, as reported in Beyond Backups: Designing Systems That Survive the Inevitable. The guide to keeping your app online during an AWS region outage walks through the pattern.

The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Control Plane’s global endpoints are DNS-based, so clients that cache DNS answers beyond their TTL can keep sending traffic to a withdrawn location for a short time. Teams that want an anycast IP or a specific CDN in front of their traffic can place a global load balancer or CDN ahead of Control Plane endpoints. Failover options beyond routing are compared in the best multi-cloud failover solutions in 2026.

FAQ

Short answers on deployment, DNS failover speed, TTLs, health checks, backup regions, and testing.

How do I route users to the nearest healthy region automatically?

Use latency- or geo-based DNS routing with health checks, an anycast global load balancer, or a platform with a built-in global endpoint such as Control Plane. Each method health-checks every region and sends users to the nearest one that is passing its checks.

How do I deploy one application to multiple regions with a single configuration?

Use infrastructure as code modules parameterized by region, Kubernetes GitOps tooling such as Argo CD ApplicationSets, or a platform like Control Plane, which runs one workload definition in every location of a GVC. Every region should run the same version and have spare capacity before it receives traffic.

Is DNS failover fast enough?

It depends on your tolerance. With default settings, worst-case failover on the DNS services in the table ranges from about a minute plus the TTL to several minutes, and resolver and client caching makes the tail unpredictable. If your SLA requires sub-30-second failover, use an anycast global load balancer with tuned health checks (Google Cloud’s defaults already detect in about 10 seconds), or tune DNS health checks to their fastest settings and keep TTLs very low, knowing some resolvers do not honor them, and confirm the result by testing.

What DNS TTL should I use for failover?

A TTL of 30 to 60 seconds is a common starting point for failover-critical records. Lower TTLs shorten the stale-answer window but raise query volume and cost, and some resolvers apply a minimum floor or ignore TTLs, so measure what your clients actually honor.

What is the difference between anycast and DNS-based routing?

DNS-based routing returns different IP addresses depending on policy, so failover waits for clients to look up DNS again after cached answers expire. A managed anycast load balancer gives every user the same IP, and its edge stops forwarding to a region once health checks mark it down, so DNS caching plays no part. Total failover time for both still depends on health check settings.

How do health checks decide a region is down?

A health check probes each endpoint over TCP, HTTP, or HTTPS at a fixed interval and marks the region unhealthy after a set number of consecutive failures, usually combining results from probers in several locations (Route 53 marks an endpoint unhealthy when 18% or fewer of its checkers report it healthy); Azure Front Door uses a sample-based rule instead. An HTTP check that exercises the region’s own request path and region-local dependencies catches failures a TCP port check misses.

Can I prefer one region and use others only as backup?

Yes. Most DNS routing services offer failover policies that send traffic to secondary endpoints only when the primary fails, and Azure Front Door supports origin priority. On Control Plane, assign each location in the GVC a priority tier; traffic moves to the next tier only when every location in the preferred tier is unavailable.

What happens to in-flight requests during failover?

Requests in flight to the failed region fail and need a retry. With DNS routing, existing connections keep pointing at the old IP until they close or error out; with a managed Layer 7 anycast load balancer such as Google Cloud’s global external Application Load Balancer or Azure Front Door, the client’s connection to the edge usually survives and new requests go to a healthy backend; with Global Accelerator, which works at Layer 4, clients reconnect and land on a healthy endpoint. Long-lived gRPC streams and WebSockets need idle timeouts and reconnect logic that re-resolves DNS.

How often should I test failover?

Test at least quarterly and after any change to regions, health check settings, or DNS TTLs. Automate the test in a pipeline, and measure detection time, propagation time, and surviving-region capacity under load each time.

title: A practical guide to indexing in LanceDB with Python
description:
Most of the time I reach for a vector database, the first version is slow in a way that is easy to miss. The queries return the right rows, the demo works, and then the table grows and every search starts scanning the whole dataset. Indexing is what fixes that, and LanceDB gives you more than one kind of index because "search" in a real application is rarely just vector similarity. You usually filter by price, by category, or by some text field at the same time.

This guide walks through the indexes LanceDB exposes in its Python SDK, with runnable code and a short note on when each one earns its place. I have spent a fair amount of time in LanceDB's index layer as a contributor, so the aim here is to be practical rather than exhaustive.

Setting up a table

Install the package and create a small table to work with. LanceDB stores data on disk and infers the schema from the first batch of rows, so you can start with plain dictionaries.

import lancedb

db = lancedb.connect("./lancedb-data")

rows = [
    {"id": 1, "category": "audio", "price": 79.0,
     "description": "wireless over ear headphones with noise cancelling",
     "vector": [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]},
    {"id": 2, "category": "audio", "price": 19.0,
     "description": "wired earbuds with inline microphone",
     "vector": [0.2, 0.1, 0.4, 0.3]},
    {"id": 3, "category": "camera", "price": 499.0,
     "description": "mirrorless camera body with fast autofocus",
     "vector": [0.9, 0.8, 0.1, 0.2]},
]

table = db.create_table("products", data=rows)

The vector column is the one we will search by similarity. The other columns are the ones we will filter on, and each of them can carry its own index.

Vector indexes

A vector index speeds up nearest neighbour search. Without one, LanceDB compares the query against every row, which is fine for a few thousand rows and painful past that.

The default type is IVF_PQ. IVF groups vectors into partitions so a query only looks inside the closest partitions, and PQ compresses each vector so the index stays small.

table.create_index(
    metric="l2",
    vector_column_name="vector",
    index_type="IVF_PQ",
    num_partitions=256,
    num_sub_vectors=16,
)

Two things are worth knowing before you copy this. A vector index has to be trained, so it needs a reasonable number of rows to be useful. On a tiny table you can skip it and let LanceDB scan. And the metric you train with has to match the metric you search with, or the results will be wrong in a quiet way that is hard to debug.

If index size or recall is a concern, LanceDB also exposes scalar quantization through IVF_SQ. It compresses each vector with scalar quantization instead of product quantization, which keeps more of the original precision at the cost of a larger index. You switch to it by changing one argument.

table.create_index(
    metric="l2",
    vector_column_name="vector",
    index_type="IVF_SQ",
    num_partitions=256,
)

Searching is the same regardless of which vector index you built.

results = table.search([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]).limit(5).to_pandas()

Scalar indexes for filters

This is the part that people skip and then wonder why their filtered searches are slow. If you run a vector search and also filter by a column, LanceDB can use a scalar index on that column to narrow the candidates before it does the distance work. No scalar index means the filter is applied by scanning.

A BTree index fits columns you compare with ranges or equality, such as a price.

table.create_scalar_index("price", index_type="BTREE")

A Bitmap index fits columns with a small number of distinct values, such as a category.

table.create_scalar_index("category", index_type="BITMAP")

Now a search that combines similarity with a filter can use both indexes. The prefilter=True argument tells LanceDB to apply the filter before the vector search rather than after, which is what you want when the filter removes most of the rows.

results = (
    table.search([0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4])
    .where("price < 100", prefilter=True)
    .limit(5)
    .to_pandas()
)

A quick rule that has held up for me: reach for BTree when the column is ordered and you filter by ranges, and reach for Bitmap when the column has a handful of repeated values. If a column holds lists of tags rather than single values, there is a LABEL_LIST index for that case.

Full text search

Vector search finds rows that are semantically close. It does not help when a user types an exact term and expects to see it. For that you want a full text search index on the text column.

table.create_fts_index("description")

Then you search the text directly by setting the query type.

results = (
    table.search("wireless headphones", query_type="fts")
    .limit(5)
    .to_list()
)

Full text search and vector search answer different questions, and real applications often need both. Keeping an index on the text column means you can offer a keyword search without standing up a separate search engine next to your database.

Checking what you built

After creating indexes it is worth confirming they exist, especially since some index builds run in the background. list_indices reports the indexes on a table along with the columns they cover.

for index in table.list_indices():
    print(index)

If an index you expected is missing, the usual causes are a table too small to train a vector index, or a build that has not finished yet.

Choosing an index

A short version of everything above, for when you are deciding what to add to a new table:

  • Searching by vector similarity on more than a few thousand rows: build a vector index. Start with IVF_PQ, and move to IVF_SQ if you want higher precision and can accept a larger index.
  • Filtering by a numeric or ordered column: BTree.
  • Filtering by a low cardinality column such as a status or category: Bitmap.
  • Filtering by a column that holds lists of values: LABEL_LIST.
  • Matching exact words in a text column: a full text search index.

None of these are expensive to add, and the cost of leaving them out only shows up once the table is large enough that a scan hurts. I would rather add the obvious ones early than debug a slow query under load later.

Closing

LanceDB's indexing is quieter than its vector search, but it is where a lot of the real performance lives. The pattern I keep coming back to is simple. Put a vector index on the column you search by similarity, put scalar indexes on the columns you filter by, and add a full text index wherever users type exact terms. Once those are in place, the database does the narrowing for you instead of scanning, and the queries stay fast as the data grows.

If you want to go deeper, the LanceDB documentation covers each index type and its parameters, and the source is open if you want to see how a given index is wired from the Rust core through to the Python SDK.

title: Building kakemono: A Wallpaper Manager That Comes With Me to Any OS
description:
TL;DR

  • kakemono is a wallpaper manager for macOS, Linux and Windows. A small daemon downloads wallpapers from Wallhaven, Unsplash, Reddit, Bing, NASA's Astronomy Picture of the Day, or your own folders, and changes the wallpaper on a timer
  • One Rust binary is both the daemon and the command-line tool. A Tauri app adds a tray icon, a thumbnail picker and a settings window
  • It started as a macOS-only Go app. I rewrote it in Rust so it keeps working if I ever move to Linux or Windows
  • The code is public at github.com/RielJ/kakemono, and v0.1.0 has installers for all three systems

The demo turns on a Wallhaven search in Settings, opens the picker, and clicks a thumbnail. The new wallpaper is set before the Settings window closes.

How it started

Linux has Variety. It's a plain little app that does one job well. You give it a list of sources, it downloads images in the background, and every half hour your desktop changes. If you liked the last one, you step back to it. If you hated it, you trash it.

I wanted that on my Mac, so I wrote wallpaperd: a Go daemon with a command-line client, six image sources, and a Unix socket. I wired it into sketchybar, so my menu bar showed the current wallpaper and had next and previous buttons. I used it every day.

The code had a weak spot, though. It set the wallpaper by running osascript and asking System Events, which needs the Automation permission. It checked for dark mode by running defaults read. Everything that touched the desktop went through another program, and every one of those programs exists only on macOS.

I keep thinking about moving to Linux one day. If I do, I want my wallpaper setup to come with me, and I'd like it on a Windows machine too. So I asked my coding agent whether I should rewrite the app in Rust.

Its first answer was no. The app sleeps 99.9% of the time, Go handles timers and sockets well, and nobody would notice the speed difference. That's fair. But I didn't care about speed. I cared about two things: no dependence on other apps, and one codebase for three operating systems. With those goals, Rust and Tauri made sense, and the rewrite began.

I also needed a new name. wallpaperd is very close to wpaperd, an existing Rust wallpaper daemon for Wayland. A kakemono is a Japanese hanging scroll, a picture on the wall that people swap out with the seasons. That's close enough to what the app does.

What it does

  • Sources. Wallhaven and Unsplash searches, a subreddit, Bing's daily images, NASA's APOD archive back to 1995, and local folders. You can add the same type more than once, for example two Wallhaven searches.
  • Rotation. By default the wallpaper changes every 30 minutes. A background downloader fetches one new image every 10 minutes and keeps the download folder under 500 MB, oldest files first. It never deletes favorites.
  • History, favorites and trash. kakemono prev goes back. favorite copies the current image to a favorites folder. trash moves it out and sets the next one, and the picker can undo that.
  • Light and dark. When the system switches theme, kakemono can set a new wallpaper and prefer images that suit the theme.
  • Filters. The settings copy Variety's "When possible, use images that..." section: landscape only, or at least 80% of the screen resolution.

The picker is a strip of thumbnails along one edge of the screen. It has five tabs: Sources, Downloaded, Local, Favorites and Cache. The Sources tab shows previews from your online sources without downloading anything. A click downloads the full image and sets it. Every action has a key, so I rarely touch the mouse.

The settings window lists the sources in one table. You turn each one on or off, and "Use Only These" limits rotation to the ones you selected.

How it's built

There are two programs. kakemono is the daemon and the CLI in one binary. kakemono-ui is the Tauri app. Both talk to the daemon in newline-delimited JSON over a Unix socket, or a named pipe on Windows. That means you can script it with nc or jq, and my sketchybar plugin still works.

kakemono next ────┐
tray, picker, ────┼──▶ socket (named pipe on Windows) ──▶ daemon
settings          │                                        │
sketchybar ───────┘                                        ├─ sources: download images
                                                           ├─ engine: rotation, history, cache
                                                           └─ platform: set the wallpaper

The Rust workspace has eight crates: protocol, config, engine, sources, platform, fs, cli and ui. Only platform knows which OS it's on.

Setting the wallpaper is the part that differs most between systems:

  • On macOS, kakemono calls NSWorkspace setDesktopImageURL:forScreen: through objc2, once for each screen. No osascript, and no Automation permission. One catch: macOS has no API that sets every Space, so only the current Space on each screen changes.
  • On Windows, it uses the IDesktopWallpaper COM interface from the windows crate.
  • Linux has no single API, so kakemono detects the session. It checks for a desktop environment (GNOME, KDE, XFCE and others), then for a wallpaper daemon that's already running (swww, hyprpaper), then the compositor (Hyprland, Sway, niri), then X11 tools like feh. That covers 17 backends. kakemono detect tells you which one it picked and why. If yours isn't covered, you can set your own command.

The tools:

Part Tools
Daemon and CLI Rust, tokio, clap, reqwest with rustls, serde, tracing
Native APIs objc2 (macOS), windows-rs (Windows), zbus for D-Bus (Linux)
App Tauri 2, React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS 4, Vite
Tests cargo test, insta snapshots, Vitest, Testing Library
CI and releases GitHub Actions on macOS, Linux and Windows, Docker, QEMU

How I built it

I built kakemono with coding agents in Pi. First, four models each wrote a plan, and I merged the best parts into one. Next, I wrote short contracts for the pieces that crates share: the config format, the platform API and the source interface. Then subagents built slices against those contracts in parallel, each in its own git worktree, which I wrote about in my pi-git-worktrees post. The rewrite took 152 commits over two days.

Three things kept the rewrite honest:

  1. Golden fixtures from the Go app. Before writing any Rust, I recorded what the Go daemon sent and received on its socket, and how it read its config. The Rust tests replay those recordings, so the new daemon had to answer the way the old one did.
  2. Lots of tests. There are 1,422 Rust tests and 392 frontend tests. The source tests replay recorded HTTP responses, so they never hit Wallhaven or Reddit.
  3. Testing on systems I don't own. GitHub Actions tests every push on macOS, Linux and Windows. I also wanted to catch failures before pushing, so the Linux checks run locally in Docker. The Windows checks run in a Windows 11 ARM virtual machine on my M4 MacBook, through QEMU and Apple's Hypervisor framework. A script installs Windows from an answer file with no clicks, runs the same tests CI runs, and shuts the VM down.

One surprise came at the end. I downloaded the first release on my other laptop, and macOS said the app "is damaged and can't be opened". It wasn't damaged. The app isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID, so macOS blocks it when it's downloaded from the internet. The fix is one command, and it's in the install steps below.

How to use it

Download the installer for your system from the Releases page.

macOS. Open the .dmg (aarch64 for Apple silicon, x64 for Intel) and drag kakemono to Applications. Because the build isn't signed, clear the quarantine flag before you open it:

xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine /Applications/kakemono.app

Linux. Install the .deb or .rpm, or run the AppImage:

sudo apt install ./kakemono_0.1.0_amd64.deb      # Debian, Ubuntu
sudo dnf install ./kakemono-0.1.0-1.x86_64.rpm   # Fedora

Windows. Run the .msi or the -setup.exe. When SmartScreen warns about an unknown publisher, click More info, then Run anyway.

Open the app. It starts the daemon and puts an icon in the menu bar, tray or notification area. From there you can open Settings, add a source, and open the picker.

If you prefer the terminal:

kakemono service install   # start the daemon at login
kakemono next              # set a new wallpaper now
kakemono prev              # go back to the previous one
kakemono favorite          # keep this one
kakemono trash             # never show this one again
kakemono pause             # stop rotating; `kakemono resume` starts again

Sources live in ~/.config/kakemono/config.toml, one [[sources]] table each:

[daemon]
interval = "30m"

[[sources]]
id = "wh-nature"
type = "wallhaven"
location = "nature"

[[sources]]
id = "pictures"
type = "folder"
location = "~/Pictures/Wallpapers"

On Linux, run kakemono detect once to see which backend it picked. If the wallpaper doesn't change, kakemono doctor prints the session, the command it would run, and what the daemon is doing.

The README has every command and config key. If you try it and something breaks on your desktop, please open an issue.

RielJ / kakemono

Rotating wallpapers from Bing, APOD, Reddit, Unsplash, Wallhaven and local folders, with a tray picker. macOS, Linux and Windows.

kakemono

kakemono is a wallpaper manager for macOS, Linux, and Windows. A small daemon downloads wallpapers from Bing, Wallhaven, Unsplash, Reddit, NASA APOD, or your own folders, and changes the wallpaper on a timer. It keeps a history you can step back through, saves favorites, and can prefer dark images in dark mode and light images in light mode.

The kakemono binary is both the daemon and the command-line client. The kakemono app adds a menu-bar (tray) icon, a thumbnail picker for browsing and setting wallpapers, and a settings window.

Install

Prebuilt downloads are on the Releases page. Each release has two kinds of file:

  • The app (kakemono_<version>_<arch>.dmg, .deb, .rpm, .AppImage, .msi, or -setup.exe). It contains the kakemono binary too, so most people need only this.
  • The command-line tool alone (kakemono-<version>-<target>.tar.gz, or .zip on Windows), for servers and window managers where…

title: Building QuickPOS: A Point of Sale for Small Food Businesses in the Philippines
description:
TL;DR

  • QuickPOS is a point-of-sale system for small food businesses: a register, a kitchen display, cash shifts with PIN sign-in, sales history with voids and refunds, inventory, and daily reports
  • It runs in the browser. The API is Hono and tRPC on Cloudflare Workers, the data is in Turso (SQLite), and the web app is a React SPA
  • Checkout is safe to retry. If the connection drops halfway through a charge, trying again returns the first result instead of ringing up the sale twice
  • Permissions, stock changes and optional features each have one shared definition that the web app and the API both use
  • I'm preparing it for a pilot with one counter-service food merchant. The code is private, so this post shows it through screenshots, a demo and diagrams

A cashier picks egg and add-on options for a Tapsilog, takes ₱500 cash and sees the change, and the order shows up on the kitchen display. The store, staff and menu are made up for the demo.

Why I built it

Small food stalls and counter-service shops in the Philippines often run on a notebook, a calculator and a cash box. The POS systems built for them are usually priced and designed for bigger restaurants, and many of them assume things that don't hold at a small counter: that prices exclude tax, that the Internet is always up, or that one person does everything.

I wanted to build one that fits how these shops actually work, and to build it the way I'd build software I'm paid to maintain. That second goal shaped most of the decisions in this post.

What it does

The core is the part a merchant uses every day:

Area What it covers
Register Cart, add-ons and modifiers, cash and other payments, receipts
Kitchen A display that shows each ticket from pending to ready
Shifts Open with a PIN and a starting cash count, close and count the drawer
Sales history Order list, voids and refunds
Daily totals Sales summary, shift report, payment types
Access Owner, admin and cashier roles, staff PINs

Around that core are optional modules: tables, inventory and purchasing, customers and loyalty, time clock and payroll, advanced reports, and the audit log. Each one can be switched off, which matters more than it sounds. I'll come back to it.

How it's built

One pnpm monorepo. The web app and the API both import the shared package, so a price rule, a permission or a module switch has one definition. The Rust coordinator is the start of offline mode and is paused until the pilot needs it.

It's my third attempt at the stack. The first version used TanStack Start with Postgres, the second moved the data to Convex, and in April 2026 I rebuilt it as a plain React SPA talking to a Hono and tRPC API on Cloudflare Workers, with Turso for storage. The SPA and tRPC split was the one that stuck: the API types flow into the web app, the Zod schemas live in one shared package, and Workers plus Turso cost close to nothing while there's one merchant.

The repository has about 975 unit and integration tests (Vitest) and 116 browser tests (Playwright) across the register, kitchen display, roles and module switches.

A charge must happen exactly once

The scariest bug a POS can have is charging twice, or losing a sale the customer already paid for. Both come from the same moment: the cashier taps Charge, the network is slow, nothing seems to happen, and they tap again.

The register makes one key per charge and keeps it until the charge succeeds or the cashier dismisses it. A retry with the same key gets the stored answer back, so a slow network can't ring up a sale twice.

Every money-moving call (creating an order, completing it, and refunding it) goes through one wrapper, withIdempotency. The register makes a key for the charge and reuses it on every retry. The server stores the response under that key the first time, and any repeat with the same key and the same cart gets the stored response back. A repeat with the same key and a different cart is refused, because that's a bug, not a retry.

Two smaller decisions back this up. The web app never retries a money mutation on its own; a retry is always the cashier pressing Retry in the checkout dialog. And the server checks whether an order is already finalized before completing it, which covers the rare case of two truly simultaneous requests.

Whose drawer is this money in?

At the end of a shift, the cashier counts the drawer and QuickPOS compares it with what it expected. That only means something if every sale lands in the right shift.

The client never says which shift a sale belongs to. The server works it out from the register and the device that activated it, so a browser that only knows a register id can't put money in someone else's drawer.

The rule I settled on is that the client never names a shift. It sends the register and the device, and the server works out the open shift from those. A register is activated on one browser by an owner, so knowing a register's id isn't enough to put money in it.

PINs get the care you'd give passwords, because a four-to-six-digit PIN is easy to guess. They're hashed with PBKDF2, failed attempts are rate-limited per store, and every attempt is logged. The rate limit lives in Workers KV rather than in memory: a Worker runs as many separate isolates, and an in-memory counter would let someone spread guesses across them.

Paid and cooked are different things

In a counter-service shop, customers usually pay first and wait for their food. My first version of orders had one status, so completing the payment also closed the order, and the ticket left the kitchen board before anyone had cooked it.

An order has two states that move on their own. Before the split, paying for an order took it off the kitchen board, so a counter that takes payment first lost the ticket before anyone cooked it.

The fix was to give the order two states that move on their own. The cashier moves payment; the kitchen moves fulfillment. The kitchen can only move a ticket forward, and only Cancel closes both, because cancelling also has to put the stock back. A migration closed the tickets for old paid orders so the kitchen board didn't fill up with history.

One rule, one place

By late 2026 the code had grown to about 85,000 lines of TypeScript, and I ran an architecture review over it. It found three rules that were each written in several places, and all three had already caused bugs.

Three rules that used to be written more than once. Each one now lives in a single module that both sides call, and the old way of doing it is the thing the docs tell you not to do.

Permissions. The web app decided what to show, and the API decided what to allow, each with its own checks. They disagreed: some screens showed buttons the API then refused, and some hid things the API would have allowed. Now there's one access policy in the shared package, with 25 named capabilities like products.edit and reports.export. The API enforces it and the web app reads the same rule. A misspelled capability is a type error.

Stock. More than a dozen API routes wrote stock levels directly. Some skipped the movement history, so the history didn't add up to the stock. Products could exist with no stock row at all, and replacing a product's variants deleted the product's own stock. Now one module, the stock ledger, is the only code that writes stock, and it writes the new count and the reason for the change in the same transaction.

Optional features. A pilot merchant should see only what they use, but switching a feature off used to mean finding its links, routes and API procedures by hand. Now each module has one switch in the shared package. Turning it off hides the menu entry, redirects its pages, and makes the API refuse the procedures it owns. Nothing is deleted, so turning it back on is a one-line change.

Decisions for a Philippine pilot

The module switches made the pilot scoping concrete. For a counter-service food merchant, I'm turning off tables, customers and loyalty, the time clock and payroll, and discounts for now. The kitchen display stays on.

Tax is off too, and the reason is specific to the Philippines. QuickPOS's tax rates add tax on top of the price, but prices here are shown VAT-inclusive, and most small merchants aren't VAT-registered. Adding tax at the register would charge customers more than the menu says.

I also wrote down the rules for while the pilot runs. New features are frozen, and only what blocks the merchant's day gets fixed. Correctness safeguards are never cut: accurate totals, authorization, duplicate-sale protection, and recovery from failed requests. And AI stays out of the checkout path, so a model outage can never stop a sale.

What about brownouts?

Power and Internet outages are common enough here that a POS needs an answer for them. I've designed offline mode and built its core, but I've paused it until the pilot shows how much it's needed.

The offline design, for brownouts and outages of up to eight hours. The cashier device keeps the record, the kitchen display follows it over the store's own Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot, and the cloud catches up later. The core and its tests exist; the Android shell doesn't yet.

The design has the cashier device act as the store's coordinator. It writes every sale to a local, signed, append-only event log before confirming it, and the kitchen display follows that log over the store's Wi-Fi or a phone hotspot. When the Internet comes back, the events sync to the cloud, and any conflict goes to a review list instead of overwriting data.

The core is a Rust crate of about 2,600 lines with 65 tests. It covers the event log in SQLite, Ed25519 signatures, the kitchen board rebuilt from events, QR pairing, and a LAN transport with TLS pinned to the cashier's certificate. The same test vectors run in Rust and TypeScript, so both sides agree on what a signed event looks like. The scope is deliberately narrow: no official receipts, no loyalty redemption and no menu changes while offline, and GCash or Maya payments are recorded as checked by the cashier but not confirmed.

What's next

The next step is the merchant visit. I'll watch how they work today and fill in the parts of the pilot plan I've left blank: which device they'll use, which modules they need, and what the first improvement should be. The goal is small on purpose: one merchant runs a normal day on QuickPOS, records sales, corrects mistakes, and reconciles the drawer at close.

If you run a small food business in the Philippines and want to try it, or you just want to talk about POS software, send me a message.
