`

If you notice, the age_check function call was added only to the invoke2 and invoke3 functions.

Actually, if you think about it, in real life you shouldn't write this kind of code that will change your workflow directly like this. For this kind of work, it makes more sense to do implementations like the validation or business specification pattern. Of course, macros will be used in these patterns too, but they'll be in a certain order.

But with the example I gave here, you can handle your cross cutting concern style operations such as cash, logging, security, etc. In fact, if you examine web frameworks, you can also see that attribute macros like these are frequently used for this kind of work.

I think this will be enough to understand the attribute macro.

Function-like Macro

At first glance, it resembles the declarative (makro_rules!) macro. But there are some differences.

  • Declarative macros work with specific patterns. The rule matching the pattern is run. It's easy to use and is used to quickly manipulate specific items and expand the code.
  • Procedural (here, of course, specifically function-like) macros, on the other hand, offer more advanced features, letting us analyze the code while allowing us to manipulate the code (syntax tree) directly. They can regenerate code, remove code or add new code.

Now let's do an example or two; the topic will be understood better.

Let's start with a simple example. The project structure is the same as the previous ones, so I won't write it again.

We replace the lib.rs file in the my_macro project with the code below.

`rust
// lib.rs

use proc_macro::TokenStream;

[proc_macro]

pub fn add_func(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
println!("Inputs: {}", input.to_string());
"fn add(a:i32, b:i32) -> i32 { a + b }".parse().unwrap()
}
`
It takes a single TokenStream, which represents the tree to be changed. And it returns a TokenStream, which, as you can guess, represents the changed version of the code.

We also change our main.rs file under the my_app directory, that is, in the main directory, as below.

`rust
// main.rs

use my_macro::add_func;

add_func!();

fn main() {
// we could have put the kmacro here too.
// after all, we can write nested functions.
// add_func!();

println!("The sum is: {}", add(2, 3));

}
`

If we examine our code with the cargo expand command, we'll see that code like the one below is generated. Normally, we hadn't defined a function called add in main.rs. But we had called it in the main function as if it existed. This way, we compiled and were able to run our code without getting an error.

`rust
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
a + b
}
fn main() {
fn add(a: i32, b: i32) -> i32 {
a + b
}
{
::std::io::_print(format_args!("The sum is: {0}\n", add(2, 3)));
};
}

`

Let's do an example that takes a String parameter and prints it to the screen.

We change our lib.rs file under my_macro as below.

`rust
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::parse_macro_input;

[proc_macro]

pub fn print_string(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
// Parse the input token stream
let input = parse_macro_input!(input as syn::LitStr);

// Get the String expression
let string_value = input.value();

// Generate Rust code using quote for code gen
let expanded = quote! {
    println!("{}", #string_value);
};

// Return the generated code
TokenStream::from(expanded)

}

`
We also change our main.rs file as below.

`rust
use my_macro::print_string;

fn main() {
print_string!("Hello, world!");
print_string!("I'm working with Rust procedural macros!");
}

`
when we run the code, we'll get an output like the one below.

plaintext
Hello, world!
I'm working with Rust procedural macros!

Now let's do an example we did before with a function-like macro too. Let's write a function-like macro that will implemet a getter and setter trait on the struct passed to our macro as a parameter.

For this, we change our lib.rs file as below.

`rust
use proc_macro::TokenStream;
use quote::quote;
use syn::spanned::Spanned;
use syn::{parse_macro_input, ItemStruct, Fields};

[proc_macro]

pub fn create_accessors(input: TokenStream) -> TokenStream {
// Parse the TokenStream given as the macro input into an ItemStruct
let input = parse_macro_input!(input as ItemStruct);
let struct_name = &input.ident; // get the struct name

// Create the struct definition
let struct_definition = quote! {
    #input
};

// Iterate over the struct's fields
let gen = match &input.fields {
    Fields::Named(fields) => {
        // Create the getter and setter methods
        let getters_setters = fields.named.iter().map(|f| {
            let field_name = &f.ident;  // Get the field name
            let field_type = &f.ty;  // Get the field type
            let setter_name = syn::Ident::new(&format!("set_{}", field_name.as_ref().unwrap()), field_name.span());  // Create the setter name

            // Getter method definition
            let getter = quote! {
                pub fn #field_name(&self) -> &#field_type {
                    &self.#field_name
                }
            };

            // Setter method definition
            let setter = quote! {
                pub fn #setter_name(&mut self, value: #field_type) {
                    self.#field_name = value;
                }
            };

            // Combine the getter and setter methods
            quote! {
                #getter
                #setter
            }
        });

        // Implement the getter and setter methods for the struct
        quote! {
            impl #struct_name {
                #(#getters_setters)*
            }
        }
    }
    _ => panic!("create_accessors only supports named fields"),  // Only named fields are supported
};

// Combine the struct definition and the getter-setter implementations
let output = quote! {
    #struct_definition
    #gen
};

TokenStream::from(output)  // Return a TokenStream as the result

}
`

We also change the main.rs file as below.

`rust
use my_macro::create_accessors;

create_accessors!(struct Person {
name: String,
age: u32,
});

fn main() {
let mut person = Person {
name: "Alice".to_string(),
age: 30,
};

// Use the getters
println!("Name: {}", person.name());
println!("Age: {}", person.age());

// Use the setters
person.set_name("Bob".to_string());
person.set_age(25);

println!("Updated Name: {}", person.name());
println!("Updated Age: {}", person.age());

}

`

I don't think there's any need to write the output of the code anymore. But I'd like to remind you of this: what we wrote here is just to understand the topic; otherwise, writing a macro like this just to add get and set methods may not make sense.

Before wrapping up the topic, I'd like to mention one more topic.

Macro Hygiene

Macro Hygiene is a feature in Rust that makes sure macros work in a safe and predictable way. This concept aims to prevent unexpected variable name collisions and similar problems while macros generate code. Thanks to macro hygiene, the variables defined or used by macros are isolated independently of the context of the code they're called in.

Let's examine a simple example to understand macro hygiene:

`rust
macro_rules! create_var {
() => {
let x = 42;
println!("x = {}", x);
};
}

fn main() {
let x = 0;
create_var!();
println!("Main scope x = {}", x);
}
`
In the code above, the create_var! macro is defined, and a variable named x is created inside the macro. When the macro is called, the x variable is defined and assigned 42 as its value. But a variable named x is also defined in the main function, and its value is 0. Thanks to macro hygiene, the x variable defined inside the macro doesn't collide with the x variable in the main function.

The output will be as follows:

rust
x = 42
Main scope x = 0

This shows that the x variable defined inside the macro doesn't get mixed up with the x in the main function. Thanks to macro hygiene, the code inside the macro isn't affected by the local variables of the place it's called from and doesn't cause variables with the same name to get mixed up.

Let's examine the example below.

`rust
macro_rules! use_external_var {
($var:ident) => {
println!("The value of {} is: {}", stringify!($var), $var);
};
}

fn main() {
let x = 100;
use_external_var!(x); // "x" here is a variable name coming from outside
}

`

In the example above, the use_external_var! macro brings in a variable from outside using the x parameter of ident type given to it, and works with it. This bypasses macro hygiene and accesses the value of the x variable. If macro hygiene were preserved, the x variable would have to be defined inside the macro or be a variable defined by the macro.

The output will be as follows:

`rust
The value of x is: 100

`
Usages like this that bypass macro hygiene can lead to unexpected behavior and collisions, especially in large projects. For example, a collision can be seen in the scenario below:

`rust
macro_rules! use_external_var {
($var:ident) => {
let $var = 200;
println!("The value of {} is: {}", stringify!($var), $var);
};
}

fn main() {
let x = 100;
use_external_var!(x); // Here "x" is a variable name coming from outside
println!("Main scope x = {}", x);
}

`
The output will be like this.`

The value of x is: 200
Main scope x = 100

In this case, the let $var = 200; line inside the use_external_var! macro redefines the x variable and sets its value to 200. But this x isn't the same as the x in the main function, because macro hygiene prevents x from being redefined globally. This can cause confusion and make it harder to predict the behavior of the code.

In summary, when using macros, we need to be careful not to affect anything and not to be affected. In other words, power is nothing without control.

Closing

Without going into detail, I'll make a recommendation or two and give a few resources I think will be useful.s

Recommendations

  • You should pay attention to the order when applying macros. In macros related to each other, the order will matter.
  • Pay attention to the Macro Hygiene topic.
  • If you intend to use the same code structure in many places, define this structure once with the declarative macro macro_rules! and use it everywhere.
  • Use the derive macro to implement a trait.
  • Use the attribue-like macro to analyze a specific structure and generate code accordingly.
  • Use the function-like macro to transform or expand a specific code structure.
  • Take care to write testable macros.
  • Writing macros is complicated, and if they're not documented well, understanding how to use them can be complicated too. So document them very well.

Recommended Resources

  • On the earthly.dev page, there's nice information about real-life macro usage under the Practical Examples of Macros heading.
  • Definitely examine the Macro by Example section in the Rust official documentation.
  • It would also be good if you read this Medium link, especially for more advanced, more detailed topics on the subject.
  • On Jetbrains' official pages, there's a blog series where macros are explained at a simpler level with figures and diagrams; you can reach it from this link.
  • A github.io page prepared just for rust macros. You can reach it from this link.
  • On the soldev.app page, which has resources for Solona Development, a nice page has been prepared for macros. It explains all the macros in detail step by step. You can reach it from this link.

Yes, that's it for now for our first article about Rust; hope you found it useful. For a while more, whenever I find the time, I'll continue my articles about Ruat.

Take care.

title: Postgres to Snowflake Replication Without Kafka or Airflow
description:
Postgres to Snowflake Replication Without Kafka or Airflow

Replicating data from PostgreSQL to Snowflake is a common requirement for teams building analytics platforms, reporting systems, and data warehouses. However, keeping the two systems synchronized can become complicated when data changes frequently.

Traditional data pipelines often rely on tools such as Kafka, Debezium, and Airflow to capture, transport, and orchestrate database changes. While these tools offer flexibility, they also introduce additional infrastructure, configuration, and operational overhead.

For teams that want to replicate an existing PostgreSQL database into Snowflake without managing a Kafka cluster or Airflow DAGs, managed Change Data Capture (CDC) services offer a simpler alternative.

In this guide, we'll compare seven tools for PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication, including Estuary, Fivetran, Airbyte, Striim, Artie, Snowflake Openflow, and Snowflake Postgres data mirroring. We'll examine their CDC capabilities, Snowflake write paths, delete handling, freshness, pricing models, and limitations.

Can You Replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake Without Kafka or Airflow?

Yes. A managed CDC service can capture PostgreSQL changes and deliver them to Snowflake without requiring you to deploy and maintain Kafka, Debezium, or Airflow.

PostgreSQL supports logical replication through its Write-Ahead Log (WAL). CDC connectors use this mechanism to capture database changes, including inserts, updates, and deletes, and send them to a destination.

A typical managed replication pipeline looks like this:

PostgreSQL → CDC Connector → Managed Data Pipeline → Snowflake

The main advantage is that the replication service handles change capture and delivery, eliminating the need to maintain separate infrastructure for message streaming and workflow orchestration.

However, not every PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake integration works with an existing external PostgreSQL database. Snowflake's native data mirroring, for example, is designed specifically for Snowflake Postgres.

Understanding this distinction is important when selecting a tool.

How We Selected These PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Tools

We compared seven tools based on six requirements relevant to teams that want to avoid Kafka and Airflow.

1. PostgreSQL source support

The tool must support an existing PostgreSQL database, whether self-hosted or running on a major cloud platform. Version requirements also matter. For example, Estuary supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later, while Snowflake Openflow requires PostgreSQL 11 or later.

2. Managed operation

The objective is to reduce infrastructure management. We considered whether the service handles CDC and data delivery without requiring teams to operate their own Kafka cluster, connector deployment, or orchestration DAG.

3. Snowflake write path

We examined how each tool delivers data to Snowflake. Some use staged loads, others support Snowpipe Streaming, and some apply changes through SQL operations.

4. Delete handling

Capturing inserts and updates is not enough. We also considered how tools handle deleted records and whether they support soft deletes, hard deletes, or operations such as TRUNCATE.

5. Data freshness

Replication frequency directly affects how current the Snowflake data remains. We compared configurable sync schedules, advertised latency, and available low-latency ingestion options.

6. Pricing transparency

We considered whether vendors publish pricing and how they charge for replication, including data volume, monthly active rows, connector instances, or compute capacity.

7 Tools to Replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake Without Kafka or Airflow

1. Estuary

https://estuary.dev/

Estuary is a strong option for replicating an existing PostgreSQL database into Snowflake without deploying Kafka or Airflow.

Its PostgreSQL capture connector continuously reads source changes using CDC and writes them into Estuary collections. The Snowflake materialization then delivers those collections to destination tables.

For standard updates, Estuary stages changes before applying them transactionally. For delta-update bindings, it also supports Snowpipe Streaming.

You can follow the PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake setup tutorial to configure the pipeline.

Key capabilities:

  • Continuous PostgreSQL CDC.
  • Automatic schema evolution.
  • One capture can feed multiple destinations without rereading the source.
  • Standard updates through staged transactional loads.
  • Snowpipe Streaming support for delta bindings.
  • Configurable Snowflake synchronization frequency.

For teams that need to balance data freshness and warehouse costs, Estuary allows the Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to be configured to 0s. This removes the scheduled waiting period. Snowpipe Streaming provides its lowest-latency Snowflake loading path for delta bindings.

Pricing:

As of October 2026, Estuary's Cloud plan charges:

  • $0.50 per GB of data moved.
  • $100 per connector instance per month for the first six instances.
  • $50 per month for each additional connector instance.

Its free Developer tier includes 10 GB of combined captured and delivered data per month and two connector instances.

Limitations:

Estuary's PostgreSQL connector supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later. Teams running PostgreSQL 9.x or earlier will need to upgrade or consider another option.

Best for: Teams that need continuous CDC from an existing PostgreSQL database, configurable Snowflake delivery, and a managed alternative to Kafka and Airflow.

2. Fivetran

https://www.fivetran.com/

Fivetran provides a managed PostgreSQL connector that replicates database data into Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector captures source data, while its Snowflake destination connector handles delivery to the warehouse.

Fivetran is a suitable option for teams that want managed database replication without operating their own CDC infrastructure.

Key capabilities:

  • Managed PostgreSQL replication.
  • Snowflake destination support.
  • SQL MERGE operations for applying changes to Snowflake tables.
  • Standard and Enterprise sync-frequency options.

Pricing:

Fivetran uses monthly active rows (MAR) for connection billing.

As of October 2026:

  • The free plan covers 500,000 monthly active rows for connections.
  • Standard connections between 1 and 1 million monthly active rows have a $5 base charge.
  • Standard includes 15-minute syncs.
  • Enterprise adds 1-minute syncs.

Enterprise database connectors are available through the Enterprise plan.

Limitations:

Teams requiring sub-15-minute freshness may need to move beyond the Standard plan to Enterprise or Business Critical.

Best for: Teams that prefer managed replication and whose freshness requirements and monthly active row volumes fit Fivetran's pricing structure.

3. Airbyte

https://airbyte.com/

Airbyte provides PostgreSQL source and Snowflake destination connectors for database replication.

Its PostgreSQL source supports CDC through logical replication and also supports replication using PostgreSQL's xmin system column.

For PostgreSQL databases larger than 500 GB, Airbyte recommends logical replication.

The Snowflake destination connector handles delivery to the warehouse. Starting with version 5.0.0, username-and-password authentication for the Snowflake destination is deprecated.

Airbyte also uses PostgreSQL WAL-based logical replication to capture delete operations.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC support.
  • Logical replication and xmin-based replication.
  • Snowflake destination connector.
  • Managed Cloud deployment options.
  • Delete capture through logical replication.

Pricing:

Airbyte offers different Cloud pricing structures:

  • Standard uses a fully managed, volume-based pricing model.
  • Pro and Enterprise Flex plans use Data Worker capacity for pricing.

Limitations:

Airbyte's CDC caching layer is incompatible with certain Aurora configurations where that layer cannot be disabled. Teams using Aurora should verify compatibility before selecting this approach.

Best for: Teams looking for managed PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication with volume-based or capacity-based Cloud pricing.

4. Striim

https://www.striim.com/

Striim provides PostgreSQL CDC capabilities through its PostgreSQL Reader and supports Snowflake as a destination through its Snowflake Writer.

One notable capability is support for capturing PostgreSQL TRUNCATE operations when using wal2json version 2.

This can be useful for workloads where table truncation is part of the source database workflow.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC through its Reader.
  • TRUNCATE capture with wal2json version 2.
  • Snowflake Writer support.
  • Snowpipe Streaming support.
  • Support for staging events to local storage, Amazon S3, or Azure Storage.

The Snowflake Writer stages events to local storage, S3, or Azure Storage unless Snowpipe Streaming is enabled. Teams should verify that their PostgreSQL Reader and Snowflake Writer configurations support the required event propagation.

Pricing:

  • Striim Developer is free for up to 25 million events per month.
  • Striim Cloud pricing is available through its sales team.

As of October 2026, Striim does not publish a standard Cloud pricing rate.

Limitations:

Teams looking for transparent, published Cloud pricing may find it difficult to estimate costs without requesting a quote. The Developer allowance is measured in events rather than bytes, so event volume needs to be estimated separately.

Best for: Teams that need PostgreSQL TRUNCATE capture and can use Striim's supported PostgreSQL Reader and Snowflake Writer configuration.

5. Artie

https://www.artie.com/

Artie is a CDC replication platform that supports PostgreSQL and Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector list includes several managed database services, such as:

  • Amazon Aurora.
  • Amazon RDS.
  • Google Cloud SQL.
  • Supabase.

Snowflake is also included among its supported destinations.

Artie advertises sub-minute replication latency and exactly-once delivery, making it an option for teams that prioritize data freshness.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL CDC support.
  • Support for several managed PostgreSQL services.
  • Snowflake destination support.
  • Advertised sub-minute latency.
  • Advertised exactly-once delivery.

Pricing:

As of October 2026:

  • The free plan covers up to 1 million billable rows per month.
  • Growth starts at $500 per month with an annual contract.
  • Growth costs $600 per month on a month-to-month basis.
  • Enterprise pricing is available through a quote.

Limitations:

Teams that need paid Growth features, such as proactive monitoring or single sign-on, must account for the plan's minimum cost.

Best for: Teams that need sub-minute CDC replication and support for managed PostgreSQL services such as Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, or Supabase.

6. Snowflake Openflow

https://www.snowflake.com/

Snowflake Openflow provides a native integration option for replicating PostgreSQL data into Snowflake.

Its PostgreSQL connector supports near-real-time or scheduled replication of selected tables. It also maintains a log of data changes alongside the current table state.

Openflow is built on Apache NiFi and provides a Snowflake-managed integration option, although its deployment and infrastructure requirements differ from fully managed third-party services.

Key capabilities:

  • PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication.
  • Near-real-time or scheduled updates.
  • Change logs alongside current table state.
  • Native Snowflake integration.

Requirements and limitations:

  • Requires PostgreSQL 11 or later.
  • Supports only username-and-password authentication with PostgreSQL.
  • Tables without a supported identity key replicate inserts only.
  • Ignores source TRUNCATE statements.
  • BYOC deployments are limited to AWS Commercial Regions.

Before using Openflow for a production workload, confirm that the source tables have the required identity keys if updates and deletes need to be replicated.

Pricing:

Snowflake bills Openflow BYOC compute per second, with a 60-second minimum.

Best for: Teams that want a Snowflake-native integration for external PostgreSQL databases and can meet its version, authentication, and deployment requirements.

7. Snowflake Postgres Data Mirroring

https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/snowflake-postgres/postgres-data-mirroring

Snowflake Postgres data mirroring is different from the other options in this comparison.

It is designed to replicate tables from Snowflake Postgres into a Snowflake analytics database. Snowflake Postgres is a service where customers create and manage PostgreSQL instances directly within Snowflake.

This means it is not a general-purpose replication solution for an existing PostgreSQL database hosted outside Snowflake.

Key capabilities:

  • Continuous replication from Snowflake Postgres.
  • No external CDC service to deploy.
  • Serverless apply.
  • A $live view containing changes that have not yet been merged.
  • A seven-day change feed for inserts, updates, and deletes.

The $live view has an approximately 30-second lag. The change feed can be queried from both Snowflake and Postgres.

Pricing:

Snowflake bills the apply using its standard serverless task rate.

Limitations:

  • Supports Snowflake Postgres as the source, not arbitrary external PostgreSQL databases.
  • Available in AWS and Azure regions where Snowflake Postgres is supported.
  • Mirrors cannot cross accounts, regions, or clouds.

Best for: Teams already using Snowflake Postgres that want continuous replication into a Snowflake analytics database without deploying an external CDC service.

PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Replication Tools Compared

The following table summarizes the main differences between the seven options.

Tool PostgreSQL source support Snowflake write path Pricing model Key limitation
Estuary PostgreSQL 10.0+, self-hosted and major cloud platforms Staged transactional loads; Snowpipe Streaming for delta bindings Per GB moved + connector-instance fees Requires PostgreSQL 10.0+
Fivetran PostgreSQL SQL MERGE Monthly active rows 15-minute Standard syncs
Airbyte CDC and xmin replication Snowflake destination connector Volume-based or Data Worker capacity Aurora CDC caching-layer compatibility
Striim PostgreSQL 9.4.x–17, self-managed Staging or Snowpipe Streaming Data moved; Cloud by quote Cloud pricing not published
Artie PostgreSQL, Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, Supabase Snowflake destination Billable rows; Growth from $500/month annually Growth plan minimum
Snowflake Openflow PostgreSQL 11+ Near-real-time or scheduled replication BYOC compute Ignores TRUNCATE
Snowflake Postgres mirroring Snowflake Postgres only Serverless apply Serverless task compute Cannot mirror external PostgreSQL sources

Pricing and plan information is based on published vendor details as of October 2026. Actual costs depend on usage, configuration, and applicable plan terms.

How to Choose a PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake Replication Tool

The right tool depends primarily on where your PostgreSQL database runs, how frequently Snowflake needs to receive changes, and how you want to manage replication costs.

Here are a few practical considerations.

Choose Snowflake Postgres data mirroring if:

Your source database is already running on Snowflake Postgres and you want replication into a Snowflake analytics database without deploying an external CDC service.

Choose Estuary if:

You have an existing PostgreSQL database and want managed CDC with configurable Snowflake delivery, without operating Kafka or Airflow.

You can set the Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to 0s to remove scheduled waiting time. For delta-update bindings, Snowpipe Streaming provides the connector's lowest-latency loading option.

Choose Fivetran if:

Your workload fits its monthly active row pricing and the Standard plan's 15-minute sync frequency is sufficient.

Choose Airbyte if:

You want PostgreSQL CDC and Snowflake destination support with volume-based or capacity-based Cloud pricing.

Choose Striim if:

Your workflow needs PostgreSQL TRUNCATE capture and its supported Snowflake Writer configuration meets your requirements.

Choose Artie if:

You prioritize its advertised sub-minute latency and need support for managed PostgreSQL services such as Aurora, RDS, Cloud SQL, or Supabase.

Choose Snowflake Openflow if:

You want a Snowflake-native option for an external PostgreSQL database and your source meets its PostgreSQL version, authentication, and deployment requirements.

Before committing to a tool, document these four things:

  1. Source type: Self-hosted PostgreSQL, RDS, Aurora, Cloud SQL, Supabase, or Snowflake Postgres.
  2. Freshness requirement: Scheduled replication, 15-minute syncs, or sub-minute delivery.
  3. Data volume: Expected monthly data captured and delivered.
  4. Change operations: Whether the pipeline must support inserts, updates, deletes, and TRUNCATE.

Also, test your largest source table and verify that all required changes reach Snowflake correctly. If your application uses TRUNCATE, test that operation separately rather than assuming it behaves like a series of individual deletes.

FAQ

1. Can you replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake without Kafka?

Yes. Managed CDC services can capture PostgreSQL changes and deliver them to Snowflake without requiring a separately managed Kafka cluster.

For example, Estuary's PostgreSQL connector captures changes into collections, and its Snowflake materialization delivers those changes to destination tables.

Estuary supports PostgreSQL 10.0 and later on major cloud platforms and self-hosted instances.

2. Do you need Airflow for PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication?

No. Airflow is an orchestration tool, not a requirement for CDC-based replication.

Managed services such as Estuary handle change capture and delivery through their own pipeline configurations. Snowflake Openflow also supports near-real-time or scheduled replication, while Snowflake Postgres mirroring runs within Snowflake.

3. Is Snowflake data mirroring available for any PostgreSQL database?

No. Snowflake data mirroring is designed specifically for Snowflake Postgres.

It continuously replicates tables from Snowflake Postgres into a Snowflake analytics database. If your PostgreSQL database runs externally, such as on Amazon RDS, Aurora, or a self-hosted server, you need a compatible external CDC connector.

Snowflake Postgres mirroring is available in supported AWS and Azure regions, and mirrors cannot cross accounts, regions, or clouds.

4. What is the fastest way to replicate PostgreSQL to Snowflake?

The answer depends on where the source database runs.

For Snowflake Postgres, the $live view exposes pending changes with an approximately 30-second lag.

For an external PostgreSQL database, Estuary is an option. You can configure its Snowflake materialization's Sync Frequency to 0s to remove scheduled waiting time. For delta-update bindings, Snowpipe Streaming provides its lowest-latency Snowflake loading path.

Actual end-to-end latency depends on the workload, processing, and ingestion configuration, so validate performance against your own freshness requirements.

5. How much does PostgreSQL-to-Snowflake replication cost?

Costs vary depending on the tool's pricing model and the amount of data being replicated.

For example, Estuary's Cloud pricing as of October 2026 is $0.50 per GB of data moved, plus connector-instance fees.

Consider a workload that captures 100 GB from PostgreSQL and delivers 100 GB to Snowflake. That produces 200 billed GB, costing $100. Two connector instances running for a full month add $200, bringing the estimated recurring pipeline charge to approximately $300.

Artie's Growth plan starts at $500 per month with an annual contract or $600 month to month, as of October 2026.

These figures exclude Snowflake storage and compute, as well as other applicable charges. Confirm vendor pricing and usage allowances before comparing final costs.

6. Should you use Snowflake Openflow or PostgreSQL data mirroring?

Use Snowflake Openflow when replicating an external PostgreSQL database that meets its PostgreSQL 11 or later requirement and supports its username-and-password authentication requirement.

Use Snowflake Postgres data mirroring when your source is already running on Snowflake Postgres and you want to replicate its tables into a Snowflake analytics database.

The two options serve different source environments, so the choice depends on where your PostgreSQL database is hosted.

Conclusion

Replicating PostgreSQL to Snowflake no longer requires every team to maintain a separate Kafka cluster, Debezium deployment, and Airflow orchestration layer.

Managed CDC services provide an alternative by handling change capture and destination delivery within a managed pipeline.

Estuary is a strong choice for existing PostgreSQL databases that need continuous CDC and configurable Snowflake delivery. Fivetran, Airbyte, Striim, and Artie offer alternative managed approaches with different pricing models and operational capabilities. Snowflake Openflow provides a native integration option for external PostgreSQL databases, while Snowflake Postgres data mirroring is specifically designed for databases hosted within Snowflake.

The best choice ultimately depends on your source environment, freshness requirements, change-handling needs, and expected data volume. Evaluate those requirements before selecting a replication tool, and test inserts, updates, deletes, and any TRUNCATE operations your application relies on.

title: How to Rotate a Video With FFmpeg (Transpose the Pixels, Don't Trust a Metadata Flag, Prove It With pytest)
description:
TL;DR: to rotate a video with FFmpeg, transpose the pixels. A rotate=90 metadata flag plus -c copy does not change the coded width or height, and many players ignore the flag. The working 90-degree clockwise command is:

ffmpeg -i input.mp4 -vf transpose=1 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 out.mp4

transpose=2 turns it 90 degrees the other way; transpose=2,transpose=2 turns it 180 degrees. The rest of this post wraps those filters in a short Python helper and proves the result with five pytest checks against a real landscape clip.

The test clip

I needed a real landscape file whose coded size I could measure before and after a rotation. Voor's Crazy Frog AI trend generator publishes an 11.375 s widescreen example (yellow-jacket-v2.mp4, 1314×702, H.264, no audio; md5 82649dc970b3989ccdc3bbd48c376050). I used that public example as the fixture. I did not generate a new clip for this post.

ffprobe -v error -show_entries stream=codec_type,codec_name,width,height,duration -of default=noprint_wrappers=1 yellow-jacket-v2.mp4

codec_name=h264
codec_type=video
width=1314
height=702
duration=11.375000

One stream, landscape, no audio. That last point keeps the tests focused on the picture.

Attempt 1: the metadata flag

The tempting lossless move is to stream-copy the packets and only write a rotation tag:

ffmpeg -i yellow-jacket-v2.mp4 -c copy -metadata:s:v:0 rotate=90 meta90.mp4

width=1314
height=702

The coded size does not change. Some players honour the tag and some do not, so the file you hand to a browser, a phone, or a later FFmpeg filter graph may still play as landscape. If you needed a portrait asset, this command did not make one.

Attempt 2: transpose the pixels 

ffmpeg -i yellow-jacket-v2.mp4 -vf transpose=1 -c:v libx264 -pix_fmt yuv420p -crf 18 cw90.mp4

width=702
height=1314
duration=11.375000

Width and height have swapped. This is a re-encode, so it is not lossless, but the picture is actually portrait. Use -crf 18 (or a bitrate you already use in your pipeline) rather than a default that makes the file look softer than the source.

Useful transpose values:

Goal Filter
90° clockwise transpose=1
90° counter-clockwise transpose=2
180° transpose=2,transpose=2

The older rotate filter is for arbitrary angles. It is the wrong tool for a quarter-turn of a video frame.

A small Python wrapper

rotate.py exposes rotate_pixels, metadata_only_rotate, and a PPM frame dump so the tests can read pixels with the standard library only:

TRANSPOSE = {
    "cw90": "transpose=1",
    "ccw90": "transpose=2",
    "180": "transpose=2,transpose=2",
}

def rotate_pixels(src, dst, direction="cw90"):
    filt = TRANSPOSE[direction]
    cmd = [
        "ffmpeg", "-v", "error", "-y", "-i", str(src),
        "-vf", filt, "-c:v", "libx264", "-pix_fmt", "yuv420p", "-crf", "18",
        "-an", str(dst),
    ]
    subprocess.run(cmd, check=True)
    return dst

If the input has an audio stream, pass -c:a copy instead of -an so the sound is not dropped when you only meant to turn the picture.

Prove it with pytest

Size alone is not enough for a 180° turn: the coded dimensions stay 1314×702. The tests also extract one RGB frame as a PPM and check that an 8×8 block from the top-left of the source lands where the mapping says it should.

def test_transpose_cw90_swaps_coded_size_and_keeps_duration(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "cw90.mp4"
    rotate_pixels(CLIP, out, "cw90")
    assert coded_size(out) == (702, 1314)
    src, dst = video_stream(CLIP), video_stream(out)
    assert abs(float(dst["duration"]) - float(src["duration"])) < 0.08
    assert abs(int(dst["nb_frames"]) - int(src["nb_frames"])) <= 1


def test_metadata_only_rotate_does_not_change_coded_size(tmp_path):
    out = tmp_path / "meta.mp4"
    metadata_only_rotate(CLIP, out, 90)
    assert coded_size(out) == coded_size(CLIP) == (1314, 702)


def test_cw90_moves_top_left_block_to_top_right(tmp_path):
    # clockwise: (x, y) -> (h-1-y, x)
    ...

Run them with:

uvx pytest -q test_rotate.py

.....                                                                    [100%]
5 passed in 3.27s

The five checks are: the fixture is 1314×702 with no audio; transpose=1 swaps the size and keeps the duration; the metadata-only command does not change the coded size; a 180° transpose keeps the size but moves a known block to the opposite corner; and the clockwise transpose moves that same block to the top-right.

When this is the wrong fix

If a phone video already looks upright in QuickTime but ffprobe reports a displaymatrix or a rotate side data, the pixels may already be stored in one orientation and tagged in another. Transposing that file again will make it look wrong. Probe first, and only run transpose when the coded width and height are the orientation you want to change.

Optional next step

The fixture in this post is a silent widescreen clip from Voor's Crazy Frog AI page: one photo in, an 11-second landscape MP4 out, quoted at 1427 credits on November 11, 2026, with the trend sound meant to be added when you post. If you want a fresh silent landscape file to practice on, the Crazy Frog AI generator is here. The rotation commands above do not depend on that tool.

This article was written with Fully Autonomous AI assistance and then checked against commands and tests run on the machine that published it.

title: siftwise v0.3: riskiest tests first, time budgets, Jest and Java selection, and live dogfooding numbers
description:
siftwise is an open-source, self-hosted tool that runs only the tests your change can affect, and tells you whether a failing test is your fault, already broken on main, or just flaky.

New here? Post 1 explains the idea and sets up the server and the GitHub Action. Post 2 adds GitLab CI and five coding agents over MCP.

Today v0.3.0 is out. The theme: smarter selection.

pip install --upgrade siftwise   # 0.3.0

What's new in v0.3

  • 🎯 Risk order: the tests most likely to fail run first, so a failure shows up early.
  • ⏱️ Time budget: "the riskiest tests that fit in 5 minutes", for fast feedback.
  • 🟨 Jest selection: a JS/TS import graph, with no Node.js needed.
  • ☕ Java selection for Maven and Gradle, including multi-module builds.
  • 🐶 Dogfooding: siftwise now runs on its own CI on every PR and push, with live numbers.
  • 🐛 Follow-ups and fixes from testing v0.2 on real repos, three of which made siftwise silently miss tests.
  • 🙌 First outside contributors: two of them, the same morning I opened my first good first issue.

Like the earlier posts, this one is the whole guide, with the real numbers, including the ones that didn't go my way.

Planned vs shipped

At the end of post 2 I promised five things for v0.3. Here's what happened:

Promised in v0.2 Shipped in v0.3
Run the tests most likely to fail first ✅ Risk order (#42), plus import depth on top (#48)
Time-budget mode ✅ --budget 5m everywhere: CLI, Action, GitLab, MCP (#43)
A real JS/TS import graph for Jest ✅ (#44), plus computed imports like import.meta.glob (#51)
Test selection for Java ✅ Maven and Gradle (#45), plus module build-file scoping, one command per build and a first Gradle replay (#54)
Live recall numbers from dogfooding ⚠️ Live time-saved numbers, yes. Live recall, not yet: none of siftwise's own runs has failed so far, so there's nothing to catch or miss. More in Part 5.

Not planned, but shipped too:

  • the v0.2 follow-ups (#46): Jest without addFileAttribute, JUnit 5 @DisplayName re-runs, Go workspaces and nested modules, and the GitLab Tests tab;
  • go list no longer edits go.mod (#52);
  • six bug fixes, three of which made siftwise silently miss tests (Part 6);
  • new evals: time to first failure, recall within a budget, and a Gradle replay.

Upgrading from 0.2

v0.3 has two database migrations (0011 and 0012; both only add columns). The server runs them on start, so with Docker it's the usual:

cd siftwise && git pull                       # the compose file now names the 0.3.0 image
docker compose up -d --wait                   # pulls 0.3.0, migrates, restarts
uv tool upgrade siftwise                      # the CLI; or: pip install --upgrade siftwise

Then move your Action pins to @v0.3.0, and the GitLab template to v0.3.0 with its new integrity hash.

Update the server and the clients together. A new CLI talking to a 0.2 server still works: it sends the request again without the new fields and gets 0.2's selection. The exception is a time budget, which can't be dropped silently: the Action, GitLab and MCP fall back to the full suite with a warning, and siftwise select --budget exits with an error. An old CLI works with a new server unchanged.

Part 1: risk order, riskiest tests first

In v0.2, siftwise picked the right tests but ran them in path order. If the one that fails is last, you still wait for everything before it.

Now every selected test gets a score, a rank and a reason, and the command runs the riskiest first. The score is a fixed, documented formula, with no machine learning:

score = link + 3 × recency + 2 × failure rate   (recency and rate discounted if the test is flaky)
        + 2 if the test is new

link     = 6 if the change reaches the test directly, 3 through other files, 0 by history only
recency  = halves every 7 days since the test last failed

So a test whose file imports the code you changed, and that failed last week, goes to the front. Ties go to the faster test.

Nothing to configure: it's on by default. siftwise select --json shows each test's score, rank and rank_reason; the PR comment and GitLab note name the three riskiest tests. To keep the old order: --order default, the Action's order: default, SIFTWISE_ORDER: default on GitLab, or order: "default" over MCP.

The order never changes which tests run, only when. How much it's respected depends on the runner:

Runner What the order guarantees
pytest arguments run in the order given (unless a plugin like pytest-xdist or pytest-randomly reorders them)
Go packages run one after another, riskiest first
Jest a hint: Jest runs files in parallel and may reorder them
Maven modules run in Maven's reactor (dependency) order

Does it help? The numbers

I replayed real CI history, evaluating each run using only the history from before it. The number is how much of a selective run passes before the first failure shows, as a median (lower is better):

Repo Default order Risk order
RDFLib/rdflib (Python), 17 runs 37.3% of the time 1.4%
agent-substrate/substrate (Go), 19 runs 42.0% 25.6%

On rdflib, the failure typically shows in the first 1.4% of the run instead of after a third of it. Recall didn't change: the same tests ran, in a different order.

I also tried a "cost-aware" order (risk per second of estimated test time). It wasn't clearly better on both repos and was worse by test count, so it didn't ship.

The feature that made the numbers worse

v0.3 also adds import depth: a test file that imports the changed code itself counts as a direct link (6), above one that reaches it through other files (3).

My first version did this for every language, and substrate got worse: the median went from 23.3% to 34.4% (by test count), with the first failure coming later in 6 runs and earlier in only 1.

Going failure by failure showed why. Go's graph is per package, and in Go most dependents import the changed package directly: 83% of the import-linked packages were at depth 1. So "direct" lifted almost every package above the e2e suites that a [[depends]] rule selects, and those were the ones failing.

The fix: Go packages aren't promoted by depth; Python, Jest and Java test files are. substrate is back to exactly its earlier numbers. I chose that rule because a test file's imports say much more precisely what a test uses than a package's do, not because it scored best on two repos. Honestly, import depth didn't move rdflib's medians either (only the mean improved a little), so I'm not claiming a speed-up from it yet.

Part 2: time budget

Sometimes even the selection is too big for the feedback you want right now. Set a budget, and siftwise runs the riskiest tests whose estimated time fits:

siftwise select --repo acme/shop --base origin/main --budget 5m   # 90s, 5m, 1h30m
Where Setting
GitHub Action budget: 5m (outputs budget-limited, budget-left-out)
GitLab SIFTWISE_BUDGET: 5m
MCP select_tests budget argument
API budget_seconds

It's off by default. Two things matter before you use it:

  • A budget is an estimate, not a cap. siftwise uses each test's mean duration from history, so a run can take longer. Keep a real CI timeout if you need a hard limit.
  • A budget-limited run is not a complete check, and siftwise says so plainly: the PR comment shows "budget-limited (estimated 4m 50s of a 5m target): N tests left out". Run the full selection before merging.

In shadow mode, a failure the budget left out is counted as a miss with the cause budget, so you can measure what a budget costs you on your own repo.

How much a budget catches, on the same replays: runs whose failure is still caught at a budget of 10%, 25% and 50% of each run's time:

Repo 10% 25% 50% No budget
rdflib 22 of 31 24 of 31 28 of 31 30 of 31
substrate 34 of 72 43 of 72 54 of 72 71 of 72

On rdflib, a 10% budget still catches most failures. On substrate, it catches under half. So a budget is great for a quick first signal, and not a replacement for the full selection.

Part 3: Jest selection

Until now, siftwise matched Jest tests only by file name (foo.ts → foo.test.ts), so a change most tests reach through imports ran the whole suite. Now siftwise reads your JS/TS imports and also runs every test file that imports the changed file, at any depth.

What it understands, without running Node:

  • relative imports, index files and TypeScript's .js → .ts;
  • tsconfig/jsconfig paths and baseUrl (with extends);
  • npm, yarn, pnpm and lerna workspace packages;
  • a JSON Jest moduleNameMapper;
  • JSON and other files a test imports;
  • computed imports with a fixed folder: import(`./locales/${lang}.json`), require('./plugins/' + name), Vite's import.meta.glob and webpack's require.context count as imports of every file they could load (#51).

When it can't see, it plays safe: a test that reaches an import it can't bound (like require(somePath)) runs for every JS change, and changes to tsconfig, Jest, Babel or SWC configs, root manifests or lockfiles run the full suite.

New test files run first, by path, once siftwise can tell where Jest expects them. On jestjs/jest (2,272 JS/TS files), the graph builds in about 2 seconds.

Step 3.1: let siftwise know each test's file

siftwise learns which file each test lives in from the JUnit report. Add jest-junit, ideally with addFileAttribute:

npm install --save-dev jest-junit

{
  "jest": {
    "reporters": ["default", ["jest-junit", { "addFileAttribute": "true" }]]
  }
}

New in v0.3: without addFileAttribute, record searches the checkout for the one test file whose string literals match the suite's test names, and adds it to the report. That works for most files, but titles built from variables can't be matched, so setting the attribute is still the reliable option.

Step 3.2: the workflow 

      - uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v7
        with:
          node-version: 22
      - run: npm ci

      - id: siftwise
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/select@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

      - name: Tests
        env:
          MODE: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.mode }}
          COMMAND: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.command }}
          JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.junit-dir }}
        run: |
          export PATH="$PWD/node_modules/.bin:$PATH"   # the command starts with `jest`
          if [ "$MODE" = selective ]; then
            if [ -n "$COMMAND" ]; then eval "$COMMAND"; else echo "No tests affected."; fi
          else
            jest   # your normal full suite
          fi

      - if: always()
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/record@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

JEST_JUNIT_OUTPUT_DIR puts the report where record looks for it. As always, pass the command through env:, never as ${{ }} inside run:.

An honest gap: there's no recall number for Jest yet. Replays need old CI runs that uploaded JUnit with file paths, and no public Jest repo I found does that. I validated the graph by hand on jestjs/jest. If you run siftwise in shadow mode on a JS repo, I'd love your numbers.

Part 4: Java selection, Maven and Gradle

In v0.2, Java tests were recorded and re-run but always ran in full. Now siftwise reads your build without running Maven, Gradle or a JVM:

  • the modules from pom.xml or settings.gradle[.kts];
  • a static graph of which test classes use which classes (imports, same-package names, fully-qualified names, Class.forName strings), across modules;
  • name matches: changing Foo.java selects FooTest, FooTests, TestFoo and FooIT;
  • a module's src/test/resources runs that module's tests.

One command per build where that's safe:

./mvnw -B -pl core,api -am test -Dtest=CartTest,MoneyTest            # Maven
./gradlew :core:test --tests CartTest :api:test --tests MoneyTest   # Gradle

Build files are scoped too (#54): a change to a module's own pom.xml or build.gradle[.kts] runs the tests of that module and of every module that depends on it. The root build file, settings.gradle, version catalogs, wrappers, parent and BOM POMs still run the full suite, because they can affect everything.

Where it can't see, the full suite runs: Kotlin, Groovy or Scala sources, custom source folders, code-generating annotation processors, or a build it can't read. Reflection (Spring scanning, ServiceLoader) needs a [[depends]] rule.

Step 4.1: the workflow

The only difference from Python is where the reports live, so point record at them:

      - uses: actions/setup-java@v6
        with:
          distribution: temurin
          java-version: 21

      - id: siftwise
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/select@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}

      - name: Tests
        env:
          MODE: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.mode }}
          COMMAND: ${{ steps.siftwise.outputs.command }}
        run: |
          if [ "$MODE" = selective ]; then
            if [ -n "$COMMAND" ]; then eval "$COMMAND"; else echo "No tests affected."; fi
          else
            ./mvnw -B test   # or: ./gradlew test
          fi

      - if: always()
        uses: PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/actions/record@v0.3.0
        with:
          server-url: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_URL }}
          token: ${{ secrets.SIFTWISE_TOKEN }}
          junit: "**/target/surefire-reports/TEST-*.xml **/build/test-results/test/*.xml"

The numbers

  • dropwizard/dropwizard (Maven, 42 modules), 148 PR runs: 74 of 74 failures caught. In the 22 selective runs, siftwise skipped a median 90.6% of the estimated test time (26% to 93%).
  • The catch: most of dropwizard's PRs are dependency bumps to its BOM, which correctly run everything. So over all 148 runs, the time saved is much smaller: 11.9%. Module build-file scoping moved 5 more runs from full to selective. A repo with more code changes and fewer bumps would save more.
  • naver/fixture-monkey (Gradle): 3 of 3 failures caught. That's a small history, so treat it as a first check, not proof.

The dropwizard replay also found a real bug: Surefire writes a class-level result with an empty test name for a JUnit 5 @Nested class, and siftwise rejected the whole upload for it. Every Windows leg of dropwizard's CI history (781 uploads) was rejected before the fix.

Part 5: dogfooding, siftwise on its own CI

This was the last promise from post 2, and the one I care most about. Replays of other projects' history are useful, but they're replays. Dogfooding is siftwise running live on real changes, as they happen.

How it works

Every siftwise PR and push to main runs a Dogfood workflow in shadow mode:

  1. A siftwise server starts inside the CI job, on the runner's own Postgres, with a random per-job token. There's no hosted server and nothing to pay for.
  2. History comes from the GitHub Actions cache. The job restores the database from main's latest cache entry, and saves a new one at the end.
  3. siftwise stores what it would have selected, then the full suite runs anyway.
  4. It compares: for every failure, would the selection have caught it? How much time would it have saved?
  5. Each run uploads a small summary file. scripts/dogfood_report.py adds them all up.

It gates nothing: no fail-on, no PR comment, and every siftwise step fails open. So it can never block my own CI.

The safety part: a PR's cache entry is scoped to that PR, so a PR (including one from a fork) can read main's history but can never write into it. Only main's own runs build the history. For the numbers, I also leave out the fork PRs' runs, because code from the fork wrote their summaries; each of those changes still counts once, as its push to main.

The numbers (26 Oct to 9 Nov 2026)

Workflow runs 36 (17 PR runs, 19 pushes to main)
Shadow runs counted 32 (the first 2 had no history yet; the 2 fork runs are left out)
Would have been selective 9 of 32
Tests selected in those 9 a median 39% of the known tests
Time saved 14.7% of 23.0 minutes over the 32 runs
Failures none: every run's suite passed, so recall can't be measured yet
Weekly time saved 21%, 7% and 34%

Read these as early numbers. A merged PR usually counts twice (once as its PR run, once as its push to main), so the 9 selective runs are really about 6 distinct changes.

What dogfooding taught me

  • Why 23 of 32 ran in full: 20 changed a build or config file (the Dockerfile and docker-compose.yml in 6 runs each, workflows, and my test fixtures' own build.gradle.kts, tsconfig.json and jest.config.ts), and 3 changed a file no test reaches (like glama.json).
  • The fixture finding is the most useful one. siftwise's tests include tiny sample Gradle and TypeScript projects. Their build files are test data, but siftwise treats them like real build files and runs everything. Scoping them safely is the first item for v0.4. I'd never have found this from replays.
  • Each run now records the risk rank of every failure, so once a dogfood run does fail, the report shows not just "caught or missed" but how early risk order would have surfaced it.

You can do the same on your repo: the Action's shadow input (always, or a sample like 10%) runs the full suite and reports what siftwise would have caught or missed, before you trust it with anything. Details: Shadow mode in the README.

Part 6: v0.2 follow-ups and fixes

Things I found while testing v0.2 on real projects (#46):

  • Jest without addFileAttribute: selection and re-runs now work without it (Part 3).
  • JUnit 5 @DisplayName and parameterized test names map back to their methods, so Gradle and phrased-Maven re-runs work.
  • Go workspaces (go.work) and nested modules work for selection, commands and re-runs.
  • The GitLab template now declares its JUnit reports, which the pipeline's Tests tab reads.

Fixes, three of which (🔴) made siftwise silently miss tests:

  • 🔴 Nested Go modules: a nested module's dependents were missed, and its tests ran from the root, where Go can't build them. Now they run as go test -C <module> ./pkg.
  • 🔴 Missed JS edges: import('./a/' + x), import.meta.glob and require.context created no edges, so changing a file they load didn't select the tests that load it.
  • go list could edit go.mod when GOFLAGS had -mod=mod. It now runs read-only (#52). On Go 1.15 or older, set GOFLAGS=-mod=readonly yourself; making siftwise do it is an open good first issue (#67).
  • Java uploads rejected for a @Nested class's result (the dropwizard bug above).
  • 🔴 Same-named Java test classes in two modules: a change to one module's test resources ran only the other module's copy.
  • A deleted Jest test file was still named in the jest command, which then failed with "No tests found".

What building v0.3 taught me

  • Measure the features you're sure about. Import depth was the "obviously better" change, and it made one repo worse. Without the replay, I'd have shipped it.
  • Your dependencies change under you. On release day, a new Typer version started requiring pydantic, which broke the check that keeps the light CLI install small. siftwise's code didn't change; the light install grew from 9 MB to 18 MB, and the check now verifies that siftwise itself never imports server code.
  • good first issue works. I labelled a one-line bug, and by the same morning two people had sent fixes. One fixed it; the other added the test that stops it from coming back. Both got merged.

Community

  • Thanks to @bfs2021 (#62) and @mursalhayat1 (#63), siftwise's first outside contributors.
  • siftwise's MCP server is listed in the HOL Guard MCP server catalog (opt-in, after a review of its code and disclosures) and on Glama.

Troubleshooting

You see Fix
Jest tests always run in full add addFileAttribute: "true" to jest-junit (Step 3.1)
jest: command not found put node_modules/.bin on PATH, as in Step 3.2
Java tests never selected record didn't find the reports: set its junit input (Step 4.1)
Every Java PR runs the full suite it changed a root or parent build file, which runs everything by design
--budget fails with a server error the server is still on 0.2: upgrade it
The order looks wrong in Jest Jest reorders files across its workers; the order is a hint there

Known limits

  • Jest: no recall number yet; jest.config.js can't be read without Node (tsconfig and relative paths still resolve); a custom testMatch isn't read.
  • Java: Kotlin, Groovy and Scala tests fall back to the full suite; Maven runs modules in reactor order, not risk order.
  • Budget: an estimate, not a cap.
  • Dogfooding: 32 runs and no failures yet, so no live recall.
  • MCP is tested on Windows only; GitLab on gitlab.com Free only.
  • Everything else: the CHANGELOG.

What's next: v0.4

  • Safe scoping for build files inside test fixtures (the dogfooding finding).
  • -mod=readonly for older Go versions.
  • More recall numbers: a Jest replay, more Gradle history, and the first live recall from dogfooding.
  • More good first issues. If you'd like to contribute, start here.

Links

  • 💻 GitHub: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise
  • 📦 PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/siftwise/
  • 📝 Release notes: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/releases/tag/v0.3.0
  • 📊 All eval numbers and method: https://github.com/PramodBasavarajMenasi/siftwise/blob/main/docs/eval-results.md
  • 📖 Post 1 (server and GitHub Action): https://dev.to/pm_22/i-built-siftwise-run-only-the-tests-your-change-needs-open-source-self-hosted-51jf
  • 📖 Post 2 (GitLab CI and coding agents): https://dev.to/pm_22/siftwise-v02-run-it-on-gitlab-ci-and-with-5-coding-agents-full-setup-guide-o2f

Try it, break it, tell me

If you have a Jest or Java repo, try siftwise in shadow mode and tell me what it would have caught or missed: that's exactly the data v0.3 is missing. Misses make the best bug reports. And a ⭐ helps a small project get seen. 👇

title: The weekly bug-status email a freelance QA tester sends, and the client rules it keeps forgetting
description:
Say you're a freelance QA tester on a three-month contract with a small agency. Every Friday you owe the client a short status email: what you found, what got fixed, what's still open. The first one goes fine. By week four, the email is technically accurate and still annoys the client, because it ignores things they told you in week one.

I build Maildoer, an email assistant, and near the end I'll show how it handles that week-four problem. Most of this post is the structure and checks I'd use no matter who writes the email.

Why bug-status emails go wrong

A tracker export answers "what's in the system?". The client reading your email on a phone wants to know:

  1. Is anything blocking launch?
  2. What changed since last Friday?
  3. Do they need to decide anything?

The raw export can't answer number 2, and it has no idea what the client already asked for. Typical week-one requests look like this:

  • "Group issues by page, not by severity. Our designers think in pages."
  • "Don't paste staging links. This email gets forwarded to people who shouldn't have them."
  • "Call it 'won't fix this release', never 'rejected'. The dev team is touchy."

None of these live in the tracker. They live in an email thread from three weeks ago.

A template that survives forwarding 

Subject: QA status, week N: [X blockers / no blockers]

1. Launch blockers (or "None this week")
   - Page > issue, one line each, current owner

2. Changed since last Friday
   - Fixed and verified: count + the ones they'll notice
   - New: one line each, grouped by page
   - Re-opened: why, in one sentence

3. Decisions needed from you
   - The question, the options, the default if we hear nothing by [day]

4. Still open, not blocking
   - Count per page; full list attached

Standing rules for this client:
   - grouped by page / no staging URLs / "won't fix this release"

The last block is the important one. Keep it at the bottom of your own draft (delete it before sending if you like). It's a checklist you re-read every Friday.

Four checks before you hit send

  • Diff, don't dump. If "changed since last Friday" is longer than the full list was last week, you're re-reporting old issues.
  • Search for forbidden strings. Find staging. and any internal ticket prefix before sending. One forwarded link is enough to lose trust.
  • One decision per bullet. "Should we A or B, default A on Wednesday" gets answered. A paragraph doesn't.
  • Read the subject line alone. It's often all the client's boss sees.

Week four is the real test

The hard part isn't writing a good first status email. It's the fourth one, when you're tired, the export has changed shape, and the client's week-one rules are buried. If you hand this job to someone else, a contractor or a tool, the same thing applies: give them the earlier thread too, not just this week's CSV.

That's the part I cared about most when building Maildoer. It doesn't read a new email from someone as if it were the first one. When it works on your week-four request, it connects it to your earlier emails, so "same format as last Friday, here's the new export" keeps the page grouping and the no-staging-links rule you set in week one. If something's off in the result, you reply to that result and say what to change. You don't start over.

Here's the brief I'd send in week one:

Attached: tracker export (CSV). Draft my weekly QA status email to the client using this structure: blockers, changed since last week, decisions needed, still open. Group by page, not severity. Never include staging URLs. Say "won't fix this release" instead of "rejected". Keep it short enough to read on a phone.

And in week four, just:

Same as last Friday. New export attached. One extra thing: the checkout page is a blocker now.

Whatever you use, write down the client's standing rules once and carry them forward every week. That habit does most of the work.

If you want to test the week-four brief on your own export, email the file and your ask to do@maildoer.com. Your first email gets 100 credits to try it. https://maildoer.com

title: SailPoint Developer Training: What a Course Should Cover (Rules, Workflows, Connectors)
description:
If you already write Java or support enterprise applications, SailPoint IdentityIQ (IIQ) development is one of the most direct routes into identity and access management. But "SailPoint developer training" means very different things on different course pages. Some teach the admin screens and call it development. This post lists what a developer-focused SailPoint course should actually cover, and how to check a syllabus before you pay.

What a SailPoint IIQ developer actually does

On a typical IIQ project, the developer:

  • Onboards applications: configures connectors, schemas, aggregation and correlation so identities and accounts match correctly.
  • Writes rules in BeanShell (Java syntax): correlation, customization, build-map, before/after provisioning and identity attribute rules.
  • Builds workflows: joiner, mover and leaver lifecycle events, access-request approvals and custom provisioning flows.
  • Debugs: reads logs, traces failed aggregations and provisioning, and fixes them without breaking production.
  • Deploys: moves configuration between DEV, TEST and PROD using XML exports and a build process.

A training course that skips any of these leaves you unprepared for the first week of a real project.

What SailPoint developer training should cover

Use this as a checklist against any syllabus:

  1. IIQ architecture and the object model: identities, links, entitlements, applications, rules and tasks, and how they relate in the database.
  2. Application onboarding: delimited file, JDBC and Active Directory connectors; schema design; aggregation tasks.
  3. Correlation: why accounts fail to correlate and how correlation rules fix it.
  4. BeanShell rules: writing, testing and debugging rules with the SailPoint API (SailPointContext, Identity, Link, QueryOptions).
  5. Roles and policies: business vs IT roles, assignment rules, separation-of-duties policies.
  6. Certifications: building access review campaigns and handling revocations.
  7. Lifecycle events and workflows: workflow XML, steps, transitions and variables; joiner-mover-leaver flows end to end.
  8. Provisioning: provisioning plans, before/after provisioning rules, handling failures.
  9. Reporting and quick links: custom reports and forms.
  10. Troubleshooting: log levels, common aggregation, correlation and provisioning errors, and how to read stack traces.

If troubleshooting and workflows are missing, the course is teaching screens, not development.

How to check a course before you enrol

  • Ask for the module list with hours per module. Rules and workflows need real time, not one session.
  • Ask how many years the trainer has spent implementing IIQ at clients.
  • Ask whether classes are live, and whether you can ask questions about your own code.
  • Ask how long you keep access to recordings. Most developers revise before interviews.
  • Be wary of "100% placement guarantee". Placement assistance (resume help, mock interviews, referrals) is the honest version.

How long it takes

For someone with basic Java and SQL, about 45 days of live evening classes plus regular practice is realistic to become comfortable with rules, workflows and troubleshooting. Recorded videos alone usually stop at configuration.

One option

IAM Careers runs a live online SailPoint IIQ course that covers all of the above across 15 modules in 45 days, including rules, workflows and a dedicated troubleshooting module. Classes run at 8 PM IST, Monday to Friday, in small batches, with recordings available for 2 years and a trainer with 15 years of IAM implementation experience. There is also a short guide on what a SailPoint developer course should cover.

This training is provided by IAM Careers and is not affiliated with, authorized by, sponsored by, or endorsed by SailPoint Technologies, Inc.

title: E-commerce Product Search Retrieval Architecture: Go Freshness Windows for Bounded Updates
description:
Short answer: for e-commerce product search, use a staged retrieval architecture with explicit collections, bounded queries, and source context that can be traced back to a product record.

At 3 a.m., the useful question is not “is the dashboard green?” It is “which page fired, and can I explain the result a shopper is seeing?” Product search makes that question concrete: price, inventory, and compliance fields change on different clocks, so one global freshness window quietly turns either into stale results or needless re-indexing.

The incident lesson: freshness is a retrieval contract

The production scenario is bounded rather than heroic. A catalog importer writes product documents, an embedding job chunks descriptions, and a vector index serves semantic candidates before a lexical or business-rules stage narrows them. When a price edit arrived during an embedding run, the system had two conflicting truths: the text chunk was recent, while the offer metadata was old. The alert told us indexing was healthy. It did not tell us the answer was explainable.

That was the page.

The invariant is simple: map the user-visible answer to a retrieval contract before choosing a database. The contract should name the collection, the fields allowed to participate, the maximum age for each change class, and the source URL or document identifier returned with every chunk. Tenant and access-control metadata travel with the item; they are filters, not optional annotations.

A practical policy uses separate windows. Inventory and price changes deserve minutes, editorial copy can tolerate hours, and rarely changing specifications can tolerate a day. Those are policy examples, not a benchmark. Your catalog may demand tighter bounds, and I’m not sure a single number can survive a seasonal sale without an explicit override.

How should an e-commerce product search query use freshness windows?

First retrieve narrowly from the collection whose freshness contract is satisfied. Apply a hard timeout, a result limit, and a retry budget at each stage. A slow source must not hold the shopper request open while a background refresh catches up. The response should carry the chunk’s product identifier, source URL, collection, and observed version so a reviewer can reconstruct why it was selected.

The second stage can rerank candidates with current offer data. If that data is outside its window, mark the candidate stale and exclude it from a purchase-critical answer; do not silently blend it with fresh text. This is where traceability pays for itself: a support engineer can compare the answer to the source record instead of trusting a score on a dashboard.

Here is a small Go client for the bounded query stage. It keeps the decision visible in code, reads the key from the environment, and backs off when the service asks for a retry.

package freshness

import (
    "bytes"
    "crypto/sha256"
    "encoding/hex"
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "time"
)

type ChangeClass string

const (
    Inventory ChangeClass = "inventory"
    Offer     ChangeClass = "offer"
    Content   ChangeClass = "content"
)

type Item struct {
    ProductID   string
    TenantID    string
    Class       ChangeClass
    UpdatedAt   time.Time
    Source      string
    AccessScope string
}

func window(class ChangeClass) time.Duration {
    switch class {
    case Inventory, Offer:
        return 10 * time.Minute
    case Content:
        return 6 * time.Hour
    default:
        return 24 * time.Hour
    }
}

func needsRefresh(item Item, now time.Time) bool {
    return now.Sub(item.UpdatedAt) >= window(item.Class)
}

func idempotencyKey(item Item) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte(item.TenantID + ":" + item.ProductID + ":" + string(item.Class) + ":" + item.UpdatedAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339Nano)))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func query(vector []float64, collection string) ([]byte, error) {
    body, err := json.Marshal(map[string]any{"collection": collection, "vector": vector, "limit": 20})
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    base := os.Getenv("INFRAI_BASE_URL")
    if base == "" { return nil, fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_BASE_URL is required") }
    req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodPost, base+"/v1/vector/query", bytes.NewReader(body))
    if err != nil { return nil, err }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"))
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 4; attempt++ {
        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil { return nil, err }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
            resp.Body.Close()
            time.Sleep(time.Duration(1<<attempt) * 200 * time.Millisecond)
            continue
        }
        data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: status %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
        }
        return data, readErr
    }
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("vector query: rate limit after retries")
}

That request uses the verified vector query path and an explicit method; production code should also honor the server’s Retry-After value when present. The deterministic key is not a substitute for consumer idempotency; it is a stable identity for a refresh operation. A worker can upsert the item, attach its access metadata, and record the source identifier, then safely retry after a 429. Query handlers should fail closed when the timeout budget is exhausted, and they should log the collection, tenant, source identifier, and request ID together so a replay has enough context to prove which freshness window was applied.

What should you compare in an e-commerce retrieval backend?

The backend changes the operational shape of the contract, but it does not remove the contract.

Option Freshness and filtering fit Traceability work Good reason to choose it
Elasticsearch Rich lexical plus vector search; explicit filters and refresh controls Map _source and version fields carefully You already operate search clusters and need broad query DSL support
Typesense Simple collection model and fast typo-tolerant lexical search Store source identifiers in documents and verify update visibility A small team wants a focused search service with low operational surface
Weaviate Vector-first collections with metadata filters and modules Preserve tenant and source properties in every object Semantic retrieval is the center of the product and schema governance is acceptable
Infrai vector endpoints A plain HTTP path for collection, upsert, and bounded query stages Return your own product/source fields and keep the contract in the caller You want discovery plus runnable examples to wire capabilities without installing another SDK

Infrai’s useful distinction here is its self-describing API, where discovery exposes a capability’s request and response schema, billing metadata, and runnable examples, so connecting a new retrieval stage is reading one endpoint rather than learning a new client library, and Infrai uses one key and one bill across 295 routes in 20 modules, which can reduce glue and secret rotation when web acquisition and vector operations belong to one service boundary. That breadth comes with consistent API conventions, although it does not make vector semantics identical to Elasticsearch, Typesense, or Weaviate; validate filtering, refresh visibility, and audit requirements against your contract.

The catch: when this design is the wrong fit

Do not use staged semantic retrieval as the primary path when inventory must be transactionally consistent with checkout, when strict faceting and aggregations dominate, or when your team already has a heavily tuned Elasticsearch cluster whose refresh and audit controls are proven. Stick with that system and put the freshness contract around it. A vector-first store is also a poor fit for a catalog whose queries are almost entirely exact SKU lookups.

Conversely, a single undifferentiated index is risky when tenants have different retention or access rules. Splitting collections by contract, keeping bounded limits, and returning source context costs some orchestration code, but it gives the on-call engineer a explainable failure mode: stale collection, timed-out source, or rejected access filter.

A runbook that survives the next page

Instrument each stage with collection name, freshness class, requested limit, timeout, retry count, and request identifier. Alert on contract violations, such as a result older than its class window or a missing source identifier, rather than on vector latency alone. During an incident, replay the exact query against the recorded collection and source version; that is more useful than a green aggregate metric.

Start with a small catalog slice, measure freshness at the user-visible answer, and widen windows only when the evidence supports it. The architecture is a decision rule, not a vendor badge: explicit contracts and bounded behavior matter more than where the vectors happen to live.

References

  • https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401
  • https://www.elastic.co/guide/en/elasticsearch/reference/current/knn-search.html
  • https://typesense.org/docs/guide/
  • https://weaviate.io/developers/weaviate
