title: Turning a Home Care Audit Evidence List into Data: An Outcome Coverage Index for Support at Home Providers
description:
Originally based on our article the 7 strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards explained for home care on rostery.com.au. This version is rewritten for developers, data people and operations staff who look after the systems behind a Support at Home provider.

When a Category 4 home care provider renews its registration, the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission asks for evidence in a fairly structured way. Its Care Delivery Evidence Collection Tool for Categories 4 and 5 (the CDECT, last updated 17 July 2026) lists 31 numbered documents and records to send before the audit opening meeting. Each row names the evidence, the outcomes it relates to and the time period it should cover. A second, shorter list sets out what the audit team may ask for while it's on site.

That's a schema, even if it arrives as a Word document. If you treat it as one, you can answer useful questions weeks before an audit letter: which outcomes have nothing behind them, which registers are stale for the window being asked about, and which older people are likely to end up in the sample.

This post builds a small Python model for each of those questions. It's deliberately plain: dataclasses, sets and a few pure functions. You can port it to SQL or whatever your reporting layer uses.

General information only, not legal advice. The outcome list comes from the Commission's Strengthened Quality Standards guidance pages and the evidence list from the CDECT for Categories 4 and 5, both read on 11 November 2026. Check the current versions before relying on any of this.

Start with the outcomes that apply to you

The strengthened standards have 7 standards and 33 outcomes. Three outcomes are written in two parts (2.2a and 2.2b, 2.6a and 2.6b, 4.1a and 4.1b), so in practice you work with outcome statements rather than outcome numbers.

Which statements apply depends on registration category. A Support at Home provider is registered in Category 4 with the service type "Care management", which brings in Standards 1 to 4 plus Outcome 5.1, clinical governance. The CDECT itself carries a footnote saying Outcome 5.1 applies only to the care management and restorative care management service types. A provider that also delivers nursing is in Category 5 and meets all of Standard 5.

Put that in a table rather than in someone's head:

from dataclasses import dataclass

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Outcome:
    code: str        # "2.6a"
    title: str
    standard: int

OUTCOMES = [
    Outcome("1.1", "Person-centred care", 1),
    Outcome("1.2", "Dignity, respect and privacy", 1),
    Outcome("1.3", "Choice, independence and quality of life", 1),
    Outcome("1.4", "Transparency and agreements", 1),
    Outcome("2.1", "Partnering with individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.2a", "Culture that supports aged care workers", 2),
    Outcome("2.2b", "Culture that supports individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.3", "Accountability, quality system, policies", 2),
    Outcome("2.4", "Risk management", 2),
    Outcome("2.5", "Incident management", 2),
    Outcome("2.6a", "Complaints and feedback: workers", 2),
    Outcome("2.6b", "Complaints and feedback: individuals", 2),
    Outcome("2.7", "Information management", 2),
    Outcome("2.8", "Workforce planning", 2),
    Outcome("2.9", "Human resource management", 2),
    Outcome("2.10", "Emergency and disaster management", 2),
    Outcome("3.1", "Assessment and planning", 3),
    Outcome("3.2", "Delivery of funded aged care services", 3),
    Outcome("3.3", "Communicating for safety and quality", 3),
    Outcome("3.4", "Planning and coordination", 3),
    Outcome("4.1a", "Environment: services in the person's home", 4),
    Outcome("4.1b", "Environment: services elsewhere", 4),
    Outcome("4.2", "Infection prevention and control", 4),
    Outcome("5.1", "Clinical governance", 5),
    # 5.2 to 5.7 omitted here: they apply in full to Category 5 and 6
]

def applicable(categories: set[int], service_types: set[str]) -> list[Outcome]:
    out = []
    for o in OUTCOMES:
        if o.standard <= 4 and categories & {4, 5, 6}:
            out.append(o)
        elif o.code == "5.1" and (
            categories & {5, 6}
            or (4 in categories and service_types & {"care management", "restorative care management"})
        ):
            out.append(o)
    return out

sah = applicable({4}, {"care management", "personal care"})
assert len(sah) == 24

That assert is worth keeping in your test suite. Twenty-three statements from Standards 1 to 4 plus 5.1 gives the 24 a Support at Home provider is assessed against, and if a refactor ever changes the count you want to know straight away.

Encode the evidence list as rows

Each CDECT row has four fields that matter to us: a number, a description, the outcomes it relates to, and a time period. Some rows say "Various" instead of listing outcomes. Keep that as its own value, because "Various" is not the same as "none".

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass(frozen=True)
class EvidenceRequest:
    no: int
    title: str
    outcomes: frozenset[str] = field(default_factory=frozenset)
    various: bool = False
    window: str = "Current"

CDECT = [
    EvidenceRequest(1, "List of current management and workers", frozenset({"2.2a", "2.6a", "2.8", "2.9"}), window="Latest"),
    EvidenceRequest(5, "Worker roster or shift allocation sheet", frozenset({"2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 4 weeks"),
    EvidenceRequest(8, "Training and induction register", frozenset({"2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(11, "Data on unfilled shifts", frozenset({"2.2a", "2.8", "2.9"}), window="Last 4 weeks"),
    EvidenceRequest(12, "List of older people with risk factors", various=True),
    EvidenceRequest(17, "Risk register", frozenset({"1.3", "2.4", "2.10", "3.1", "3.2", "4.1b", "4.2", "5.3", "5.5"})),
    EvidenceRequest(18, "Complaints and feedback register", frozenset({"2.6a", "2.6b"}), window="Past 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(19, "Incident registers incl. SIRS notifications", frozenset({"2.5", "3.1", "3.3"}), window="Past 3 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(20, "Trend analysis of incidents and complaints", frozenset({"2.3", "2.5", "2.6a", "2.6b"}), window="Past 12 months"),
    EvidenceRequest(27, "Clinical meeting minutes", frozenset({"5.1"}), window="Last 4 meetings"),
    EvidenceRequest(29, "Older people and supporter meeting minutes", frozenset({"1.1", "1.3", "2.1", "3.3"}), window="Last 4 meetings"),
    # ...the full list has 31 rows; copy them from the current CDECT
]

Notice that outcomes from Standard 5 beyond 5.1 turn up in some rows (the risk register is tagged 5.3 and 5.5). The tool covers Category 4 and 5 together, so filter the tags against your own applicable set rather than trusting the row.

Check coverage, and read the gaps carefully

Now the first useful report: which of your applicable outcomes has no numbered pre-audit request tagged against it?

def coverage(requests, outcomes):
    codes = {o.code for o in outcomes}
    tagged = set().union(*(r.outcomes for r in requests)) & codes
    return sorted(codes - tagged)

print(coverage(CDECT, sah))   # with all 31 rows loaded
# ['1.2', '1.4', '2.2b', '2.7', '3.4']

We ran this over all 31 rows of the July 2026 version. Five Support at Home outcomes aren't tagged on any numbered pre-audit document: dignity, respect and privacy (1.2), transparency and agreements (1.4), the culture that supports individuals (2.2b), information management (2.7), and planning and coordination (3.4).

That doesn't mean the Commission ignores them. It means the evidence for them comes from somewhere else: the "Various" rows, interviews with older people and workers, observation, and the second list of records the audit team may ask for during the audit. That list includes agreements with older people, budgets and monthly statements, consent and dignity of risk forms, the tools used to share information with older people and workers, and progress or file notes for the previous 60 days. It carries no outcome tags, so map it yourself. Our own mapping, not the Commission's, looks like this:

DURING_AUDIT = {
    "Agreements with older people": {"1.4"},
    "Budget and monthly statements": {"1.4"},
    "Consent and dignity of risk forms": {"1.3"},
    "Communication tools, interpreters, other formats": {"2.7", "3.3"},
    "Progress or file notes, previous 60 days": {"3.2", "3.3"},
    "Current care and services plans": {"1.1", "3.1"},
}

The practical point is that outcome 1.4 sits almost entirely on records the auditors may ask for on the day. Those are exactly the records where home care has been weakest. The Department's first Support at Home payment integrity review found only 21% of the 262 monthly statements it reviewed had every required item, and the Commission's April to June 2026 data counted 1,011 home care concerns about fees and charges, or how they were communicated. Your coverage report should flag 1.4 for a manual check even though nothing is "missing" from the pre-audit list.

Normalise the time windows

The "Time period" column mixes three kinds of window:

  • Point in time: "Latest" and "Current".
  • Rolling date ranges: "Last 4 weeks", "Past 3 months", "Past 12 months", and "previous 60 days" for progress notes.
  • Counts: "Last 4 meetings".

The count-based one catches people out. If a team meets every quarter, the last four meetings reach back a year. If it met twice and then stopped, no date filter will tell you; you need the count.

from datetime import date, timedelta

def window_ok(records: list[date], window: str, today: date) -> bool:
    if window in ("Latest", "Current"):
        return bool(records)                      # plus a "still in force" check elsewhere
    if window == "Last 4 meetings":
        return len(records) >= 4
    days = {"Last 4 weeks": 28, "Past 3 months": 92,
            "Past 12 months": 366, "Previous 60 days": 60}[window]
    since = today - timedelta(days=days)
    return any(d >= since for d in records)

A rolling window passing doesn't prove much on its own. An incident register with one entry in three months passes the check but may tell an auditor something about reporting culture. Report the count alongside the pass, and let a person decide what's normal for the service.

"Current" also needs its own rule per record type. For care plans it means a plan in force with a review date in the future. For worker checks it means not expired. For an emergency plan it means reviewed on the cycle your own policy sets. Keep those rules next to the request, not buried in a report query.

Build the sample list before you're asked for it

Row 12 asks for a complete list of older people receiving care, and a list of those with particular risk factors. The factors include palliative and end of life care needs, specialised nursing needs, communication difficulties (cognitive or sensory impairment, disability, culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds), high-risk medications such as psychotropics or insulin, any restraint or seclusion, a recent history of falls, a transition to or from hospital or another provider in the last 3 months, living alone with limited outside contact, oxygen, a stoma, enteral feeding, a catheter, needing a higher level of care than they currently receive, greater than expected unspent funds, self-managing Support at Home funding, and being represented by a public guardian.

Most of these can be derived from data you already hold. A few can't, and the honest design is to say so:

from enum import Enum

class Source(Enum):
    DERIVED = "derived from records"
    CONFIRM = "needs a care manager to confirm"

RISK_FLAGS = {
    "recent_falls":        (Source.DERIVED, "incident type = fall, last 90 days"),
    "hospital_transition": (Source.DERIVED, "hospital or transfer record, last 3 months"),
    "high_risk_meds":      (Source.DERIVED, "active medication in a high-risk class list"),
    "restraint":           (Source.DERIVED, "restrictive practice recorded"),
    "unspent_funds_high":  (Source.DERIVED, "unspent balance above your own threshold"),
    "self_manages":        (Source.DERIVED, "funding management flag"),
    "lives_alone_limited": (Source.CONFIRM, "living situation plus contact pattern"),
    "needs_higher_care":   (Source.CONFIRM, "care manager judgement or pending reassessment"),
    "communication":       (Source.CONFIRM, "cognitive, sensory, disability or language needs"),
}

"Greater than expected" unspent funds has no number in the tool, so the threshold is yours to set and to explain. Write it down. The same goes for "limited contact outside of the provider".

This list does more than satisfy row 12. The people on it are the ones whose records an auditor is most likely to read closely, so it's also a good list for your own file reviews in the months before an audit.

Map each request to its system of record

Last step: for every request, record where the evidence lives and who owns it. In most small providers the answer is spread across a rostering tool, an HR folder, spreadsheets for registers and an accounting package for statements. A short table makes the gaps obvious:

Request System of record Owner Window
Worker list, roster, unfilled shifts Rostering system Rostering lead Latest / 4 weeks
Worker checks, training register HR or worker compliance HR Current / 12 months
Incident register, SIRS notifications Incident system Quality manager 3 months
Complaints register Complaints system Quality manager 12 months
Care and services plans Care management Care partners Current
Agreements, budgets, monthly statements Billing and statements Finance Current
Meeting minutes Shared drive Each meeting's chair Last 4 meetings

If a row has two systems in the owner column, expect a reconciliation problem at audit time.

In Rostery, a few of these joins are built in. The aged care complaints register has a Linked Quality Standard field on each complaint, so the register can be filtered by the standard it's evidence against. Aged care care plans carry a Review due date that turns amber within 30 days and red once it has passed, which maps neatly onto a "Current" rule. Support at Home statements and claims are generated for each participant's plan every month, including months with no services. None of that replaces the mapping exercise; it just means fewer columns of the table point at spreadsheets.

For a plain-language refresher on the standards themselves, the Aged Care Quality Standards glossary entry is a quick read, and our Blogger post on which Aged Care Quality Standards a home care provider actually meets walks through the registration categories. If incidents are your next build, our earlier dev.to post on a SIRS triage workflow for aged care compliance teams covers reportability and deadlines.

A short checklist for your own build

  • Derive the applicable outcome list from registration category and service types, and test the count.
  • Store evidence requests as rows with outcomes, a "various" flag and a window.
  • Run coverage against applicable outcomes only, and treat untagged outcomes as manual checks, not gaps.
  • Map the during-audit records yourself, and label that mapping as yours.
  • Normalise windows into point-in-time, rolling and count-based rules, and report counts next to passes.
  • Build the risk-factor sample list from data, and mark the flags that need human judgement.
  • Give every request one system of record and one owner.

Sources: Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission, Strengthened Quality Standards guidance (outcome pages for Standards 1 to 4 and Outcome 5.1); Strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards page (audit types and ratings); Support at Home provider requirements (Category 4 with care management, Outcome 5.1); Care Delivery Evidence Collection Tool, Categories 4 and 5 (last updated 17 July 2026); Sector performance data, April to June 2026. Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Support at Home Payment Integrity Rolling Review, cycle 1 summary report. Rostery help and feature pages read 11 November 2026.

Written by the Rostery team in Sydney. Rostery makes rostering, care and billing software for NDIS and aged care providers.

title: SQL Challenge: Can You Group Customers by Income Using CASE WHEN?
description:
Here is a practical problem you might face while preparing a customer analysis report.

You have a customers table containing customer IDs, names and annual income.

The business team wants to understand how many customers fall into each income category.

The categories are:

  • Low Income: Below ₹3,00,000
  • Middle Income: ₹3,00,000 to ₹7,00,000
  • High Income: Above ₹7,00,000

How would you create this report using SQL?

customers

customer_id | name | annual_income
101 | Rahul | 250000
102 | Priya | 450000
103 | Amit | 850000
104 | Sneha | 300000
105 | Karan | 650000
106 | Neha | 950000
107 | Rohan | 200000

Your Challenge

Write a query to:

  1. Categorize customers using CASE WHEN.
  2. Count the number of customers in each category.
  3. Display the income category along with the total customer count.
  4. Do not change the original table data.

Think before you scroll!

The SQL Solution (Oracle)

SELECT
CASE
WHEN annual_income < 300000
THEN 'Low Income'
WHEN annual_income <= 700000
THEN 'Middle Income'
ELSE 'High Income'
END AS income_category,
COUNT(*) AS total_customers
FROM customers
GROUP BY
CASE
WHEN annual_income < 300000
THEN 'Low Income'
WHEN annual_income <= 700000
THEN 'Middle Income'
ELSE 'High Income'
END;

Expected Output

income_category | total_customers
Low Income | 2
Middle Income | 3
High Income | 2

Why Does This Work?

CASE WHEN checks the annual income of each customer and assigns an income category.

Customers earning below ₹3,00,000 are placed in Low Income.

Customers earning from ₹3,00,000 to ₹7,00,000 are placed in Middle Income.

All remaining customers are placed in High Income.

GROUP BY combines customers belonging to the same category.

COUNT(*) calculates how many customers belong to each group.

That's it. CASE WHEN and GROUP BY help convert individual customer records into a useful business report.

One Thing to Remember:

The order of conditions in CASE WHEN matters.

Once a condition is satisfied, SQL returns its corresponding result without checking the remaining conditions.

Your Turn

Suppose you want to display the actual customer names along with their income categories instead of just counting customers.

How would you modify this query?

Share your SQL query in the comments!

SQL #SQLChallenge #OracleSQL #DataAnalytics #LearnSQL

title: Put a test message on a Kafka topic without writing a producer first
description:
You wrote a consumer and want to see it handle one message. Writing a throwaway producer app for that is slow. Here are three ways to do it, from fastest to most realistic.

1. One message with kcat

kcat reads from stdin and produces to a topic. -K: tells it the key and value are separated by a colon, and -H adds a header.

echo 'user_1001:{"eventId":"evt_001","userId":"user_1001","status":"ACTIVE"}' \
  | kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -P -K: \
      -H "eventType=USER_CREATED" -H "version=v1"

Two things trip people up:

  • The delimiter splits at its first occurrence. With -K: a key such as user:1001 is cut at the first colon. Pick a delimiter that cannot appear in the key, for example -K'|'.
  • Quote the JSON with single quotes so the shell leaves the double quotes alone.

2. Several messages from a file

Put one key:value pair per line and pass the file with -l:

kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -P -K: -l messages.txt

Messages with the same key go to the same partition, so if your consumer depends on per-key ordering, reuse a key across lines to test it.

3. From Java, when headers and types matter

When the consumer reads headers or you want the same serializer as production, a ProducerRecord is the honest test:

ProducerRecord<String, String> record = new ProducerRecord<>(
    "user.events", "user_1001", objectMapper.writeValueAsString(payload));
record.headers().add("eventType", "USER_CREATED".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
record.headers().add("version", "v1".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
producer.send(record).get();

Header values are bytes. If the consumer decodes them with a different charset than the producer used, the header looks corrupted, so state UTF-8 on both sides.

Check what landed

Read the last message of each partition back, including key and headers:

kcat -b localhost:9092 -t user.events -C -o -1 -e \
  -f 'key=%k headers=%h value=%s\n'

If the key is empty here, the -K delimiter did not match when you produced.

Getting a payload that matches the schema

The slow part is usually not the command but writing JSON that satisfies the schema: every required field, the right types, the nested records. I built a small browser tool for that step. You paste an Avro schema or a JSON Schema, set the topic, key field and headers, and it returns a matching sample payload, the full message, a ProducerRecord snippet and a kcat command:

  • Kafka message generator
  • Avro schema generator if you only have a sample JSON message and need the schema first

The values are fixed placeholders based on field type and name, not random data, and it makes up to 20 messages per run. That is enough to check that a consumer parses the message; it is not a load generator. Everything runs in the browser and the schema is not uploaded.

Summary

Need Use
One message, right now `echo ... \
A batch, or ordering per key {% raw %}kcat -P -K: -l file
Headers and production serializers ProducerRecord in a test
Confirm key, headers and value kcat -C -o -1 -e -f ...

title: LibreFang 2026.11.11 Released
description:
LibreFang 2026.11.11 Released

LibreFang v2026.11.11 is out now — a release focused on reasoning depth, memory reliability, and the kind of production hardening that keeps agents running smoothly at scale.

87 PRs from 5 contributors since v2026.10.16.

What's New

Reasoning Depth Now Tunable Per Message

Set how deep your agent thinks on each turn. The chat UI, CLI, and agent editor all gain reasoning-effort controls that let you pick from the levels your model supports (none, minimal, low, medium, high, xhigh, max), with:

  • Per-message override: Click a level to arm it for the next message only, then it resets.
  • Session pinning: Lock a level for the whole conversation via a new /think command or dashboard toggle.
  • Agent defaults: Set [thinking] reasoning_effort in your agent manifest for all automated turns.

The backend's offered_efforts are mirrored in the UI so you only see what's actually available — no dead choices. Works with streaming and HTTP fallback. (#8616, #8617, #8618)

Memory That Sticks

Two key fixes restore context across compaction and iteration limits:

  • Trimmed messages now folded into summaries: When a session compacts, messages older than the window are no longer dropped — they fold into that session's own summary, so later turns can still reconstruct what happened. Other sessions on the same agent no longer lose their history. (#8736, #8646, #8730)
  • Capped turns record themselves: If your agent hits the iteration limit mid-turn, that attempt is now saved to memory as a failed exchange with a clear [Unfinished — this turn reached the iteration limit] marker, so the next turn knows it happened. (#8688)
  • Memory misses are now hints, not dead ends: When memory_recall finds no match, it surfaces similar keys that do exist in your namespace, so agents can correct typos or try variations. (#8628)

Session Stability and Correctness

Three subtle but high-impact fixes prevent silent data loss:

  • Compaction mirrors are per-session (#8646): The old agent-level canonical summary is now also tracked per session, so multiple conversations on the same agent no longer clobber each other's compressed history.
  • History fold respects turn boundaries (#8653, #8731): A single long agent turn no longer compacts its own tool results mid-loop. The fold now stops at the running turn's start, and the boundary is found by tool ID so it survives session repair and compression.
  • Injections stay out of long-term storage (#8737): Ephemeral context (current time, recalled memory, search results) is no longer persisted when inline compression merges it into adjacent messages, so it doesn't replay forever.

Combined, these mean your agent's memory is accurate, and compacting sessions doesn't accidentally erase history across the workspace.

DeepSeek V4 and MCP OAuth Work Reliably

Two integration suites are now solid:

  • DeepSeek reasoning echoes correctly (#8639, #8652): The runtime now sends full reasoning content on every historical turn with a thinking block (as DeepSeek's API requires), and recognizes DeepSeek's native DSML markup as text so it doesn't leak into the transcript.
  • OAuth discovery follows RFC 9728 (#8670, #8728): MCP servers behind path prefixes, self-hosted gateways, and services with dynamic client registration all work now. Discovery probes authorization-server metadata and handles both header-based and headerless variants.

API and Routing Consistency

Reasoning effort now flows through all dispatch paths identically:

  • Channel, cron, trigger, and agent_send turns now use the routed model's reasoning policy, not a pre-routing downgrade. (#8729)
  • Streaming turns apply agent routing, pinned_model, and tier/cost routing the same way scheduled turns do. (#8591)
  • Session model picks win everywhere via /model override.

Security and Isolation

From a comprehensive workspace audit:

  • /api/sessions and transcripts are now owner-scoped — non-admin roles can no longer read every user's conversations. (#8588)
  • web_fetch cache is per-agent — one agent can't read another's authenticated response. (#8591)
  • MCP credentials never leak in config endpoints or sidecar environment. (#8591)
  • Shell flags in exec allowlists are now validated individually (-lc can't slip through as one token). (#8588)
  • Three critical RustSec advisories closed: lru 0.18.2 (unsound eviction), wasmtime 48.0.8 (Cranelift jump bug on aarch64), rmcp 3.9 (OAuth SSRF, tool schema cache). (#8610, #8722)

Developer Experience Improvements

  • Form lists are now chips in the dashboard: paste a comma or newline-separated list and each value becomes a removable chip. (#8657)
  • Manifest history is readable: The TUI and dashboard now show human labels (Model change, Suspended, Pre-restore snapshot) instead of wire tokens. (#8603, #8604, #8607, #8609)
  • Tab accessibility fixed: The dashboard's tab strips now carry proper aria-controls, aria-labelledby, and keyboard semantics (Arrow/Home/End navigation, roving tabindex). (#8608)
  • Identity file locks don't deadlock in parallel tests anymore. (#8620)
  • Telegram sidecar has a poll deadline (50s) — no more wedged workers after a 502. (#8662)

Under the Hood

  • apply_patch anchoring: Hunks that match multiple locations are now rejected; use @@ <line> scope headers or add context to disambiguate. (#8588)
  • Sidecar SDK MSRV raised to Rust 1.85 to track tokio 1.54. (#8695)
  • Per-agent config overrides now live in agent.toml (not config.toml) — the kernel emits a targeted warning if it finds them in the wrong place. (#5476)
  • Session mode resolution is documented in docs/architecture/session-mode-resolution.md for triggers, cron, and channels. (#8736)

Install / Upgrade 

# Binary
curl -fsSL https://get.librefang.ai | sh

# Rust SDK
cargo add librefang

# JavaScript SDK
npm install @librefang/sdk

# Python SDK
pip install librefang-sdk

  • GitHub Release
  • GitHub
  • Discord
  • Contributing Guide

title: Reading Reddit without an API key: RSS endpoints, a parser, and the limits
description:
Reddit's login wall is now the default path for a lot of readers. I read public threads for research, and I didn't want another account just to open a link. The official API can do the job, but it means OAuth, an app registration, and a token refresh path before the first request.

The public RSS feeds are still there. No key, no OAuth, Atom XML. I built a small Android client around them (105 KB, no server, no analytics). This post is about the feed format, the parsing problems, and the limits that decide what kind of reader you can build.

The endpoints 

Listing:
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/hot.rss?limit=25
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/new.rss?limit=25
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/top.rss?limit=25

Thread:
https://www.reddit.com/r/{subreddit}/comments/{post_id}/.rss?limit=100

{subreddit} is the name without r/. hot, new, and top are the listing sorts. The thread URL returns the post plus the comments Reddit includes in the feed.

A few details that matter:

  • The response is application/atom+xml, not JSON.
  • The feed caps what it returns. The app asks for 25 posts per listing and 100 entries for a thread. The listing is the latest 25; I haven't found a working pagination parameter.
  • Reddit rate-limits these endpoints per IP. Two quick requests to the same subreddit can return HTTP 429. Treat 429 as "back off and retry", not as an empty feed.
  • Send a normal browser User-Agent. A bare Java client UA is more likely to get a 403.

What is inside an entry

A listing entry has the fields you'd expect: title, author name, updated timestamp, a permalink in link rel="alternate", and an HTML content block. The id looks like t3_abc123, which is handy as a stable key.

A thread feed uses the same entry shape. The first entry is the post; the rest are comments. Each comment has an author, a timestamp, and HTML content. There is no score, no depth, and no reliable parent pointer in the RSS payload, so comments render as a flat list.

Parsing it with XmlPullParser

Android already ships a streaming XML parser, so the RSS mode does not need a third-party XML library. The core loop looks like this:

XmlPullParser parser = Xml.newPullParser();
parser.setFeature(XmlPullParser.FEATURE_PROCESS_NAMESPACES, false);
parser.setInput(connection.getInputStream(), "UTF-8");

int event = parser.getEventType();
String title = null, author = null, link = null, updated = null;

while (event != XmlPullParser.END_DOCUMENT) {
    String name = parser.getName();

    if (event == XmlPullParser.START_TAG) {
        switch (name) {
            case "entry":
                title = author = link = updated = null;
                break;
            case "title":
                title = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "name":
                author = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "updated":
                updated = parser.nextText();
                break;
            case "link":
                String rel = parser.getAttributeValue(null, "rel");
                if (rel == null || "alternate".equals(rel)) {
                    link = parser.getAttributeValue(null, "href");
                }
                break;
        }
    } else if (event == XmlPullParser.END_TAG && "entry".equals(name)) {
        emit(title, author, link, updated);
    }

    event = parser.next();
}

The important part is not the switch statement; it is the event loop. nextText() reads the text of the current tag and leaves the parser on its end tag. Emit a row on the entry end tag, and keep the parser streaming so a long thread does not build a DOM in memory.

Two practical notes:

  • Namespaces are not worth the trouble here. Reddit's Atom feed is simple enough that disabling namespace processing keeps getName() returning local names.
  • If you render content, sanitize it first. It is HTML from Reddit, and a WebView will execute whatever is in it.

The limits, and why they shape the app

RSS is read-only and shallow:

  • No score and no comment depth. You get the text, not the ranking.
  • No pagination that I could make work. The listing ends at the latest batch.
  • No voting, posting, or replying.
  • Fields can be missing. Deleted authors and removed comments still show up as entries.
  • A shared server is the wrong architecture. If every user fetches through your proxy, Reddit sees one IP and rate-limits everyone together. The app makes the request from the phone's own IP, one request per user action, with no polling.

That last point is also why a web page cannot just do this in the browser: fetch to reddit.com is blocked by CORS, and Reddit sends X-Frame-Options, so an iframe stays blank. A native client avoids both.

What I shipped

I wrapped the feed into a 105 KB Android app. The RSS mode has a native list for Hot/New/Top and a thread screen; a separate WebView reader handles pages the feeds do not cover. It is free, has no analytics and no background service, and distinguishes 429, 403, and no-connection errors instead of showing a generic failure.

The app is here: https://www.wappkit.com/tools/reddit-reader-android?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=community&utm_campaign=reddit_reader_0_2

Disclosure: I built the app, so that link is mine. There are no affiliate links in this post.

Open question

If you have parsed Reddit's Atom feeds, have you found a pagination parameter that actually works for listings? That is the one limit I have not solved. I would also like to know whether a Play Store listing matters more than extra RSS features for a read-only reader.

title: Go, from zero to a running service · 2. Setup, modules and the shape of a project
description:
Go, from zero to a running service · Chapter 2 of 12 · Languages · new chapter every Tuesday night

By the end of this chapter: Create, build and run a Go project laid out the way the ecosystem expects.

The problem

Emma is a junior backend engineer on a fintech startup that just landed its first B2B client. The client wants a new “transaction‑validation” service that will sit behind the existing Java monolith. The product manager has pushed the deadline to two weeks because the client’s contract starts next month.

Emma, eager to prove herself, decides to write the service in Go because the team’s senior engineer swore it would “just work faster”. She clones a starter repository, adds a single http.Handler that parses JSON, validates a few fields and returns a 200 OK. She runs the binary locally and everything looks fine.

However, when she tries to build the project using the command go build, she gets an error message: go: cannot find main module; see 'go help modules'. She is not sure what this means or how to fix it. The error is costing her time, and the deadline is looming. Emma needs to get her project set up correctly and build a working Go service.

Before you start

To follow along with this chapter, you need to have Go installed on your machine. You can verify this by running the command go version in your terminal. You should see a version number, such as go1.19. You also need to have a code editor or IDE set up. If you have completed the previous chapter, you should have a basic understanding of why Go exists and what it optimises for.

Understanding Go modules

To create a new Go project, we need to understand how Go modules work. Go modules are the package management system for Go. They allow us to manage dependencies and ensure that our project is reproducible. A Go module is a collection of Go packages stored in a directory with a go.mod file. The go.mod file contains the module path, which is the unique identifier for the module, and the dependencies required by the module.

Creating a new Go project

To create a new Go project, we need to create a new directory for our project and navigate to it in our terminal. We can then run the command go mod init to create a new Go module. The go mod init command will prompt us to enter the module path, which should be in the format of github.com/username/repository. Once we have created the module, we can start adding dependencies to our project using the go get command.

Working with dependencies

When working with dependencies in Go, it's essential to understand the concept of versions. Go modules use semantic versioning, which means that each version of a dependency is identified by a unique version number. We can specify the version of a dependency in our go.mod file using the require directive. For example, to require version 1.2.3 of the github.com/gorilla/mux package, we would add the following line to our go.mod file:

require github.com/gorilla/mux v1.2.3

We can also use the go get command to update the version of a dependency. For example, to update the github.com/gorilla/mux package to the latest version, we would run the following command:

go get github.com/gorilla/mux@latest

Build it

Here are the steps to create, build and run a Go project:

  1. Create a new directory for your project: Run the command mkdir transaction-validation to create a new directory for your project.
  2. Navigate to the new directory: Run the command cd transaction-validation to navigate to the new directory.
  3. Create a new Go module: Run the command go mod init transaction-validation to create a new Go module.
  4. Create a new Go file: Run the command touch main.go to create a new Go file.
  5. Add the http.Handler code: Add the following code to the main.go file: 
package main

import (
    "encoding/json"
    "fmt"
    "log"
    "net/http"
)

type Transaction struct {
    ID   string `json:"id"`
    Amount float64 `json:"amount"`
}

func main() {
    http.HandleFunc("/validate", func(w http.ResponseWriter, r *http.Request) {
        var transaction Transaction
        err := json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(&transaction)
        if err != nil {
            http.Error(w, err.Error(), http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        if transaction.Amount < 0 {
            http.Error(w, "Invalid transaction amount", http.StatusBadRequest)
            return
        }
        w.WriteHeader(http.StatusOK)
    })
    log.Fatal(http.ListenAndServe(":8080", nil))
}
  1. Build the project: Run the command go build to build the project. To confirm that the project has been built successfully, you should see a transaction-validation executable file in your project directory.
  2. Run the project: Run the command ./transaction-validation to run the project. To confirm that the project is running successfully, you should be able to access the /validate endpoint using a tool like curl. For example: 
curl -X POST -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"id": "123", "amount": 10.99}' http://localhost:8080/validate

This should return a 200 OK response.

When this breaks

One common issue that can occur when building a Go project is the go: cannot find main module error. This error occurs when the go build command cannot find the go.mod file. To fix this error, make sure that you are in the correct directory and that the go.mod file exists.

Another issue that can occur is the undefined: Transaction error. This error occurs when the Transaction struct is not defined. To fix this error, make sure that the Transaction struct is defined in the main.go file.

What it costs

Using Go modules has several benefits, including reproducibility and dependency management. However, it also has some costs, such as the need to manage the go.mod file and the potential for version conflicts. Additionally, Go modules can make it more difficult to work with local dependencies, as they require a go.mod file to be present in the dependency directory.

In the interview

In an interview, you may be asked to explain how Go modules work and how to create a new Go project. A weak answer might be: "Go modules are a way to manage dependencies, but I'm not really sure how they work." A strong answer would be: "Go modules are a package management system for Go that allows us to manage dependencies and ensure that our project is reproducible. To create a new Go project, we need to create a new directory, navigate to it in our terminal, and run the command go mod init to create a new Go module."

A follow-up question might be: "How do you handle version conflicts in a Go project?" A strong answer would be: "To handle version conflicts in a Go project, we can use the go mod tidy command to remove any unnecessary dependencies and the go mod vendor command to vendor our dependencies. We can also use the go mod verify command to verify that our dependencies are correct."

As a senior engineer, you may be asked more advanced questions, such as: "How do you optimize the performance of a Go project?" or "How do you handle errors in a Go project?" A strong answer would demonstrate a deep understanding of Go and its ecosystem, as well as the ability to apply best practices to real-world problems.

Your tasks

  1. Create a new Go project using the go mod init command. Verify that the project has been created successfully by checking for the presence of a go.mod file.
  2. Add a new dependency to your project using the go get command. Verify that the dependency has been added successfully by checking the go.mod file.
  3. Run the go mod tidy command to remove any unnecessary dependencies. Verify that the command has been run successfully by checking the go.mod file.
  4. Run the go mod vendor command to vendor your dependencies. Verify that the command has been run successfully by checking for the presence of a vendor directory.
  5. Create a new Go file and add a new http.Handler to it. Verify that the handler is working correctly by using a tool like curl to access the endpoint.

Your tasks this week

Do the exercises above before the next chapter. Reading a tutorial and doing
one are different activities and only one of them changes what you can build.

Stuck on any of them? Say so — describe what you tried and what happened:
tell me where you got stuck. I read every one, and the questions
that come back more than twice get answered in the next chapter.

Go, from zero to a running service

Chapter 2 of 12. New chapter every Tuesday night.
Next: Types, structs and methods without inheritance.

recap of everything the series has covered, and the extended guidance:

title: IaaS Explained: A Beginner's Guide Using Amazon EC2 as a Case Study
description:
By Samuel Andong, Cloud Computing student
When I started my cloud computing course, I kept hearing three terms: IaaS, PaaS and SaaS. This article explains the first one, Infrastructure as a Service, in simple language. It then looks at Amazon EC2 as a real case study.
What is IaaS?
Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS) is a cloud model where a provider rents you computing resources over the internet. These resources are virtual servers, storage, and networking. You do not buy or maintain any physical hardware. You create what you need in minutes, and you pay for what you use.
Think of renting an empty building. The owner looks after the land, the walls, the electricity and the security guards. You decide what goes inside, how to arrange it, and who comes in.
IaaS vs PaaS vs SaaS
The main difference is who manages what.
Model
You manage
The provider manages
Example
IaaS
Operating system, runtime, apps, data
Servers, storage, networking, virtualization
Amazon EC2, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
PaaS
Your app and data
Everything below the app, including the OS
Cloudflare Workers, Railway
SaaS
Only your own use of it
The whole application
Gmail, Google Docs
IaaS gives you the most control, but also the most responsibility. If you rent a server, you must install updates, secure it and set it up yourself.
Key characteristics of IaaS
• On-demand: you can create or delete a server in minutes.
• Pay as you go: you are billed for usage, not for owning hardware.
• Scalable: you can add more servers when traffic grows and remove them when it drops.
• Full control: you choose the operating system, software and network rules.
• Global: you can place servers in data centers around the world.
Case study: Amazon EC2
Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) is the IaaS service from Amazon Web Services (AWS). It lets you rent virtual machines, called instances, and it is one of the best-known IaaS products in the world.
The main building blocks
• Instances: the virtual servers. You pick a type based on CPU, memory and cost. Some are small for tests, and others are large for heavy workloads.
• AMI (Amazon Machine Image): a template that holds the operating system and software. You pick an AMI, such as Ubuntu or Windows, when you launch a server.
• EBS (Elastic Block Store): storage disks that attach to your instance, like a hard drive.
• VPC and security groups: your private network and the firewall rules that decide which traffic can reach your server, for example port 80 for web traffic and port 22 for SSH.
• Key pairs: a secure login method, so you connect with a private key file instead of a password.
• Regions and Availability Zones: AWS has data centers in many parts of the world. You choose where your server runs, and you can spread servers across zones for reliability.
How you pay
EC2 offers several pricing options:
• On-Demand: pay per use with no commitment. This is best for beginners and short projects.
• Reserved or savings plans: commit to a period of usage for a lower price.
• Spot instances: use spare capacity at a large discount, with the risk that AWS may take it back.
AWS has offered a free tier for new accounts. Always check the current terms and set a billing alert so you are not surprised by a bill.
Scaling
Auto Scaling can add EC2 instances when traffic rises and remove them when it falls. A load balancer spreads visitors across the servers. This is how a busy website can survive a sudden spike without crashing.
Comparison: Amazon EC2 vs Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI) is another major IaaS provider. It offers the same core idea as EC2, which is virtual servers, storage and networking on demand, but it uses different names for many things.
Feature
Amazon EC2 (AWS)
Oracle Cloud Infrastructure
Virtual server
Instance
Compute instance
Server sizes
Instance types
Shapes
OS templates
AMI
Images
Disk storage
EBS
Block Volume
Private network
VPC
VCN (Virtual Cloud Network)
Firewall rules
Security groups
Security lists and network security groups
Organizing resources
Accounts and tags
Compartments
Server login
Key pair
SSH key pair
Free option
Free tier for new accounts
Always Free resources and a trial credit
The terms differ, but the workflow is almost the same: pick an image, choose a server size, set the network rules, add an SSH key and launch. Once you understand one IaaS provider, learning another is mostly learning its vocabulary. Free offers and limits change often, so check each provider's current terms before you sign up.
Example: hosting a website on EC2
Here is the typical flow for putting a small website online on IaaS:

  1. Create an AWS account and choose a region.
  2. Launch an instance and select an Ubuntu AMI.
  3. Create a key pair and download the private key.
  4. Set the security group to allow SSH (port 22) from your own IP and HTTP (port 80) from anywhere.
  5. Connect with SSH, install a web server such as Nginx, and copy your files to it.
  6. Open the instance's public address in a browser to see the site. Compare this with a PaaS platform. On a platform like Cloudflare, I connected my GitHub repository and the platform published my site. With IaaS, I would have to create the server, install the web server and secure it myself. That is more work, but it gives me full control. Benefits of IaaS • No upfront hardware cost • Fast setup and easy experimentation • Flexible scaling up and down • Full control of the operating system and software • Reliable infrastructure run by experts Challenges of IaaS • More responsibility: you handle patches, security settings and backups. • Cost surprises: a forgotten running server keeps charging you. • Skills needed: you need to understand servers, networking and security. • Vendor lock-in: moving to another provider can take effort. When should you choose IaaS? Choose IaaS when you need full control, custom software, or special network settings. Choose PaaS when you just want to deploy code quickly, and SaaS when you only need a ready-made tool. Conclusion IaaS is the foundation of cloud computing. It gives you virtual servers, storage and networks on demand, with control over everything above the hardware. Amazon EC2 shows how this works in practice: you choose a server, set up the network, install your software and pay for what you use. For a student, IaaS is a great way to learn how real systems run, as long as you secure your servers and watch your costs. References • AWS documentation: What is Amazon EC2? (docs.aws.amazon.com) • AWS Pricing for EC2 (aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing) • NIST definition of cloud computing, Special Publication 800-145

title: Rotating mTLS Certificates Across Clouds Without Dropping Connections
description:
Mutual TLS fails in a particular way during rotation. The new certificate is valid, the old one has not expired yet, and traffic still breaks — because the two sides of a connection stopped trusting each other at different moments. In a single cloud that gap is usually minutes. Across clouds, where each platform has its own certificate authority, its own distribution mechanism, and its own reload behaviour, the gap can stretch to hours if nobody designed for it.

The problem is rarely cryptography. It is sequencing.

Two rotations, not one

Every mTLS rotation is actually two separate changes. First, what a service presents: its leaf certificate and key. Second, what a service trusts: the bundle of issuing roots it will accept from peers.

Those two changes must happen in opposite orders depending on direction, and they cannot safely happen at the same time. If a service starts presenting a certificate from a new authority before its peers trust that authority, peers reject it. If a service stops trusting the old authority before peers have stopped presenting certificates from it, it rejects them.

The safe sequence is always the same: widen trust first, wait until the wider trust bundle has actually reached every workload, then change what workloads present, wait again, and only then narrow trust back down. Skipping the waiting steps is where most rotation incidents come from.

Trust bundles do not propagate instantly, and they do not propagate the same way

Each cloud delivers trust material differently. One platform may push a new bundle when a workload restarts. Another may mount it as a file that a sidecar polls. A third may require a deployment to pick it up at all.

That means "the bundle was updated" is three different statements in a three-cloud estate, each true at a different time. A rotation plan that records a single timestamp for the whole estate is recording something that never happened.

Track propagation per platform, and verify it from the workload's point of view — what roots does this running process accept right now — rather than from the control plane's point of view. Control planes report intent. Workloads enforce reality, and they enforce the old reality until the new material is loaded and the process has actually re-read it. Some servers cache the bundle for the lifetime of a connection listener, so a file update alone changes nothing until a reload or a graceful restart.

Long-lived connections hide the change, then expose it all at once

Existing connections are usually not re-authenticated when certificates rotate. A connection established under the old trust keeps working, which makes early testing look reassuring — and misleading.

The break appears later, all at once, when connections churn: a deployment, a load balancer draining a node, a network blip that forces reconnects. Suddenly many clients reconnect under the new rules at the same moment, and any trust mismatch that was latent becomes an outage. This is also why rotation incidents often appear to be caused by an unrelated deploy hours later.

Plan for that. Rotate during a window where forced reconnects can be tested deliberately, in stages — reconnect a small slice of clients first and watch handshake failures before widening. A handshake failure rate, broken down by presenting authority and trusting side, is the signal that tells you which half of the sequence went wrong.

Short-lived certificates reduce one risk and raise another

Automated issuance with lifetimes measured in hours or days makes a missed rotation less catastrophic, because there is no single annual cliff edge, and it limits how long a compromised key stays useful. It also means issuance becomes a production dependency: if the issuer or the distribution path in one cloud stalls, workloads there start failing authentication as their certificates expire, with very little slack.

If certificates are short-lived, monitor time-to-expiry the way latency is monitored — as a distribution, not an average, and alerted well before the shortest lifetime in the estate. And test the issuer-outage case explicitly: what happens in each cloud when no new certificate can be issued for twice the normal renewal interval?

A rotation sequence that survives contact with three clouds

  1. Inventory every issuing authority in the estate and which workloads present and trust each one. Unknown authorities found in trust bundles are a finding in themselves.
  2. Publish the new authority into trust bundles everywhere, alongside the old one. Verify, from inside running workloads on each platform, that both are accepted.
  3. Force a controlled reconnect for a small slice of traffic and confirm handshakes succeed in both directions.
  4. Start presenting certificates from the new authority, platform by platform, watching handshake failures by authority pair.
  5. Wait until no workload still presents from the old authority — verified from observed handshakes, not from deployment status.
  6. Remove the old authority from trust bundles, again platform by platform, with the same workload-level verification.
  7. Record the measured propagation time for each platform. The next rotation plan should be built from those numbers, not from assumptions.

None of this needs a particular product. It needs the rotation to be treated as a distributed-systems change that happens to involve certificates, with the same staging, observation, and rollback discipline as a schema migration.

Teams that run these estates day to day — including the work described at CloudVerg around VergShield zero-trust controls and VergMesh private connectivity — tend to keep the trust inventory in the same place as the network design, so a new authority or a new cloud cannot be added without both being updated together. However the estate is built, the principle holds: widen trust, prove it arrived, then change what is presented — never the other way round.

title: WCAG Levels A, AA and AAA: What's the Difference?
description:
The short answer
A, AA and AAA are the three conformance levels in the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG). Level A is the minimum. Level AA is the standard most laws and policies require. Level AAA is the highest level.

Each level is a set of specific success criteria, and each higher level includes everything below it.

How the levels fit together
First, we must acknowledge that the levels stack. To claim AA, a page must meet every Level A criterion as well as every Level AA criterion. To claim AAA, it must meet all three sets, this means the website must meet Level A, Level AA and Level AAA.

WCAG 2.2 has 86 active success criteria:

Level A: 31 criteria
Level AA: 24 more (55 total for an AA claim)
Level AAA: 31 more (86 total for an AAA claim)
A few rules decide whether a claim holds up:

It's all or nothing. Missing one AA criterion means the page doesn't conform at AA. There's no "mostly AA."
Whole pages only. You can't claim conformance for part of a page.
Levels are about impact, not difficulty. Level A covers barriers that block some people completely. AA covers barriers that make content hard to use. AAA adds extra support for specific needs.
Level A: the baseline
Level A removes the barriers that lock people out entirely. If a site fails Level A, some people can't use it at all.

Examples of Level A criteria:

Text alternatives (1.1.1). Images that carry meaning have alt text. A screen reader user can't learn what a chart shows without it.
Keyboard (2.1.1). Everything works with a keyboard alone. Someone who can't use a mouse can still open menus and submit forms.
Info and relationships (1.3.1). Headings, lists, tables and form labels are coded, not just styled. Assistive tech can then announce the structure.
Use of color (1.4.1). Color isn't the only way to show meaning. An error field also gets an icon or a message, not just a red border.
Page titled (2.4.2). Each page has a title that says what it is.
Level A alone isn't enough for most real-world users. It's the floor, not the target.

Level AA: the practical target
Level AA is the level nearly every law, policy and contract asks for. It removes barriers that don't fully block people but make content hard or tiring to use.

Examples of Level AA criteria:

Contrast (1.4.3). Regular text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against its background. Large text needs 3:1.
Non-text contrast (1.4.11). Buttons, input borders and focus indicators have at least 3:1 contrast.
Resize text (1.4.4). Text can zoom to 200% without breaking the page.
Reflow (1.4.10). Content fits a 320-pixel-wide screen without scrolling sideways.
Focus visible (2.4.7). Keyboard users can always see where they are on the page.
Captions, live (1.2.4). Live video and audio have captions.
Target size, minimum (2.5.8). Click and tap targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels, or have enough space around them. New in WCAG 2.2.
Accessible authentication, minimum (3.3.8). Logging in doesn't depend on remembering or solving a puzzle unless there's a way around it, like allowing paste or a password manager. New in WCAG 2.2.
AA is achievable for almost any site with good design and development habits. That's why it's the standard.

Level AAA: enhanced support
Level AAA adds the highest level of support for specific needs. The W3C itself doesn't recommend requiring AAA for entire sites. Some content simply can't meet every AAA criterion.

Examples of Level AAA criteria:

Enhanced contrast (1.4.6). Regular text has at least 7:1 contrast. Large text needs 4.5:1.
Sign language (1.2.6). Prerecorded video includes sign language interpretation.
Reading level (3.1.5). When text needs more than a lower-secondary reading level, a simpler version or summary is available.
Unusual words (3.1.3). Jargon and idioms are defined.
No timing (2.2.3). Nothing has a time limit, except live events.
Target size, enhanced (2.5.5). Targets are at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels.
Here's why AAA site-wide isn't realistic. A live auction must have time limits, which fails 2.2.3. A medical research article can't always be rewritten at a lower-secondary reading level without losing meaning.

Still, AAA criteria are worth meeting where you can. Plain language, extra contrast and bigger targets help many people, including people with learning and thinking differences.

What to aim for
Target WCAG 2.2 Level AA across your whole site, then add AAA criteria where they help your audience most.

Fix Level A failures first. They block people completely.
Work through Level AA until every page and process conforms.
Test with automated tools, manual checks, assistive tech and real users.
Publish an accessibility statement that names the WCAG version and level, and lists known gaps honestly.

title: When Is an AI Rewrite Finished?
description:
AI makes it easier to attempt a replacement. The harder question is what the new software still owes the people using the old version.

Imagine rewriting a game engine and getting the same winner in both versions. That looks promising. Then you inspect the match record. The new engine has counted a move supplied by the software as though the AI model chose it. The game still ended, but the experiment changed.

I am exploring a Rust version of eSlams alongside its Python engine. eSlams lets AI models play games so we can investigate their decisions. That gives a rewrite a particular obligation: preserve what a result means. Which moves did the model choose? What could it see? What happened when it failed to return a usable response?

These questions make the appeal of AI-assisted rewrites more interesting to me. A replacement that once looked too expensive may now be worth attempting. We can explore a different language, remove an awkward dependency or reconsider an architecture. But generating the replacement is only part of finding out whether it can take over.

Cloudflare's Vinext offers a useful example. The company described building its initial reimplementation of the Next.js API on Vite in under a week, with one engineer directing AI and about $1,100 in model tokens. It called the release experimental. Seven months later, its account of version 1.0 described the work of making the replacement behave correctly across real applications.

An October security advisory showed how small a consequential difference can look. Two different cached functions could share an entry when they used the same extra cache keys and arguments. In the advisory's example, a public summary route could return data cached by a private receipt route. Vinext 1.2.0 fixed that defect by including the function's source code in the key.

That distinction mattered because the functions had different jobs. A caller could supply the expected arguments, receive a valid response and still get information the route should never have returned. Matching the visible shape of an API had left a gap in its behaviour.

The lesson I take from this is to make the obligations of a rewrite explicit before celebrating its completeness. Some will be documented. Others live in tests, old incidents and the assumptions of whoever calls the software. A particular error may tell another service to retry. The order of two events may determine whether a customer is charged again.

For eSlams, I would want the two engines to encounter the same positions and recorded actions, then compare the state after each move. An identical final score could hide an earlier disagreement. I would also want to know whether they reject the same invalid action and preserve the same information boundaries between players.

The same approach applies elsewhere. Compare a write followed by a read, a request repeated after a timeout, or two customers making otherwise identical requests. Include the stored data and emitted events in the comparison. A response body can look correct while the next request inherits the mistake.

Some differences will be improvements we intended to make. An old bug need not become a permanent feature merely because a comparison found it. But someone needs to decide which behaviour is wanted, understand who depends on it and record that decision. Otherwise, convenient differences can quietly become accepted ones.

Those decisions also affect the release. I would begin with a bounded part of the workload and keep a way back. Running both versions can help, provided the comparison does not send two emails or make two payments. Switching back only works if the old software can still understand the data the new version has written.

I find the possibility of building a better engine exciting. AI gives a small team more room to attempt work it might previously have postponed. That is a meaningful change even before anyone claims a fully autonomous rewrite.

But the finish line has to include the people and programs that depend on the result. They need the replacement to keep working when an input is unusual, a request repeats or a component fails. I would call the rewrite finished when I can explain which promises survived, which changed deliberately and how we checked.
