title: What a "song for dad" form taught me about asking users for input
description:
I build SongUp AI, an AI song maker. People type a few lines about someone, pick a voice and a mood, and get a song back. One of the most common reasons to open it is a gift for a parent, and the "song for dad" flow has taught me more about input design than any dashboard I have built. These are the notes I wish I had before writing the first form.

Adjectives are the wrong question

The first version of the gift form had a box that said, more or less, "Describe him". People answered with adjectives: kind, funny, hard-working, the best. A language model can write a verse from that, and the verse is fine, and it fits every father on earth. Nobody cries at "you were always there for me".

What works is the opposite of a description: small true details. So the prompts now ask for things like:

  • one thing he always says,
  • one thing he fixed, built or drove you to,
  • what you never say to him out loud.

The last one does most of the work. It is also the on-screen hook of the short video we made for the page: "Write what you never say out loud". A question that is slightly uncomfortable to answer gives you the line the whole song hangs on.

The general lesson for any generative product: the quality of the output is capped by how specific the input is, and users do not volunteer specifics unless the form asks for them one at a time.

Names are the hardest field

A gift song has one word that must be right: the name. Text models spell it fine; singing voices do not always pronounce it the way the family does, and "Dad" itself is Papa, Baba, Abba, Appa or Tata depending on the house. We sing in 76 languages, so this comes up daily.

Two things helped. First, treating the name as its own piece of input instead of something buried in a paragraph. Second, a pronunciation hint: a place to write the name the way it sounds. It is a tiny field, and it removed a class of "the song is lovely but that is not his name" messages.

If your product reads user text aloud, in any voice, give names their own handling early. It is cheaper than apologising later.

Long input needs a decision, not a silent cut

People who write to their fathers write a lot. Some paste a full page. A song has a length, so something has to give. Quietly trimming the text is the worst option: the user notices the missing verse, which is always the one that mattered.

Now, when the lyrics run past roughly 1,700 characters, the Create step asks what to do: split it into parts, shorten it, or go ahead anyway. One extra question, asked only when needed, and the choice stays with the person who wrote the words.

Let people hear it before the price matters

The piece of the flow I would defend hardest is the order: you hear the first 30 seconds of your own lyrics, sung, before paying anything. One full song is then $2.99.

For a gift this matters more than usual. The buyer is not judging audio quality in the abstract; they are checking one thing, "does this sound like it is about my dad?" No landing page copy answers that. Thirty seconds of their own words does. It also keeps us honest: if the preview is not good, nobody has paid for it.

What I would tell another builder

  1. Ask for facts, not opinions. "What does he always say?" beats "Describe him".
  2. Find the one field that must be right (for us, the name) and give it its own input and its own check.
  3. When input does not fit, ask; never cut silently.
  4. Put the proof before the price.

None of this is specific to music. It applies to any tool where a model turns a few lines from a person into something that is supposed to feel personal.

If you want to see the flow as a user would, it is here: a song for dad, in your own words.

P.S. The 28-second version of the idea: https://youtube.com/shorts/Fvye5ikx-Ck

title: How to Cut Cloud Costs Without Giving Up Multi-Region Redundancy: A Redundancy Cost Ledger
description:
To cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy, remove spend that does not buy recovery and keep spend that does. The right approach matches each workload tier to the cheapest architecture that still meets its recovery time objective (RTO) and recovery point objective (RPO), then verifies every cut with a failover drill. The redundancy cost ledger in this post itemizes multi-region spend and flags the cuts that quietly remove redundancy.

Disclosure: Control Plane publishes this guide.

TL;DR

  • Where redundancy spend goes. A second region adds compute, database replicas, cross-region data transfer, duplicated networking, duplicated observability ingestion, backup copies, DNS health checks, and capacity reservations. Itemize each one.
  • Spend that buys recovery versus spend that does not. Replicated critical state, failover-ready capacity, and tested routing buy recovery. Full-size idle standby VMs, replicated staging data, and a second region’s telemetry pipeline that nobody reads do not.
  • Tier workloads by criticality. Not every service needs multi-region. Revenue-critical APIs get active-active or hot standby. Internal batch jobs get backup-and-restore.
  • Standby capacity math. Active-active across N regions needs N/(N-1) times peak capacity: 200% for two regions, 150% for three, roughly 133% for four. Adding a third region can lower total provisioned capacity compared with two.
  • Cross-region data transfer. Selective replication and batched sync windows cut a cost that grows with every GB replicated. Replicate only the data you need to recover.
  • Storage and backup copies. Lifecycle policies move cold backups to cheaper tiers, but archive retrieval times must stay within your RTO.
  • Commitments. The discount from commitments that apply across regions, such as AWS Compute Savings Plans, follows a workload when it fails over. These commitments do not reserve capacity, so Tier 1 failover still needs a capacity reservation.
  • Cuts that quietly remove redundancy. Running standby on spot only, region-locked reservations, shrinking standby without load testing, and dropping the second region’s observability all look like savings until a real failure hits.
  • Drills. Follow every cost cut with a failover test. Revert any cut that fails the drill.
  • Where Control Plane fits. A Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC) runs a workload active-active across its locations from one definition, so redundancy runs without idle standby capacity.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy?

Work through the steps in order. Skipping one risks cutting spend that was buying recovery.

1. Inventory the redundancy line items. Pull billing data and tag every resource that exists solely because you have a second region. Record each one in the redundancy cost ledger in the next section.

2. Tier workloads by RTO and RPO. Group services into three or four criticality tiers. A payment API that needs sub-minute RTO and a nightly analytics pipeline that tolerates hours of downtime belong in different tiers. Document the business impact of each tier’s failure so finance and engineering agree on what redundancy is worth paying for.

3. Pick the cheapest pattern per tier. Active-active or hot standby for Tier 1. Warm standby or pilot light for Tier 2. Backup-and-restore for Tier 3. Each step down the ladder keeps less compute running in the second region.

4. Shrink idle standby. If you run warm standby, right-size the standby instances to the minimum that can absorb traffic while new capacity scales out. Do not mirror production sizing one-to-one unless your RTO requires instant full-capacity failover.

5. Cut cross-region transfer and duplicated telemetry. Replicate only the data needed for recovery: transaction logs, user state, encryption keys, container images. Stop replicating intermediate build outputs, CI caches, staging databases, and cache warming data. Consolidate logs and metrics into a single multi-region observability backend instead of running parallel ingestion stacks. How to cut cloud compute costs covers compute spend in more depth.

6. Tier backup storage. Move backup copies older than your shortest recovery window to infrequent-access or cold storage. Keep the most recent backup in a standard tier so retrieval time stays within RTO.

7. Buy commitments that move with failover. AWS Compute Savings Plans, the Azure savings plan for compute, and Google Cloud compute flexible committed use discounts apply across regions. EC2 Instance Savings Plans, EC2 Reserved Instances, Azure reservations, and Google Cloud resource-based committed use discounts are tied to one region. Do not put all commitments into reservations locked to the primary region, because during a failover they go unused and the secondary region runs at on-demand rates. Savings Plans and regional Reserved Instances discount usage without reserving capacity, so Tier 1 failover capacity still needs a capacity reservation.

8. Drill after every cut. Run a failover test within days of any change to redundancy spend. Measure actual RTO, RPO, and throughput under load. If the drill fails, revert the cut.

What does a second region add to the bill?

Line item What drives the cost Lever that cuts it Resilience risk of the lever
Standby or second-region compute Instance hours for VMs or containers sitting idle or at reduced load Right-size standby, use pilot light, or run active-active with autoscaling so standby capacity also serves live traffic Medium: under-provisioned standby may not absorb traffic fast enough during failover
Standby database instances or clusters Per-hour cost of read replicas or hot-standby clusters in the second region Use a cross-region read replica instead of a full standby cluster; promote it on failover Medium: promotion adds about a minute (Aurora Global Database) to several minutes or longer (RDS read replica) of RTO; replication lag sets RPO
Cross-region replication data transfer Volume of data synchronized between regions, billed per GB by every major provider (AWS data transfer pricing, Azure bandwidth pricing, Google Cloud network pricing) Replicate selectively; batch non-urgent sync; compress payloads High if critical data is excluded from replication
Inter-region service-to-service calls Latency-driven retries and egress charges when services in one region call services in another Co-locate tightly coupled services in the same region; use async messaging Low if every region runs a full copy of the co-located services; High if co-location leaves a dependency in one region only
Duplicated load balancers, NAT gateways, and firewalls Per-hour and per-GB charges for networking infrastructure in each region Use one global load balancer or traffic manager in front of regional endpoints; remove NAT gateways in AZs that run no workloads; send Amazon S3 and DynamoDB traffic through gateway VPC endpoints Low if each active AZ keeps its own NAT gateway or a regional NAT gateway is used; Medium if consolidated to one zonal NAT gateway, since that AZ’s loss cuts outbound access for every AZ
Duplicated logs, metrics, and traces ingestion Per-GB ingestion and retention in a second observability stack Centralize observability into one multi-region backend Medium: losing regional telemetry delays diagnosis during a partial failure
Backup and snapshot copies in a second region Storage volume and cross-region copy transfer Lifecycle-tier older backups; replicate only the most recent recovery set Medium: if the latest set is corrupted, for example by ransomware, no older restore point exists in the second region; archive retrieval delays may exceed RTO
Global DNS and health checks Per-query and per-health-check fees for global traffic management Use standard 30-second health checks instead of fast 10-second checks, and drop optional health-check features, where faster detection is not required Low: slower failover detection, which adds to RTO
Capacity reservations for failover On-Demand rates charged for reserved capacity whether or not instances run in it Reserve capacity in the failover region, for example with AWS On-Demand Capacity Reservations, only for Tier 1 workloads; cover the discount with a commitment that applies across regions High if no reservation exists and on-demand capacity is unavailable during a regional event

No prices are listed because rates vary by provider, region, instance family, and negotiated discount. The point of the ledger is to ensure every line item is visible, owned, and justified.

How much extra capacity does multi-region redundancy need?

Active-active deployments must provision enough capacity in each region so that surviving regions can absorb a failed region’s traffic. The arithmetic is straightforward when traffic is evenly distributed.

Regions Capacity per region (share of total peak) Total provisioned capacity (share of peak)
2 100% 200%
3 50% 150%
4 ~33% ~133%

With two regions, each must handle 100 percent of peak load on its own, so you provision 200 percent of peak across both. With three regions, each needs only 50 percent of peak (each serves a third of peak normally and half of peak after one region fails), totaling 150 percent. A third region therefore lowers total provisioned compute compared with two. The saving covers compute only. A third region adds its own networking, observability, and a third copy of replicated data, and the 150 percent figure covers the loss of one region at a time. Active-active versus active-passive cost compares the two cost profiles.

This is arithmetic on peak load that assumes even traffic distribution and no headroom buffer. Real deployments add headroom for traffic spikes and uneven distribution. Warm standby keeps a scaled-down, working copy of production in the standby region. Pilot light keeps data replicated and core infrastructure running, with application compute off or minimal. Both accept a longer RTO because capacity must scale out before it absorbs full traffic. Running active-active across AWS and Azure without idle standby works through the capacity math for two clouds.

Which cost cuts quietly remove redundancy?

Each of these cuts looks safe on a spreadsheet and can remove the recovery capability you are paying for.

Cut Why it looks safe What it breaks Safer alternative
Running standby capacity only on spot or preemptible instances Spot prices are far below on-demand rates Spot capacity can be interrupted when the provider needs it back and is not guaranteed during regional demand spikes, which is exactly when you need failover capacity Mix spot with a baseline of on-demand or reserved instances for Tier 1 workloads
Region-locked reservations in the primary region only Maximizes discount on the region that handles most traffic Reservations become waste when you fail over; standby region runs at on-demand rates Use commitments that apply across regions, such as AWS Compute Savings Plans, the Azure savings plan for compute, or Google Cloud compute flexible committed use discounts, plus capacity reservations in the failover region for Tier 1
Shrinking standby without a load test Billing drops immediately and nobody notices in steady state Standby cannot absorb production traffic during failover; RTO blows past target Load-test the standby at expected failover traffic before shrinking
Replicating data but skipping its encryption keys, secrets, or container images Saves cross-region transfer and secrets management complexity Data is present but unusable; applications cannot decrypt, authenticate, or start Replicate secrets, keys, and images alongside the data they protect
Keeping control dependencies in one region (identity provider, DNS, CI/CD, secrets store) Simplifies operations and reduces cost A regional failure takes out the tooling needed to execute failover Distribute control dependencies or use providers with built-in multi-region resilience
Dropping the second region’s observability entirely Eliminates duplicated ingestion costs You cannot diagnose failures in the standby region during or after failover Centralize observability with a multi-region backend; keep minimal regional collection
Moving standby backups to an archive tier whose retrieval time exceeds the RTO Archive storage is the cheapest tier available S3 Glacier Deep Archive retrieval takes up to 12 hours with Standard retrieval or up to 48 hours with Bulk retrieval; if the latest standard-tier backup is also lost, recovery stalls Keep the most recent backup set in a standard or infrequent-access tier; archive only older copies
Consolidating to fewer availability zones in the surviving region Reduces per-AZ networking and compute costs If the surviving region runs in one AZ, an AZ failure there during a regional failover causes a full outage; with two AZs, it halves surviving capacity Maintain at least two AZs in every region that participates in failover

Which workloads need multi-region redundancy at all?

Not every service justifies the cost of a second region. Matching the redundancy pattern to the workload’s actual business impact is usually the largest cost lever.

Tier Example workloads Pattern Indicative RTO Indicative RPO
Tier 1: Revenue-critical, user-facing Payment processing, authentication, core API Active-active or hot standby Seconds to low minutes Near-zero to seconds
Tier 2: Important but tolerant of brief outage Order management, notification services, dashboards Warm standby or pilot light Minutes to tens of minutes Seconds to minutes
Tier 3: Internal or batch Analytics pipelines, dev/staging environments, batch ETL Backup-and-restore or single region with multi-AZ Hours Hours to a day

Multi-AZ deployments inside a single region protect against the failure of a data center or availability zone. Multi-region adds protection against region-wide failures, which are less frequent and higher impact. For Tier 3 workloads, multi-AZ with regular backups copied to a second region is usually sufficient and far cheaper than running live standby capacity. Cloud disaster recovery RTO and RPO targets covers target setting.

Backup-and-restore is enough when the business can tolerate hours of downtime and the data can be restored from a recent snapshot. If that matches the workload’s actual impact profile, spending on warm standby or active-active is waste.

How do you keep the savings without losing the failover?

Savings erode as infrastructure drifts and new services ship without a redundancy review. Four checks keep both the savings and the failover in place.

Drill on a schedule. Beyond the drill after each cut in step 8, run a failover drill at least quarterly so drift shows up before a real failure. Measure actual RTO, RPO, and throughput against targets.

Measure failover capacity continuously. Track the ratio of standby capacity to expected failover traffic. Alert when standby drops below the minimum needed to absorb a region loss. Autoscaling helps, but autoscaling from zero to full production load takes time that counts against your RTO.

Alert on replication lag. With asynchronous replication, current lag is the data you would lose if the primary failed now. If lag exceeds your RPO target, a failover at that moment would lose more data than the target allows. Alert before lag reaches the target, for example at half of it, so teams can investigate before a failure turns lag into data loss.

Review the ledger quarterly. Reassess every line item in the redundancy cost ledger. New services may have been deployed without replication. Old replication rules may cover data that is no longer critical. Assign ownership of each line item to a team or product so accountability is clear.

How does Control Plane fit?

Control Plane is the unbreakable platform for running production workloads. It runs serverless, standard, stateful, and cron workloads natively on AWS, GCP, Azure, and Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI), VM workloads on locations joined through Control Plane’s Managed Kubernetes, and workloads on Kubernetes clusters you already run or your own machines, including on premises, active-active across regions and clouds.

A GVC is Control Plane’s named set of locations drawn from cloud regions, Kubernetes clusters you register, and your own hardware; a workload deployed to a GVC runs active-active in every location of that GVC from one definition, so redundancy runs without paying for idle standby capacity. Each workload’s canonical endpoint uses health-aware DNS geo-routing to send clients to the nearest location where the workload passes its readiness probes. Location routing options set a priority tier per location and latency offsets. A failover location can sit in a lower tier that receives traffic only when every higher-tier location is unavailable. Per-location overrides can give the workload a smaller replica range there than in the primary, for a warm standby layout on the same GVC.

During the October 20, 2025 AWS us-east-1 outage, Control Plane customers with us-east-1 in their GVC had workloads “active and running in healthy locations within 10 seconds,” with no customer downtime, according to Control Plane’s internal incident telemetry.

Control Plane handles Day 2 operations for you, including autoscaling, built-in observability, and security. Autoscaling sets each location’s replica count between minScale and maxScale, and maxScale caps each location separately, so a GVC spanning three locations at maxScale 5 can run 15 replicas. Capacity AI is Control Plane’s feature that right-sizes a workload’s CPU and memory reservation between a minimum and maximum based on historical usage. Built-in logs and metrics carry a location label, and logs, metrics, and traces from every location are queried in one place, so teams do not need a separate telemetry stack per region and still see each location’s health during a failover. A Cost & Usage view per org and per resource with a projected total, plus a monthly spend alert to billing admins, gives finance and engineering shared visibility into redundancy spend. The billing API breaks cost down by GVC, workload, or location, so each location’s workload and storage cost can be its own line in the redundancy cost ledger.

Control Plane customers typically see 30 to 50 percent lower compute costs compared with running directly on AWS, GCP, or Azure. You pay for the CPU and memory a workload reserves, billed per millicore and per MB, with no contracts or minimums. Egress, storage, observability, dedicated load balancers, and GPUs are billed too.

The 99.999% availability SLA applies to workloads running at least two replicas in at least two locations. Control Plane is PCI DSS Level 1, SOC 2 Type II, HIPAA, and GDPR compliant.

Active-active removes idle standby, but each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic. minScale sets the capacity running at the moment of failover, and maxScale sets what autoscaling can add afterward. Adding a location to a GVC runs every workload there with no change to the workload definition. To move a two-location layout at 200 percent of peak to three locations at 150 percent, add the third location and lower each location’s minScale so it holds half of peak. Databases still set RPO based on replication lag, and that remains true regardless of the platform running the application tier.

FAQ

Short answers on cost, high availability, active-active, spot capacity, multi-AZ, hidden costs, and testing.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up multi-region redundancy?

Remove spend that does not buy recovery, such as idle full-size standby compute, replicated non-critical data, and duplicated telemetry. Keep replicated critical state, obtainable failover capacity, and tested failover paths. Match each workload tier to the cheapest architecture that meets its RTO and RPO, then verify every cut with a failover drill.

How do I cut cloud costs without giving up high availability?

Use multi-AZ inside a region, with autoscaling and health-checked load balancing, for high availability. Reserve multi-region for Tier 1 workloads where regional outages are unacceptable.

How much does multi-region high availability cost compared with a single region?

Two-region active-active provisions about twice peak compute, warm standby adds a partial second copy plus data transfer, and pilot light keeps compute minimal but still pays for replication and storage. Itemize your own mix with the redundancy cost ledger.

Is active-active more expensive than active-passive?

It depends on standby size and region count. Two-region active-active and active-passive with a full-size standby both provision about 200 percent of peak. Active-passive with a scaled-down standby provisions less compute and accepts a longer RTO. Three-region active-active provisions about 150 percent of peak.

Are spot instances safe for a standby region?

Not as the only source of failover capacity for Tier 1 workloads. Providers can reclaim spot capacity, and it is scarcest during regional demand spikes. Use spot for non-critical standby and keep a baseline of on-demand or reserved capacity for critical services.

Does multi-AZ count as redundancy?

Yes, against the failure of a data center or availability zone within a region. It does not protect against region-wide outages. Multi-AZ alone is enough only when the business accepts the risk of a regional outage.

What is the biggest hidden cost of multi-region?

Cross-region data transfer is often the most underestimated cost. Replication traffic, inter-region API calls, and telemetry shipped across regions generate per-GB charges that grow with volume and frequency.

How often should I test failover after cutting costs?

Test within days of any change and run automated, non-destructive failover drills at least quarterly.

How does Control Plane reduce the cost of multi-region redundancy?

Control Plane runs a workload active-active in every location of its Control Plane Global Virtual Cloud (GVC), so redundancy runs without paying for idle standby capacity. Per-location autoscaling, Capacity AI right-sizing, built-in observability, and health-aware DNS geo-routing reduce the scaling, telemetry, and traffic-management tooling each extra region would otherwise duplicate. Each location still needs headroom to absorb a failed location’s traffic.

To size a multi-region layout on Control Plane, talk to the Control Plane team or sign up free.

title: AWS Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations Explained (Beginner Guide)
description:
A simple beginner guide to AWS Global Infrastructure: what Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations are, how they differ, and how to choose between them."
tags: aws, beginners, cloud, tutorial

series: AWS Beginner Journey

When I started learning AWS, one thing confused me before I even launched my first server: Region, Availability Zone, Edge Location. What's the difference?

If you are preparing for the Cloud Practitioner exam or just starting your cloud journey, this is one of the most important concepts to get right. In this article, I explain it in simple words with real examples.

Why Does AWS Have a "Global Infrastructure"?

AWS doesn't run from one giant building. It runs from data centers spread across the world. This is done so that:

  • Your app stays available even if one data center fails
  • Your users get low latency (faster response) from nearby locations
  • You can follow data rules of your country or company
  • You get fault tolerance and disaster recovery options

AWS organizes this global network into three main building blocks: Regions, Availability Zones and Edge Locations.

1. AWS Region

A Region is a separate geographic area in the world where AWS has multiple data centers grouped together.

Each Region has a name and a code. Some examples:

Region Name Code
Asia Pacific (Mumbai) ap-south-1
Asia Pacific (Hyderabad) ap-south-2
US East (N. Virginia) us-east-1
Europe (Ireland) eu-west-1

Key points about Regions:

  • Regions are completely independent of each other
  • Your data stays in the Region you choose unless you move or replicate it yourself
  • Most services are Region-specific. An EC2 instance in Mumbai will not appear when you switch to N. Virginia
  • Pricing can differ from Region to Region
  • Not every service is available in every Region

How to choose a Region

  1. Latency: Choose a Region close to your users. For users in India, Mumbai (ap-south-1) is a natural choice.
  2. Compliance: Some businesses must keep data within a country.
  3. Service availability: New services often launch in a few Regions first.
  4. Cost: Prices vary between Regions.

2. Availability Zone (AZ)

An Availability Zone is one or more separate data centers inside a Region, each with its own power, cooling and networking.

AZs inside a Region are named like this:

  • ap-south-1a
  • ap-south-1b
  • ap-south-1c

Key points about AZs:

  • Every Region has multiple AZs (at least three in most Regions)
  • AZs are physically separated so that a fire, flood or power failure in one does not affect the others
  • AZs in the same Region are connected with high-speed, low-latency private networking
  • Some resources, like subnets and EC2 instances, live in a single AZ

Why AZs matter

If you run your whole application in a single AZ and that AZ has a problem, your app goes down. If you spread it across two or more AZs, your app keeps running.

This is exactly why services like Application Load Balancer, Auto Scaling Group and RDS Multi-AZ are built around AZs. They help you create a highly available architecture.

3. Edge Location

An Edge Location is a site that AWS uses to deliver content closer to users. It is not where you launch your servers. It is where content is cached and served.

Edge Locations are mainly used by:

  • Amazon CloudFront (CDN) to cache websites, images and videos
  • Amazon Route 53 (DNS) to answer DNS queries quickly
  • AWS Global Accelerator to route traffic over the AWS network

Simple example

Imagine your website's origin is an S3 bucket in the US, but your visitors are in India.

  • Without an Edge Location: every request travels all the way to the US and back, so it is slower.
  • With CloudFront: a copy of your content is cached at a nearby Edge Location, so users get it much faster.

Region vs AZ vs Edge Location: Quick Comparison

Feature Region Availability Zone Edge Location
What is it? Geographic area Data center(s) inside a Region Content delivery site
Purpose Host your resources High availability Low-latency delivery
You launch EC2/RDS here? Yes (you choose the Region) Yes (you choose the AZ) No
Example ap-south-1 (Mumbai) ap-south-1a CloudFront cache site

An Easy Real-Life Analogy

Think of AWS like a courier company:

  • Region = a city where the company operates
  • Availability Zone = separate warehouses inside that city. If one warehouse has a power cut, the others keep working
  • Edge Location = small pickup points in different neighborhoods so customers get parcels faster

Other Terms You May Hear

  • Local Zones: extend a Region closer to large cities for ultra-low latency
  • Wavelength Zones: bring AWS services to the edge of 5G networks
  • Outposts: AWS infrastructure installed in your own data center

You don't need these as a beginner, but it's good to know they exist.

Hands-On: See It Yourself in the AWS Console

  1. Log in to the AWS Management Console
  2. Click the Region selector at the top right and switch between Regions
  3. Open EC2 → Launch instance, then under Network settings choose a Subnet. Each subnet shows the AZ it belongs to (for example, ap-south-1a)
  4. Open CloudFront and notice that it is a global service and does not ask you to pick a Region

Try this once and the concept will stay in your mind for good.

Key Takeaways

  • A Region is a geographic area, and Regions are independent of each other
  • An Availability Zone is an isolated data center location inside a Region, and using multiple AZs gives you high availability
  • An Edge Location caches and delivers content closer to users, mainly through CloudFront
  • Choose your Region based on latency, compliance, service availability and cost
  • Design for failure: spread your resources across multiple AZs

Cloud Practitioner Exam Tip

A common exam question: "How can you make your application highly available on AWS?" The answer is usually deploy across multiple Availability Zones. And "Which service uses Edge Locations?" The answer is Amazon CloudFront.

Final Thoughts

Understanding AWS Global Infrastructure is the foundation for everything else you will learn, from EC2 and S3 to VPC and load balancing. Once you know where your resources live and why, designing reliable and fast applications becomes much easier.

I'm sharing what I learn step by step as part of my cloud journey. If this helped you, feel free to like, comment or share your own experience.

Connect with me

  • LinkedIn: Vishal Patil
  • GitHub: VishalPatil-DevOps-AWS
  • Portfolio: vishalpatil-devops-aws.github.io/portfolio

title: CI/CD #01 - I finished my app locally. Now what?
description:
These days, what I see most often is people generating an entire app with AI and stopping the moment it runs on localhost. It works on my machine, and then what? This series covers what happens under the hood when an application has to go to a real server, and how I plan to improve that process step by step.

I’ll start from the most honest place possible: my process is raw today, and I’m going to show you what it looks like.

The context

S.O Manager is a service order management system I’m building with a colleague. He built the Android app in Kotlin, and I built the API with Java and Spring Boot, using PostgreSQL as the database and MinIO for file storage. Everything runs on a VPS that I set up from scratch, with Nginx, a firewall, and a domain.

Today, the system has two access levels: Administrator, who manages the creation and progress of service orders (SOs), and Technician, who sees the SOs assigned to them, fills in the relevant information, and collects the client’s signature and feedback. Everything is automated, removing bottlenecks in order management and in filling out manual spreadsheets.

How I deploy today

When I finish a feature, this is the process:

On my machine

  1. I bump the version in pom.xml to mark which version is going to production, and commit it.
  2. I build the Docker image with Google Jib, tagged with the current version.
  3. I docker push the image to the registry.

On the VPS, via SSH

  1. I run git pull on the repository to update docker-compose.prod.yml.
  2. I run docker pull to download the new image.
  3. I take the application down with docker container kill.
  4. I edit .env to point to the new version and bring everything up with docker compose -f docker-compose.prod.yml --env-file .env.prd up -d.

Compose starts three services together: Postgres, MinIO, and the application. Database migrations run with Flyway when the application starts. And if something breaks, the rollback is to edit .env back to the previous image and bring everything up again.

One note: I don’t build on the VPS. It only pulls a ready-made image, which keeps the server simple and guarantees that what ran on my machine is what goes to production.

Two environments

I just set up a staging subdomain. api.mydomain.com.br is production, with real data, and hml.api.mydomain.com.br is where I’ll validate versions before promoting them.

What hurts

The process works, but it has clear problems:

  • Too many steps, all manual. There are seven steps across two machines, and any slip becomes a bug in production.
  • Downtime. Since I take the container down before bringing the new one up, the API is offline for a few seconds.
  • Manual rollback. Reverting a version requires editing a file on the server.
  • Almost no automated tests, and none run before the deploy. Today, the only barrier between a bug and production is me.
  • I depend on memory. If I forget a step or the order, nobody notices until something goes wrong.

A concrete example: I once hit a conflict with an existing container when bringing up the new version. I thought docker container kill removed the container, but it only stops it. (This deserves its own post.)

What’s next

In the next posts of the series, I’ll evolve this process with GitHub Actions:

  1. A first pipeline that runs the build and tests on every push.
  2. Automatic deploy to the VPS, going through the staging environment first.
  3. How to handle secrets outside the repository.
  4. Rollback and reducing downtime.

The idea isn’t to show a perfect process, but to record the evolution of one that started raw. If you’ve been through this, tell me in the comments: what was the first step you automated?

title: Fintech Cleanup Sweeps: Webhook Queue Rate Limits, Delayed Retries, and a DLQ
description:
The trade-off that settles this is not price per message. It's whether the queue hands you delayed jobs, per-destination rate limiting, and a DLQ you don't have to rebuild in application code — pick the one whose retry semantics you can make idempotent cheaply, because retry amplification, not the invoice, is what gets a periodic cleanup paged at 03:00.

Everything below is that one decision, taken apart.

Cleanup that outlives the HTTP request

The job is unglamorous. A fintech ledger carries card authorization holds that expire on a schedule; once a hold passes its expiry, the money has to be released in the ledger and the merchant has to be told over a webhook so their own reconciliation lines up. US and EU tenants live in separate regions for residency reasons, so it is two sweeps with two queues, not one global one. Every merchant endpoint publishes a limit — 5 requests per second is a normal number — and some of them enforce it with a hard 429 rather than a queue of their own. So the sweep is not "release N rows"; it is "release N rows at a pace someone else controls, exactly once, in two jurisdictions, without a human watching."

Running that inside an HTTP handler is the original sin.

The shape of that failure is always the same: someone wires the sweep to an admin endpoint, the gateway cuts the connection at its 60-second limit, the caller (or the load balancer, or an impatient operator) retries, and now two sweeps walk the same rows. Half the holds get released twice, the merchant gets two webhooks with different payload ids, and their reconciliation opens a ticket that lands back on you. Missed jobs are annoying. Duplicate deliveries are the ones that generate finance-side work, and they are the reason the idempotency question outranks the pricing question in this design.

The trigger is not the reliability boundary either. Scheduled CI triggers are convenient — GitHub's own documentation says scheduled workflows can be delayed during periods of high load, so treat the tick as a hint, not a guarantee. Whatever fires the sweep, the sweep itself has to be safe to run twice, late, or concurrently with its own previous run.

What a rate-limited sweep actually costs

Per-message pricing is the smallest line in this system, and reasoning about it first is how teams end up with a cheap queue and an expensive on-call rotation.

Do the arithmetic on amplification instead. Take 50,000 expired holds in a nightly window, a 2% slice of destinations answering 429, and a worker that retries five times on a fixed one-second backoff with no jitter: that slice turns 1,000 deliveries into 6,000 requests, all aimed at the endpoints that were already asking you to slow down, all in the same second because fixed backoff synchronizes retries. The queue charge for those extra messages is rounding error. The costs that actually show up are the merchant's rate limiter escalating to longer bans, your egress and log volume (per-attempt structured logs are what you need in a postmortem, and they are billed per line), and the engineer who has to decide at 03:00 whether the DLQ contains 400 poison payloads or one broken endpoint.

There is a deployment cost too. A queue with server-side pacing means the limit is a config value you can change without a deploy; a queue without it means the limiter lives in your worker, and every limit change is a code change, a rollout, and a chance to get it wrong under pressure.

Should a rate-limited webhook queue own delayed jobs, retries, and the DLQ?

Compare the candidates on where each mechanism lives, not on the sticker. Caps and defaults move, so I re-read these pages before I commit a design to them.

Option Delayed jobs Pacing per destination Failure landing zone
Amazon SQS (standard) DelaySeconds up to 15 minutes consumer-side; you write the limiter redrive policy to a DLQ after maxReceiveCount
RabbitMQ / CloudAMQP delayed-message-exchange plugin, or TTL plus dead-letter routing consumer-side, via prefetch and your own token bucket dead-letter exchange; quorum queues add a delivery-limit
Google Cloud Tasks scheduleTime up to 30 days out queue-level: max dispatches per second and max concurrent dispatches retry config only — no dead-letter queue, so you record the terminal failure yourself
Upstash QStash delay on publish, HTTP push model per-endpoint controls, no long-lived consumers inspectable DLQ you can re-publish from

Read that table as four different answers to one question: who holds the pacing state. Cloud Tasks puts it in the queue and gives you nothing to catch terminal failures; SQS and RabbitMQ put it in your worker and give you a real landing zone for poison messages. Neither arrangement is wrong. But the one you choose decides how much of the next section you have to build yourself, and that is the real bill.

For a two-region sweep the practical constraint is usually duller than any feature matrix: a queue you can run in both us-east and eu-central with the same worker binary, so the EU deployment isn't a fork of the US one.

Idempotency keys make redelivery boring

At-least-once delivery is the contract every one of these systems actually offers. The design goal is not zero duplicates in flight — it is that a duplicate does nothing the second time.

That starts before the queue. The sweep plans work and hands out keys; it never releases a hold itself.

// sweep.go — the sweep only plans work. Nothing is released in here.
type Hold struct {
    ID        string
    AccountID string
    Region    string // "us" or "eu": separate queues, same binary
    ExpiresAt time.Time
}

// Stable across every redelivery: no attempt counter, no run id, no wall clock.
func idemKey(h Hold) string {
    sum := sha256.Sum256([]byte("hold.released|" + h.ID + "|" + h.ExpiresAt.UTC().Format(time.RFC3339)))
    return hex.EncodeToString(sum[:])
}

func planSweep(ctx context.Context, db *sql.DB, q Queue, now time.Time) (int, error) {
    tx, err := db.BeginTx(ctx, nil)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer tx.Rollback()

    rows, err := tx.QueryContext(ctx, `
        SELECT id, account_id, region, expires_at
          FROM auth_holds
         WHERE state = 'active' AND expires_at < $1
         ORDER BY expires_at
         LIMIT 500
           FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, now)
    if err != nil {
        return 0, err
    }
    defer rows.Close()

    n := 0
    for rows.Next() {
        var h Hold
        if err := rows.Scan(&h.ID, &h.AccountID, &h.Region, &h.ExpiresAt); err != nil {
            return n, err
        }
        // Spread the batch instead of firing 500 messages at one endpoint.
        delay := time.Duration(n/25) * time.Second
        if err := q.Enqueue(ctx, h.Region, Message{Key: idemKey(h), HoldID: h.ID}, delay); err != nil {
            return n, err
        }
        n++
    }
    if err := rows.Err(); err != nil {
        return n, err
    }
    return n, tx.Commit()
}

Enqueue-then-commit is a dual write, and I left it that way on purpose: if the process dies between the last Enqueue and Commit, the next tick re-plans the same holds and the queue receives the same keys again. That's survivable precisely because each key comes from the hold and its expiry rather than from the run. A transactional outbox removes the dual write entirely and is the better shape once the sweep matters enough to justify the extra table — the reason to know both is that the key discipline is what makes either one safe.

The worker side does one attempt and reports one of three outcomes. Retry policy is data, not if statements scattered through delivery code.

// worker.go — one attempt, three outcomes. The queue decides what happens next.
type Outcome int

const (
    Done Outcome = iota
    RetryLater
    DeadLetter
)

func attempt(ctx context.Context, d Delivery, lim *rate.Limiter, secret []byte, hc *http.Client) (Outcome, time.Duration, error) {
    if err := lim.Wait(ctx); err != nil { // one bucket per endpoint, never one global bucket
        return RetryLater, 5 * time.Second, err
    }

    ts := strconv.FormatInt(time.Now().Unix(), 10)
    mac := hmac.New(sha256.New, secret) // HMAC-SHA256, RFC 2104
    mac.Write([]byte(ts))
    mac.Write([]byte("."))
    mac.Write(d.Body)

    req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost, d.Endpoint, bytes.NewReader(d.Body))
    if err != nil {
        return DeadLetter, 0, err // a malformed endpoint will not get better on attempt 4
    }
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", d.Key)
    req.Header.Set("X-Hold-Signature", ts+"."+hex.EncodeToString(mac.Sum(nil)))

    resp, err := hc.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return RetryLater, backoff(d.Attempt), err
    }
    defer resp.Body.Close()
    io.Copy(io.Discard, resp.Body) // drain, so the connection gets reused

    switch {
    case resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests:
        // The receiver's own limiter outranks ours.
        return RetryLater, retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"), backoff(d.Attempt)), nil
    case resp.StatusCode >= 500:
        return RetryLater, backoff(d.Attempt), nil
    case resp.StatusCode >= 400:
        return DeadLetter, 0, fmt.Errorf("rejected: %d", resp.StatusCode)
    default:
        return Done, 0, nil
    }
}

Three details in there carry most of the reliability. backoff must include jitter, or every retry from a batch lands in the same millisecond and re-triggers the limit that caused it. Retry-After is a documented HTTP header and receivers that send it are telling you the exact answer — honouring it is cheaper than guessing. And the Idempotency-Key header only helps if the receiver stores it; when a merchant ignores it, the fallback is that your own release step writes to a ledger table with a unique constraint on the key, so the second delivery is a no-op insert and the webhook is just noise.

Testing this is less work than it sounds. A fake endpoint that returns 429 for the first two calls, then 200, then 500 forever, exercises every branch above in a unit test, and a counter of distinct Idempotency-Key values versus total requests is the single metric worth alerting on. If that ratio drifts above 1.0 in normal operation, your retry policy is louder than your idempotency guarantees.

Where this advice stops working

The catch is scale in the other direction. If the sweep touches a few hundred rows in one region and no external endpoint is rate limiting you, a queue is a second system to operate for no benefit — a cron-triggered job with an advisory lock, a LIMIT clause, and an in-process limiter is honestly fine, and it is less to page on.

Ordering is the other boundary. Standard queues are not suitable when releases for one account must land in order; that pushes you toward FIFO-style grouping or an ordered log, and both cost throughput. If the cleanup grows human approvals, compensation steps, or multi-day waits, a message queue isn't the right tool at all — that's workflow-engine territory, and bolting state machines onto retry policies is how the state machine ends up in your DLQ.

I'm not sure there's a universal answer on where the limiter belongs. Queue-side pacing has fewer moving parts, worker-side pacing gives you finer control per destination and works identically in both regions; your mileage may vary with how many endpoints you deliver to. What doesn't vary is the ordering of the decision: settle idempotency first, then retry policy, then the DLQ, and only then look at what any of it costs per million messages.

Sources

  • Amazon SQS delay queues — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-delay-queues.html
  • Amazon SQS dead-letter queues — https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • RabbitMQ quorum queues: delivery-limit and dead lettering — https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/quorum-queues
  • Google Cloud Tasks queue configuration: rate limits and retry — https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/configuring-queues
  • Upstash QStash documentation — https://upstash.com/docs/qstash
  • RFC 2104: HMAC keyed-hashing for message authentication — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc2104
  • RFC 9110 section 9.2.2: idempotent methods — https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110#section-9.2.2
  • GitHub Actions: events that trigger workflows (schedule) — https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows
  • MDN: Retry-After header — https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Headers/Retry-After

title: We tracked 62 major cloud outages since 2020. Here's what actually takes the cloud down.
description:
We've been tracking 62 major AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and Cloudflare outages since 2020 that have a public write-up. Each one has the provider's own root cause, the region, and how long it lasted.

Once you line them up, a few patterns jump out, and most of them aren't what people expect. Here's the cheat sheet.

The 30-second version

  • The median major outage lasted 6 hours and 8 minutes. Not a blip. A full workday.
  • 55% were caused by a change or a bug. Config pushes and deployments (32%) and software bugs or automation (23%). Fires and floods are the minority.
  • Power and cooling failures are rarer but brutal. 18% of outages, with a median of about 21 hours.
  • 37 of the 57 outages with a known end ran longer than 4 hours. 16 ran longer than 12.
  • Only 7 were fixed within an hour. Plan for "hours," not "minutes."
  • 2025 and 2026 had the most incidents we recorded (16 and 18). Partly more outages, partly more detailed public write-ups.

What actually takes the cloud down

Cause Share of outages Median duration
Configuration or deployment change 32% 5h 21m
Software bug or automation 23% 5h 35m
Power or cooling 18% ~21h
Network 6% 3h 17m
Capacity or overload 6% 9h 22m
Physical damage (fire, water, drones) 5% 27h to months (2 still ongoing)
Other or not stated 5% n/a
DNS 5% 1h 35m

Two things stand out. Most outages start with the provider's own changes or code, and the physical ones (power, cooling, fire) are rare but last the longest, because you can't roll back a flooded room.

Five lessons, and what to do about each

1. "Multi-AZ" won't save you from a regional outage

Plenty of these outages took out a whole region, or a regional control plane that every zone depends on. In Paris, a cooling-water leak flooded a UPS room and started a fire, and shutting down that one building took the region's control plane offline for over a day. When an outage is regional, spreading across zones doesn't help, and the median outage in this data lasted about six hours.

Do this: run critical services in at least two regions, and know which managed services you use are regional (they often are, even when compute is zonal).

2. The scariest outages start with a routine change

Paused gateway OS updates resuming all at once. A cache optimization that reordered DNS records. A release that withdrew about 1,100 customer IP prefixes. None of these were exotic. They were routine changes.

Do this: roll out your own changes the way you wish your provider did: one location at a time, gated on health metrics, with automatic rollback. Your config changes count too, not only code.

3. DNS breaks fast and heals slow

DNS outages had the shortest median (about an hour and a half), but the effects can outlast the fix: resolver caching keeps bad answers alive, and downstream systems take time to catch up. One CloudFront DNS incident caused 1h 35m of errors, while CloudFront configuration propagation stayed delayed for up to 7h 48m.

Do this: know your TTLs, keep them low on records you might need to fail over, and don't assume a fixed DNS problem is fixed for your users.

4. Backups that live in the same region aren't backups

In March 2026, drone strikes in the UAE and near a facility in Bahrain damaged AWS infrastructure. AWS later said some data held only in the affected UAE zones, and data held only in the Bahrain region, cannot be restored. The teams that recovered had copies somewhere else.

Do this: copy backups to another region (or another provider) and actually test a restore from there.

5. Your recovery plan has a human bottleneck

With a median outage of six hours, the question isn't whether you'll get paged. It's whether your system shifts traffic by itself or waits for someone to wake up, read the status page, and run a runbook for the first time.

Do this: automate the failover path and rehearse it. A failover you've never tested is a guess.

The cheat sheet

If this fails... ...this is what saves you
One availability zone Running in 3 zones with load balancer health checks
A whole region Active capacity in a second region and health-checked traffic routing
The provider's control plane Workloads that keep serving without new API calls (no scaling or deploys needed to survive)
DNS Low TTLs, a failover plan, and patience with resolver caches
A bad config push Gradual rollouts with automatic rollback
Your only copy of data Cross-region backups with tested restores
Power or cooling at a facility Not being in only one facility

How the data was built

Most entries come from the provider's official status page or post-incident report; a handful of older or thinly documented incidents rely on press coverage. Every source is linked in the full tracker. It only includes major outages with a public write-up, so smaller incidents are missing, and recent years look busier partly because providers now publish more detail. Durations are the provider's own numbers where they give them.

The full tracker, with every incident, cause, and source link, is here: Cloud Outage Tracker. It's updated every week.

If you want the math on why one bad hour wrecks a 99.99% SLA, I wrote that up separately: Four nines is 4 minutes and 19 seconds. Nobody on your team can respond that fast.

Disclosure: I work at Control Plane, where we build a platform for running apps active-active across regions and clouds. The data above comes from the providers' own reports, plus press coverage for a few older incidents.

What's the worst outage you've lived through, and what would have saved you? Curious what people's real failover setups look like.

title: 7 Things to Check Before Buying a Full-Stack Website Template
description:
Buying a ready-made website can save weeks of development work. However, choosing the wrong template may introduce hidden costs, security problems, and unnecessary maintenance.

Whether you're a freelance developer or launching a startup, here are seven practical things to check before purchasing a full-stack website template.

1. Examine the Technology Stack

Start by identifying which technologies power the application.

A modern full-stack project might use Next.js, React, Node.js, TypeScript, and PostgreSQL. However, not every project needs the same stack.

Choose technologies your team understands and can maintain.

2. Review the Source Code Quality

Clean code matters more than impressive screenshots.

Before buying, look for:

  • A clear project structure
  • Reusable components
  • Environment variable documentation
  • Consistent naming conventions
  • Setup and deployment instructions

If a live demo is available, test its important features rather than judging the design alone.

3. Understand Authentication and Security

Security should never be an afterthought.

Check whether the project uses secure authentication, properly validates inputs, and protects sensitive routes.

For applications handling customer information, examine authorization rules, dependency updates, and data protection measures.

Remember that purchasing source code does not automatically make a website production-ready.

4. Evaluate Database Design

A full-stack application often depends on a database.

Review its schema, relationships, migration files, and configuration instructions.

A well-organized database makes future feature development easier.

Also check whether sample data is included and whether it can be safely removed before deployment.

5. Check Customization Options

Your business requirements may change after launch.

Therefore, select templates with reusable UI components, clear configuration files, and flexible styling.

For example, a React or Next.js template with organized components is often easier to customize than a project containing duplicated code.

However, actual flexibility depends on how the project was built.

6. Read the Licensing Terms

Licensing is an important part of buying website source code.

Before purchasing, clarify whether the license allows:

  • Commercial projects
  • Client work
  • Modifications
  • Multiple deployments
  • Redistribution or resale

Never assume that purchasing a template gives you exclusive ownership of its source code.

7. Test Deployment and Documentation

Finally, review how the application moves from development to production.

Check whether the seller provides environment setup instructions, build commands, required services, and deployment guidance.

If possible, test the project in a staging environment before going live.

Good documentation can reduce troubleshooting time and unnecessary expenses.

Final Thoughts

Full stack website templates can be a useful starting point for developers, agencies, and startups. Nevertheless, the best choice is not always the cheapest or most visually attractive option.

Focus on code quality, security, maintainability, licensing, and deployment requirements.

If you're exploring ready-made web applications or source code for your next project, you can browse SellOnBay, a marketplace for website templates and digital development resources.

Choose carefully, review the documentation, and build on a foundation that suits your project.

title: Why vLLM and SGLang might not be the best option to run AI agents
description:
vLLM and SGLang are great inference engines. If you serve chat or batch jobs, use them. But AI agents are a different workload, and I wanted to see how well these engines handle it. So I measured it.

How an agent talks to the model

A coding agent works in turns:

  1. It sends the whole conversation to the model.
  2. The model answers with a tool call (run a command, edit a file).
  3. The agent runs the tool, appends the result, and sends the whole conversation again.

In the traces I used, a median session has about 60 turns and grows to tens of thousands of tokens. Every turn re-sends everything before it.

To answer a turn, the engine needs the KV cache for the full history. If the cache from the last turn is still in GPU memory, only the new tokens need computing. If it was evicted while the agent was running its tool, the engine computes the whole history again.

What vLLM and SGLang do between turns

Both engines have a prefix cache: blocks from earlier requests stay in memory and get reused if the next prompt starts the same way. But they don't know that a request belongs to an agent that will come back in half a second.

  • vLLM 0.33.0 accepts a session_id on chat requests, but it's only used as metadata for KV cache events. There's no pinning and no time-to-live. When memory runs out, blocks are evicted least recently used first.
  • SGLang 0.5.23 has real sessions (/open_session, /close_session), but its OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint only forwards the session_id, not the session parameters. The mode that keeps a session's KV pinned (--enable-streaming-session) is off by default and needs the /generate API. Eviction is LRU by default, with options like TLRU.

So under load, while one agent waits on its tool, other agents' requests push its history out of memory. When it comes back, the engine pays for that history again.

The test

I wrote a small serving engine in Rust (about 1,700 lines) that keeps each agent's session in GPU memory between turns, shares the common prompt start (system prompt, tool definitions) across sessions, and only admits new sessions when the ones already running still fit. I compared it with vLLM and SGLang:

  • Workload: 24 real coding-agent sessions from the SWE-rebench-OpenHands dataset (791 turns), all running at once.
  • Same conditions for every engine: Qwen3-8B, one NVIDIA L40S, and the same KV cache size (173,200 tokens).
  • Tool time: a fixed wait between turns of 0.5 s, 5 s or 60 s. Measured coding-agent tool calls have a median gap of about 0.42 s, so 0.5 s is the realistic one.
  • Two runs per configuration. I wrote down before each run what result would count as a pass.

Results

Total time for all 24 sessions with a 0.5 s tool wait (lower is better):

Engine Run 1 Run 2 History recomputed First token (median)
vLLM 0.33.0 2264 s 2222 s 55% 28.6 s
SGLang 0.5.23 (LRU) 2013 s 2048 s 51% 35.0 s
SGLang 0.5.23 (TLRU) 2067 s 2024 s 52% 36.3 s
Rust session engine 1506 s 1586 s 8-16% 4.5 s

More than half of all the prompt tokens vLLM and SGLang processed were history they had already computed once and then evicted. Keeping sessions in memory cut that to 8-16% and made the whole run 1.31x faster than SGLang and 1.45x faster than vLLM. The first token came about 5x sooner.

The gain shrinks as tools get slower:

Tool wait vs best baseline vs vLLM
0.5 s 1.31x faster 1.45x faster
5 s 1.13x faster 1.24x faster
60 s about the same about the same

With a 60 s wait, few agents need the GPU at the same time, so there's less memory pressure and every engine does about as well. My engine was also slower to the first token there.

What this doesn't mean

  • vLLM and SGLang aren't slow. Token for token, they're faster than my engine: its decoding is 15-21% slower per token than vLLM. The gain comes only from not recomputing history.
  • The idea isn't new. InferCept, Pensieve and Continuum, among others, already proposed keeping agent KV caches alive across tool calls. What I added is a measurement against the current versions of both engines on real agent traces.
  • It's one setup. One model, one GPU, one load level, fixed tool waits. I didn't test CPU offload (LMCache, SGLang HiCache) or SGLang's streaming sessions, which might close part of the gap.
  • Not everything worked. Three of my pinning policies lost to vLLM with 60 s waits. Pinning sessions for too long blocks memory other agents could use. The paper lists them all.

So should you switch?

Probably not yet. My engine is a research prototype, and the right fix is for vLLM and SGLang to learn about agent sessions. Both projects have open proposals for exactly that: vLLM PR #38514 and RFC #37003, and SGLang RFC #24656.

But if you run many agents on your own GPUs, check how much of your prompt traffic is recomputed history. Both engines can report cached tokens per request (--enable-prompt-tokens-details in vLLM, --enable-cache-report in SGLang). If it's over half, like in my test, you're paying for the same tokens twice.

Code and paper

Everything is open: the engine, the replay client, the raw results and the scripts that produce every number above.

  • Code: https://github.com/Nahuel990/agent-session-engine
  • Paper: When Does Keeping Agent Sessions in GPU Memory Pay Off? A Rust Serving Engine and a Replay Study on Real Agent Traces (in the repo under paper/)

title: Lovable app not deploying or "Publishing failed"? Find the cause, then fix it
description:
Most of the "my Lovable app won't deploy" messages I see come down to one of a handful of causes. Some are inside Lovable (the change was never published, the build failed, a security scan or a workspace policy blocked it). The rest happen when you move the app to Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare and the host is set up for the wrong kind of build.

Here is how I find which one it is, and the fix for each.

The messages you might see

  • Publishing failed
  • Fix security issues to publish
  • Publishing is blocked by workspace policy
  • You don't have permission to publish this project
  • Or no message at all: the deploy on Vercel or Netlify fails, or the live site still shows old changes.

Why it happens

  • The changes were never published. Lovable does not push edits to the live site by itself, and accepting a draft does not publish it. A small dot on the Publish button means there are unpublished changes.
  • The build fails. An error in the code stops the deploy. The Publish button turns into Try to fix, or a Publishing failed banner appears.
  • A security scan blocks it. The Publish dialog runs a quick security scan. Its findings don't block publishing by default, but with Block publishing with critical issues turned on, you get Fix security issues to publish until the critical findings are resolved.
  • A policy or a missing permission blocks it. By default editors and above can publish. On Enterprise workspaces a policy can require approval (Publish requires approval) or block publishing.
  • The outside host is set up for the wrong kind of app. A React and Vite project from Lovable builds static files into dist. A TanStack Start project needs a host that runs a server, and its build fails if nitro is missing from package.json.
  • Build-time values are missing. VITE_SUPABASE_URL and VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY are written into the app when it builds. Set them after the build, or not at all, and the app loads but can't reach its backend.

Find the cause first

  1. Open the Publish dialog and read what it says. Publishing failed, Try to fix, Fix security issues to publish and a policy message each point to a different cause above.
  2. Look for the dot on the Publish button. If it's there, the live site is behind the editor.
  3. Visit the exact published address. Changing the URL subdomain moves the site to a new address, and a new custom domain serves the app only once it shows Live.
  4. On Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare, open the failed deploy's build log and read the first error, not only the last line.
  5. Open package.json in the Code tab. @tanstack/react-start means a TanStack Start app that needs a server; otherwise it's a React and Vite app that builds to static files.

Fix 1: Publish from Lovable, then publish every change

  1. Click Publish (top right, next to Share), check the Website URL and who can see the site, then click Publish. The dialog says Your website is live when the deploy finishes.
  2. For every later change, open the Publish dialog again and click Publish changes.
  3. If a Publishing failed banner appears, use what it offers: Try again for a temporary problem, Try to fix for an error in the app or its configuration, and Ask the assistant to help for a database conflict. Internal errors go to Lovable support.

Fix 2: Clear a build error or a blocked publish

  1. Click Try to fix, or paste the exact error into the chat and ask Lovable to fix only that error.
  2. If the dialog says Fix security issues to publish, open the scan findings and fix the critical ones rather than turning the block off.
  3. For Publish requires approval or Publishing is blocked by workspace policy, ask a workspace admin. For You don't have permission to publish this project, ask for editor access.
  4. If the build keeps failing after each fix, open History, revert to the version marked Published (the last one that went live) and make the change again in smaller steps. Reverting restores code, not database data.

Fix 3: Deploy outside Lovable (Vercel, Netlify, Cloudflare)

  1. Connect the project to GitHub with Git sync, then import that repository on the host.
  2. For a React and Vite app, use the build command npm run build, the output directory dist and Node 22.
  3. If npm ci fails because the repository has only bun.lock, build with Bun, or generate and commit a package-lock.json.
  4. Set the VITE_ values from the project's .env file on the host before the build, and redeploy after any change: they are fixed at build time.
  5. Add the fallback that serves index.html for app routes (a _redirects file on Netlify and Cloudflare, vercel.json on Vercel), and add the new domain to your sign-in provider's allowed redirect URLs.
  6. For a TanStack Start app, use a host that runs a server (Vercel, Netlify and Cloudflare Pages detect it automatically) and check that nitro is in package.json.

These are the settings for the common case:

React + Vite app from Lovable, on Vercel, Netlify or Cloudflare Pages

Build command     npm run build
Output directory  dist
Node version      22
Environment       VITE_SUPABASE_URL
                  VITE_SUPABASE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY
                  VITE_SUPABASE_PROJECT_ID
                  (values from the project's .env file, set before the build)

Check the fix worked

  • The Publish dialog says Your website is live, and the Publish button shows no dot.
  • Open the published address in a private window: your latest change is there.
  • On an outside host, open a deep link directly and refresh it: the page loads instead of a 404.
  • Sign in on the live domain: you come back to the app, not to the preview address or localhost.

Stop it coming back

  • Check the live address after you publish, not only the preview.
  • Ask a workspace admin or owner to turn on Block publishing with critical issues (Workspace settings > Security), so a change with critical findings can't go live unnoticed.
  • Keep the project in GitHub with Git sync, so an outside host builds every push and a failed build shows up at once.

Quick answers

Why does my Lovable app work in the preview but not on the live site? The preview shows the version you're editing; the live site is the snapshot you last published. Click Publish changes to update it, and check you're visiting the exact published address.

Can I deploy a Lovable app to Vercel or Netlify? Yes. Connect it to GitHub with Git sync and import the repository; a React and Vite app builds with npm run build into dist on Node 22. The frontend can move while the app keeps using its Lovable Cloud backend.

Do I need a paid plan to publish? No. Free and Pro projects can publish with public or invite-only access. Connecting a custom domain needs a paid plan.

Sources: Lovable: Publish your Lovable project, Lovable: Deploying and hosting outside Lovable, Lovable: Revert and restore your project with version history.

I keep the full checklist, with related fixes for 404s on refresh and undefined env variables, on our fix page. Once it's live, you can run the free Launch Check on the published address to catch exposed keys and missing security headers.
