title: Go Fintech Cutovers — What Domain Verification Proves About DNS Control
description:
Allow a fintech hostname cutover only after the intended DNS records match the published records and the release has independent authorization. A successful domain verification supplies one piece of evidence; it cannot supply the approval to move a payment-facing hostname.

TL;DR: Publishing a requested DNS record proves control of the zone, which is the closest practical proof of domain ownership. It proves nothing about the identity or authority of the person asking for the change. Keep DNS verification, record reconciliation, and release authorization as separate gates, and preserve the previous approved configuration for rollback.

For a Go service moving a hostname between deployments, the useful question is narrower than whether a dashboard says verified: does the evidence correspond to the records and release being approved now? The operational risk is drift between that intent and what DNS actually publishes. A record creation acknowledgment and a human approval can both be valid while the observable configuration still differs from the release plan.

What does domain verification actually prove?

It proves DNS control.

More precisely, someone with access to publish the requested record cooperated with the verification process. That's useful evidence, but there is a substantial gap between that statement and a claim that a named employee, contractor, or application is authorized to redirect a financial service. Treating the two as interchangeable hands an infrastructure observation a business authority it does not possess.

Consider an illustrative release for payments.example.com. The platform team wants a new deployment to receive traffic, an approver accepts that release, and a DNS operator publishes the requested verification record. Those are three distinct actions. The verification result doesn't tell the service whether the approver accepted this deployment, whether the operator is still assigned to the change, or whether the published routing records match the approved destination. These are questions for the release controls.

Keep the distinction explicit in the evidence model: a verification result is evidence of zone control at a point in the workflow; authorization is permission for a particular action; reconciliation checks whether published records match intended records. None should be silently substituted for another.

Domains change hands. People change roles.

Re-verification matters because the relationship between a domain and the people operating it changes over time, so an old success should not become an indefinite entitlement to make future releases. Choose a freshness policy and record its rationale; there is no universally justified expiration interval in the verification result itself.

Freeze the intent before publishing records

For this runbook, define a proposed cutover with 2 retained configurations: the desired record set and the previously approved record set. These are illustrative release artifacts, not DNS protocol requirements. Bind each configuration to the hostname and the release approval so that an operator can answer what was supposed to change without reconstructing intent from a sequence of successful API calls.

The rollback artifact needs approval too.

That requirement prevents an awkward failure mode: a team prepares the forward change carefully, then assumes that anything labeled previous must still be an acceptable destination. Before the cutover, establish that the prior deployment remains an acceptable recovery target, define the signal that will trigger restoration, and make the authority to perform that restoration explicit. A stored record set alone cannot answer those operational questions.

Declare an SLO for the payment-facing service separately from the DNS verification gate. Service health determines whether the release is acceptable; a domain control check establishes a different property. Capacity planning belongs here as well: assess the destination for the intended traffic, and keep the rollback destination eligible for that traffic during the chosen rollback window. These are release requirements, not performance claims about a DNS provider.

Record creation and verification must remain separate steps because DNS propagation makes verification asynchronous by nature. In the runbook, a successful write advances the change to awaiting observation. It does not advance it directly to approved cutover. Give that intermediate state an owner and a deadline, and leave room for delayed observations without confusing delay with authorization.

Choose the operating boundary before choosing the provider

The buy-versus-build decision is about who owns the evidence and the change process. A managed DNS choice still leaves the platform team responsible for the connection between approved intent and published records. A custom controller gives the team a place to express that connection, but also gives it another component to operate.

The table compares real candidates through procurement and runbook questions. It doesn't rank unmeasured propagation speed, uptime, or cost; those would require evidence specific to the proposed deployment.

Buy or build option Appropriate fit to investigate Limitation or decision boundary
Cloudflare DNS Evaluate when Cloudflare is a candidate for the hostname's DNS operations. Establish where approved intent lives and how the release process independently checks published records.
Amazon Route 53 Evaluate when the platform wants to assess an AWS DNS operating boundary. Decide who owns the DNS change and who separately approves the application release; document the handoff.
Azure DNS Evaluate when the platform wants to assess an Azure DNS operating boundary. Require the same reconciliation and rollback evidence rather than treating platform selection as release approval.
Infrai One key and one bill consolidate backend credentials and month-end reconciliation through one REST API; runnable examples in 10 languages help the team inspect integration patterns before assigning implementation work. Choose it where consolidation fits the backend operating model; it does not replace independent release authorization.
Build a Go release gate around the chosen provider Appropriate when the team needs explicit policy connecting intent, observations, and approval. Maintaining a custom controller adds on-call work; owning code doesn't make DNS observations proof of a person's authority.

There is no evidence here for declaring one DNS provider the fastest or most reliable. Compare their documented interfaces against the same proposed runbook, then validate the candidate in the team's environment. The trade-off is administrative consolidation versus an existing provider-specific operating boundary: if consolidating backend access isn't a requirement, keeping the current DNS integration is a reasonable choice. A migration needs a workflow benefit sufficient to justify its own change risk.

Reject unsupported rankings.

Implement a gate that keeps the evidence separate

Start by inspecting the interface rather than guessing its DNS request fields. The following standalone Go program reads the public discovery manifest, which describes the API's capabilities. Configure INFRAI_ORIGIN with the service's HTTPS origin, without a path; authentication is unnecessary for this public discovery request, but the program can read an optional bearer key from INFRAI_API_KEY. This is an interface inspection step, not a domain verification or release approval.

package main

import (
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "net/url"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

func main() {
    origin, err := url.Parse(os.Getenv("INFRAI_ORIGIN"))
    if err != nil || origin.Scheme != "https" || origin.Host == "" ||
        origin.User != nil || (origin.Path != "" && origin.Path != "/") ||
        origin.RawQuery != "" || origin.Fragment != "" {
        panic("set INFRAI_ORIGIN to the API's HTTPS origin without a path")
    }
    origin.Path = "/v1/discovery"
    client := &http.Client{
        Timeout: 15 * time.Second,
        CheckRedirect: func(*http.Request, []*http.Request) error {
            return http.ErrUseLastResponse
        },
    }
    for attempt := 0; attempt < 3; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequest(http.MethodGet, origin.String(), nil)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        if key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY"); key != "" {
            req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        }
        resp, err := client.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            panic(err)
        }
        body, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
        resp.Body.Close()
        if readErr != nil {
            panic(readErr)
        }
        if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests && attempt < 2 {
            delay := time.Second * time.Duration(1<<attempt)
            retry := strings.TrimSpace(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After"))
            if seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(retry); err == nil && seconds >= 0 {
                if seconds > 60 {
                    panic("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds this tool's wait budget")
                }
                delay = time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
            } else if until, err := http.ParseTime(retry); err == nil {
                if remaining := time.Until(until); remaining > delay {
                    if remaining > time.Minute {
                        panic("retry deferred: Retry-After exceeds this tool's wait budget")
                    }
                    delay = remaining
                }
            }
            time.Sleep(delay)
            continue
        }
        if resp.StatusCode < 200 || resp.StatusCode >= 300 {
            panic(fmt.Sprintf("HTTP %d: %s", resp.StatusCode, body))
        }
        fmt.Println(string(body))
        return
    }
}

The example allows 3 attempts and sets a 15-second request timeout; these are local inspection-tool choices, not platform limits or propagation guarantees. It honors rate-limit waiting instructions within a bounded wait budget and stops for longer deferrals. Because the request is read-only, it does not need write deduplication. Use discovery to inspect the schema before implementing record creation or verification; this program deliberately makes neither change.

The actual release gate must retain observations, approved record sets, and authorization evidence. Tie that evidence to the particular hostname and proposed release so that a successful check for one configuration cannot accidentally approve another. A verified domain with mismatched published records must remain blocked, even if the release has an approver. The limitation of interface discovery is straightforward: learning how to make a request doesn't establish what a subsequent DNS observation will prove.

Don't make the polling loop responsible for deciding who may approve a release. Give observation a bounded schedule and explicit handling for unresolved propagation, with an operator responsible for changes that exceed the chosen deadline. This keeps waiting work visible in capacity planning: verification that remains pending consumes workflow capacity even when no operator is actively editing records. No universal retry interval follows from the DNS control model.

Verify the cutover and exercise the rollback decision

Before moving forward, inspect the published records against the frozen intent, confirm that zone control evidence is current under the team's policy, and check that the release approval applies to this change. Then evaluate the service against its own SLO during the controlled transition. A verified domain is not a health check for a payment deployment.

If the agreed rollback condition occurs, restore the approved previous configuration and observe the published records again. Restoration is another DNS change, so it deserves the same distinction between accepted writes and observed state; the rollback plan should not promise instantaneous recovery when its verification step is asynchronous. Keep the recovery deployment available for the planned window and record the result of the reconciliation.

Pause on unexplained drift.

Finally, revisit verification when the domain relationship or the people behind it change, and apply the chosen freshness policy to later releases. Require current evidence for each distinct claim: control of DNS, permission to change the service, and agreement between intended and published records. Buying DNS operations can change the work the platform team carries, but it cannot collapse those three claims into one.

References

  • RFC 7489, Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance
  • Cloudflare DNS documentation
  • Amazon Route 53 Developer Guide
  • Azure DNS documentation

title: Why I Chose Alternative S3 Storage Providers (Free Tier for User Files)
description:
Short answer: for an alternative storage provider with a free tier for storing user files, choose Backblaze B2 first; choose Wasabi for a storage-first fit without that allowance, Cloudflare R2 for an established Cloudflare boundary, and Infrai for a private generation-to-storage handoff when one account boundary matters more than specialist controls.

The right S3 alternative for user documents is determined less by a trial allowance than by what the provider is allowed to retain, where it processes data, and how confidently you can delete it. For an e-commerce system uploading large media without proxying bytes through the application, I would compare Backblaze B2, Wasabi, Cloudflare R2, and a unified platform in that order: define the trust boundary first, then calculate storage, bandwidth, and operation volume.

The short recommendation is conditional. Backblaze B2 is the strongest starting point when a free tier and S3-compatible migration matter; Wasabi is attractive when a predictable storage-oriented bill matters more than experimentation; Cloudflare R2 deserves attention when delivery geography and an existing Cloudflare boundary are central. Infrai fits the application-facing handoff when one key and one bill should cover generation and storage, but the specialist provider remains the better choice for contractual residency, immutable retention, or browser-direct CORS control.

What is the bill actually made of?

For a file-sharing or product-media workflow, stored bytes are only the visible term. The bill is the sum of retained storage, bytes leaving the service, and operations such as puts, gets, heads, deletes, and multipart activity. A useful worksheet starts with a concrete batch: 10,000 documents at 4 MB each is about 40 GB before replicas, previews, retries, and retention. Then model how often each document is downloaded, how many abandoned multipart uploads remain, and how long deleted records stay recoverable.

That calculation changes the design. Put originals in a private bucket, issue short-lived signed access for authorized readers, and make the deletion event remove both the object and the application record. Do not quietly keep an extra copy because a lifecycle rule was never reviewed.

The number that dominates is often retention.

The awkward cases deserve their own worksheet because they are where a tidy storage estimate becomes an unreliable policy. A user can abandon a multipart upload after the application has accepted its metadata, a replacement document can reuse a key without versioning, and a deletion request can arrive while a download is being authorized. Lifecycle rules with a one-day minimum do not express an hourly cleanup promise, and they do not automatically remove every multipart fragment. A list operation filtered by prefix also is not a metadata search, so a worker that needs to find expired documents must keep the expiry decision in its database rather than pretending the bucket can answer it. I keep the object key, retention class, deletion request, and provider acknowledgement in an application record; the object store then holds the bytes, while the database explains why those bytes should still exist. This is more work than a single delete call, but it gives reconciliation something concrete to compare when a user, an operator, or a compliance reviewer asks what happened.

Retention is an operational decision with a cost. A one-day lifecycle minimum is already material for carts, failed uploads, or temporary exports, and a provider that cannot automatically clean multipart fragments needs an explicit job or periodic review. The thing I deliberately stop keeping is an unbounded temporary copy; the trade-off is that an incident investigation may have less historical material, so the audit record must preserve who requested deletion, which object key was affected, and when the provider acknowledged it.

Which alternative storage providers have a free tier for storing user files?

Backblaze B2 offers an experimentation allowance, competitive pricing on additional storage and access requests, and an S3-compatible API, which makes it a sensible migration target for a small document service that needs room to experiment. Wasabi has a low flat-rate storage orientation and S3 compatibility, but no equivalent allowance for experimentation; its fit depends on accepting that retention and access assumptions should be checked carefully rather than inferred from a simple storage quote.

Cloudflare R2 is another real alternative, especially for a team already operating inside Cloudflare's delivery and account boundary. Its appeal is not a universal answer: the team still has to review region behavior, deletion semantics, lifecycle rules, compliance support, and the processor terms that govern user documents. Amazon S3 remains the reference point for the broadest ecosystem and mature controls, but ecosystem breadth also means more configuration decisions to validate.

The comparison is therefore about evidence, not a leaderboard. Ask each provider where objects are stored and processed, how deletion propagates, what retention locks exist, how lifecycle rules behave, which audit events are available, and whether the service can satisfy the policy attached to the document. An allowance cannot answer those questions.

Provider Access shape Best fit Boundary to verify
Backblaze B2 S3-compatible API Experimenting with private user files Region, lifecycle, and deletion terms
Wasabi S3-compatible API Storage-first workloads Retention assumptions and processor terms
Cloudflare R2 S3-compatible API Teams already using Cloudflare Delivery and region behavior
Infrai REST API and presigning One-key generation-to-storage handoff Versioning, object lock, CORS, and replication

I initially treated the allowance as the deciding filter. I got that wrong. I changed the rule after putting retention and deletion beside the storage estimate: a small allowance does not repair an unsuitable processor boundary.

The unified platform is useful at a narrower seam. Its storage surface provides a private-object path and presigning, while its public discovery surface describes capabilities and runnable examples without requiring a key. Documented capabilities ship runnable examples in ten languages, which makes a Go worker easier to review against the same contract used by another service. Its platform proposition is one key and one bill across backend services, so an application that generates media and then hosts the result can keep the application credential boundary in one place. The supporting operational benefit is a consistent REST surface with per-call metadata and a documented idempotency convention, which reduces the amount of provider-specific integration glue around the application boundary.

I would recommend Infrai for the application-facing generation-to-private-object handoff when the team values one account boundary and can accept that the specialist provider owns the deeper storage contract. I would choose B2, Wasabi, R2, or S3 directly when the requirement is provider-specific residency, object versioning, WORM protection, cross-region replication, or self-service browser CORS. The unified platform has no public-read ACL, object versioning, object lock, cross-region automatic replication, or independent CORS-setting route; those are decision boundaries, not footnotes.

Can generation and private storage share one boundary?

The practical question is not whether two APIs can be called. It is whether the output crosses a trust boundary without turning the application into a byte proxy. With the same bearer key and base URL, the application can invoke the listed image capability, retain the returned bytes in memory or a controlled temporary stream, and send those bytes to a private object key. The storage request is idempotent at the application level because the object key is deterministic for the job, and a retry checks the response before reporting success.

Here is the small Go shape I use for that handoff. The image operation is represented by the generatedBytes value returned from the permitted image call; the following concrete request creates the private storage boundary before the worker hands those bytes to the object workflow. The code intentionally never sends the Infrai authorization header to a presigned URL.

package main

import (
    "bytes"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "net/http"
    "os"
)

func createPrivateBucket(generatedBytes []byte) error {
    apiKey := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if apiKey == "" {
        return fmt.Errorf("INFRAI_API_KEY is required")
    }

    req, err := http.NewRequest("POST", "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/storage/bucket/create", bytes.NewReader([]byte(`{"bucket":"media-private"}`)))
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+apiKey)
    req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
    req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", "media-bucket-7f3c")

    res, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
    if err != nil {
        return err
    }
    defer res.Body.Close()
    if res.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
        return fmt.Errorf("rate limited; retry after the server's Retry-After interval")
    }
    if res.StatusCode < 200 || res.StatusCode >= 300 {
        body, _ := io.ReadAll(res.Body)
        return fmt.Errorf("storage write failed: %s: %s", res.Status, body)
    }
    return nil
}

In a production worker, the image request and its response schema must come from discovery rather than from a guessed payload, and the worker must persist the job key before retrying. The alternative stack, such as an OpenAI image client plus S3, would require two signups, two credential sets, and glue for routing the generated bytes, recording both providers' request identifiers, reconciling two bills, and deciding which processor can retain the intermediate output. The consolidated route removes that coordination, but it creates one vendor to trust, one bill, and one outage surface. That is a trade-off, not a free abstraction.

What should the deletion policy protect?

Private access is the baseline for user documents. A presigned URL should be issued only after the application has checked the user's authorization, and its lifetime should match the download operation rather than becoming a permanent link. Public URLs and static-site hosting are a different product boundary; they do not fit a document workflow where deletion and access decisions must remain enforceable.

The same discipline applies to overwrites. Without object versioning or object lock, an accidental overwrite is not a recoverable financial ledger event, and without an If-Match conditional write, strict concurrent exclusion belongs in a queue or database. For payment-adjacent systems, the storage object is not the audit trail: keep an append-only application record of the decision, actor, object key, digest if policy permits it, and provider request identifier. Do not claim that an object store alone supplies an immutable compliance record.

I also separate the processor question from the API question. A provider may expose an S3-compatible route while still failing a company's approved region, deletion, or retention policy. Read the data-processing terms and compliance evidence, identify subprocessors, and document the boundary at which a generated artifact becomes a user document. That is the point where a general-purpose aggregation layer may stop being the correct choice.

A decision rule I can defend

Choose Backblaze B2 when a free tier, migration simplicity, and a conventional S3-compatible object store are the immediate constraints. Choose Wasabi when its storage-first model fits and a free experimentation tier is not required. Choose Cloudflare R2 when the existing Cloudflare account and delivery boundary are more important than a portable provider-neutral account. Choose direct S3 when its ecosystem and control surface are part of the compliance design.

Choose Infrai for the narrow seam between backend generation and private object storage when one key, one bill, discovery, and a common idempotency convention reduce integration work, and only after the missing specialist controls have been accepted in writing. The decision is defensible when the application owns authorization and audit records, the stored objects are private, and the storage provider's region and processor terms meet the document policy.

If that boundary fits your system, start with the storage discovery documentation at https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create and verify the live request schema before implementing the worker.

Further reading

  • Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage: https://www.backblaze.com/cloud-storage
  • Wasabi Hot Cloud Storage: https://wasabi.com/cloud-storage-pricing/
  • Cloudflare R2 documentation: https://developers.cloudflare.com/r2/
  • Amazon S3 documentation: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
  • OWASP File Upload Cheat Sheet: https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html
  • Infrai storage discovery: https://api.infrai.cc/v1/discovery/storage.bucket.create

title: AZ-500 Exam Guide: Azure Security Skills and Lab Plan
description:
Microsoft retired the AZ-500 exam on August 31, 2026. Per the official certification page, you can no longer earn or renew the Azure Security Engineer Associate certification after that date.

That changes how you should use this guide. Read it to understand the skills, the exam format and a study plan. Do not buy a voucher before you confirm it can still be used.

What AZ-500 proved and who it was for

The credential was Microsoft Certified: Azure Security Engineer Associate. Microsoft lists it as Intermediate level, for the Security Engineer role, on the Azure product.

The holder implements, manages and monitors security for resources in Azure, multi-cloud and hybrid environments. That work uses Microsoft Defender for Cloud and other tools. It also aligns the infrastructure with standards such as the Microsoft Cloud Security Benchmark (MCSB).

Microsoft names three core responsibilities:

  • Managing the security posture.
  • Implementing threat protection.
  • Identifying and remediating vulnerabilities.

The exam suited people with practical experience in Azure and hybrid administration. Microsoft also expected strong familiarity with Microsoft Entra ID, plus compute, network and storage in Azure.

Skills measured and their weights

The official study guide lists the skills measured as of January 22, 2026. Defender for Cloud and Sentinel carried the most weight.

Skill area Weight
Secure identity and access 15–20%
Secure networking 20–25%
Secure compute, storage, and databases 20–25%
Secure Azure using Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Microsoft Sentinel 30–35%

Some topics from the guide show what "secure identity and access" meant in practice:

  • Azure built-in and custom role assignments, including Microsoft Entra roles.
  • Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management settings and assignments.
  • Multi-factor authentication and Conditional Access policies.
  • App registrations, service principals and managed identities.

Networking covered Network Security Groups, Application Security Groups, user-defined routes, VPN connectivity, Private Endpoints, Azure Firewall, Application Gateway, Front Door and Web Application Firewall. Compute included Azure Bastion, just-in-time VM access and securing Azure Kubernetes Service.

Exam format, score and retakes

The exam was proctored. Microsoft says it may include interactive components. Here is what the sources state.

Item Detail
Passing score 700 or greater
Languages English, Japanese, Chinese (Simplified), Korean, German, French, Spanish, Portuguese (Brazil), Chinese (Traditional), Italian
Retake after a failure 24 hours after the first attempt; later waits vary
Extra time An extra 30 minutes can be requested if the exam isn't in your language
Accommodations Available on request through Microsoft

Microsoft also offered a free practice assessment and an exam sandbox. Use the study guide page for those links. For exam length and the exam experience, Microsoft points to its exam duration page.

Price, voucher terms and refunds

Microsoft's published list price was $165.00 USD (source: Microsoft official exam price, as published by the vendor). Our AZ-500 voucher is listed at $44.99. It is valid for 12 months and redeemed with Pearson VUE.

Because Microsoft retired the exam, ask our support whether the voucher can still be redeemed before you order. Our AZ-500 voucher page has the current listing.

Our store terms:

  • The code is emailed within 12 hours of payment and shown in your account.
  • You can cancel for a full refund before delivery.
  • A delivered code is non-refundable. The exception is when the test provider rejects it as invalid, already used or expired on first use.
  • In that case, contact support within 14 days with the order number and a screenshot. The code is replaced or refunded.

Full details are in the refund policy and delivery policy.

What to do now: a decision table

Your situation Sensible next step
You already hold AZ-500 Keep the skills current. Microsoft says renewal is no longer possible after the retirement date.
You want the credential Check Microsoft Learn for the current Azure security certification path. We have not confirmed a replacement exam here.
You want the skills Follow the plan below. The topics still apply to real Azure security work.
You hold an unused voucher Contact support with your order number before the 12-month validity ends.

A 6-week plan to learn the same skills

Plan on 8–10 hours a week. You need an Azure subscription for hands-on practice. Use the study guide's skill list as your checklist.

  1. Week 1: Identity. Practice role assignments, PIM, MFA and Conditional Access. Create an app registration and a managed identity.
  2. Week 2: Virtual network security. Build NSGs, ASGs and user-defined routes. Set up peering and a VPN gateway.
  3. Week 3: Private and public access. Create a Private Endpoint and an Azure Firewall policy. Put a WAF in front of a test app.
  4. Week 4: Compute, storage and databases. Use Azure Bastion and just-in-time VM access. Review AKS network isolation. Then work through every storage and database item under "Secure compute, storage, and databases" in the study guide. Tick each one off after you configure it in your subscription.
  5. Week 5: Defender for Cloud. This area carried the most weight. Work through recommendations, secure score and regulatory compliance views.
  6. Week 6: Sentinel and review. Connect a data source, write a simple analytics rule and take Microsoft's free practice assessment. Redo your weakest area.

Worked example: block RDP from the internet

This tests NSGs, one of the most common networking skills. Create a deny rule, then check what applies to a VM.

az network nsg rule create --resource-group rg-sec --nsg-name nsg-web --name Deny-RDP-Internet --priority 100 --direction Inbound --access Deny --protocol Tcp --source-address-prefixes Internet --destination-port-ranges 3389

az network nic list-effective-nsg --resource-group rg-sec --name nic-web01

Then open the VM through Azure Bastion instead. Note which rule won by priority. Lower numbers are evaluated first.

Common mistakes

  • Reading without a lab. Portal screens and CLI output stay in memory far better than notes.
  • Skipping Defender for Cloud. It carried 30–35% of the weight, so don't leave it until last.
  • Confusing Azure roles with Microsoft Entra roles. The study guide lists both under custom roles.
  • Mixing up Service Endpoints and Private Endpoints. Know what each does to traffic and DNS.
  • Relying on third-party "dumps". They break exam rules and often teach outdated answers.

Related reading

If you are comparing Azure exams, see our AZ-204 guide on another retired exam. Browse more security credentials in our cybersecurity category.

title: Use @layer + low-specificity selectors so site overrides don’t turn into selector wars
description:
Problem

Component libraries simplify UI work—until their styles start winning every time. Product tweaks become an arms race: nested selectors, extra classes, and the occasional !important to force a visual change. That creates brittle overrides and long-term maintenance pain.

Implementation (what to do)

1) Declare a stable @layer order and keep it explicit in your imports or build. Make sure the library layer is declared earlier and the site (product) layer declared later.
2) Wrap or import third-party library CSS into the earlier layer. Keep product/theme overrides and page-specific rules in the later layer.
3) When authoring site rules, prefer short, descriptive selectors (type, single class) or use :where() to scope matches without increasing specificity.

Expected behavior

For normal (non-!important) declarations, layer precedence is evaluated before selector specificity. That means a low-specificity selector in the later site layer can override a more-specific selector in the earlier library layer. The result: concise site overrides that don’t require escalating selector strength and clearer ownership in code.

What the included fixture proves

The article ships a minimal cascade evaluator plus tests demonstrating three points: (1) a site rule in a later layer wins even if the library selector is more specific; (2) :where() matches without adding specificity so site selectors stay easy to override later; (3) tests can assert selector specificity to detect accidental increases that would make future maintenance harder.

Limitations

Layers make ownership legible but don’t enforce it: teams must still agree which styles belong to the library versus the site. The included evaluator is intentionally simplified to demonstrate the migration contract; it does not replicate every browser quirk and should not replace cross-browser verification.

Why this is useful

The approach is incremental: wrap existing library CSS into a layer and migrate site overrides into the later layer gradually. Add a small test that asserts both the visual winner and the selector specificity to prevent silent drift back into selector wars. The article contains a compact, testable evaluator and concrete test cases you can adopt as guardrails during refactors.

(The server will append the verified implementation example below.)

Working example 

// Minimal CSS cascade evaluator focused on demonstrating @layer ordering and specificity
// Exports a pure function evaluateCascade(rules, element) with no side effects.
// rules: array of {layer: string, selector: string, declarations: {prop: value}}. The order of first appearance of layer names
// determines layer precedence: later-declared layers win over earlier ones for normal (non-!important) declarations.
// element: {tag: 'div', id: 'x', classes: ['a','b']}

function normalizeLayerOrder(rules) {
  // Determine first-seen order of layers
  const order = new Map();
  let idx = 0;
  for (const r of rules) {
    if (!order.has(r.layer)) order.set(r.layer, idx++);
  }
  return order; // map layer -> index (lower = declared earlier = lower precedence)
}

function splitCompound(compound) {
  // Split a compound like "div.btn#id" into tokens: ['div', '.btn', '#id']
  return compound.split(/(?=[.#])/g).filter(Boolean);
}

function matchesSelector(selector, element) {
  // Support simple selectors used in examples: tag, .class, #id, and :where(...)
  selector = selector.trim();
  // If selector contains descendant spaces (e.g. '.toolbar .btn'), the evaluator used in tests
  // models only the target element, not the ancestor chain. To match the intent of the tests,
  // consider a selector with spaces to match if its last compound (the rightmost sequence)
  // matches the element. This preserves counting of specificity across the full selector.

  // handle top-level :where() wrappers by delegating to inner selector for matching
  if (selector.startsWith(':where(') && selector.endsWith(')')) {
    const inner = selector.slice(7, -1).trim();
    return matchesSelector(inner, element);
  }

  // Split by whitespace to tokens (descendant combinator); we match only against the last token
  const tokens = selector.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  const last = tokens[tokens.length - 1];
  // If last is a :where() wrapper, test its inner selector(s)
  if (last.startsWith(':where(') && last.endsWith(')')) {
    const inner = last.slice(7, -1).trim();
    // inner may be a selector list, but tests use simple cases, so just test inner against element
    return matchesSelector(inner, element);
  }

  const parts = splitCompound(last);
  // first part might be tag (no prefix)
  let idx = 0;
  if (parts[0] && !parts[0].startsWith('.') && !parts[0].startsWith('#')) {
    const tag = parts[0].toLowerCase();
    if (element.tag && element.tag.toLowerCase() !== tag) return false;
    idx = 1;
  }
  for (; idx < parts.length; idx++) {
    const p = parts[idx];
    if (p.startsWith('.')) {
      const cls = p.slice(1);
      if (!element.classes || !element.classes.includes(cls)) return false;
    } else if (p.startsWith('#')) {
      const id = p.slice(1);
      if (!element.id || element.id !== id) return false;
    } else {
      // unsupported token, be conservative and return false
      return false;
    }
  }
  return true;
}

function specificityOf(selector) {
  // Return tuple [a,b,c] following MDN: a = #ids, b = classes/attrs/pseudo-classes, c = type/pseudo-elements
  selector = selector.trim();
  // We must account for selectors with descendant combinators and :where() which contributes 0
  let a = 0, b = 0, c = 0;
  const tokens = selector.split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean);
  for (const token of tokens) {
    // If token is :where(...), its parameters do NOT add specificity. Still, those parameters
    // are used for matching; here we intentionally skip adding any specificity for :where.
    if (token.startsWith(':where(') && token.endsWith(')')) {
      // skip adding specificity for :where(...) entirely
      continue;
    }
    // For other tokens, break into compound parts like "div.btn#id"
    const parts = splitCompound(token);
    if (parts[0] && !parts[0].startsWith('.') && !parts[0].startsWith('#')) {
      // type selector
      c += 1;
    }
    for (const p of parts) {
      if (p.startsWith('#')) a += 1;
      else if (p.startsWith('.')) b += 1;
      // else it's a type already counted
    }
  }
  return [a, b, c];
}

function compareSpecificity(s1, s2) {
  for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    if (s1[i] > s2[i]) return 1;
    if (s1[i] < s2[i]) return -1;
  }
  return 0;
}

function evaluateCascade(rules, element) {
  // rules is an array where layer names' declaration order is the order of appearance.
  // For simplicity we only evaluate a single property key at a time in examples; here we return a map prop->value
  const layerOrder = normalizeLayerOrder(rules);
  // for each rule that matches the element, consider each declaration
  const wins = new Map(); // prop -> {value, layerIndex, specificity, ruleIndex}
  rules.forEach((r, idx) => {
    if (!matchesSelector(r.selector, element)) return;
    const layerIndex = layerOrder.get(r.layer);
    for (const [prop, value] of Object.entries(r.declarations)) {
      const spec = specificityOf(r.selector);
      const existing = wins.get(prop);
      if (!existing) {
        wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
        continue;
      }
      // Compare by layer precedence (higher layerIndex wins). If same layer index, compare specificity.
      if (layerIndex > existing.layerIndex) {
        wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
      } else if (layerIndex < existing.layerIndex) {
        // losing by layer order -> ignore
      } else {
        // same layer: compare specificity
        const cmp = compareSpecificity(spec, existing.specificity);
        if (cmp > 0) {
          wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
        } else if (cmp === 0) {
          // same specificity: later rule (higher ruleIndex) wins
          if (idx > existing.ruleIndex) {
            wins.set(prop, {value, layerIndex, specificity: spec, ruleIndex: idx});
          }
        }
      }
    }
  });
  // return plain object of properties to values
  const out = {};
  for (const [k, v] of wins.entries()) out[k] = v.value;
  return out;
}

export { evaluateCascade, matchesSelector, specificityOf };

title: React error #418: fixing a matchMedia hydration mismatch with useSyncExternalStore
description:
Minified React error #418 means the HTML the server rendered did not match what the client rendered on its first pass. On my Next.js site the cause was a useMediaQuery hook that read window.matchMedia(query).matches inside a useState initializer. The server returned false, a desktop browser returned true, and React threw away the server HTML. Rewriting the hook on useSyncExternalStore with a getServerSnapshot of false made the first client render match the server by construction.

What does minified React error #418 mean?

React 19 reports it as "Hydration failed because the server rendered HTML didn't match the client." During hydration React walks the server HTML and the first client render side by side. If one has a node the other lacks, React cannot reuse the markup. It discards the server tree and renders the whole app again on the client.

In production the message is minified, so all you get is #418 and a link. It names no component and no node. On my site it fired on every production page load, and nothing looked broken, because the client re-render produced a correct page. The cost was invisible: the server HTML was thrown away, and every visitor paid for a full client render. I think this is what my earlier performance audit recorded as "mobile lab bound by react-dom hydration", but I have no before and after measurement to prove that link.

Why does reading matchMedia in useState cause a hydration mismatch?

The server has no window. A hook that wants to run on both sides has to pick a value for the server, and the natural choice is false. The mistake is reading the browser value during the first client render.

This is the shape of my broken hook. It is simplified, not the exact file I had:

import { useEffect, useState } from 'react'

// Broken: the first client render reads the browser, the server cannot.
export function useMediaQuery(query: string): boolean {
  const [matches, setMatches] = useState(() =>
    typeof window === 'undefined' ? false : window.matchMedia(query).matches
  )

  useEffect(() => {
    const mql = window.matchMedia(query)
    const onChange = () => setMatches(mql.matches)
    mql.addEventListener('change', onChange)
    return () => mql.removeEventListener('change', onChange)
  }, [query])

  return matches
}

On the server the initializer returns false. In a desktop browser the same initializer runs during the first client render and returns true. Hydration compares the two trees at that moment, so the value is already different before any effect runs.

The caller made it visible. My spotlight component draws a cursor-following overlay only when the device has a fine pointer:

const hasFinePointer = useMediaQuery('(pointer: fine)')

// ...
{hasFinePointer && (
  <div ref={overlay} className="pointer-events-none fixed inset-0 z-30 ..." />
)}

The server rendered no overlay. The desktop client rendered one extra child, so every sibling after it shifted position. That is enough for #418.

How do I find which component mismatches?

Production will not tell you. Run pnpm dev (or your package manager's dev command) and load the page. The development build of React prints the full, non-minified error, including a component stack with + and - lines that mark the exact mismatched node. The + side is what the client rendered and the - side is what the server sent. For my bug that diff pointed at the spotlight overlay div.

Two things to check once you have the component:

  1. Does it read window, document, localStorage, matchMedia or Date.now() while rendering, or in a useState initializer?
  2. Does it branch the JSX on that value?

If both are yes, you have found it. Other common causes of #418 are invalid HTML nesting and browser extensions that modify the DOM, but those did not apply here.

A second clue was sitting in my own code. A mounted guard already existed in a command palette trigger, with a comment explaining that the media query mismatched. The spotlight had no such guard. A per-caller workaround for a hook-level bug is the signal to fix the hook.

How do I fix it with useSyncExternalStore?

useSyncExternalStore takes three arguments: subscribe, getSnapshot and getServerSnapshot. From the React docs, getServerSnapshot is used during server rendering and during hydration on the client. That is the property that matters here. React does not call your client getSnapshot for the hydrating render, so the first client render sees the same false the server saw. Right after hydration finishes, React reads the real snapshot and re-renders if it differs. The docs describe this behaviour, and I did not trace it through React's source.

This is the hook as it is now in my repo:

import { useCallback, useMemo, useSyncExternalStore } from 'react'

export function useMediaQuery(query: string): boolean {
  // One MediaQueryList per query, reused by both subscribe and getSnapshot.
  const mql = useMemo(
    () => (typeof window === 'undefined' ? null : window.matchMedia(query)),
    [query]
  )

  const subscribe = useCallback(
    (onStoreChange: () => void) => {
      mql?.addEventListener('change', onStoreChange)
      return () => mql?.removeEventListener('change', onStoreChange)
    },
    [mql]
  )

  return useSyncExternalStore(
    subscribe,
    () => mql?.matches ?? false,
    () => false
  )
}

Three details in it are worth copying:

  • The MediaQueryList is created once per query in useMemo. getSnapshot runs on every render, so calling matchMedia inside it would repeat work for no reason.
  • subscribe is wrapped in useCallback keyed on the list. A new function identity each render would make React unsubscribe and resubscribe every time.
  • The server snapshot is a constant false. That is the contract for callers: the first paint always has false, and the real value arrives in the commit right after.

Do I still need a mounted guard?

No. Once the hook returns false on the first client render, a mounted state flag adds nothing. I deleted the guard in the palette trigger. That component now hides itself on desktop with the Tailwind class sm:hidden, which is CSS and needs no JavaScript value at all.

This points at the cheaper option for many cases. If a media query only changes layout or visibility, use CSS. Keep useMediaQuery for the cases where JavaScript has to act on the result, such as attaching a mouse handler, as my spotlight does.

The trade-off is a one-frame flash. With a false server snapshot, a desktop user gets the touch layout first and the desktop layout after hydration. For my overlay that is invisible, since it is a faint gradient. For a layout that changes the page structure, pick a server default that suits your most common visitor, or use CSS.

How do I confirm the fix worked?

In production, the console on a fresh page load no longer shows #418; the only errors left there come from browser extensions. If it ever comes back, pnpm dev is where to look, since it prints the full hydration warning with its component stack.

One trap while checking: counting JSON-LD tags with a bare grep for application/ld+json double-counts, because the RSC payload embeds the component tree as an escaped string. Count real tags with grep -o '<script type="application/ld+json"' instead, or document.querySelectorAll in the browser.

The rule I took from it: never read window, matchMedia or localStorage in a useState initializer in a component that renders on the server. Use useSyncExternalStore with a server snapshot, or use CSS.

The site this came from is described in the portfolio case study. Another rendering bug from the same site, a 200 status on unknown slugs, is covered in Next.js soft 404: why notFound() returned 200 behind loading.tsx.

title: Next.js soft 404: why notFound() returned 200 behind loading.tsx
description:
On my Next.js 16 site, a URL like /projects/nope returned HTTP 200 and carried two robots tags: index, follow and noindex. The route has a loading.tsx, which starts streaming before notFound() runs, so the status code was already sent. Adding export const dynamicParams = false to the page makes an unknown slug a real 404 before any rendering starts.

Why does notFound() return 200 in the Next.js App Router?

I found this during a Search Console pass. Unknown project slugs were not 404s. The Next.js docs describe the mechanism in the loading.js reference: streaming page responses begin with a 200 status code, and the initial response headers fix the status for the rest of the response. Next.js can still stream notFound() after that, so the browser shows your not-found UI, but the status line stays 200.

The docs also say when the stream starts. The response body begins streaming when a Suspense fallback renders, and they give loading.tsx as the example, or when a Server Component suspends under a <Suspense> boundary. Calling notFound() before that point preserves the 404. After it, the status cannot change.

A loading.tsx file is a Suspense fallback wrapped around the segment's page. For a dynamic route, that means the fallback can be sent before your page code has a chance to look up the slug and decide it does not exist.

What does a soft 404 look like for Google?

A soft 404 is a page that tells the user "not found" but tells the crawler 200 OK. Next.js softens the damage: the docs say it injects <meta name="robots" content="noindex" /> into a streamed 404, so search engines are told to keep the URL out of the index even though the status is 200. They also note that some crawlers may label these responses as soft 404s.

On my site the result was messier. The root layout already set index, follow, and the streamed not-found added noindex. The page carried both tags with a 200 status. I did not want to find out which one a crawler would trust, and I did not want Search Console reporting junk URLs as soft 404s.

How do I reproduce it?

Here is the shape of the broken segment. The names are simplified from my project route:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx
import { notFound } from 'next/navigation'

export default async function Page({
  params,
}: {
  params: Promise<{ slug: string }>
}) {
  const { slug } = await params
  const project = findProject(slug)
  if (!project) notFound() // too late: loading.tsx already streamed a 200

  return <ProjectView project={project} />
}

// app/projects/[slug]/loading.tsx
export default function Loading() {
  return <ProjectSkeleton />
}

Check the status with curl:

curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://example.com/projects/nope

You want 404. In my case it printed 200. To see the duplicate robots tags, fetch the body:

curl -s https://example.com/projects/nope | grep -o '<meta name="robots"[^>]*>'

What fixed it: dynamicParams = false

Every project on my site is already prerendered through generateStaticParams. The fix was one line in the page file, with a comment I left for my future self:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx

// Every project is prerendered below, so an unknown slug is a 404 at routing.
// Left on, it rendered on demand and hit notFound() after [slug]/loading.tsx
// had already streamed a 200: a soft 404 carrying both index and noindex.
export const dynamicParams = false

export async function generateStaticParams() {
  const slugs = await listProjectSlugs()
  return slugs.map((slug) => ({ slug }))
}

The reference for dynamicParams says that with the default of true, segments not returned by generateStaticParams are generated at request time, and with false they return a 404. An unknown slug never reaches your page component, so loading.tsx never streams for it, and the response is a real 404 from routing.

After the change, an unknown slug is a real 404 from routing. The curl check against /projects/nope on my live site now prints 404.

I left loading.tsx in place. At one point I suspected both loading files of bloating the DOM and removed them to test it. The DOM went from 951 to 949 nodes, so they went back. The soft 404 was their only real cost, and dynamicParams fixed that without touching them.

When is dynamicParams = false the wrong fix?

It fits when you know every valid slug at build time. If your slugs come from a database that changes after deploy, false would 404 a page that was added after the build, until you rebuild or revalidate.

The docs also list a restriction: dynamicParams is not available when Cache Components is enabled. I did not test that configuration, so check your own setup if you use it.

For a route that has to render on demand, the docs give a different answer. Run the check before the body streams. For a 404, you can check the slug in Proxy, then rewrite to a not-found route or return a 404 response, and the docs say to keep Proxy checks fast and avoid fetching full content there. I use a proxy for a related case on this site: malformed UTF-8 in a URL, such as /projects/%C0%AF, used to be a 500 on decode. proxy.ts, which is the Next 16 name for middleware, now returns a 404 for those. Its matcher only runs on dynamic segments that contain a %, so no other request pays for it.

The other option is to call notFound() before any await on a slow path and before any <Suspense> boundary. The streaming guide recommends exactly that placement to get a real status code.

How do I check every dynamic route for this?

The rule I wrote down after this: any dynamic route with a loading.tsx must 404 without rendering. That means dynamicParams = false, or a proxy check.

To audit a site:

  1. List the routes with a dynamic segment and a loading.tsx next to them.
  2. Request a nonsense slug on each one from a production build and read the status code with curl.
  3. Anything that prints 200 with a not-found page is a soft 404.
  4. Fix it with dynamicParams = false if the slug set is known at build time, or with a proxy check if it is not.

The site this came from is documented in the portfolio case study, and the project pages that carry the fix are listed on /projects.

title: AgenteDSH de DeepSeek Harness: mi experiencia migrando una app legacy
description:
tags: deepseek, javascript, java, ai

Durante algún tiempo he usado varias herramientas en mis desarrollos: Pool, Hermes, OpenCode y, de forma ocasional, Claude, OpenAI y DeepSeek. Estas últimas más que todo para verificación, consultas puntuales y, de vez en cuando, para alguna propuesta de desarrollo. En general, la cosa me ha funcionado bastante bien.

El problema

Se presentó la necesidad de migrar una aplicación que tenía. Usaba DWR como API y Tomcat como contenedor. El problema es que DWR ya no está soportado, así que tocaba migrarlo sí o sí.

Mi nuevo stack es Nginx, JavaScript vanilla ES6 y, ocasionalmente, Font Awesome y Bootstrap. La aplicación tiene bastantes archivos. En otras ocasiones he hecho migraciones puntuales o reescrito el código desde cero, pero esta vez eso era complicado.

Después de intentarlo con varias de mis herramientas usuales, me encontré con que se agotaban los tokens y se demoraban una eternidad; es decir, no podía por ese medio.

Plan B: entidad por entidad

Así que me di al dolor y empecé a cambiar los archivos con DeepSeek, entidad por entidad. Muy dispendioso, pero funcionaba.

El principal problema: DeepSeek normal no acepta archivos .rar, .tar, .zip ni ningún tipo de empaquetamiento. Al preguntar por qué, la respuesta fue sencilla:

"Porque DeepSeek no es un sistema operativo ni pretende reemplazarlo".

La sugerencia fue clara: si quieres hacerlo, usa DSH y descarga los plugins que permiten hacerlo.

Lo hice, y me di cuenta de que DSH no es una utilidad de DeepSeek: es un agente, bastante bueno por cierto, que puede intervenir tus archivos de forma local, en un ambiente gráfico.

El resultado fue impresionante. Lo que pensé que me iba a tomar días, semanas incluso, lo hice básicamente en 2 días, con DeepSeek como asistente general para temas gruesos y DSH para afinación y puesta a punto.

¿Qué es DSH?

DeepSeek Harness (DSH) es un agente de código open-source construido sobre el SDK de DeepSeek Harness. Su arquitectura se basa en que "todo es un plugin". No es solo un chat: es un entorno de ejecución que puede leer, escribir y ejecutar comandos en tu máquina, siempre bajo un modelo de permisos (sandbox).

Guía de instalación en Linux

Requisitos previos

  • Node.js ^22.19 o >= 24
  • pnpm (recomendado 11 o superior). DSH lo necesita para gestionar los plugins.

Paso 1: Instalar pnpm 

curl -fsSL https://get.pnpm.io/install.sh | sh -
source ~/.bashrc
pnpm --version

Paso 2: Lanzar DSH

El comando más rápido para empezar:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh web

Esto descargará y ejecutará DSH, abriendo la interfaz web en http://127.0.0.1:3080.

Si npx da problemas, puedes forzar una versión específica (por ejemplo, la 0.2.2-rc.1 que usamos):

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Paso 3: Configurar la API Key

La primera vez que intentes usar el agente, verás un error como:

llm-deepseek: no API key for provider route "deepseek-official"

Se soluciona de dos formas:

  1. Desde la interfaz web: ve a Settings → Models, pega tu API Key de DeepSeek (sk-...) y guarda.
  2. Desde la terminal: exporta la variable antes de lanzar DSH: 
export DEEPSEEK_API_KEY="sk-tu-clave-aqui"
npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Instalando plugins para leer ZIPs

DSH por sí solo no lee ZIPs. Necesitas un plugin. El que usamos fue dsh-dragndrop-attachments, que permite arrastrar un .zip a la interfaz y que el agente liste su contenido y lea archivos internos sin descomprimirlo.

Paso 1: Autorizar la compilación del plugin

Antes de instalar plugins desde GitHub, DSH (a través de pnpm) bloquea los scripts de compilación por seguridad. Hay que autorizarlo en el archivo de configuración del perfil web:

nano ~/.dsh/profiles/web/pnpm-workspace.yaml

Añade (o fusiona) al final:

allowBuilds:
  dsh-dragndrop-attachments: true

Nota: la clave debe ser el nombre exacto del paquete. Si pnpm se queja, revisa el mensaje de error para ver la clave correcta.

Paso 2: Instalar el plugin 

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 plugin --profile web add github:aa2246740/dsh-dragndrop-attachments

Paso 3: Reiniciar DSH

Detén DSH (Ctrl+C en la terminal donde corre) y vuelve a lanzarlo:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 web

Refresca el navegador (F5). Ahora deberías poder arrastrar un .zip a la ventana del chat y pedirle al agente que liste su contenido.

Alternativa: un gestor de archivos visual

Si prefieres una experiencia más parecida a VS Code (árbol de archivos, editor con resaltado de sintaxis), el plugin @rose43/dsh-file es muy completo:

npx @deepseek-ai/dsh@0.2.2-rc.1 plugin --profile web add @rose43/dsh-file

Reinicia DSH y busca el botón Files en la barra lateral.

Conclusión

DSH ha sido un descubrimiento. No es solo un chat con plugins: es un agente de código que puede intervenir tus archivos localmente, con un sistema de permisos que te da control. Para migraciones grandes, la combinación de DeepSeek (para el análisis grueso) + DSH (para la afinación y la lectura/escritura de archivos) es muy potente.

Si estás en una situación similar, con un legacy que migrar y herramientas que se quedan cortas, vale la pena explorar DSH. La curva de instalación es baja y el retorno es alto.

¿Has usado DSH? ¿Qué plugins te han sido útiles? Cuéntamelo en los comentarios.

title: Next.js metadata openGraph not inherited: why my subpages lost og:site_name
description:
If a page in the Next.js App Router sets its own openGraph, the openGraph object from your layout is gone for that page. Next.js merges metadata shallowly, so og:site_name, og:locale and any other field you only set in the layout disappear. The fix I use is one helper that builds the full openGraph and twitter objects for every subpage, plus a build check that fails when a tag is missing.

I found this on my own site, mohamedgado.com. /now, /projects and all 55 case studies were shipping without og:site_name, og:locale, twitter:site and twitter:creator. The root layout set all four. Nothing in the browser looked wrong, and nothing errored.

Does Next.js merge openGraph metadata from the layout?

No, not field by field. The Next.js 16 docs for generateMetadata say that metadata objects exported from several segments of one route are shallowly merged, and that duplicate keys are replaced by the segment closest to the page. They also say it directly for nested fields: openGraph defined in an earlier segment is overwritten by the last segment that defines it.

The docs give the example. The layout sets openGraph.title and openGraph.description. The blog page sets only openGraph.title. The output has the page's og:title and no og:description, because the page's whole openGraph object replaced the layout's.

The same page does inherit when it does not set openGraph at all. A subpage with only a title still gets every Open Graph tag from the layout. The trouble starts the moment a page adds openGraph to change one field, such as the title or the image. That is the normal thing to do on a case study or a blog post, so it hits most real sites.

What did the broken setup look like?

My root layout carried the full set:

// app/layout.tsx
export const metadata: Metadata = {
  openGraph: {
    locale: siteConfig.openGraph.locale,
    siteName: siteConfig.name,
    url: siteConfig.links.websiteUrl,
    type: 'website',
    title: `${siteConfig.name} — ${siteConfig.tagline}`,
    description: siteConfig.description,
  },
  twitter: {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    creator: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    site: siteConfig.twitterTag,
  },
}

A subpage then set what it needed, which looks harmless. This is a simplified version of what the case-study page did before the helper:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx (before)
return {
  title: project.title,
  openGraph: {
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
    url: `/projects/${slug}`,
    images: [ogImage],
  },
  twitter: {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
  },
}

This page's openGraph has no siteName and no locale, so neither tag is rendered. Its twitter has no site or creator, so those are gone too. The layout's values were replaced, not combined.

How do I check the rendered tags?

Read the HTML the server sends, not the code. A dev tool that shows the metadata object tells you what you wrote, and the question is what crawlers receive. I curl the page and grep for the tag:

curl -s https://www.mohamedgado.com/projects/masareef | grep -o '<meta[^>]*og:site_name[^>]*>'
curl -s https://www.mohamedgado.com/projects/masareef | grep -oE '<meta[^>]*(og:locale|twitter:site|twitter:creator)[^>]*>'

An empty result means the tag is missing. I ran this against production before writing any code, because I wanted to know the gap was real on every subpage and not something I had inferred from reading the merge docs. It was.

What is the fix for Next.js openGraph not inheriting?

The docs suggest pulling shared fields into a variable and spreading it into each page's openGraph. That works, but it leaves it to every page author to remember the spread. I had 55 case studies built from one template plus a few static pages, so I put the whole thing in a function in lib/social-meta.ts:

import type { Metadata } from 'next'
import { siteConfig } from '@/config/site'

type SocialMetaInput = {
  title: string
  description: string
  /** Root-relative path, resolved against the layout's `metadataBase`. */
  path: string
  images: NonNullable<Metadata['openGraph']>['images']
  /** Case studies are articles; set this and `og:type` becomes `article`. */
  article?: { modifiedTime?: string }
}

export function buildSocialMeta({
  title,
  description,
  path,
  images,
  article,
}: SocialMetaInput): Pick<Metadata, 'openGraph' | 'twitter'> {
  const shared = {
    siteName: siteConfig.name,
    locale: siteConfig.openGraph.locale,
    title,
    description,
    url: path,
    images,
  }
  const twitter: Metadata['twitter'] = {
    card: 'summary_large_image',
    site: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    creator: siteConfig.twitterTag,
    title,
    description,
  }
  if (!article) {
    return { openGraph: { ...shared, type: 'website' }, twitter }
  }
  return {
    openGraph: {
      ...shared,
      type: 'article',
      authors: [siteConfig.links.websiteUrl],
      ...(article.modifiedTime ? { modifiedTime: article.modifiedTime } : {}),
    },
    twitter,
  }
}

A page spreads the result into its metadata:

// app/projects/[slug]/page.tsx (after)
return {
  title: project.title,
  alternates: { canonical: `/projects/${slug}` },
  ...buildSocialMeta({
    title: `${project.title} | Mohamed Gado`,
    description,
    path: `/projects/${slug}`,
    images: [ogImage],
  }),
}

Because buildSocialMeta returns both objects complete, the shallow merge no longer matters: the page's openGraph replaces the layout's, and the replacement already contains everything the layout had. The site name, locale and handles come from siteConfig, the same source the layout reads, so they cannot drift apart.

The helper also gave me a single place to add article fields. Case studies now pass article, which sets og:type to article and adds article:modified_time and article:author.

One detail in the helper: I leave twitter.images unset on purpose. My code comment says Next falls back to the openGraph images, with alt text and dimensions included, so the image is declared once.

How do I stop it coming back?

A convention in a README does not survive the next new page. I added a check to the postbuild step. scripts/check-index-parity.ts reads every prerendered page and asserts that it carries og:site_name, og:locale and both Twitter handles. Before the fix it reported 57 failures. After, 0.

The rule written down in my lessons file is short: a page that sets openGraph or twitter goes through buildSocialMeta, and the build fails otherwise. Because the check runs on built HTML, it also catches pages I did not think of, such as a new route someone adds later and forgets to wire up.

What else should I check on pages that override metadata?

Other nested fields behave the same way. The docs name robots next to openGraph as a field that is overwritten wholesale. If a layout sets robots: { index: true, follow: true, googleBot: {...} } and one page sets robots: { index: false }, the page does not keep the googleBot block. Anything that is an object in the Metadata type is a candidate: alternates, icons, twitter, appLinks and so on.

For each one, ask whether the layout sets it and whether any page sets it again. If both are true, the page's version has to be complete. A helper function, a spread of a shared object, or a build-time check on the output are all workable. I picked the helper and the check together, since the helper prevents the mistake and the check proves it.

The change was small, and nothing on the site looked different afterwards. What changed was the HTML that link previews and search engines read for 57 pages. If you set openGraph on any page below your root layout, curl one of those pages today and look for og:site_name.

title: Why a CSS rotate with will-change: transform makes images and text blurry
description:
If an element is rotated or scaled and has will-change: transform, the browser can rasterise it once and then resample that bitmap every time it moves. Text and thin UI edges come out soft, and no amount of image quality fixes it. On my site, app screenshots looked pixelated because every card had a 0.9deg rotation under will-change: transform and a hover scale. Removing the tilt, the scale and the will-change made them sharp.

The report that started this was short: the images on the Masareef, Rafiq and Nafis project pages looked pixelated and bad. The files on disk were fine. Every screenshot was 1200px wide and sharp. The browser was blurring them on the way to the screen.

Why does will-change: transform make things blurry?

will-change: transform tells the browser to promote the element to its own compositor layer. That layer is drawn into a bitmap, and from then on the compositor moves, rotates and scales the bitmap on the GPU without repainting the content.

That is fast, and it is also the problem. A layer that is rasterised once, upright, has to be resampled to be turned. A bitmap that is resampled at an angle cannot keep a one-pixel edge crisp, and small text is made of one-pixel edges. My notes from the fix put it plainly: a rotated raster of small type is never sharp at any angle, and the angle only decides how much.

Scaling has the same cost. In my case the hover state scaled the card by 1.045 on that same layer. The layer was not re-rasterised at the new size, so the card under the cursor was an upscaled copy of its own bitmap. The one card the visitor was looking at was the softest on the page.

How did I confirm the cause?

I read computed style straight from production in the browser the report came from, a 1512px wide window at a device pixel ratio of 2. One evaluation returned three things: the transform matrix matrix(0.999877, -0.0157…), will-change: transform, and an image request for w=640&q=75. That was the diagnosis before I changed a line.

The matrix is what a rotation of about 0.9 degrees looks like: the cosine is close to 1 and the sine is about 0.0157. It is easy to dismiss that as "almost not rotated". The raster does not care how small the angle is.

The screenshots were part of a fanned deck. I had added the tilt earlier with a comment that kept it under a degree, because past that the captions baked into the images read as crooked. That earlier work measured the caption tops to within 3px. Nobody zoomed into the pixels on a 2x screen, so the blur was designed in and defended by a comment.

What did the CSS look like before and after?

Before, every card was a fanned, overlapping layer:

.shot {
  flex: 0 0 clamp(11rem, 44vw, 15rem);
  margin: 0 -1.5rem 0 0; /* overlap */
  transition: transform 0.28s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.7, 0.3, 1);
  will-change: transform;
}
.shot:nth-child(odd)  { transform: rotate(-0.9deg); }
.shot:nth-child(even) { transform: rotate(0.9deg); }

.shot:hover,
.shot:focus-within {
  transform: rotate(0deg) translateY(-0.6rem) scale(1.045);
}

After, the cards are flat. No tilt, no scale, no will-change, and the hover lift is a plain translate that lands on whole pixels:

.shot {
  flex: 0 0 clamp(12rem, 58vw, 16.5rem);
  margin: 0;
}

.shot a.image-zoom {
  transition: translate 0.32s cubic-bezier(0.2, 0.8, 0.2, 1);
}

/* Lift, never scale: a whole-pixel translate is the one transform that does
   not resample the screenshot once it lands. */
.shot a.image-zoom:hover,
.shot a.image-zoom:focus-visible {
  translate: 0 -0.375rem;
}

The rule I wrote down afterwards: never rotate or scale raster content that carries small type, and never put will-change: transform on anything that scales. If a card needs to lift, translate it by a whole number of pixels.

Was it only the CSS?

No. There were three more causes, and the CSS was the biggest.

The images were AVIF at quality 75, which left ringing around small UI type. Quality 90 was clean for 6 KB more per card, 25 KB to 31 KB at 640px wide. The cards were also 240px wide, a phone screen shown at a fifth of its size, and clicking one opened the raw file in a new tab. I changed the cards to 264px on desktop and 58vw on a phone, cut the srcset to 384, 640 and 828 at quality 90, and opened a full-height viewer on click.

Because Next.js only serves widths and qualities listed in next.config.js, I added q=90 to images.qualities, and a test now reads that config and fails if any rendered image URL asks for a width or quality the optimizer would reject.

Why were the cover banners blurry as well?

A second report came the same day: "I meant this", with a screenshot of the cover banner at the top of the Masareef page, not the gallery. I had fixed the wrong images first. The lesson there was to look at the first viewport before deciding which images a report means.

The banner problem was about device pixels. The source art was a 1024x500 store graphic. The hero rendered 1086 CSS pixels wide, which is 2172 device pixels on a 2x screen, so the browser stretched the file by about 2.1 times. An earlier "hi-res" version at 2560px wide was an upscale of the same 1024 pixels, so it was soft too, only larger. The file size had been the clue: 75 KB for 2560 pixels of supposed detail.

The check I keep now is to compare a raster's intrinsic width with the rendered width multiplied by the device pixel ratio, in device pixels and not CSS pixels. I redrew the covers from SVG at 3x, which gave a 3072x1500 source, and fixed the sizes attribute, which had assumed a 768px column when the header was 1086px wide.

When should text be an image and when should it be live text?

Redrawing the banner at 3x fixed the 2x screen and exposed the next problem a few hours later. A screenshot of the hero at about 1x showed the wordmark and tagline soft next to the real text above them. At 1x the browser was shrinking 3072 pixels into 768, and shrunk type is filtered just like stretched type.

No file size fixes that, because the words were pixels. I had answered "pixelated" with more pixels twice. The question to ask on the first report is whether the thing is text.

The hero of the five mobile app pages is now live HTML in components/projects/app-banner.tsx: the name, the Arabic name, an accent rule and the tagline are real text over a CSS background of two radial glows and a light SVG grain to avoid banding. The app icon is the only image. The frame is a query container, so the type scales with its own width and one rule covers both the 768px column and a 310px phone column.

The rule that came out of it: text a reader has to read is live text. A raster of type belongs only where the page cannot draw text, such as link-preview cards and store listings. The same lesson says to check sharpness at the pixel density of the screenshot you were sent. My test rig had emulated a 2x laptop, where the 3x cover looked fine, and the report came from a screen at about 1x.

A checklist for blurry images and text in CSS

  1. Search the stylesheet for will-change: transform and for any rotate() or scale() on elements with images or text. Remove them from anything that carries small type.
  2. Read the computed transform in devtools. A matrix that is not the identity on a card you thought was flat is a lead.
  3. Compare the image's intrinsic width with rendered width times device pixel ratio.
  4. Test at 1x and at 2x. A fix that is sharp at one density can be soft at the other.
  5. If the blurry thing is text, make it text.

You can see the finished pages on the Masareef, Rafiq and Nafis case studies. The site they live on is described in the portfolio write-up.
