title: Applying ReAct Agents to Exception Recovery in Distributed Sagas
description:
The Saga pattern is the industry standard for maintaining eventual consistency across microservices without distributed two-phase commits (2PC). In a Saga, a sequence of local transactions executes across domain boundaries. If any step fails forward execution, the Saga orchestrator (such as Temporal) executes compensating transactions in reverse order to undo previously committed changes.

However, modern distributed systems face a critical failure mode: The Failed Compensation Paradox. What happens when a compensating action itself fails?

For instance, in a Payment Execution workflow, if a downstream ledger debit succeeds, but a subsequent sanctions check fails, the orchestrator triggers a compensating refund activity. If that refund API returns a 500 Internal Server Error, times out, or encounters an unexpected schema constraint, the Saga enters a stalled, indeterminate state.

Historically, core banking architectures handle failed compensations by halting the workflow and emitting an operational alert to a manual exception queue. In high-volume environments, this creates massive operational queues, inflates Recovery Time Objectives (RTO), and exposes customer balances to inconsistent holds.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms eliminate manual triage bottlenecks by deploying Autonomous ReAct (Reasoning + Acting) Agents as dynamic self-healing nodes. When a Temporal Saga compensation branch fails, an isolated ReAct agent analyzes the failure context, queries live microservice telemetry, executes corrective tool actions in real time, and either restores the compensation path or cleanly escalates to human operators.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

BIAN Service Domain Exception Recovery Matrix

Within a Banking Industry Architecture Network (BIAN) topology, compensation failures vary in operational complexity. The ReAct agent exception recovery framework establishes clear toolsets and boundary limits mapped by domain criticality.

BIAN Service Domain Failed Compensation Scenario ReAct Agent Toolset Maximum Autonomy Bounds Fallback Action
Payment Execution Refund API returns 500 due to temporary ledger lock inspectLedgerLock(), retryWithBackoff(), forceReleaseLock() Retry count <= 3; Max amount <= $50,000 Escalate to Payment Ops Task
Position Keeping Reversing balance hold fails due to account status change getAccountState(), rerouteToSuspenseAccount(), logAudit() No direct balance overrides; Suspense routing only Route to Risk Officer Queue
Foreign Exchange (FX) Unwinding FX spot rate lock fails due to expired quote fetchCurrentFxRate(), negotiateSlippage(), rebookFxLock() Slippage tolerance <= 0.10% Freeze FX Position & Alert Desk
Consumer Loan Origination Reverting collateral reservation fails due to lock contention queryCollateralState(), clearLockKeys() Non-destructive database lock release Re-queue for Scheduled Batch Worker

Mathematical Model: Self-Healing Reliability & Unresolved Saga Risk

To quantify the risk reduction achieved by autonomous ReAct compensation repair, we model the overall unresolved Saga probability Punresolved-saga​ across distributed banking transactions.

Let Pforward-fail​ be the probability of a forward transaction step failing, and Pcomp-fail​ be the conditional probability that a registered compensating action fails due to transient infrastructure outages or state locks. The baseline unresolved Saga rate without AI self-healing is:

Pbaseline-risk​=Pforward-fail​×Pcomp-fail​

By introducing a ReAct agent to inspect and repair failed compensations across K reasoning iterations, the joint unresolved Saga probability becomes:

Punresolved-saga​=Pforward-fail​×Pcomp-fail​×i=1∏K​(1−Pagent-repair-i​)

Where Pagent-repair-i​ is the probability that the agent successfully diagnoses the root cause and executes an authorized corrective tool action during iteration i . Assuming Pagent-repair​≈0.85 over 2 reasoning loops, the manual operational exception queue footprint is reduced by over 97%.

Architectural Topology: The ReAct Saga Repair Engine

The architecture separates Deterministic Workflow Orchestration (Temporal) from Autonomous Reasoning (ReAct Agent). The workflow definition remains 100% deterministic, while non-deterministic AI reasoning executes inside a specialized Temporal Activity.

                       REACT SAGA COMPENSATION RECOVERY TOPOLOGY

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | TEMPORAL SAGA WORKFLOW ENGINE                                                   |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Forward Transaction Steps ] ───► ( Fail ) ───► [ Execute Compensation ]      |
  |                                                               │                 |
  |                                                      Compensation Fails         |
  |                                                               │                 |
  |                                                               v                 |
  |  [ Saga Suspended ] ◄── ( Return Final Status ) ─── [ Invoke ReAct Activity ]   |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------|------------------+
                                                                 |
                                       1. Pass Execution Trace & | Payload
                                                                 v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | REACT AGENT REPAIR ACTIVITY (Non-Deterministic Reasoning Loop)                  |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  |  | ReAct Execution Loop (Max 3 Iterations)                                  |  |
  |  |                                                                           |  |
  |  |  1. THOUGHT: "Refund failed with HTTP 500. Inspecting ledger locks..."   |  |
  |  |  2. ACTION:  Call tool `inspectLedgerLock(accountId)`                     |  |
  |  |  3. OBSERVE: "Stale optimistic lock found on row #9012."                  |  |
  |  |  4. THOUGHT: "Clearing stale lock key and retrying refund API..."         |  |
  |  |  5. ACTION:  Call tool `clearLockKey(accountId)` -> `retryRefund()`       |  |
  |  |  6. OBSERVE: "Refund API succeeded with Transaction ID TX-8812."          |  |
  |  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------+  |
  +--------------------------------------------------------------|------------------+
                                                                 |
                                       2. Return Repaired Status | Payload
                                                                 v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | IMMUTABLE COMPLIANCE AUDIT STORE                                                |
  |  [ Persists Complete ReAct Thought-Action-Observation Trace & Signatures ]      |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Technical Implementation: Temporal Workflow & ReAct Engine

1. Temporal Workflow with Compensation Fallback (Java 21)

The workflow executes forward steps within a try-catch block. If a compensating activity throws an unrecoverable exception, control shifts to the ReActSagaRepairActivity.

package com.xenon.banking.saga.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.saga.activity.PaymentActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.activity.ReActRepairActivity;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.PaymentSagaInput;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.RepairResult;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflow {
    @WorkflowMethod
    void processPaymentSaga(PaymentSagaInput input);
}

public class ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl implements ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflow {

    private final PaymentActivities paymentActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            PaymentActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build()
    );

    private final ReActRepairActivity repairActivity = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            ReActRepairActivity.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(45)).build()
    );

    @Override
    public void processPaymentSaga(PaymentSagaInput input) {
        boolean ledgerDebited = false;

        try {
            // Step 1: Debit Source Ledger Account
            paymentActivities.debitSourceAccount(input.getPaymentId(), input.getSourceAccount(), input.getAmount());
            ledgerDebited = true;

            // Step 2: Perform Real-time Sanctions Screening (Fails intentionally for demonstration)
            paymentActivities.executeSanctionsScreening(input.getPaymentId(), input.getDebtorName());

        } catch (Exception forwardException) {
            Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .warn("Forward execution failed. Starting compensation. Error: " + forwardException.getMessage());

            if (ledgerDebited) {
                try {
                    // Attempt Standard Compensation: Refund Source Account
                    paymentActivities.refundSourceAccount(input.getPaymentId(), input.getSourceAccount(), input.getAmount());
                    Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class).info("Compensation succeeded standard execution.");

                } catch (Exception compensationException) {
                    Workflow.getLogger(ResilientPaymentSagaWorkflowImpl.class)
                            .error("CRITICAL: Compensation failed! Invoking Autonomous ReAct Repair Agent...");

                    // Invoke ReAct Repair Activity to autonomously triage and repair state
                    RepairResult repairResult = repairActivity.repairFailedCompensation(
                            input.getPaymentId(),
                            input.getSourceAccount(),
                            input.getAmount(),
                            compensationException.getMessage()
                    );

                    if (!repairResult.isRepaired()) {
                        // ReAct agent failed or reached maximum safety limits -> Escalate to Human Queue
                        repairActivity.escalateToHumanQueue(input.getPaymentId(), repairResult.getReasoningTrace());
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
}

2. ReAct Engine Repair Activity Implementation (Java 21)

This Java activity executes the Thought-Action-Observation reasoning loop. It inspects diagnostic tools, analyzes exception context, and takes corrective action within strict safety bounds.

package com.xenon.banking.saga.activity;

import com.fasterxml.jackson.databind.ObjectMapper;
import com.xenon.banking.saga.model.RepairResult;
import io.temporal.activity.Activity;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;

@Component("reActRepairActivity")
public class ReActRepairActivityImpl implements ReActRepairActivity {

    private final MicroserviceDiagnosticToolSet toolSet;
    private final ObjectMapper objectMapper;

    public ReActRepairActivityImpl(MicroserviceDiagnosticToolSet toolSet, ObjectMapper objectMapper) {
        this.toolSet = toolSet;
        this.objectMapper = objectMapper;
    }

    @Override
    public RepairResult repairFailedCompensation(String paymentId, String accountId, double amount, String failureMessage) {
        var activityContext = Activity.getExecutionContext();
        String workflowId = activityContext.getInfo().getWorkflowId();

        List<String> reasoningTrace = new ArrayList<>();
        reasoningTrace.add("INITIAL OBSERVATION: Compensation failed for payment [" + paymentId + "]. Error: " + failureMessage);

        int iteration = 0;
        int maxIterations = 3;
        boolean repaired = false;

        while (iteration < maxIterations && !repaired) {
            iteration++;
            reasoningTrace.add("--- REACT ITERATION " + iteration + " ---");

            if (iteration == 1) {
                // THOUGHT 1: Inspect database locks and service availability
                reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 1: Inspecting if account [" + accountId + "] is currently locked by concurrent workers.");

                // ACTION 1: Invoke Diagnostic Tool
                String lockStatus = toolSet.inspectAccountLock(accountId);
                reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 1: Called tool inspectAccountLock(" + accountId + "). Result: " + lockStatus);

                if (lockStatus.contains("STALE_LOCK_FOUND")) {
                    // THOUGHT 2: Clear stale lock key
                    reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 2: Stale lock detected. Attempting non-destructive lock clearance.");

                    // ACTION 2: Clear stale lock
                    boolean lockCleared = toolSet.clearStaleLock(accountId);
                    reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 2: Called tool clearStaleLock(" + accountId + "). Success: " + lockCleared);
                }
            } 
            else if (iteration == 2) {
                // THOUGHT 3: Retry the refund transaction API after lock cleanup
                reasoningTrace.add("THOUGHT 3: Retrying compensating refund transaction API...");

                // ACTION 3: Retry Refund Execution
                Map<String, Object> refundResponse = toolSet.retryRefundApi(paymentId, accountId, amount);
                reasoningTrace.add("ACTION 3: Called tool retryRefundApi(). Response: " + refundResponse.get("status"));

                if ("SUCCESS".equals(refundResponse.get("status"))) {
                    repaired = true;
                    reasoningTrace.add("OBSERVATION: Compensation successfully repaired and executed!");
                } else {
                    reasoningTrace.add("OBSERVATION: Refund API failed again. Details: " + refundResponse.get("error"));
                }
            }
        }

        return new RepairResult(repaired, String.join("\n", reasoningTrace));
    }

    @Override
    public void escalateToHumanQueue(String paymentId, String reasoningTrace) {
        System.err.println("ESCALATING TO HUMAN OPS: Payment " + paymentId + "\nTrace:\n" + reasoningTrace);
        // Create Flowable Human User Task for operational staff review
    }
}

Bounded Autonomy & Deterministic Safety Guardrails

Allowing an autonomous agent to execute diagnostic tools over financial databases introduces operational risk if left unconstrained. ReAct repair activities must operate within strict Safety Guardrails:

                       REACT AGENT BOUNDED AUTONOMY MATRIX

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | REACT AGENT REASONING ENGINE                                                    |
  +----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
                                           |
                                 Proposed Tool Execution
                                           |
                                           v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | POLICY-AS-CODE GUARDRAIL INTERCEPTOR (OPA / DMN)                                |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  Check 1: Is Tool Permitted? ────► `clearStaleLock()` ──► [ ALLOWED ]          |
  |  Check 2: Is Action Destructive? ─► `deleteAccount()`   ──► [ BLOCKED ]          |
  |  Check 3: Max Monetary Value? ───► `overrideBalance()`  ──► [ BLOCKED > $10k ]   |
  +----------------------------------------+----------------------------------------+
                                           |
                                   Validated Tool Call
                                           |
                                           v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | MICROSERVICE DIAGNOSTIC LAYER                                                   |
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+

Core Safety Rules

  1. Max Reasoning Iterations: The ReAct loop is strictly bounded (e.g., maximum 3 iterations). If the agent cannot diagnose and repair the issue within 3 cycles, it must halt and escalate.
  2. Forbidden Tool Actions: ReAct agents are strictly prohibited from invoking destructive API endpoints (e.g., deleteRecord(), truncateLedger(), or directBalanceCredit()). Agent tools must be read-only diagnostics or safe, idempotent retry handlers.
  3. Monetary Value Limits: If a failed compensation involves an amount exceeding a defined threshold (e.g., > $50,000), the ReAct activity bypasses autonomous repair entirely and routes the transaction directly to human underwriters.

Observability, Forensic Lineage, and Regulatory Audit

Financial regulators (such as OCC, EBA, and MAS) require full explainability for autonomous self-healing actions. System history must record not only the outcome, but the complete Thought-Action-Observation chain.

Audit Payload Structure (react-saga-audit.json)

For every self-healing execution, the ReAct activity logs an immutable audit event to the central compliance data lake (Elasticsearch / ClickHouse):

{
  "auditId": "AUDIT-REACT-2026-770192",
  "temporalWorkflowId": "PaymentSaga-PAY-90128",
  "temporalRunId": "c89f102a-331b-429a-b802-991204812a41",
  "bianDomain": "PaymentExecution",
  "paymentId": "PAY-90128",
  "failedCompensationActivity": "refundSourceAccount",
  "originalError": "HTTP 500 Internal Server Error: LockWaitTimeoutException",
  "reActExecutionTrace": [
    {
      "step": 1,
      "thought": "Inspecting account lock state to determine root cause of 500 error.",
      "action": "inspectAccountLock",
      "actionInput": {"accountId": "ACC-GB-40912"},
      "observation": "Found stale lock held by dead worker pod payment-worker-77b"
    },
    {
      "step": 2,
      "thought": "Lock is stale. Clearing lock key to allow compensation API to proceed.",
      "action": "clearStaleLock",
      "actionInput": {"accountId": "ACC-GB-40912"},
      "observation": "Lock key cleared successfully."
    },
    {
      "step": 3,
      "thought": "Retrying refund compensation activity now that lock is cleared.",
      "action": "retryRefundApi",
      "actionInput": {"paymentId": "PAY-90128", "amount": 1250.00},
      "observation": "Refund API responded HTTP 200 OK. Transaction ID: TX-88120"
    }
  ],
  "repairStatus": "SUCCESSFULLY_REPAIRED",
  "executionDurationMs": 1420,
  "timestamp": "2026-09-16T12:30:00Z"
}

Integrating autonomous ReAct agents into Temporal Saga exception workflows resolves the long-standing challenge of failed compensations in distributed core banking. By isolating non-deterministic reasoning inside bounded Temporal Activities, enforcing Policy-as-Code safety limits, and maintaining cryptographic auditability, modern financial architectures eliminate operational queue bloat, achieve sub-second self-healing, and protect end-to-end data integrity across all BIAN service domains.

title: Enforcing Maker-Checker Approvals in Financial AI Agents: A Hybrid Gateway-Orchestration Topology
description:
As enterprise core banking platforms integrate Large Language Model (LLM) agents to automate operational decisions, governing AI Tool-Calling (Function Calling) has emerged as a primary architectural challenge. When an AI agent generates tool calls to execute REST APIs—such as initiating wire transfers, adjusting credit limits, or waiving fees—the system must enforce strict regulatory controls.

A common design pitfall is confusing Structural Access Control with Stateful Business Process Logic. Attempting to force an Identity and Access Management (IAM) provider like Keycloak to evaluate stateful financial metrics (such as fetching database balances or evaluating $10,000 threshold routing) introduces tight coupling, database latency, and broken execution flows. Throwing a 403 Forbidden error at the gateway for a high-value transaction kills the request entirely, preventing the system from ever instantiating the required human supervisor approval task.

Under the Xenon Architecture Standards, modern core banking platforms govern AI tool-calling through a Hybrid Gateway-Orchestration Topology. Structural capability authorization ("Is this AI agent allowed to invoke the wire transfer tool?") is handled at the perimeter gateway via Keycloak. Stateful context evaluation ("Does a $10,000 transfer require a human supervisor sign-off?") is handled within the durable execution layer via Temporal Sagas and Flowable DMN Engines.

💡 Explore the Xenon Architecture Standard For comprehensive architectural blueprints, BIAN service domain mappings, and dual-orchestration integration patterns, visit the official Xenon Architecture Guide. To inspect reference code, infrastructure templates, and open-source banking modules, explore the VecPay-Tech GitHub Organization.

Architectural Taxonomy: Capability vs. Context Governance

Separating Identity Capability from Business Context establishes clear boundaries across the BIAN (Banking Industry Architecture Network) ecosystem.

Governance Layer Primary Component Evaluation Scope State Requirement System Action on Positive Match System Action on Failure / Boundary Match
Structural Capability (Gateway) Keycloak IAM Token OAuth2 scopes (wire:execute), role claims, identity validity Stateless (Evaluates JWT claims) Pass request to API Ingress Gateway 403 Forbidden (Hard stop; blocks malicious calls)
Stateful Context (Orchestration) Temporal + Flowable DMN Transaction amounts, stateful balance lookups, DTI ratios Stateful (Queries core databases & DMN tables) Execute automated transaction Saga Suspend & Route (Generate Flowable Checker task)

Mathematical Model: Risk-Driven Workflow Routing

To evaluate whether an AI agent's tool payload requires human intervention, the durable workflow layer calculates a Contextual Risk Index Rcontext​ by combining real-time database facts with agent execution metrics:

Rcontext​=w1​⋅(ThresholdmaxRequested-Amount​)+w2​⋅(1−Cagent)+w3​⋅(Current-LimitRequested-Limit​)

Where:

  • Requested-Amount is the transaction value normalized against the BIAN domain cap Thresholdmax​ .
  • Cagent​ is the LLM agent's reported confidence score ( 0.0≤Cagent​≤1.0 ).
  • Current-Limit is fetched statefully from the core database during activity execution.
  • w1​,w2​,w3​ are policy weight vectors such that ∑wi​=1.0 .

If Rcontext​ exceeds defined DMN thresholds, Temporal does not fail the execution. It suspends the workflow state, generates a cryptographic approval token, and creates a Flowable Human Checker User Task.

Hybrid System Topology

The system separates perimeter identity validation from stateful business process routing.

                           HYBRID GOVERNANCE ARCHITECTURE

  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | PERIMETER GATEWAY LAYER (Stateless Capability Enforcement)                     |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  AI Agent Tool Call ---> [ API Gateway + Keycloak Filter ]                       |
  |                           ├── Missing Scope `wire:write` ──► [ 403 Forbidden ]  |
  |                           └── Has Valid Scope ───────────────► [ PASS ]         |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                      |
                           1. Dispatch Authorized Tool Call
                                      |
                                      v
  +---------------------------------------------------------------------------------+
  | DURABLE ORCHESTRATION LAYER (Stateful Context Execution - Temporal)             |
  |                                                                                 |
  |  [ Start PaymentExecutionWorkflow ]                                             |
  |    ├── Activity: Fetch Stateful DB Balances & Credit Limits                     |
  |    └── Activity: Evaluate Business Rules (Flowable DMN)                         |
  +-----------------------------------|---------------------------------------------+
                                      |
            ┌─────────────────────────┴─────────────────────────┐
            | DMN Decision: AUTO_APPROVE                        | DMN Decision: REQUIRES_CHECKER
            v                                                   v
  +-----------------------------------+               +-----------------------------------+
  | MICROSERVICE SETTLEMENT           |               | FLOWABLE HUMAN WORKFLOW           |
  |                                   |               |                                   |
  | [ Executes Ledger Mutation ]      |               | 1. Create Human Checker Task      |
  +-----------------------------------+               | 2. Temporal Suspends (Awaits Sig) |
                                                      | 3. Human Checker Signs Off        |
                                                      +-----------------+-----------------+
                                                                        |
                                                               4. Send Temporal Signal
                                                                        |
                                                                        v
                                                      +-----------------------------------+
                                                      | MICROSERVICE SETTLEMENT           |
                                                      | [ Executes Ledger Mutation ]      |
                                                      +-----------------------------------+

Technical Implementation

1. Keycloak Gateway Filter (Stateless Capability Check)

This gateway component validates that the calling AI agent possesses the required structural OAuth2 scope (wire:execute) before allowing the request to enter the orchestration mesh.

package com.xenon.banking.gateway.filter;

import org.springframework.http.HttpStatus;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;
import org.springframework.web.server.ServerWebExchange;
import org.springframework.web.server.WebFilter;
import org.springframework.web.server.WebFilterChain;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

import java.util.List;

@Component
public class KeycloakCapabilityGatewayFilter implements WebFilter {

    @Override
    public Mono<Void> filter(ServerWebExchange exchange, WebFilterChain chain) {
        String path = exchange.getRequest().getURI().getPath();

        // Target AI tool-calling execution endpoints
        if (path.startsWith("/api/v1/tools/wire-transfer")) {
            List<String> authHeaders = exchange.getRequest().getHeaders().get("Authorization");

            if (authHeaders == null || authHeaders.isEmpty()) {
                exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED);
                return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
            }

            // Extract JWT and verify structural capability scope
            String token = authHeaders.get(0).replace("Bearer ", "");
            boolean hasWireScope = extractScopesFromJwt(token).contains("wire:execute");

            if (!hasWireScope) {
                // Structural failure: Hard fast-fail at gateway
                exchange.getResponse().setStatusCode(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN);
                return exchange.getResponse().setComplete();
            }
        }

        // Structural check passed: Forward request to Temporal Workflow trigger
        return chain.filter(exchange);
    }

    private List<String> extractScopesFromJwt(String jwtToken) {
        // Standard stateless JWT claims parsing logic
        return List.of("wire:execute", "account:read");
    }
}

2. Temporal Workflow (Stateful Business Process & Signal Gateway)

The workflow orchestrates stateful database reads, evaluates dynamic DMN rules, and handles asynchronous human checker approval signals without terminating execution.

package com.xenon.banking.workflow;

import com.xenon.banking.activity.AccountStateActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.activity.BusinessRuleActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.activity.PaymentSettlementActivities;
import com.xenon.banking.model.DmnEvaluationResult;
import com.xenon.banking.model.PaymentExecutionPayload;
import io.temporal.activity.ActivityOptions;
import io.temporal.workflow.Workflow;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowInterface;
import io.temporal.workflow.WorkflowMethod;
import io.temporal.workflow.SignalMethod;

import java.time.Duration;

@WorkflowInterface
public interface PaymentExecutionWorkflow {

    @WorkflowMethod
    void executePayment(PaymentExecutionPayload payload);

    @SignalMethod
    void receiveCheckerApproval(String checkerUserId, String approvalSignature);
}

public class PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl implements PaymentExecutionWorkflow {

    private final AccountStateActivities accountActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            AccountStateActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()
    );

    private final BusinessRuleActivities ruleActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            BusinessRuleActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5)).build()
    );

    private final PaymentSettlementActivities settlementActivities = Workflow.newActivityStub(
            PaymentSettlementActivities.class,
            ActivityOptions.newBuilder().setStartToCloseTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(10)).build()
    );

    private boolean checkerApproved = false;
    private String approvingCheckerId;

    @Override
    public void executePayment(PaymentExecutionPayload payload) {

        // 1. Stateful Data Fetching via Temporal Activity (Core DB lookup)
        double currentAccountBalance = accountActivities.fetchCurrentBalance(payload.getSourceAccount());
        String customerRiskTier = accountActivities.fetchCustomerRiskTier(payload.getSourceAccount());

        // 2. Evaluate Dynamic Business Rules via Flowable DMN Engine
        DmnEvaluationResult dmnResult = ruleActivities.evaluatePaymentRules(
                payload.getAmount(),
                currentAccountBalance,
                customerRiskTier,
                payload.getAgentConfidenceScore()
        );

        // 3. Process Execution Path Based on Business Rules
        if ("REQUIRES_CHECKER".equals(dmnResult.getDecision())) {

            // Instantiates Flowable Human Task for Supervisor Review
            String taskId = ruleActivities.createFlowableCheckerTask(
                    payload.getPaymentId(),
                    payload.getAmount(),
                    dmnResult.getReasoning()
            );

            Workflow.getLogger(PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .info("Payment " + payload.getPaymentId() + " requires Maker-Checker sign-off. Created Task: " + taskId);

            // Suspend workflow execution and await external Human Approval Signal
            Workflow.await(() -> checkerApproved);

            Workflow.getLogger(PaymentExecutionWorkflowImpl.class)
                    .info("Human Sign-Off received from Checker: " + approvingCheckerId + ". Resuming settlement.");
        }

        // 4. Final Settlement Execution
        settlementActivities.executeSettlement(payload.getPaymentId(), payload.getAmount(), approvingCheckerId);
    }

    @Override
    public void receiveCheckerApproval(String checkerUserId, String approvalSignature) {
        this.checkerApproved = true;
        this.approvingCheckerId = checkerUserId;
    }
}

3. Flowable Human Checker Task Signaling Bridge

When a human supervisor approves the task within the operational dashboard, this service emits a Temporal signal to wake up the suspended workflow.

package com.xenon.banking.bridge;

import io.temporal.client.WorkflowClient;
import org.flowable.engine.TaskService;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
public class FlowableTemporalBridgeService {

    private final TaskService flowableTaskService;
    private final WorkflowClient temporalWorkflowClient;

    public FlowableTemporalBridgeService(TaskService flowableTaskService, WorkflowClient temporalWorkflowClient) {
        this.flowableTaskService = flowableTaskService;
        this.temporalWorkflowClient = temporalWorkflowClient;
    }

    public void approveCheckerTask(String taskId, String checkerUserId, String cryptographicSignature) {
        // 1. Complete Flowable Task
        var task = flowableTaskService.createTaskQuery().taskId(taskId).singleResult();
        String paymentId = (String) flowableTaskService.getVariable(taskId, "paymentId");

        flowableTaskService.complete(taskId);

        // 2. Signal Temporal Workflow to resume execution
        var workflowStub = temporalWorkflowClient.newWorkflowStub(
                com.xenon.banking.workflow.PaymentExecutionWorkflow.class,
                "PaymentWorkflow-" + paymentId
        );

        // Emit signal directly into Temporal's event history
        workflowStub.receiveCheckerApproval(checkerUserId, cryptographicSignature);
    }
}

Analysis of Architectural Trade-Offs

Analyzing the hybrid architecture highlights how responsibilities are balanced across the stack.

1. Separation of Concerns & System Governance

  • Keycloak manages IAM scopes, OAuth2 client identities, and role assignments.
  • Temporal & Flowable DMN handle business logic, stateful database queries, and workflow routing.
  • Outcome: Security policies remain clean and stateless, while business workflows retain full access to operational context.

2. Dynamic Rule Management

  • Business parameters (such as lowering an approval threshold from $10,000 to $5,000) are managed inside the Flowable DMN Engine or dynamic configuration services.
  • Outcome: Rule adjustments take effect instantly without re-deploying microservices or updating Temporal workflow code.

3. Fast-Fail Security Protection

  • Invalid requests (e.g., an AI agent attempting an unauthorized API call without proper scopes) are blocked at the API Gateway by Keycloak.
  • Outcome: Malicious or malformed requests fail fast at the perimeter, preventing invalid state entries from polluting Temporal's event store.

4. Enterprise Audit Trails & Compliance

  • Keycloak logs authentication and token issuance events for IAM auditing.
  • Temporal maintains an event history recording the complete execution lineage: AI Agent initiated -> DMN evaluated -> Flowable task generated -> Human Checker signed off -> Settlement executed.
  • Outcome: Provides financial regulators (OCC, EBA, BCBS 239) with proof of non-repudiation and process compliance.

Decoupling structural access control from stateful business process routing establishes a resilient architecture for financial AI agents. Assigning capability validation to Keycloak at the gateway while executing contextual Maker-Checker workflows within Temporal and Flowable DMN allows core banking systems to preserve security perimeter defenses, maintain sub-second operational execution, and meet stringent regulatory requirements across all BIAN service domains.

title: UNDERSTANDING IaaS THROUGH AMAZON EC2: A BEGINNER'S GUIDE
description:
Understanding Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS): A Case Study of Amazon EC2

Introduction

Technology has changed the way individuals and organizations store data, run applications, and manage their computing resources. In the past, organizations had to purchase physical servers, storage devices, and networking equipment to operate their IT systems. This required significant financial investment, maintenance, and technical expertise.

Cloud computing provides an alternative by allowing organizations to access computing resources over the internet. One of its major service models is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS).

This article explains IaaS, how it works, its benefits and challenges, using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), a service offered by Amazon Web Services (AWS), as a case study.

What is Infrastructure as a Service (IaaS)?

Infrastructure as a Service is a cloud computing model in which a cloud provider offers computing resources such as virtual servers, storage, and networking over the internet.

Instead of purchasing and maintaining physical hardware, customers rent these resources from a cloud provider and use them according to their needs.

IaaS gives customers control over important computing resources, including their operating systems, applications, and data, while the provider manages the underlying physical infrastructure.

Case Study: Amazon EC2

Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is a computing service provided by AWS. It allows users to create and manage virtual servers called instances in the cloud.

These instances provide computing capacity without requiring customers to own physical servers.

For example, imagine a small business in Cameroon that wants to develop and host its own website. Traditionally, the business would need to purchase a physical server, install an operating system, provide storage, and maintain the equipment.

With Amazon EC2, the business can rent a virtual server, install its preferred operating system, configure the necessary software, and host its website through the internet.

This demonstrates how IaaS makes computing infrastructure available without requiring customers to purchase the physical equipment.

How Amazon EC2 Works

Amazon EC2 operates by providing virtual computing resources through AWS’s cloud infrastructure.

The process involves the following steps:

  1. Creating an AWS account: The user creates an account and accesses the AWS Management Console.

  2. Selecting a virtual server: The user chooses an EC2 instance with suitable computing resources, such as processor capacity and memory.

  3. Selecting an operating system: The user selects an operating system, such as Linux or Windows, using an Amazon Machine Image (AMI).

  4. Configuring security and networking: The user configures network access and security settings to control communication with the virtual server.

  5. Launching the instance: AWS provisions the virtual server, making it available for the user to access and manage.

  6. Installing and running applications: The user can install software, host websites, store and process data, or run other applications.

Major Features of Amazon EC2

Amazon EC2 provides several features that make it useful for individuals and organizations.

  1. Virtual servers: EC2 allows users to create virtual machines without purchasing physical servers.

  2. Scalability: Users can increase or decrease their computing capacity depending on their requirements.

  3. Flexible pricing: Users can choose different purchasing options, including On-Demand Instances, where they pay for the computing capacity they use.

  4. Storage: EC2 works with Amazon Elastic Block Store (EBS), which provides persistent storage volumes for virtual servers.

  5. Security: EC2 provides security groups, which act as virtual firewalls to control incoming and outgoing network traffic.

  6. Networking: Users can configure networking resources and control how their virtual servers communicate with other systems.

Benefits of Using Amazon EC2 as an IaaS Solution

Amazon EC2 offers several advantages:

  • Reduced hardware costs: Organizations do not need to purchase expensive physical servers before deploying applications.
  • Flexibility: Users can select computing resources that suit their workloads.
  • Scalability: Computing resources can be adjusted as demand changes.
  • Accessibility: Virtual servers can be accessed and managed remotely through the internet.
  • Faster deployment: Users can provision virtual servers without waiting to purchase and install physical hardware.
  • Resource management: Organizations can monitor and manage their computing resources according to their requirements.

Challenges of Using Amazon EC2

Despite its advantages, Amazon EC2 also has some challenges.

  1. Internet dependency: Accessing and managing cloud resources generally requires a reliable internet connection.

  2. Security responsibilities: Although AWS provides security tools, customers must properly configure their operating systems, access permissions, applications, and data protection measures.

  3. Cost management: Poor resource management can result in unexpected expenses, especially when users leave unnecessary resources running.

  4. Technical knowledge: Users need some technical understanding to configure, secure, and maintain their virtual servers.

Conclusion

Infrastructure as a Service has transformed how individuals and organizations obtain and manage computing resources. Through services such as Amazon EC2, users can access virtual servers, storage, and networking without purchasing and maintaining their own physical infrastructure.

Amazon EC2 demonstrates how virtualization, scalability, flexible resource allocation, and cloud-based infrastructure work together to make IaaS possible.

As organizations continue to adopt cloud computing, IaaS remains an important solution for reducing hardware investments, improving flexibility, and supporting the development and deployment of modern applications.

References

  1. Amazon Web Services. What is Amazon EC2? https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/concepts.html
  2. Amazon Web Services. Amazon EC2 Security Groups. https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSEC2/latest/UserGuide/ec2-security-groups.html
  3. Amazon Web Services. Amazon EC2 Pricing. https://aws.amazon.com/ec2/pricing/

title: Seven Java changes that pass your build and break your users
description:
Each change below compiles, passes the library's own tests and looks harmless in a code review. Each one breaks code that depends on the library, either when it is recompiled or, worse, when it runs against the new jar without being recompiled. We checked every example on Java 25.

Two ways to break a caller

A Java library can break its users in two different ways, and a change can break one without the other.

  • Source compatibility: does the caller's code still compile against the new version?

  • Binary compatibility: does code that was compiled against the old version still run with the new jar?

Binary compatibility matters more than it seems. When an application updates your library, it rarely recompiles the other libraries that use it. Those were compiled once, against your old version, and they keep calling it exactly as they did then. The Java Language Specification describes the rules in chapter 13, Binary Compatibility.

In each example, version 1.0 is the release that callers use and 1.1 is the change. The error messages are the real ones.

1. A wider parameter type 

// 1.0
public static int twice(int x)

// 1.1: accepts more values, so it looks compatible
public static long twice(long x)

Recompiled callers: compile. An int argument widens to long automatically.

Old binaries: fail. The JVM looks up a method by its exact descriptor, parameter and return types included:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'

Instead: add the long version as an overload and keep the int one, delegating to the new method if you like.

2. A more general return type 

// 1.0
public static List<String> names()

// 1.1
public static Collection<String> names()

Recompiled callers: compile if they only use what Collection has, such as size() or a for loop, and fail if they assign the result to a List or call get(i).

Old binaries: fail, even the ones that only call size(). The return type is part of the descriptor:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'java.util.List Lib.names()'

Instead: keep the return type. If the new type is the right one, add a new method under a new name and deprecate the old one.

3. A new method in an interface 

// 1.0
public interface Lib { String name(); }

// 1.1, and the library now calls id()
public interface Lib { String name(); String id(); }

Recompiled callers: every class that implements the interface stops compiling until it implements id().

Old binaries: load without any error. The failure comes later, at the first call to the missing method, which can be deep inside your library and long after startup:

java.lang.AbstractMethodError: Receiver class Client does not define or inherit
an implementation of the resolved method 'abstract java.lang.String id()' of interface Lib.

Instead: give the new method a default implementation, for example default String id() { return name(); }. Old implementations then keep working, compiled or not. Interfaces that callers only use and never implement can grow freely; say so in the documentation, or mark them with an annotation such as @DoNotImplement.

4. Making a class final 

// 1.0
public class Lib { ... }

// 1.1: "nobody should extend this"
public final class Lib { ... }

Recompiled callers: subclasses stop compiling.

Old binaries: a subclass compiled against 1.0 cannot even be loaded:

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: class Client cannot inherit from final class Lib

Adding final to a public or protected method breaks the classes that override it in the same way. Removing final is always safe.

Instead: decide before the first release. If the class is already open, deprecate extension first and make it final in the next major version.

5. A static method becomes an instance method 

// 1.0
public static String version()

// 1.1
public String version()

Recompiled callers: every Lib.version() call stops compiling.

Old binaries: fail at the call. The opposite change, from instance to static, fails the same way:

java.lang.IncompatibleClassChangeError: Expected static method 'java.lang.String Lib.version()'

Instead: add the instance method with a new name and keep the static one.

6. A new checked exception 

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


0

Recompiled callers: fail, unless they already catch or declare the exception:

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


1

Old binaries: run. The JVM does not check throws clauses, so old callers get the exception at runtime without any code to handle it.

This is the reverse of the first two changes: old jars keep working, and the break appears the next time a user upgrades and recompiles. It is still a breaking change, and it belongs in a major version.

Instead: throw an unchecked exception, or add a new method that declares the checked one.

7. A new value for a constant 

java.lang.NoSuchMethodError: 'int Lib.twice(int)'


2

Nothing fails, and that is the problem. A static final field of a primitive type or String, set to a constant expression, is copied into the class files of the code that uses it when that code is compiled. Callers compiled against 1.0 keep using 10 with the 1.1 jar, until they are recompiled. We printed the field from a client compiled against 1.0 and run with the 1.1 jar: it printed 10.

So two parts of one application can disagree about the value, depending on when each part was compiled.

Instead: if a value can change, don't make it a compile-time constant. Expose it through a method, or initialise the field in a way that is not a constant expression.

The seven at a glance

Change in a minor release Recompiled callers Old binaries
Wider parameter type Compile NoSuchMethodError
More general return type Some fail NoSuchMethodError
New abstract method in an interface Implementations fail AbstractMethodError at the first call
Class or method made final Subclasses fail IncompatibleClassChangeError when loaded
Static to instance, or back Fail IncompatibleClassChangeError
New checked exception Fail Run, with no handler for it
New constant value Get the new value Keep the old value

None of them fails the library's own build, and most of them get past at least one of the two checks. That is why they reach a release.

Why tests don't catch them

The library's tests are compiled together with the new code, so they always match it. They test the library as it is now. What they cannot see is the code that was written, or compiled, against the version you released before.

These are not rare cases either. A study of 119,879 library upgrades on Maven Central found a breaking change in 1 in 5 minor and patch upgrades (Ochoa et al., 2022). The numbers and their sources are in our report.

How to catch them

Compare your public API with the last release, not with your tests. Tools that do this for Java:

  • japicmp: compares two jars and reports binary and source incompatibilities. It has a Maven plugin, and there are Gradle plugins for it.

  • Revapi: API analysis with configurable rules, for Maven and Gradle.

  • binary-compatibility-validator: for Kotlin libraries, built on a committed API dump.

  • Bumpwise: our IntelliJ IDEA plugin. It compares the code in the editor with the last published release, highlights each breaking change while you type, offers the compatible alternative (such as keeping the old signature as @Deprecated) and calculates the next version.

The first three run in the build, usually in CI. Bumpwise runs before the change is committed. They work well together: one check while you write, one before you release.

Disclosure: Gilware makes Bumpwise, a paid plugin with a free edition for Java libraries published on Maven Central.

How we checked

For each change we compiled the 1.0 library, compiled a small client against it, compiled the 1.1 library, then ran the old client with the new jar and recompiled the client against 1.1. OpenJDK 25.0.5. The error messages above are copied from those runs.

Found a mistake? Write to hello@gilware.com.

Originally published at gilware.com.

title: AI Prototyping inside your design system. A hands-on guide for design & product teams.
description:
In-System Design

Why builders hand you a lookalike, what has to exist before an agent can use your components, and the MCP setup I use.

Prototyping in code is what designers do now, at least according to LinkedIn. I tried it, and after two days I wanted to throw my laptop into the sea. Good news: I came out with a process I actually like, and that works, and that is what this article is. So here is what happened:

It started with every team I worked with suddenly turning up with the same frustration. They had connected their design system to an AI builder, described a screen, and got back something that looked finished. Leadership loved it. Then a developer opened the code, said something unrepeatable, and rebuilt it from scratch with the actual design system.

I did not understand it either at first. It was connected to the real design system, so what was wrong? So I started poking around the code, comparing it to the original.

The answer sits in the code, and that is the whole problem. Developers see it in a glance and are quietly furious: why are you handing me this? Everyone else sees a screen that works: looks fine, just ship it. Both are right; neither can explain it to the other, and this is how I ended up in my favourite workshops again: translating between the two.

This gap is not just awkward; it is expensive. Plans get made as if the AI prototype were most of the work, dates get promised on it, and then the rebuild happens quietly under pressure, while capable people work late to keep up with a speed AI promised, not understanding what went wrong and trying to fix it with more DESIGN.md files.

It happens often enough to have a name. Writing in Forbes, Yunhao Jiao calls it the prototype wall: excitement in week one, concerns around week three, abandonment by month two.

Before the solution (and yes, there is one, actually more than one), a quick look at what is actually going on. It takes a minute, and I know you want to skip ahead, but don’t; it helps you tell whether the next prototyping product you launch is useful when you work in a design system.

Why ready-made AI builders will not give you the output you need when working with a design system

The Lovables, Bolts and Claude Designs of this world all have a little button that says connect your design system. Not false advertising; that would be harsh, and nobody is trying to trick anyone (who would do that in tech and AI?!). They do read your design system indeed, then build their own version of it, usually (but not all) on shadcn and Tailwind.

The first screen looks close. The more you prompt, the more it invents, and nothing that comes out points at your real components. Totally fine for a quick idea, but useless for something you have to build and maintain inside a design system to scale and ship. Different tools for different jobs.

Prompting harder will not fix it, and neither will another markdown file. The problem is not the instructions. The components are not real.

I started writing a breakdown of each builder, got halfway, and realised it will be out of date by the time you read it. So, two prompts instead.

Ask the builder, after it has generated a screen:

Show me the code for the primary button on this screen. Which file is that component imported from, and which props did you set? Do not change anything. Compare it to my original design system button and show me similarities or differences.

Or ask an AI to read the docs for you:

Read the official documentation for [tool]. Using only the docs, with quotes and links: when I connect my design system, does it install my component package and use my components with their props, or does it copy and rebuild them? Where does the generated code live, and how do I get it out?

Example: Claude Design.
I have to admit Claude Design surprised me; it does a better job than I expected. However, let’s look at the details because it is still (and this might change rapidly) not what we need: The marketing says it builds with your real design system components and checks its output against your system. The setup docs say Claude “extracts” them from whatever you give it: a codebase, design files, even slide decks. Those are two different sentences, so I gave it my own repo to prototype with and had a closer look at our all-time favourite component: the button.

Every prop, value and default came back right, and my CSS came with it, every token name intact, no invented colours. But Base UI had been dropped for its own helpers, my scoped classes had become global copies, and the types were gone. Its own handover note says it plainly: “This is a recreation for design and prototyping.” A very good copy, frozen the day it was made, that a developer cannot simply merge.

📌 Note, 26 October 2026. Claude Design moves into Claude in December, and their setup already flags the Claude Code route as the higher-fidelity one for React. So this recreation step may quietly disappear. Run the prompt above and you will know before I do.

What you actually need: a component list and an MCP

The difference isn’t a better prompt. It is two pieces: a list of what your design system really contains, and a connection the agent can ask through.

A list to pick components from: the manifest

A component in code is correct, complete and something you would have to read line by line to work out what it offers. A designer gives up halfway, and an agent burns through its budget wading through thousands of files doing the same.

What an agent needs instead is the component as a list. One entry per component: its name, what it is for, every property, every allowed value, every default. Write it once, generate it from the code, and add nothing. In most setups, that file is JSON and it is called a manifest, and it looks a bit like this:

Read it the way the agent does: there is a Button; it is the primary action trigger; it comes in four variants and three sizes; and unless told otherwise, it is primary and medium. That list has no room for a fifth variant.

Three things worth knowing about it:

  • It is generated, not written. Storybook, for example, produces one from your stories and your component types. A script can write one. A custom setup usually keeps a richer version with tokens and patterns alongside the components.
  • It is not documentation and not a design file. It is the facts, written once, so nobody has to interpret them. A very boring inventory list.
  • It is yours. Any agent can read it, so it does not tie you to one tool. More important than you might think.
And it is why everything else becomes possible: the agent picks instead of inventing; it is cheap to read compared with a whole repository; checks become possible because there is something to compare against; and gaps become visible because anything that cannot go in the list becomes a conversation.

No list, no AI prototyping, however good your components are.

The connection: MCP, so the agent asks instead of remembering

The list has to be reachable while the agent works, and the standard for that is MCP, the Model Context Protocol: the plug that connects your design system, so the agent can ask what exists instead of guessing. You may know it from the Figma MCP, which lets an AI read your Figma file directly. In Claude, these are called connectors, same thing.

Without it, an agent answers from memory, and it has seen thousands of design systems, so you get the most common version of a button, with bits of yours mixed in. With it, every answer comes from your system, in this session.

Why it holds: no step trusts the one before it

Five things have to happen in a solid setup, and none of them is visible to you:

  1. Look it up, do not remember. Every session starts by asking the system what exists today. A model’s memory of your Button is the one thing you can be sure is out of date.
  2. Choose, do not invent. The agent composes from a closed list: these components, these values, these tokens. Nothing in the prompt should be able to add a fifth variant.
  3. Check against the system, not against taste. Automatically, before a human looks: are these real components, real tokens, does it meet the rules your team wrote down.
  4. Look at the rendered thing. Code that parses is not UI that works, and neither of you can tell from the code alone.
  5. A person decides. Everything green means the machine found nothing. It does not mean the work is good.

Two ways to get one

For prototyping with your own system in code, there are currently two realistic routes (check the date; this stuff moves fast). Both are built by developers. Your job is to know which one to ask for and what it costs them.

(There is a third, on the canvas side, where you prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code. Figma clicks into this far more smoothly than most people think, and it gets its own article, part 3 of this series, on 10 November 2026.)

Wait, can’t I just send the agent straight into the code?

In a small system, yes. My own website has a handful of components, and setting all of this up there was overkill. In a real system it breaks in two ways. The first is noise: the agent wades through thousands of files, internal helpers and types, which is slow and expensive. Storybook’s own test found its MCP used 27% fewer tokens and finished almost three times faster. The second is drift: code shows what exists, not what was intended. A product repo holds every old version, every one-off and every hand-built copy, and an agent copies whatever it finds most of, so the drift spreads. The MCP answers only with what the system sanctions. A custom one adds what code can’t say at all: the patterns your team agreed on and the rules that check them.

Where exactly the line sits, I don’t know, and I haven’t seen anyone put a number on it. The signs are easier to spot: the agent rebuilds a component that already exists, copies an old pattern instead of the current one, or sessions get noticeably slower and pricier. If you’ve found where that point is for your team, I’d be happy to hear it. Till then let’s have a look at our option and you just give it a go:

1. The Storybook MCP, the quick and easy route.

Most design systems already have a Storybook, which is why I start here with teams.

In case you have not met it: Storybook is a website that shows every component in your codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the code itself, with a small stories file next to each component listing its examples, so what you click through is built from the real thing.

That part you probably already have. The Storybook MCP add-on is what lets an agent use it too: it passes your component list over, so you prompt and get a prototype made of real components. Most of what I described above comes with it, the list, the preview, running your tests, and even the wording for your rules file, since the docs hand you a snippet that tells your agent never to invent a property. What does not come with it are the gates at the end, which stay with your team’s checks.

Normally your developers set this up once and give you a branch to prototype on, and that is the version I would ask for. You can also do it yourself, which is what I did. Start on a playground design system rather than the real product: I keep a small one for trainings, and any little open-source system works too. If it has no Storybook yet, that is fine, your agent can add one.

One thing to sort out first: you need an agent that works inside your project, like Claude Code or Codex. What that means in practice is that a design system is a folder of files. You download it, you open that folder with Claude Code, and from then on the AI can read those files, change them and start things up on your machine. A chat window only ever sees what you paste into it.

Then give your agent this:

Set up the Storybook MCP in this repo, following the official docs at https://storybook.js.org/docs/ai/mcp/overview. Install the add-on, switch on the components manifest, add the MCP server to my agent, and paste the agent instructions snippet from the docs into my agent’s rules file, whichever one this project uses. Then verify by listing all documented components, and tell me what you changed and anything you could not do.

What it needs: Storybook 10 or newer (it will tell you if you do not have it, and the prompt above updates it), the components manifest switched on since it is off by default, and either a branch you are allowed to work on, which your dev team sets up, or a local playground folder you connect to. After that the agent can see your components and their guidelines, find and write stories, show you a preview, and run your tests.

Using the Storybook MCP to prototype

Point your agent at the folder or branch you are allowed to work in, then ask it to open Storybook. It starts on your own machine, at an address like localhost:6001, which is a website only you can see. Nothing is published, nothing leaves your laptop, and you can close it again by stopping it.

Then I just talk to it:

Using the Storybook MCP, make a separate section for prototyping, and create my first prototype: a sign-in and a register page. Use only components from my system. If something does not exist, piece it together from what is there, mark it clearly, and tell me what you had to invent.

A minute later there is a prototyping section in my Storybook with a page made of real components, clickable, running locally.

📌 Tip: I always ask for a short list underneath of what it used and what it had to make up. I still do “need” to invent here and there, but I need to know.

That is the whole experience from where I sit. A prompt and a result, with all the machinery out of sight, and something to hand over that makes sense to a developer.

Add a skill long term
By the third run you will be typing the same corrections. That is the moment for a skill: a packaged set of instructions your agent loads automatically for this job. Mine says which components may be used, how to mark anything invented, and what to write underneath. One safety note, since a skill can run code on your machine: install them from people you trust, or have a developer look first.

2. A custom design system MCP, the serious route

What a team with engineers builds for its own system, and where the best results come from, because everything in it is shaped around what that system actually holds.

The gist is always the same. A server answers from machine-readable files about the system: every component with its real properties, every token, and the compositions the team has agreed are the right way to build a pattern. The agent has to query that before it writes anything, the generated code gets checked back against the same files, rendered so somebody can look at it, reviewed by you, and run through the team’s automated checks before anything merges.

Beyond that they differ a lot, and the ones I have seen vary in what they hold, how strict they are, and where the checks sit. Brad Frost was kind enough to give me a tour of his, which goes by the name Eddie, and it was quietly mad: I had a conversation with it and watched a page assemble itself in front of me, theme changes and all, in something that is not a chat window. I later worked through the course he runs with Ian Frost and TJ Pitre (no advert; it just truly helped me), which is where the pieces finally clicked for me. I am building a small MCP for my own products and for teaching now, from the design side rather than the engineering one, enjoying it more than I expected and learning a ton.

Another interesting read about building custom prototyping tools with AI is this one by Atlassian, published in November 2025

Using a custom design system MCP

You still point your agent at a branch and describe a screen. And this is the experience you should have working with it.

The difference is what happens out of sight: it asks a system built for exactly this, so it knows your patterns as well as your components; it knows which combinations your team has blessed, and it follows your rules rather than a generic snippet. You notice it in the small things: fewer corrections, fewer invented layouts, and a gaps list that is about your product instead of about the tooling. The one I saw was also significantly faster, close to real time at times. The cost is that somebody has to build and keep it, which is why it belongs to teams who ship a system rather than to one designer with a playground.

Which one to ask for

  • No Storybook, no engineers to spare: fix that first. Nothing here works without a component list, and Storybook is the cheapest way to get one.
  • Small teams, Storybook already there: ask for the MCP add-on, the manifest switched on, and a branch to work on. An afternoon of developer time.
  • Enterprise with a design system team: they will most likely build a custom MCP, because they can staff it. More power, and more governance to agree before anything moves.
  • Nothing is ready: do not reach for a builder to fill the gap. Clean up what you have, and prototype in Figma against a library that mirrors the code until the code side catches up.

Either way, this infrastructure is development work. What a designer can do is ask for the right three things: a component list, a connection, and branch access.

Oh no, but I already have so much vibe-coded work!

In the long run, I recommend one of these approaches outlined above; however, there is a really fun Skill by called vibe killer by Brad Frost that gets all your vibed mess back into the system. I haven’t personally used it in a real setup yet, but go for it and tell me how it went. It looks very promising, and I love the name.

Handing off an AI prototype

The prototype still gets rebuilt, and knowing what happens next changes how you build it.

In a decent setup, you work on a design branch (it could be called anything; I took the naming from this article by TJ Pitre, as it makes a lot of sense) and hand over what you built. The design branch itself is never merged. Accepted ideas are rebuilt on a feature branch, and that is where the pull request happens: a formal way of saying, come and look at this before it goes in.

Then: developers add what a prototype does not have: real data, loading, errors, empty states. Then come the automated checks that run on every proposed change, which is what people mean when they say CI: tests, accessibility, responsiveness, whether everything used is a real component, and performance. Some teams add an AI eval that reads the change and asks whether it follows the rules and does what the ticket asked. Then a person approves it, because a green build is not a yes. It runs through all of this stuff; you don’t need to know the details, but you need to know it is there.

So why bother, if it gets checked and partly rebuilt anyway? Because the rebuild is cheap when the parts already exist. A developer transcribes decisions instead of reverse-engineering a picture.

Also, you find out now, while it is still a prototype, whether the system can express what you designed. And the thing you hand over behaves, so you can test it with people instead of asking them to imagine a click.

If you get the chance, ask your developers to show you what their checks do with your prototype. One session of that will teach you more than a year of handover templates.

📌 Tip: this is the step your prototype walks into, and somebody has already automated it. Brad Frost has published skills that carry a finished Storybook page into the product’s codebase and all the way to a pull request, with a build, a side-by-side comparison and accessibility checks on the way. Send it to your developers, and read it yourself: it spells out what a careful handover actually involves, which is useful the next time somebody tells you the prototype is basically done.

What this does not solve

  • It needs a system worth prototyping with. Messy components produce tidy-looking nonsense.
  • It does not tell you what to build. Perfect components plus no knowledge of your users gives you consistent, average screens.
  • It is not production code, however real it looks.
  • There is no established workflow yet, mine included. This is a few months of my own trial and error, and the parts I would bet on are the component list and the checks, not my exact prompts.
  • Both sides, design and dev, have to move. Designers need to get near a codebase, which starts with asking for access. Developers need to make the system readable and open the door. Neither is a tooling problem.

And the canvas? Very much alive

Remember the laptop I wanted to throw into the sea? Everything above fixes most of that, not all of it. Prototyping in code is useful, and handing over in code matters more than ever, but I still do my best thinking on a canvas, with several versions next to each other and notes beside them.

Ditching Figma has become a sort of credential this year, and I have yet to see a link between how loudly a tool gets declared dead and the quality of what ships. Figma is also moving: it has shown something called Code Sources, still in closed beta, which would let a Figma file point at the real components in a codebase instead of at a copy of them (neither Make nor Code Layers do that today). And now you know what that means! If it ships the way it was demoed, a good part of what I do by hand disappears. Nothing here depends on it, and it is the release I am watching most closely.

Until then, I do not have to choose. When your Figma library mirrors the code, the same agent works on both sides, and a prototype can move between them made of the same real components. I want to work where the work is best done, wherever the job needs me that day, and I call that In-System Design. The canvas half of it is part 3 of this series, out on 10 November 2026.

Sources:
The custom MCP thinking in this article owes a lot to Brad Frost, Ian Frost and TJ Pitre’s course.
The Storybook details come from their MCP documentation.

📖 Words in this article

  • MCP (Model Context Protocol): a standard plug that lets an AI connect to a tool like Figma or Storybook and read from it or act in it.
  • Manifest: the component as a list. Every property, allowed value and default, written once, generated from the code. Storybook can produce one, switched on in its config.
  • Storybook: a website that shows every component of a codebase, live and clickable. It lives inside the codebase rather than keeping its own copy.
  • Story: one example of a component, written next to it in the code.
  • Props: the options a component has in code (size, variant, disabled). Figma calls them component properties.
  • Design branch: a parallel copy of the codebase that developers set up for designers. Nothing you do there can reach the product. I read this idea first in an article by TJ Pitre.
  • Pull request: a formal proposal to change the real product, reviewed before it is accepted.
  • CI (continuous integration): checks that run automatically on every proposed change.
  • Eval: an AI reading the work and judging it against a standard. Useful, not deterministic.
  • Skill: a packaged set of instructions an agent loads automatically for a recurring job. Powerful, and worth vetting before you install one.
  • In-System Design (my term): designing with the real components of the system, on whichever surface the task needs, instead of next to the system in a tool that rebuilds it.

About the author: Christine Vallaure

I’m Christine Vallaure. I design, I teach, and I spend an unreasonable amount of my time on articles like this one. Through moonlearning.io I teach Figma, design systems and AI workflows to designers and teams. Along the way I speak at conferences like Figma Config and Smashing Conference, mostly about where design meets code, and I am a member of the Awwwards jury.

I write these articles with an AI assistant, from my own notes, recordings and repositories. The thinking, the examples and the opinions are mine, and so is the final wording and tone.

Sign up for the newsletter to keep up.
