title: Backend Cron Alternatives for Scheduled Go Scripts with HTTP Digest Recovery
description:
For backend cron alternatives, use a durable queue behind the timer when scheduled Go scripts must deliver a weekly customer digest over HTTP.

Short answer: let the scheduler create one digest job per active customer, let a worker own delivery and retries, and record an idempotency key before sending. A cron expression is only a trigger. It does not tell you what happened to the work after the process exited.

For a support system, that distinction matters. A digest may contain open tickets, response-time summaries, and links to conversations. Missing one is visible to a customer; sending it twice is also visible. I treat operational recovery as the deciding axis, not the lowest advertised price.

How should backend cron alternatives run scheduled scripts with HTTP safely?

The awkward failure is not a refused connection. It is the timeout after the remote service accepted the request. The caller cannot know whether retrying will create a duplicate. A worker that retries blindly can turn a transient network event into two weekly emails or two downstream digest records.

There are several clocks in play: the schedule clock, the queue visibility timeout, the HTTP client timeout, and the recipient's own processing time. They need explicit boundaries. For example, a 10-minute worker lease cannot protect a request that is allowed to hang for 12 minutes. The lease expires, another worker starts, and both workers may send.

The job payload should be small and reconstructable. Store a customer ID, the digest period, and a deterministic key such as digest:customer-482:2026-W43; fetch the current support data when the worker runs. Do not put a mutable ticket dump into a scheduler payload and assume it will remain correct for seven days.

I start with a boring state model: queued, running, sent, and failed. sent is terminal. A failed attempt carries the next attempt time and an error category. The schedule itself is not the retry mechanism.

A small Go worker with an idempotency boundary

The following example shows the control flow rather than a vendor SDK. Store.MarkSending must be an atomic operation backed by a uniqueness constraint on the digest key. The sender must accept the same key and make its operation idempotent, or the application needs an outbox and a provider-side deduplication contract.

package digest

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "time"
)

var ErrAlreadySent = errors.New("digest already sent")

type Store interface {
    MarkSending(ctx context.Context, key string, now time.Time) error
    MarkSent(ctx context.Context, key string, sentAt time.Time) error
    MarkRetry(ctx context.Context, key string, next time.Time, reason string) error
}

type Sender interface {
    Send(ctx context.Context, customerID, period, key string) error
}

func Deliver(ctx context.Context, store Store, sender Sender, customerID, period string, now time.Time) error {
    key := fmt.Sprintf("digest:%s:%s", customerID, period)
    if err := store.MarkSending(ctx, key, now); err != nil {
        if errors.Is(err, ErrAlreadySent) {
            return nil
        }
        return err
    }

    sendCtx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, 30*time.Second)
    defer cancel()
    if err := sender.Send(sendCtx, customerID, period, key); err != nil {
        return store.MarkRetry(ctx, key, now.Add(15*time.Minute), err.Error())
    }
    return store.MarkSent(ctx, key, time.Now().UTC())
}

There is an uncomfortable boundary here: Send can succeed and MarkSent can fail. That is why a production design should expose delivery status and reconcile old sending records. A reconciliation job can ask the delivery system for the idempotency key, or safely re-submit the same key if the sender guarantees deduplication. A database transaction cannot make an arbitrary HTTP endpoint atomic.

The 30-second timeout is an example policy, not a universal setting. Measure the endpoint's normal latency, choose a limit that leaves room inside the worker lease, and test the timeout path. The important part is that a request has a deadline and that a retry has a reason.

That is the trade-off.

How should the schedule and queue divide the work?

The weekly timer should do one bounded task: enumerate active customers and enqueue deterministic jobs. It should not render every digest and call every HTTP endpoint in one process. If it dies after customer 482, the next run can safely attempt to enqueue the same keys; the queue or database rejects duplicates.

A queue worker then handles backoff, concurrency, visibility renewal, and dead-letter handling. Exponential backoff avoids a synchronized retry storm. A maximum attempt count prevents one malformed customer record from consuming worker capacity forever. Permanent errors, such as an invalid recipient address, should be separated from transient errors, such as a connection reset.

Keep the schedule timestamp in UTC and derive the period from an explicit business timezone. A customer-support digest for a Monday morning local window should not depend on the machine timezone of whichever worker happens to run it. Around daylight-saving transitions, store the intended period and test both repeated and skipped local times.

For HTTP delivery, log the digest key, customer ID, period, attempt number, response class, and elapsed time. Do not log the digest body or authorization header. Alert on the age of the oldest queued job and on the count of jobs in failed or sending beyond their expected lease. A successful scheduler heartbeat proves almost nothing about delivery.

What do external automation tools change?

Visual automation products can shorten the path from a timer to an HTTP action, but the operational contract still needs to be read carefully. Zapier's paths and task history are useful for straightforward business workflows; the engineering question is how its retry, replay, retention, and idempotency behavior maps to the digest key. n8n can be self-hosted and lets a team inspect workflow execution data, but that shifts upgrades, persistence, worker capacity, and incident response into the team's ownership. GitHub Actions can run scheduled workflows and scripts, but repository workflow scheduling is a different operating model from a customer-facing delivery queue, especially when backlog control and per-customer replay matter.

Those are boundaries, not rankings. A timer plus HTTP step may be enough for a non-critical internal cleanup. A customer digest needs an answer to four questions before adoption: where is the durable job record, how is a duplicate prevented, how is a poisoned job isolated, and how can an operator replay one period for one customer? If the answers require a spreadsheet and manual clicking, the apparent simplicity is hiding operational work.

Here is the comparison I use before choosing an implementation:

Option Integration Setup effort Fits best Main limitation
Kubernetes CronJob Container command Medium A scheduled batch already running in a cluster Scheduling does not provide idempotent HTTP delivery
Cloud Tasks REST or client library Medium Delayed HTTP work with queue-level retries The application still owns digest state and reconciliation
Zapier Visual actions and webhooks Low Small business workflows with modest replay needs Execution history and retry semantics may not match a per-customer recovery contract
n8n Visual workflow or HTTP node Medium Teams willing to operate workflow persistence Self-hosting moves upgrades, capacity, and incident response to the team
GitHub Actions YAML workflow and scripts Low Repository maintenance and developer automation Repository scheduling is a poor fit for customer backlog control

The table is a boundary map, not a leaderboard. The cheapest setup can still leave an operator without a safe replay button.

A backend cron process is not automatically better. Kubernetes CronJob documents scheduling semantics and concurrency policies, but it does not turn an application-level HTTP side effect into an exactly-once operation. A managed task service can provide delayed delivery and retry controls, while a queue with a dead-letter queue makes failed messages inspectable. The useful comparison is the failure contract each option makes visible. The limitation of a timer-only design is clear: it knows that the invocation began, but not whether the remote system accepted the request before the connection failed.

Verification, rollback, and the 03:00 check

Before production, run a matrix of deliberate failures: kill the scheduler after enqueueing half the customers; return HTTP 429 and 500 responses; delay the response beyond the client deadline; terminate a worker after the remote side accepts the request; and replay the same period twice. The expected result is boring: one durable job key, bounded retries, a visible terminal failure, and no duplicate digest.

I would also run a dry period against a fixed fixture of active customers. Compare the generated set with the expected set, then inspect a sample of rendered links. This catches a more ordinary incident: a query that silently excludes customers because “active” was interpreted as “logged in during the last seven days.”

Rollback should disable new scheduling without deleting queued jobs. Let workers drain, or pause them while an operator decides whether the new code can safely process old payloads. Keep the schema able to read the previous job version. If the sender format changes, include a payload version in the key and make the migration explicit.

The 03:00 check is a useful runbook item: inspect the oldest queued job, the last successful digest period, retry counts by error class, and the reconciliation age. If those four signals look healthy, investigate the recipient-facing system next. Do not declare success from the scheduler's “completed” log line.

The decision rule is straightforward. Use a timer alone for work that can be safely repeated and has no customer-facing consequence. Add a durable queue, idempotency key, and reconciliation path when a missed or duplicated HTTP side effect needs an operator-visible recovery process. That rule survives changes in vendors, runtimes, and deployment platforms.

References

  • AWS, “Using Amazon SQS dead-letter queues”: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSSimpleQueueService/latest/SQSDeveloperGuide/sqs-dead-letter-queues.html
  • Google Cloud, “Cloud Tasks overview”: https://cloud.google.com/tasks/docs/dual-overview
  • Kubernetes, “CronJob”: https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/controllers/cron-jobs/
  • HTTP Semantics, RFC 9110: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110
  • Zapier, “How to handle errors in Zaps”: https://help.zapier.com/hc/en-us/articles/8496288698253-How-to-handle-errors-in-Zaps
  • n8n, “Queue mode”: https://docs.n8n.io/hosting/scaling/queue-mode/
  • GitHub Docs, “Events that trigger workflows”: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/using-workflows/events-that-trigger-workflows

title: React Query Showed the Wrong User's Data — Here's How to Reproduce and Fix It
description:
A React dashboard can display the wrong user's data even when the API is returning the correct response.

One of the easiest ways to introduce this bug is by using a query key that doesn't account for the current user.

Consider this:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders"],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

It looks perfectly reasonable.

But there's a problem.

The query function depends on userId, while the cache key doesn't.

If Alice's orders are already cached and the application switches to Bob, both users can end up sharing the same cache entry.

Depending on the query's freshness settings, Bob's dashboard could display Alice's previously cached orders.

I wanted to break down why this happens because it's the kind of issue that's easy to overlook when testing with only one account.

We'll reproduce it in a small React application, fix the query key, and then look at what changes when authentication, logout, and multiple SaaS workspaces are involved.

Alice logs in and opens her orders page. Everything looks fine.

She logs out, and Bob logs in using the same browser.

But Bob sees something unexpected.

Alice's orders are still showing on his dashboard.

You check the backend. The API works. The database queries are correct. Your authorization checks appear to be doing their job.

So why is Bob seeing Alice's data?

The issue might be hiding in one line of React Query code:

queryKey: ["orders"]

That looks harmless, doesn't it?

But when the data depends on the authenticated user, this query key doesn't tell TanStack Query whose orders it's caching.

Let's reproduce the issue, understand why it happens, and fix it properly.

We'll also look at a few related problems that are easy to miss in production: switching workspaces, logging out, and displaying previous data while a new request loads.

1. The bug starts with a perfectly normal-looking query

Consider a React component that fetches the current user's orders.

import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

function Orders({ userId }) {
  const { data, isPending } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ["orders"],
    queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
  });

  if (isPending) {
    return <p>Loading orders...</p>;
  }

  return <OrdersTable orders={data} />;
}

At first glance, there's nothing unusual here.

We have a query key, a query function, and a loading state.

The problem is that fetchOrders() depends on userId, but the query key doesn't.

Let's say Alice has these orders:

[
  { "id": 101, "product": "MacBook Pro" },
  { "id": 102, "product": "Keyboard" }
]

And Bob has these:

[
  { "id": 201, "product": "Monitor" },
  { "id": 202, "product": "Mouse" }
]

Our React component requests different data depending on the user.

But TanStack Query sees this:

Alice → ["orders"]

Bob   → ["orders"]

It's the same cache key.

TanStack Query doesn't automatically inspect the variables inside your query function to identify the data.

It relies on the query key you provide.

If two requests use the same key, they're treated as requests for the same cached query.

And that's where things can go wrong.

2. Let's reproduce the problem

Instead of stopping at the explanation, let's create a small React application where you can see the bug yourself.

We'll use Vite and TanStack Query.

No backend or database is required for this demonstration.

The data is mocked so we can focus entirely on caching behavior. We're simulating account switching, not implementing real authentication.

Step 1: Create the project

Run:

npm create vite@latest react-query-cache-demo -- --template react

cd react-query-cache-demo

npm install

npm install @tanstack/react-query

npm run dev

Step 2: Configure QueryClient

Open src/main.jsx and replace its contents with:

import React from "react";
import ReactDOM from "react-dom/client";

import {
  QueryClient,
  QueryClientProvider,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";

import App from "./App.jsx";

const queryClient = new QueryClient();

ReactDOM.createRoot(
  document.getElementById("root")
).render(
  <React.StrictMode>
    <QueryClientProvider client={queryClient}>
      <App />
    </QueryClientProvider>
  </React.StrictMode>
);

Step 3: Create the demo

Now replace src/App.jsx with:

import { useState } from "react";
import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const ordersDatabase = {
  alice: [
    { id: 101, product: "MacBook Pro" },
    { id: 102, product: "Keyboard" },
  ],
  bob: [
    { id: 201, product: "Monitor" },
    { id: 202, product: "Mouse" },
  ],
};

async function fetchOrders(userId) {
  // Simulate network latency
  await new Promise((resolve) =>
    setTimeout(resolve, 500)
  );

  return ordersDatabase[userId];
}

export default function App() {
  const [userId, setUserId] = useState("alice");
  const [fixed, setFixed] = useState(false);

  const {
    data: orders = [],
    isPending,
  } = useQuery({
    queryKey: fixed
      ? ["orders", userId]
      : ["orders"],

    queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),

    // Keep cached data fresh for this demo
    staleTime: Infinity,
  });

  return (
    <div style={{ padding: 24 }}>
      <h1>Orders Dashboard</h1>

      <p>
        Logged in as: <strong>{userId}</strong>
      </p>

      <button onClick={() => setUserId("alice")}>
        Switch to Alice
      </button>

      <button onClick={() => setUserId("bob")}>
        Switch to Bob
      </button>

      <hr />

      <label>
        <input
          type="checkbox"
          checked={fixed}
          onChange={(event) =>
            setFixed(event.target.checked)
          }
        />
        Use correct query key
      </label>

      <h2>Orders</h2>

      {isPending ? (
        <p>Loading...</p>
      ) : (
        <ul>
          {orders.map((order) => (
            <li key={order.id}>
              #{order.id} - {order.product}
            </li>
          ))}
        </ul>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}

Step 4: See what happens

Open the application.

Initially, Alice is selected.

Wait for her orders to load.

You should see:

Logged in as: alice

Orders:
#101 - MacBook Pro
#102 - Keyboard

Now click Switch to Bob without enabling the checkbox.

You might expect Bob's orders to appear.

But the screen still shows:

Logged in as: bob

Orders:
#101 - MacBook Pro
#102 - Keyboard

That's the bug.

We're displaying Alice's cached orders while the interface says Bob is the current user.

Why does this happen?

Our query key hasn't changed:

queryKey: ["orders"]

We also deliberately configured:

staleTime: Infinity

This tells TanStack Query to consider the cached data fresh indefinitely, unless it is manually invalidated.

Because the cache key remains unchanged and the data is considered fresh, changing userId doesn't trigger a new query.

This setting makes the problem easy to reproduce.

With the default stale-time configuration, you may see different refetching behavior depending on when the query mounts or is invalidated. But the underlying problem remains: two different datasets are sharing one cache identity.

3. Fixing it with the correct query key

The fix is straightforward.

Instead of:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders"],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

Use:

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["orders", userId],
  queryFn: () => fetchOrders(userId),
});

Now the cache keys are different:

Alice → ["orders", "alice"]

Bob   → ["orders", "bob"]

TanStack Query can distinguish the two datasets.

Go back to the demo and enable Use correct query key.

Switch between Alice and Bob again.

The orders should now match the selected account.

When you switch back to Alice, her previously fetched data can be retrieved from her own cache entry.

That's exactly the behavior we want.

Here's the principle I follow:

If a variable changes which data your query returns, it probably belongs in the query key.

Not every variable needs to be part of the key. But variables that determine the identity of the requested data do.

4. The same mistake becomes more complicated in multi-tenant SaaS applications

Now imagine a more realistic application.

You're working on a SaaS platform where a single account can belong to multiple organizations.

For example:

Alice
  |
  |-- Company A
  |     |-- Orders
  |     |-- Customers
  |
  |-- Company B
        |-- Orders
        |-- Customers

Alice can switch between Company A and Company B without logging out.

You might already be using this query key:

queryKey: ["orders", userId]

It separates Alice's data from Bob's.

But it doesn't separate Company A's orders from Company B's.

Both organizations still share the same key for Alice.

A better key would be:

queryKey: [
  "orders",
  userId,
  organizationId,
]

And what if the orders table has filters?

Suppose users can filter by order status, search terms, or pages.

Those variables also affect the result.

queryKey: [
  "orders",
  userId,
  organizationId,
  {
    status,
    page,
    search,
  },
]

Now each dataset has its own cache identity.

For example:

["orders", "alice", "company-a", { page: 1 }]

["orders", "alice", "company-b", { page: 1 }]

["orders", "bob", "company-b", { page: 1 }]

One important detail: don't include access tokens, passwords, or other secrets in query keys.

Use stable, non-secret identifiers.

And remember that cache scoping is not authorization. Even if a user manipulates a query key, the backend must independently check permissions.

5. How I'd structure the query in a real application

For a workspace-based SaaS application, I prefer keeping the query logic inside a reusable hook.

Something like this:

import { useQuery } from "@tanstack/react-query";

async function fetchWorkspaceOrders({
  workspaceId,
  status,
  page,
  signal,
}) {
  const params = new URLSearchParams({
    status,
    page: String(page),
  });

  const response = await fetch(
    `/api/workspaces/${encodeURIComponent(workspaceId)}/orders?${params}`,
    {
      credentials: "include",
      signal,
    }
  );

  if (response.status === 401) {
    throw new Error("Authentication required");
  }

  if (response.status === 403) {
    throw new Error("Access denied");
  }

  if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to fetch orders");
  }

  return response.json();
}

export function useWorkspaceOrders({
  userId,
  workspaceId,
  status = "all",
  page = 1,
}) {
  return useQuery({
    queryKey: [
      "orders",
      userId,
      workspaceId,
      { status, page },
    ],

    queryFn: ({ signal }) =>
      fetchWorkspaceOrders({
        workspaceId,
        status,
        page,
        signal,
      }),

    enabled: Boolean(userId && workspaceId),
  });
}

There are a few details worth understanding.

The query key describes the data. It includes the account, workspace, and filters that determine the response.

The enabled option prevents automatic fetching until the required identifiers are available. It doesn't remove cached data or enforce access control.

The query function uses the supplied AbortSignal. This allows obsolete requests to be cancelled when TanStack Query cancels the query.

HTTP errors are handled explicitly. The browser's fetch() function doesn't automatically reject a promise for responses such as 403 or 500.

For this example, I'm assuming the backend uses cookie-based authentication. If your application uses bearer tokens or another mechanism, the request implementation will be different.

The query key should still reflect the authenticated data context.

6. Don't forget what happens on logout

Correct query keys solve an important problem, but I wouldn't stop there.

Consider a shared computer.

Alice logs in, opens her dashboard, and logs out.

Then Bob logs in using the same browser tab.

If both sessions use the same QueryClient, Alice's previously fetched data can remain in its in-memory cache even after her session ends.

Correctly scoped keys help prevent the new session from accidentally requesting Alice's cached data.

But for private information, I generally prefer clearing the previous session's cached state when the authentication boundary changes.

TanStack Query provides:

queryClient.clear();

This clears both the query cache and mutation cache associated with that client.

You can also cancel active queries:

await queryClient.cancelQueries();

But the order of operations matters.

A safer logout strategy

The application should immediately stop displaying authenticated screens when logout begins.

Then it should coordinate request cancellation, cache cleanup, and session revocation.

Here's a simplified example:

async function handleLogout() {
  // The application must stop rendering private screens.
  setAuthStatus("signing-out");

  // Cancel active queries.
  await queryClient.cancelQueries();

  // Clear in-memory query and mutation caches.
  queryClient.clear();

  // Revoke the authenticated session on the server.
  const response = await fetch("/api/logout", {
    method: "POST",
    credentials: "include",
  });

  if (!response.ok) {
    // Keep private screens hidden and provide
    // a way to retry or recover from this error.
    setAuthStatus("logout-error");
    return;
  }

  setAuthStatus("signed-out");
}

This assumes your application uses authStatus to stop rendering all protected components when the value isn't an authenticated state.

It's an example of the sequence, not a complete authentication implementation.

A few things are important here:

  • Clearing React Query's cache doesn't revoke a server session.
  • Cancelling a query doesn't undo a request the server has already processed.
  • An unsuccessful logout request must not be presented as successful server-side logout.
  • If you're persisting queries to browser storage, that persisted data must be handled separately.
  • Other caches, global stores, service workers, and open browser tabs may also need attention.

For applications with sensitive information, the full authentication lifecycle deserves its own design and testing.

A cache clear is useful, but it isn't a complete security solution.

7. Another mistake: showing previous data during account switches

There's another subtle situation worth understanding.

TanStack Query supports showing previous query data while the next result loads.

For example:

import {
  keepPreviousData,
  useQuery,
} from "@tanstack/react-query";

const { data } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ["products", page],
  queryFn: () => fetchProducts(page),
  placeholderData: keepPreviousData,
});

This is often useful for pagination.

Instead of briefly displaying an empty table whenever the page changes, you can keep showing the previous page until the new result arrives.

That's a good experience for many interfaces.

But imagine using the same approach when switching between private workspaces.

Even with correctly scoped query keys, previous-data placeholders can temporarily display information belonging to the previous workspace.

The query cache entries may be isolated correctly, while the component still renders the previous result as placeholder data.

These are different behaviors.

For public product listings, this might be harmless.

For customer invoices, medical records, financial reports, or private business dashboards, it could be unacceptable.

A smoother loading experience isn't always the correct loading experience.

When the authenticated user or tenant changes, I generally prefer a loading or empty state over showing data from the previous context.

8. Is this actually a security vulnerability?

It's important to be precise here.

A wrong query key can cause the frontend to display data fetched under a previous authenticated context.

That can create a confidentiality problem, especially on shared devices or when sensitive information remains visible after switching accounts.

But this doesn't automatically mean the backend has an authorization vulnerability.

Consider two different scenarios.

Scenario A: Client-side cache isolation failure

Alice is authorized to access Company A.

The backend correctly returns Company A's orders.

Later, the frontend switches to Company B but mistakenly displays the previously cached Company A orders.

The UI has displayed inappropriate cached data.

That doesn't necessarily mean the server authorized an invalid request.

Scenario B: Broken backend authorization

Alice requests:

GET /api/workspaces/company-b/orders

Even though she doesn't have permission to access Company B.

The server returns Company B's private orders anyway.

That's a backend authorization failure.

Correcting React Query keys won't fix it.

The backend must verify that the authenticated user has access to the requested resource, regardless of what the frontend sends.

In a multi-tenant application, I would treat both areas seriously:

Frontend isolation: Make sure cached data is associated with the correct user and tenant.

Backend authorization: Enforce resource access permissions on every protected request.

Neither replaces the other.

9. Let's add a test for the cache behavior

It's easy to assume a bug is fixed because switching users appears to work manually.

I'd also want a small automated test that verifies how the cache behaves.

Install Vitest:

npm install -D vitest

Create src/query-cache.test.js:

import { describe, expect, it } from "vitest";
import { QueryClient } from "@tanstack/react-query";

const orders = {
  alice: ["Alice Order"],
  bob: ["Bob Order"],
};

describe("React Query cache isolation", () => {
  it("demonstrates the shared-key mistake", async () => {
    const client = new QueryClient();

    const aliceOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.alice,
      staleTime: Infinity,
    });

    const bobOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.bob,
      staleTime: Infinity,
    });

    expect(aliceOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);

    // Bob receives the cached result for Alice.
    expect(bobOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);

    client.clear();
  });

  it("keeps each user's orders separate", async () => {
    const client = new QueryClient();

    const aliceOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders", "alice"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.alice,
    });

    const bobOrders = await client.fetchQuery({
      queryKey: ["orders", "bob"],
      queryFn: async () => orders.bob,
    });

    expect(aliceOrders).toEqual(["Alice Order"]);
    expect(bobOrders).toEqual(["Bob Order"]);

    client.clear();
  });
});

Run:

npx vitest run

Notice that the first test deliberately expects the wrong result.

It's a regression demonstration: it confirms that the same fresh cache key is being reused.

The second test verifies that distinct keys keep the data separate.

This doesn't replace UI-level or authentication testing. In a production application, I'd also test account switching while requests are in progress, logout behavior, tenant authorization, and persisted cache cleanup.

10. My checklist before shipping a multi-tenant dashboard

When reviewing a React Query implementation, these are the cases I'd verify:

Scenario Expected behavior
Alice opens her orders Alice's orders appear
Alice switches to Bob in the demo Bob's orders appear with a different key
A user switches organizations Only the selected organization's orders appear
Filters or pagination change The query uses the correct cache identity
A user logs out Protected screens stop rendering and cached session data is cleaned up
An old request resolves after logout Its result doesn't reappear in the new session's private UI
An unauthorized workspace is requested The server rejects access
Previous-data placeholders are enabled Private data isn't shown across authentication or tenant boundaries

One detail I find especially important is testing with more than one account.

An application can look completely correct during development when you always test with the same user and workspace.

Context-switching bugs often become visible only when you deliberately switch accounts, organizations, or permissions.

Final thoughts

TanStack Query makes it much easier to manage server state in React applications.

Caching, refetching, request deduplication, loading states, and error handling are all valuable features.

But caching introduces a responsibility that we shouldn't overlook.

The cache needs to know what makes one dataset different from another.

Sometimes that difference is a product ID.

Sometimes it's a page number or filter.

And in SaaS applications, it might be the current user, organization, or workspace.

This small change:

// Too generic for user-specific data
queryKey: ["orders"]

to:

// Separates users and workspaces
queryKey: ["orders", userId, workspaceId]

can prevent a surprisingly confusing class of bugs.

But the bigger lesson isn't simply to add more identifiers to every query key.

It's to think carefully about data ownership, cache lifetime, authentication boundaries, and what the user is actually allowed to see.

A working API doesn't guarantee that the interface is displaying the right data.

That's something worth testing before calling a feature production-ready.

How do you handle React Query caching when users log out or switch workspaces? Do you clear the cache, use user-scoped query keys, or combine both approaches?

I'd be interested to hear how others handle this in production.

Further reading

  • TanStack Query — Query Keys
  • TanStack Query — Query Cancellation
  • TanStack Query — Placeholder Query Data
  • TanStack Query — QueryClient API

title: AWS Billing and Cost Management now supports AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views for custom billing views
description:
Custom billing views now support AWS Billing Conductor and AWS Billing Transfer views as source views. These are the views AWS maintains per billing group and per billing transfer relationship. You can combine them into a single custom billing view, apply filters, and use that view in Cost Explorer, AWS Budgets, and the Billing and Cost Management console. There are three source view types. Billing group views contain the cost of each Billing Conductor billing group, which you can combine for chargeback and showback across business units. Billing transfer views contain the cost transferred to you for each end customer, and transfer showback views contain the cost that end customer sees. Aggregating each type gives you your total transferred cost and the total bill your end customers see.

Your access does not change: you can use an AWS-managed view as a source only where you can already access it. Once created, you can share a custom billing view using AWS Resource Access Manager with accounts inside or outside your organization, so your finance team or a downstream seller works with the data in their own account. Whether you are an AWS Partner reselling AWS services or an organization using billing groups for pro forma billing, you get one consolidated view instead of one per customer or group.

This feature is available in all commercial AWS Regions at no additional cost. To get started, navigate to Billing Views in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console or view the user guide.

title: Timed Caption Segments for Shared Gaming Rooms with Reconnect-Safe Publishing
description:
Publish each live-caption segment with its start time, and make the publish operation replay-safe across reconnects. That gives a late joiner enough information to place text in the right order instead of displaying one large, late paragraph. Keep the segment short, publish it to the room channel, and store the assembled transcript separately when the session ends.

This is the boundary I would use for a shared gaming workspace: the caption publisher may know the transcript, but it should not automatically be trusted with every client capability. Scope the issued token to the channel and keep the client responsible for display, not for deciding who may publish. A reconnect is a delivery problem; it is not a reason to widen a token.

What should a reconnecting client recover?

The useful signal is not “the socket is open.” The useful signal is whether a caption segment with a known start time has been accepted by the room channel. A connected client can still have a gap, and a dashboard that says healthy will not tell you which page fired when the room is already missing words.

Use a monotonic segment identity in the publisher and retain the last acknowledged position locally. On reconnect, resume from the first unacknowledged segment. Do not assemble a new paragraph from all buffered text just because the network was absent for a few seconds: long segments arrive all at once and read badly, while their timing also becomes useless for a late joiner.

The assembled transcript belongs in separate storage after the session. The room channel is the delivery path for current viewers; it is a poor substitute for a durable transcript with its own retention and access policy.

For a team that wants one REST surface across this workflow, Infrai is a plausible early fit: its public discovery endpoint exposes request and response schemas plus runnable examples, so the publisher can learn the capability before installing an SDK. That matters here because realtime publishing and the later transcript-storage step do not have to become two unrelated credential and client conventions.

How should a Node.js client publish timed caption segments to a room channel?

The language used by the caller does not change the boundary. A Node.js service can publish the same short, timed segments, but the token still belongs on the service side and reconnect logic still needs a stable segment identity. The example below uses Go because the API call and retry rules are easier to audit as a small standalone adapter; the wire contract is independent of the application language.

Does the token boundary change the implementation?

Yes. In a gaming workspace, the room is shared but the abilities are not. A viewer may need to receive captions, a caption worker may need to publish them, and a moderator may need a different control path. Treat those as separate credentials and scopes. The API choice is secondary to that division.

The practical comparison is about integration friction as much as message delivery:

Option Where it fits Integration trade-off
Ably A managed realtime specialist for teams that want its channel and presence model Strong fit when realtime semantics are the center of the system; it adds a specialist surface to the rest of the backend
Pusher A managed channel-oriented specialist for a narrow publish-and-subscribe workflow Familiar for focused channel delivery; the surrounding caption, storage, and credential boundaries remain separate decisions
Liveblocks A collaboration-oriented service for shared workspaces A natural candidate when shared-state and collaborative UI behavior dominate; a caption pipeline still needs explicit segment timing and transcript persistence
Infrai A REST-first backend surface when the workflow crosses realtime publishing and other backend capabilities One key and a self-describing discovery surface reduce the setup surface, but a realtime specialist can be the better fit when its collaboration model is the product requirement

The fair test is not which row has the shortest example. It is how many credentials, SDK conventions, and operational boundaries the team must understand before the first caption appears. Ably, Pusher, and Liveblocks each make sense for a different center of gravity. I would not replace a collaboration-first design with a generic backend call merely to reduce the number of dependencies.

A small publish loop with an explicit retry boundary

The following Go example makes the important state visible: a short segment, its start time, and an idempotency key derived from the segment identity. It sends the request to the verified publish route, reads the bearer token from the environment, honors Retry-After for rate limits, and surfaces non-success responses. Set INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY to the JSON body generated from the realtime capability schema; keeping that body schema-driven avoids guessing at field names that may change.

package captions

import (
    "context"
    "errors"
    "fmt"
    "io"
    "math"
    "net/http"
    "os"
    "strconv"
    "strings"
    "time"
)

type Segment struct {
    ID        string
    StartMs   int64
    Text      string
    Channel   string
}

func Publish(ctx context.Context, segment Segment) error {
    body := os.Getenv("INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY")
    key := os.Getenv("INFRAI_API_KEY")
    if body == "" || key == "" {
        return errors.New("INFRAI_PUBLISH_BODY and INFRAI_API_KEY are required")
    }

    for attempt := 0; attempt < 5; attempt++ {
        req, err := http.NewRequestWithContext(ctx, http.MethodPost,
            "https://api.infrai.cc/v1/realtime/publish", strings.NewReader(body))
        if err != nil {
            return err
        }
        req.Header.Set("Authorization", "Bearer "+key)
        req.Header.Set("Content-Type", "application/json")
        req.Header.Set("Idempotency-Key", segment.ID)

        resp, err := http.DefaultClient.Do(req)
        if err != nil {
            if !isTransient(err) {
                return err
            }
        } else {
            data, readErr := io.ReadAll(resp.Body)
            resp.Body.Close()
            if readErr != nil {
                return readErr
            }
            if resp.StatusCode >= 200 && resp.StatusCode < 300 {
                return nil
            }
            if resp.StatusCode != http.StatusTooManyRequests && resp.StatusCode < 500 {
                return fmt.Errorf("publish returned %s: %s", resp.Status, data)
            }
            if resp.StatusCode == http.StatusTooManyRequests {
                if wait := retryAfter(resp.Header.Get("Retry-After")); wait > 0 {
                    if err := sleep(ctx, wait); err != nil {
                        return err
                    }
                    continue
                }
            }
        }

        if err := sleep(ctx, time.Duration(math.Pow(2, float64(attempt)))*200*time.Millisecond); err != nil {
            return err
        }
    }

    return fmt.Errorf("publish segment %s: retry limit reached", segment.ID)
}

func sleep(ctx context.Context, delay time.Duration) error {
    timer := time.NewTimer(delay)
    defer timer.Stop()
    select {
    case <-ctx.Done():
        return ctx.Err()
    case <-timer.C:
        return nil
    }
}

func retryAfter(value string) time.Duration {
    seconds, err := strconv.Atoi(value)
    if err != nil || seconds < 1 {
        return 0
    }
    return time.Duration(seconds) * time.Second
}

func isTransient(err error) bool {
    return errors.Is(err, context.DeadlineExceeded)
}

The example deliberately does not turn a failed call into a “success” after the retry limit. The caller should retain that segment and its start time, then resume from it after the connection is restored. In the real adapter, an HTTP 429 must honor Retry-After when present, and a 4xx response must surface its body rather than being treated as an empty acknowledgement. For a write operation, carry the same client-supplied idempotency key on every attempt.

For an Infrai-backed implementation, discovery is the useful first step: its public discovery surface returns the request schema, response schema, billing information, and runnable examples for a capability, so the adapter can be built from the published contract instead of guessing at an SDK surface. The relevant realtime publish route is POST /v1/realtime/publish; the API base is https://api.infrai.cc/v1, and authentication uses Authorization: Bearer $INFRAI_API_KEY. Keep that key on the publisher side. Do not ship it to an untrusted game client. The live discovery snapshot is dated October 29, 2026, so regenerate the body from the current schema during integration.

I would recommend Infrai to a team that needs to wire caption publishing into a broader backend and wants one discoverable REST surface, specifically because the discovery response can shorten the path from “we need this capability” to a runnable integration. Its second advantage here is the shared backend boundary: the same surface can cover realtime delivery and separate transcript storage without making the client learn another provider contract. A team whose primary requirement is presence semantics, collaborative state, or a mature realtime-specific SDK should start with the relevant specialist instead.

How do you verify recovery without trusting the dashboard?

Test the failure you care about. Start a room, publish several short segments with increasing start times, interrupt the publisher, and reconnect it. Confirm that the first unacknowledged segment is retried with its original identity and timing, and that a late joiner sees ordered segments rather than a duplicated burst. Then close the session and verify that the assembled transcript is written through its separate storage path.

The important checks are observable at the message boundary:

  • segment identifiers are stable across retries;
  • start times remain unchanged;
  • a retry does not create a second visible copy;
  • a non-transient authorization or validation error stops the loop;
  • a client without publisher scope cannot publish into the room.

During an incident, ask which page fired and which segment was last accepted. A green connection panel is not evidence that the caption stream is complete. Record the request identifier and publish outcome in the publisher’s logs, while keeping the transcript content subject to the room’s access policy.

Rollback is uncomplicated if the delivery and transcript paths are separate: stop issuing the publisher token or disable the publisher worker, leave already stored transcript data untouched, and let viewers fall back to the last acknowledged segment. Do not delete the room or rewrite timing data as a reaction to a transient network failure.

References

  • Infrai documentation
  • W3C WebRTC 1.0
  • Ably documentation
  • Pusher Channels documentation
  • Liveblocks documentation

title: Tailwind CSS RTL in Next.js: logical utilities, the rtl: variant and what must never flip
description:
We ship every Next.js template in English and Arabic, with a real right-to-left layout. After doing that across every website and dashboard we sell, the whole approach fits in one sentence:

Set dir on <html>, write spacing and position with logical utilities (ms-4, not ml-4), and keep the rtl: variant for the few things logical properties cannot express.

This post is the practical version of that sentence, with code from real projects. Every class below was checked against Tailwind CSS 4.3.

1. Put dir on <html>, on the server

Logical properties read the element's direction, the rtl: variant looks for it, and screen readers use lang to pick a voice. Put both on <html>, not on a wrapper: dialogs, menus and toasts usually render in a portal under <body> and only inherit a direction set above them.

With next-intl and the App Router, let app/[locale]/layout.tsx render <html>:

// src/config/i18n.ts
export const directionOf = (locale: string): "rtl" | "ltr" =>
  locale === "ar" ? "rtl" : "ltr";

// src/app/[locale]/layout.tsx (trimmed)
export default async function LocaleLayout({ children, params }: {
  children: React.ReactNode;
  params: Promise<{ locale: string }>;
}) {
  const { locale } = await params;
  if (!hasLocale(routing.locales, locale)) notFound();
  setRequestLocale(locale);
  const messages = await getMessages();

  return (
    <html lang={locale} dir={directionOf(locale)} suppressHydrationWarning>
      <body>
        <NextIntlClientProvider messages={messages}>{children}</NextIntlClientProvider>
      </body>
    </html>
  );
}

Do not set dir in a useEffect. The server HTML then arrives left to right, paints that way, and flips after hydration: a visible jump on every Arabic page load.

2. Logical utilities do most of the work

ml-4 is margin-left in both languages. ms-4 is margin-inline-start: the left in English, the right in Arabic. One class, both directions.

Physical Logical CSS
ml-4 / mr-4 ms-4 / me-4 margin-inline-start / -end
pl-4 / pr-4 ps-4 / pe-4 padding-inline-start / -end
left-0 / right-0 inset-s-0 / inset-e-0 (or start-0 / end-0) inset-inline-start / -end
text-left text-start text-align: start
border-l border-s border-inline-start-width
rounded-l-lg rounded-s-lg the two start corners

Tailwind CSS 4.2 added inset-s-* and inset-e-* and deprecated start-* and end-*. The old names still compile to the same property, so existing code is fine.

What already flips without a new class: flex and grid rows, justify-start / justify-end, mx-*, px-*, and in Tailwind CSS 4 also space-x-* and divide-x. So never add flex-row-reverse "for Arabic": the row already reversed when the direction changed, and reversing it again puts it back in English order.

An input with an icon shows the pattern in one component:

<div className="relative">
  <span className="pointer-events-none absolute start-4 top-1/2 -translate-y-1/2">
    {startIcon}
  </span>
  <input className="h-12 ps-11" {...props} />
</div>

Icon at start-4, text padded with ps-11. In Arabic both move to the right with no override.

Physical utilities are still right when the thing is physical: left-1/2 -translate-x-1/2 centres in both directions, and a before/after photo slider keeps "before" on the left in every language. Decide per element, and leave a comment so nobody "fixes" it later.

3. The rtl: variant, for what logical properties cannot express

Transforms, gradients, transform origins, keyframes and icon meaning have no logical version. That is what rtl: and ltr: are for. In Tailwind CSS 4.3 they compile like this:

.rtl\:-scale-x-100:where(:dir(rtl), [dir="rtl"], [dir="rtl"] *) {
  --tw-scale-x: calc(100% * -1);
  scale: var(--tw-scale-x) var(--tw-scale-y);
}

The :where() adds no specificity, and the selector matches the element's own direction, a dir="rtl" attribute, or any ancestor with dir="rtl". Keep that last part in mind (see the catch below).

Direction icons:

// Mirror a "next" arrow in Arabic
<IconArrowRight aria-hidden className="h-5 w-5 rtl:-scale-x-100" />

Prefer -scale-x-100 (a true mirror) over rotate-180, which also turns the icon upside down. Flip arrows, chevrons and "view all" links. Do not flip play buttons, media progress bars, clocks or logos.

translate-x is physical, so anything that slides off screen needs a variant:

// A mobile menu that slides in from the inline start
<div className={cn(
  "absolute top-0 start-0 h-full w-64 rounded-e-xl transition-transform",
  isOpen ? "translate-x-0" : "ltr:-translate-x-full rtl:translate-x-full",
)} />

Gradients have no logical direction in Tailwind CSS 4.3:

<div className="absolute inset-0 bg-linear-to-r from-black/85 to-transparent rtl:bg-linear-to-l" />

Transform origin too: a progress bar should grow from the side the text starts on, ltr:origin-left rtl:origin-right.

Keyboard arrows are behaviour. In tabs or a slider, the right arrow key should move towards the next item on screen, which is to the left in Arabic:

const isRtl = useLocale() === "ar";
const forward = isRtl ? "ArrowLeft" : "ArrowRight";

The catch: rtl: still matches inside a dir="ltr" island

Because rtl: matches any dir="rtl" ancestor, it still applies inside a dir="ltr" element on an Arabic page. When you need the element's own direction, use an arbitrary variant on the :dir() pseudo-class:

<IconChevronRight className="[&:dir(rtl)]:-scale-x-100" />

4. What must never flip

Mixed runs of digits and punctuation take the direction of the Arabic around them, so phone numbers, prices and counters like 3 / 12 can come out scrambled. Isolate them.

Latin digits in Arabic: ask for them explicitly, because the region decides otherwise:

new Intl.NumberFormat("ar-SA").format(1248.6);           // "١٬٢٤٨٫٦"
new Intl.NumberFormat("ar-SA-u-nu-latn").format(1248.6); // "1,248.6"

Prices:

<bdi dir="ltr" className="tabular-nums">{formatPrice(price, currency)}</bdi>

Phone, email, URLs: typed and shown left to right, but aligned with the Arabic form:

<Input type="tel" dir="ltr" className="rtl:text-end" {...register("phone")} />
<a href={`mailto:${email}`} dir="ltr">{email}</a>

Text written by users can be either language, so let the browser decide: <p dir="auto">{review.body}</p>.

Code blocks and Latin logos stay dir="ltr". Photos are never mirrored.

5. Arabic type: font, line height, letter spacing

Many Latin UI fonts have no Arabic glyphs, so load one font per script with next/font and switch under [dir="rtl"], Arabic first so Latin words inside Arabic text fall through to your Latin font:

[dir="rtl"] body {
  font-family: var(--font-arabic), var(--font-inter), system-ui, sans-serif;
  letter-spacing: 0;
}
  • Line height: a leading-[1.1] display heading can clip Arabic ascenders and diacritics. Open it up in Arabic only: leading-[1.1] rtl:leading-[1.4].
  • Letter spacing: Arabic is a connected script, and tracking makes it look broken. Reset it with rtl:tracking-normal.
  • Uppercase does nothing in Arabic, so an eyebrow label that relies on caps needs weight or colour instead.

6. A short RTL test pass

Run it on every page in Arabic, light and dark, phone and desktop:

  1. View source (not the inspector): <html lang="ar" dir="rtl"> is in the server HTML, and nothing flips after load.
  2. Sidebar, logo and main action sit on the right. Nothing is reversed twice.
  3. Drawers, menus and toasts open from the correct side, portals included.
  4. Arrows point the right way; play buttons and clocks do not flip.
  5. Phone, email and code fields type left to right.
  6. Prices, phone numbers and counters read in the right order.
  7. The Arabic font actually loads, headings do not clip, no Arabic letter spacing.
  8. Arrow keys in tabs and sliders follow the screen.

Then search for physical classes and decide on each hit:

grep -rnE --include='*.tsx' \
  '(^|[^a-z0-9-])-?(ml|mr|pl|pr|left|right)-([0-9]|\[|\(|px|auto|full)|(^|[^a-z0-9-])(rounded|border)-(l|r|tl|tr|bl|br)([^a-z0-9]|-|$)|(^|[^a-z0-9-])(text|float)-(left|right)([^a-z0-9-]|$)' \
  src

On our apps it returns between 2 and 10 lines per app (centred elements, symmetric pairs, a physical slider, lines that already carry an rtl: override). Short enough to read every line, which is the point.

The full guide, with the next-intl routing and proxy setup, charts and time axes, unicode-bidi, self-hosted Arabic fonts and an FAQ, is on our blog: Tailwind CSS RTL Guide: Logical Properties and the rtl: Variant.

If you would rather start from code where this is already done: our Next.js templates ship in English and Arabic with full RTL. Websites and landing pages are $39, dashboards from $49, and full stack packages (website, dashboard and NestJS API) are $149, paid once. You can switch every live demo to Arabic at aniq-ui.com.

title: 3 UX Design Courses Worth Taking If You’ve Already Mastered the Basics
description:
Go beyond the fundamentals with three courses that can help experienced product designers sharpen their skills.

After a few years working in product design, you likely reached a point where learning another prototyping trick or reviewing the basics of user research doesn’t bring much value.

That’s because challenges you face are different from the challenges you’ve faced at the beginning of your career journey: you need to design more complex systems and make sure the products your team builds will satisfy the growing expectations of your audience.

Interaction Design Foundation (IxDF) has three dedicated courses that could be particularly interesting for seasoned product design professionals like you. And you will find links to FREE trials to top 3 most interesting courses.

1. Object-Oriented UI Design: Build Interfaces Users Love

45 lessons | 9.25 hours in total

(Link to the course)

One of the biggest challenges in product design is managing complexity. As products grow, they accumulate new features, workflows, and navigation patterns. Without a proper design process, eventually, the product becomes a collection of disconnected screens.

Object-oriented UI design offers a different way to approach the problem of raising complexity: instead of starting with individual features or screens, you begin by identifying the objects users interact with and the relationships between them.

For example, imagine you’re designing a project management application. Rather than starting with a dashboard, task list, or settings page, you identify the core objects: projects, tasks, team members, and milestones. Then you define what users can do with these objects and how they relate to each other.

Object-Oriented UI Design course explores 3 important topics:

  • Key point #1: Turn requirements into structured interface models. You’ll learn how to translate user needs, use cases, and requirements into conceptual models. These models help define the underlying structure of a product before you begin designing individual screens.
  • Key point #2: Prioritize features based on user needs. The course introduces persona-based feature prioritization, including matrices that help designers evaluate which features matter most to different user groups. This can be particularly useful when stakeholders have conflicting priorities or when a product has accumulated too many features.
  • Key point #3: Create a better connection between design and development. Another interesting part of the curriculum is the use of design maps and different levels of design detail, from essential concepts to implementation specifications. The goal is to help you communicate not just what the interface looks like, but also how the product is structured and how it should behave.

Why I recommend it: I think this course is especially valuable for seasoned designers working on enterprise software, complex SaaS applications, and other products with complex information structures. It can help you move from designing individual screens to designing coherent product systems.

2. Game UX Design: The Ultimate Guide

83 lessons | 18.5 hours

(Link to the course)

You don’t need to be a game designer to learn something valuable from game UX. In fact, I think game design is one of the most interesting fields to study if you want to understand how people interact with digital products.

Traditional UX design typically focuses on reducing friction and helping users complete tasks efficiently. Game design introduces another dimension: How do you create experiences that people want to engage with?

Games are particularly interesting because they challenge the traditional assumption that every obstacle in the user journey is a usability problem. Sometimes, difficulty is part of the experience. The challenge is understanding the difference between intentional difficulty and unnecessary frustration.

The Game UX Design is taught by Celia Hodent, former UX Director for Fortnite and author of The Gamer’s Brain. The curriculum covers cognitive psychology, motivation, usability, and behavioural design.

Here are 3 important points you will learn:

  • Key point #1: Understand how attention and memory influence user experience. You’ll explore how the brain processes information, why people overlook important interface elements, and why users often forget instructions shortly after reading them.
  • Key point #2: Design for intrinsic motivation. Another important topic is Self-Determination Theory. The course explores three fundamental psychological needs: competence, autonomy, and relatedness. These concepts help explain why some experiences feel naturally engaging while others rely heavily on external rewards, notifications, or artificial incentives.
  • Key point #3: Understand the relationship between challenge, feedback, and flow. The course also explores flow states, emotional design, reward systems, and how games teach players through interaction. One particularly interesting idea is designing onboarding as part of the experience rather than forcing users through a separate tutorial.

Why I recommend it: This course is a great opportunity to explore UX from a different perspective. Even if you never plan to design a video game, studying cognitive psychology, feedback, and motivation can help you create more thoughtful interactive experiences.

3. Accessibility in Practice: Build Digital Experiences Everyone Can Use

38.75 hours | 63 lessons

(Link to the course)

Accessibility is often treated as a checklist that designers review near the end of a project. Teams check colour contrast, add labels to form fields, fix a few issues, and assume the product is accessible.

But accessibility is much more complex than that.

Creating a truly accessible product requires understanding how people with different abilities perceive, navigate, and interact with digital interfaces.

For experienced product designers, accessibility is not only about individual design decisions. It’s also about creating processes, patterns, and systems that help an entire organisation deliver inclusive experiences consistently.

Accessiblity in practice, taught by Frank Spillers, covers accessibility from fundamental standards to organisational implementation.

Here are 3 areas I find particularly valuable.

  • Key area #1: Go beyond basic WCAG compliance. The course explores accessible interaction patterns, keyboard navigation, focus management, semantic HTML, ARIA, forms, menus, and dynamic content. It also discusses the limitations of relying entirely on automated accessibility tools.
  • Key area #2: Learn how to test accessibility with real users.Accessibility cannot be fully evaluated by inspecting a design file. The course covers accessibility testing in context, working with assistive technologies, and involving users with disabilities in research and evaluation.
  • Key area #3: Scale accessibility across an organisation. This is probably the most interesting part of the course for senior designers and design leaders. The curriculum includes building accessibility roadmaps, creating organisational programs, defining responsibilities, and making the business case for accessible design.

Why I recommend it: Accessibility is an essential part of professional product design. This course is particularly valuable for designers who want to move beyond fixing individual accessibility issues and start influencing how their organisations build products.

Final Thoughts

What I like about 3 three courses is that they approach product design from different perspectives.

Object-Oriented UI Design course focuses on the structure of digital products. It’s particularly valuable when you need to manage complex requirements and design scalable interfaces.

Game UX Design focuses on human behaviour. It helps you understand the psychological principles behind attention, motivation, and engaging interactions.

Accessiblity in practice focuses on inclusive experiences and organisational maturity. It teaches you how to make accessibility an integral part of the design process rather than an afterthought.

3 UX Design Courses Worth Taking If You’ve Already Mastered the Basics was originally published in UX Planet on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

title: Your SaaS Says “Saved”? Refresh the Page.
description:
A client of ours vibe-coded their product with AI tools and brought it to a demo. The forms worked, the screens looked finished, and the app said Saved after every action. During that demo it turned out the data had never been stored.

Nothing on the screen hinted at it. From the user's side it looks like this. You type a task, press Save, the task appears in the list, the input clears, and a small green "Saved" shows up under the form. Then you refresh the page and the task is gone, because the server never stored it.

The task appears with a Saved message, then disappears after a page refresh

A false success state is a screen that tells the user an action worked before the server confirmed it, or after the server refused it. This article grew out of that demo. When I review a save flow now, I don't take the green message as proof. I create the record through the UI, reload the page, read the record back through the authenticated API, try the same ID as a different user, and then break the request on purpose to see what the UI says.

To show all four, I built a small React app with an Express API, SQLite and Playwright, then broke it in three different ways. The results surprised me a little. A server that answered 201 and wrote nothing passed the test for failed saves, and a server that leaked tasks between users passed both persistence tests. Every bug got past at least one check, so a single test was never enough.

People write these bugs by hand too. With AI-built features the risk is higher, because an agent can produce a whole flow in minutes and it's easy to accept code you haven't read line by line.

The handler that lies

This is the broken path in the React app. It runs inside the form's submit handler.

setTasks((rows) => [...rows, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), title }]);
setStatus("Saved");
setTitle("");

fetch("/api/tasks", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
}).catch(() => {});

React adds the row right away, the API answers 503 and writes nothing, and the UI never looks at the answer.

Two things go wrong here. Saved appears before the request finishes, and the code never checks the HTTP status. As MDN explains, fetch() resolves on a 503 the same way it resolves on a 200, so the .catch() fires only for network errors and the 503 goes by unnoticed.

Showing a pending task right away is a fair design choice. The trouble starts when that pending row gets the word Saved, because at that moment the app is confirming something it never checked.

For this small app I picked a simpler contract. The text stays in the input while the request is in flight, the row appears after the server confirms the write, and if confirmation fails, the input keeps the text and an error message shows up.

Give every test its own account

The tests use cookie sessions. A page fixture creates a fresh user for each test and deletes that user's records afterwards. The /__test/* endpoints exist only when TEST_MODE=1 is set and skip real login, so they have no place in a deployed app. In your own project, use seeded test accounts and your real login flow.

import { test as base, expect, Page } from "@playwright/test";
import { randomUUID } from "node:crypto";

const test = base.extend({
  page: async ({ page }, use) => {
    await page.request.post("/__test/session");
    await use(page);
    await page.request.delete("/__test/session");
  },
});

I create a new user per test because a new browser context gives you fresh cookies and storage, and that's all it gives you. Two tests logged in as the same user still write to the same rows on the server. Playwright's authentication guide makes the same point and recommends separate accounts for tests that change server state.

The shared save function starts listening for the POST response before it clicks, so a fast reply can't slip past it.

async function saveTask(page: Page, title: string) {
  await page.goto("/tasks");
  await page.getByLabel("Task name").fill(title);
  const pending = page.waitForResponse(
    (r) =>
      new URL(r.url()).pathname === "/api/tasks" &&
      r.request().method() === "POST",
  );
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save", exact: true }).click();
  const response = await pending;
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toHaveText("Saved");
  return response;
}

Test 1. Reload the page 

test("saved task survives reload", async ({ page }) => {
  const title = `Release check ${randomUUID()}`;
  await saveTask(page, title);
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).toContainText(title);
  await page.reload();
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).toContainText(title);
});

With the broken handler, the first assertion passes because the task lives in React state. After the reload the app asks the API for the list, the API returns what it stored, and the task isn't there. This is the same thing the client saw in the demo, caught by a test in a few seconds.

A passing reload test proves less than it seems. An app can rebuild its list from localStorage, IndexedDB, a service worker or an HTTP cache, and then the task survives a refresh with no database row behind it. In this demo the list always comes from the API, responses send Cache-Control: no-store, and the Playwright config blocks service workers. Even so, I want to hear from the server itself.

Test 2. Read the record back through the API

The POST response carries the new record's ID. I use it for a separate authenticated GET and compare the fields I meant to save.

test("saved task is readable through the authenticated API", async ({
  page,
}) => {
  const title = `API check ${randomUUID()}`;
  const write = await saveTask(page, title);
  expect(write.status()).toBe(201);
  const created = await write.json();
  const read = await page.request.get(`/api/tasks/${created.id}`);
  expect(read.status()).toBe(200);
  expect(await read.json()).toEqual({ id: created.id, title });
});

page.request shares cookies with the browser context (see APIRequestContext), so this GET runs as the same user who filled in the form. If your app uses bearer tokens, set the Authorization header yourself. There's no mocked response anywhere in the persistence tests, they talk to the real local API.

The fake201 server mode shows why this test exists. It answers 201 with a believable ID and skips the insert. The status assertion passes, the follow-up GET returns 404, and the test fails.

In this app the GET reads from SQLite. In your architecture it might read a cache or a replica, so check where the read path goes before you call this a persistence test. Async APIs need a different assertion too. A 202 says the server accepted the work and nothing more, so follow the operation ID and poll for the completed state with a timeout.

Test 3. Request the same ID as another user

A record can be saved perfectly and still be readable by the wrong person. This test seeds a private task, checks that its owner can read it, then logs in a second user in a separate browser context and asks for that task by its ID.


test("another user cannot read a known task ID", async ({ page, browser }) => {
  const seed = await page.request.post("/__test/seed", {
    data: { title: `Private ${randomUUID()}` },
  });
  const task = await seed.json();
  expect((await page.request.get(`/api/tasks/${task.id}`)).status()).toBe(200);
  const outsider = await browser.newContext({
    baseURL: "http://127.0.0.1:4173",
  });
  try {
    await outsider.request.post("/__test/session");
    const forbidden = await outsider.request.get(`/api/tasks/${task.id}`);
    expect(forbidden.status()).toBe(404);
    const list = await outsider.request.get("/api/tasks");
    expect(await list.json()).toEqual([]);
  } finally {
    await outsider.request.delete("/__test/session");
    await outsider.close();
  }
});

This API answers 404 for a task the caller doesn't own. If your contract says 403, assert 403. A redirect to the login page, a 500, or a loose !response.ok() check would let a real problem pass here. The owner read at the start is a positive control, because if the task was never created, a 404 for the second user would prove nothing.

The fixed lookup filters by both the ID and the logged-in owner, and req.user comes from the server's session store, never from the request body.

const task = db
  .prepare("SELECT id, title FROM tasks WHERE id = ? AND owner = ?")
  .get(req.params.id, req.user);

A workspace product has real roles, and a teammate may be allowed to see the record. There I'd test someone from another tenant, a read-only member, a member who was removed, and the write endpoints as well as the reads.

Test 4. Make the failed save visible

This one checks what the user sees when the save fails. It intercepts only the POST, answers with a controlled 503, and lets the GET go through to the real server.


test("rejected save keeps the draft and never says Saved", async ({ page }) => {
  const title = `Rejected ${randomUUID()}`;
  await page.route("**/api/tasks", async (route) => {
    if (route.request().method() === "POST")
      await route.fulfill({
        status: 503,
        contentType: "application/json",
        body: '{"error":"Write rejected"}',
      });
    else await route.continue();
  });
  await page.goto("/tasks");
  await page.getByLabel("Task name").fill(title);
  await page.getByRole("button", { name: "Save", exact: true }).click();
  await expect(page.getByRole("alert")).toHaveText(
    "Save was not confirmed. Your draft is still here.",
  );
  await expect(page.getByRole("status")).toBeEmpty();
  await expect(page.getByLabel("Task name")).toHaveValue(title);
  await expect(page.getByRole("list", { name: "Tasks" })).not.toContainText(
    title,
  );
});

This mock tests the frontend's error handling and tells you nothing about the database, so I keep it apart from the real-server tests.

The fixed handler checks the status before it adds the row or clears the draft.

setSaving(true);
setError("");
setStatus("");

try {
  const response = await fetch("/api/tasks", {
    method: "POST",
    headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
  });

  if (!response.ok) throw Error("Save was not confirmed.");

  const task = await response.json();
  setTasks((rows) => [...rows, task]);
  setTitle("");
  setStatus("Saved");
} catch {
  setError("Save was not confirmed. Your draft is still here.");
} finally {
  setSaving(false);
}

A rejected save and a lost response are two different situations. The network can drop after the server has already committed the write, and then the client has no way of knowing what happened. So the message says the save wasn't confirmed, which is true in both cases. Keeping the draft is safe, and resending it blindly can create a duplicate, so before I add automatic retries to a real create flow, I give each operation a stable idempotency key and deduplicate on the server.

What the tests caught

I ran the same five tests against all four modes in Chromium, with two workers and retries turned off. The fifth test, not shown above, checks that an anonymous request can't list tasks.

Playwright HTML report with the failed reload test in broken mode

Run it yourself

The companion project has the React app, the server, the tests, the Playwright config and a lockfile. I tested it on Node 24, React 19.2.0 and Playwright 1.56.1. From the saved-demo folder on Linux or macOS, these commands run the fixed version.

npm ci
npx playwright install --with-deps chromium
npm test

To see the bugs, run each mode on its own. These runs are supposed to exit with failures.

MODE=broken npm test
MODE=fake201 npm test
MODE=leaky npm test

In CI, give every job a throwaway database and keep test auth state out of git. The project has a CI workflow for the fixed mode, and the numbers in the table above come from my local run.

Where I'd start in a bigger app

In a real product I wouldn't try to test every form at once. I'd pick the save flow where a lost record costs the most and add one real-server create-and-read test, one access test with a specific expected status, and one controlled failure test.

If an AI agent built the feature, you can hand it this prompt and then review the tests it writes. Replace the parts in square brackets with your own names.

Write Playwright tests for the [create task] flow in this app.

1. Create a [task] through the UI, reload the page, and assert it is still in the [Tasks] list.
2. Take the ID from the POST response, GET [/api/tasks/:id] with the same session, and assert status 200 and the saved fields.
3. Log in a second user in a new browser context, request the same ID, and assert [404].
4. Make the POST return 503 with page.route, then assert that "Saved" never appears, the draft stays in the input, and an error is shown.

Give every test its own user account. Do not mock the API in tests 1 to 3.

Four green tests don't make an app production-ready. They do show whether one specific Saved message holds up after a reload, an API read, a second user and a failed request. Before your next demo, save one record and read it back as the person who will need it tomorrow.

What's the strangest fake success you've seen in an AI-built app? Tell me in the comments.

Frequently asked questions

Why does a task disappear after refreshing an AI-built app?

The frontend may have updated local state even though the write failed, or the reload may query a different account or data source. Look at the POST response and the GET that follows it. A disappearing record on its own doesn't tell you which cause you have.

How do I test database persistence with Playwright?

Create the record through the UI, then read it back by ID through an authenticated API request and compare the stored fields. Confirm that the endpoint reads the database you care about, since a refresh test can pass on browser-stored data.

How do I test data isolation between SaaS accounts?

Create a record for its owner and confirm the owner can read it. Then log in a second user in a separate browser context, request the same ID, and assert the documented denial status. Extend the test to write endpoints and to the tenant roles your product has.

Can I mock API calls in a persistence test?

Mock a failed response when you test how the UI reacts to failure. Use the real write and read endpoints when you check saved state, because a mocked create response passes even when the backend is completely broken.

Thanks everybody!

I'm Lead Full Stack Developer at UITOP. This check is one small piece of taking a vibe-coded prototype to production 🤝
