title: Rust is amazing, as long as I’m not the one writing it
description:
The creator of Ruby on Rails says reading Rust is like “pouring acid in my eyes.” Yet he loves it. I wanted to understand why.

I’m the JavaScript and PHP guy.

Web apps, full stack, a bit of infrastructure: Docker, servers, deploys.

Systems programming? Never needed it. Never wrote about it.

Then my timeline changed. Suddenly everybody is talking about Rust.

Rust this. Rewritten in Rust that. “Blazingly fast” under every other post.

I haven’t written a single line of Rust. So this is the view from outside the fence.

The picture we had of Rust

From where I sat, Rust was what you reach for when you write system code. The low-level stuff, close to the machine.

Same shelf as C and C++. The shelf you need a ladder for.

And the syntax. Here’s a function from the official Rust book:

fn longest<'a>(x: &'a str, y: &'a str) -> &'a str {
    if x.len() > y.len() {
        x
    } else {
        y
    }
}

It’s the simplest case in the book, and all it does is return the longer in bytes of two strings. Yes.

In JavaScript, that’s one line and nobody gets hurt.

That 'a? Not a typo. It's called a lifetime. I'll tell you what it is when I find out.

Even the Rails guy flinches

I’m not the only one squinting.

DHH, the creator of Ruby on Rails, at his Rails World 2026 keynote:

Rust to me is like pouring acid in my eyes when I have to look at the code.

He kept going:

It is, in my opinion, the ugliest programming language that has been invented in probably the last 40 years.

And going:

Absolutely inhumane to ask people of flesh and blood to subject their eyeballs to this.

He loves it. As long as he doesn’t have to look at it:

"If all I have to do is revel in applications being 30 or 100 times faster, compiling down to minuscule executables that start up in sub milliseconds. I love Rust."

Rust is amazing. As long as you never, ever have to read it yourself.

I think he was talking about a world where AI writes the low-level code.

So why the sudden outburst?

Did everybody get smarter overnight?

No. I checked. I didn’t.

My theory: AI does most of the typing now, and typing was the part of Rust that scared people off.

AI doesn’t make ownership and lifetimes any easier to understand. It just means you no longer have to type them from scratch. Once AI removed that bottleneck, what’s left is the part everyone wanted anyway: the speed and the safety.

Rust is also unusually friendly to AI.

Why Rust and AI get along

It’s statically typed. Every variable and every function call has a type, and the compiler knows it before the code runs. So do Go, Java and TypeScript. The difference is what Rust’s compiler does with that knowledge.

The compiler is strict. Most mistakes get caught before your code runs, not in production at 2am. For an AI, that’s a feedback loop: write, compile, read the error, fix, repeat. The compiler marks the AI’s homework.

No null. If a value might be missing, the type says so, and the compiler makes you handle it. No more Cannot read properties of undefined at the worst possible moment. Rust still panics, but at a line you can point to.

Rust’s compiler is just the strictest teacher in the room.

And when it finally compiles, you get the speed: same category as C and C++.

So the AI writes, the compiler checks and nobody’s eyes get hurt.

The rewrites are already on my timeline

Once the intimidation went, people started building. And rewriting. A lot.

  • PHP, reimplemented in Rust, mostly by AI (php-rust).
  • An experimental Rust port of the TypeScript compiler (ts-rust). Funny detail: Microsoft’s own native TypeScript compiler is written in Go. Someone ported that to Rust. With AI.
  • Your JavaScript build tools. More on this one below.

I went down the php-rust rabbit hole in an earlier post if you want the details.

You’re probably running Rust already

Vite 8 “ships with Rolldown as its single, unified, Rust-based bundler.”

And it’s not alone:

  • SWC: compiles and minifies JavaScript and TypeScript
  • Biome: linting and formatting
  • Oxc: parser, linter, transformer
  • Lightning CSS: parses, transforms and minifies CSS
  • Rspack: a webpack-compatible bundler

You npm install them like anything else. Under the hood it's a compiled Rust binary doing the heavy lifting, and that's much faster for CPU-heavy work: parsing, compiling, transforming code.

To be fair, a lot of these tools started before AI got good at writing code. The speed was always the selling point. AI didn’t put Rust in your build tools. It put Rust on your timeline.

You’ve been using Rust every day without having to look at it. DHH would approve.

Rust in the browser? Yes, really.

Rust also compiles to WebAssembly, which runs in the browser next to your JavaScript.

So the heavy part of a web app (image processing, parsing a huge file, anything that makes the tab freeze) can be Rust, while the rest stays JavaScript.

Will Rust replace JavaScript?

No.

JavaScript is still the language of the browser. Your web app is not getting rewritten in Rust. (Please don’t.)

But I think Rust will replace many of the JavaScript-based tools in the build pipeline, because it’s faster and it’s safer.

The future I see is Rust plus JavaScript, not Rust versus JavaScript.

If you’re a JavaScript developer feeling the FOMO

Don’t leave JavaScript. Add to it.

  1. Learn the basics of Rust: types, ownership, the borrow checker. Enough to read what the AI writes.
  2. Use AI to get your code right, and read the compiler errors with it.
  3. Keep reading. As you use AI to work, you get better at it too. Every error it fixes in front of you is a free lesson.

From outside the fence

I don’t know what the future of Rust looks like.

But from where I’m standing, it’s getting a lot less scary.

Keep building software someone can still read.

title: Why Developer Experience Needs Continuous Improvement?
description:
What I Learned From My Open-Source Journey

When I started working on open-source projects such as Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe in the cloud-native community, I began to understand the importance of user experience (UX) in developer tools.

Today, many organizations and open-source communities are focusing on building new products, introducing AI features, and improving existing technologies. Engineers are busy developing new features, fixing technical issues, and releasing new versions of their software.

During my journey, I noticed that developer experience (DevEx) is important, but it does not always receive the same attention as product development.

Many engineers understand the value of UX, but they often do not have enough time to focus on improving the developer experience. Some engineers are interested in participating in UX research, but their busy schedules make it difficult to attend interviews or contribute to UX-related activities.

I also noticed that some engineers try to apply UX research methods themselves. However, without enough knowledge of UX research, they may choose methods or solutions based on what they personally feel is appropriate rather than following a structured research process.

At the same time, UX designers also face challenges when entering the developer experience field.

Unlike designing everyday applications, working on developer tools requires technical and domain knowledge. Designers need to understand how developers work, what tools they use, and what challenges they face.

For example, I have been learning about Kubernetes and the cloud-native ecosystem for almost two years. Even today, I feel there is still a lot to learn before I can fully understand the technical challenges developers experience.

Developer experience requires both UX knowledge and an understanding of the developer's technical environment.

These experiences made me think about an important question:

How can organizations improve developer experience without spending too much time, money, and effort?

1. Why Improving Developer Experience Can Be Challenging

During my open-source journey, I interacted with people from different organizations and learned how they approach developer experience.

I noticed that some large organizations have dedicated UX teams, budgets, and resources to improve their products. However, smaller organizations and open-source projects may not have enough time, money, or people to focus on UX improvements.

This does not necessarily mean they do not care about user experience. In many cases, they are already busy maintaining their products, developing new features, and supporting their users.

The challenge is not always a lack of interest in UX. Sometimes, it is a lack of time, resources, and a clear process for making improvements.

Another challenge is finding UX professionals who are interested in developer tools and have enough technical knowledge to work in this field.

As a result, even when engineers experience difficulties using a product, those challenges may not receive immediate attention.

2. Why UX Should Be a Continuous Improvement Process

One of the most important lessons I learned is that user experience is not a one-time activity. It is a continuous process of learning, testing, and improving.

Imagine an organization develops an application, tests it, and launches the first version.

During the first few months, users start exploring the application and using its features. After six months or one year, they may begin to experience challenges that were not identified during the initial development and testing stages.

These challenges may include confusing workflows, difficult navigation, unclear documentation, or features that do not work as users expected.

Even if the organization improves these issues and releases another version, users may discover new challenges as the product continues to grow.

This means UX improvements should not stop after a product is launched.

Every new version, feature, or workflow can create new opportunities to understand users and improve their experience.

In simple terms:

Build the product → Release it → Listen to users → Identify challenges → Improve the experience → Release the next version → Continue learning.

This cycle should continue throughout the product's life.

3. The Time, Cost, and Effort Behind UX Improvements

From my experience working as a Senior UX Designer at Super Purposes, I learned that even small UX improvements can require significant time, money, and organizational effort.

For example, imagine an organization decides to improve the user experience of an existing application.

The first step may be to hire a UX designer or build a UX team.

At Super Purposes, I was involved in hiring UX talent, assigning tasks, managing UX activities, and reviewing design work.

From this experience, I learned that hiring suitable UX talent can take approximately two to three months(For immediate hire, many be different time line for regular hiring talent), depending on the organization's requirements, candidate availability, interviews, and evaluation process.

During this period, the organization is already spending time and money on recruitment, hiring teams, and tools.

Once the UX designer joins the organization, the next stage involves understanding the existing product, discussing improvement opportunities with managers and developers, and identifying user challenges.

The UX improvement process may include:

  • Understanding the existing application: Learning how the product works and identifying its current limitations.

  • Conducting UX research: Interviewing users, running usability studies, and collecting feedback.

  • Analyzing research findings: Identifying common challenges, patterns, and opportunities for improvement.

  • Designing solutions: Creating design improvements and exploring multiple iterations.

  • Testing improvements: Evaluating whether the proposed solutions actually solve users' problems.

  • Collaborating with teams: Working with developers, managers, and stakeholders to review and approve changes.

  • Documenting the research: Recording findings, decisions, and improvements for future reference.

Depending on the size and complexity of the project, this entire process can take several months. In some cases, a major one feature UX improvement initiative may take nine to twelve months or longer.

For a solo UX designer, managing all these activities can be especially challenging, so it leads the organization to hire multiple talents.

Before AI tools became widely available, completing these activities often required more manual effort. Today, AI can help designers with tasks such as organizing research findings, preparing documentation, analyzing feedback, and exploring design ideas.

However, AI cannot completely replace the need to understand users, validate findings, and make thoughtful design decisions.

Even with AI assistance, a solo designer may need many months to complete a large UX improvement project (Start working on improvements and deliver the results and then documenting the project).

This helped me understand that UX improvements are not only about design. They also involve organizational time, money, people, collaboration, and long-term planning.

Why UX documentation is equally important

Another important lesson from my experience is the value of UX documentation.

Imagine a company completes user research and makes several improvements but does not document the findings or decisions.

After a year, the company decides to improve the same application again. If the previous research findings are unavailable, the new team may need to repeat some of the earlier work.

This can increase the time and cost of future improvements.

Good UX documentation helps organizations preserve knowledge, avoid repeating research unnecessarily, and make better decisions in future product versions.

4. New Features vs. Better Developer Experience

In software development, organizations often follow planned release cycles to introduce new features, fix bugs, and improve product capabilities.

For example, while working with the KServe project, I observed how the project continues to evolve with new releases and capabilities.

KServe has supported traditional predictive model serving, while its development has also expanded toward generative AI and large language model (LLM) workloads.

This is an example of how developer tools continue to evolve as technology and user requirements change.

However, releasing new features does not automatically mean the developer experience is improving.

A product may offer powerful technical capabilities while developers still face challenges understanding documentation, configuring the system, deploying applications, or troubleshooting errors.

In many organizations, engineering teams are already focused on delivering new releases. Conducting UX research and improving existing workflows may require separate planning, resources, and approval.

As a result, new feature development may move faster than UX improvements.

This creates an important question:

What if organizations could collect developer feedback continuously instead of waiting until they have enough time and resources to start a large UX research project?

I believe this approach could help organizations identify problems earlier and make improvements more regularly.

5. How Can We Improve Developer Experience With Less Time and Effort?

Based on my experience with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe, I started thinking about practical ways to improve developer experience without always depending on large UX research projects.

I believe small, consistent UX activities can help organizations understand developers' challenges and make meaningful improvements over time.

Here are three approaches that I believe can help.

Approach 1: Collect Feedback Directly From Developers

One of the simplest ways to understand user challenges is to ask users for feedback while they are using the product.

For example, after a developer completes an important workflow, the application could invite them to share their experience through a short feedback form.

The form should take only two to three minutes to complete.

It could include simple questions such as:

  • What were you trying to accomplish?
  • Did you experience any difficulties?
  • What could we improve to make this task easier?

This approach allows organizations to collect feedback regularly without requiring every user to participate in a long interview.

Over time, the organization can build a useful collection of feedback that helps identify common problems and prioritize improvements.

Many organizations already use feedback surveys in their applications.

I believe developer tools and open-source projects can also benefit from making short feedback activities part of their regular workflows.

The important point is to collect feedback at the right moment without interrupting developers' work.

Approach 2: Use Existing GitHub Issues as a UX Research Resource

Sometimes, organizations may not receive enough responses from surveys or may struggle to recruit developers for interviews.

In these situations, valuable user feedback may already exist in the project's GitHub repository.

Developers regularly create GitHub issues to report bugs, ask questions, describe technical difficulties, and request new features.

These issues can provide useful information about the challenges developers experience while using a product.

For example, instead of starting a completely new research study, a UX designer or engineer can review existing GitHub issues and identify patterns such as:

  • Repeated deployment and configuration difficulties.
  • Confusing error messages or troubleshooting processes.
  • Missing or unclear documentation.
  • Challenges with maintenance and observability.
  • Feature requests that reveal unmet developer needs.

By organizing these issues into common themes, teams can identify areas that may need UX improvements.

During my KServe research, I explored GitHub issues to understand the challenges developers experience while working with the project.

This experience helped me recognize that GitHub repositories can be a valuable source of existing user feedback for developer experience research.

However, GitHub issues do not always explain the complete user journey or the reasons behind a problem. When possible, teams should validate their findings through interviews, usability testing, or additional feedback.

Approach 3: Use Developer Conferences to Collect Quick Feedback

Another opportunity I noticed during my open-source journey is the value of developer-focused conferences and community events.

Many open-source projects participate in conferences, organize booths, and introduce their technologies to developers.

For example, KServe participates in cloud-native community events where engineers can learn about the project and interact with contributors.

These events are already bringing developers and project teams together.

Why not use a few minutes of these conversations to understand developers' challenges?

Instead of only explaining the product or introducing new features, project contributors could ask developers a simple question:

"What is the biggest challenge you face while using our project?"

A developer may need less than five minutes to explain a challenge they recently experienced.

Even a short conversation can help the team discover a problem, understand a confusing workflow, or identify an opportunity for improvement.

Imagine speaking with ten developers during a conference. Their feedback may reveal common challenges that deserve further investigation.

These conversations do not replace formal UX research, but they can help teams identify important questions and decide where to focus their research efforts.

Sometimes, a five-minute conversation can be the starting point for a meaningful developer experience improvement.

6. Small UX Activities Can Create Long-Term Value

From my experience, I believe organizations do not always need to wait until they have a dedicated UX team or a large research budget to start improving developer experience.

They can begin with activities that fit into their existing development and community workflows.

For example, collecting short feedback surveys, reviewing GitHub issues, and talking to developers during community events can help teams understand user challenges continuously.

However, collecting feedback is only the beginning.

The real value comes from reviewing the feedback, identifying common patterns, prioritizing problems, making improvements, and checking whether those improvements actually help developers.

Over time, these small activities can build a stronger understanding of users and help teams make better product decisions.

They can also create useful research documentation that supports future improvements.

For smaller organizations and open-source communities, this approach may be more practical than waiting to launch a large UX initiative.

Conclusion: Developer Experience Is Everyone's Responsibility

My journey with Kubernetes SIG-Multicluster and KServe has helped me understand that improving developer experience is not always easy.

Engineers are busy building and maintaining products. UX designers need time to understand complex developer tools. Organizations must balance product development, budgets, and available resources.

But I also learned that improving developer experience does not always require a large team, a big budget, or a lengthy research project.

Sometimes, meaningful improvements can begin with simple activities:

Ask developers for feedback. Listen to their challenges. Learn from existing GitHub issues. Have short conversations at community events. Document what you discover.

These small efforts can help organizations understand their users and make better decisions.

As technology continues to evolve, especially with AI and cloud-native tools, I believe developer experience should receive continuous attention alongside new feature development.

Building powerful developer tools is important, but making those tools easier to understand, use, and maintain is equally important.

And most importantly, developer experience is not a one-time improvement. It is a continuous journey of listening, learning, and making things better for developers.

These are my personal observations and lessons from working on UX research in the cloud-native open-source community. I would love to hear how other engineers, maintainers, and UX designers approach developer experience improvements in their projects.

What small UX activities have helped your team improve developer experience?

title: You're Still Optimizing Re-Renders Wrong: The Vue 3 Architecture That Outsmarted the Virtual DOM
description:
If you have built applications in modern frontend frameworks, you have almost certainly encountered the re-render nightmare.

In traditional Virtual DOM architectures, updating a single state variable often causes an entire component tree to re-execute from top to bottom. To prevent performance bottlenecks, developers must manually wrap calculations in memoization hooks, carefully manage dependency arrays, and worry about stale closures:

// The manual dependency tightrope
const userProfile = useMemo(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user, filters);
}, [user.id, filters.activeStatus]); // Miss a dependency, and your UI breaks

One missing dependency in that array creates subtle, agonizing bugs. One unnecessary dependency triggers expensive cascading re-renders across dozens of child components.

Then you look at Vue 3:

// In Vue 3: No dependency array. No manual memoization.
const userProfile = computed(() => {
  return calculateComplexMetrics(user.value, filters.activeStatus);
});

You mutate user.value.name, and only the exact paragraph rendering that name updates. The parent component does not re-render. Sibling components do not recalculate. There are no dependency arrays, no stale closures, and no manual memoization hooks.

To many developers, this behavior looks like magic or dangerous hidden reactivity.

In reality, Vue 3 is powered by one of the most sophisticated engineering architectures in modern software: a fine-grained Proxy dependency graph coordinated with a Compiler-Informed Block Tree.

Here is how Vue 3 actually tracks state, updates the DOM, and eliminates the re-render cascade.

1. The Reactivity Engine: Proxies, track(), and trigger()

In Vue 2, reactivity was implemented using Object.defineProperty(). The engine recursively traversed every property of your data object on initialization and converted them into getters and setters.

This approach suffered from notorious limitations:

  • Adding a new property (obj.newKey = 123) went undetected, requiring Vue.set().
  • Deleting a property went undetected, requiring Vue.delete().
  • Direct array index mutations (arr[0] = 'new') were unobservable without overriding prototype methods.
  • Deeply nested objects incurred heavy upfront performance costs during initialization.

Vue 3 replaced Object.defineProperty() entirely with modern JavaScript Proxy objects.

The Global Dependency Store (targetMap)

At the core of Vue 3 is a private, module-level data structure named targetMap.

targetMap is a nested multi-level registry that maps objects and their properties to the functions that depend on them:

targetMap (WeakMap)
 └── [target object] ──► depsMap (Map)
                          └── [property key] ──► dep (Set of ReactiveEffects)
  1. targetMap (WeakMap): Holds raw target objects as keys. Because it is a WeakMap, if your application discards the original object, the garbage collector cleans it up automatically, preventing memory leaks.
  2. depsMap (Map): Maps each specific property name of that object (e.g., 'count', 'username') to its dependency tracker.
  3. dep (Set): A Set containing all active ReactiveEffect instances (such as a component render function, a watch callback, or a computed value) that read that specific property.

How track() Registers Dependencies (The Getter Trap)

When you write:

const state = reactive({ count: 0 });

Vue wraps your raw object in a Proxy.

When a component renders, it executes inside a ReactiveEffect wrapper, setting a global pointer named activeEffect to point to that component's render function.

When your template evaluates state.count:

  1. The Proxy's get trap intercepts the property read.
  2. The proxy invokes Vue's internal track(target, 'count') function.
  3. track() checks: Is there currently an activeEffect running?
  4. If yes, it fetches or creates the dep Set for target.count inside targetMap and adds activeEffect to the Set.

You never declare dependency arrays because JavaScript's runtime call stack declares them for you. Any property read while activeEffect is running is automatically recorded as an exact subscriber.

How trigger() Fires Updates (The Setter Trap)

When you execute:

state.count = 42;
  1. The Proxy's set trap intercepts the mutation.
  2. The proxy assigns the new value to the raw underlying object using Reflect.set().
  3. It invokes Vue's internal trigger(target, 'count') function.
  4. trigger() looks up targetMap.get(target).get('count').
  5. It retrieves the Set of subscribed effects and schedules them for execution.

Only the exact components and computed properties subscribed to state.count are scheduled to run. Unrelated components are completely untouched.

2. The Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM: Block Trees and Patch Flags

Virtual DOMs earned a reputation for being heavy and resource-intensive because traditional implementations (like React's standard reconciler) operate on brute-force tree diffing.

In a traditional Virtual DOM:

  • When state changes, the component function executes again.
  • It allocates a brand-new tree of Virtual DOM nodes (VNodes) in memory.
  • The reconciler recursively compares every old VNode with every new VNode, checking tags, props, and children, even if 95% of those nodes are purely static HTML that can never change.

Vue 3 solved this through an architectural breakthrough: the Compiler-Informed Virtual DOM.

The Static Analysis Advantage

Because Vue templates have a deterministic structure, the Vue compiler analyzes your template at build time to identify which parts are dynamic and which parts are static.

Consider this template:

<div class="user-card">
  <header>
    <h1>User Profile</h1>
    <span class="badge">Verified</span>
  </header>
  <p class="bio">{{ user.bio }}</p>
  <button :class="{ active: isActive }">Follow</button>
</div>

In a traditional framework, updating user.bio requires diffing the <div class="user-card">, the <header>, the <h1>, the <span>, and the <button>.

The Vue 3 compiler does something radically different:

1. Static Hoisting

The <header> containing <h1>User Profile</h1> and <span class="badge"> contains zero dynamic bindings.

The compiler pulls those VNodes completely outside the component render function. They are created once when your application loads and reused across every future render. Their memory allocation during updates is zero.

2. Patch Flags (Bitwise Optimization)

For dynamic elements, the compiler attaches a numeric PatchFlag representing precisely what can change:

// Compiled output snippet
_createVNode("p", { class: "bio" }, _toDisplayString(_ctx.user.bio), 1 /* TEXT */)
_createVNode("button", { class: _normalizeClass({ active: _ctx.isActive }) }, "Follow", 2 /* CLASS */)

The number 1 is a bitmask for TEXT. The number 2 is a bitmask for CLASS.

When diffing the <p> tag, Vue performs a single bitwise check (patchFlag & PatchFlags.TEXT). If true, it updates node.textContent directly, skipping any checks for attributes, event listeners, or styles.

3. The Block Tree (dynamicChildren)

The root <div> is compiled into a Block.

A Block maintains a flat array called dynamicChildren. Instead of traversing the nested DOM tree recursively, the Block collects only the dynamic elements:

Block (div.user-card)
 └── dynamicChildren: [
       VNode (p.bio, PatchFlag: 1),
       VNode (button, PatchFlag: 2)
     ]

When user.bio updates, the diffing algorithm does not traverse the tree. It iterates over a flat array of two items!

The diffing cost becomes proportional to the number of dynamic bindings on the page, rather than the total size of your HTML tree.

3. ref() vs reactive(): The Destructuring Trap

One of the most frequent points of confusion for developers adopting Vue 3 is choosing between ref() and reactive().

Both create reactive state, but their underlying implementation mechanisms differ fundamentally.

The Mechanism of ref()

JavaScript primitive types (number, string, boolean, null, undefined) are passed by value, not by reference. You cannot wrap a primitive in a JavaScript Proxy.

To make primitives reactive, Vue introduces the RefImpl class:

class RefImpl {
  private _value;
  public dep = new Set();

  constructor(val) {
    this._value = val;
  }

  get value() {
    trackRefValue(this);
    return this._value;
  }

  set value(newVal) {
    this._value = newVal;
    triggerRefValue(this);
  }
}

A ref() is simply an object with a single property: .value.

Reading .value triggers the getter and tracks dependencies. Mutating .value triggers the setter and notifies subscribers.

Because it is wrapped in an object container, you can pass a ref across composable functions, return it from stores, and pass it as function arguments without losing reactivity.

The Mechanism of reactive()

reactive() accepts an object and wraps it directly in a Proxy.

It feels more natural to write because you do not need to append .value in your script code:

const user = reactive({
  name: "Emma",
  age: 26,
});

user.age++; // Natural syntax

The Destructuring Trap

Here is where thousands of developers run into unexpected silent failures:

// A common fatal mistake
const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// Destructuring breaks reactivity!
const { name, age } = user;

Why does destructuring destroy reactivity?

Remember: user is a Proxy intercepting property access on the user object.

When you write const { age } = user, JavaScript evaluates user.age, retrieves the raw primitive number 26, and assigns it to a new local variable named age.

The variable age is now just the plain number 26. It is completely disconnected from the Proxy. When the original user.age mutates later, age remains 26. The Proxy's getter and setter traps are never invoked.

The Solution: toRefs()

If you need to destructure a reactive object, you must convert its properties into individual ref objects using toRefs():

import { reactive, toRefs } from 'vue';

const user = reactive({ name: "Emma", age: 26 });

// toRefs wraps each property in a custom getter/setter proxy pointing back to user
const { name, age } = toRefs(user);

age.value++; // Reactivity is fully preserved!

4. The Batching Engine: Scheduler and nextTick()

What happens if you update a reactive variable fifty times inside a loop?

const count = ref(0);

function runStressTest() {
  for (let i = 0; i < 50; i++) {
    count.value++;
  }
}

Does Vue re-render the DOM fifty times in rapid succession, thrashing the browser layout engine?

No. Vue updates the DOM asynchronously using an internal Scheduler.

The Microtask Queue

When a reactive state change invokes trigger():

  1. Vue does not execute the component's render function immediately.
  2. It passes the render job to queueJob(job).
  3. The scheduler checks if this specific component's render job is already queued. If it is already in the queue, it ignores the duplicate call.
  4. The scheduler flushes the entire job queue in a single batch on the browser's next Microtask tick using Promise.resolve().then(flushJobs).

Regardless of how many times you mutate reactive state synchronously during a function execution, the component's render function runs exactly once.

Accessing Updated DOM via nextTick()

Because DOM updates are queued on a microtask, reading the physical DOM immediately after mutating state returns the old layout:

count.value = 5;
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Still prints old value!

To wait until the scheduler has completed its microtask flush and committed the updates to the physical DOM, Vue provides nextTick():

import { nextTick } from 'vue';

count.value = 5;
await nextTick();
console.log(document.querySelector('.counter').textContent); // Now prints "5"

nextTick() simply attaches a callback to the exact same microtask promise chain, guaranteeing that your inspection logic runs immediately after the DOM update commits.

5. The Evolution: Vue 2, Vue 3, and Vapor Mode

Frontend framework design is moving away from heavyweight runtime Virtual DOM reconciliation toward compile-time direct DOM operations.

We have seen this trend through frameworks like Svelte and SolidJS.

Vue is uniquely positioned in this landscape because of its architectural progression across three distinct eras:

Era 1: Vue 2 (Runtime Virtual DOM + Object.defineProperty)

  • Relied on ES5 getters and setters.
  • Full-tree recursive Virtual DOM diffing.
  • Required manual workarounds for array mutations and dynamic properties.

Era 2: Vue 3 (Proxy Reactivity + Compiler-Informed Block Trees)

  • Native ES6 Proxies for complete reactivity coverage.
  • Build-time static hoisting, PatchFlags, and Block Trees.
  • Up to 300% faster VDOM reconciliation than traditional brute-force diffing engines.

Era 3: Vue Vapor Mode (Opt-In Direct DOM Compilation)

  • The next major leap in Vue's architecture.
  • For opted-in components, Vapor Mode completely eliminates the Virtual DOM.
  • The template compiler translates your template into fine-grained direct DOM creation and update calls tied directly to reactivity signals: 
// Conceptual Vapor Mode compilation output
import { renderEffect, setText } from 'vue/vapor';

const n0 = document.createElement('h1');
renderEffect(() => {
  setText(n0, count.value);
});

When count.value updates in Vapor Mode:

  • Zero VNodes are allocated in memory.
  • Zero diffing algorithms run.
  • The signal directly triggers setText(n0, count.value) to mutate the physical DOM node in place.

Best of all, Vapor Mode uses the exact same Single-File Component syntax (<template>, <script setup>). You do not need to learn a new templating language or rewrite existing components to benefit from zero-VDOM performance.

6. Three Common Vue Reactivity Traps

Understanding Vue's internal architecture immediately arms you against the three most frustrating pitfalls developers encounter:

Trap 1: Storing Heavy External Objects in reactive()

If you store non-primitive third-party objects (such as a Three.js scene, a Monaco Editor instance, a Chart.js canvas, or a Mapbox map) inside a standard reactive() or ref():

// DANGEROUS: Destroys performance
const editorInstance = ref(monaco.editor.create(...));

Vue will recursively wrap the thousands of internal properties, prototypes, and event listeners of that third-party library in reactive Proxies. This creates massive memory overhead and frequently causes third-party libraries to crash when their internal this contexts are proxied.

The Fix: Use shallowRef() or markRaw():

import { shallowRef } from 'vue';

// Safe: Only the .value pointer is reactive; inner properties are untouched
const editorInstance = shallowRef(monaco.editor.create(...));

Trap 2: Infinite Watch Loops

Because Vue tracks dependencies automatically during execution, creating circular reads and writes inside watchEffect() will crash your application:

// CRASHES: Maximum recursive update cycle exceeded
watchEffect(() => {
  total.value = items.value.length;
  // If reading total somewhere triggers items to update, an infinite loop ensues
});

The Fix: Prefer explicit computed() for derived state, and reserve watchEffect() strictly for side effects (such as making API calls or updating local storage).

Trap 3: Direct Mutation of Props

In Vue, data flow is strictly unidirectional. Passing a reactive object as a prop and mutating it directly in a child component bypasses parent state tracking and leads to unpredictable rendering inconsistencies.

The Fix: Emit events using defineEmits() or use v-model with defineModel() to maintain clear ownership over state mutations.

The Mental Shift

The difference between struggling with frontend performance and building scalable interfaces comes down to your mental model:

Stop thinking of reactive components as functions that need to re-execute repeatedly from top to bottom.

Vue 3 is an event-driven signal graph paired with an intelligent compiler.

  • State is a Proxy network, registering dependencies automatically on access.
  • Templates are Block Trees, diffing only the slots marked with PatchFlags.
  • DOM updates are batched asynchronously through microtask queues.
  • And with Vapor Mode, the Virtual DOM step disappears entirely, connecting state directly to DOM nodes.

Once you understand this architecture, the need for complex memoization hooks disappears, re-render cascades vanish, and building reactive user interfaces becomes natural, predictable, and exceptionally fast.

How has Vue's fine-grained reactivity model influenced how you design your frontend state? Have you experienced the performance shift between traditional re-render engines and Proxy-based tracking, or experimented with early Vapor Mode builds? Share your thoughts and architecture experiences in the comments below.

title: Five Users Is a Stop Rule, Not a Sample Size
description:
Every front-end team has inherited some version of this: "we don't need real usability data, Nielsen said five users is enough." The recommendation is real. The way it gets quoted into standups is not. Five users is a stopping rule for problem discovery. It is not a sample size for anything you want to measure, and the difference is arithmetic you can implement in about twenty lines.


Conceptual AI-generated cover for this article, composited with the unchanged official Design Den Solutions logo. The logo artwork itself is not AI-generated.

The model behind the number

Jakob Nielsen's original claim (Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users, NN/g, 18 March 2000) is a coverage model, not a headcount heuristic:

P(n) = 1 - (1 - L)^n
  • n = testers in the round
  • L = the proportion of the total problem set that one tester finds
  • P = cumulative proportion of the problem set found after n testers

Nielsen used L = 0.31, which lands at ~85% at n = 5. He was explicit that this is a cost/benefit stopping point, not a completeness claim: "The best results come from testing no more than 5 users," and in the same article, "You need to test with at least 15 users to discover all the usability problems." His 2012 restatement (How Many Test Users in a Usability Study?) keeps "test 5 users in a qualitative usability study" and gives the reason not to inflate n: "ROI drops like a stone with a bigger N."

const coverage = (L, n) => 1 - (1 - L) ** n;

for (let n = 1; n <= 8; n++) {
  const prev = n === 1 ? 0 : coverage(0.31, n - 1);
  console.log(
    `n=${n}  total=${(coverage(0.31, n) * 100).toFixed(1)}%  ` +
    `this tester adds ${((coverage(0.31, n) - prev) * 100).toFixed(1)} pts`
  );
}
// n=1 total=31.0% this tester adds 31.0 pts
// n=3 total=67.1% this tester adds 14.8 pts
// n=5 total=84.4% this tester adds  7.0 pts
// n=8 total=94.9% this tester adds  2.3 pts

That marginal column is the entire argument. Tester five returns roughly a fifth of tester one's yield. The model assumes equal findability across problems, which is false in practice: a label nobody clicks is nearly invisible to every tester, while a broken button is found by the first person who touches it. So L is not measurable before the round, and 85% is a planning figure, not a guarantee. At L = 0.20, five testers cover 67.2%; at L = 0.15, 55.6%.

Implement the stop rule, not the magic number

The useful engineering artefact is a uniqueness curve over the problems you have actually logged:

function shouldStop(problemLog, testersNeeded = 2) {
  const firstSeen = new Map();
  problemLog.forEach((p, i) => { if (!firstSeen.has(p.id)) firstSeen.set(p.id, i); });

  const newPerTester = Array.from({ length: problemLog.length }, (_, t) =>
    [...firstSeen.values()].filter((i) => i === t).length
  );

  const tail = newPerTester.slice(-testersNeeded);
  return {
    newPerTester,
    stop: tail.every((x) => x === 0),
    reason: `last ${testersNeeded} testers surfaced ${tail.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)} new problem classes`
  };
}

"Stop" is not "five reached". It is "the last two testers produced no problem class you had not already recorded". On a checkout flow with one obvious blocker, that can happen at three. On a genuinely untested dashboard, it may not happen until seven. Five is the expected cost of a round, not the exit condition.

What five people cannot tell you

This is where teams write a number into a deck that the data cannot carry.

Three of five testers abandon the enquiry form. Someone reports "60% of users fail the form". Five is not a survey; the correct statement is an interval.

function wilson(k, n, z = 1.96) {
  const p = k / n, d = 1 + (z * z) / n;
  const c = (p + (z * z) / (2 * n)) / d;
  const h = (z * Math.sqrt((p * (1 - p)) / n + (z * z) / (4 * n * n))) / d;
  return [Math.max(0, c - h), Math.min(1, c + h)];
}

wilson(3, 5);   // [0.23, 0.88]  -> "23% to 88%"
wilson(12, 20); // [0.39, 0.78]

A 65-point-wide interval is not a conversion finding. To hold ±10 points around a 60% success rate you need n = z²p(1−p)/e² ≈ 93. If the goal is a rate — task success, completion time, benchmark against a competitor — that is a quantitative study with a different budget, and no amount of qualitative rounds substitutes for it.

Two more things five users will not do:

  • Prove the redesign worked. Before/after on five people each is anecdote with a delta.
  • Establish accessibility conformance. WCAG is a standard you audit against, not a headcount. Contrast under SC 1.4.3 is 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text, computed from relative luminance. Five sighted testers will not tell you whether your orange-on-white passes, and neither will fifty.

And one that is easy to get wrong: five per study is not five per audience. The NN/g guidance is "you'll need close to 5 users per group". Split across two personas, each group gets 2.5 people and the model's single-population assumption no longer applies.

Rounds beat bigger N

A second round of five after the fixes is not a repeat of the first. It runs against a changed interface, so it can surface problems the first round structurally could not reach — the flow you just unblocked, the copy you just rewrote, the regression you just shipped. One round of ten would find 97.6% of the problems that existed at the start, and 0% of the ones created by your fixes. Iteration is the point; Nielsen's own phrasing is to "plan for a lot of iterations".

Make each session produce a bug, not a vibe

Instrument the same fields every time so the round aggregates:

{
  "task": "find out whether installation is included",
  "tester": "T3",
  "completed": false,
  "helpRequested": true,
  "timeOnTaskSec": 143,
  "firstClick": ".pricing-card",
  "quote": "I can't tell if they fit it or just sell it",
  "problemIds": ["pricing-scope-ambiguous"],
  "severity": "serious"
}

Severity rubric that survives review: blocker = cannot complete without help; serious = completes with visible struggle or a wrong assumption; cosmetic = preference, no task impact. Then write the finding the way you would write a defect: task, page or selector, observed action, user's stated goal, consequence. pricing-scope-ambiguous with two testers and a quote is actionable. "Users find pricing confusing" is not.

Two operational constraints worth putting in the test script before you invite anyone:

  1. Consent and data. Record only with explicit consent, store the minimum, and never let a tester enter real personal data, make a payment, or fire a live enquiry into your own production system. Use a staging environment or stop at the boundary.
  2. Recruit for the actual population. Colleagues share your mental model and will silently repair your copy for you. Five strangers beat five teammates every time.

The honest summary

Five users is the cheapest round that reliably produces a ranked fix list, because the marginal yield collapses right after it. Use it to decide what to build next. Do not use it to report a percentage, to certify accessibility, or to claim a lift. Those are different studies, and the arithmetic above will tell you the sample size you actually need before you promise anyone a number.

References

  • Nielsen, J. Why You Only Need to Test with 5 Users. Nielsen Norman Group, 18 Mar 2000.
  • Nielsen, J. How Many Test Users in a Usability Study? Nielsen Norman Group, 3 Jun 2012.
  • W3C, Understanding SC 1.4.3 Contrast (Minimum), WCAG 2.2.

Disclosure: this article was prepared with AI assistance and reviewed for accuracy by Design Den Solutions. The cover image is a conceptual AI-generated illustration with the official company logo composited unchanged. All percentages come from the discovery model and the code shown above, which was executed before publishing; no client data or user metrics are represented.
